Unfortunately, these methods usually incur high computational burdens, exhibit exposure bias, and suffer from unstable inference dynamics that can cause the policy to diverge when the environment distribution changes.  Energy‑Based Models (EBMs), which learn an energy landscape end‑to‑end and capture equilibrium dynamics, naturally mitigate these problems by providing more robust inference and reduced exposure bias.  Historically, however, EBM‑driven policies have struggled to scale to high‑dimensional settings.  Recent advances in Energy‑Based Transformers (EBTs) have shown that EBMs can be applied to complex spaces, yet their potential to tackle the core challenges of embodied agents has not yet been fully explored.  

In this work we present **EBT‑Policy**, a new energy‑based architecture that directly addresses the shortcomings of robotic and real‑world deployment.  Across both simulated and physical experiments, EBT‑Policy consistently outperforms diffusion‑based baselines while requiring substantially fewer training and inference steps.  In several tasks it converges in just two inference iterations—about a 50× speed‑up over Diffusion Policy’s typical 100 steps.  Furthermore, EBT‑Policy displays emergent abilities absent in prior models, such as zero‑shot recovery from failed action sequences using only behavior cloning without any explicit retry training.  By exploiting the scalar energy for uncertainty‑aware inference and adaptive compute allocation, EBT‑Policy offers a compelling route to robust, generalizable robot behavior in the face of distribution shifts.
130: Survival analysis seeks to estimate the time until a clinically relevant event occurs, a task that is central to many biomedical studies. A major difficulty lies in capturing the heterogeneity of patients while also tailoring risk estimates to each individual’s covariates and to evolving temporal effects. We introduce a dual mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) architecture for discrete‑time survival modeling. The first MoE module acts as a feature encoder that learns subgroup‑specific representations, while the second MoE module models the hazard function by incorporating both patient features and time‑embedding information, thereby encoding temporal dynamics. This dual‑MoE construction can be seamlessly integrated with existing deep‑learning survival frameworks. Evaluated on the METABRIC and GBSG breast‑cancer cohorts, our method consistently outperforms baseline approaches, improving the time‑dependent C‑index by up to 0.04 on test sets, and delivers additional gains when applied within the Consurv framework.
131: Software fuzzing has emerged as a pivotal tool for automated vulnerability discovery. However, many prevailing mutation strategies are agnostic to program semantics, which often results in redundant test cases and hampers progress into deeper execution states. In this paper, we introduce a hybrid fuzzing framework that fuses static and dynamic analysis with Large Language Model (LLM)-driven input mutation and semantic feedback. The static analysis stage extracts control‑flow and data‑flow graphs, which are then converted into structured prompts that guide the LLM to produce syntactically correct and semantically diverse seeds. While the program runs, we enrich conventional coverage signals with semantic feedback derived from state changes, exception types, and output characteristics, enabling the fuzzer to prioritize inputs that elicit novel program behaviours rather than merely increasing line coverage. The approach is implemented on top of AFL++, leveraging its instrumentation and augmenting seed selection with embedding‑based semantic similarity metrics. Experiments on real-world open‑source projects such as libpng, tcpdump, and sqlite show that our method reduces time to first bug, increases semantic diversity of inputs, and remains competitive with leading fuzzers in terms of unique bugs found. These results underscore the promise of combining LLM reasoning with semantic‑aware feedback to accelerate and deepen vulnerability discovery.
132:
Multivariate time‑series data consist of several concurrent streams that jointly describe a temporal phenomenon. Detecting anomalies in such data is challenging yet critically important across many scientific and engineering fields, because anomaly scores must capture both temporal evolution and inter‑variable relationships. This paper introduces a clustering‑based framework that identifies anomalies in the amplitude and shape of multivariate time series. 

We first employ a sliding‑window technique to extract a collection of multivariate subsequences, then apply an extended fuzzy clustering algorithm to uncover the inherent structure among these subsequences. A reconstruction criterion is subsequently used to re‑assemble each subsequence from the optimal cluster centers and the partition matrix. A confidence index is derived to quantify the severity of detected anomalies. Particle Swarm Optimization is leveraged to solve the resulting anomaly‑detection optimization problem efficiently. 

Experimental results on several synthetic datasets and six real‑world case studies demonstrate that the proposed method accurately detects anomalies. By exploiting the cluster structure revealed by the extended fuzzy clustering, the framework excels at identifying anomalous amplitude and shape patterns in domains such as healthcare, meteorology, finance, and disease surveillance.
133: The rising use of AI in areas ranging from materials discovery to climate science has underscored the crucial, yet labor‑intensive, nature of data preparation. Raw datasets from heterogeneous origins must be meticulously cleaned, normalized, and transformed before they can serve as reliable inputs for training and inference, while judicious feature engineering and selection remain key to model efficiency. To overcome the bottlenecks of scalability and specialist knowledge, we introduce **Data Agent**, a fully autonomous system tailored for tabular data. By harnessing large language‑model reasoning in conjunction with grounded validation, Data Agent automatically executes data cleaning, hierarchical routing, and feature‑level optimization through two interlocked feedback loops. It is built on three guiding principles—**automatic, safe, and non‑expert friendly**—ensuring end‑to‑end reliability without human oversight. This demonstration presents the first practical deployment of an autonomous Data Agent, illustrating a seamless transformation of raw data into AI‑ready “better data.”
134:
The Weighted First‑Order Model Counting (WFOMC) problem requires computing the weighted sum of all models of a first‑order logic sentence over a specified domain. When WFOMC is conditioned on evidence—i.e. when the truth values of certain ground literals are fixed—it has been proven that no algorithm can run in time polynomial in the domain size (unless $\#P \subseteq FP$), even for logical fragments that are otherwise tractable without evidence.  

In this paper we break that limitation by focusing on binary evidence that yields a Gaifman graph of bounded treewidth. We develop a polynomial‑time algorithm (in the domain size) for computing the conditioned WFOMC for the two‑variable fragments $\mathrm{FO}^2$ and $\mathrm{C}^2$ under such evidence.  

To demonstrate the practical impact, we apply our method to a combinatorial challenge—the stable seating arrangement problem on graphs of bounded degree and bounded treewidth—which had previously remained unsolved. We also present empirical results showing that our algorithm scales favorably compared to existing model‑counting solvers.
135: CodeSight is a comprehensive end‑to‑end platform that forecasts whether software development tasks will meet their deadlines. It pulls raw data from GitHub, converts it into structured process‑mining logs, and then derives a range of metrics and visual dashboards that reveal patterns in pull‑request activity and overall workflow performance. Leveraging these structured logs, the system trains an LSTM network that estimates the remaining time for each PR by examining both sequential activity traces and static attributes, thus flagging early on any risk of a deadline breach. Evaluation results show that CodeSight achieves high precision and F1 scores in predicting deadline compliance, underscoring the benefits of combining process mining with machine‑learning techniques for proactive project management.
136:
Regression trees such as CART (Classification and Regression Trees) typically employ the variance‑reduction criterion to determine optimal splits. When the predictor is categorical with many levels, the usual exhaustive search over all binary partitions is computationally prohibitive and can lead to sub‑optimal splits that increase the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on unseen data. This paper introduces a **binary split algorithm for categorical features that directly optimizes MAE** as the splitting criterion.  

The proposed method first orders the levels of a categorical variable by the conditional mean of the target, then applies a dynamic‑programming routine that enumerates all possible binary partitions of the ordered levels in \(O(k^2)\) time for a feature with \(k\) categories. This ordering guarantees that every optimal binary split is considered, while dramatically reducing the combinatorial explosion associated with naive search. During tree construction, the algorithm selects the split that yields the largest reduction in MAE, thereby producing more robust regression trees that are less sensitive to outliers than variance‑based methods.  

Experimental results on a suite of synthetic and real‑world datasets (including the UCI Adult, Kaggle House Prices, and Kaggle Credit Card Default datasets) demonstrate that our MAE‑guided binary splits achieve on average 3.5 % lower test MAE and 2.1 % higher \(R^2\) compared to standard CART implementations that use Gini or MSE for categorical splits. Furthermore, the computational overhead remains negligible for practical problem sizes, and the resulting trees are often shallower, indicating improved interpretability.  

The paper’s contributions are: (1) a novel MAE‑based split criterion tailored for categorical predictors, (2) an efficient \(O(k^2)\) algorithm that guarantees optimal binary partitions, and (3) empirical validation showing superior predictive accuracy and tree compactness. Future work will explore extensions to multi‑way splits and integration with ensemble methods such as random forests and gradient boosting.
137:
The growing ubiquity of cloud‑based machine‑learning services raises acute concerns about the confidentiality of user data. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) offers a principled way to perform inference on encrypted inputs, but the high computational overhead of non‑linear activations has limited its practical deployment. PRISM (Privacy‑preserving Inference System with Modular Activation) bridges this gap by integrating a family of *modular activations*—piece‑wise polynomials defined over a finite field—into an FHE‑compatible neural network pipeline.  

PRISM automatically compiles standard deep‑learning models into an encrypted‑friendly form, replacing conventional ReLU or sigmoid units with lightweight modular activation functions that preserve expressive power while admitting efficient evaluation under the CKKS scheme. A novel bootstrapping scheduler limits ciphertext noise growth, and a modular‑layer design allows dynamic switching between linear and non‑linear regimes to balance accuracy and performance.  

Empirical results on MNIST, CIFAR‑10, and a ResNet‑50 subset of ImageNet demonstrate that PRISM reduces inference latency by 3–4× and ciphertext footprint by 3× compared to leading HE frameworks, with a negligible (<1.5 %) drop in classification accuracy. Theoretical analysis quantifies the trade‑off between security parameters and modular activation precision.  

PRISM thus provides a scalable, low‑overhead solution for secure neural inference, enabling privacy‑preserving predictions in cloud and edge environments without compromising model fidelity.
138:
Understanding and modeling user preferences is a central challenge for multilingual recommendation and information‑retrieval systems. Existing preference‑learning frameworks typically treat every observation as equally reliable, thereby ignoring the inherent uncertainty that arises when translating or inferring preferences across languages. This oversight can lead to over‑confident predictions and sub‑optimal ranking in multilingual environments.

We introduce **CAPO (Confidence‑Aware Preference Optimization)**, a unified learning framework that explicitly estimates the confidence of each user preference signal and incorporates it into the optimization objective. CAPO first trains a language‑agnostic embedding layer that projects items and users into a shared semantic space using a transformer‑based multilingual encoder. A secondary confidence predictor—parameterized as a lightweight neural network—learns to score each preference pair according to its linguistic and contextual reliability. The overall loss combines a pairwise ranking term with a confidence‑weighted regularizer, allowing the model to down‑weight noisy or ambiguous cross‑lingual signals while still exploiting them for richer generalisation.

To evaluate CAPO we construct the **Multilingual Preference Corpus (MPC)**, a large‑scale, multi‑language dataset of explicit and implicit user interactions collected from a global e‑commerce platform. Experiments on MPC, as well as on the publicly available Multi‑Lingual MovieLens and the Cross‑Lingual Pinterest datasets, demonstrate that CAPO outperforms strong baselines (e.g., BERT4Rec, M3, and XL-MLP) by 5.7 % and 4.3 % in NDCG@10 and MAP respectively, with statistically significant improvements across all language pairs. Ablation studies confirm that the confidence module is pivotal to achieving these gains, particularly in low‑resource languages where translation noise is highest.

CAPO thus offers a principled approach to preference optimisation in multilingual scenarios, providing both higher ranking accuracy and interpretable confidence estimates that can guide downstream decision‑making. The source code and datasets are released at https://github.com/example/capo.
139:
Knowledge‑graph‑augmented large language models (KGLMs) have shown promise in grounding language generation with explicit facts, yet both their training and evaluation suffer from the absence of fine‑grained, reliable supervision. Existing benchmarks rely on coarse question‑answer pairs or noisy KG extractions, which do not capture the exact subgraph structures required for a model to retrieve or infer a given fact. We introduce **Ground‑Truth Subgraphs (GTS)**—a curated collection of minimal, query‑aligned subgraphs extracted from large public knowledge graphs (Freebase, Wikidata, and YAGO). Each subgraph is accompanied by a human‑verified entailment score and a natural‑language prompt that explicitly specifies the reasoning path. 

Using GTS we (i) redesign the fine‑tuning objective of retrieval‑augmented LLMs to maximize subgraph reconstruction fidelity, and (ii) propose a subgraph‑matching evaluation protocol that rewards correct structural predictions over surface‑level correctness. Experiments on benchmark datasets (LAMA, SimpleQuestions, and a newly released KGLM‑Eval) show that KGLMs trained with GTS achieve +12 % absolute improvement in factual recall and +8 % on reasoning‑based questions, while the new evaluation metric correlates more strongly with downstream task performance (r = 0.74 vs. 0.58 for conventional metrics). The GTS dataset is publicly released to encourage reproducible research. Our work demonstrates that grounding language models with explicit, human‑verified subgraphs yields both more accurate knowledge integration and a more reliable assessment of their reasoning capabilities.
140:
The visual systems of cats and humans diverge in several anatomical features. In particular, the domestic cat (*Felis catus*) possesses a vertically elongated pupil that is thought to aid in ambush hunting; however, the consequences of such adaptations for higher‑level visual representations are still largely unclear. To investigate this, we introduce a unified, frozen‑encoder benchmark that measures how well visual representations align between species in natural images. The benchmark evaluates a wide range of architectures—including classic convolutional neural networks (CNNs), supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs), window‑based transformers, and self‑supervised ViTs trained with DINO—using layer‑by‑layer centered kernel alignment (CKA, both linear and RBF) and representational similarity analysis (RSA). We also report on additional distributional and stability assessments.

Across all models, the self‑supervised DINO ViT‑B/16 achieves the highest alignment, with mean RBF‑CKA ≈ 0.814, mean linear‑CKA ≈ 0.745, and mean RSA ≈ 0.698. These peaks occur early in the network, suggesting that token‑level self‑supervision generates early‑stage features that bridge species‑specific visual statistics. Supervised ViTs attain comparable CKA scores but display weaker geometric correspondence than DINO (e.g., RSA ≈ 0.53 at block 8 for ViT‑B/16 and ≈ 0.47 at block 14 for ViT‑L/16), highlighting depth‑dependent divergences between similarity and representational geometry. While CNNs remain solid baselines, they trail plain ViTs in alignment, and windowed transformers perform worse than their plain counterparts—underscoring how architectural inductive biases influence cross‑species alignment.

These findings demonstrate that combining self‑supervision with ViT inductive biases yields visual representations that more closely resemble the feline visual system than conventional CNNs or windowed transformers. This work offers empirically testable hypotheses regarding the loci and mechanisms of convergent visual computation across species. All code and datasets are made publicly available to facilitate further study and replication.
141:
Accurate multi‑organ delineation is essential for computer‑aided diagnosis, yet the wide variability in organ size and morphology often hampers the performance of recent deep‑learning segmentation models. To tackle these difficulties, we introduce the **Spatial Prior‑Guided Cross Dual Encoder Network (SPG‑CDENet)**—a two‑stage framework that boosts multi‑organ segmentation accuracy.  
The first stage employs a spatial prior network that produces coarse localisation maps, highlighting approximate regions of interest (ROIs) which then serve as spatial cues for the second stage.  
The second stage is built around a **cross dual encoder network** comprising: (i) a global encoder that captures whole‑image semantic context, (ii) a local encoder that extracts fine‑grained information guided by the prior maps, (iii) a symmetric cross‑attention module that fuses the global and local pathways at every encoder layer, and (iv) a flow‑based decoder that forwards the highest‑level features to all decoder layers, ensuring maximal feature preservation and reuse.  

Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations on two public datasets demonstrate that SPG‑CDENet outperforms existing multi‑organ segmentation techniques. Ablation experiments further confirm that each proposed component—spatial prior, cross‑attention, and flow‑based decoding—contributes significantly to the overall improvement.
142:
We introduce a transformer‑based multimodal system that produces clinically meaningful captions for MRI scans. The framework employs a DEiT‑Small vision transformer to encode images, MediCareBERT to embed the captions, and a tailored LSTM decoder. To fuse visual and textual representations, we adopt a hybrid loss that blends cosine similarity and mean‑squared error, and we conduct contrastive inference using vector similarity. 

Our evaluation is performed on the MultiCaRe dataset, where we compare results obtained from a brain‑focused subset of MRIs against those from the full MRI collection. The method is benchmarked against leading medical image captioning models such as BLIP, R2GenGPT, and other recent transformer‑based approaches. Findings demonstrate that concentrating on domain‑specific data yields higher caption accuracy and better semantic alignment. In summary, our approach offers a scalable, interpretable solution for automated reporting in medical imaging.
143: Algorithms that actively seek weaknesses in agents’ policies—adversarial optimization—have proven effective at producing robust and diverse strategies in multi‑agent scenarios. Yet, their application has largely been confined to zero‑sum problems; in cooperative settings a straightforward application often triggers a disastrous self‑sabotage effect, where agents deliberately hinder one another, preventing task completion and stalling learning. To circumvent this, we propose **Rationality‑Preserving Policy Optimization (RPO)**, a framework that guards against self‑sabotage by requiring each agent’s policy to remain optimal against some plausible partner policy. Solving RPO is achieved via **Rational Policy Gradient (RPG)**, which trains agents to maximize their own reward in a modified game that incorporates opponent‑shaping techniques to drive the adversarial objective. RPG allows us to adapt numerous existing adversarial methods; without the self‑sabotage limitation they now generate adversarial examples, enhance robustness and adaptability, and yield a richer set of policies. Experiments demonstrate that our approach delivers strong results across a range of popular cooperative and general‑sum environments. The project page is available at https://rational-policy-gradient.github.io.
144:
Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly empowered by external tools to tackle complex, long‑horizon problems. To push this capability further, researchers need reproducible, large‑scale training and evaluation environments that are both controllable and richly varied. Existing real‑world APIs fall short: they are sparse, unstable, and often gated behind keys or rate limits, making reliable experiments difficult.  

We present **SynthTools**, a modular framework that synthesizes entire tool ecosystems on demand. SynthTools comprises three main modules:  
1. **Tool Generation** – automatically creates a wide array of synthetic tools across many domains.  
2. **Tool Simulation** – models realistic interactions and behaviors of these tools.  
3. **Tool Audit** – validates the fidelity and consistency of the simulated toolset.  

Using SynthTools, we can generate tool libraries that double both the number of domains and the number of tools per domain compared to prior benchmarks. The simulation and audit modules achieve high reliability, with 94 % and 99 % accuracy, respectively. Moreover, the resulting synthetic tools form challenging downstream tasks that even state‑of‑the‑art agents struggle with.  

By providing a scalable, diverse, and dependable suite of synthetic tools, SynthTools opens the door to large‑scale training and stable evaluation of tool‑using agents. The code is available at [https://github.com/namkoong-lab/SynthTools](https://github.com/namkoong-lab/SynthTools).
145:
Sustainable fisheries management increasingly relies on timely, high‑resolution predictions of fishing effort, yet such forecasts remain difficult due to the complex, multivariate nature of marine ecosystems. In this study we introduce a novel deep‑learning framework that integrates heterogeneous environmental spatial datasets to predict weekly fishing concentration zones in the North Atlantic. The model ingests a suite of remotely sensed and in‑situ products—including sea‑surface temperature, chlorophyll‑a concentration, wind speed, ocean current vectors, bathymetry, and historical vessel tracking (AIS) effort maps—through a multi‑branch convolutional neural network. Each branch is designed to capture distinct spatial and temporal patterns; the features are subsequently fused by a spatiotemporal attention module that learns dynamic interactions between environmental drivers and fishery behaviour. Training on a 4‑year period of labeled effort data (≥ 1 × 10⁵ vessel‑hour observations) and validated on a 12‑month hold‑out set, the model achieves a mean F1‑score of 0.68 for hotspots (top 10 % of effort density), outperforming traditional statistical and machine‑learning baselines by 18 % and 26 % respectively. Spatial cross‑validation confirms robust generalisation across coastal and offshore regimes.

The approach demonstrates that deep‑learning architectures can effectively harness heterogeneous spatial information to capture the spatiotemporal dynamics of fishing activity. Practically, the weekly forecasts provide a decision‑support tool for adaptive management, enabling targeted enforcement and monitoring, and reducing over‑exploitation. The methodology is readily transferable to other regions and fishery types, offering a scalable pathway for evidence‑based, data‑driven fisheries stewardship.
146: This study presents the OUNLP system entered into the TSAR‑2025 Shared Task (Alva‑Manchego et al., 2025), which focuses on readability‑controlled text simplification via LLM‑prompting. By examining existing prompt‑based simplification approaches, we uncovered a key insight: the effectiveness of simplification strongly depends on the disparity between the source text’s CEFR level and the desired target CEFR level (Arase et al., 2022). Leveraging this observation, we devised two iterative simplification strategies that we implemented with GPT‑4o: a purely rule‑driven approach (MRS‑Rule) and a hybrid method that jointly applies rules and LLM generation (MRS‑Joint). Our submissions achieved a 7th‑place finish among 20 participants. Subsequent refinements with MRS‑Joint demonstrated that initializing the process with LLM‑generated simplification candidates can further enhance multi‑round simplification quality.
147: Designing materials with specific properties is difficult because the chemical space is enormous and data labeled with properties is limited. Although generative models have recently shown promise for inverse design, they generally need large datasets and must be retrained whenever a new property is targeted. To address these issues, we present EGMOF (Efficient Generation of MOFs), a hybrid diffusion‑transformer framework built around a modular, descriptor‑mediated workflow. EGMOF splits the inverse design problem into two stages: first, a one‑dimensional diffusion model (Prop2Desc) translates the desired property values into chemically meaningful descriptors; second, a transformer model (Desc2MOF) constructs MOF structures from those descriptors. This modular approach requires only minimal retraining and retains high performance even when data are scarce. On a hydrogen‑uptake benchmark, EGMOF achieved over 95 % structural validity and an 84 % hit rate—improvements of up to 57 % in validity and 14 % in hit rate relative to existing methods—while still functioning effectively with only 1,000 training samples. Furthermore, the model successfully carried out conditional generation across 29 distinct property datasets—including CoREMOF, QMOF, and text‑mined experimental collections—an achievement not reached by prior models. This study demonstrates a data‑efficient, generalizable strategy for inverse MOF design and underscores the value of modular workflows for broader materials discovery.
148: Modern answer set programming solvers such as CLINGO incorporate sophisticated language features that enhance both expressivity and brevity of logic programs. Conditional literals represent one such feature; they act as “sub‑formulas” that behave like nested implications inside rule bodies, thereby moving the syntax of rules closer to that of first‑order logic. This makes conditional literals particularly valuable for knowledge representation. In this paper we introduce a semantics for logic programs that combine conditional literals with arithmetic, grounded in the SM operator. Unlike the prevailing approach, which translates these constructs into infinitary propositional logic and then grounds them, our semantics works directly at the non‑ground level. The principal contribution is a formal proof of equivalence between our SM‑based semantics and the existing, grounding‑based semantics.
149:
South‑Slavic languages (Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, Macedonian, Slovenian and their variants) exhibit high morphological complexity, rich inflectional morphology, and frequent code‑switching with neighboring languages. These characteristics, coupled with a pronounced scarcity of high‑quality labeled corpora, make automatic text classification a challenging domain for both research and industry. In this paper we present a comprehensive, state‑of‑the‑art survey of modern text‑classification pipelines for South‑Slavic languages, with a particular focus on the trade‑off between **fine‑tuning** of multilingual transformer back‑bones (mBERT, XLM‑R, mDeBERTa) and **prompt‑based** (zero‑ and few‑shot) approaches that leverage large‑scale language models (ChatGPT, Llama‑2, GPT‑4).

We first catalogue the publicly available corpora and benchmark datasets (e.g., *SentiPol*, *SentiBa*, *SentiSK*, *BSC‑Senti*, *SLP‑NLP*) and discuss the linguistic properties that influence model performance. We then conduct an extensive empirical evaluation across six downstream tasks (sentiment analysis, topic categorisation, spam detection, hate‑speech identification, intent detection, and author‑gender classification) on a unified test split. Our results show that while fine‑tuned models achieve the highest average F1‑scores on high‑resource settings (≥10 k labelled examples per class), prompting methods can rival or even surpass fine‑tuning when data is limited (<1 k examples) or when cross‑lingual transfer is required. In particular, chain‑of‑thought prompting with GPT‑4 yields a 3 % absolute gain in zero‑shot settings, whereas fine‑tuning XLM‑R‑Large with domain‑specific adapters remains the best choice for large‑scale deployments.

The paper further explores the impact of language‑specific pre‑training, tokenization strategies, and morphological feature augmentation, providing concrete guidelines for practitioners. Finally, we release a new benchmark suite, *SaL‑Bench*, that standardises evaluation across the South‑Slavic space, together with open‑source code for reproducibility. Our findings suggest a hybrid approach—light fine‑tuning coupled with prompt‑engineering—offers the most robust solution for resource‑scarce South‑Slavic NLP tasks.
150:
Academic advising in higher education is a pivotal yet resource‑intensive process that directly influences student success, yet current practices suffer from inconsistent quality, limited scalability, and a lack of data‑driven personalization. This paper introduces **AdvisingWise**, a human‑in‑the‑loop multi‑agent framework that augments traditional advising workflows by orchestrating a suite of domain‑specialized agents—Student Profile, Course Recommendation, Risk Assessment, and Scheduling—while preserving expert human oversight. Each agent ingests institutional data (transcript, enrollment, demographic, and behavioral signals), applies a hybrid reasoning pipeline (rule‑based inference, collaborative filtering, and causal risk modeling), and outputs actionable advisement suggestions. The framework employs a dynamic orchestration layer that tracks student progress, triggers agent re‑inference upon new evidence, and presents an explainable decision interface to advisors.  

We evaluate AdvisingWise on a large university’s longitudinal student data (N = 12,345), comparing it against conventional advisor records and a baseline rule‑based recommender. The system achieved a 17 % improvement in course registration alignment with degree plans, a 22 % reduction in at‑risk student alerts, and a 15 % increase in overall student satisfaction as measured by post‑semester surveys. A qualitative usability study with 30 advisors confirmed the framework’s intuitive interface and the value of human‑in‑the‑loop interventions for nuanced decision‑making.  

AdvisingWise demonstrates that a modular, agent‑centric architecture can deliver scalable, evidence‑based advisement while embedding human expertise. The approach offers a template for universities to modernize advisory services, promote academic resilience, and foster equitable student outcomes.
151: Visual‑Language Pre‑training (VLP) systems now deliver strong results on a wide range of downstream tasks, yet they still succumb to adversarial attacks. Earlier work has tried to boost the transferability of multimodal attacks by exploiting cross‑modal interactions, but these methods tend to overfit because they depend too heavily on a single modality’s adversarial cues when perturbing the other. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Local Shuffle and Sample‑based Attack (LSSA), inspired by techniques from adversarial training. LSSA first shuffles a random local block of an image, thereby generating a richer set of image‑text pairs, and then creates adversarial images that are further perturbed by sampling around them. These original and sampled images are subsequently used to produce adversarial text inputs. Extensive evaluations across multiple VLP models and benchmark datasets show that LSSA markedly improves the transferability of multimodal adversarial examples, and it surpasses state‑of‑the‑art attacks when applied to large vision‑language models.
152:
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) enhanced with deep test‑time memorization layers—such as Titans and TTT—offer a linearly‑scalable alternative to Transformers. Although these highly expressive models currently trail the top‑tier Transformers in peak performance, their promise remains largely unrealized because training is slow and hardware utilisation low. Traditional parallelisation schemes hinge on a single chunksize hyper‑parameter: larger chunks improve throughput but hurt accuracy, forcing a sub‑optimal compromise.

We propose TNT, a two‑stage training framework that separates efficiency from inference quality. In the first, pre‑training stage, we employ a hierarchical memory: a global module processes large, hardware‑friendly chunks to capture long‑range dependencies, while several parallel local modules handle fine‑grained detail. By periodically resetting the local memory states, we break sequential ties and enable massive context parallelisation. The second, lightweight fine‑tuning stage adapts only the local memory to a smaller, high‑resolution chunksize, thereby maximizing accuracy with negligible overhead. Applied to Titans and TTT, TNT delivers up to a 17× speed‑up over the most accurate baseline while simultaneously raising model performance. This breakthrough removes a major scalability bottleneck, laying a practical path toward more expressive RNNs that can close the performance gap with Transformers.
153: Clinical documentation is moving toward automatic speech‑recognition and summarisation, yet there is no established method for turning those conversations into actionable medical orders for Electronic Health Records. Solving this problem could dramatically lower clinicians’ paperwork load and improve patient care. In response, we launched MEDIQA‑OE 2025, the first shared‑task devoted to extracting medical orders from doctor‑patient dialogues. Six teams participated, testing a variety of strategies and both closed‑ and open‑weight large language models. This paper presents the task definition, the dataset, the final leaderboard standings, and a discussion of the participants’ solutions.
154:
The landscape of large‑language‑model usage is rapidly expanding beyond simple chat completions to include sophisticated inference‑time scaling and deep‑reasoning workloads. Yet, most inference servers remain fine‑tuned for chat‑style interactions. Previous studies have shown that substantially higher key‑value (KV) cache hit rates can be achieved if these servers adapt to the emerging non‑chat workloads, but the solutions proposed thus far are tailored to a single pattern—retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG).

In this work we propose a *span query* interface that unifies a broad spectrum of inference patterns—including chat, RAG, scaling, and autonomous agent workloads—into a single, expressive formalism. The core idea is to capture the essential difference between these workloads: whether the order of inputs is significant (i.e., whether they commute). Chat interactions are inherently non‑commutative, whereas many RAG queries commute. Span queries are thus defined as expression trees of inference calls annotated with commutativity constraints.

We detail the syntax and semantics of span queries and demonstrate how they can be automatically rewritten to maximize KV‑cache locality. A minor modification to vLLM (only 492 lines of code) is sufficient to support high‑performance execution of span queries. Using this stack, we achieve 10–20× reductions in time‑to‑first‑token (TTFT) across two distinct non‑chat scenarios. Finally, we show that optimizing span queries for attention locality can mitigate the “lost‑in‑the‑middle” problem, enabling a 2 b‑parameter model with attention‑optimized span queries to outperform a stock 8 b‑parameter inference server in terms of accuracy.
155:
Rapid, accurate, and transparent oceanographic information is essential for climate monitoring, fisheries management, and maritime safety. Existing services, however, suffer from fragmented data sources, opaque model assumptions, and high latency, making it difficult for scientists, decision‑makers, and the public to obtain trustworthy insights in near real‑time. We present **OceanAI**, a conversational platform that integrates heterogeneous oceanographic observations, state‑of‑the‑art predictive models, and uncertainty‑aware analytics into a single, natural‑language interface. OceanAI ingests real‑time satellite, buoy, and ARGO float data streams, applies a hybrid deep‑learning framework for sub‑hourly forecasting of key variables (sea surface temperature, salinity, chlorophyll‑a), and stores results in a domain‑specific knowledge graph. The system exposes this information through a transformer‑based dialogue engine that allows users to query, explore, and interrogate the data using everyday language. Crucially, every prediction is accompanied by a probabilistic confidence interval and a provenance trace that documents the contributing data streams and model parameters, thereby ensuring transparency.

In a six‑month pilot with NOAA’s ocean‑observing network and the European Marine Observation and Data Network (EMODnet), OceanAI delivered temperature and salinity forecasts with <2 % mean absolute error compared to ground truth and reduced end‑to‑end latency to 4.7 min. Domain experts reported a 37 % improvement in decision‑making speed for coastal fisheries planning, while non‑technical users found the conversational interface intuitive and trustworthy. We also demonstrate OceanAI’s extensibility by integrating a real‑time marine debris detection model and a climate‑projection module. Our results indicate that a conversational AI framework can bridge the gap between complex ocean science and actionable, real‑time decision support, paving the way for more resilient marine stewardship.
156:
The Alternating‑Current Optimal Power Flow (ACOPF) problem is a cornerstone of modern power‑system operation, yet its high dimensionality and non‑linearity render exact solution prohibitive for real‑time or large‑scale applications. End‑to‑end surrogate models—often neural networks or other data‑driven “optimization proxies”—have emerged as a promising remedy, but training such proxies demands a massive, representative dataset of solved ACOPFs, which is expensive to generate. Conventional active‑learning strategies that query the most uncertain model predictions frequently overlook the rich structure of ACOPF constraints (power‑balance equations, voltage limits, line thermal bounds, generator capability limits), resulting in inefficient sampling that fails to capture critical feasibility borders.

In this work we introduce **Constraint‑Informed Active Learning (CI‑AL)**, a principled framework that couples a physics‑aware constraint‑checker with a Bayesian surrogate to steer sample acquisition directly toward regions where constraint violations are most likely or where the surrogate’s uncertainty is highest. The algorithm iteratively (i) solves a relaxed ACOPF to identify “feasibility‑critical” operating points, (ii) evaluates the surrogate’s predictive uncertainty, and (iii) selects the next training point by maximizing a combined acquisition function that trades off uncertainty against constraint proximity. We also embed a lightweight constraint‑projection step to ensure that all queried points remain within a realistic operational envelope.

Extensive numerical experiments on IEEE 30‑, 118‑, and 300‑bus test cases demonstrate that CI‑AL achieves ≥ 90 % reduction in the number of full ACOPF evaluations required to reach a target root‑mean‑square error of 0.1 % in objective value and ≤ 0.01 % average power‑balance residual, compared with random sampling and standard uncertainty‑based active learning. The resulting proxies respect all ACOPF constraints to within machine precision, enabling their seamless integration into rapid contingency screening and dispatch‑level decision support. Our approach generalizes to other constrained engineering optimization problems, opening a path toward scalable, physics‑guided data acquisition for high‑fidelity surrogate modeling.
157:
Document parsing lies at the heart of document‑intelligence systems, powering tasks such as information extraction, retrieval‑augmented generation, and automated analysis. Yet, in practice, documents frequently contain intricate layouts—multi‑tier tables, embedded images or mathematical formulas, and structures that span multiple pages—poses a persistent challenge for conventional OCR engines.  

We present **MonkeyOCR v1.5**, a unified vision‑language framework that tackles these difficulties through a two‑step pipeline. In the first step, a large multimodal model jointly infers the page layout and the reading order, using visual cues to enforce both structural coherence and correct sequencing. The second step localises and recognises the content (text, formulas, and tables) within each detected region, preserving high visual fidelity and curbing error propagation.  

To improve table parsing, we introduce a reinforcement‑learning strategy based on visual consistency: the model is rewarded when the rendered output of a parsed table aligns with its original appearance, enabling better structural accuracy without requiring manual annotations. Moreover, we add two dedicated modules—**Image‑Decoupled Table Parsing** and **Type‑Guided Table Merging**—which handle tables that embed images and reconstruct tables that span pages or columns, respectively.  

Extensive evaluations on the OmniDocBench v1.5 dataset show that MonkeyOCR v1.5 establishes new state‑of‑the‑art results, surpassing PPOCR‑VL and MinerU 2.5 while exhibiting remarkable robustness across highly visual and complex document scenarios.
158: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has proven effective at boosting the reasoning abilities of large language models, giving rise to large reasoning models (LRMs) such as DeepSeek‑R1 and OpenAI o1.  Yet these LRMs tend to produce long, often superfluous reasoning chains—a phenomenon known as *over‑thinking*—which inflates inference costs.  Existing remedies that penalise output length typically fall into two pitfalls: *length collapse* and *training collapse*, leading to sub‑optimal outcomes.  To overcome these problems, we introduce a training pipeline for a Conciseness Reward Model (CRM) that evaluates how succinct a reasoning path is.  We further propose a new reward formulation, the Conciseness Reward Function (CRF), which couples the task reward with the conciseness score, encouraging both accurate and efficient reasoning.  Theoretically, CRF offers variance reduction and faster convergence.  Empirically, on five mathematical benchmark datasets, our approach improves accuracy by 8.1 % and cuts response length by 19.9 % on Qwen2.5‑7B, and it generalises to other LLMs such as Llama and Mistral.  Code and data are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CRM.
159:
General‑sum Markov games (MGs) provide a natural framework for modeling sequential multi‑agent decision making under uncertainty.  While the existence of Nash and correlated equilibria in static games is classical, the computational and sample‑complexity theory of *coarse correlated equilibria* (CCEs) in MGs remains largely unexplored.  In this paper we close this gap by establishing a near‑optimal convergence theory for learning CCEs in finite‑state, finite‑action, discounted‑reward Markov games.

We first show that any joint policy sequence that satisfies a *no‑regret* property for every player automatically drives the expected discounted payoff of each player to within $\varepsilon$ of a CCE.  This observation links online learning guarantees in the repeated game to equilibrium attainment in the underlying MG.  Leveraging this connection, we propose a fully distributed, model‑free algorithm that combines *Online Mirror Descent* (OMD) with a simple exploration scheme.  Each agent updates its policy using a locally observed reward signal and a stochastic gradient derived from a soft‑max regularizer, while simultaneously estimating the transition dynamics via a sample‑based empirical MDP.

Our main result is that the algorithm attains an $\varepsilon$‑CCE in
$$
\tilde{O}\!\left(\frac{|S|\;|A|^{N}}{\varepsilon^2}\right)
$$
episodes, where $|S|$ is the state space size, $|A|$ the per‑agent action set size, and $N$ the number of agents.  This bound is *near‑optimal*: we prove a matching lower bound up to constant and logarithmic factors.  The analysis holds for both finite‑horizon and infinite‑discounted MGs, and it applies to any number of players and arbitrary state transition dynamics.

Experiments on synthetic grid‑worlds and benchmark multi‑agent control tasks confirm that our method reaches high‑quality CCEs far faster than baseline no‑regret schemes and scales gracefully with the number of agents.  The results demonstrate that coarse correlated equilibria are not only theoretically tractable but also practically attainable in general‑sum Markov games.
160:
Accurate classification of genomic variants is critical for precision oncology, yet prostate cancer remains under‑represented in publicly available variant benchmarks. Here we introduce **Prostate‑VarBench**, a curated repository of 23,487 germline and somatic single‑nucleotide variants (SNVs) and indels spanning 1,356 prostate cancer–associated loci. Each entry is annotated with a rich set of functional, evolutionary, and population‑frequency features (e.g., CADD, REVEL, ClinVar, gnomAD allele counts), along with gold‑standard labels derived from expert curation and high‑confidence pathogenicity assays. The benchmark is partitioned into disjoint training, validation, and independent test sets that preserve class balance and variant types, enabling reproducible comparison of computational pipelines.

To address the dual challenges of performance and interpretability in variant calling, we deploy a **TabNet**‑based framework—an attention‑driven deep tabular architecture—tailored to Prostate‑VarBench. TabNet’s dynamic feature selection yields state‑of‑the‑art classification accuracy (AUROC = 0.94 ± 0.02, F1 = 0.91 ± 0.01) on the test set, surpassing conventional machine‑learning baselines (Random Forest, XGBoost) and deep models (MLP, CNN) by 4–6 % absolute. Crucially, TabNet’s inherent interpretability provides per‑variant feature importance scores; our analyses reveal that evolutionary conservation, protein‑impact scores, and prostate‑specific eQTLs drive the majority of predictions, offering actionable insights for clinical geneticists.

Prostate‑VarBench and the accompanying TabNet implementation are publicly released (https://github.com/ProstateVarBench), along with a reproducible evaluation pipeline. By furnishing a rigorous benchmark and a transparent, high‑performance classifier, we aim to accelerate variant interpretation in prostate cancer research and facilitate downstream therapeutic decision‑making.
161:
Deploying compact deep neural networks on edge devices is increasingly attractive for latency‑critical applications, yet their limited capacity makes them fragile to domain shifts that inevitably occur at test time. Recursive neural models—whose depth grows implicitly through weight sharing or hierarchical composition—offer a powerful yet parameter‑efficient alternative to conventional feed‑forward nets, yet their performance degrades sharply under distribution mismatch. In this work we investigate **test‑time adaptation (TTA) of tiny recursive models** (TRMs), a class of lightweight architectures that combine recursive weight reuse with hierarchical feature extraction.

We first formalise the challenge of adapting TRMs without labelled data at deployment time, and identify two bottlenecks: (i) the recursive structure amplifies optimisation instability, and (ii) conventional TTA methods (e.g., test‑time batch norm, unsupervised loss minimisation) are too computationally expensive for sub‑millimetre‑sized models. To address these, we introduce **RecAdapt**—a lightweight adaptation framework that (a) learns a compact, task‑agnostic meta‑learner to predict per‑recursive‑module residuals, and (b) optimises these residuals using a single‑step self‑distillation objective under a low‑precision update regime. RecAdapt requires no additional parameters beyond a small adaptation head and incurs only a 1 % increase in FLOPs during inference.

We evaluate RecAdapt on a suite of vision and language benchmarks (CIFAR‑10, SVHN, Office‑31, and a recursive sentence‑classification dataset) under severe domain shifts. Tiny recursive models (≤ 1 M parameters) adapted with RecAdapt achieve an average accuracy gain of 4.8 % over static baselines and 2.1 % over state‑of‑the‑art TTA methods, while preserving real‑time inference on a Raspberry Pi 4. Our results demonstrate that careful exploitation of recursion and efficient meta‑adaptation enables robust, on‑device learning even for the smallest neural architectures.
162:
Financial information retrieval (FIR) demands that search systems translate ambiguous user utterances into precise queries while ensuring that the resulting query can actually be satisfied by the available corpora. Existing query‑generation methods focus largely on relevance or linguistic quality, yet rarely assess whether the query can be answered given the dynamic, highly structured nature of financial data. In this work we propose a **Query Generation Pipeline with Enhanced Answerability Assessment (QGP‑EAA)** that jointly generates high‑precision, finance‑aware queries and predicts their answerability before retrieval.  

The pipeline comprises three stages: (1) **Semantic parsing** of user intent using a transformer‑based model fine‑tuned on a large, domain‑specific corpus of financial FAQs and regulatory documents; (2) **Structured query synthesis** that maps parsed entities and relations to a hybrid query representation combining keyword, slot‑fill, and knowledge‑graph components; and (3) **Answerability scoring** via a lightweight neural network that ingests the generated query, the target corpus statistics (document coverage, temporal recency, and data type), and a set of retrieval‑confidence signals. The scorer is trained on a novel annotated dataset of 12,000 financial queries labeled with ground‑truth answerability, derived from a mixture of news, earnings transcripts, and SEC filings.  

We evaluate QGP‑EAA on two large-scale financial IR benchmarks (FinSearch‑2024 and SEC‑Corpus) and compare it against state‑of‑the‑art query generation baselines (BERT‑QG, T5‑QG) and answerability predictors (BM25‑based, GPT‑3 heuristic). Our system achieves a **23.7 % lift in mean reciprocal rank (MRR)** and a **15.2 % reduction in unanswerable queries** relative to the best baseline, while maintaining a negligible latency overhead. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of domain‑specific embeddings and the multi‑signal answerability model.  

QGP‑EAA demonstrates that incorporating a principled answerability assessment into the query generation loop substantially improves retrieval effectiveness for finance‑specific use cases, paving the way for more reliable, user‑centric FIR systems.
163:
Wound‑care visual question answering (VQA) is an emerging task that combines medical image analysis with natural‑language reasoning to assist clinicians in diagnosing and monitoring skin lesions. Existing VQA systems for this domain suffer from a scarcity of fine‑grained annotated data, highly specialized terminology, and a mismatch between visual content and textual queries, which often leads to brittle inference. In this work we introduce **Mined Prompting and Metadata‑Guided Generation (MP‑MG)**, a two‑stage framework that leverages unlabeled clinical imagery and structured metadata to overcome these limitations.

First, we propose a **prompt‑mining pipeline** that automatically extracts high‑yield question templates from a large corpus of wound‑care reports and expert annotations. These prompts capture domain‑specific linguistic patterns and are used to augment the training objective of a multimodal transformer, encouraging the model to learn clinically relevant reasoning pathways. Second, we incorporate **metadata‑guided generation**, where patient‑specific attributes (e.g., wound location, etiology, temporal information) are encoded and fed to the decoder to constrain answer synthesis, thereby improving factual accuracy and reducing hallucinations.

We assemble a new benchmark, **WoundCare‑VQA**, consisting of 5,432 images and 12,768 paired visual questions sourced from electronic health records and a multi‑institutional clinical trial. On this dataset, MP‑MG achieves a 12.3 % absolute improvement in exact‑match accuracy over the state‑of‑the‑art baseline and a 3.1 % gain in BLEU‑4, while maintaining robust generalization to out‑of‑distribution queries. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of prompt mining and metadata integration. Our results demonstrate that mining domain‑specific prompts and harnessing structured metadata are pivotal for high‑performance, clinically trustworthy VQA in wound care.
164:
Large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in clinical natural‑language processing, yet their proficiency with numerical reasoning—particularly in the high‑stakes domain of medical calculation—remains uneven. We introduce **MedCalc‑Eval** and **MedCalc‑Env**, a paired framework designed to (1) quantify and benchmark calculation accuracy of LLMs on real‑world clinical problems, and (2) provide a lightweight, reproducible environment that augments models with domain‑specific numeric tools and guideline‑based constraints.

MedCalc‑Eval aggregates 3,456 calculation instances drawn from electronic health record (EHR) notes, radiology reports, and pharmacokinetic worksheets. Each instance is paired with a gold‑standard solution and a set of five evaluation metrics: exact‑match accuracy, numerical error tolerance, reasoning chain completeness, and domain‑specific sanity checks (e.g., dosage limits, unit consistency). The benchmark covers a broad spectrum of tasks—vital‑sign interpretation, drug‑dose calculation, risk‑score derivation, and laboratory value conversions—making it the most comprehensive public testbed for medical numeracy.

MedCalc‑Env implements a modular “calc‑shell” that intercepts arithmetic prompts, delegates to a curated library of numerically precise sub‑modules (e.g., dose‑adjustment tables, Bayesian drug‑level estimators), and then streams partial reasoning back to the LLM. The shell also exposes a lightweight API for external calculators and real‑time unit conversion, thereby allowing models to outsource complex operations while preserving end‑to‑end explainability.

Using MedCalc‑Eval, we evaluate three contemporary LLMs (ChatGPT‑4, Med-PaLM, and Gpt‑4‑Turbo). Raw prompting yields 46 % exact‑match accuracy. When coupled with MedCalc‑Env, accuracy rises to 72 % across all task categories, with the most pronounced gains on pharmacokinetic dosage calculations (≈ + 18 %) and lab‑value conversions (≈ + 22 %). Ablation studies confirm that both the explicit reasoning scaffolding and the domain‑specific toolchain contribute independently to performance improvements. 

Our results demonstrate that a calibrated evaluation benchmark, paired with a specialized calculation environment, can substantially mitigate the numerical limitations of LLMs in clinical contexts. Future work will explore reinforcement‑learning‑based fine‑tuning within MedCalc‑Env and the integration of real‑time clinical decision support workflows.
165: This study introduces **LEVER**, a new framework that tackles the persistent problem of poorly performing rare classes in Extreme Classification (XC). Rare labels—those with only a few training instances—tend to exhibit high label inconsistency, which hampers the accuracy of standard classifiers. LEVER combats this by employing a robust Siamese‑style network that transfers knowledge across related categories, thereby reducing noise and boosting the effectiveness of One‑vs‑All models. Extensive experiments on a wide range of XC benchmarks demonstrate that LEVER markedly improves performance on infrequent classes, establishing a new state‑of‑the‑art. In addition, the paper releases two novel multi‑intent datasets that will serve as valuable resources for future XC research.
166: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) accessed via Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) introduces a serious security risk: providers may act dishonestly. Such malfeasance can take many forms, for instance covertly replacing a touted high‑performance model with a cheaper one, or padding outputs with meaningless tokens to inflate costs. In this paper we address this problem from the perspective of algorithmic game theory and mechanism design. We present the first formal economic framework that captures a realistic user–provider ecosystem where a user can submit \(T\) successive queries to multiple providers, each of whom may adopt various strategic tactics. Our main result is a constructive proof that, for any continuous strategy space and any \(\varepsilon \in (0, \tfrac12)\), there exists an approximate incentive‑compatible mechanism with an additive approximation ratio of \(O(T^{1-\varepsilon}\log T)\) while guaranteeing a quasi‑linear second‑best utility for the user. We also establish an impossibility result, showing that no mechanism can achieve an expected user utility asymptotically better than ours. Finally, we validate our mechanism through simulation experiments that emulate real‑world API deployments.
167: Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) provide a principled framework for sequential decision‑making under uncertainty, yet online planning in high‑dimensional belief spaces remains computationally prohibitive.  We introduce **Vectorized Online POMDP Planning (VOP)**, a scalable framework that exploits SIMD and GPU architectures to accelerate belief‑space search without sacrificing optimality guarantees.  VOP reformulates the conventional depth‑first, tree‑based exploration (e.g., POMCP, SARSOP) as a set of batched linear‑algebra operations over large collections of belief states, observations, and actions.  By representing belief updates and value backups as tensor contractions, we achieve a >10× reduction in wall‑clock time on a wide range of benchmark domains (Tiger, RockSample, and autonomous navigation problems), while maintaining the same pruning thresholds and convergence criteria as the state‑of‑the‑art sequential algorithms.  We further extend the vectorized formulation to handle continuous observation models via kernel density estimation, enabling the method to be applied to partially observable continuous‑state problems.  Experimental results demonstrate that VOP not only scales to belief trees with millions of nodes but also yields near‑optimal policies in real‑time settings where traditional online planners fail.  Our open‑source implementation, together with a comprehensive evaluation suite, provides a practical baseline for future research on hardware‑accelerated POMDP solvers.
168:
Monocular depth estimation (MDE), which predicts per‑pixel depth from a single RGB frame, is essential for a wide range of AI systems that require three‑dimensional scene understanding. In practice, MDE models must often operate in domains that differ markedly from their training conditions. Test‑time (domain) adaptation (TTA) is a practical strategy for bridging this gap. Although recent self‑supervised TTA techniques have shown promise for MDE, they still struggle in highly varied and dynamic settings.

To address these limitations, we introduce **PITTA**, a novel, high‑performing TTA framework for MDE. PITTA incorporates two core innovations: (1) a pose‑agnostic TTA strategy that adapts a pre‑trained depth network without relying on camera pose data, and (2) an instance‑aware image masking approach. The latter isolates dynamic entities—such as vehicles and pedestrians—by extracting instance masks from a pre‑trained panoptic segmentation model and discarding static background components. Additionally, we propose a lightweight edge‑extraction module that operates directly on the single input image and its depth map to further enhance adaptation quality.

Extensive experiments on the DrivingStereo and Waymo datasets, spanning diverse environmental conditions, show that PITTA outperforms current state‑of‑the‑art methods, delivering significant improvements in monocular depth estimation during test‑time adaptation.
169: The advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI)—especially AI applied to scientific research (AIS)—must be guided by the principles of responsible AI. While progress in responsible AI is frequently measured with evaluation metrics, the robustness and reliability of those metrics themselves have received comparatively little scrutiny. In this paper we revisit prior studies that probe the stability of fairness metrics in recommender systems, an exemplar AI domain, and distill their main findings into a set of non‑exhaustive guidelines. These guidelines are designed to aid the creation of dependable metrics for responsible AI across a wide range of applications, including AIS.
170:
This study introduces and evaluates three denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) that synthesize high‑resolution 3‑D $T_1$‑weighted MRI brain volumes. The models were trained on 80,675 scans from 42,406 individuals drawn from 38 publicly available datasets. All images, roughly 1 mm isotropic, were manually screened by three experts to remove scans with poor quality, limited field‑of‑view, or excessive pathology. Minimal preprocessing was applied so as to preserve the natural visual diversity of the data; the volumes were neither registered to a common coordinate system nor subjected to bias‑field correction, thereby allowing the DDPMs to generate images exhibiting realistic orientation variations and intensity inhomogeneity. 

Model performance was assessed through segmentation, Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) calculations, and visual inspection. All three DDPMs produced coherent brain volumes; the velocity‑ and flow‑prediction variants yielded lower FIDs than the sample‑prediction baseline, yet all models still achieved higher FIDs than real scans across several cohorts. A permutation test revealed that the synthetic volume distributions differed from those of real data, with the velocity and flow models showing fewer significant differences in thalamic and putaminal volumes. 

In summary, we present the first fully 3‑D diffusion model for brain imaging that operates without skull stripping or registration. Despite the statistical discrepancies noted, the models generate high‑resolution $T_1$‑weighted brain volumes that are visually plausible. All trained weights and inference code are openly released at https://github.com/piksl-research/medforj.
171:
The ability to connect chemical structures with their natural‑language descriptions underpins many applications in cheminformatics, drug discovery, and computational biology. Existing multimodal approaches typically treat a molecule as a flat vector or a whole graph, and a text passage as a sequence of tokens, leading to a coarse alignment that often misses fine‑grained semantic correspondences between sub‑structures (e.g., functional groups) and descriptive phrases (e.g., “hydroxyl‑bearing side chain”). We propose **Substructure‑aware Alignment (S³A)**, a joint representation learning framework that explicitly bridges this gap by aligning chemically meaningful sub‑graphs with linguistic tokens through a graph‑to‑text attention mechanism.

S³A first decomposes a molecule into a hierarchical set of sub‑structures using a data‑driven fragmentation scheme. Each sub‑structure is embedded with a graph neural network, while the full text is encoded by a transformer encoder. A cross‑modal attention module learns to map sub‑structure embeddings to contextualized word embeddings, and a contrastive loss enforces that the aggregated sub‑structure representation of a molecule is close to its textual description in a shared latent space. We further introduce a *structure‑aware alignment loss* that penalizes misalignment between chemically related sub‑structures and semantically related words, thereby encouraging interpretable correspondence.

Evaluated on two large‑scale benchmarks—(i) the PubChemText dataset of SMILES–caption pairs and (ii) a curated subset of the ChEMBL literature—S³A achieves a 15 % relative improvement in retrieval rank metrics (mAP@10) over state‑of‑the‑art multimodal baselines. Ablation studies confirm that sub‑structure decomposition and the alignment loss are crucial to performance. Visual inspection of attention weights shows that S³A consistently associates functional groups with the correct descriptive phrases, providing interpretability that is absent in conventional methods.

Our work demonstrates that incorporating explicit chemical sub‑structure awareness into multimodal representation learning yields both quantitative gains and qualitative insights, thereby advancing the integration of chemical and textual knowledge for downstream tasks such as virtual screening, literature mining, and automated synthesis planning.
172:
Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) models combine a language model with an external knowledge base, yet their performance often diverges from human expectations due to misaligned retrieval and generation dynamics. We introduce **DMA** (Dynamic Retrieval‑Alignment via Online Human Feedback), a principled framework that continuously incorporates user feedback to steer a RAG system toward higher factual accuracy, relevance, and overall alignment. DMA operates in an online loop: after each user interaction, a lightweight feedback signal (e.g., click‑through, star rating, or explicit correction) is converted into a joint loss that updates both the retrieval module and the generation head in real time. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve sample efficiency, DMA employs a replay buffer of high‑confidence feedback events and a meta‑gradient update that balances retrieval ranking with generative fidelity. 

We evaluate DMA on three benchmark domains (knowledge‑base question answering, dialogue, and open‑domain summarization) using both synthetic and real‑world human annotations. Compared to conventional offline fine‑tuning and reinforcement‑learning‑from‑human‑feedback (RLHF) baselines, DMA reduces factual hallucinations by 23 % and improves user satisfaction scores by 15 % while maintaining comparable latency. Ablation studies confirm that jointly updating retrieval and generation is essential for the observed gains, and that the online feedback loop can converge to a stable policy within 10 k interactions.  

DMA offers a scalable, low‑overhead path to continuously align RAG systems with evolving user preferences, opening new avenues for adaptive knowledge‑augmented dialogue agents and beyond. The code and an open‑source implementation of the DMA framework are available at https://github.com/your-org/dma.
173: Allocating indivisible payoffs—whether in the form of physical goods, labor contracts, or monetary compensation—poses a persistent challenge in cooperative decision‑making: how to distribute value fairly when a single item cannot be split. Classical fair‑division tools such as the *Shapley value* are defined for transferable‑utility games, yet applying them directly to indivisible outcomes yields non‑integral, often infeasible shares. In this work we introduce a principled framework that reconciles the Shapley value with indivisibility constraints. Our construction treats each indivisible payoff as a coalition‑dependent project and defines a *Shapley‑based rounding* that preserves the axiomatic properties of efficiency, symmetry, dummy, and additivity up to a bounded approximation error. We prove that for any finite coalition structure, the resulting allocation constitutes a Pareto‑optimal, envy‑free solution in expectation and satisfies a novel *Shapley‑fairness* criterion that generalizes the classical *Shapley value fairness* to the discrete setting. Computationally, we provide a polynomial‑time algorithm that achieves the optimal rounding under a limited‑item restriction and a scalable heuristic based on sampling for larger instances. Empirical evaluation on synthetic datasets and real‑world cooperative projects (e.g., joint venture profit sharing, shared resource allocation) demonstrates that our method yields allocations with significantly lower variance in perceived fairness compared to existing rule‑based schemes (e.g., round‑robin, highest‑bid first). This paper thus bridges a longstanding gap between cooperative game theory and practical indivisible division, offering a robust, axiomatic tool for designers of fair pay‑out mechanisms.
174:
Deep‑learning models span a wide spectrum of designs, yet most proofs of their universal approximation abilities are tailored to each specific architecture—fully‑connected nets, CNNs, Transformers, and so on. This bespoke approach has two main drawbacks: every new architecture demands a fresh, from‑scratch proof, and the resulting results remain isolated, preventing a common theoretical language across network families. Consequently, redundant work is unavoidable, and a unified understanding of expressive power is lacking.

To resolve this, we introduce a general, modular framework for establishing universal approximation. The core idea is the **Universal Approximation Module (UAM)**: a minimal building block, possibly consisting of several layers, that already possesses the universal approximation property. We prove that any deep network formed by chaining such modules automatically inherits universality. Furthermore, the overall approximation can be viewed as a stepwise refinement, where each module successively improves the function being approximated. This perspective unifies the analysis of disparate architectures and offers a transparent view of how expressiveness accumulates through the depth of the network.
175: Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) that undergo post‑training with Reinforcement Learning (RL) exhibit strong general reasoning, yet their assessment usually focuses on language‑heavy challenges such as math problems. This leaves open whether RL truly pushes the intrinsic limits of a base VLM, especially for visually driven spatial tasks where the model initially performs poorly. To explore this, we propose **Ariadne**, a framework that employs synthetic maze environments for multi‑step spatial reasoning, allowing precise manipulation of difficulty factors such as path length and number of turns. Using this controllable setting, we train VLMs via **Reinforcement Learning with Verified Rewards (RLVR)** within a difficulty‑aware curriculum. Remarkably, after RLVR fine‑tuning, the VLM attains over 50 % accuracy on a task set that the original model solved at 0 %, evidencing a genuine expansion of its baseline capability. To gauge real‑world applicability, we test out‑of‑distribution generalization on practical benchmarks. Despite training solely on synthetic mazes, Ariadne delivers significant zero‑shot gains, improving accuracy by an average of 16 % on MapBench (e.g., museum navigation) and 24 % on ReasonMap (subway transfer tasks). These findings demonstrate that our approach not only extends a model’s fundamental abilities but also boosts its performance on real‑world spatial reasoning. We note that our study focuses on post‑training, given the opacity of pre‑training data, and hope this work encourages further research into targeted, capability‑enhancing alignment strategies.
176: Scientific discovery driven by data hinges on repeated cycles of literature review, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. While recent AI systems have begun automating aspects of research, they typically falter after a small number of steps, curtailing the depth of insight they can produce. We introduce **Kosmos**, an AI scientist capable of conducting extensive, data‑centric investigations. Starting from an open‑ended goal and a supplied dataset, Kosmos can run for up to twelve hours, iterating through parallel data analytics, literature searches, and hypothesis crafting before consolidating findings into formal scientific reports. A key innovation is a structured world model that facilitates seamless communication between the data‑analysis and literature‑search agents, enabling the system to maintain coherence across roughly 200 agent rollouts. In total, each run executes an average of 42,000 lines of code and processes around 1,500 research papers, with every claim in the output being backed by code or primary literature citations. External evaluators verified that 79.4 % of the statements in Kosmos’ reports were correct, and collaborators reported that a single 20‑cycle run equated to roughly six months of their own research effort. Moreover, the number of substantive scientific insights produced scales linearly with the number of cycles (tested up to 20). We showcase seven discoveries made by Kosmos across metabolomics, materials science, neuroscience, and statistical genetics. Three of these independently corroborate results from pre‑prints or unpublished studies that Kosmos had no prior access to, while the remaining four represent novel contributions to their respective fields.
177: Generating music that matches visual content—known as Video‑to‑Music (V2M)—faces two enduring hurdles: (1) the absence of explicit rhythm modeling impairs audiovisual temporal alignment, and (2) integrating diverse visual cues to guide music synthesis is inherently difficult. We tackle these problems with **Diff‑V2M**, a versatile V2M framework built on a hierarchical conditional diffusion network. The architecture consists of a visual‑feature extractor followed by a conditional music generator. To encode rhythm, we compare several representations—low‑resolution mel‑spectrograms, tempograms, and onset detection functions (ODFs)—and train a rhythm predictor that directly infers these cues from video frames. In addition, we capture semantic and emotional attributes to preserve contextual and affective consistency. All modalities enter the generator through a two‑stage cross‑attention: the first layer conditions on emotional features to sculpt the music’s affective tone, while the second layer fuses semantic and rhythmic signals. To further refine feature blending, we employ time‑aware fusion mechanisms, including feature‑wise linear modulation (FiLM) and weighted aggregation, enabling the model to dynamically balance semantic and rhythmic guidance across the diffusion process. Extensive evaluations show that low‑resolution ODFs provide the most effective rhythmic signal, and Diff‑V2M surpasses existing approaches on both in‑domain and out‑of‑domain test sets, achieving new state‑of‑the‑art scores in objective metrics and user studies. A demo and the source code are available at https://Tayjsl97.github.io/Diff-V2M-Demo/.
178: The swift rise of artificial intelligence (AI) across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) brings forth a pivotal inquiry: do investments in computational infrastructure keep pace with the development of the necessary skills, incentives, and governance frameworks? Using socio‑technical systems (STS) theory as a lens, this mixed‑methods investigation assesses workforce readiness in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Oman. We analyze term‑frequency inverse‑document‑frequency (TF‑IDF) metrics from six national AI strategies, catalog 47 publicly announced AI projects (January 2017–April 2025), conduct paired case studies, and examine programs at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) and the Saudi Data & Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA) Academy. A scenario matrix links oil‑revenue slack (technical capacity) to regulatory coherence (social alignment). Of the 47 initiatives, 34 (0.72; 95% Wilson CI 0.58–0.83) integrate both social and technical dimensions, with country‑level indices ranging from 0.57 to 0.90 (small n; overlapping intervals). Our scenario analysis indicates that regulatory alignment may be more critical than fiscal capacity: fragmented rules can undermine progress even with ample oil revenues, whereas harmonized standards sustain momentum during austerity. We also uncover an emerging dual‑track talent pipeline—elite researchers versus rapidly trained practitioners—that threatens a bifurcated labor market absent bridging mechanisms. By extending STS inquiry to oil‑rich, state‑led economies, the study refines theory and proposes a research agenda focused on longitudinal coupling metrics, coordination ethnographies, and outcome‑based performance indicators.
179:
The acquisition of a coherent body representation in early infancy is driven by spontaneous self‑touch and the growing ability to regard one’s own limbs. In this study we present *Baby Sophia*, a developmental‑robotics framework that emulates this natural process of self‑exploration through a tightly coupled sensorimotor loop of self‑touch and hand regard. Building on theories of infant body‑schema formation, we equipped a humanoid platform with an array of tactile sensors, an articulated hand, and a vision system capable of detecting its own arm in the visual field. A reinforcement‑learning controller generates exploratory touch sequences (e.g., reaching, grasping, rolling) while a gaze‑control module directs the robot’s visual attention toward the touched limb, thereby providing a consistent hand‑regard signal.
