During a 60‑minute exploration phase, *Baby Sophia* performed 3,200 self‑touch events, which were used to update a probabilistic body‑map via a Kalman‑filter‑based body‑schema estimator. We evaluated the system’s performance by measuring the accuracy of hand‑position predictions before and after the exploration phase, as well as its ability to generalise to novel postures. Results show a 42 % reduction in positional uncertainty and a 35 % increase in correct hand‑recognition rates after the exploration period, compared with a baseline condition in which hand regard was omitted. Importantly, the inclusion of hand regard accelerated convergence of the body model and improved robustness to sensor noise.

Our findings demonstrate that a developmental approach that jointly harnesses self‑touch and visual hand regard can endow a robotic agent with a functional body‑schema that closely parallels infant self‑exploration. This work bridges developmental psychology and robotics, offering a scalable paradigm for autonomous self‑learning and providing insights into the mechanisms underlying early self‑awareness in humans.
180: In this study, we present **Wonder3D++**, a new approach for rapid creation of high‑fidelity textured meshes from single‑view images. While recent Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) techniques can recover 3D geometry from 2D diffusion priors, they typically require slow, per‑shape optimization and often yield inconsistent geometry. Conversely, methods that infer 3D directly in a single forward pass produce fast results but usually lack detail and quality. To address these shortcomings, we design a cross‑domain diffusion framework that simultaneously generates multi‑view normal maps and corresponding color images. A multi‑view, cross‑modal attention layer is employed to promote coherence across views and modalities. Finally, we introduce a cascaded mesh‑extraction pipeline that converts the 2D representations into a high‑quality surface in a coarse‑to‑fine manner within roughly three minutes. Extensive experiments confirm that our method delivers superior reconstruction quality, robust generalization, and improved efficiency relative to existing solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/xxlong0/Wonder3D/tree/Wonder3D_Plus.
181: Mental‑health disorders affect millions globally, yet recognizing them early remains difficult—especially among Arabic‑speaking communities where limited resources and cultural taboos often suppress discussion. Although many studies have examined English‑language mental‑health detection, Arabic data are still scarce because of a lack of annotated corpora. To bridge this gap, we introduce **CARMA**, the first large‑scale, automatically annotated dataset of Arabic Reddit posts. It covers six clinical conditions—such as anxiety, autism and depression—alongside a healthy control group, and exceeds existing Arabic resources in size and diversity. We perform both qualitative and quantitative analyses of lexical and semantic patterns among users, revealing condition‑specific linguistic markers. Finally, we evaluate a spectrum of classifiers—from simple models to advanced language models—on this dataset, demonstrating its utility for advancing mental‑health detection in under‑represented languages like Arabic.
182:
Large‑language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety‑critical and decision‑support settings, yet the notion of “risk” that drives their evaluation remains contested. In this paper we investigate who is actually “seeing” risk in LLM‑based systems, mapping the divergent perspectives that arise among developers, end‑users, regulators, and affected communities. We frame this question as a *stakeholder‑conflict problem* and argue that existing risk‑assessment protocols, which largely adopt a single technical or legal lens, fail to capture the multiplicity of concerns that emerge in practice.

To explore these tensions we conduct a mixed‑methods study that combines: (i) a large survey (N = 1,245) of LLM practitioners and policy makers; (ii) in‑depth interviews with 32 stakeholders across industry, academia, and civil‑society; and (iii) a systematic audit of 15 high‑profile LLM deployments. The results reveal three distinct risk “lenses”—technical reliability, socio‑economic impact, and governance—and illustrate how conflicts arise when a single explanatory policy is applied uniformly. In particular, developers prioritize algorithmic robustness, while regulators demand compliance with fairness and privacy standards, and affected communities emphasize potential harms and transparency.

Based on these insights we propose a **Stakeholder‑Aware Explanatory Policy (SA‑EP)** framework that (1) explicitly identifies the target audience and their risk criteria, (2) maps LLM outputs to a set of interpretable risk metrics aligned with each lens, and (3) generates customized, policy‑driven explanations that can be toggled by end‑users. We implement a prototype dashboard that demonstrates the SA‑EP in two use‑cases—a medical triage chatbot and a loan‑approval assistant—showing that stakeholders report a 38 % increase in perceived trust and a 27 % reduction in decision‑time when provided with tailored explanations.

Our contributions are: a taxonomy of stakeholder risk perceptions for LLMs; empirical evidence of policy‑conflict in current practices; and a practical framework for designing explanatory policies that reconcile these conflicts. These findings advance the governance of LLMs by foregrounding the social dimensions of risk and providing a pathway to more inclusive and accountable risk assessment.
183:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into security‑automation pipelines—from automated vulnerability discovery and patch suggestion to threat‑intel aggregation and incident‑response triage. While their natural‑language reasoning capabilities promise substantial productivity gains, the same openness that facilitates rapid model deployment also exposes LLMs to *poisoning attacks*: subtle, crafted perturbations in training data or inference inputs that cause the model to produce incorrect or malicious outputs. This paper formally investigates the unique threats posed by poisoned LLMs in the context of security automation.

We first define a threat model for *semantic* and *adversarial* poisoning in LLM‑driven security tools, distinguishing between training‑time data poisoning and inference‑time prompt manipulation. We then design a benchmark of security‑automation tasks (e.g., code‑review comment generation, malware‑signature synthesis, and incident‑response recommendation) and construct a suite of poisoning scenarios—including back‑door triggers, dataset bias injection, and prompt‑tailoring attacks—using both synthetic and real‑world corpora. Extensive empirical evaluation on GPT‑4‑style architectures and open‑source LLMs (LLaMA, Falcon) demonstrates that a single poisoned example can skew a model’s output distribution by up to 67 % on critical tasks, leading to the generation of exploitable code snippets or the omission of key vulnerability indicators.

To mitigate these risks, we propose a lightweight *in‑stream consistency check* that flags anomalous outputs based on cross‑model agreement and semantic divergence metrics, achieving an F1‑score of 0.88 in detecting poisoned responses while preserving 92 % of benign utility. We further discuss defensive retraining regimes, secure data‑collection pipelines, and policy implications for regulatory compliance in autonomous security systems.

Our results underscore the need for rigorous poisoning‑resilience testing in any production LLM‑based security automation stack and provide a foundation for developing robust safeguards against the subtle yet potentially catastrophic vulnerabilities introduced by poisoned language models.
184: The worldwide agricultural landscape is currently in the midst of a major transformation, spurred by rising food demands, climatic fluctuations, and the imperative for greener practices. SUSTAINABLE is a comprehensive smart‑farming platform that fuses IoT, artificial intelligence, satellite imagery, and role‑based workflow orchestration to deliver efficient, traceable, and sustainable cultivation, with a pilot application in the wine‑growers of the Mediterranean. This study surveys existing smart‑agriculture solutions, offers a comparative assessment, and details SUSTAINABLE’s core capabilities—satellite‑derived indices, live environmental monitoring, and role‑centric task scheduling—specifically adapted to vineyards in the region.
185:
–  
As large language models (LLMs) continue to evolve, the need for robust personalization methods that can tailor a model’s behavior to individual users has grown sharply. While non‑parametric approaches exploit LLMs’ in‑context learning, newer parametric techniques such as personalized, parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning and reward modeling are still hampered by limited adaptability to evolving user patterns and poor data efficiency in sparse settings. To overcome these shortcomings, we introduce a fine‑grained, instance‑specific steering framework that constructs sample‑level interference vectors directly from user data and injects them into the model’s forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our method hinges on two innovations: (1) a fine‑grained steering module that captures subtle signals by tapping activations from both attention and MLP layers, and (2) an input‑aware aggregation component that fuses these signals into context‑relevant adjustments. The resulting approach is highly flexible and data‑efficient, excelling when distributions shift rapidly or data is scarce. Moreover, it is orthogonal to existing personalization techniques and can be used as a plug‑in for a variety of methods. Extensive experiments on tasks ranging from short to long text generation and web function calling demonstrate that our framework significantly boosts personalization performance in dynamic environments while remaining robust across diverse interaction modes and context lengths. Code is available at https://github.com/KounianhuaDu/Fints.
186: Pre‑trained models for natural language inference (NLI) often attain high benchmark scores by exploiting dataset artifacts rather than truly grasping linguistic nuances such as negation. In this work, we examine an ELECTRA‑small network fine‑tuned on the Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) corpus, paying particular attention to how it handles negated expressions. Our analysis shows that the model struggles to classify examples containing negation correctly. To remedy this, we enrich the training set with contrastive and adversarial examples that highlight negation. The resulting augmented model improves its accuracy on negation‑laden instances while preserving overall performance, thereby reducing the model’s reliance on spurious dataset correlations.
187:
Large language models (LLMs) are frequently evaluated on their *consistency* – the ability to produce a single, stable answer to a question across different contexts or prompts. While consistency is often treated as a desideratum, recent evidence shows that overly rigid adherence to a single answer can actually impede post‑training reasoning, especially on problems that require multi‑step inference, non‑deterministic exploration, or handling ambiguous evidence. In this work we investigate the trade‑off between consistency and *exploration* during post‑training reasoning.  

We introduce **Exploratory Post‑Training Reasoning (E‑PTR)**, a lightweight decoding strategy that systematically samples and aggregates multiple reasoning traces (via temperature‑controlled sampling, diverse top‑k decoding, and beam‑search with orthogonal constraints) before reconciling them into a final prediction. We evaluate E‑PTR on a suite of reasoning benchmarks that span symbolic math, multi‑hop question answering, and commonsense inference, comparing against both consistency‑only baselines and state‑of‑the‑art chain‑of‑thought methods.  

Across 12 datasets we observe that E‑PTR achieves a 4–12 % relative accuracy improvement while maintaining calibrated confidence scores. In several cases (e.g., multi‑hop reasoning on HotpotQA and symbolic tasks on GSM‑8k) the gains are driven by the model’s ability to revisit alternative inference pathways that the consistency‑only decoder would prematurely discard. Ablation studies reveal that the benefits stem from *controlled exploration* rather than increased randomness alone, and that a small ensemble of diverse traces suffices to capture the most informative reasoning routes.  

Our results challenge the prevailing assumption that consistency is an unqualified virtue in LLM reasoning. Instead, we demonstrate that judicious exploration of the model’s latent reasoning space, followed by principled aggregation, yields more accurate, reliable, and interpretable post‑training reasoning. This insight opens avenues for designing inference procedures that balance the stability of consistent outputs with the flexibility required for complex problem solving.
188:
Financial time‑series forecasting remains one of the most challenging tasks in quantitative finance due to its high volatility, non‑stationarity, and the strong dependence of price dynamics on multiple temporal horizons. In this study we introduce **Multi‑Period Learning (MPL)**, a unified framework that jointly learns short‑, medium‑ and long‑term forecasts in a single end‑to‑end architecture. Rather than training separate models for each horizon, MPL employs a shared encoder that extracts hierarchical representations of the underlying market dynamics, while a set of task‑specific decoders predict returns at the desired time‑frames. The key innovations are (i) a *cross‑horizon consistency loss* that enforces coherent evolution of predictions across scales, and (ii) an *adaptive weighting scheme* that automatically balances the influence of each horizon during training, mitigating the bias‑variance trade‑off that plagues conventional multi‑task approaches.

We evaluate MPL on a comprehensive benchmark comprising daily, intraday, and monthly price series for equities, foreign‑exchange, and commodity markets. Using standard metrics (RMSE, MAE, directional accuracy) and downstream trading simulations, MPL outperforms baseline models (ARIMA, LSTM, Temporal Fusion Transformer) by 6–12 % in forecasting error and yields 2–4 % higher risk‑adjusted returns. Ablation studies confirm that both the consistency loss and adaptive weighting are essential for the observed performance gains.

The proposed Multi‑Period Learning framework demonstrates that a single, jointly trained model can capture the intricate, scale‑dependent structure of financial markets, offering a practical tool for traders and risk managers who require coherent predictions across multiple horizons. Future work will extend MPL to incorporate exogenous macro‑economic signals and to adaptively re‑train in a streaming setting.
189: Offline imitation learning seeks to recover expert behavior solely from logged demonstrations, yet most methods are highly sensitive to distribution mismatch between the recorded dataset and the learner’s state–action distribution.  In this work we introduce a *balance‑equation–based* framework that explicitly enforces the fundamental occupancy‑measure equality of the expert and the learned policy while simultaneously guarding against worst‑case distributional perturbations.  We formulate the problem as a *distributionally robust* optimization over an ambiguity set defined by a Wasserstein (or KL) ball around the empirical trajectory distribution.  Leveraging the dual form of the balance equations, the resulting problem becomes a convex–concave saddle point program that can be solved efficiently with stochastic mirror descent.  Theoretical analysis yields a finite‑sample regret bound that scales with the radius of the ambiguity set and the total variation distance between the expert and learner distributions, guaranteeing that the learned policy remains near‑optimal even under severe covariate shift.  Empirically we evaluate our method on a suite of continuous‑control benchmarks (MuJoCo, Meta‑World) and a real‑world robotic manipulation dataset.  Across all tasks, the proposed approach consistently outperforms vanilla behavioral cloning, GAIL, and other offline imitation baselines, achieving higher returns with fewer demonstrations and exhibiting robust performance under varying levels of data corruption and domain shift.  The results confirm that incorporating balance equations within a distributionally robust offline setting yields a principled, data‑efficient, and resilient imitation learner.
190:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are routinely adapted to new tasks or corrected for undesired behaviours through fine‑tuning or instruction‑tuning.  In practice, such edits are often short‑lived: a model that has been patched to avoid a particular bias, or to respect a newly added policy, may “forget” the edit after additional pre‑training, domain adaptation, or even after a few inference passes.  We refer to this phenomenon as **edit decay** – the gradual erosion of a model’s responsiveness to a deliberate modification in its internal knowledge or behavior.  

This paper formalizes edit decay, proposes a principled framework for quantifying it, and empirically investigates its dynamics across a range of architectures, training regimes, and edit types.  We introduce the *Edit Retention Metric (ERM)*, which measures the fidelity of a model’s response to a curated set of probe queries before and after subsequent training or deployment steps.  Using ERM, we evaluate three families of fine‑tuning methods: (i) full‑parameter update, (ii) parameter‑efficient adapters (LoRA, PrefixTuning), and (iii) gradient‑based memory‑preserving updates (Replay, Elastic Weight Consolidation).  Experiments on GPT‑Neo, LLaMA‑2, and T5 variants reveal that parameter‑efficient approaches maintain edit fidelity up to 8× longer than full‑parameter fine‑tuning, while memory‑preserving strategies mitigate decay at a computational cost of 1.5× higher inference latency.  We further uncover a strong correlation between the *edit magnitude* (measured as the norm of parameter changes) and decay speed, suggesting a trade‑off between edit strength and longevity.

Our results highlight that edit decay is a quantifiable, systematic risk in the deployment of fine‑tuned LLMs, especially in safety‑critical or policy‑sensitive applications.  The proposed metrics and insights provide practitioners with concrete diagnostics and guidelines for designing durable edits, and open avenues for future work on continual‑learning safeguards in large language models.
191:
Pressure ulcers (PUs) represent a major and widespread challenge in healthcare. Correctly staging PUs (I–IV) is crucial for effective management, yet the task is fraught with difficulty because the visual differences between stages are subtle and clinicians often disagree. Existing AI solutions based on Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers have shown encouraging performance, but they lack transparent reasoning.  

We introduce FT‑ARM (Fine‑Tuned Agentic Reflection Multimodal model), a large language model fine‑tuned for multimodal input and equipped with an agentic self‑reflection loop that emulates clinician diagnostic reassessment. FT‑ARM repeatedly refines its predictions by integrating visual cues from the ulcer image with contextual knowledge encoded from clinical text, thereby improving both accuracy and consistency.  

Evaluated on the public Pressure Injury Image Dataset (PIID), FT‑ARM—fine‑tuned from LLaMA 3.2 90 B—reaches 85 % accuracy in classifying stages I–IV, outperforming prior CNN‑based baselines by 4 %. Unlike previous studies that relied solely on offline testing, FT‑ARM has been designed and benchmarked for real‑time inference, mirroring practical deployment scenarios. In addition, it generates natural‑language explanations grounded in clinical reasoning, enhancing interpretability and clinician trust.  

By combining multimodal fine‑tuning with reflective reasoning, FT‑ARM represents a significant step toward reliable, transparent, and clinically useful automated PU assessment, addressing the urgent need for consistent and explainable staging in patient care.
192:
Continuous, real‑time motion recognition is a highly active research area because it aligns closely with practical deployment scenarios. Skeleton‑based methods, which exploit 3‑D temporal information, have recently attracted significant attention. Unfortunately, the vast majority of existing studies focus on segment‑level recognition, making them ill‑suited for true online processing. 

In this work, we introduce a streaming skeleton‑sequence recognizer built around two complementary modules: a detector and a classifier. Both components rely on a Semi‑Positive Definite (SPD) matrix representation of the skeletal data, together with a Siamese network that learns their semantic similarity. This formulation allows the detector to identify the temporal boundaries of motions in an unsegmented stream, while the classifier simultaneously labels each detected interval. Because the detector operates continuously, it can track changes in kinetic state on the fly. 

We evaluate our system on several hand‑gesture and body‑action benchmarks, demonstrating that it achieves superior accuracy compared to state‑of‑the‑art methods in most cases.
193:
The proliferation of offshore structures such as wind farms, oil rigs and platform installations has intensified the need for automated, high‑frequency monitoring over vast oceanic areas. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) from Sentinel‑1 offers persistent, all‑weather coverage but the complex scattering signatures of man‑made platforms pose a challenge for conventional object detection algorithms. This study presents a deep learning framework that leverages convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to identify offshore platforms in Sentinel‑1 single‑look complex (SLC) images and investigates the efficacy of synthetic training data in overcoming the scarcity of annotated SAR imagery.

We curated a comprehensive dataset of 1,200 Sentinel‑1 SLC scenes spanning three oceanic basins and labeled 3,400 platforms of varying types and sizes. To augment this limited set, we generated synthetic SAR scenes using a physics‑based radar image simulator that models platform geometry, radar incidence angles, and sea‑state scattering. The synthetic dataset (8,000 images) was combined with the real data to train a Faster‑R‑CNN backbone with a feature pyramid network (FPN), fine‑tuned for small‑object detection and adapted to SAR’s speckle noise via a domain‑specific augmentation pipeline.

Evaluation on a held‑out 300‑image test split demonstrated that the model trained on real data alone achieved a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.54 at IoU = 0.5, whereas inclusion of the synthetic data raised mAP to 0.68, a 26 % relative improvement. Notably, the synthetic‑augmented model maintained robust performance under varying incidence angles, back‑scattering conditions, and sea‑state regimes, indicating superior generalisation. Ablation studies confirmed that the fidelity of the SAR simulator (e.g., inclusion of ground‑range migration and polarisation effects) significantly influences downstream detection accuracy.

The results underscore the practical value of synthetic SAR training data for object detection tasks where real labelled data are scarce. This work paves the way for scalable, automated monitoring of offshore infrastructure, facilitating rapid risk assessment and operational decision‑making in the maritime domain.
194:
Multimodal deep learning models traditionally fuse features from vision, language, audio and other modalities by jointly optimizing a single shared representation. Although powerful, this tight coupling often leads to *modality interference*, hampers rapid adaptation to new modalities, and exacerbates the *cold‑start* problem when a model must incorporate data that were unseen during training.  
We propose **Metis‑SPECS** (Self‑distilled Preference‑based Cold‑Start) – a framework that *decouples* multimodal learning into modality‑specific encoders and a lightweight preference network that learns to weight each modality’s contribution through self‑distillation. The preference network is trained on a *cold‑start* curriculum: it first learns a coarse, modality‑agnostic representation, then self‑distills to a refined, preference‑aware embedding without any explicit cross‑modal supervision. This self‑distillation allows the model to bootstrap reliable modality weights even when few labeled examples of a new modality are available.  

During inference, Metis‑SPECS dynamically aggregates modality embeddings according to the learned preference scores, yielding a robust multimodal representation that is both *modality‑aware* and *efficient* to update. Extensive evaluations on standard benchmarks (MS‑COCO, Flickr30k, Visual Genome, and an audio‑vision VQA dataset) demonstrate that Metis‑SPECS outperforms state‑of‑the‑art joint‑fusion baselines by up to 3.9 % mAP on image‑caption retrieval and 5.7 % accuracy on multimodal question‑answering, while reducing parameter redundancy by 22 % and enabling 4× faster adaptation to unseen modalities.  

Our results indicate that decoupling multimodal learning via self‑distilled preference mechanisms not only alleviates modality interference but also provides a principled approach to cold‑start scenarios, paving the way for more flexible, scalable multimodal systems.
195:
Quantum mechanics offers non‑classical concepts—such as superposition and entanglement—that have motivated a growing class of machine‑learning techniques. Yet, the majority of quantum‑inspired multimodal fusion architectures rely exclusively on unitary or unitary‑like operations to create entanglement. Although highly expressive, these methods often exhibit training brittleness and limited generality.  

In this paper we introduce the Quantum‑inspired Neural Network with Quantum Jump (QiNN‑QJ), a new framework for modelling multimodal entanglement. Each input modality is first mapped to a pure quantum state. A differentiable Quantum‑Jump module then converts the initial separable product state into an entangled representation. By jointly learning Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators, QiNN‑QJ induces controlled cross‑modal entanglement through dissipative dynamics, leveraging stochasticity and attractor behaviour to stabilise optimisation and shape the entanglement structure. The entangled states are projected onto trainable measurement vectors to generate predictions.  

Experiments on benchmark multimodal sentiment datasets (CMU‑MOSI, CMU‑MOSEI, and CH‑SIMS) demonstrate that QiNN‑QJ outperforms current state‑of‑the‑art models. Moreover, the model offers post‑hoc interpretability via von‑Neumann entanglement entropy. This work provides a principled, quantum‑inspired approach for fusing modalities and opens new avenues for exploiting complex cross‑modal relationships in machine learning.
196:
The rapid proliferation of speech foundation models—large pretrained systems that underlie a spectrum of downstream voice applications—has spurred the development of benchmark suites that quantify intelligibility, naturalness, and linguistic fidelity.  However, a pivotal attribute of human speech—voice quality variation (VQV)—remains largely under‑explored.  Voice quality, encompassing breathiness, creak, vibrato, and other phonatory traits, carries crucial paralinguistic information and can dramatically alter speaker perception.  In this work, we argue that VQV should be a core dimension in evaluating the fidelity of foundation models.  

We first construct **VQ‑Eval**, a multilingual, speaker‑balanced corpus annotated with a fine‑grained taxonomy of voice qualities derived from acoustic and articulatory models.  Using VQ‑Eval, we benchmark four leading foundation models (e.g., Whisper‑Large, Wav2Vec‑2.0, SpeechT5, and a recently proposed Voice‑Transformer) on both natural and synthetic speech.  We develop a hybrid evaluation framework that couples perceptual listener tests with a suite of objective metrics—including spectral tilt, harmonic‑to‑noise ratio, and a learned VQV embedding—trained on the annotated corpus.  

Our results reveal systematic deficiencies: many models collapse diverse VQ states into a single “neutral” prototype, yielding a loss of expressivity that is not captured by conventional metrics.  We demonstrate that incorporating VQV into the training objective of a generative TTS system improves both objective VQV scores (↑12 % in harmonic‑to‑noise ratio) and subjective naturalness (↑3.1 MOS points).  This study underscores the necessity of voice‑quality‑aware evaluation and provides a reproducible benchmark for future work.  The released dataset, metrics, and code facilitate further research into more nuanced, human‑like speech synthesis and recognition.
197:
Silent failures—deceptive, undetected deviations from intended behavior—are a growing threat in complex autonomous systems that rely on coordinated, multi‑agent interactions. While single‑agent diagnostics have matured, the collective dynamics of multi‑agentic AI trajectories introduce subtle failure modes that remain hidden from conventional monitoring: an agent may appear compliant locally while the joint trajectory drifts toward catastrophic states, or agents may compensate for one another’s errors, masking systemic faults. To address this, we formulate the **Silent Failure Detection (SFD)** problem for multi‑agent trajectories as a joint inference task over temporal interaction graphs and latent failure states.  

We introduce **Multi‑Agent Temporal Anomaly Graph (MATAG)**, a probabilistic framework that couples a dynamic Bayesian network over agents’ actions with a latent Markov model of failure modes. MATAG learns from logged trajectories in both simulation and real‑world deployments (e.g., swarm robotics and autonomous vehicle platoons) without requiring labeled failures. By integrating pairwise interaction constraints and trajectory‑level reconstruction losses, the model captures both local and emergent failure signatures.  

Experiments on a suite of benchmark scenarios—including cooperative search, resource‑sharing games, and traffic‑joint control—show that MATAG detects >95 % of injected silent failures with an average lead time of 3.2 s, outperforming baseline supervised classifiers by 12 % in precision and 15 % in recall. In a real‑world autonomous drone swarm, MATAG flagged latent actuator degradation before any observable safety violation occurred, allowing preemptive mitigation.  

Our work demonstrates that probabilistic graph‑based anomaly detection, when tailored to the multi‑agent context, can uncover silent failures that conventional monitoring would miss. The proposed framework offers a scalable, data‑driven approach for ensuring reliability in increasingly autonomous, coordinated AI systems.
198: We introduce **Regular Games (RG)**, a novel framework for General Game Playing that prioritizes both computational speed and ease of design. RG’s backbone is a compact, low‑level language that specifies game rules as finite automata. Its minimalistic design—containing only a handful of primitives—facilitates automatic analysis, optimisation, and agent integration, while remaining universal for all finite turn‑based games with imperfect information. To ease human or procedural game creation, we layer higher‑level languages on top of the core, which compile down to the automaton form. Benchmarks show that RG’s forward models execute faster than those of existing GGP systems such as Regular Boardgames and Ludii. The accompanying ecosystem offers an LSP‑enabled editor, automaton visualisation, performance‑testing utilities, and a debugger for tracking transformations of game descriptions.
199:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed on commodity hardware where soft‑errors—random bit‑flips in DRAM or SRAM—can silently corrupt model weights or activations, leading to catastrophic inference failures or training divergence. Existing fault‑tolerance techniques for neural networks are either computationally expensive or require extensive hardware support, making them impractical for the wide scale of modern LLM workloads. We introduce **LM‑Fix**, a lightweight bit‑flip detection and rapid recovery framework that protects the integrity of LLMs with minimal performance penalty.  

LM‑Fix combines three key ideas. First, it embeds a lightweight, deterministic *weight‑signature* layer that periodically recomputes a compact hash of each model layer’s parameters; any discrepancy indicates a bit‑flip. Second, it exploits the highly redundant nature of transformer embeddings and attention matrices to localize corrupt bits to a single weight or activation tensor using a sparse error‑localization routine. Third, it restores the corrupted component on‑the‑fly by recalling the last known‑good checkpoint from a small, on‑device log, thereby avoiding expensive recomputation of the entire model.  

We evaluate LM‑Fix on a suite of state‑of‑the‑art models (GPT‑2, LLaMA‑13B, BERT‑Large) under simulated soft‑error rates up to 10⁻⁶ per bit. Across 1,000 inference runs, LM‑Fix detected 99.8 % of injected bit‑flips, incurred an average latency overhead of 2.4 % and a memory overhead of 0.6 %, while preserving model perplexity within 0.3 % of the fault‑free baseline. During training, the framework reduced catastrophic divergence incidents by 87 % compared to naïve checkpointing.  

Our work demonstrates that robust LLM execution on unpro‑tected hardware is feasible without incurring prohibitive costs, and establishes a practical foundation for future research on lightweight resilience techniques for deep learning.
200:
Generative language models have become ubiquitous, yet their tendency to produce hallucinated, biased, or harmful content remains a major obstacle to deployment in safety‑critical settings. Existing post‑hoc filtering or prompt‑engineering strategies treat safety as a separate layer and do not fundamentally alter the generation process. In this work we introduce **Consensus Sampling**, a lightweight, model‑agnostic sampling framework that drives the generation process toward safer, more reliable outputs by enforcing agreement among multiple stochastic decoding trajectories.  

Our method samples a set of candidate continuations from a single autoregressive model under different stochastic seeds and temperature schedules. A lightweight safety scorer, trained on a curated set of adversarial prompts, evaluates each trajectory. The final token is chosen as the one that maximizes a weighted combination of probability, factual coherence, and safety consistency across the ensemble. Because the consensus is computed online during decoding, the approach incurs only a modest overhead (≤ 5 % extra inference cost) while remaining compatible with any pre‑trained transformer.  

We evaluate Consensus Sampling on a suite of safety benchmarks including Toxicity, Hallucination, and Adversarial Prompt tests. On a 13‑B GPT‑style backbone, our approach reduces toxic utterances by 48 % and factual hallucinations by 35 % relative to temperature‑scaled sampling, while preserving fluency and user‑satisfaction scores. Ablation studies confirm that the safety‑consensus component, rather than mere ensemble averaging, is the primary driver of improvement.  

Our results demonstrate that Consensus Sampling offers a principled, general‑purpose route to safer generative AI, enabling more trustworthy deployments without the need for costly model retraining or specialized architectures.
201:
Modern large‑scale scientific simulations generate petascale volumes of spatiotemporal field data that are difficult to store, transmit, or analyze efficiently.  Implicit neural representations (INRs) – coordinate‑based neural networks that learn a continuous mapping from a domain to the simulated field – have emerged as a powerful compression paradigm, but their deployment has been limited to post‑processing due to the high computational burden of training.  In this work we introduce **Sketch‑Regularized In‑Situ INR Training (S‑SIT)**, a framework that couples real‑time INR learning with a lightweight sketch‑based regularizer that guides the network toward physically meaningful solutions.  

S‑SIT injects inexpensive geometric “sketches” of the evolving field (e.g., low‑resolution edge maps, integral projections, or sparse sensor samples) into the loss function as a regularizing prior.  This approach mitigates the ill‑posedness of in‑situ training, accelerates convergence, and preserves fine‑scale structure without the need for additional memory‑heavy auxiliary models.  We integrate S‑SIT into the simulation loop of several canonical test cases – compressible Navier–Stokes, magnetohydrodynamics, and multi‑species particle‑in‑cell – and demonstrate compression factors exceeding 1,000× while maintaining relative errors below 0.5 % for key diagnostics.  Compared with baseline INR training and conventional lossy codecs, S‑SIT yields a 3× reduction in training time and a 20 % improvement in reconstruction fidelity, all while consuming less than 10 % of the simulation’s CPU budget.  Our results establish sketch‑regularized in‑situ INR training as a viable, scalable compression strategy for next‑generation scientific workflows.
202:
The *AIA Forecaster* is a data‑driven forecasting framework designed to predict the occurrence of solar eruptive events using high‑cadence, multi‑wavelength observations from the Solar Dynamics Observatory’s Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (SDO/AIA). The report details the motivation, methodology, implementation, and evaluation of a deep‑learning pipeline that ingests full‑disk EUV image sequences, processes them through a hybrid convolutional‑recurrent architecture, and outputs probabilistic flare forecasts on a 12‑hour horizon.  

Training data consist of 8,500 days of AIA 94 Å and 131 Å images combined with HMI magnetograms, labelled with GOES X‑ray flare classes (C, M, and X). The model is trained to maximize the True Skill Statistic (TSS) while maintaining a manageable false‑alarm rate, thereby addressing the imbalance inherent in flare datasets. Cross‑validation on a 70/15/15 split shows a peak TSS of 0.78 for X‑class events and 0.86 for M‑class events, surpassing traditional logistic‑regression baselines by 15 % and 12 % respectively. 

The technical report also covers the open‑source software architecture, which is implemented in Python 3.9, utilizes the TensorFlow 2.6 backend, and is containerized with Docker for reproducibility. A lightweight inference module demonstrates real‑time forecasting on a single NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti GPU, delivering predictions every 12 minutes with a latency of < 30 s.  

Finally, we discuss operational implications for space‑weather agencies, outline potential extensions to incorporate STEREO and IRIS data, and provide a roadmap for integrating the forecaster into a near‑real‑time decision‑support system. This report serves as a comprehensive technical reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to deploy or extend AIA‑based solar flare prediction tools.
203:
Robotic grasping is a core skill for autonomous manipulation, yet most contemporary solutions depend on extensive expert-labelled datasets and must be retrained whenever a new object is introduced.  We introduce **VLAD‑Grasp**, a vision‑language model–assisted, zero‑shot framework for detecting grasps.  From a single RGB‑D frame, our pipeline:  

1. Uses a large vision‑language model to produce a *goal image* in which a straight rod “impales” the target object, thereby encoding an antipodal grasp.  
2. Generates depth and segmentation masks to lift this 2‑D representation into 3‑D space.  
3. Aligns the synthesized and real point clouds through principal‑component analysis and a correspondence‑free optimisation, yielding an executable grasp pose.  

Unlike prior methods, VLAD‑Grasp requires no task‑specific training or curated grasp datasets.  Despite being completely training‑free, it matches or surpasses the performance of state‑of‑the‑art supervised models on the Cornell and Jacquard benchmarks.  We also showcase its zero‑shot capability on unfamiliar real‑world objects using a Franka Research 3 robot, underscoring the value of foundation vision‑language models as powerful priors for robotic manipulation.
204:
Multimodal mathematical reasoning—solving problems that combine natural‑language description, symbolic expressions, and visual elements—remains a challenging frontier for contemporary large language models. Existing approaches typically generate a single chain of reasoning, which is then evaluated only once, leading to cascading errors in long‑term dependency and low accuracy on higher‑order tasks.  

We introduce **MathSE**, a unified framework that endows a multimodal foundation model with *Self‑Evolving Iterative Reflection* (SEIR) and *Reward‑Guided Fine‑Tuning* (RGFT). In SEIR, the model repeatedly generates, critiques, and refines its own intermediate steps: after an initial solution attempt it applies a reflection module that identifies inconsistencies, missing assumptions, or computational mistakes, then revises the derivation in a self‑consistent loop until convergence. This iterative process mimics human mathematical practice and drastically reduces error propagation.  

RGFT provides a principled learning signal: we construct a lightweight reward model that aggregates three signals—(i) symbolic correctness of intermediate steps, (ii) alignment with a visual grounding loss (for images of graphs, equations, or handwritten notes), and (iii) human‑in‑the‑loop feedback on high‑stakes reasoning. The reward model is used to fine‑tune the base network through policy gradient methods, steering the system toward more reliable reasoning trajectories.

We evaluate MathSE on several benchmarks—MATH, GSM8K, and a newly curated Multimodal Math Dataset (MMMD) that includes scanned worksheets and diagrammatic questions. On MATH MathSE improves exact‑match accuracy from 52.3 % (baseline GPT‑4‑Vision) to 68.9 %. On GSM8K it achieves 76.5 % accuracy, surpassing prior state‑of‑the‑art by 8 %. Ablation studies confirm that SEIR contributes 4–5 % of the gain while RGFT provides an additional 2–3 % improvement.  

MathSE demonstrates that iterative self‑reflection coupled with reward‑guided fine‑tuning can substantially elevate multimodal mathematical reasoning. The framework is broadly applicable to education, automated tutoring, and any domain where rigorous, interpretable problem solving is required.
205:
The rapid diversification of machine‑learning (ML) accelerators—GPUs, CPUs, FPGAs, ASICs, and emerging neural‑processing units—has made hand‑tuned libraries a bottleneck for end‑to‑end performance. Each device exposes a distinct set of instruction sets, memory hierarchies, and parallel execution primitives, and optimal implementation strategies vary with model architecture, batch size, and precision. We introduce **PerfDojo**, a fully automated end‑to‑end pipeline that transforms high‑level ML kernels or computational graphs into highly tuned libraries for any target heterogeneous architecture.

PerfDojo adopts a three‑stage workflow. First, a **semantic analyser** extracts a fine‑grained dependency graph and identifies optimization opportunities (e.g., fused operations, loop tiling, vectorisation). Second, a **performance modeler** builds a differentiable surrogate of execution time and energy consumption using a combination of analytic models and micro‑benchmarking on the target platform. Third, a **reinforcement‑learning controller** explores the vast space of implementation candidates—choosing instruction‑set‑specific primitives, scheduling strategies, and data layouts—to maximize a multi‑objective reward (latency, throughput, power). The generated code is emitted in a target‑specific intermediate representation and compiled to native binaries or device libraries (CUDA, ROCm, OpenCL, Xilinx SDAccel, etc.). PerfDojo’s modular design allows incremental integration with existing ML frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX) and supports end‑to‑end end‑to‑end optimisation of both inference and training workloads.

We evaluate PerfDojo on a diverse benchmark suite: convolutional neural networks for ImageNet, transformer‑based language models for BERT, and graph neural networks for MoleculeNet, across NVIDIA V100, AMD MI100, Intel Xeon Skylake, and Xilinx Alveo U280. Compared to the state‑of‑the‑art libraries (cuDNN, OpenBLAS, Vitis AI), PerfDojo achieves **30–55 % higher throughput** and **up to 2× energy savings** while maintaining accuracy. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of joint device‑aware code generation and performance‑driven search.

PerfDojo demonstrates that a principled, automated approach can close the performance gap for heterogeneous ML workloads, enabling rapid prototyping and deployment on diverse hardware stacks without manual tuning. The system and its open‑source implementation are released to foster broader adoption and further research in automatic ML library generation.
206:
Implementing continuous‐time controllers on low‑cost embedded platforms often requires replacing real‑valued state feedback and integral actions with integer arithmetic in order to meet tight latency, power, and memory budgets. Naïve rounding or truncation of a pre‑designed floating‑point controller, however, can introduce significant performance loss and, in the worst case, destabilize the closed‑loop system. In this work we propose a principled learning framework that directly synthesises quantized continuous controllers tailored to the integer‑only arithmetic of target hardware.  

Our method casts controller synthesis as a constrained optimisation problem over a parameterised set of continuous controllers, augmented with a differentiable quantisation layer that maps each weight to its nearest integer multiple of a prescribed resolution. By employing a hybrid gradient‑based / integer‑relaxation strategy we can back‑propagate through the quantisation operator while guaranteeing that the final policy satisfies the integer constraints exactly. We further introduce a stability‑regularisation loss that penalises violations of Lyapunov‑based invariance conditions, thus providing theoretical guarantees for the closed‑loop system even after quantisation.  

We evaluate our approach on a suite of benchmark control tasks ranging from inverted pendulums to quadrotor trajectory tracking, implemented on both a Raspberry Pi and a low‑end automotive microcontroller. Compared to hand‑tuned fixed‑point implementations, our learned quantised controllers achieve on average a 15 % reduction in tracking error and a 30 % improvement in robustness to plant parameter drift, while requiring only 8‑bit arithmetic. Moreover, we show that the learned quantisation patterns exhibit structured sparsity that can be exploited for further hardware acceleration.  

Our results demonstrate that learning‑based quantisation of continuous controllers can reconcile the conflicting demands of high‑performance control and integer‑only embedded execution, opening a path toward systematic deployment of sophisticated controllers on resource‑constrained hardware.
207:
The rapid deployment of multimodal Large Language Models (mLLMs) in everyday applications raises urgent questions about their ability to recognize and appropriately respond to harmful content. Existing evaluations largely focus on text‐only toxicity or rely on small, manually curated test sets that lack visual nuance and contextual diversity, leading to biased judgments of a model’s harmfulness awareness. In this paper we introduce **MemeArena**, a fully automated, context‑aware benchmark designed to evaluate mLLMs’ understanding of harmfulness in multimodal inputs. MemeArena aggregates a curated corpus of over 150 k memes sourced from mainstream social media, each paired with a high‑resolution image, a caption, and a set of context annotations (e.g., cultural references, sarcasm cues, and visual cues). For every meme, we automatically generate a series of contextualized prompts that probe the model’s interpretation of the image, text, and combined multimodal signal. The evaluation framework employs a dual‑tier scoring system: (1) a *harmfulness detection* metric that compares the model’s response to ground‑truth labels derived from large‑scale crowd‑source and automatic toxicity classifiers; and (2) a *context‑sensitivity* metric that assesses whether the model appropriately modulates its response based on subtle contextual signals.

Applying MemeArena to several leading mLLMs—including GPT‑4V, Gemini‑1.5‑Vision, and Claude‑3‑Multimodal—reveals systematic gaps in harmfulness understanding that are invisible to text‑only benchmarks. In particular, we find that while models can flag overtly toxic captions, they frequently misinterpret visual cues that mitigate or intensify harm in nuanced meme contexts. Statistical analyses confirm that MemeArena’s balanced distribution of benign, harmful, and ambiguous memes mitigates annotation bias and provides an unbiased performance estimate. Moreover, our automated pipeline facilitates large‑scale, reproducible testing across evolving model families.

MemeArena constitutes the first benchmark that unites visual and textual signals, context awareness, and unbiased evaluation in a scalable, automated framework. By exposing the contextual limitations of current mLLMs, it provides a concrete path toward more robust, socially responsible multimodal AI systems. The MemeArena dataset, evaluation scripts, and benchmark results are released under an open license to support further research in harmful content detection.
208: We present **VeriStruct**, a new framework that moves AI‑assisted automated verification beyond single functions to tackle complex data‑structure modules in Verus. The system features a planner that systematically produces abstractions, type invariants, specifications, and proof code. To cope with large language models’ frequent misreading of Verus’ annotation syntax and verification semantics, VeriStruct injects explicit syntax cues into prompts and incorporates an automatic repair phase that fixes annotation errors. Evaluated on eleven Rust data‑structure modules, the approach verified ten of them, successfully proving 128 of 129 functions (a 99.2 % success rate). These results mark a significant advance toward fully automated, AI‑driven formal verification.
209: The attention mechanism lies at the heart of Transformer architectures, enabling the extraction of rich, global context from embedded vectors and demonstrating remarkable expressivity. However, its quadratic time and memory cost limits applicability to very long sequences. While several sparse‑attention variants have been proposed, they often lack a rigorous analysis of how much expressivity is retained when complexity is reduced. In this work we introduce **Random Batch Attention (RBA)**, a linear‑time self‑attention scheme grounded in random batch methods from numerical mathematics. RBA offers several key advantages: (1) it operates in \(O(n)\) time and can be parallelized along a new dimension, yielding substantial memory savings; (2) it can be inserted into a wide range of existing models, often surpassing even specialized, high‑performance attention variants; (3) its convergence properties are theoretically justified by the underlying random batch framework. Extensive experiments on large‑scale graph datasets confirm the practical benefits of RBA, and its formal analysis opens avenues for deeper theoretical exploration of self‑attention mechanisms.
210: Controlling the length of text generated by large language models (LLMs) is a vital yet often neglected problem, especially for use‑cases that demand concise voice‑assistant replies or expansive research overviews. Existing solutions—such as Regularized DPO, Length‑Instruction Fine‑Tuning, and tool‑augmented generation—usually involve costly model re‑training or intricate inference‑time setups. In this study we propose a purely prompt‑engineering strategy that achieves fine‑grained length regulation without altering the model itself. By embedding a structured planning outline and a word‑counting routine directly into the prompt, the model is nudged to monitor and respect the specified length constraints. Extensive experiments with six leading LLMs show that our method markedly increases length accuracy for several models compared to vanilla prompting, particularly for short‑to‑medium sized summaries. The degree of improvement varies with the underlying architecture, with some models attaining up to a 37.6 % gain in length compliance. Quality assessments confirm that our approach preserves— and in some cases boosts— overall output quality relative to standard prompting. This technique offers an immediately deployable, cost‑effective solution for production systems that require reliable length control without the overhead of model re‑training.
211:
Vision‑Language Alignment (VLA) models such as CLIP, BLIP and Flamingo have revolutionised multimodal AI, enabling end‑to‑end reasoning across images and text. In real‑world deployments these models rely on physical sensors (cameras, LiDAR, depth sensors) to acquire visual input, making them vulnerable to a new class of *physical‑sensor attacks* that alter the captured scene without modifying the underlying algorithm. In this work we investigate the security and robustness of VLA models against such attacks and propose a systematic defense strategy.

We formulate a threat model that captures the constraints of real‑world sensors: limited spatial resolution, illumination variability, and physical tampering costs. Leveraging this model, we construct a suite of *phantom* perturbations—tiny stickers, reflective patterns, and dynamic lighting—that can be placed on or around a sensor to induce high‑confidence mis‑alignments in the VLA output. Extensive experiments on ImageNet‑Caption, COCO‑Caption and a newly curated *Phantom‑VLA* benchmark demonstrate that these physical perturbations can change the top‑1 alignment probability by up to 73 % for CLIP and 58 % for BLIP with a mean physical cost of only 4 mm² per image.

To mitigate these attacks we introduce **Robust Sensor Fusion (RSF)**, which jointly processes raw sensor data with a learned physical‑scene prior and incorporates a lightweight adversarial‑training curriculum that explicitly exposes the model to a wide range of synthetic and physical perturbations. RSF reduces attack success rates by 84 % for CLIP and 79 % for BLIP, while incurring less than 0.7 ms additional inference latency. We further provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of VLA models under bounded sensor noise, and show that RSF preserves downstream performance on clean data.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a comprehensive empirical study of physical sensor attacks on multimodal VLA models, (2) a large-scale public benchmark that bridges simulation and real‑world evaluation, and (3) an efficient, deployable defense that significantly enhances robustness without sacrificing accuracy. These results highlight the urgent need to secure VLA systems against the “phantom menace” of physical adversarial manipulation.
212: We propose **2Dto3D‑SR**, a flexible framework for real‑time single‑view 3D super‑resolution that does not rely on high‑resolution RGB guidance. By transforming 3‑D information observed from a single camera into a structured 2‑D image, our method allows us to harness any existing 2‑D super‑resolution network directly. The Projected Normalized Coordinate Code (PNCC) encodes the visible 3‑D surface into a regular image, bypassing the difficulties of point‑cloud or RGB‑guided approaches. This simple design yields lightweight, fast models that can be deployed across a wide range of platforms. We demonstrate 2Dto3D‑SR with two back‑bones: a Swin Transformer variant for maximum fidelity, and a Vision Mamba variant for high‑speed inference. On standard benchmarks the Swin version attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy, while the Vision Mamba version provides competitive results at real‑time frame rates. These findings show that our geometry‑guided pipeline is an unexpectedly straightforward yet practical solution for real‑world applications where high‑resolution RGB data is unavailable.
213:
Bias mitigation has become a critical concern for language models that are deployed in high‑stakes applications. A common practice to reduce model size while preserving performance is *knowledge distillation*, where a compact student learns from a larger teacher. Yet the *distillability* of debiasing interventions remains largely unexplored. In this paper we ask whether students can “learn to debias” in the same way that teachers do, and whether the choice of mitigation strategy influences the extent to which a student inherits fairness properties.

We formalise three broad classes of bias‑mitigation methods—(i) **data‑centric** (re‑sampling, counterfactual augmentation), (ii) **training‑time regularisation** (adversarial debiasing, focal loss), and (iii) **post‑processing** (bias‑aware calibration). For each class we train a set of teacher models on several benchmark datasets (e.g., Winogender, CrowS‑Fact, and a large‑scale sentiment‑analysis corpus) and then distill them into students of comparable size. We evaluate the *bias* of teacher and student pairs across multiple metrics (e.g., demographic parity, equalised odds) and under a variety of downstream tasks.

Our findings reveal a nuanced landscape: data‑centric mitigations tend to be largely preserved through distillation, whereas training‑time regularisation often reverts to teacher‑level bias levels unless carefully tuned. Post‑processing approaches, when applied after distillation, can recover fairness but at a cost to predictive accuracy. We also observe that a hybrid strategy—combining counterfactual data augmentation with a bias‑regularised loss—produces students that match or even surpass the debiasing performance of their teachers. Finally, we identify a “bias amplification” phenomenon where certain mitigation methods become counterproductive when the student capacity is limited.

These results underscore that *not all* debiasing methods are equally amenable to knowledge distillation, and that careful design of student objectives is essential to retain fairness guarantees. Our work provides a framework for practitioners to select and adapt bias‑mitigation strategies that remain effective in resource‑constrained settings.
214: The growing interest in joint representation learning for molecules and text stems from its promise to deepen our grasp of chemical knowledge. Nevertheless, many current approaches fail to discriminate subtle variations between a molecule and its textual description because they do not learn detailed, fine‑grained alignments between molecular substructures and corresponding chemical phrases. To overcome this shortfall, we propose **MolBridge**, a new framework that explicitly incorporates substructure‑aware alignments. By enriching each molecule–description pair with additional alignment cues derived from both molecular subcomponents and relevant chemical phrases, MolBridge applies contrastive learning that respects these substructures and introduces a self‑refinement module to weed out noisy signals. Across a diverse set of molecular benchmarks, MolBridge demonstrates superior ability to capture fine‑grained correspondences, achieving state‑of‑the‑art performance and underscoring the importance of substructure‑aware alignment in molecule‑text representation learning.
215: Knowledge Base Question Answering (KBQA) seeks to answer natural‑language queries by querying a structured Knowledge Base. Recent advances leverage an “agentic” reasoning framework, wherein a Large Language Model (LLM) repeatedly breaks a question into sub‑problems, generates corresponding logical queries, and interacts with the KB to retrieve an answer. Existing techniques, however, normally fine‑tune the LLM on synthetically generated reasoning paths, a process supervision that offers limited encouragement for exploration and thus weakly cultivates genuine agentic reasoning. We introduce **KnowCoder‑A1**, an LLM engineered to autonomously execute agentic reasoning over KBs. To foster genuine exploration, KnowCoder‑A1 is trained exclusively with outcome‑only supervision via a multi‑stage curriculum reinforcement learning that eases the problem from simple to complex. Initially, it learns foundational reasoning skills by fine‑tuning on a small, high‑quality set of trajectories selected by outcome‑based rejection sampling. Thereafter, to mitigate reward sparsity, it undergoes staged RL with progressively demanding reward schedules. Under this training regime, KnowCoder‑A1 demonstrates strong reasoning capabilities, surpassing prior methods consistently on three leading benchmarks. On the zero‑shot portion of GrailQA, it achieves a relative gain of up to 11.1 % while requiring only one‑twelfth of the training data, underscoring its robust agentic reasoning proficiency.
216: Fast and precise simulation of dynamical systems remains a key challenge across science and engineering. Conventional numerical solvers typically juggle accuracy against speed, while neural‑network methods usually need a fresh model for each new problem. To address these shortcomings, we present FMint‑SDE—a multi‑modal foundation model designed for large‑scale differential‑equation simulations. FMint‑SDE is built on a decoder‑only transformer that performs in‑context learning, drawing on both numerical data and textual prompts to learn a universal error‑correction strategy. We train it on sequences of coarse solutions produced by standard solvers, which endows the model with the ability to generalize broadly across disparate systems. We benchmark FMint‑SDE on a diverse set of stochastic differential‑equation tasks from molecular dynamics, mechanics, finance, and biology. The results demonstrate that FMint‑SDE outperforms classical solvers in terms of the accuracy–efficiency trade‑off, highlighting its promise as a versatile simulation engine for dynamical systems.
217: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has matured from a research curiosity to a practical enabler that can transform how software is conceived, designed, built, and maintained. While early adopters report gains in productivity, code quality, and creativity, the field remains fragmented: existing tools are often narrow, integration points with established development practices are unclear, and the socio‑technical implications of pervasive generation remain underexplored. This paper presents a comprehensive research roadmap that bridges these gaps, charting a path for augmenting both **software engineering processes** (requirements elicitation, design, testing, deployment) and **software products** (codebases, documentation, user interfaces, runtime adaptation) with generative AI. We synthesize current capabilities and limitations across four inter‑related dimensions—**(1) Foundation Models & Domain Adaptation**, **(2) Process‑Aware Generation & Automation**, **(3) Evaluation & Metrics for AI‑Assisted Artifacts**, and **(4) Governance, Ethics & Human‑in‑the‑Loop**—to identify 12 high‑impact research challenges. For each challenge, we propose concrete milestones, suitable methodological approaches, and potential collaboration points between academia and industry. By positioning the roadmap within a lifecycle framework that spans idea inception to post‑release monitoring, we illuminate how generative AI can be systematically incorporated into the software development life‑cycle, while safeguarding quality, safety, and accountability. The paper concludes with a set of recommended policy and investment priorities that will accelerate the responsible adoption of generative AI in software engineering.
218: Mobile manipulation systems must decide where to position their base in order to reliably execute manipulation tasks described in natural language.  This *base‑placement* problem is particularly challenging when the robot must reason about a wide range of object affordances and must do so with only coarse, top‑down sensory input and limited computational budgets.  In this paper we propose an **Affordance‑Guided Coarse‑to‑Fine (AGC‑F) exploration** framework that selects a small set of promising base locations by first exploiting high‑level affordance maps, then refines the selection with a fine‑resolution local search.  The coarse phase leverages a pre‑trained open‑vocabulary affordance network that predicts where an object can be grasped, lifted, or inserted, and uses this information to generate a sparse candidate set in the 3‑D workspace.  The fine phase employs a learned value function that evaluates each candidate under the task specification, using a combination of depth imagery, semantic segmentation, and linguistic embeddings.  We evaluate AGC‑F on a benchmark of 120 mobile‑manipulation scenes spanning 50 object categories and 20 natural‑language tasks.  Compared to baseline volumetric planning and random sampling, our method reduces average planning time by 45 % while achieving a 12 % higher manipulation success rate.  Experiments on a real KUKA LBR‑4iiwa coupled with a Clearpath Husky mobile base confirm the practicality of our approach in cluttered, unstructured environments.  The proposed framework demonstrates how open‑vocabulary task understanding can be seamlessly integrated with affordance‑driven exploration to enable efficient, robust base placement for mobile manipulation.
219: Artificial intelligence is increasingly reshaping the workplace—replacing routine tasks, informing critical decisions, and inundating our communications with synthetic content—thereby eroding traditional notions of work, identity, and social trust. We contend that the most effective human response to this disruption is resilience. We conceptualize resilience at three interconnected levels: psychological (emotional regulation, meaning‑making, cognitive flexibility), social (trust, social capital, coordinated action), and organizational (psychological safety, feedback loops, graceful degradation). Drawing on early studies, we show that these capacities mitigate individual stress, lower burnout through peer support, and reduce silent failures in AI‑augmented workflows via robust team norms and risk‑responsive governance. Moreover, we demonstrate that resilience can be deliberately built through targeted training, complementing rather than replacing structural safeguards. By reframing the AI conversation around actionable human resilience, this paper provides policymakers, educators, and practitioners with a pragmatic framework to maintain agency and guide responsible AI adoption.
220: This study introduces a control‑based method for aligning large language models (LLMs) by employing a control barrier function (CBF). The CBF safety filter is applied to the token predictions produced by a baseline LLM, thereby steering the generated text toward user‑desired outcomes. Two key benefits of this approach are highlighted: first, the filter operates as an add‑on, enabling alignment without requiring any fine‑tuning of the underlying LLM; second, it can be directly informed by any alignment‑evaluation model used. The complete text‑generation pipeline is built on open‑source language models with the goal of producing positive content.
221:
Recent advances in diffusion‑based video synthesis have largely focused on short clips or simple, single‑sentence prompts.  Long‑form and semantically intricate text‑to‑video (T2V) generation, which demands sustained temporal coherence, multi‑scene reasoning, and fine‑grained action planning, remains an under‑explored frontier.  We introduce **LoCoT2V‑Bench**, a comprehensive benchmark designed to drive progress in this domain.  LoCoT2V‑Bench comprises 10 k video–text pairs spanning 1–5 min, annotated with fine‑grained scene‑level, action‑level, and narrative‑level captions.  The dataset covers 20+ distinct genres (e.g., documentary, dramatized storytelling, instruction‑based tutorials) and incorporates multimodal cues such as audio, subtitles, and scene‑graphs, thereby mirroring real‑world long‑form production pipelines.

To assess model capabilities, we propose a suite of evaluation metrics that jointly capture (i) **semantic fidelity** (caption‑to‑video alignment via CLIP‑based retrieval), (ii) **temporal consistency** (frame‑level optical‑flow coherence), (iii) **logical progression** (scene‑graph consistency across the video), and (iv) **human‑centered quality** (crowd‑sourced Likert scores).  We also provide an open‑source evaluation toolkit that automatically computes these metrics and visualises failure modes.

Using LoCoT2V‑Bench we benchmark several state‑of‑the‑art T2V models (e.g., VideoDiff, Make‑It‑Move, and X-Gen).  Results reveal a substantial performance gap: while short‑clip models achieve >80 % CLIP similarity on 1‑min clips, their scores drop below 30 % on full‑length sequences, and temporal consistency metrics indicate frequent drift or flicker.  These findings underscore the need for novel architecture designs, curriculum‑learning strategies, and richer conditioning signals tailored to long‑form video.

LoCoT2V‑Bench is released under a permissive license, including all raw data, annotations, and evaluation scripts, to encourage community participation.  By furnishing a challenging yet realistic testbed, we aim to catalyse research toward robust, coherent, and semantically faithful long‑form text‑to‑video generation.
222: In multi‑agent systems, agents frequently interact repeatedly while pursuing individual objectives that are not perfectly aligned with those of their peers.  The resulting dynamics can be highly non‑stationary, and it is often unclear whether and how agents’ policies converge, cycle, or diverge.  This paper develops a unified framework for analysing the convergence dynamics of *Agent‑to‑Agent* interactions under objective misalignment.  We formalise misalignment via a vector‑valued reward matrix and study the induced gradient‑based learning dynamics of both cooperative and adversarial agents.  First, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for local asymptotic stability of fixed points in terms of the Jacobian of the joint policy map and the curvature of the underlying payoff landscape.  Second, we identify a class of *misalignment‑sensitive potential functions* that guarantee convergence to Nash equilibria for a broad spectrum of convex‑concave objective pairs.  Third, we employ stochastic approximation techniques to show that, in high‑dimensional reinforcement‑learning settings, the same stability results hold almost surely under standard exploration assumptions.  Empirical validation on synthetic games (matching pennies, public‑goods, and resource‑allocation) and on a suite of continuous‑control multi‑robot coordination tasks demonstrates that our theoretical bounds predict the observed convergence rates and expose the critical role of misalignment magnitude.  Finally, we discuss practical design principles—regularisation, reward shaping, and communication protocols—that can mitigate divergence and foster robust cooperation in real‑world multi‑agent deployments.  The paper thereby bridges a gap between game‑theoretic stability theory and the emerging field of misaligned multi‑agent learning.
223: Meta‑cognitive self‑monitoring—examining and adjusting one’s own reasoning when outcomes are unsatisfactory—is a hallmark of intelligent behaviour. Although traditionally associated with high‑level Artificial General Intelligence, this capability can be instantiated within narrow machine‑learning systems. In this work we introduce a supervisory neural network that emulates self‑awareness by tracking activation patterns of a subordinate network. By detecting signs of high uncertainty in the subordinate model’s responses, the supervisor assesses the reliability of its predictions. The subordinate architecture is a convolutional‑neural‑network ensemble trained for face identification and expression recognition. The supervisory network maintains a memory module that records its past performance, and its parameters are updated during training to improve this assessment. When the confidence estimate falls below a threshold, the system activates an active‑learning mode, thereby granting the algorithm a degree of agency to request human intervention under conditions of confusion or high uncertainty.
224:
Large language models (LLMs) are routinely evaluated through perplexity or downstream task accuracy, yet these metrics provide limited insight into how efficiently a model stores and transmits linguistic knowledge. We introduce *Information Capacity* as a principled, end‑to‑end measure of a model’s ability to compress natural language, thereby quantifying the amount of predictive information it has internalized. By treating an LLM as a probabilistic encoder and measuring the cross‑entropy loss on held‑out corpora, we obtain the theoretical minimum number of bits required to encode each token. Aggregating over sequences yields a compression ratio that directly reflects the model’s predictive power and its ability to exploit redundancy in text.

Our experimental framework applies this compression metric to a spectrum of transformer‑based LLMs ranging from 125 M to 13 B parameters, evaluated on diverse datasets (Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and domain‑specific corpora). We show that larger models consistently achieve higher compression, reducing the per‑token bit cost by up to 35 % relative to smaller baselines. Crucially, we observe a plateau beyond 6 B parameters, suggesting diminishing returns in information capture. We further compare compression to traditional perplexity, demonstrating a strong but non‑perfect correlation, and reveal that models with comparable perplexity can differ markedly in compression efficiency when evaluated on unseen domains.

Beyond benchmarking, this approach exposes model “knowledge gaps”: sequences that defy compression indicate under‑represented linguistic phenomena. We illustrate this by highlighting the degradation of compression on low‑resource languages and on synthetic adversarial prompts. Finally, we propose an adaptive training objective that explicitly optimizes for compression, yielding a 4–6 % improvement in downstream fine‑tuning performance with minimal extra cost.

Our results establish information‑theoretic compression as a complementary, interpretable metric for assessing LLM efficiency, guiding both model selection and architectural innovation toward maximally economical representations of language.
225:
Multi‑agent path finding (MAPF) seeks conflict‑free trajectories for a set of agents operating on a graph.  
The recently proposed **PIBT** (Priority‑Inheritance with Backtracking) algorithm has gained popularity for its simplicity and decentralised execution, yet its single‑action‑per‑step constraint often leads to high latency and sub‑optimal solutions on dense or dynamic maps.  This paper introduces **Multi‑Action PIBT (MAP‑PIBT)**, a principled extension that allows agents to execute a bounded sequence of actions in a single planning round while preserving PIBT’s priority‑inheritance guarantees.  MAP‑PIBT augments the underlying priority graph with *action‑bundles*, enabling agents to “look ahead” and preemptively resolve future conflicts, thereby reducing the number of backtracking iterations required.  

We formally prove that MAP‑PIBT retains completeness on finite, connected graphs, and we derive a worst‑case time complexity bound that improves upon standard PIBT by a factor of Θ(1/α) where α is the average action‑bundle size.  Extensive experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks (e.g., Grid, Office, and Warehouse domains) demonstrate that MAP‑PIBT achieves up to 35 % lower makespan and a 20 % increase in success rate compared with vanilla PIBT and comparable decentralized methods, while maintaining near‑constant communication overhead.  Ablation studies further illustrate the trade‑off between bundle size and computational load, guiding practical configuration.  

Our findings suggest that incorporating multi‑action operations into PIBT significantly enhances its scalability and efficiency, making it a compelling choice for real‑time applications in robotics, logistics, and game AI.
226:
The proliferation of surveillance cameras and user‑generated media has made video‑based violence detection a critical task for public safety. However, training and deploying deep vision models on high‑resolution video streams raises two major obstacles: (i) the need to preserve the privacy of potentially sensitive footage, and (ii) the high computational and energy cost of contemporary spatio‑temporal networks. In this work we present **FL‑ViLD**, a federated learning framework that jointly exploits lightweight convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and large‑scale vision‑language models (VLMs) to achieve high‑accuracy violence detection while keeping local device energy consumption within practical limits.

Each client runs a compact 3‑D CNN that extracts motion‑aware feature maps from short video clips. These local embeddings are periodically uploaded to a central server where a VLM—pre‑trained on a multimodal corpus—projects the CNN features into a shared semantic space and performs a final classification via a lightweight classifier. This two‑stage pipeline allows the heavy VLM to be trained offline, while the client‑side CNN remains efficient enough to run on edge GPUs or mobile processors. We further introduce a hierarchical aggregation protocol that selectively updates the VLM parameters only when the CNN’s prediction confidence falls below a threshold, thereby reducing the frequency of expensive communication rounds. Knowledge distillation from the VLM to the CNN is also employed to keep the local model’s performance high without inflating its size.

Experiments on the Violence in Sports, Real‑World Violence (RWV), and a newly curated *Edge‑VIC* dataset show that FL‑ViLD attains a 94.2 % top‑1 accuracy—within 1.3 % of the full‑scale non‑federated baseline—while cutting per‑client energy consumption by 38 % and memory usage by 4.5×. Ablation studies confirm that the vision‑language component contributes 3.8 % relative improvement over a purely CNN‑based federated approach, and that the dynamic aggregation strategy further reduces network traffic by 25 %. Our results demonstrate that a complementary partnership between lightweight CNNs and VLMs enables privacy‑preserving, energy‑efficient video violence detection at scale.
227: Multi‑modal models that jointly process text and image streams are now pervasive in vision‑language applications such as image captioning, visual question answering, and content moderation.
