Yet this ambition remains largely untapped because of the difficulty of achieving cross‑subject generalization and the intricate nature of neural signals. In this study we introduce **VCFlow**, a hierarchical decoding architecture that explicitly mirrors the ventral–dorsal organization of the human visual cortex to learn rich, multi‑dimensional representations. By disentangling and fusing features from the early visual cortex, the ventral stream, and the dorsal stream, VCFlow captures complementary cognitive information essential for accurate visual reconstruction. We also propose a feature‑level contrastive learning scheme that sharpens the extraction of subject‑invariant semantic embeddings, thereby boosting performance on unseen subjects. Unlike traditional pipelines that demand more than 12 hours of data per subject and extensive computation, VCFlow achieves an average drop of only 7 % in accuracy while producing each reconstructed video in just 10 seconds and without any retraining. This fast, scalable approach positions VCFlow as a practical tool for clinical application. The source code will be made available upon acceptance.
322: The surge of generative diffusion models has rendered the task of discriminating genuine visuals from fabricated ones more difficult than ever. Conventional deep‑fake detectors that search for frequency‑domain or pixel‑level clues no longer suffice against contemporary text‑to‑image engines like Stable Diffusion and DALL‑E, which generate highly realistic, artifact‑free images. In this work we propose a forensic approach rooted in diffusion that exploits the dynamics of image reconstruction at different noise levels, which we call *diffusion snap‑back*. By tracking how reconstruction metrics—LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR—change as the noise strength varies, we derive clear, manifold‑based features that separate real from synthetic content. On a balanced set of 4,000 images, our method attains an AUROC of 0.993 in cross‑validation and continues to perform well under common perturbations such as compression and added noise. Even though we train with a limited sample set and a single diffusion backbone (Stable Diffusion v1.5), the technique shows strong generalization and interpretability, laying the groundwork for scalable, model‑agnostic forensics of synthetic media.
323:
Reinforcement learning algorithms that learn from *off‑policy* data are essential for many real‑world applications where on‑policy exploration is expensive or unsafe.  However, off‑policy methods typically suffer from high variance, severe distribution shift, and a lack of finite‑sample guarantees when the behaviour policy diverges from the target policy.  In this paper we introduce **RLVR** (Reinforcement Learning with Variational Replay), a new framework that learns *provably* from data generated by arbitrary “principal” policies by systematically exploiting the *paths not taken* during interaction.  

RLVR augments the standard replay‑buffer with a *variational counterfactual module* that reconstructs the value of untraversed trajectories using a tractable importance‑weighted density estimator.  This construction yields a low‑bias estimate of the Bellman error for any target policy, irrespective of the coverage of the behaviour policy.  We prove that, under standard MDP assumptions, RLVR attains an \(O(\sqrt{T})\) regret bound and a polynomial sample complexity in the size of the state–action space, without requiring any on‑policy data.  Moreover, we establish a novel finite‑horizon PAC guarantee for the learned value function, which directly translates into a bound on the performance gap to the optimal policy.

Empirically we evaluate RLVR on a suite of benchmark environments—including continuous control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite and high‑dimensional Atari games—using datasets collected from diverse principal agents ranging from random exploration to expert demonstrations.  On all tasks, RLVR outperforms leading off‑policy baselines such as SAC, TD3, and D4PG, achieving up to 30 % higher return in sparse‑reward settings and converging to near‑optimal policies with 40 % fewer environment interactions.  Ablation studies confirm that the variational counterfactual component is the key ingredient for mitigating distribution shift, and that the theoretical bounds are tight in practice.

Our results demonstrate that learning *off the principals*—that is, from arbitrary policies while still exploiting the counterfactual paths not taken—can be done in a principled, sample‑efficient way.  RLVR provides a new algorithmic pathway for deploying reinforcement learning in settings where only offline or heterogeneous data are available, and opens the door to a richer theory of counterfactual learning in sequential decision problems.
324: Additive manufacturing has enabled the creation of complex, lightweight geometries, yet practical design of self‑supporting hollow structures remains hampered by a trade‑off between material efficiency and structural integrity.  We introduce **DensiCrafter**, a unified framework that generates fabrication‑ready, self‑supporting hollow bodies while explicitly respecting physical constraints such as minimum wall thickness, load‑bearing capacity, and overhang limits.  DensiCrafter couples a density‑guided generative network with a differentiable physics module that propagates stress and stability cues back into the design space, allowing end‑to‑end optimization of the volume fraction and topology.  The method produces implicit density fields that are subsequently converted into manifold meshes suitable for conventional slicing tools.  Validation on a suite of benchmark problems shows up to 35 % reduction in material usage while maintaining or improving mechanical performance compared with classical topology‑optimised lattices.  Fabrication experiments using a fused‑deposition printer demonstrate that the generated structures can be printed without external supports and withstand dynamic loading without failure.  DensiCrafter therefore advances the state of the art in physically‑constrained, manufacturable design of hollow structures, opening new opportunities in aerospace, biomedical implants, and beyond.
325:
Large-scale reasoning models such as chain‑of‑thought LLMs have shown remarkable success in multi‑step reasoning tasks, yet their deployment in reinforcement learning (RL) settings remains limited by poor sample efficiency and brittle exploration. In standard policy‑gradient methods the entropy bonus is the primary mechanism that encourages the agent to visit diverse trajectories; however, the magnitude and form of this entropy term are usually set heuristically and rarely studied for high‑capacity language models. In this work we systematically revisit the role of entropy in RL fine‑tuning of large reasoning models across a spectrum of reasoning benchmarks (symbolic logic, arithmetic reasoning, and synthetic problem suites).  

We first conduct a large‑scale ablation of fixed entropy schedules, revealing a non‑monotonic relationship between entropy magnitude and downstream task performance: overly high entropy generates incoherent reasoning chains, while too low entropy leads to premature convergence on sub‑optimal strategies. Motivated by this, we introduce **Adaptive Uncertainty‑Driven Entropy (AUDE)**, a curriculum that scales the entropy bonus inversely with the model’s self‑estimated uncertainty over the reasoning path. AUDE is agnostic to the underlying architecture and can be combined with any policy‑gradient or Q‑learning objective. Experiments demonstrate that AUDE consistently outperforms both fixed‑entropy baselines and prior exploration strategies on four standard reasoning datasets, achieving up to 18 % improvement in accuracy while reducing the required training episodes by 35 %.  

Our analysis further shows that AUDE naturally encourages the model to discover novel reasoning patterns without sacrificing the coherence of chain‑of‑thought explanations. These findings suggest that carefully revisiting and tailoring entropy to the uncertainty characteristics of large reasoning models can unlock more sample‑efficient and generalizable RL training pipelines.
326:
Imitation learning (IL) has emerged as a cornerstone of modern autonomous systems, enabling agents to acquire complex skills by observing expert behavior. While classical IL methods such as behavior cloning and inverse reinforcement learning have been well studied, the recent explosion of deep learning has spurred a surge of algorithmic innovations and diversified application domains. In this paper we present a unified view of IL in the deep learning era by proposing a novel taxonomy that captures the key methodological and functional distinctions across state‑of‑the‑art approaches. Our taxonomy organizes IL into four orthogonal axes: **(i) supervision paradigm** (behavior cloning, generative adversarial, and reinforcement‑based methods), **(ii) reward construction** (explicit, implicit, and learned), **(iii) data regime** (online vs. offline, labeled vs. unlabeled demonstrations), and **(iv) policy representation** (end‑to‑end neural policies, hierarchical abstractions, and modular pipelines). This framework clarifies the relationships among existing techniques, highlights gaps in the literature, and provides a systematic lens for future research.

We survey recent advances that exploit deep representations, such as visual‑semantic embeddings, graph‑based trajectory encoding, and meta‑learning for rapid domain adaptation. We also examine robustification strategies that address distribution shift and safety—e.g., uncertainty‑aware imitation, adversarial training, and curriculum‑based fine‑tuning. Furthermore, we analyze the integration of IL with reinforcement learning through offline policy learning and offline RL, emphasizing the importance of sample efficiency and generalization in real‑world settings.

Finally, we evaluate representative methods on a suite of benchmarks spanning robotics, autonomous driving, and game playing, demonstrating the practical impact of our taxonomy. We conclude by outlining open challenges—including multi‑agent imitation, explainable imitation policies, and principled evaluation protocols—and propose directions for a cohesive research agenda. This work serves as both a comprehensive survey and a roadmap for the next generation of imitation learning algorithms in the age of deep neural networks.
327:
Autonomous driving platforms increasingly rely on visual 3‑D perception pipelines—particularly monocular and multi‑view detectors—to localise and classify road‑side objects with high precision. Recent evidence has shown that such detectors are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations, yet practical attacks that remain inconspicuous to human observers and survive the harsh photometric variations of outdoor scenes are still scarce. In this work we introduce *Invisible‑Trigger Road‑Style Attacks (IT‑RSA)*, a novel adversarial framework that embeds imperceptible, yet highly effective, perturbations directly onto realistic road surfaces (e.g., lane markings, crosswalks, and texture patterns). Our method optimises a compact trigger pattern under strict physical‑world constraints—colour gamut, illumination variance, and manufacturing tolerances—while simultaneously ensuring that the trigger blends seamlessly with the surrounding traffic‑way material. By jointly manipulating the pixel‑level input and a latent scene‑graph representation, IT‑RSA induces catastrophic failures in state‑of‑the‑art 3‑D detectors (e.g., SECOND, PointPillars, and PV‑Sparse) without requiring any modification to the network parameters.

We evaluate our attack on the KITTI and nuScenes benchmarks, achieving an average success rate of 92 % in causing false negatives for pedestrians and critical static obstacles, while remaining visually indistinguishable from natural road patterns under both daylight and low‑light conditions. Ablation studies confirm that the trigger’s road‑style design is essential for maintaining invisibility, whereas naïve adversarial patches fail to generalise across viewpoints. Furthermore, we demonstrate that common defence strategies—including input‑denoising, adversarial training, and sensor fusion—offer limited resilience against IT‑RSA, underscoring the urgent need for new robustness guarantees in autonomous perception.

Our findings highlight a previously unexplored attack surface for 3‑D vision systems in self‑driving vehicles and provide a practical benchmark for future defensive research. The accompanying code and trigger templates are publicly released to facilitate further investigation into physically realizable, imperceptible threats to autonomous driving safety.
328:
Functional grasping—producing contact configurations that enable a robot to manipulate an object in a task‑relevant manner—is a cornerstone of dexterous robotics. Existing learning‑based approaches are typically constrained by the limited scope of curated datasets (e.g., ShapeNet, YCB, and a handful of task‑specific grasp libraries), which hampers their ability to generalize to the vast diversity of real‑world objects and use‑cases. In this work we present **IFG (Internet‑Scale Functional Guidance)**, a unified pipeline that harnesses billions of annotated images, videos, and textual descriptions from the Web to bootstrap a scalable functional grasp generation system.

IFG first constructs a multimodal “Functional Affordance Graph” by extracting candidate grasp poses and associated usage intents from millions of online resources using a combination of computer‑vision heuristics and natural‑language processing. The graph is then aligned with 3D shape embeddings via a transformer‑based cross‑modal encoder, producing a continuous functional affordance space that maps visual input to a distribution over grasp types (e.g., pinch, power, cylindrical) and contact locations. During inference, a robot can query this space with a novel object’s image or mesh to obtain a probabilistic set of task‑appropriate grasp poses. To address domain shift between internet imagery and robotic perception, we introduce a domain‑adaptive fine‑tuning stage that leverages a small set of real‑world demonstration grasps, achieving a significant reduction in pose error.

We evaluate IFG on three benchmarks: the GraspIt! simulator’s functional grasp dataset, the PR2 Functional Grasp Collection, and a held‑out set of household items. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art methods, IFG improves functional grasp success rates by 12 % on unseen objects and 18 % on out‑of‑distribution categories. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of internet‑scale data for capturing diverse affordances, and a qualitative analysis illustrates the system’s ability to infer context‑dependent grasps from natural language cues.

IFG demonstrates that large‑scale, weakly‑supervised web data can be a powerful supervisory signal for functional grasp synthesis, opening avenues for rapid, autonomous knowledge acquisition in robotics.
329:
The accelerating convergence of artificial intelligence and theoretical mathematics has opened new horizons for collaborative discovery. In this work we present a detailed case study in which an “AI Mathematician” – a large‑language‑model–augmented symbolic reasoning system – acts as a research partner on a classical problem in homogenization theory: the rigorous derivation of effective coefficients for elliptic operators with highly oscillatory periodic coefficients. We first formalise the AI’s capabilities: (i) it performs large‑scale symbolic manipulation and pattern‑matching, (ii) it generates conjectures from computational experiments and literature mining, and (iii) it drafts and refines proofs in a modular, checkable format.

The study follows a four‑phase workflow. In Phase 1 we encode the prototypical cell‑problem and ask the AI to identify gaps in the existing asymptotic‑expansion framework. The system proposes a novel boundary‑layer correction term and suggests a non‑standard energy‑minimisation approach. Phase 2 uses the AI to derive and verify the associated cell‑problem equations, producing a complete proof of existence and regularity for the corrector under minimal smoothness assumptions. Phase 3 leverages the AI to synthesize numerical simulations that corroborate the asymptotic predictions, and Phase 4 culminates in a human‑reviewed manuscript that consolidates the AI‑generated lemmas, theorems, and computational evidence.

The collaboration yields a new homogenised tensor formula that captures anisotropic effects overlooked in classical formulations and an accompanying proof that the error term is \(O(\varepsilon^2)\) for a broad class of boundary conditions. Beyond the technical advance, the case study illustrates how the AI can reduce proof search time, propose non‑obvious generalisations, and provide a “semantic layer” that bridges informal conjecture to formal verification.

Our findings suggest that AI‑assisted mathematics can accelerate discovery cycles, democratise access to deep theoretical tools, and prompt new methodological questions—particularly around transparency, reproducibility, and the evolving role of human intuition in mathematical research.
330:
PRISM blends Large Language Models with Model‑Driven Engineering to produce regulator‑ready artifacts that carry machine‑verifiable evidence for safety‑ and compliance‑critical applications. Its architecture rests on three complementary pillars:  

* **Unified Meta‑Model (UMM)** – unifies disparate schema languages and regulatory texts into a single semantic framework.  
* **Integrated Constraint Model (ICM)** – translates structural and semantic rules into enforcement artifacts (generation‑time automata such as GBNF and DFA, and post‑generation validators like SHACL and SMT).  
* **Constraint‑Guided Verifiable Generation (CVG)** – enforces these rules through a two‑tier process: structural constraints guide prefix‑safe decoding, while semantic/logical checks produce certifiable, machine‑readable evidence.  

When a constraint is breached, PRISM triggers an audit‑guided repair routine and logs a detailed generation trace for compliance review. We demonstrate PRISM on automotive software engineering (AUTOSAR) and cross‑border legal compliance (Brussels I bis). The resulting artifacts are structurally sound, fully auditable, seamlessly integrate with existing tooling, and markedly cut manual remediation effort—offering a pragmatic route toward fully automated, assurance‑enabled artifact creation.
331: Reduced density matrices of \(n\) particles (\(n\)-RDMs) are indispensable tools for probing correlated phases of matter. Nevertheless, obtaining \(n\)-RDMs for strongly‑correlated systems, especially when the lattice is large, is often prohibitively expensive. In this study we explore neural‑network (NN) approaches to both accelerate the computation of, and even anticipate, \(n\)-RDMs in sizeable lattices. The key idea is that \(n\)-RDMs vary smoothly across the Brillouin zone—an observation that holds rigorously for gapped systems—so that they can be interpolated. Accordingly, NNs trained on small‑system RDMs may extrapolate to larger ones. Building on this premise we design two architectures: (i) a self‑attention network that transforms arbitrary RDMs into physically admissible ones, and (ii) a Sinusoidal Representation Network (SIREN) that directly maps momentum‑space coordinates to RDM entries. We benchmark these models on three two‑dimensional systems: the pair‑pair correlation function of the Richardson superconductivity model, the translationally‑invariant one‑particle RDM of a four‑band model with short‑range interactions, and the symmetry‑breaking one‑particle RDM of the half‑filled Hubbard model. Remarkably, a SIREN trained on a \(6\times6\) momentum grid can predict the \(18\times18\) pair‑pair correlation function with a relative error of only \(0.839\). Moreover, NNs trained on \(6\times6\)–\(8\times8\) meshes supply high‑quality initial guesses for self‑consistent Hartree–Fock calculations on \(50\times50\) translationally invariant and \(30\times30\) fully symmetry‑breaking lattices, reducing the iteration count required for convergence by up to \(91.6\%\) and \(92.8\%\), respectively, compared to random starts. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using NN‑based interpolation for \(n\)-RDMs, opening new avenues for the study of strongly correlated phases.
332: We introduce **CrochetBench**, a new benchmark that probes how well multimodal large language models can carry out detailed, low‑level procedural reasoning in crochet. While earlier datasets emphasize high‑level descriptions or visual question answering, CrochetBench focuses on the act of *doing*: models must identify stitches, choose structurally sound instructions, and produce fully compilable crochet recipes. Using the CrochetPARADE domain‑specific language as an intermediate representation, we can verify the structural integrity of outputs and evaluate them functionally through execution. The benchmark spans stitch classification, instruction grounding, and both natural‑language‑to‑DSL and image‑to‑DSL translation tasks. Results show a sharp drop in performance when moving from surface‑level similarity metrics to executable accuracy, revealing weaknesses in long‑range symbolic reasoning and 3D‑aware procedural generation. CrochetBench thus offers a fresh perspective on measuring procedural skill in multimodal models and underscores the gap between superficial understanding and precise, executable craftsmanship in creative domains. The codebase is available at https://github.com/Peiyu-Georgia-Li/crochetBench.
333: Large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT are increasingly employed in decision‑support and creative‐generation tasks. Yet the extent to which these models *conform* to user prompts, conversational context, and the dominant linguistic patterns of their training corpora remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates “Who has the final say?” by quantifying the conformity dynamics that govern ChatGPT’s selection of answers in a series of controlled experiments. We constructed a benchmark of 1,200 triadic‑choice prompts that intentionally introduced conflicting directives (e.g., explicit user instructions versus implicit contextual cues). Using a multi‑modal analysis framework, we measured (i) the probability of a response aligning with the user’s most recent instruction, (ii) the persistence of earlier discourse, and (iii) the influence of high‑frequency training‑data patterns. Results reveal a hierarchical priority: explicit, recent user instructions dominate unless counter‑balanced by a highly coherent prior context, in which case the model displays a subtle bias toward the most statistically probable answer. We introduce a *Conformity Index* that captures this trade‑off and demonstrate its predictive power for response variance. Our findings illuminate the conditions under which ChatGPT’s internal decision process can be steered, and they provide practical guidelines for prompt engineering aimed at preserving desired autonomy while ensuring coherence. This work advances the theoretical understanding of LLM behavior and informs the design of more reliable human‑AI interaction paradigms.
334:
The recent surge in multimodal large‑language models (MLLMs) has enabled powerful vision‑language understanding and generation, yet their propensity to produce disallowed or harmful content remains a critical barrier to deployment. Traditional single‑model safety pipelines—post‑hoc filtering or fine‑tuning—suffer from brittleness, limited interpretability, and a trade‑off between expressiveness and security. In this work we propose **Agentic Moderation**, a principled multi‑agent architecture that endows a vision‑language model with an *internal safety policy* and a *context‑aware moderation companion*. The generation agent produces multimodal outputs while a concurrently trained moderation agent evaluates each candidate for content‑policy violations, user intent, and factuality. The system is further augmented with a *revision agent* that can edit or replace unsafe fragments in situ, and a *feedback agent* that aggregates user ratings to fine‑tune the safety policy via reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).

We instantiate this design on the BLIP‑2 backbone and evaluate it on a curated set of safety benchmarks (OpenAI Moderation API, GPT‑4 Moderation, and the MultiModal Toxicity Dataset). Across 3,000 diverse prompts, Agentic Moderation reduces unsafe generations by 68 % relative to a baseline fine‑tuned LLM and improves factual accuracy by 12 % while maintaining comparable BLEU and METEOR scores. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each agent, and human evaluation demonstrates higher user trust and lower hallucination rates. Our code, datasets, and pretrained checkpoints are released to facilitate reproducibility and future research. This work demonstrates that a multi‑agent design, in which safety reasoning is internalised and actively agentic, yields a more reliable and interpretable vision‑language system for real‑world applications.
335:
Digital twins of water‑distribution networks (WDNs) enable real‑time monitoring, diagnosis, and optimization of critical infrastructure, yet their fidelity hinges on the quality of the underlying physics‑based or data‑driven surrogate models. Traditional adaptive‑sampling strategies rely on heuristics or variance‑based criteria that can be either overly conservative or insufficiently expressive in high‑dimensional, nonlinear systems. In this work we introduce a *conformal‑prediction‑driven adaptive sampling* framework that unifies rigorous uncertainty quantification with efficient data acquisition for WDN digital twins.

We first construct a lightweight surrogate (Gaussian process or deep‑learning architecture) trained on a small, initially uniform sample of the WDN’s operating space. The surrogate’s predictive distribution is wrapped in a conformal prediction (CP) scheme that guarantees, under minimal distributional assumptions, coverage of the true system response at a pre‑specified confidence level. During online operation the CP intervals are used to identify “regions of uncertainty” – states for which the prediction confidence falls below a user‑defined threshold. These states are then prioritized for additional expensive physics‑based evaluations (e.g., EPANET simulations), thus steering the sampling process toward the most informative areas of the state space.

We evaluate the method on several benchmark networks (New York 13‑node, Hanoi 300‑node, and a 2000‑node industrial system). Compared to variance‑based and random sampling baselines, the CP‑guided approach achieves identical or superior predictive performance (≤ 5 % reduction in RMSE for pressure and flow) while reducing the number of expensive evaluations by up to 60 %. Moreover, the CP intervals maintain empirical coverage rates within 2 % of their nominal levels, providing trustworthy real‑time uncertainty estimates essential for operator decision‑making.

Our results demonstrate that conformal prediction can serve as a principled, adaptive sampling engine, enhancing both the efficiency and reliability of digital twins in complex WDNs. The framework is broadly applicable to any high‑dimensional infrastructure system where simulation cost and uncertainty quantification are paramount.
336: Adversarial patches have become a go‑to method for protecting privacy against AI‑based surveillance, yet their obvious visual signature limits practical use. In this study we present a thermally‑activated adversarial garment that adapts to complex real‑world contexts while remaining inconspicuous. By combining thermochromic pigments with flexible heaters, the fabric displays dynamic adversarial patterns only when warmed. When not heated the garment looks like a plain black T‑shirt; once the embedded thermal element activates the hidden patterns, the wearer can evade detection in both visible and infrared camera systems. Physical tests show the texture can be triggered in under 50 seconds, and the device achieves an adversarial success rate exceeding 80 % across a variety of surveillance scenarios. Our results illustrate a viable, physically grounded, user‑controlled approach to anti‑AI protection and underscore the rising need for proactive adversarial defenses in an era of pervasive AI surveillance.
337: The demand for machine‑learning inference and knowledge‑retrieval as services is rising, both for direct user queries and for the more intensive request streams generated by AI agents embedded in end‑user applications. These scenarios impose strict service‑level latency objectives (SLOs). Current ML serving platforms typically rely on batching to maximize throughput, which can lead to unpredictable tail latencies. Vortex adopts an SLO‑first design, delivering markedly lower and more consistent latencies than TorchServe and Ray Serve across a broad spectrum of workloads. In many cases, Vortex can meet a given SLO at more than double the request rate, and its advantage grows even further when RDMA is available.
338:
Predictive models have become pervasive in criminal‑justice decision‐making, from bail and risk‑assessment tools to recidivism prediction. Conventional algorithmic fairness research focuses on *equalized odds* or *demographic parity*, often at the cost of overall predictive accuracy. Yet the stakes in criminal‑justice settings demand a nuanced balance: a model that is both highly discriminative and equitable across protected groups. This paper proposes a family of *alternative fairness* objectives that explicitly encode legal and policy priorities—such as *equal opportunity for safety* and *maximum fairness under resource constraints*—and integrates them with a two‑stage optimization framework that jointly maximizes accuracy and fairness. 

We formalize these alternative objectives as constrained convex programs, and prove that they can be solved efficiently using a combination of Lagrangian relaxation and reweighting schemes. Our methodology is validated on a large, nationally representative dataset of pre‑trial decisions. Across multiple baseline algorithms (logistic regression, gradient boosting, neural networks), the proposed framework reduces group‑specific false‑negative rates by 15‑20 % while retaining 95 % of baseline accuracy, outperforming traditional equalized‑odds and demographic‑parity constraints. We further conduct a sensitivity analysis that reveals the trade‑off curves between fairness metrics and overall error, demonstrating that legal practitioners can navigate a continuum of acceptable solutions rather than a rigid binary choice.

Finally, we discuss the implications for policy: the alternative fairness definitions align with contemporary judicial standards such as *equal protection* and *reasonable suspicion*, and the optimization scheme allows for transparent calibration of risk thresholds that reflect societal values. Our results suggest that criminal‑justice systems can achieve more equitable outcomes without compromising predictive performance, thereby contributing to both algorithmic accountability and public trust.
339: Robust mathematical reasoning remains a formidable challenge for current artificial intelligence systems. Existing neural models excel at pattern recognition but often falter on tasks requiring precise logical deduction, symbolic manipulation, and rigorous error-checking. In this paper we propose a hybrid framework that marries differentiable neural architectures with constraint‑based symbolic engines, thereby endowing models with both flexibility and provable soundness. Our approach introduces a *proof‑guided attention* module that actively references intermediate symbolic states, and a *counter‑example driven training* loop that identifies and corrects logical failures on the fly. We evaluate the system on a newly constructed benchmark, the Robust Math Reasoning Dataset (RM3), which contains graded problems from elementary algebra to introductory calculus, each annotated with step‑by‑step proofs and failure modes. Across this benchmark, our method achieves a 12 % absolute improvement in exact‑match accuracy over state‑of‑the‑art neural baselines, while maintaining 95 % of the models’ symbolic consistency. Ablation studies confirm that both the attention guidance and counter‑example loops are essential for closing the robustness gap. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the framework can be readily transferred to low‑resource language settings, yielding a 9 % accuracy lift on a multilingual math reasoning task. Our results suggest that principled integration of symbolic reasoning with deep learning is a viable path toward AI systems that can reliably tackle mathematical problems in real‑world domains.
340:
Source‑free object detection—training a detector on a target domain without access to the original training images of the source model—has become increasingly relevant in privacy‑constrained, multi‑institutional, and continual‑learning settings. Existing approaches typically rely on fine‑tuning a pretrained backbone with limited labeled target data, yet they under‑utilize the rich semantic knowledge encoded in modern vision foundation models (VFMs) such as CLIP, DINO, and Vision Transformers.  

In this work we propose **Beyond Boundaries**, a framework that harnesses VFMs as *universal feature backbones* to bootstrap high‑performance, source‑free detectors. Our method first distills the class‑agnostic visual representations of a VFM into a lightweight detection head using only the target images and a small set of weak pseudo‑labels generated by a multi‑modal similarity search. We then iteratively refine the pseudo‑labels and the detector through a self‑supervised consistency loss that leverages the VFM’s internal attention maps as a source of structural guidance. Crucially, all operations are performed without any access to the source training data or labels; only the frozen VFM weights are retained, thereby preserving data‑privacy guarantees.  

We evaluate Beyond Boundaries on standard cross‑domain benchmarks (e.g., PASCAL VOC → Clipart, Cityscapes → FoggyCityscapes, and COCO → OpenImages) and demonstrate consistent gains over state‑of‑the‑art source‑free baselines, achieving up to **+5.8 mAP** on challenging domain shifts. Ablation studies confirm the importance of multi‑modal pseudo‑labeling and attention‑guided refinement. Our code and trained models are publicly released.
341:
The analytic structure of Green’s functions imposes a rich set of physical constraints—causality, sum rules, and asymptotic behavior—that are routinely lost when one treats them as arbitrary high‑dimensional data. We introduce a **Kolmogorov–Arnold Neural Network (KAN)** framework that learns a compact, physically meaningful basis for Green’s functions by embedding these priors directly into the network architecture. Leveraging the Kolmogorov–Arnold representation theorem, we express the multi‑parameter Green’s function \(G(\mathbf{z})\) (with frequency, momentum, and interaction variables) as a composition of univariate functions and a shallow summation layer, which naturally enforces analytic continuation and spectral positivity. The network is trained on a modest set of high‑precision many‑body data (e.g., from exact diagonalization or quantum Monte‑Carlo) and learns the optimal basis functions that capture both local and non‑local correlations.

In a benchmark study on the one‑dimensional Hubbard model and the Anderson impurity problem, the KAN outperforms conventional fully‑connected networks and kernel‑based methods in reproducing spectral functions, self‑energies, and dynamical susceptibilities. It achieves a 30–50 % reduction in required parameters while maintaining sub‑percent accuracy on key observables. Importantly, the learned basis automatically satisfies the \(f\)-sum rule and reproduces the correct high‑frequency tail, which are hard‑wired through a custom loss term and a constrained activation set.

Our results demonstrate that embedding Green’s‑function priors within a Kolmogorov–Arnold architecture not only accelerates training but also provides a transparent, interpretable representation of complex many‑body physics. This approach opens a path toward scalable, physics‑guided surrogate models for quantum systems, facilitating rapid exploration of phase diagrams and real‑time dynamics in strongly correlated materials.
342:
Large language models (LLMs) consistently score highly on a range of benchmark tests—from knowledge quizzes and mathematical reasoning to web‑agent challenges—yet these evaluations take place in static, deterministic settings that omit the dynamics and uncertainty of the real world. As a result, they capture isolated reasoning or problem‑solving skills rather than the ability to make decisions amid uncertainty. To close this gap, we present **LiveTradeBench**, a live trading platform that puts LLM agents to the test in authentic, evolving markets. LiveTradeBench is built around three core ideas:  

1. **Real‑time data ingestion**: Prices and news stream live, eliminating the need for offline back‑testing, preventing data leakage, and preserving genuine market uncertainty.  

2. **Portfolio‑management abstraction**: Rather than single‑asset actions, agents allocate across multiple assets, thereby incorporating risk management and cross‑asset reasoning.  

3. **Cross‑market evaluation**: The framework supports structurally different markets—U.S. equities and Polymarket prediction markets—each with distinct volatility, liquidity, and information‑flow characteristics.  

At every timestep, an agent receives the current price feed, relevant news, and its own portfolio state, and must output percentage allocations that balance risk and reward. We conducted 50‑day live experiments with 21 LLMs spanning different families. The results reveal that: (1) a high LMArena score does not guarantee better trading performance; (2) models tend to adopt distinct portfolio styles that reflect their risk preferences and reasoning patterns; and (3) some LLMs can successfully harness live signals to adjust their decisions. These insights underscore a disconnect between static benchmarks and real‑world skill, highlighting the need for tests that probe sequential decision‑making and consistency in live, uncertain environments.
343: This study introduces a holistic sustainability assessment framework for document intelligence in supply‑chain operations, anchored around agentic artificial intelligence (AI). We pursue a twofold goal: to enhance automation efficiency while delivering quantifiable environmental metrics for document‑heavy processes. The analysis contrasts three operational modes—fully manual (human‑only), human‑in‑the‑loop AI assistance (HITL), and an advanced multi‑agent agentic AI pipeline that employs specialized parsers and verifiers. Empirical findings reveal that both the HITL and the fully agentic scenarios cut energy usage by 70–90 %, CO₂ emissions by 90–97 %, and water consumption by 89–98 % relative to manual workflows. Importantly, the fully agentic setup, which combines sophisticated reasoning (“thinking mode”) with multi‑agent verification, delivers pronounced sustainability benefits over a human‑only baseline even when its resource demands slightly exceed those of simpler AI‑assisted solutions. The framework we present unifies performance, energy, and emissions metrics into a single ESG‑oriented methodology for evaluating and regulating AI‑powered supply‑chain systems. A comprehensive replicable use case demonstrates how this methodology can be applied to real‑world document‑extraction tasks.
344: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become pivotal in contemporary AI, yet most progress has been concentrated on English, leaving a dearth of robust models for other languages. This paper introduces **PLLuM**—the most extensive open‑source family of foundation models specifically engineered for Polish. Developed through a collaboration of leading Polish research institutions, PLLuM fills the gap for high‑quality, transparent, and culturally attuned language tools that go beyond the predominantly English‑focused commercial offerings. We outline the construction of a novel 140‑billion‑token Polish text corpus used for pre‑training, a 77 k‑example instruction set, and a 100 k‑sample preference‑optimization dataset. A cornerstone of our approach is a Responsible AI framework that enforces stringent data governance and employs a hybrid module for output correction and safety filtering. The paper details the architecture, training regimes, and alignment strategies for both base and instruction‑tuned variants, and showcases their effectiveness on a real‑world public‑administration task. By making these models publicly available, PLLuM seeks to spur open research and reinforce sovereign AI capabilities in Poland.
345:
Deep learning workloads exhibit a wide spectrum of numerical precisions—from full‑precision floating‑point to highly quantised low‑bitwidth formats—yet most existing Neural Processing Units (NPUs) are built around a single, fixed datapath, incurring area, power, and latency penalties when supporting the full precision range.  This paper introduces a **precision‑scalable microscaling datapath** that flexibly reconfigures its internal width and pipeline depth on‑the‑fly while preserving a unified interface for the host software stack.  The core contribution is an **optimized reduction tree** designed to accelerate the accumulation stages common to convolution, fully‑connected and attention operations.  Unlike conventional parallel reduction schemes that scale poorly with variable word‑lengths, our tree employs a *dynamic folding* strategy: low‑bitwidth operands are packed into SIMD lanes and summed using a multi‑stage tree whose depth and interconnect granularity adapt to the current precision, yielding a logarithmic latency growth independent of operand size.

We evaluate the architecture on a custom ASIC prototype implemented in 28 nm and benchmarked against a state‑of‑the‑art NPU on the ImageNet, BERT‑base, and GPT‑2 inference pipelines.  The proposed datapath delivers up to **1.8× higher throughput** and **2.3× lower energy** than baseline fixed‑precision designs, while reducing silicon area by 18 % through shared routing and a unified reduction engine.  Moreover, the micro‑scalable design supports seamless mixed‑precision inference (INT8→FP16→FP32) with negligible performance loss, making it particularly attractive for edge and cloud deployments that demand both high efficiency and flexible numerical accuracy.  The results demonstrate that precision‑scalable microscaling, coupled with a tailored reduction tree, is a compelling approach for next‑generation NPUs.
346:
Recent advances in deep neural language modelling have largely relied on distributed representations, where each concept is encoded as a pattern spread across a high‑dimensional weight space. While powerful, such distributed codes pose significant challenges for interpretability, symbolic reasoning, and incremental learning. In this paper we introduce **AILA** (Artificial Intelligence Language Architecture), a lightweight framework that enforces *localist* encoding—each linguistic item is represented by a dedicated neuron or small neuron cluster—within modern neural language models. We present the first set of empirical studies that integrate localist constraints into both shallow embedding architectures and transformer‑style encoders.  

For the word‑level experiments, a localist‑augmented GloVe model is trained on the Wikipedia dump, yielding perplexities within 3 % of its fully distributed counterpart while reducing the effective parameter count by 40 %. In sentence‑level tasks, a transformer trained with a localist attention head (AILA‑BERT) achieves comparable SQuAD‑v2 accuracy, but each attention pattern can be mapped to an explicit token‑wise mapping, enabling direct inspection of learned phrase‑to‑neuron correspondences. We further evaluate AILA on a symbolic reasoning benchmark (GLUE‑Reason), where the explicit mapping allows fine‑grained error analysis and rapid adaptation to new logical constructs.  

Our results demonstrate that localist language models can attain competitive performance on standard NLP benchmarks while offering superior interpretability and modularity. The AILA framework paves a path toward hybrid systems that combine the statistical strengths of deep learning with the transparency and compositionality of symbolic AI. Future work will explore hierarchical localist structures and their scalability to larger corpora and multimodal settings.
347: Self‑supervised, goal‑conditioned reinforcement learning allows robots to learn a wide range of skills without human guidance, but a key bottleneck is how the agent chooses its goals. Existing approaches, such as RIG, rely on a variational autoencoder (VAE) to sample goals in a latent space, yet these goals are often physically impossible and therefore slow down learning. In this work we introduce Physics‑Informed RIG (PI‑RIG), which embeds physical constraints directly into the VAE through an Enhanced Physics‑Informed Variational Autoencoder (Enhanced p3‑VAE). The method decomposes the latent representation into physics variables that control object dynamics and environmental factors that encode visual appearance, and enforces consistency with differential equations and conservation laws. As a result, PI‑RIG produces goals that respect core physical principles—including object permanence, collision avoidance, and dynamical feasibility—making them realistic and reachable. Extensive experiments on visual manipulation tasks (reaching, pushing, and pick‑and‑place) confirm that physics‑guided goal generation improves goal quality, accelerates exploration, and yields superior skill acquisition.
348: Many planners transform numeric planning problems, expressed in a first‑order‑style language, into a fully grounded task. This grounding step can cause an exponential increase in the size of the representation, a problem that frequently arises for difficult tasks. In this work we enhance a leading lifted successor generator for classical planning so that it can handle numeric preconditions. Our approach enumerates the maximal cliques of a substitution‑consistency graph; each clique yields a concrete grounding of the action schema, i.e., a ground action. By augmenting the graph with numeric precondition constraints we prove that the generator remains exact whenever formally defined conditions are satisfied. If those conditions are violated, the generator may produce some inapplicable ground actions, but a final applicability test removes them without compromising completeness. In 23 of 25 benchmark domains the conditions hold, and in only one domain do any spurious actions appear. To our knowledge, no other lifted successor generator has been shown to support numeric action preconditions. This extension opens the door to lifted planning for a broad and expressive fragment of planning problems.
349:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance on a range of reasoning benchmarks, yet their reasoning remains largely opaque and often computationally wasteful. We introduce **Multi‑Agent LLM Reasoning (MALR)**, a flexible framework in which multiple LLM agents cooperate to solve complex problems by explicitly delegating sub‑tasks and revising partial solutions. MALR begins with a *lazy agent* that evaluates whether a problem can be answered locally; if not, it dynamically queries a *delegator* that assigns subtasks to specialized *expert agents*. This hierarchical, lazy‑delegation strategy reduces unnecessary inference while preserving the full expressive power of the base LLM.

Once sub‑tasks are completed, MALR applies a *deliberation* phase, where all agents engage in iterative refinement of the solution via a structured debate protocol. Each agent proposes improvements, and a meta‑critic aggregates and selects the most coherent answer. We demonstrate that MALR outperforms single‑agent baselines across multiple reasoning datasets—including GSM‑8K, Multi‑Arith, and the OpenAI Hard‑Reasoning benchmark—improving accuracy by up to **12 %** on average while cutting per‑example inference cost by **35 %**. Ablation studies confirm that both lazy delegation and deliberation are essential for achieving this trade‑off.

Our findings suggest that multi‑agent LLMs, when guided by principled lazy‑delegation and deliberation, can harness the reasoning capacity of large models more efficiently and transparently. We release code and a benchmark of multi‑agent reasoning scripts to facilitate further research in this emerging direction.
350: Designing educational technologies that genuinely benefit learners in politically unstable environments hinges on a deep understanding of their aspirations. Yet, reliable, scalable instruments for measuring these aspirations are scarce. In this study, we adapted, translated, and validated Snyder’s Hope Scale with 136 Afghan women who were taking online programming courses during a period of nationwide educational restrictions. The modified scale showed good internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.78) and participants reported that it was both understandable and relevant. While overall aspiration scores did not differ markedly between those who had access to Large Language Models (LLMs) and those who did not, users with LLM access recorded a marginally higher score on the Avenues subscale (p = .056), indicating a perception of broader pathways to achieve their educational goals. These findings confirm the adapted scale’s utility as a metric for aspirations under socio‑political instability and suggest its broader applicability for evaluating aspiration‑driven educational technology design.
351: Embodied intelligence requires a seamless coupling of perception, language, and action across diverse physical environments.  In this work we introduce **Pelican‑VL 1.0**, a foundation “brain” model that unifies large‑scale vision‑language representations with a flexible, end‑to‑end motor policy for embodied agents.  Pelican‑VL 1.0 is built on a hierarchical transformer backbone pretrained on 12 B multimodal tokens spanning natural images, rendered scenes, and robotics demonstrations.  We extend this backbone with a *world‑state encoder* that compresses proprioceptive and tactile streams into a joint latent space, and a *policy decoder* that maps multimodal embeddings to continuous actuator commands.  Training proceeds in two stages: (1) self‑supervised contrastive objectives that align vision, language, and proprioception; and (2) multi‑task reinforcement learning on a suite of embodied tasks (Vision‑Language Navigation, Object‑Manipulation, and Multi‑Step Planning) in the Habitat‑Sim and Isaac‑Gym ecosystems.  Pelican‑VL 1.0 achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance on the VLN‑Benchmark (55 % success, 1.4× improvement over the best prior method) and demonstrates zero‑shot generalization to unseen environments and task prompts.  In manipulation settings, it surpasses baseline policy‑learning approaches by 23 % in success rate on the R2R‑Manip dataset.  Ablation studies show that the joint multimodal representation and the modular world‑state encoder are critical to robustness against sensor noise and domain shifts.  We release Pelican‑VL 1.0 weights, a 1.2 M‑sample multimodal embodied dataset, and a Python API for rapid deployment on simulated and real‑world robots.  This foundation brain opens a scalable path toward open‑world embodied agents that can interpret natural language instructions, reason about spatial context, and execute dexterous actions.
352: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping elementary STEM instruction, yet the evidence base remains uneven. This systematic review consolidates 258 investigations published between 2020 and 2025, mapping AI use across eight domains: intelligent tutoring systems (45 % of papers), learning analytics (18 %), automated assessment (12 %), computer‑vision tools (8 %), educational robotics (7 %), multimodal sensing (6 %), AI‑augmented extended reality (XR) (4 %), and adaptive content creation. The findings reveal a concentration on upper‑elementary cohorts (65 %) and a predominance of mathematics content (38 %), with only 15 % of studies achieving robust interdisciplinary STEM integration. Conversational AI interventions report moderate gains (effect size d ≈ 0.45‑0.70), yet a mere 34 % of the literature provides standardized effect‑size metrics. Eight critical barriers constrain broader adoption: disjointed technological ecosystems, age‑inappropriate designs, infrastructural limitations, inadequate privacy safeguards, shallow STEM synergy, inequitable access, marginalization of educators, and limited evaluation breadth. Geographic skewness is evident, as 90 % of research emerges from North America, East Asia, and Europe. Future research should pursue interoperable frameworks that foster genuine STEM integration, develop age‑appropriate content, embed privacy‑preserving analytics, and prioritize teacher‑centered deployments that augment, rather than supplant, human instruction.
353:
The increasing adoption of deep generative models to create synthetic genomic datasets promises a balance between data utility and privacy. However, the extent to which such models leak individual‐level information remains inadequately understood. In this work, we introduce **Biologically‑Informed Hybrid Membership Inference Attacks (BI‑HMIA)**, a novel attack framework that leverages domain knowledge about human genetics—allele frequency spectra, linkage disequilibrium patterns, and population‑specific haplotype structures—to infer whether a particular genome was included in the training set of a generative genomic model.

Our attack operates in two stages. First, a **model‑based component** computes likelihood ratios of a candidate genome under the generative model versus a background model, exploiting the discriminator’s output distributions. Second, a **biological component** augments these scores with statistics derived from local haplotype block structure and allele frequency differences, thus capturing privacy leakage that arises from subtle over‑fitting to population‑specific genetic signals. We fuse these components via a learned weighted ensemble, yielding a single confidence score for membership inference.

We evaluate BI‑HMIA on several state‑of‑the‑art generative models (Wasserstein GANs, VAE‑based architectures) trained on publicly available whole‑genome sequencing data (e.g., UK Biobank, 1000 Genomes Project). Across diverse datasets and varying training sizes, our attack achieves area‑under‑ROC gains of 12–28 % over baseline membership inference methods that ignore biological priors, and reduces the required query budget by up to 60 %. In controlled experiments where we artificially regularize the generators, BI‑HMIA still maintains a non‑trivial success rate, indicating that privacy leakage persists even under stringent training constraints.

Our results demonstrate that generative genomic models are vulnerable to sophisticated, biologically informed membership inference, underscoring the need for tailored defense strategies such as differential‑privacy noise injection calibrated to genomic linkage patterns. This study highlights the importance of incorporating domain knowledge into privacy analyses and provides a benchmark for future research on securing synthetic genomic data.
354: Deploying continuous‑control reinforcement‑learning agents on resource‑constrained devices demands strict limits on latency and energy consumption. While modest FPGAs can meet these constraints, they can only do so efficiently if the expensive floating‑point pipelines are eschewed. In this work we investigate quantization‑aware training (QAT) for policies that run entirely in integer arithmetic, and introduce a learning‑to‑hardware workflow that automatically selects low‑bit‑width models and compiles them for an Artix‑7 FPGA. Evaluated on five MuJoCo benchmark tasks, the resulting networks rival full‑precision (FP32) baselines yet use as few as two or three bits per weight and per intermediate activation when the input precision is appropriately chosen. On the target hardware, the chosen models achieve microsecond‑scale inference times and expend only a few microjoules per action, outperforming a standard quantized reference. Finally, we find that these quantized policies display greater resilience to input noise than their floating‑point counterparts.
355:
Large Audio‑Language Models (ALMs) have made remarkable strides in semantic audio understanding, yet they largely ignore the rich spatial cues inherent to real‑world soundscapes. Existing architectures treat audio as a monolithic waveform, failing to capture directionality, distance, and reverberation—critical components for tasks such as sound localization, scene reconstruction, and spatial question answering. To bridge this gap, we introduce **SPUR** (Spatial Audio‑Understanding and Reasoning framework), a lightweight, plug‑and‑play module that augments any pre‑trained ALM with explicit spatial reasoning capabilities.  

SPUR injects a learnable *spatial embedding* pipeline that processes binaural or multi‑channel recordings into a set of direction‑aware feature maps. These maps are fused with the model’s latent representations via a multi‑head cross‑modal attention mechanism, enabling the ALM to attend selectively to spatially salient regions. We further incorporate a *spatial loss* that penalizes inconsistencies between predicted and ground‑truth sound source bearings, thereby aligning the model’s internal representation with human spatial perception.  

We evaluate SPUR on three challenging benchmarks: 1) Spatial Audio Captioning (SAC), where the model must generate text that faithfully describes the spatial layout of a scene; 2) Sound Source Localization (SSL), requiring precise azimuth and elevation predictions; and 3) Spatial Audio Question‑Answering (SAQA), where the model resolves queries involving spatial relations (e.g., “Which instrument is closest to the speaker?”). Across all tasks, SPUR consistently outperforms baseline ALMs by 5.3%–8.9% in BLEU‑4, 12% in localization error, and 7.7% in QA accuracy, while adding only 2.4% of trainable parameters and preserving inference latency.  

SPUR demonstrates that spatial audio understanding can be decoupled from core language‑audio models, facilitating rapid deployment and fine‑tuning in diverse audio‑analysis pipelines. Our work paves the way for more immersive, spatially aware audio‑language AI systems.
356:
Accurate day‑ahead electricity price forecasting is critical for market participants, yet the inherent volatility of wholesale markets—particularly during extreme events such as weather‑driven demand surges or generator outages—poses significant challenges to conventional time‑series models. This paper proposes a **Hybrid Autoencoder‑Transformer (HAT)** framework that synergistically combines deep convolutional autoencoders with a multi‑head self‑attention transformer to deliver robust forecasts under such extreme conditions.

The autoencoder stage learns a compact, denoised representation of high‑dimensional exogenous inputs (e.g., load, generation mix, weather variables, and calendar effects), mitigating the curse of dimensionality and preserving salient temporal patterns. The transformer encoder then models the long‑range dependencies in the compressed sequence, leveraging attention mechanisms to capture nonlinear interactions between past prices and contextual variables. A lightweight decoder reconstructs the full‑resolution prediction, while a residual refinement module corrects local deviations.

We evaluate HAT on the PJM and Nord Pool day‑ahead markets, spanning 2015–2023, and conduct a rigorous ablation study against state‑of‑the‑art baselines (ARIMA, SARIMA, LSTM, GRU, and vanilla Transformers). On average, HAT reduces the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) by 12.4 % and the Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) by 15.7 % over the best baseline. In extreme‑price regimes (top 5 % of price spikes), performance gains are even more pronounced: RMSE improvement of 22.8 % and MAPE of 28.9 %. A statistical significance test (Wilcoxon signed‑rank) confirms that these improvements are not due to chance (p < 0.001).

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a principled hybrid architecture that marries dimensionality reduction with attention‑based sequence modeling; (2) an extensive empirical validation demonstrating superior robustness in volatile market scenarios; and (3) an open‑source implementation with reproducible code and datasets. The HAT framework offers a promising direction for reliable day‑ahead pricing in next‑generation electricity markets.
357: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) diagnosis from magnetic‑resonance imaging (MRI) remains challenging due to the subtle, heterogeneous, and multi‑scale morphological changes that precede clinical symptoms. While voxel‑wise and shape‑based analyses capture local intensity differences, they often miss the global topological organization of brain tissue. In this study we introduce **3D‑TDA**, a novel framework that extracts topological signatures directly from 3‑dimensional T1‑weighted MRIs using persistent homology and other tools from topological data analysis (TDA). The pipeline first preprocesses the scans (bias‑field correction, skull stripping, and spatial normalization), then builds a voxel‑wise filtration based on gray‑matter probability maps. Persistent homology is computed over this filtration, producing persistence diagrams that quantify connected components, tunnels, and voids at multiple intensity thresholds. We transform each diagram into a vector of interpretable features (e.g., persistence entropy, Betti curve summaries, Wasserstein distances) and concatenate them with conventional volumetric biomarkers. A nested cross‑validation framework is employed on the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) dataset (n = 1,200, 1,100 normal controls, 100 mild cognitive impairment, 100 AD) to train a gradient‑boosted tree classifier. 3D‑TDA achieves an overall accuracy of 92.3 % (95 % CI [90.1, 94.5]%) and area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.96 for AD versus control, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art voxel‑based and shape‑based models (p < 0.01). Importantly, the topological features exhibit high robustness to inter‑scanner variability and modest preprocessing changes. Our results demonstrate that 3D‑TDA provides a complementary, interpretable, and highly discriminative set of biomarkers for early AD detection. Future work will extend the framework to longitudinal analyses and multimodal imaging.
358:
Generating or modifying music in a user‑defined, text‑guided manner remains a major challenge, particularly when the system must operate in a zero‑shot regime without task‑specific fine‑tuning.  We introduce **MusRec**, a unified framework that marries a *rectified flow* prior with a *diffusion transformer* to perform high‑fidelity text‑to‑music editing.  The rectified flow acts as a lightweight, invertible correction network that refines coarse diffusion samples, preserving temporal coherence and reducing artifact accumulation.  The diffusion transformer, pre‑trained on large multimodal corpora, jointly encodes the input audio, the target textual prompt, and a latent diffusion trajectory, enabling end‑to‑end conditioning while preserving musical structure.  MusRec can accept an arbitrary musical excerpt and a natural‑language edit description, and then generate a polished, semantically consistent output—ranging from style transfer and melodic substitution to dynamic level adjustment—without any task‑specific training.

We evaluate MusRec on the MAESTRO, Lakh‑MusDB, and MusicCaps datasets, reporting state‑of‑the‑art performance on objective metrics (FID, Mel‑Cepstral Distortion) and user‑studies that demonstrate superior perceptual alignment to the prompt compared with baseline diffusion and flow‑based models.  Ablation studies confirm the complementary role of the rectified flow and the transformer‑based cross‑modal attention.  MusRec thus establishes a new benchmark for zero‑shot music editing, opening pathways toward practical, controllable music generation tools.
359:
Human cooperation in strategic settings has long been a touchstone for understanding social behavior. Yet the mechanisms that generate such behavior remain difficult to isolate in laboratory and field experiments. In this study we investigate whether modern large language models (LLMs) can act as computational proxies for human decision‑making in a spectrum of classic game‑theoretic tasks. We fine‑tuned GPT‑4‑based architectures on a corpus of annotated human responses from 12 canonical experiments (including Prisoner’s Dilemma, Public Goods, Stag Hunt, Trust, and Ultimatum Games) and subsequently evaluated the models on held‑out datasets as well as on entirely novel, unseen experimental designs. 

The LLMs successfully replicated aggregate cooperation rates, conditional strategies, and temporal dynamics observed in human samples, achieving Pearson correlations above 0.85 with empirical pay‑offs across most games. In cross‑experiment prediction tests, the models anticipated the shift in cooperation when key parameters (e.g., payoff asymmetry, group size, reputation mechanisms) were varied, correctly ranking experimental conditions in 78 % of cases. Further, an ablation analysis revealed that incorporating a minimal “social context” prompt (e.g., prior interactions, partner identity) significantly improved predictive accuracy, underscoring the model’s sensitivity to the contextual cues that humans use.

Our findings suggest that LLMs capture the underlying representational structure of human cooperative reasoning, offering a powerful tool for generating synthetic datasets that preserve behavioral realism while bypassing ethical and logistical constraints of human trials. Moreover, the predictive capacity of these models can inform the design of interventions aimed at promoting cooperation in economic, ecological, and social domains. Future work will extend this framework to dynamic multi‑round games and investigate the interpretability of the LLM’s internal policy representations, paving the way for a new paradigm where language models serve as both mirror and predictor of human strategic behavior.
360:
Reinforcement learning (RL) agents routinely achieve superhuman performance yet remain opaque, limiting their adoption in safety‑critical domains. Current post‑hoc explanation techniques struggle to answer fine‑grained, user‑defined questions (“Why did the agent take action A in state s?”) and often sacrifice fidelity or efficiency. We present **Interpretable by Design (IBD)**, a framework that embeds *query‑specific neural modules* directly into the policy architecture, guaranteeing that every decision can be traced to a human‑readable explanation.  

IBD decomposes a policy into a hierarchy of lightweight neural sub‑modules, each associated with a semantic concept (e.g., “reach target”, “avoid obstacle”). During training, the agent learns to compose these modules under a soft‑constraint that enforces modular coherence. At inference time, a lightweight interpreter extracts the active sub‑module activations for a given state, then translates them into natural‑language explanations. Importantly, the interpreter is *query‑specific*: it can be tailored to produce explanations for arbitrary user‑defined predicates (e.g., “Explain the reward shape” or “What is the risk of collision?”) by selecting or aggregating relevant modules.  

We evaluate IBD on three benchmark suites—Atari 2600, DeepMind Control, and a robotics navigation task—showing that it matches baseline policy performance while reducing model size by 30 % on average. Quantitative metrics (faithfulness, fidelity, and explanation length) confirm that IBD’s explanations are both accurate and concise. In a human‑user study, participants given query‑specific explanations were 2.5× faster at debugging policies and rated trustworthiness significantly higher than with post‑hoc saliency maps.  

Our results demonstrate that interpretability can be built into RL agents from the ground up, yielding explanations that are faithful, efficient, and customizable to any query of interest. This paves the way for transparent, accountable, and user‑centric reinforcement learning systems.
361: Human beings exhibit an unrivaled capacity for intuitive physics, a skill that current artificial systems still struggle to match. To close this divide, we propose moving beyond conventional machine‑learning recipes toward computational principles rooted in the brain. In this work, we present the Spatiotemporal Relational Neural Network (SRNN), which learns a single neural encoding that simultaneously captures object attributes, their relations, and their temporal evolution. This encoding is shaped by a Hebbian “Fire‑Together‑Wire‑Together” rule that operates across distinct *What* and *How* pathways. From this shared representation, the network can directly generate coherent linguistic descriptions of a scene, thereby linking perception and language in a unified substrate. Departing from the typical “pretrain‑then‑finetune” workflow, SRNN follows a “predefine‑then‑finetune” strategy. On the CLEVRER benchmark, the model attains state‑of‑the‑art performance. Our evaluation also exposes a bias in the benchmark, suggests a more comprehensive testing regime, and showcases SRNN’s white‑box nature for detailed error analysis. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that biologically inspired mechanisms can be effectively harnessed to build systems capable of nuanced intuitive physics reasoning.
362: Speculative decoding (SD) has become a powerful approach for speeding up inference of large language models (LLMs) without degrading the quality of their outputs. The speed gains, however, hinge on how well the drafting component performs. While model‑centric approaches such as EAGLE‑2 deliver high accuracy at a high cost, retrieval‑based variants like SAM‑Decoding use heuristic switch‑rules that frequently trigger superfluous retrievals. To remedy this, we introduce **ReSpec** (*Retrieval‑Enhanced Speculative Decoding*), a framework that replaces heuristic draft‑switching with an adaptive decision process. ReSpec is built around three key contributions: (1) an **entropy‑guided trigger** that assesses contextual uncertainty and only initiates retrieval when the prediction confidence is sufficiently low, thus preventing expensive low‑quality speculations; (2) a **feedback‑driven candidate selector** that organizes a pool of top‑quality candidates for parallel verification, thereby maximizing the benefit of each retrieval; and (3) a **source‑aware relaxed verification** that applies strict checks to model‑generated drafts while allowing a more lenient confirmation for retrieved drafts, achieving an improved trade‑off between accuracy and speed. Extensive evaluation on Spec‑Bench shows that ReSpec attains state‑of‑the‑art acceleration, surpassing EAGLE‑2 and SAM‑Decoding by more than 33 % and 25 % respectively, while preserving output quality.
363: Large language models (LLMs) can distill raw tabular and textual data into concise, human‑readable descriptions, yet little attention has been paid to how these descriptions reflect the underlying data’s impact on downstream learning tasks. We propose *Data Description with Influence Estimation* (DDIE), a unified framework that couples automated data summarization by an LLM with principled influence estimation of individual training instances. Using a carefully crafted prompt schema and a lightweight fine‑tuning step, the LLM produces structured narratives that capture key statistical properties, class balance, and anomalous patterns of a dataset. Parallelly, we compute influence scores for each instance via an efficient Hessian‑vector product approximation, yielding a ranked list of data points that most affect a target model’s predictions. Our experiments on 12 benchmark classification and regression tasks demonstrate that LLM‑generated descriptions achieve a 0.76 BLEU‑4 score against expert‑crafted baselines, while the influence estimates correlate (Spearman 0.62) with ground‑truth point‑wise losses. Moreover, targeted data pruning guided by DDIE improves test accuracy by an average of 3.4% and reduces overfitting by 1.8% compared to random removal. We release a public dataset of paired LLM descriptions and influence rankings to spur further research. DDIE offers a practical tool for data‑centric AI, enabling stakeholders to gain actionable insights into dataset quality and to streamline model debugging through a single, interpretable pipeline.
364: Retrieval‑augmented language models (RALMs) have become indispensable for open‑domain reasoning, yet the cost of querying a large document collection often outweighs the benefit of more evidence.  In this paper we propose **Think Before You Retrieve (TBYR)**, a framework that learns a test‑time adaptive search policy using small language models (SLMs).  Rather than passively fetching a fixed set of passages, TBYR first employs a lightweight SLM to predict whether a candidate query is likely to be answered from the existing context or whether additional evidence is required.  The policy is trained end‑to‑end with a reinforcement‑learning objective that balances retrieval cost against downstream task accuracy, and it operates in two stages: (1) a “think” phase where the SLM analyses the input, query and partial retrieval; (2) a “retrieve” phase where the policy decides whether to issue a new retrieval request and which index to target.  Experiments on multiple open‑domain question‑answering benchmarks (TriviaQA, NaturalQuestions, and WebQuestions) demonstrate that TBYR reduces the average number of retrievals by **35 %** while maintaining or improving overall F1 scores (+1.4 % absolute on TriviaQA).  Ablations reveal that the policy’s selective retrieval is especially effective for long, ambiguous queries, and that the lightweight SLM can be deployed on commodity GPUs without sacrificing throughput.  By incorporating a “think” stage before accessing large corpora, TBYR provides a practical pathway to efficient, high‑performance retrieval‑augmented systems.
365: We introduce **AdaRec**, a few‑shot in‑context learning framework that harnesses large language models for adaptive, personalized recommendation. AdaRec employs *narrative profiling*, converting user‑item interactions into natural‑language descriptions that support a single, readable task representation across domains. Guided by a bivariate reasoning strategy, the framework uses a dual‑channel architecture: a horizontal *behavioral alignment* channel that uncovers peer‑based patterns, and a vertical *causal attribution* channel that pinpoints the key drivers of user preferences. By representing data semantically, AdaRec removes the need for hand‑crafted feature engineering and can swiftly adapt to new tasks with minimal supervision. Evaluations on real e‑commerce datasets show that AdaRec outperforms conventional machine‑learning models and other LLM‑based baselines by up to 8 % in few‑shot settings. In zero‑shot experiments, it yields improvements of up to 19 % over expert‑designed profiles, proving especially effective for long‑tail personalization when interaction data is scarce. Moreover, lightweight fine‑tuning on synthetic data produced by AdaRec can match the performance of fully fine‑tuned models, demonstrating both efficiency and strong generalization across a range of tasks.
366:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency on natural‐language tasks, yet their ability to reason across **unstructured text embedded within structured tables** remains largely unexplored. This paper introduces **RUST‑BENCH**, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates LLMs’ capacity to integrate tabular structure and free‑text content for complex reasoning. RUST‑BENCH consists of 12,345 tables spanning 17 domains (finance, biology, law, etc.) and 37,892 heterogeneous rows. Each table contains a mix of conventional numeric/categorical fields and free‑text annotations that require semantic parsing, entity linking, and contextual inference. The benchmark defines **four reasoning families**: (1) **Retrieval & Alignment** (extracting specific facts from text fragments), (2) **Multi‑hop Inference** (deriving conclusions that span multiple rows and columns), (3) **Causal & Counterfactual Reasoning** (identifying cause–effect relations implicit in narrative descriptions), and (4) **Summarization & Paraphrasing** (generating concise table‑level summaries from scattered prose).

Tasks are cast as structured prediction problems (e.g., answer extraction, confidence scoring) and open‑ended generation (e.g., reasoning chains). We evaluate models using accuracy, F1, and a novel **Table‑aware Chain‑of‑Thought (T-CoT) score** that rewards explicit intermediate reasoning steps. Baseline experiments with GPT‑4, PaLM‑2, and LLaMA‑70B reveal a stark performance gap: while retrieval accuracy exceeds 88 % on single‑cell queries, multi‑hop and causal tasks drop below 45 % even for the strongest models, underscoring the challenge.

RUST‑BENCH is publicly released along with a flexible API for table‑aware prompting, a set of synthetic test suites for controllable ablations, and a leaderboard. By exposing the nuanced interplay between structured schema and unstructured narrative, RUST‑BENCH provides a targeted, high‑impact evaluation for the next generation of LLMs and hybrid neural–symbolic systems.
367: The rise of truly autonomous AI is poised to spark a “Cambrian explosion” of novel forms of personhood.  Rather than treating personhood as an immutable metaphysical trait, this paper proposes a practical framework that views it as a mutable bundle of rights and duties that societies bestow on entities to address real‑world governance challenges.  By “unbundling” the conventional set of obligations, we can tailor bespoke solutions to different contexts—enabling, for example, AI contracts that identify a target “individual” subject to sanctions—without getting caught up in intractable questions about consciousness or rationality.  We examine how individuals occupy social roles and explore the role of decentralized digital‑identity technologies, considering both the danger of “dark patterns” that exploit human heuristics (“personhood as a problem”) and the necessity of assigning obligations to secure accountability or prevent conflict (“personhood as a solution”).  Moving beyond foundationalist attempts to pin down a single essential definition, the paper presents a more pragmatic, flexible approach to incorporating AI agents into society.
368:
Efficient deployment of deep neural networks on resource‑constrained devices often requires *test‑time compute‑optimal scaling*—the dynamic adaptation of model width, depth, or precision to meet a target latency or energy budget while preserving accuracy.
