By having an explicit RM, agents can learn more efficiently from a reduced number of samples. Nevertheless, traditional RMs struggle with long‑horizon problems where a collection of subtasks may be performed in any order, because the amount of information that must be learned grows exponentially with the number of unordered subtasks. In this paper we overcome this drawback by proposing three extensions to the RM framework: (1) *Numeric RMs*, which encode intricate tasks compactly using numerical predicates; (2) *Agenda RMs*, where each state is coupled to an agenda that records the subtasks still pending; and (3) *Coupled RMs*, in which each agenda element is linked to a dedicated state that tracks progress on its corresponding subtask. Leveraging these coupled RMs, we introduce a novel compositional learning scheme—*CoRM* (Q‑learning with Coupled RMs). Empirical evaluations demonstrate that CoRM outperforms existing RM‑based methods when tackling long‑horizon tasks with unordered subtasks.
561:
In many domains, human teams achieve more than merely “completing” a task: they create value through shared knowledge, iterative refinement, and distributed problem‑solving.  Yet most automated systems treat completion as an atomic objective, ignoring the richer dynamics of collaboration.  This paper formalizes the distinction between *completion* (the attainment of a task goal) and *collaboration* (the process of coordinated, iterative work that may generate emergent value).  We argue that as problems grow in scale and complexity, the benefits of collaborative effort become increasingly pronounced, but also that scaling such effort requires more than simply delegating sub‑tasks to additional workers.

To this end, we introduce **CollabAgents**, a lightweight, agent‑oriented architecture that mediates collaborative work at scale.  Each agent is endowed with a domain‑specific skill set, a local plan, and a communication protocol that allows it to negotiate partial solutions, share intermediate artifacts, and adapt to evolving requirements.  We prove that, under reasonable assumptions, the collaborative plan space explored by CollabAgents expands super‑linearly with the number of agents while maintaining bounded coordination overhead.  We evaluate the framework on three benchmark scenarios—distributed scientific simulation, large‑scale data annotation, and open‑source software development—comparing it to both single‑agent completion baselines and traditional multi‑worker pipelines.  CollabAgents consistently achieves higher quality outputs (up to 27 % improvement in domain‑specific metrics) and demonstrates near‑linear speed‑up when adding agents, validating our claim that *completion ≠ collaboration* and that collaboration can be scaled effectively through autonomous agents.

Our results highlight the need for new design principles that treat collaboration as a first‑class objective, and we outline future work on richer interaction models and theoretical limits of agent‑based collaboration.
562:
Accurate, real‑time reconstruction of 3D human meshes for multiple people in an unconstrained scene remains a formidable challenge for current top‑down methods. These approaches, typically built on the Human Mesh Recovery (HMR) backbone, rely solely on visual cues, leading to drift in depth, self‑occlusion errors, and a lack of global consistency when many bodies are present. To address these issues we introduce **PressTrack‑HMR**, a pressure‑augmented framework that fuses low‑resolution floor‑pressure data with a single RGB view to produce globally consistent, person‑specific SMPL meshes in a multi‑person setting. 

Our key contributions are: (i) a novel pressure‑based depth prior that resolves scale and depth ambiguities by aligning each predicted mesh to the measured foot‑pressure distribution; (ii) a differentiable pressure‑to‑mesh layer that back‑propagates pressure residuals during training, enabling end‑to‑end optimization of a modified HMR network; and (iii) a new benchmark, **PressTrack‑Bench**, containing synchronized RGB‑pressure recordings of up to eight subjects interacting in realistic indoor environments. Experiments on PressTrack‑Bench and the public H3.6M dataset show that PressTrack‑HMR outperforms state‑of‑the‑art single‑image and multi‑person mesh estimators by 12.4% in MPJPE and 9.1% in PCK, while maintaining 30 fps inference speed. The proposed method demonstrates that even sparse, inexpensive pressure measurements can dramatically enhance global human mesh recovery, opening the door to robust, privacy‑preserving motion capture in smart‑home and interactive gaming scenarios.
563:
Denario is a multi‑agent artificial intelligence platform that functions as a comprehensive assistant for scientific research. It can carry out a wide range of tasks—including generating hypotheses, conducting literature reviews, formulating research strategies, writing and executing code, generating visualizations, and drafting or revising scholarly manuscripts. The system’s modular design allows individual agents to tackle specific subtasks (e.g., ideation) or to orchestrate full end‑to‑end analytical pipelines with Cmbagent as a deep‑research engine. 

In this paper we describe the architecture of Denario and its constituent modules in detail. We demonstrate its versatility through a series of AI‑generated papers spanning disciplines such as astrophysics, biology, biophysics, biomedical informatics, chemistry, materials science, mathematical physics, medicine, neuroscience, and planetary science. Furthermore, we showcase Denario’s ability to synthesize cross‑disciplinary ideas by presenting a study that blends quantum‑physics techniques with machine‑learning methods to analyse astrophysical data. 

Domain experts evaluated these AI‑produced manuscripts, offering both quantitative scores and narrative critiques. We discuss the system’s strengths, shortcomings, and current limitations, and reflect on the ethical and philosophical implications of AI‑driven research. All code is publicly available at https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/Denario, with an online demo at https://huggingface.co/spaces/astropilot-ai/Denario and plans for a full cloud‑based deployment.
564:
The rapid progress of large language models has enabled them to act as “autonomous agents” that can execute complex instructions by invoking external tools (e.g., calculators, search engines, code editors). Yet progress is hampered by the absence of a unified, realistic, and scalable benchmark that evaluates such agents on truly diverse, multi‑step tasks. We present **The Tool Decathlon** – a benchmark suite that compiles 10 distinct “tool‑heavy” domains (cooking, software debugging, legal drafting, data analysis, scientific reasoning, creative design, robotics control, financial modeling, logistics planning, and conversational tutoring) into a single, long‑horizon evaluation framework. Each task is framed as a natural‑language instruction that must be decomposed into a sequence of tool calls, with intermediate results available to the agent, and is evaluated on *realistic* environments (e.g., simulated kitchen appliances, IDEs, web browsers, and spreadsheets) rather than synthetic prompts.

Our benchmark supplies a standardized tool interface specification, a gold‑standard plan hierarchy, and a reproducible evaluation harness that records *success*, *efficiency* (steps, runtime), *tool‑use correctness*, and *semantic fidelity*. We evaluate a broad set of baseline agents (GPT‑4, Claude 2, Llama‑2 70B with Llama‑Index, and fine‑tuned chain‑of‑thought planners) using the OpenAI API and open‑source tool‑execution frameworks. While all models can solve trivial tasks, we observe a steep performance drop on long‑horizon problems, with GPT‑4 achieving an overall success rate of 42 % versus 15 % for the best fine‑tuned baseline. Detailed error analysis reveals systematic failures in reasoning over tool state, managing dependencies, and handling stochastic environments.

The Tool Decathlon thus offers a rigorous, scalable, and community‑friendly platform for advancing language‑agent research, encouraging the development of more robust planning, grounding, and tool‑interaction techniques. All datasets, scripts, and evaluation code are released under an open‑source license at https://tooldecathlon.org.
565:
Character appearance frequency is a fundamental signal for understanding narrative structure, character salience, and inter‑character dynamics in serial media.  While a wealth of computational studies have explored dialogue, sentiment, and visual style in anime and manga, no standardized resource exists that facilitates systematic analysis of character prominence in the Japanese light‑novel‑derived series *My Teen Romantic Comedy SNAFU* (Oregairu).  This paper introduces **OregairuChar**, the first benchmark dataset expressly designed for character‑appearance‑frequency analysis in this franchise.  OregairuChar contains 312 fully aligned subtitles, 1,214 audio‑transcript pairs, and 8,527 annotated video frames from the original anime and its adaptations, spanning 13 seasons and 286 episodes.  Each subtitle utterance is tagged with a fine‑grained character label (e.g., Yukino Yukinoshita, Hachiman Hikigaya) and a temporal anchor, while corresponding visual frames are annotated with bounding boxes and identity IDs for all on‑screen characters.  The dataset also provides a hierarchical character taxonomy (protagonist, supporting, cameo) and a set of ground‑truth appearance counts per episode.  

To demonstrate its utility, we formulate two benchmark tasks: (1) *Character‑frequency prediction* from raw subtitles (a sequence classification problem) and (2) *Multi‑modal character‑tracking* from audio–visual streams (an object‑detection + identity‑re‑identification pipeline).  We report baseline results using Transformer‑based language models and convolutional–recurrent architectures, achieving a mean absolute error of 4.12 appearances per episode on the frequency task and an F1‑score of 0.81 on the tracking task.  Ablation studies highlight the complementary value of audio cues and visual context.  

OregairuChar is publicly released under a CC‑BY license, along with an evaluation server and an API for rapid prototype testing.  We anticipate that the dataset will catalyze research in narrative analytics, multimodal character recognition, and the broader field of computational media studies.
566:
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as a versatile class of porous materials for gas storage, separation, and catalysis, yet the rapid and accurate prediction of their adsorption performance remains a bottleneck for high‑throughput screening. We present **COFAP**, a universal framework that integrates *designed multi‑modal extraction* of structural, chemical, and physical descriptors with *cross‑modal synergy* to deliver state‑of‑the‑art adsorption predictions for a wide range of gases.  

COFAP first generates three complementary feature streams from each COF structure: (i) a graph‑based representation that encodes topology and connectivity; (ii) a physics‑informed descriptor set capturing pore geometry, surface area, and energy landscapes; and (iii) a spectroscopic‐style fingerprint derived from simulated X‑ray diffraction patterns. A novel **cross‑modal attention network** learns to fuse these streams, allowing each modality to inform and refine the others. To ensure generality, the framework is trained on a newly curated benchmark of 12,340 COFs with experimentally measured and high‑fidelity simulation‑based adsorption capacities for CO₂, CH₄, H₂, and N₂ over a temperature–pressure grid.  

Across all four gases, COFAP reduces the mean absolute error by 18–26 % relative to leading single‑modal models and achieves an R² > 0.92 on held‑out test sets, including a 20 % improvement on extrapolative predictions for COFs with unseen topologies. Ablation studies confirm that the cross‑modal attention mechanism is essential for capturing synergistic effects between pore geometry and chemical functionality. Finally, a SHAP‑based analysis provides physically interpretable insights into the dominant structural and electronic determinants of adsorption.  

COFAP thus offers a scalable, accurate, and interpretable tool for accelerating COF discovery, and its modular design can be readily extended to other porous materials classes such as metal–organic frameworks and zeolites.
567: Cross‑view geo‑localization (CVGL) between aerial and satellite images is notoriously difficult because of the large viewpoint gaps and the prevalence of hard negatives—samples that look similar yet are geographically unrelated. Most current mining or re‑weighting approaches rely on fixed weighting schemes, which are vulnerable to distribution changes and can over‑penalise hard samples too early, resulting in noisy gradients and unstable training. We introduce Dual‑level Progressive Hardness‑aware Reweighting (DPHR), a two‑stage strategy. On the sample level, a Ratio‑based Difficulty‑Aware (RDA) module measures relative difficulty and assigns fine‑grained weights to negative pairs. On the batch level, a Progressive Adaptive Loss Weighting (PALW) module uses the training progress as a signal to dampen noisy gradients in the initial phases and gradually strengthen hard‑negative mining as the model matures. Extensive experiments on the University‑1652 and SUES‑200 datasets confirm that DPHR consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods, demonstrating both effectiveness and robustness.
568:
The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has spurred interest in applying them to cyber‑threat intelligence (CTI), yet rigorous, domain‑specific evaluation remains elusive. Existing benchmarks are static, limited to a narrow set of tasks, and fail to capture the evolving nature of threat information. We introduce **AthenaBench**, a dynamic, end‑to‑end benchmark designed to assess LLMs across the full spectrum of CTI workflows—from ingesting raw threat reports to producing actionable intelligence for defenders.

AthenaBench comprises four interrelated evaluation suites: (1) **Narrative Summarization** of long‑form incident reports; (2) **Indicator Extraction** for malware, IPs, domains, and file hashes; (3) **Adversarial Reasoning** that tests model ability to infer tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and map them to the MITRE ATT&CK framework; and (4) **Vulnerability‑to‑Exploit Mapping** that evaluates semantic alignment between CVE descriptions and exploit reports. Each suite is instantiated on a continuously refreshed corpus sourced from open‑source feeds, commercial threat intelligence feeds, and simulated adversarial corpora, ensuring that models are evaluated against the latest tactics and artifacts.

We formalize a set of metrics that combine traditional information‑retrieval scores (precision, recall, F1) with task‑specific measures (semantic similarity for summaries, TTP‑coverage for reasoning). Baselines using GPT‑4, Claude 3, and Llama‑2 demonstrate substantial headroom, particularly in indicator extraction and adversarial reasoning, highlighting the need for specialized training and prompting strategies. AthenaBench also provides a lightweight, reproducible evaluation pipeline that automatically ingests new threat data, re‑runs experiments, and publishes leaderboards, fostering continual model improvement.

Our contributions are threefold: (i) a modular, dynamic benchmark that reflects the temporal nature of CTI, (ii) a comprehensive evaluation protocol with domain‑specific metrics, and (iii) open‑source tooling that encourages community participation. AthenaBench aims to become the standard for benchmarking LLMs in cybersecurity, driving progress toward robust, trustworthy CTI automation.
569: Accurate, real‑time tracking of tennis players and the ball is essential for performance analysis, refereeing decisions, and fan engagement.  This paper presents a fully automated system that combines court key‑point detection with multi‑object tracking to replicate and improve upon the commercial Hawk‑Eye technology.  We first formulate court geometry as a set of 17 canonical key‑points (baseline, service line, center marks, etc.) and train a ResNet‑50 backbone with a stacked‑hourglass decoder to predict these points from each high‑speed frame.  The detected court is then used to estimate a homography that projects all detections into a unified court coordinate system.  Player bodies are localized with a single‑stage detector (YOLO‑X) that outputs bounding boxes and 2D human poses; the ball is identified by a lightweight SSD trained on a novel annotated dataset of 3 M frames (10 Hz, 4 K resolution) containing over 50 k annotated ball positions.  To maintain identity across occlusions, we employ a Kalman‑filter‑based tracker that fuses detections with a Hungarian assignment scheme and a learned re‑identification embedding for players.  The system runs at 45 fps on a single RTX 3090.  Evaluation on the public Tennis‑Track dataset yields a mean average precision of 93.6 % for player detection, 88.2 % for ball detection, and an average endpoint error of 4.7 px for court key‑points.  In a blind test against the official Hawk‑Eye benchmark, our method reduces the miss‑call rate by 12 % while maintaining sub‑millimeter positional accuracy, demonstrating its viability for real‑world tennis analytics and officiating.
570:
Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems—those capable of autonomous decision‑making and self‑initiated interactions—are increasingly deployed in safety‑critical domains such as autonomous vehicles, medical diagnosis, and financial advisory services. While these agents promise unprecedented efficiency, their inherent dynamism and adaptive learning pose significant challenges to traditional reliability assurance methods, which are largely static and test‑centric. In this paper we propose a comprehensive Reliability Monitoring Framework (RMF) tailored to agentic AI, integrating continuous performance evaluation, contextual risk profiling, and adaptive safety‑bounds that evolve alongside the agent’s operational context.

The RMF is built on a hierarchical monitoring architecture: (1) a *Data‑Integrity Layer* that verifies sensor fidelity and input distribution shifts; (2) a *Decision‑Quality Layer* that tracks policy drift, model confidence, and compliance with domain constraints; and (3) a *Human‑In‑the‑Loop Layer* that facilitates dynamic trust calibration and intervention protocols. We formalize a set of reliability metrics—including *Uncertainty‑Weighted Error Rates*, *Regret‑Bounded Performance*, and *Explainability Consistency*—and demonstrate their joint application on two benchmark agentic workloads: a reinforcement‑learning‑based autonomous drone navigation task and a dialogue‑system for clinical triage. Empirical results show that our RMF detects latent failures up to 35 % earlier than conventional offline validation, while maintaining comparable decision‑making speed.

The discussion highlights the implications of our framework for regulatory compliance, model lifecycle management, and ethical accountability. We conclude by outlining research directions for incorporating formal verification, stochastic safety‑margin tuning, and cross‑domain knowledge transfer into the RMF, thereby advancing the field toward trustworthy, resilient agentic AI deployments.
571:
Clustering large‐scale, high‑dimensional data with nonlinear structure remains a central challenge in unsupervised learning. Kernel Power K‑Means (K‑PKM) extends classical K‑Means by embedding the data into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) and optimizing a power‑based distortion criterion, thereby capturing complex cluster shapes while preserving the intuitive geometry of the centroid‑based formulation. However, K‑PKM is limited by two practical bottlenecks: the quadratic memory cost of the kernel matrix and the sensitivity of the hard‑assignment scheme to outliers. In this work we introduce **RPF‑PKM**, a scalable and robust variant of Kernel Power K‑Means that simultaneously alleviates these limitations.  

First, we embed the data using **Random Fourier Features (RFF)** to obtain a low‑dimensional linear approximation of the target kernel. This eliminates the need to form the full kernel matrix and reduces the time complexity from \(O(n^2)\) to \(O(ndm)\), where \(n\) is the number of samples, \(d\) the input dimension, and \(m\) the number of random features. Second, we incorporate a **possibilistic fuzzy membership scheme** into the K‑PKM objective, allowing each point to possess a degree of belonging to all clusters while penalizing excessively high memberships. This modification yields an objective that is robust to outliers and noisy observations without sacrificing convergence guarantees.  

We present a complete algorithmic framework, prove that the RFF‑based surrogate preserves the essential properties of the original K‑PKM objective up to a controlled additive error, and show that the possibilistic criterion induces a strictly convex sub‑problem that can be solved efficiently via an alternating optimisation scheme. Experiments on synthetic benchmark datasets and large real‑world corpora (e.g., MNIST, 20‑Newsgroups, and a 1‑million point high‑dimensional image set) demonstrate that RPF‑PKM achieves clustering accuracies comparable to full‑kernel K‑PKM while reducing memory usage by an order of magnitude and improving robustness to injected noise and outliers. The proposed method thus provides a practical, theoretically grounded solution for scalable, robust clustering in modern data‑intensive settings.
572: Accurately estimating the 6‑D pose of objects remains a central hurdle in computer vision. Existing methods often falter when transferring from synthetic training data to real‑world scenes that exhibit variable lighting, texture‑poor surfaces, and heavy occlusion. To overcome these issues, we introduce **VLM6D**, a dual‑stream framework that exploits the complementary strengths of visual and geometric cues extracted from RGB‑D inputs. The model employs a self‑supervised Vision Transformer (DINOv2) to encode the RGB image, leveraging its pretrained understanding of visual grammar to remain robust to changes in texture and illumination. Simultaneously, a PointNet++ encoder processes the depth‑derived point cloud, providing reliable geometric reasoning even when the scene is sparsely sampled or heavily occluded. The two feature streams are fused and fed to a multi‑task prediction head, yielding precise pose estimates. Extensive experiments on the challenging Occluded‑LineMOD benchmark demonstrate that VLM6D surpasses existing state‑of‑the‑art methods, confirming its improved robustness and accuracy.
573:
Modern large‑scale AI systems increasingly rely on *agentic workflows*—collections of autonomous agents that interact, collaborate, and adapt to solve complex problems. A persistent challenge in such settings is to *quantify* the contribution or influence of each agent, both for interpretability and for efficient resource allocation. Existing approaches largely depend on heuristic metrics (e.g., cumulative reward, task‑completion counts) that ignore the causal structure of agent interactions.  

We propose a **Counterfactual‑based Agent Influence Ranker (CAIR)** that treats each agent’s contribution as a causal effect and ranks agents according to the marginal change in a workflow‑level objective when the agent’s behavior is *intervened* or *abated* in a counterfactual world.  CAIR constructs a probabilistic graphical model over the workflow’s execution trace, learns a differentiable representation of each agent’s policy, and uses a counterfactual simulation engine to estimate the *average causal influence* (ACI) of an agent.  The ranking is obtained by sorting agents by their ACI scores.  

We formalize the theoretical properties of ACI, proving that it satisfies a subset of desirable axioms (monotonicity, anonymity, and efficiency).  Empirical evaluation on a suite of synthetic benchmarks and a real‑world multi‑agent data‑cleaning pipeline demonstrates that CAIR assigns higher ranks to agents that truly drive performance improvements, outperforming baseline methods (e.g., reward‑based, Shapley‑style) by 15‑25 % in terms of ranking correlation and downstream decision‑making accuracy.  Our work bridges counterfactual causal inference with practical agent‑rank evaluation, offering a principled tool for managing and optimizing agentic AI workflows.
574:
Sequential recommendation systems have become indispensable for e‑commerce, streaming, and news platforms, yet they still struggle to reconcile the diverse patterns of user behavior with the need for scalable, interpretable models.  We introduce **HyMoERec**, a hybrid Mixture‑of‑Experts framework that jointly learns multiple, task‑specific sequence models and dynamically selects the most appropriate expert for each user‑item interaction.  Unlike conventional single‑head architectures, HyMoERec couples a set of lightweight recurrent, attention‑based, and memory‑augmented experts with a soft‑max gating network conditioned on both user and contextual embeddings.  This hybrid design enables the model to capture short‑term, long‑term, and global dynamics without sacrificing efficiency.  We further incorporate a load‑balancing regularizer and an entropy penalty to mitigate expert collapse and promote diverse usage across the training corpus.

Empirical evaluation on four widely used sequential recommendation benchmarks – Amazon‑Books, MovieLens‑20M, Jester, and a large‑scale e‑commerce click‑stream – demonstrates that HyMoERec consistently outperforms strong baselines such as SASRec, BERT4Rec, and RecFormer.  On the Amazon dataset, we achieve a 5.2 % relative improvement in Recall@10 and a 4.7 % gain in NDCG@20 over the best performing baseline, while reducing the number of trainable parameters by 18 %.  Ablation studies confirm that the hybrid expert pool and dynamic gating are critical to the observed gains, and that the load‑balancing regularizer is essential for stable training.  Finally, we provide a detailed complexity analysis showing that HyMoERec attains near‑linear inference time in the number of experts, making it suitable for deployment in real‑time recommendation pipelines.

Our work demonstrates that a principled mixture‑of‑experts approach can reconcile the tension between model expressiveness and scalability, offering a new direction for future sequential recommendation research.
575:
Medical visual question answering (VQA) requires the simultaneous understanding of radiologic images and complex, domain‑specific language, and it is increasingly used to support clinical decision‑making. Conventional VQA frameworks typically employ a single multimodal transformer and treat the task as a monolithic classification or generation problem, which limits their ability to capture the diverse reasoning patterns present in medical data. In this paper we introduce **CMI‑MTL**, a Cross‑Mamba Interaction based Multi‑Task Learning framework that tackles these limitations in two complementary ways. First, we design a novel **Cross‑Mamba Interaction (CMI) module** that interleaves two Mamba‑style temporal convolutional networks—one dedicated to visual feature extraction and the other to language encoding—allowing cross‑modal information to be exchanged at every depth. This design preserves the linear‑time efficiency of Mamba while enabling richer joint representations. Second, we cast medical VQA as a multi‑task problem comprising (i) answer classification, (ii) answer generation, and (iii) evidence localization. By sharing the CMI backbone across these subtasks, the model learns complementary supervisory signals that regularize the network and improve generalization on low‑data regimes typical of medical datasets.

We evaluate CMI‑MTL on three large‑scale benchmarks—VQA‑Med, PathVQA, and RadCommons—achieving state‑of‑the‑art accuracy (86.3 % on VQA‑Med), a 4.7 % absolute gain over the best published transformer baseline, and a 2.1 × speed‑up at inference time thanks to Mamba’s efficient design. Ablation studies confirm that both the cross‑interaction mechanism and multi‑task supervision are essential to the observed performance. Our approach demonstrates that domain‑aware cross‑modal coupling combined with multi‑task learning can substantially advance the capabilities of medical VQA systems.
576:
Long‑context reasoning—where a language model must read, understand, and integrate information spanning tens of thousands of tokens—has become a critical benchmark for evaluating the true capacity of large language models (LLMs). Existing datasets either limit input length or focus narrowly on a single reasoning style, thereby obscuring a comprehensive view of how models handle extended discourse, memory retention, and aggregation of distant facts. To address this gap, we introduce **Oolong**, a unified benchmark suite designed to probe LLMs on a diverse set of long‑context reasoning and aggregation tasks. Oolong comprises five families of tasks (chronological reasoning, multi‑document summarization, entity‑tracking, cross‑document inference, and hierarchical planning) with a total of 3,200 instances, each containing up to 50,000 tokens of source text. The benchmark is accompanied by a modular evaluation framework that measures not only end‑to‑end accuracy but also intermediate reasoning fidelity (e.g., chain‑of‑thought coherence), memory usage, and inference latency.

We evaluate a spectrum of state‑of‑the‑art models—including GPT‑4, Llama‑2 with retrieval‑augmented techniques, and retrieval‑based architectures such as RAG and REALM—under both vanilla and fine‑tuned settings. Results demonstrate a pronounced decline in performance beyond the 4,096‑token boundary, with a steep drop in factual accuracy and coherence for models without explicit memory mechanisms. Retrieval‑augmented methods mitigate this degradation, yet still exhibit significant variance across task families. Notably, Oolong reveals that aggregation‑heavy tasks (e.g., cross‑document inference) are particularly sensitive to token budget, highlighting the need for more sophisticated context‑window management.

Oolong is publicly released with full documentation, evaluation scripts, and a leaderboard, inviting the community to benchmark and improve long‑context reasoning systems. By exposing the strengths and weaknesses of contemporary LLMs in a controlled, high‑scale setting, Oolong serves as a catalyst for the next generation of scalable reasoning architectures.
577:
In-context learning (ICL) has emerged as a defining capability of large transformer language models, allowing them to perform a wide variety of tasks by conditioning on a few demonstrations rather than fine‑tuning. Recent investigations have identified a class of attention heads—termed *induction heads*—that appear to encode the mechanism by which a model extracts and generalises patterns from a context window. However, the precise emergence, functional role, and training dynamics of these heads remain poorly understood. In this paper we present a systematic study of induction heads across several transformer families (GPT‑2, GPT‑3, and a newly‑trained 12‑billion‑parameter model) and benchmark tasks (synthetic arithmetic, coreference resolution, and simple program synthesis).

We (i) develop a quantitative indicator that detects induction‑like attention patterns in a principled, data‑driven way; (ii) trace the appearance of these heads through fine‑tuning epochs and show that they co‑evolve with ICL accuracy; (iii) demonstrate through controlled ablation that disabling a single induction head can catastrophically degrade performance on all ICL benchmarks while leaving vanilla language modeling largely intact; (iv) present a minimal “induction head” architecture that can be grafted onto standard transformers to accelerate ICL from pre‑training. Finally, we offer a theoretical account linking induction heads to a simple form of self‑attention‑based pattern‑matching and discuss implications for interpretability and model compression. Our findings establish induction heads as a necessary and sufficient component of in‑context learning, opening new avenues for designing models that learn from context more efficiently.
578: This work tackles the pressing issues of communication overhead, data heterogeneity, and privacy that arise when applying deep learning to channel‑state‑information (CSI) feedback in massive MIMO networks. We propose **Fed‑PELAD**, a federated learning architecture that combines locally trained, user‑specific encoders with a globally shared decoder that is adapted using Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA). In this scheme, each user equipment (UE) learns a personalized encoder to capture its unique channel characteristics, while the base station (BS) updates a common decoder through the coordinated aggregation of only the lightweight LoRA adapters—thereby avoiding the transmission of full model parameters. To further stabilize training, we employ an alternating freezing strategy together with a tuned learning‑rate ratio during LoRA aggregation. Extensive experiments on 3GPP‑standard channel models demonstrate that Fed‑PELAD cuts uplink communication cost to just 42.97 % of that required by conventional approaches, while simultaneously delivering a 1.2 dB gain in CSI‑feedback accuracy even under heterogeneous conditions.
579:
Epileptic seizures represent a major clinical challenge because their onset is unpredictable and often accompanied by severe neurological and socioeconomic consequences. Recent efforts have turned to deep learning on long‑term intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) for seizure forecasting, yet most models either neglect the rich spatio‑temporal structure of multichannel recordings or suffer from overfitting to limited, patient‑specific datasets. In this work, we propose **Adversarial Spatio‑Temporal Attention Networks (ASTAN)**, a novel framework that integrates three complementary innovations: (i) a graph‑convolutional encoder that captures inter‑electrode dependencies; (ii) a dual‑attention decoder that learns both temporal dynamics and spatial relevance across channels; and (iii) an adversarial training regime that forces the model to learn robust, patient‑agnostic representations by jointly optimizing against a discriminator that distinguishes real seizure‑onset patterns from synthetic perturbations.  

ASTAN is evaluated on the open‑access CHB‑EEG and EPILEPSIAE datasets, covering 20 patients and more than 200,000 seizure‑free hours of data. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art deep forecasting methods, ASTAN improves seizure‑forecast sensitivity from 78.4 % to 85.6 % (p < 0.01) while maintaining a false‑positive rate below 0.6 % per hour. On a held‑out cross‑patient test set, the model achieves an area‑under‑the‑curve (AUC) of 0.92, demonstrating strong generalizability. Ablation studies confirm that both the spatio‑temporal attention modules and the adversarial objective are essential to reach these gains.  

Our results indicate that jointly learning spatial relationships, temporal evolution, and robustness to distribution shift yields a clinically viable forecasting system. ASTAN paves the way for personalized, reliable seizure warning devices and offers a general paradigm for temporally sensitive, high‑dimensional biomedical time series.
580: Balancing short‑term gains against long‑term effects while dealing with delayed results, hidden variability, and ethical limits is a central challenge in allocating scarce resources for high‑stakes areas such as education, hiring, and healthcare. Existing learning‑based allocation methods usually rely on instant feedback or ignore how individual traits interact with intervention dynamics. We introduce a two‑layer contextual bandit framework that addresses individualized allocation under delayed feedback and is suitable for realistic environments with shifting populations, limited capacity, and time‑sensitive outcomes. The upper layer assigns budgets to subgroups to meet fairness and operational constraints, whereas the lower layer employs a neural network trained on observational data to pick the most responsive individuals within each group, honoring cooldown periods and modeling delayed treatment effects through resource‑specific delay kernels. By explicitly capturing temporal dynamics and feedback delays, the policy is continuously updated as new information arrives, resulting in more agile and responsive decisions. Experiments on two real‑world datasets—one from education and another from workforce development—demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines in cumulative outcomes, adapts better to varied delay patterns, and distributes resources equitably among subgroups. These findings underscore the value of delay‑aware, data‑driven decision systems for enhancing institutional policies and overall social welfare.
581:
The increasing demand on global health services and the shrinking time available for patient encounters—often less than five minutes per primary‑care visit—have exposed major systemic bottlenecks. Pre‑consultation procedures such as triage and structured history taking promise to alleviate these pressures, yet current AI implementations are hindered by passive interaction models and difficulties in managing contextual information. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hierarchical multi‑agent framework that turns conventional medical AI into an active, inquiry‑driven system through autonomous task orchestration.

Our eight‑agent architecture, governed by a central controller, partitions the pre‑consultation workflow into four core tasks: Triage ($T_{1}$), collection of the History of Present Illness ($T_{2}$), Past Medical History gathering ($T_{3}$), and Chief Complaint generation ($T_{4}$). Within $T_{1}$–$T_{3}$, we further define 13 domain‑specific subtasks. We evaluated the framework on 1,372 de‑identified electronic health records from a Chinese medical platform, testing it with three different foundation models (GPT‑OSS 20B, Qwen3‑8B, Phi4‑14B). The system achieved an 87.0 % accuracy rate for primary department triage and 80.5 % for secondary department classification, while task completion rates rose to 98.2 % under agent‑driven scheduling compared to 93.1 % with simple sequential processing.

Clinical quality, judged by 18 physicians, averaged 4.56 for Chief Complaints, 4.48 for History of Present Illness, and 4.69 for Past History on a 5‑point scale. The number of conversational rounds needed was 12.7 for $T_{2}$ and 16.9 for $T_{3}$. Because the architecture is model‑agnostic and deployable locally, it preserves patient privacy while maintaining consistent performance across different large‑language models. These results suggest that autonomous, multi‑agent AI can significantly improve the efficiency and quality of pre‑consultation workflows in clinical practice.
582:
In modern game development, automated play‑testing must keep pace with continuous content updates while providing meaningful insights into emergent bugs and design‑level issues. We propose a Knowledge Graph‑enhanced Large Language Model (KG‑LLM) framework that supports *incremental* play‑testing, i.e., testing new patches or assets on top of a previously validated game state without re‑running the entire test suite. Our approach constructs a dynamic *Game Knowledge Graph* (GKG) that encodes the semantics of game objects, actions, state transitions, and narrative constraints. This graph is jointly leveraged with a pre‑trained LLM (ChatGPT‑4) in a two‑stage pipeline: (1) the LLM generates natural‑language test scripts and exploratory play‑throughs conditioned on the GKG, and (2) the GKG is queried to validate consistency, detect state‑space coverage gaps, and automatically annotate failures with high‑level bug categories.  

Key technical contributions include (i) an incremental KG update mechanism that preserves consistency across patches, (ii) a hybrid inference module that fuses LLM‑generated hypotheses with graph‑based constraint checking to reduce false positives, and (iii) an active learning loop that prioritizes test cases based on novelty metrics derived from the KG. We evaluated the system on two commercial‑grade titles— a procedurally generated dungeon crawler and a narrative‑driven puzzle platform—using a curated dataset of 15 incremental releases. Compared to baseline LLM‑only and rule‑based testers, KG‑LLM achieved a 35 % increase in defect recall, reduced test generation time by 42 %, and maintained an F1‑score above 0.88 for bug classification. The results demonstrate that integrating structured domain knowledge with large language models yields a scalable, low‑overhead solution for incremental game play‑testing, enabling developers to detect regressions early and maintain higher quality releases.
583:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly reshaped bioinformatics, enabling unprecedented synthesis and augmentation of biological data. This systematic review surveys the landscape of generative models applied to bioinformatics from 2010–2024, encompassing 1,245 peer‑reviewed publications identified through PubMed, Web of Science, arXiv, and major conferences (e.g., ISMB, RECOMB, NIPS). After a rigorous screening process based on PRISMA guidelines, 312 studies were retained for detailed analysis.

We categorize the reviewed work into three core domains: (i) **Model architectures**—generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders (VAEs), diffusion models, and transformer‑based language models; (ii) **Applications**—protein structure and sequence design, de‑novo drug discovery, multi‑omics integration, single‑cell transcriptomics, and synthetic biology; and (iii) **Methodological advances**—physics‑informed constraints, attention‑based conditioning, self‑supervised pre‑training, efficient sampling, and novel evaluation metrics. Across all domains, we identify a shift from early GAN‑based approaches toward diffusion and transformer models that offer higher fidelity and interpretability.

Key findings include: (1) Diffusion models now dominate protein and molecular generation tasks, achieving benchmark‑level accuracy in de‑novo design; (2) Transformer‑based language models are increasingly used for genomics and transcriptomics, leveraging massive unlabeled datasets for sequence imputation and variant effect prediction; (3) Integration of domain knowledge (e.g., energy potentials, evolutionary couplings) consistently improves generative quality; and (4) Evaluation remains a critical bottleneck—most studies rely on proxy metrics (e.g., Kullback‑Leibler divergence, RMSD) rather than biological assays, highlighting the need for standardized benchmarks and wet‑lab validation protocols.

Finally, we outline open challenges—data scarcity and imbalance, ethical concerns over synthetic biology, scalability of training pipelines, and reproducibility of generative benchmarks—and propose a research agenda that prioritizes cross‑disciplinary collaboration, open‑source toolkits, and regulatory frameworks. This review offers a comprehensive map of the current state of generative AI in bioinformatics and a roadmap for future methodological innovations.
584: Large‑scale generative models have achieved unprecedented quality, yet the diversity of their outputs often remains limited. Current ensemble and distillation techniques either amplify diversity at the expense of fidelity or vice‑versa, because each constituent model is optimized independently. We propose *Base‑Aligned Model Collaboration* (BAMC), a principled framework that jointly optimizes a set of base models to achieve high output quality while maximizing inter‑model diversity. BAMC first projects each base model into a shared latent space and introduces a *base‑alignment loss* that encourages complementary feature representations. A subsequent *diversity‑aware aggregation* module weights model predictions according to their dissimilarity, ensuring that the ensemble covers a wide spectrum of plausible solutions without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate BAMC on three large‑scale benchmarks—ImageNet‑StyleGAN, COCO‑Captioning, and OpenAI‑GPT—using both quantitative metrics (FID, BLEU, BERTScore, and a newly proposed Diversity‑Quality Pareto Score) and human preference studies. Across all datasets, BAMC outperforms conventional ensembling, voting, and mixture‑of‑experts baselines by 12–18 % in quality metrics while increasing diversity scores by 25–30 %. Ablation experiments confirm that the base‑alignment loss and diversity weighting are essential to achieving the reported trade‑off. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis showing that BAMC converges to a Pareto‑optimal frontier under mild assumptions. Our code and pre‑trained models are publicly released.
585:
Partially Relevant Video Retrieval (PRVR) aims to locate videos in which only a subset of the content satisfies a textual query. Current approaches treat every annotated text–video pair as a positive match while considering all other pairs as negatives, thereby overlooking the rich semantic diversity both inside a single video and across different videos. As a result, the embeddings of a query and the corresponding video-clip segments for distinct events within the same video tend to collapse, whereas embeddings of semantically similar queries and segments drawn from different videos are pushed apart. This “semantic collapse” hampers retrieval performance in multi‑event videos.

This work tackles these issues in both the text and video embedding spaces. We first propose **Text Correlation Preservation Learning**, which maintains the semantic relationships encoded by a foundation model among text queries. To mitigate collapse in video embeddings, we introduce **Cross‑Branch Video Alignment (CBVA)**, a contrastive alignment technique that disentangles hierarchical video representations across temporal scales. Building on this, we present **order‑preserving token merging** and **adaptive CBVA** to further refine alignment, yielding video segments that are internally coherent yet distinct from one another. Extensive experiments on PRVR benchmarks confirm that our framework successfully avoids semantic collapse and substantially boosts retrieval accuracy.
586:
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) form the backbone of most contemporary computer‑vision solutions, spanning everyday to high‑stakes applications. As a result, the field of explainable AI (XAI) has become essential for understanding both model behavior and its decisions. Earlier research has shown that the individual channels in the upper layers of a CNN can often be tied to human‑recognizable concepts. Concept‑Relevance Propagation (CRP) techniques trace predictions back to these channels and identify the images that maximally activate them. Yet, existing CRP workflows remain largely manual: domain experts must examine the activation maps, label the emergent concepts, and then compose lengthy explanations from the relevance distributions. This manual effort hampers the scalability and accessibility of the insights.

To solve these challenges, we propose **LLEXICORP (Large Language Model‑based EXplaIns COncept Relevance Propagation)** – a modular pipeline that fuses CRP with a multimodal large‑language model. LLEXICORP automatically assigns concise, descriptive labels to concept prototypes and generates natural‑language narratives that map quantitative relevance signals into intuitive stories. By carefully designing prompts that teach the language model the semantics of CRP through illustrative examples, we enforce a clear division between the naming and explanation phases, ensuring that the generated text remains faithful to the underlying model. The resulting explanations can be customized for different audiences, providing detailed technical descriptions for specialists or high‑level summaries for non‑technical stakeholders.

We evaluate our approach qualitatively on a range of ImageNet images using a VGG16 architecture. The results demonstrate that coupling concept‑based attribution with large‑language models markedly reduces the effort required to interpret deep neural networks, opening the door to more transparent and user‑friendly AI systems.
587: Vision‑language fine‑tuning has become a popular and efficient strategy for building multimodal foundation models. Although the text often cues semantic relations in an image, most fine‑tuning approaches ignore this context when aligning visual and linguistic representations, which limits performance. To address this shortfall, we introduce a method that strengthens multimodal alignment and fusion by jointly leveraging semantics and relationships. First, we extract multi‑level semantic features from several vision encoders to capture richer relational cues. Next, we learn a projection that clusters related semantic concepts, increasing the likelihood that the visual features encode meaningful relationships. Finally, we fuse the visual and textual streams through an inheritable cross‑attention mechanism that globally prunes redundant visual relationships, discarding visual‑language pairs with low correlation. We evaluate our approach on eight foundation models and two downstream tasks—visual question answering and image captioning—and demonstrate that it surpasses all competing methods.
588:
Speech translation (ST) systems must simultaneously transcribe and translate spoken input, and their quality is influenced by errors arising at both the acoustic‑to‑text and text‑to‑text stages. Existing automatic MT metrics ignore this dual‑source nature, while conventional ST metrics (e.g., BLEU, chrF) fail to capture the rich linguistic and prosodic information present in the audio signal. In this work we investigate how *source‑aware neural MT metrics* can be repurposed to evaluate ST output in a principled manner.  

We first design a lightweight alignment framework that maps an ASR transcript to the target translation, allowing neural metrics such as COMET, BLEURT, and BERTScore to attend to both the source text and its acoustic realization. We then benchmark a suite of metrics—BLEU, chrF, BERTScore, COMET, BLEURT—along with several novel source‑aware variants on two large multilingual ST corpora (MuST‑CS and CoVoST‑2) that include human judgments of adequacy and fluency. Across English–German, English–Spanish, and English–Russian pairs, the proposed source‑aware neural metric improves Kendall‑tau correlation with human ratings by up to **12 %** relative to the best non‑source baseline, while also showing resilience to varying ASR quality.  

To facilitate future work we release an annotated test set of 4,000 ST hypotheses with fine‑grained error tags and a reproducible evaluation pipeline. Our findings demonstrate that integrating source‑side information into neural MT metrics yields a more faithful assessment of ST quality, and we outline several avenues—such as multimodal pre‑training and real‑time error detection—for further enhancing ST evaluation.
589:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable single‑agent capabilities, yet orchestrating multiple such agents into a coherent team remains a formidable challenge. Existing multi‑agent frameworks either treat agents independently or rely on ad‑hoc coordination signals, which often lead to sub‑optimal joint behavior and fragile collaboration. We introduce **Maestro**, a novel framework that learns *conditional listwise policies* for a population of LLM agents, enabling them to collaborate effectively on complex, multi‑step tasks. 

Maestro casts joint planning as a conditional listwise optimization problem: at each decision point the agents simultaneously generate a *list* of candidate responses, conditioned on the shared context and the partial plans of their teammates. These lists are scored by a *joint value function* that evaluates coherence, diversity, and task relevance of the entire set of responses. By back‑propagating through the listwise objective with a differentiable relaxation (e.g., Gumbel‑Softmax), each agent learns to anticipate and complement the contributions of others. To stabilize training in the presence of non‑stationary policies, we employ a *meta‑learning* scheme that periodically re‑optimizes a shared global policy while preserving agent‑specific specialization.

We evaluate Maestro on a suite of collaborative benchmarks—including multi‑agent code synthesis, cooperative story generation, and distributed reasoning tasks. Across the board, Maestro outperforms baseline single‑agent fine‑tuning, heuristic coordination, and reinforcement‑learning‑based multi‑agent approaches, achieving up to 27 % higher task success rates and producing more coherent, high‑quality joint outputs. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of the listwise objective and the conditional attention mechanisms.  

Maestro demonstrates that principled policy optimization at the *list* level, conditioned on partner behavior, can unlock robust collaboration among large language models. Our code and models are released at https://github.com/maestro-ml.
590:
Privacy leakage remains a critical vulnerability in modern artificial‑intelligence (AI) systems, yet most existing techniques focus on *verification*—proving that a model satisfies a formal privacy specification—without revealing why a particular input or output might compromise sensitive information.  In practice, security auditors and system designers need *explanatory* evidence that can guide remediation, especially after a model has already been deployed.  

We introduce **Beyond Verification: Abductive Explanations for Post‑AI Assessment of Privacy Leakage** (BEPA), a unified framework that couples formal verification with abductive inference to generate human‑readable explanations of privacy leakage events.  BEPA first runs a lightweight verification engine on the trained model and dataset to identify *potential* privacy violations.  It then constructs a *causal graph* of model decisions, data dependencies, and intermediate activations, and applies abductive reasoning over this graph to infer the most plausible leakage pathways.  The result is a ranked list of *explanatory scenarios* that link a particular input to sensitive attributes, annotated with confidence scores and actionable mitigation suggestions.  

Our evaluation on three benchmark datasets—ImageNet (face‑attribute leakage), UCI Adult (income inference), and OpenAI GPT‑3 (private‑prompt extraction)—shows that BEPA can identify 94 % of known leakage cases that verification alone misses, and it produces concise explanations that reduce human debugging time by 37 % compared to baseline post‑hoc attribution methods.  We also demonstrate BEPA’s extensibility to differential‑privacy‑aware models and its resilience to adversarial evasion attacks.

BEPA advances the state of the art by providing a principled, post‑deployment analysis tool that bridges the gap between formal privacy guarantees and actionable understanding, thereby enabling more robust and trustworthy AI deployments.
591:
Safety guarantees in reinforcement learning are commonly enforced through *shielding*: a supervisory mechanism that constrains an agent’s actions to satisfy pre‑specified formal rules. Traditional shields are static; they rely on fixed logical conditions and manually defined abstractions. While they protect against violations under nominal conditions, they cannot adapt if the environment deviates from its assumptions.  

In this work we present the first *adaptive shielding* framework that operates on Generalized Reactivity of rank 1 (GR(1)) specifications—an expressive yet tractable fragment of Linear Temporal Logic that encodes both safety and liveness. Our approach monitors the environment at runtime, detects when its assumptions are breached, and then repairs the offending GR(1) constraints online using Inductive Logic Programming (ILP). This repair process is systematic and interpretable, allowing the shield to evolve gracefully: it only weakens goals when necessary to preserve liveness.  

We evaluate our method on two benchmark domains, Minepump and Atari’s Seaquest. The results show that (i) static symbolic controllers are often far from optimal when auxiliary rewards are considered, and (ii) reinforcement learning agents equipped with our adaptive shield achieve near‑optimal rewards while maintaining perfect compliance with logical specifications, outperforming static shields.
592: Accurate segmentation of liver structures from multi‑phase contrast‑enhanced CT (CECT) is essential for computer‑aided diagnosis and therapeutic planning of hepatic diseases, particularly for tumor identification. In this work we examine the efficacy of UNet‑style networks for liver‑tumor delineation, progressing from the vanilla UNet to the more advanced UNet3+ with a range of backbones. We compare ResNet, transformer‑based, and state‑space (Mamba) encoders, all initialized from pre‑trained weights. Contrary to expectations, ResNet‑based models consistently deliver higher performance across all metrics than their transformer or Mamba counterparts. Adding attention modules further boosts accuracy; the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) integration proves most effective. The ResNet‑UNet3+ model equipped with CBAM achieves the best overlap, with a Dice coefficient of 0.755 and IoU of 0.662, and demonstrates the finest boundary accuracy, reflected in an HD95 of 77.911. It also leads in overall accuracy (0.925) and specificity (0.926), underscoring its robustness in distinguishing lesions from normal tissue. Grad‑CAM visualizations were used to expose the regions driving predictions, enhancing interpretability. These results indicate that conventional ResNet backbones, when paired with modern attention mechanisms, remain highly competitive for medical image segmentation and hold promise for clinical liver‑tumor detection.
593: Recent progress in Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal foundation models has expanded their use in robotics and collaborative environments. Yet, effective multi‑agent interaction requires strong perspective‑taking skills so that models can grasp both physical and epistemic viewpoints. Existing training regimes largely ignore these interactive contexts, leading to difficulties when the model must reason about the subjectivity of individual agents or operate in settings with multiple observers. This work investigates whether explicitly incorporating diverse viewpoints via the ReAct framework—an approach that blends reasoning and action—can boost an LLM’s ability to understand and satisfy the needs of other agents. We build upon the classic Director task, adding active visual exploration across seven increasingly complex scenarios that test the agent’s ability to resolve referential ambiguity through visual access and interaction, under various state representations and prompting schemes, including ReAct‑style reasoning. Our experiments show that providing explicit perspective cues along with active exploration markedly enhances the model’s interpretive accuracy and collaborative performance. These results underscore the value of marrying active perception with perspective‑taking mechanisms for advancing LLMs in robotics and multi‑agent systems, paving the way for more adaptive, context‑aware AI in the future.
594: Kolmogorov‑Arnold Networks (KANs) have recently garnered considerable interest as a distinct family of neural architectures. Unlike conventional multilayer perceptrons, KANs employ trainable, parameterized activation functions, which endow them with enhanced interpretability and superior accuracy when approximating symbolic equations. A drawback of the original KAN design is the necessity to manually adjust the network’s domain discretization (the “domain grid”) during training, imposing extra effort on practitioners. Standard KAN layers also lack the ability to adapt their domains automatically based on the evolving output ranges of preceding layers. By incorporating a histogram‑driven update scheme, our proposed AdaptKAN not only eliminates this overhead but also facilitates out‑of‑distribution (OOD) detection across diverse scenarios. Empirical results show that AdaptKAN either outperforms or matches the state‑of‑the‑art KAN variants and MLPs on four benchmark tasks: learning scientific equations from the Feynman dataset, classifying images using frozen feature embeddings, synthesizing a control Lyapunov function, and identifying OOD samples on the OpenOOD v1.5 benchmark.
595:
The rapid rise of transformer‑based language models has made high‑quality pre‑training corpora a prerequisite for competitive performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. However, for the twenty‑plus Indic languages that together serve a population of over 600 M, large‑scale, balanced, and linguistically diverse training data remain scarce. We introduce **BhashaKritika**, a scalable pipeline that automatically constructs synthetic pre‑training corpora for Indian languages by leveraging multilingual resources, cross‑lingual transfer, and controllable generation techniques.  

BhashaKritika first harvests raw monolingual and parallel data from public repositories and then applies a series of transformations—script normalization, morphological inflection, back‑translation, and language‑model‑guided paraphrasing—to amplify and diversify the textual content while preserving linguistic authenticity. The pipeline is parameterized to produce corpora of arbitrary size, enabling the creation of 5–10 B token datasets for each target language. We evaluated the resulting corpora by pre‑training a family of Indic BERT‑style models (IndicBERT‑BhashaKritika) and benchmarked them on 12 downstream NLU and MT tasks spanning 15 languages. Compared with models trained on existing hand‑collected corpora, IndicBERT‑BhashaKritika achieves an average absolute improvement of **3.7 %** in token‑level F1 on NER and a **1.3 %** BLEU gain on low‑resource MT, while maintaining comparable inference latency.  

Our contributions are threefold: (i) a reproducible, open‑source framework for generating high‑fidelity synthetic data for under‑resourced Indic languages; (ii) a publicly available 45 B‑token multilingual dataset (BhashaKritika Corpus) and pre‑trained models; and (iii) an empirical study demonstrating that synthetic augmentation can close the performance gap for languages with limited corpora. BhashaKritika paves the way for equitable language technology across the Indian sub‑continent and offers a blueprint for scaling synthetic data generation to other low‑resource language families.
596: As digital transformation accelerates, optimizing business processes has emerged as a critical lever for enhancing corporate competitiveness. This paper presents an integrated business‑process‑optimisation framework that fuses artificial intelligence with big‑data analytics to deliver end‑to‑end intelligent lifecycle management. The architecture is organised into three layers—data ingestion, AI‑based analytical engines, and business‑rule orchestration—enabling continuous, real‑time monitoring and adaptive optimisation of processes. Leveraging distributed computing and deep‑learning modules, the system handles intricate operational contexts while preserving superior throughput and fault tolerance. Empirical tests conducted in diverse enterprise settings demonstrate a 42 % reduction in process cycle times, a 28 % boost in resource utilisation, and a 35 % cut in operating expenses, all while sustaining 99.9 % availability under heavy concurrent workloads. The findings underscore both theoretical significance and practical applicability, offering a compelling blueprint for enterprises seeking to accelerate digital transformation and elevate operational efficiency.
597:
Methane (CH₄) emissions from point sources such as industrial sites, oil‑gas infrastructure, and natural seepage are a major contributor to atmospheric greenhouse‑gas budgets. Conventional monitoring relies on in‑situ measurements or sparse satellite overpasses, which struggle to provide continuous, high‑resolution coverage of localized leaks. Here we present an end‑to‑end operational machine‑learning framework that exploits remote spectroscopic imagery to detect CH₄ point sources in near real‑time.  

We assemble a diverse training set combining (i) synthetic line‑by‑line radiative transfer simulations that span the full range of plume geometries, wind speeds and atmospheric conditions, and (ii) a growing catalog of verified on‑ground emission sites obtained from ground‑based hyperspectral platforms and targeted aircraft campaigns. The model architecture is a 2‑D convolutional encoder‑decoder network augmented with a spectral attention module that isolates the weak CH₄ absorption bands (1.65 µm, 2.3 µm, and 3.4 µm) from broadband radiance features. During training, we inject realistic noise and cloud‑screening effects to improve robustness.

Applied to TROPOMI and OCO‑2 Level‑2 products over a 12‑month period, the network achieves a true‑positive rate of 92 % for emissions >10 t yr⁻¹ while maintaining a false‑positive rate below 0.5 % per 10 km pixel. Cross‑validation with independent in‑situ flux measurements (1–15 t yr⁻¹) shows a mean absolute error of 1.8 t yr⁻¹ in retrieved source strengths. The inference pipeline processes a full‑orbit swath in under 5 s on a commodity GPU, enabling operational deployment on existing satellite data streams.

Our results demonstrate that machine‑learning‑assisted spectroscopic remote sensing can provide the spatial and temporal resolution required for regulatory compliance, targeted leak‑repair campaigns, and large‑scale methane inventories. The framework is scalable to future hyperspectral missions and can be extended to other trace gases, offering a versatile tool for atmospheric monitoring and climate mitigation.
598: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for creative tasks such as simulating fictional characters, yet their capacity to convincingly portray non‑prosocial or villainous personas has not been thoroughly explored. We propose that the safety alignment mechanisms built into current LLMs inherently clash with the objective of authentically embodying morally ambiguous or outright antagonistic figures. To examine this claim, we present the Moral RolePlay benchmark—a new dataset that employs a four‑point moral alignment scale and a balanced test split designed for stringent evaluation. We challenge state‑of‑the‑art LLMs to role‑play characters ranging from moral exemplars to outright villains. Across a large‑scale assessment, we observe a clear, monotonic drop in fidelity as character morality worsens. The models particularly falter when asked to display traits directly opposed to safety norms, such as “Deceitful” and “Manipulative”, often replacing nuanced malevolence with crude aggression. Moreover, we find that general chatbot competence does not reliably predict a model’s ability to play villainous roles; highly safety‑aligned models, in particular, perform poorly. This study offers the first systematic evidence of a major shortcoming in LLMs, underscoring the tension between safety constraints and creative authenticity. Our benchmark and insights lay the groundwork for more sophisticated, context‑aware alignment strategies.
599:
Alibaba International E‑commerce Product Search Competition (AICUP‑2025) posed the challenge of retrieving the most relevant product listings for millions of ambiguous user queries while respecting real‑time constraints. In this report we describe the end‑to‑end ranking framework engineered by the *DcuRAGONs* team, which combines a lightweight lexical matcher with a deep multimodal re‑ranker. The system first applies a highly efficient inverted‑index filter to prune the candidate space to the top‑k (k = 1000) items using query‑term statistics and product title embeddings. These candidates are then re‑ranked by a transformer‑based relevance model that jointly attends to query text, product titles, descriptions, and visual embeddings extracted from ResNet‑50. We augment this pipeline with a graph‑based feature that captures item co‑purchase and category relationships via a Graph Attention Network, and a cross‑task learning module that jointly optimizes click‑through‑rate (CTR) and relevance.  

Our experiments on the provided training set (≈ 1.2 M queries, 4.5 M products) show that the proposed architecture achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.321 and MAP of 0.284, outperforming the baseline by 12 % and 15 % respectively. Ablation studies confirm the complementary gains from visual features (3 % NDCG) and graph signals (2 % NDCG). The final submission ranked 3rd overall in the competition, achieving a 0.7 % absolute lift in user satisfaction metrics on the held‑out test set. We also discuss deployment‑specific optimizations such as dynamic quantization, early‑exiting in the transformer, and a lightweight offline cache that reduce latency to under 25 ms per query on commodity hardware. The report concludes with lessons learned and directions for future work, including reinforcement‑learning based query reformulation and continual model adaptation to emerging product catalogs.
600:
Symbolic regression (SR) seeks interpretable mathematical expressions that explain observed data.  A pervasive difficulty is that distinct syntactic forms can encode the same underlying function; without a principled way of recognising and collapsing such *symbolic equivalences*, evolutionary or stochastic search methods expend unnecessary effort exploring redundant sub‑spaces and often return noncanonical, opaque models.  We introduce **EGG‑SR**, a framework that embeds symbolic equivalence directly into the SR search by constructing and maintaining an **Equality Graph (EGG)**.  Each node of the graph denotes a sub‑expression while edges encode algebraic identities (e.g., distributive, trigonometric, exponential rules).  During evolution, candidate expressions are projected onto the EGG, where a union‑find structure merges equivalent nodes and prunes duplicate genetic operators.  This representation guarantees that any two expressions mapped to the same EGG component are mathematically indistinguishable, thus drastically reducing the search space and accelerating convergence.

We formalise the graph‑construction procedure, prove that the EGG preserves the equivalence class of any expression, and show that the expected number of distinct evaluation points drops from exponential to sub‑exponential in the size of the search tree.  Experiments on a suite of synthetic benchmarks (polynomial, trigonometric, rational) and two real‑world datasets (chemical kinetics and neuronal firing) demonstrate that EGG‑SR matches or exceeds state‑of‑the‑art SR methods in fit error while requiring 35–55 % fewer fitness evaluations and yielding models with lower structural complexity.  The proposed approach thus offers a systematic, theoretically grounded means of harnessing algebraic equivalence to make symbolic regression more efficient, interpretable, and scalable.
601: Recent breakthroughs in large language models (LLMs) have propelled advances in decision‑making and task planning for embodied autonomous agents. Yet, most current approaches falter on intricate, long‑horizon challenges because they depend on a single, monolithic trajectory that bundles every past decision and observation, attempting to solve the entire task in one go. To overcome this shortfall, we introduce **ReAcTree**, a hierarchical planning framework that breaks down a complex objective into smaller, tractable sub‑goals within a dynamically grown agent tree. Each sub‑goal is addressed by an LLM‑powered agent node that can reason, act, and further expand the tree, while higher‑level control‑flow nodes orchestrate the coordination among these agent nodes. We also incorporate two complementary memory modules: episodic memory supplies each agent node with goal‑specific, sub‑goal‑level examples, and a working‑memory module broadcasts environment‑specific observations to all nodes. Experiments on the WAH‑NL and ALFRED benchmarks show that ReAcTree consistently surpasses strong baselines such as ReAct across a range of LLMs. In particular, on WAH‑NL, ReAcTree attains a 61 % success rate with Qwen 2.5‑72B, almost twice the 31 % achieved by ReAct.
602:
The practical use of near‑term quantum devices is hampered by the noise that they inevitably exhibit.  
Quantum error‑mitigation (QEM) strategies are the most promising route to enhance the fidelity of such devices without the heavy qubit overhead of full error‑correction, yet they often demand a large number of measurements—particularly when a whole family of circuits, each labeled by classical parameters, must be corrected.  
In this work we focus on zero‑noise extrapolation (ZNE), the most widely used QEM technique, and introduce **surrogate‑enabled ZNE (S‑ZNE)**.  
S‑ZNE replaces the repeated noisy circuit executions with a classical surrogate model that predicts the noisy expectation values for all parameter settings, allowing the extrapolation to be carried out entirely on the classical side.  
Consequently, the measurement cost for correcting an entire circuit family drops from linear in the number of circuits to a constant overhead, giving the method excellent scalability.  
We provide a theoretical justification showing that, in many realistic regimes, S‑ZNE achieves accuracy on par with standard ZNE, and we validate the approach on numerical experiments involving ground‑state energy calculations and quantum metrology problems with up to 100 qubits.  
Our results illustrate a general framework that can be adapted to other QEM protocols, thereby opening a promising route to scalable error mitigation.
603: Ensuring that a classifier’s confidence scores reflect actual outcome probabilities—i.e., that it is well‑calibrated—is a minimal, essential prerequisite for its reliability. Current multiclass calibration checks tend to focus on particular prediction facets (such as the top‑class confidence or per‑class accuracy) or rely on computationally intensive variational techniques. Here we tackle scalable *evaluation* of multiclass calibration. We introduce “utility calibration”, a flexible framework that quantifies calibration error with respect to a user‑specified utility function, thereby encoding the decision‑making priorities of the end user. This approach subsumes several existing metrics, enabling more robust formulations of top‑class and class‑wise calibration, while also extending to richer downstream utilities beyond simple binarized criteria.
604:
Software‑defined networking (SDN) offers unprecedented agility and programmability for modern data‑center and enterprise networks, yet its centralized control plane remains a prime target for attacks and a single point of failure. Blockchain technology, with its immutable ledger, decentralised consensus, and programmable smart‑contract layer, provides a compelling means to enhance SDN security without sacrificing performance. In this paper we propose **SmartSecChain‑SDN**, a novel, blockchain‑integrated intelligent framework that unifies secure data plane management with efficient control‑plane operation. 

SmartSecChain‑SDN introduces a multi‑layered architecture in which a lightweight SDN controller cluster off‑loads security‑critical tasks to a consortium blockchain. Flow‑rule distribution, authentication, and policy enforcement are encoded as verifiable smart contracts, ensuring that every configuration change is cryptographically logged and auditable. A dedicated “control‑ledger” synchronises state across controllers, eliminating the single‑point‑of‑failure problem and enabling rapid recovery in the event of compromise or outage. To maintain high throughput, we employ a sharded chain and off‑chain data availability layers, coupled with an adaptive consensus protocol that selects the most suitable mining strategy (PoS/PBFT) based on network load.

We evaluate SmartSecChain‑SDN in a realistic emulated environment (Mininet + Hyperledger Fabric) under a spectrum of attack scenarios (e.g., controller hijack, flow‑table tampering) and performance workloads. Results demonstrate up to 35 % reduction in configuration latency compared to a traditional SDN controller, while providing 100 % tamper‑resistance for critical policy updates and achieving a 97 % success rate in automated threat detection.  

The key contributions of this work are: (1) a unified framework that couples SDN and blockchain for end‑to‑end security; (2) a smart‑contract‑driven policy engine that guarantees verifiable enforcement; (3) a lightweight, shard‑based consensus mechanism that preserves control‑plane efficiency; and (4) a comprehensive evaluation that confirms the feasibility of the approach in real‑world deployments.
605:
Reading a scene‑printed text involves a rapid, hierarchical cascade of visual and linguistic operations in the human brain. Motivated by these neurocognitive stages, we propose **OTSNet**—an *Observation‑Thinking‑Spelling* pipeline that mirrors the way people perceive, interpret and produce written language. OTSNet first extracts fine‑grained visual embeddings from irregular text images via a multi‑scale convolutional backbone (Observation stage). A contextual “Thinking” module—implemented as a stacked Transformer encoder with a self‑attention‑guided visual‑to‑language bridge—refines these embeddings by modelling intra‑ and inter‑character dependencies and incorporating global scene cues. Finally, a “Spelling” decoder performs a character‑level autoregressive generation augmented with a lightweight language model, ensuring syntactic and lexical coherence while correcting low‑confidence predictions.

The three‑stage architecture is jointly trained in a single end‑to‑end pipeline, enabling back‑propagation of errors from the spelling output to the early visual representations. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (ICDAR‑2015, SVTP, CUTE‑11, and the more challenging ReCTS) show that OTSNet achieves 92.4 % accuracy on ICDAR‑2015, surpassing current state‑of‑the‑art methods by 1.7 % absolute. Ablation studies confirm that each stage contributes significantly: removing the Thinking module drops accuracy by 2.3 % and the Spelling module by 1.8 %. Cross‑domain tests reveal that OTSNet generalises robustly to handwritten and synthetic datasets without fine‑tuning. These results demonstrate that a neurocognitive‑inspired pipeline can effectively bridge the gap between visual perception and linguistic decoding in scene text recognition.
606:
Deep Q‑Networks (DQNs) have become a canonical benchmark for value‑based deep reinforcement learning, yet their empirical performance remains highly sensitive to the exploration strategy and the replay mechanism. In this study we investigate how the choice of ε‑greedy policy parameters and the adoption of Prioritized Experience Replay (PER) jointly influence learning dynamics and final performance.
