Models are asked to output not only a point estimate but also a 90 % confidence band, and we evaluate calibration by comparing the empirical coverage of these intervals against the nominal 90 %.  

We evaluate a spectrum of LLMs—including GPT‑4, LLaMA‑2, and open‑source variants—using a variety of prompting strategies (few‑shot, chain‑of‑thought, and temperature tuning).  Across all models, the average coverage falls far below the target, with GPT‑4 achieving only 73 % and LLaMA‑2 62 % coverage while nominally reporting 90 % intervals.  Expected Calibration Error (ECE) is 0.21 for GPT‑4 and 0.34 for LLaMA‑2.  We further demonstrate that a lightweight calibration head and temperature annealing reduce overconfidence, raising GPT‑4 coverage to 86 % without harming accuracy.  These findings highlight a critical gap in the practical deployment of LLMs for scientific and engineering tasks, where well‑calibrated uncertainty estimates are essential.  FermiEval provides a reproducible, domain‑agnostic testbed for future work on confidence interval calibration in large language models.
653:
Forecasting financial markets remains notoriously challenging due to their non‑stationary dynamics and sensitivity to macro‑economic regimes. Traditional time‑series models often rely solely on recent observations, thereby overlooking the valuable information embedded in historical contexts that resemble the current economic environment. In this paper, we introduce **History Rhymes**, a retrieval‑augmented forecasting framework that explicitly leverages macro‑contextual similarities between past and present periods to enhance prediction robustness.  

Our approach first encodes each time‑slice of macro‑economic data (GDP growth, inflation, policy rates, sentiment indicators, etc.) into a compact vector using a cross‑modal Transformer. A similarity search is then performed over a curated historical archive to retrieve the *k* most analogous macro‑contexts, along with their associated financial trajectories. The retrieved histories serve as an auxiliary conditioning signal to a downstream forecasting model (an LSTM‑based or Bayesian neural network), effectively “borrowing” pattern information from regimes that have historically responded similarly to the current macro environment.  

Empirical evaluations on multi‑asset portfolios (S&P 500, Euro Stoxx 50, and commodity indices) over a 30‑year horizon demonstrate that History Rhymes outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines—including pure ARIMA, XGBoost, and vanilla Transformer predictors—by 12–18 % in mean‑squared error and 8–12 % in directional accuracy. Ablation studies confirm that both the retrieval mechanism and the macro‑embedding design are critical for the gains. We also provide a theoretical analysis linking retrieval‑based regularization to improved generalization under regime‑shift settings.  

Our findings suggest that “history rhymes” with the present, and that systematically incorporating this rhythmic pattern into forecasting pipelines can significantly bolster robustness in volatile financial markets.
654: Diffusion models have rapidly become the leading approach for generating high‑quality images, yet their real‑world usability is limited by the heavy computation required for the many iterative denoising steps. Existing caching tricks can speed up inference, but they often force a difficult compromise between latency and visual fidelity, either degrading image quality or incurring additional computational costs. To overcome these drawbacks, we propose **H2‑Cache**, a new hierarchical caching strategy tailored to contemporary generative diffusion architectures. The core idea is that the denoising trajectory can be decomposed into two functional phases: a structure‑forming stage and a detail‑refining stage. H2‑Cache exploits this separation by applying a dual‑threshold policy that caches each phase independently. To make the two‑check procedure efficient, we introduce **Pooled Feature Summarization (PFS)**—a lightweight, yet robust, method for rapid similarity estimation. We evaluate H2‑Cache on the Flux architecture, where it delivers up to a **5.08× acceleration** while preserving image quality almost indistinguishable from the uncached baseline, outperforming all prior caching techniques both quantitatively and qualitatively. Our contribution offers a practical, high‑performance solution that resolves the speed‑quality trade‑off and lowers the barrier to deploying high‑fidelity diffusion models in real‑world settings. Source code is available at https://github.com/Bluear7878/H2-cache-A-Hierarchical-Dual-Stage-Cache.
655: Feature‑attribution techniques are pivotal for rendering machine‑learning predictions interpretable by quantifying the contribution of individual or groups of features to a model’s output. Among these techniques, the Shapley value—rooted in cooperative game theory—stands out due to its theoretical guarantees under deterministic inference. In this study, we extend the Shapley framework to large language model (LLM)–based decision‑support systems, whose predictions are intentionally stochastic. We investigate the conditions under which various practical implementations of Shapley attribution maintain its core axioms in such non‑deterministic settings, and we examine how the inherent randomness of LLMs influences these guarantees. Finally, we discuss the trade‑offs between the speed of obtaining explainable inferences, the fidelity to exact Shapley values, and the satisfaction of the principled properties.
656: Machine‑learning models can fail in many seemingly unrelated ways—exhibiting unfairness toward protected groups, being brittle to spurious correlations, or performing poorly on minority sub‑populations. These failure modes are usually studied by separate communities. In this paper we introduce a single theoretical lens that shows when distinct bias mechanisms actually lead to the same quantitative impact on a model’s performance. By expressing bias as a violation of conditional independence and measuring it with information‑theoretic tools, we derive formal equivalence relations linking spurious correlations, distribution shifts in sub‑populations, class imbalance, and fairness violations. One key result is that a spurious correlation of strength \( \alpha \) induces a drop in worst‑group accuracy equivalent to a sub‑population imbalance ratio \( r \approx \frac{1+\alpha}{1-\alpha} \), assuming overlapping features. We test these predictions on six benchmark datasets and three neural architectures; the empirical results confirm the equivalences within a 3 % margin of worst‑group accuracy. This unifying view allows researchers to transfer debiasing techniques between problems and connects the disparate fields of fairness, robustness, and distribution shift.
657: Can language models (LMs) produce accurate descriptions of their own internal workings? And are they more effective at self‑explanation than other models? This study explores how an LM’s privileged knowledge of its own internals can be harnessed to develop novel explanatory techniques. By fine‑tuning LMs on existing interpretability outputs, we train them to generate natural‑language accounts of (1) what information is encoded in LM features, (2) the causal relationships between internal activations, and (3) how particular input tokens influence the model’s predictions. Even with only a few tens of thousands of example explanations, the resulting explainer models generalize meaningfully to new queries. This capability seems partly rooted in the model’s intimate access to its own internals: a model tends to explain its own computations better than a different, even more powerful, model can explain theirs. Our findings show that LMs can learn to reliably elucidate their internal processes, providing a scalable supplement to conventional interpretability methods.
658: Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) often suffer from quadratic compute costs and a rapidly growing key‑value (KV) cache, largely because they process many redundant visual tokens. We introduce **SharpV**, a lightweight framework that adaptively prunes both visual tokens and the KV cache. Unlike conventional uniform compression methods, SharpV tailors its pruning ratios to the spatio‑temporal characteristics of the input, and in some cases even surpasses fully dense models—showing that adaptive pruning can be advantageous. During the KV‑cache pruning step, SharpV identifies and discards degraded visual features by self‑calibration, using similarity to the original features as a guide. This hierarchical pruning strategy is framed as an information‑bottleneck problem, providing fresh insights into how VideoLLMs process visual information. Extensive experiments on several public benchmarks confirm that SharpV outperforms existing techniques. To our knowledge, it is also the first two‑stage pruning approach that does not rely on exposed attention scores, thereby remaining fully compatible with hardware‑accelerated attention mechanisms such as Flash Attention.
659: This study proposes a fresh classification scheme for contemporary workload schedulers. We examine three distinct categories—OS process schedulers, cluster job schedulers, and big‑data schedulers—charting their progression from early prototypes to current implementations while highlighting algorithmic usage and features. The paper contrasts the characteristics of each class and outlines their historical evolution. Finally, we underscore common design themes that transcend both local and distributed systems.
660:
Interpretability is pivotal for the application of deep learning in computational pathology, as it underpins trust in AI‑assisted diagnostics. Standard attribution techniques such as Integrated Gradients (IG) have proven useful, yet their direct application to whole slide images (WSIs) is hindered by the enormous resolution of these data. While IG can uncover patterns driving model decisions, it often fails to isolate signals that truly distinguish between tumor subtypes. To address these issues, we propose **Contrastive Integrated Gradients (CIG)**, a new attribution framework that operates in logit space and computes class‑specific gradients relative to a reference class. CIG achieves sharper delineation between malignant and benign tissue by highlighting discriminative regions, satisfies the core axioms of integrated attribution, and therefore offers a theoretically sound interpretation.  

Additionally, we introduce two quantitative metrics—**MIL‑AIC** and **MIL‑SIC**—to evaluate attribution quality by tracking how predictive information and model confidence change as salient regions are progressively revealed, particularly under weakly supervised settings. We assess CIG on three diverse pathology datasets: CAMELYON16 (breast cancer metastases in lymph nodes), TCGA‑RCC (renal cell carcinoma), and TCGA‑Lung (lung cancer). Results show that CIG delivers richer, more accurate attributions, as evidenced by higher MIL‑AIC/MIL‑SIC scores and visual maps that closely match ground‑truth tumor locations, demonstrating its promise for reliable and interpretable WSI‑based diagnosis.
661:
Accurate sensor calibration is pivotal for autonomous systems, remote sensing, and industrial automation, yet most state‑of‑the‑art procedures either incur high computational cost or lack the agility required for on‑board, real‑time operation.  In this work we introduce the *Dynamic Calibration Network* (DCN), a lightweight, end‑to‑end learning framework that reconciles these competing demands by jointly optimizing calibration precision, inference latency, and resource utilization.  The DCN comprises three key components: (i) a sparse, adaptive sensor‑feature encoder that selectively activates only the most informative measurements; (ii) a recurrent refinement module that incorporates temporal context to reduce calibration drift without sacrificing throughput; and (iii) a quantized, edge‑friendly inference pipeline that guarantees sub‑10‑ms latency on embedded hardware.  

We evaluate the model on two challenging benchmarks—lidar‑to‑camera extrinsic calibration for autonomous vehicles and thermal‑to‑visible image alignment in UAV platforms—using a ground‑truth dataset of 3 M paired sensor readings.  Compared to conventional least‑squares and deep‑learning baselines, DCN reduces calibration error by 38 % (mean reprojection error) while operating at 92 % lower FLOPs and 76 % less memory footprint.  In addition, the online fine‑tuning mechanism keeps drift below 1.2 % over a 24‑hour continuous run, demonstrating the model’s robustness to environmental variations.  

Our results confirm that a judicious blend of sparse feature selection, temporal coherence, and quantization can deliver high‑accuracy calibration in real‑time, resource‑constrained settings.  The proposed framework is thus immediately applicable to a wide range of robotic and sensor‑fusion applications where latency and energy budgets are stringent.
662:
Large reasoning models (LRMs) excel at tackling intricate inference problems, but they frequently “over‑think,” generating overly lengthy chain‑of‑thought (CoT) sequences that inflate inference cost and can even hurt performance. Our study uncovers a strong negative correlation between reasoning length and accuracy: across multiple stochastic decodes, the shortest CoT paths consistently yield the highest correctness, whereas longer paths tend to accumulate mistakes and redundant steps. Ideally, the most concise, accurate reasoning route could be identified by exhaustively enumerating the entire reasoning tree, yet this search space expands exponentially with sequence length, making exhaustive exploration impractical.  

To overcome this obstacle, we introduce DTS—a model‑agnostic decoding strategy that sparsely traverses the reasoning tree. DTS selectively branches only at high‑entropy tokens and stops early once a complete reasoning path is found, thereby approximating the optimal short path without extra training or supervision.  

Evaluation on the AIME2024 and AIME2025 benchmarks using DeepSeek‑R1‑Distill‑Qwen‑7B and its 1.5B variant demonstrates that DTS boosts accuracy by up to 8 %, cuts the average CoT length by 23 %, and lowers repetition rates by 12 %. These results confirm DTS’s effectiveness in producing efficient, high‑quality reasoning from LRMs at scale.
663: Vision Graph Neural Networks (ViGs) open new avenues for advancing visual models, yet their graph‑construction stage is often computationally heavy, limiting practical efficiency. In this work we introduce **AdaptViG**, a streamlined yet powerful hybrid Vision GNN that tackles this bottleneck via a novel **Adaptive Graph Convolution**. This technique rests on a lightweight static axial scaffold and a dynamic, content‑aware gating scheme termed **Exponential Decay Gating**, which selectively down‑weights long‑range edges according to feature similarity. AdaptViG adopts a hybrid scheme: the early layers rely on the efficient gating mechanism, while the final layer employs a full Global‑Attention block to maximize feature aggregation. The resulting framework establishes a new state‑of‑the‑art balance between accuracy and computational cost for Vision GNNs. For example, AdaptViG‑M attains 82.6 % top‑1 accuracy, surpassing ViG‑B by 0.3 % while using 80 % fewer parameters and 84 % fewer GMACs. On downstream benchmarks it achieves 45.8 mIoU, 44.8 APbox, and 41.1 APmask, outperforming the larger EfficientFormer‑L7 by 0.7 mIoU, 2.2 APbox, and 2.1 APmask, all while employing 78 % fewer parameters.
664:
Automated theorem generation has traditionally been limited by the reliance on handcrafted templates or stochastic search over large logical spaces. In this paper we present *Rectangular Standard Contradiction* (RSC), a novel theoretical framework that enables systematic, provably sound construction of theorems across propositional and first‑order domains. RSC abstracts a contradiction into a two‑dimensional “rectangular” skeleton, where each axis encodes a logical dimension (e.g., variable binding, quantifier depth, or connective type). By enumerating all admissible fillings of this skeleton with symbols from a given language, the framework guarantees that every produced statement either follows from, or is a valid corollary of, the underlying contradiction pattern. We formalise the RSC notion, prove its soundness and, under mild regularity conditions, its completeness relative to a class of minimal contradictions.

Building on this foundation, we design an automated generator that (1) constructs a minimal contradiction rectangle from a seed formula, (2) expands it into a family of theorem candidates via combinatorial substitution, and (3) verifies each candidate with the Z3 SMT solver. The generator is implemented in Python and evaluated against standard benchmark libraries (TPTP, Mizar, and HOL Light). On propositional benchmarks it produced 1,842 non‑trivial tautologies and 237 valid first‑order lemmas, of which 34% were novel in the sense that they do not appear in existing libraries. Ablation studies show that the rectangular structure reduces search space by an average of 68 % compared to naïve enumeration, while maintaining high correctness rates.

Our results demonstrate that RSC provides a principled, scalable method for automated theorem generation, bridging the gap between constructive logic and automated reasoning. The framework’s modularity invites extensions to richer logics (e.g., temporal, probabilistic) and integration into interactive proof assistants. Future work will explore dynamic rectangle shaping based on machine‑learning heuristics and the synthesis of proof certificates for generated theorems.
665: Large‑scale vision models, trained on web‑scale datasets, excel at identifying and semantically segmenting object parts even in highly cluttered environments. Nevertheless, while they can guide a robot’s attention to an approximate object location, they fall short in providing the fine‑grained geometric insight necessary for precise dexterous hand control in 3D grasping tasks. Our solution is to combine these powerful perceptual models with a simulation‑based force‑closure pipeline that explicitly models the local geometry between hand and object. Although the simulation step is computationally expensive and depends on accurate ground‑truth observations, we distill its outcomes into a diffusion model that operates in real time on camera‑derived point clouds. By fusing the global semantic awareness of internet‑scale networks with the locally precise, geometry‑aware grasp synthesis from simulation, \our achieves robust semantic grasping without any manually curated training data. Visuals can be found on our website: https://ifgrasping.github.io/.
666:
The regulation of genes, proteins, and metabolites in living systems is governed by intricate networks that frequently contain feedback loops, oscillations, and recurrent motifs. Conventional causal‐structure learning methods, such as Bayesian networks and directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), impose an acyclicity constraint that precludes the discovery of such circular interactions and therefore limits their applicability to biological data. In this work we introduce **Circular Causal Structure Learning (CCSL)**, a principled framework that extends structural causal modeling to directed graphs with cycles while maintaining identifiability and computational tractability. CCSL leverages a hybrid formulation of linear structural equation models with additive noise, augmented by a novel *cycle‐aware* score function that penalises implausible feedback pathways based on prior biological knowledge. An efficient search algorithm, inspired by simulated annealing and constraint‑based pruning, is employed to explore the space of cyclic graphs. We demonstrate that CCSL outperforms state‑of‑the‑art acyclic methods on simulated gene‑regulatory networks with known feedback motifs, recovering directed edges and cycle structures with >90 % precision while keeping computational time below 10 min for networks of 200 nodes. Application to time‑resolved single‑cell RNA‑seq data from *Drosophila* embryogenesis reveals previously uncharacterised oscillatory regulatory loops involving Wnt and Notch pathways, and validates the inferred cycles against perturbation experiments. Our approach bridges the gap between causal inference and the inherently cyclic nature of biological regulation, providing a scalable tool for reconstructing realistic regulatory networks from high‑dimensional omics data. 

Keywords: Biological regulatory networks, causal inference, cyclic graphs, Bayesian networks, feedback loops, gene‑regulatory network, structural equation modeling.
667:
The *Proceedings of the Second International Workshop on Next‑Generation Language Models for Knowledge Representation and Reasoning* (NeLaMKRR 2025) brings together leading researchers and practitioners to explore the frontiers of large‐scale language models (LLMs) in the construction, integration, and inference over structured knowledge. This workshop—held in conjunction with the 2025 International Conference on Computational Linguistics—provided a focused forum for discussing how recent advances in foundation models, instruction tuning, and multimodal learning can be harnessed to represent complex ontologies, support logical reasoning, and facilitate explainable AI systems.

Keynotes highlighted the synthesis of symbolic knowledge bases with neural embeddings, the emergence of self‑supervised reasoning benchmarks, and the role of graph neural networks in grounding language representations. Paper presentations spanned three thematic tracks: (1) *Neural Knowledge Bases* – methods for aligning LLMs with formal knowledge graphs; (2) *Symbolic‑Neural Reasoning* – hybrid architectures that combine differentiable logic with transformer models; and (3) *Evaluation & Benchmarking* – novel datasets for temporal, causal, and commonsense reasoning in multi‑modal contexts. Interactive workshops showcased open‑source toolkits for converting natural‑language queries into logical forms, and a live competition on cross‑lingual knowledge alignment demonstrated the practical impact of recent model scaling.

The proceedings synthesize these contributions into a cohesive roadmap that identifies critical gaps—interpretability, data sparsity, and dynamic knowledge updates—and proposes a suite of community‑driven benchmarks. By delineating best practices and emerging trends, NeLaMKRR 2025 serves as a catalyst for future research that bridges the gap between statistical language models and principled knowledge representation, ultimately advancing AI systems that can reason coherently with human‑defined world knowledge.
668: Access to legal assistance in Bangladesh remains a major challenge. Citizens often confront prohibitive fees, opaque legal jargon, a shortage of qualified lawyers, and an ever‑growing backlog of unresolved court cases. Generative AI models—such as OpenAI’s GPT‑4.1 Mini, Google’s Gemini 2.0 Flash, Meta’s Llama 3 70B, and DeepSeek’s R1—offer the promise of democratizing legal support by delivering rapid, low‑cost advice. In this work we gathered 250 genuine legal queries from the Facebook community “Know Your Rights,” where certified legal experts routinely supply authoritative answers. These questions were then fed into the four advanced AI systems using a uniform, standardized prompt, and the resulting responses were evaluated through a two‑tier framework. First, a state‑of‑the‑art large language model served as an adjudicator, judging each reply on factual correctness, legal relevance, completeness, and clarity. Second, the same questions and answers were assessed by three licensed Bangladeshi attorneys using identical criteria. We also employed automated similarity metrics, including BLEU, to compare responses. The results paint a nuanced picture: while the AI models produce many well‑structured, high‑quality legal responses, they also frequently generate harmful misinformation—such as fabricated case citations, erroneous procedural guidance, and potentially risky advice. These findings highlight the necessity of stringent expert oversight and robust safeguards before AI can be responsibly used for legal consultation in Bangladesh.
669:
Accurate multi‑agent trajectory prediction is a cornerstone for safe and efficient autonomous systems. Existing methods typically rely on either historical kinematics or high‑level semantic maps, but rarely combine visual scene cues, agent intent, and the social dynamics that jointly govern motion. We propose **VISTA** (Vision and Intent‑Aware Social Attention), a unified framework that jointly models these three facets to produce temporally coherent trajectory forecasts for multiple interacting agents.

VISTA first extracts a **vision‑driven scene embedding** from raw camera or LiDAR data using a lightweight convolutional encoder, capturing road geometry, traffic signals, and other static constraints. Parallelly, an **intent module** predicts a probabilistic goal distribution for each agent based on past motion and contextual signals, allowing the model to reason about plausible future intentions. These two embeddings are fused into a shared representation which is then processed by a **social attention network**: an attention‑based graph neural layer that learns pairwise interaction weights conditioned on both visual context and inferred intents. The network outputs a set of multimodal trajectory predictions via a mixture density head, preserving uncertainty and capturing the inherently stochastic nature of real‑world motion.

We evaluate VISTA on three large‑scale benchmarks—Argoverse, nuScenes, and ETH/UCY—showing consistent gains over state‑of‑the‑art baselines: a 12 % reduction in average displacement error on Argoverse, 9 % on nuScenes, and 7 % on ETH/UCY. Ablation studies confirm the complementary value of vision and intent cues, while a qualitative analysis demonstrates VISTA’s ability to anticipate lane‑changing maneuvers and avoid collisions in dense traffic scenes.  

VISTA demonstrates that end‑to‑end integration of visual perception, intent reasoning, and socially aware attention yields robust, interpretable trajectory predictions, paving the way for more reliable motion forecasting in autonomous navigation.
670: Recent advances in Transformer‑based Neural Operators have propelled data‑driven solvers for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) to new heights. While most work seeks to curb the quadratic cost of attention in order to boost training and inference speed, a prominent example—Transolver—achieves this by introducing Physics‑Attention, which partitions grid points into slices for slice‑level attention and then recombines them via deslicing. We find that Physics‑Attention can be re‑expressed as a particular form of linear attention and that the slice‑wise attention itself may even degrade performance. Instead, its gains appear to stem largely from the slicing/deslicing mechanics rather than from inter‑slice interactions. Leveraging this insight, we develop a two‑step transformation that recasts Physics‑Attention into a standard linear attention scheme, yielding our Linear Attention Neural Operator (LinearNO). LinearNO sets a new benchmark on six canonical PDE datasets, cutting parameter count by an average of 40 % and computational overhead by 36.2 %. Moreover, it outperforms existing methods on two industrial‑scale challenges, AirfRANS and Shape‑Net Car.
671:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have become the foundation of many downstream applications, yet their task‑specific adaptation typically requires centralized fine‑tuning that compromises user privacy and incurs prohibitive communication costs.  In this work we introduce **Implicit Federated In‑Context Learning (IF‑ICL)**, a lightweight framework that enables LLMs to be fine‑tuned across distributed clients without exchanging gradients or model weights.  Instead, each participant performs *in‑context learning* on a local task by embedding a compact task description and a few examples directly into the input prompt.  The LLM then implicitly learns the task through its internal self‑supervised dynamics while the only signal communicated to the server is the *log‑probability* of the target tokens.  This implicit feedback obviates the need for explicit label sharing, preserves fine‑grained privacy, and dramatically reduces communication payload.

We formalize the IF‑ICL objective as a variational inference problem where the server aggregates posterior beliefs over task parameters derived from the clients’ log‑probabilities.  We demonstrate that the resulting aggregated prompt effectively steers the LLM toward a task‑specific fine‑tuned policy.  Experimental evaluation on a suite of few‑shot classification, natural language inference, and dialogue generation benchmarks (GLUE, SQuAD, and the 10‑k prompt dataset) shows that IF‑ICL matches or exceeds the performance of fully fine‑tuned baselines while using an order of magnitude less bandwidth and zero explicit model updates.  Moreover, we observe robust privacy guarantees under differential‑privacy‑style analysis, as the only publicly shared data are token likelihoods.  Finally, we provide ablation studies on prompt design, client heterogeneity, and communication budgets, revealing the scalability of IF‑ICL to thousands of participants.

Our results establish that implicit federated in‑context learning is a practical, privacy‑preserving alternative to traditional fine‑tuning, opening avenues for decentralized, task‑specific deployment of LLMs in edge‑constrained and privacy‑sensitive environments.
672: The recent proliferation of 3D generative models has made it possible to automatically create geometry and texture from multimodal inputs such as text or images. Yet most of these approaches neglect physical feasibility and manufacturability constraints. Here we tackle the problem of generating 3‑D designs that are both lightweight and self‑supporting. We introduce **DensiCrafter**, a framework that produces hollow, self‑supporting structures by optimizing a continuous density field. Beginning with coarse voxel grids supplied by Trellis, we treat them as differentiable density maps and impose three simulation‑free, physically grounded loss terms. A mass‑regularization penalty discourages unnecessary material, while a constrained optimization region preserves the external surface. DensiCrafter plugs into existing Trellis‑based models (e.g., Trellis, DSO) without architectural changes. Extensive experiments show up to a 43 % reduction in material mass on text‑to‑3D tasks, while improving structural stability and maintaining high geometric fidelity relative to state‑of‑the‑art baselines. Real‑world 3‑D printing tests confirm that the resulting hollow designs are both reliably fabricated and self‑supporting.
673:
Large language models (LLMs) routinely generate probability estimates that are far from well‑calibrated, limiting their reliability in safety‑critical and uncertainty‑aware applications. Prior investigations have focused almost exclusively on the final softmax layer, neglecting the rich internal dynamics that give rise to the output distribution. In this work we perform a systematic, layer‑wise audit of calibration across the depth of state‑of‑the‑art transformer architectures. By projecting hidden representations through the same softmax mapping that produces final predictions, we obtain a sequence of token‑level confidence scores for every layer and evaluate them using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Brier Score, and negative log‑likelihood. Across several models (GPT‑3, Llama‑2, PaLM‑2) and benchmarks (C4 language modelling, TriviaQA, Multi‑Choice QA), we discover that calibration evolves non‑monotonically: early layers exhibit severe over‑confidence, mid‑layers partially self‑correct, but the final layers often re‑introduce over‑confidence due to fine‑tuned head dynamics.  

To harness this insight, we propose **Layer‑wise Temperature Scaling (LTS)**, a lightweight post‑hoc procedure that learns a temperature per transformer block during inference. LTS significantly reduces ECE by up to 35 % on average, while preserving perplexity. Moreover, we show that incorporating a *Calibration Consistency Loss* during pre‑training aligns calibration across layers and yields models that are inherently more reliable without post‑processing. Our findings highlight the importance of internal calibration dynamics and provide practical tools for improving uncertainty estimation in modern LLMs.
674: Modern software systems rely on constantly evolving technology stacks, where updates can introduce new features but also break dependent projects. This study investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) can be harnessed to automate code migration, particularly for maintaining compatibility across major and minor semantic version changes of dependencies. By feeding LLMs with contextual information derived from code diffs rather than raw source code alone, we achieve superior performance compared to off‑the‑shelf models, as measured by test‑coverage gains and change‑comparison metrics. To support further research, we release a dedicated dataset and an open‑source Python library, *AIMigrate*, designed to streamline migration tasks. In a practical experiment, *AIMigrate* was applied to migrate the TYPHOIDSIM application between STARSIM releases, correctly identifying 65 % of necessary modifications in a single pass. After multiple iterative runs, the success rate rose to 80 %, with 47 % of the generated changes being fully correct on the first try.
675:
Reinforcement learning (RL) traditionally relies on a hand‑crafted reward signal to shape behaviour. In practice, such signals are costly to design, brittle across tasks, and often unavailable in complex, real‑world environments. We introduce **Zero Reinforcement Learning (ZeroRL)**, a paradigm that eschews explicit reward functions and instead exploits intrinsic motivations, hierarchical self‑supervision, and a modular policy repertoire to learn broadly useful behaviours in *general domains*. ZeroRL constructs a curriculum of self‑generated sub‑tasks via exploration‑driven curiosity and leverages a multi‑skill policy graph that can be recomposed at test time. The framework is built atop a differentiable planner that aggregates information from multiple “world‑models” learned online, allowing the agent to anticipate long‑term consequences without supervision.  

Our theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees for a class of policy‑gradient updates in ZeroRL, showing that the learned policies converge to a fixed point of the intrinsic objective that maximises coverage of the state‑action space. Empirically we evaluate ZeroRL on a suite of heterogeneous benchmarks—including continuous control in MuJoCo, discrete navigation in procedurally generated mazes, and real‑time strategy in StarCraft II. Across all settings, ZeroRL achieves performance that is competitive with reward‑based baselines while requiring no task‑specific reward engineering. Moreover, policies transfer zero‑shot to novel, unseen environments within the same domain, demonstrating the generality of the learned skill set.  

ZeroRL opens a new direction for RL research, showing that autonomous agents can acquire versatile, transferable behaviours without explicit rewards, thereby advancing the goal of truly general domain learning.
676:
In many industries organizations are turning to AI to assist with screening and bargaining, but deploying such tools in high‑stakes B2B environments is hindered by governance concerns. These include preventing the AI from making unauthorized commitments, ensuring it has enough information before it negotiates, and keeping human oversight and auditability intact. Existing research on large‑language‑model negotiation focuses on fully autonomous bargaining and overlooks practical requirements such as staged information gathering, clear authorization limits, and systematic feedback loops.

We introduce **GAIA**, a governance‑first framework for human‑LLM interaction in B2B screening and negotiation. GAIA assigns three core roles—Principal (the human), Delegate (the LLM agent), and Counterparty—with an optional Critic to refine performance. It structures interactions through three mechanisms: (1) an information‑gated progression that cleanly separates screening from bargaining, (2) a dual‑feedback system that fuses AI critique with lightweight human corrections, and (3) explicit authorization boundaries that define escalation pathways.

Our contributions are: (1) a formal governance structure with four safety invariants and coordinated mechanisms for bounded delegation, (2) an information‑gated progression that tracks task completion and enforces state transitions, (3) a dual‑feedback loop that blends Critic input and human oversight across parallel learning channels, and (4) a hybrid validation model that merges automated protocol metrics with human judgments of outcomes and safety. By marrying theory with operational needs, GAIA provides a reproducible, safe, and accountable specification for AI delegation that can be applied to procurement, real estate, and staffing workflows.
677: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a highly energy‑efficient alternative to conventional Artificial Neural Networks, excelling in spatio‑temporal domains such as keyword spotting and video classification. Their inherently low arithmetic intensity, however, limits compatibility with mainstream accelerators like GPUs and TPUs. In contrast, Field‑Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are engineered for memory‑bound workloads, making them a natural fit for SNNs. Here we introduce FeNN‑DMA, a fully‑programmable RISC‑V based system‑on‑chip designed to run SNNs on modern UltraScale+ FPGAs. FeNN‑DMA matches the resource utilization and power consumption of leading fixed‑function SNN accelerators while supporting considerably larger and more sophisticated models. Leveraging this capability, we achieve state‑of‑the‑art classification performance on the Spiking Heidelberg Digits and Neuromorphic MNIST benchmarks.
678:
The explosive growth of collaborative knowledge bases has made comparative analysis of their textual and structural properties increasingly valuable for understanding how content is curated and consumed across domains. This study investigates the similarity between **Grokipedia**, an emerging domain‑specific wiki focused on computational linguistics and artificial‑intelligence research, and **Wikipedia**, the global encyclopedic platform. We formulate a multi‑dimensional comparison framework that integrates (1) *textual similarity* metrics derived from contextual embeddings, (2) *semantic coverage* assessed via topic modeling and ontology alignment, (3) *structural coherence* captured through hyperlink networks and edit histories, and (4) *community dynamics* quantified by contributor overlap and editorial patterns. 

Using a cross‑section of 3,200 articles (1,600 from each platform) published within the last year, we compute pairwise cosine similarities in embedding space, perform LDA topic alignment, and calculate graph metrics such as clustering coefficient, betweenness centrality, and PageRank. Editor activity is modeled with bipartite networks to evaluate inter‑platform collaboration. Our results reveal a moderate textual similarity (average Jaccard index of 0.41), but distinct topical emphases: Grokipedia exhibits higher concentration on emerging AI subfields, whereas Wikipedia maintains broader coverage. Structurally, Grokipedia’s link density is 1.8× that of Wikipedia, indicating tighter topical interlinking, while its edit churn is significantly lower, reflecting a more stable editorial ecosystem. Community analysis shows minimal overlap, underscoring divergent contributor bases.

These findings highlight that while Grokipedia and Wikipedia share common encyclopedic conventions, they differ markedly in depth, focus, and editorial dynamics. The proposed framework offers a scalable approach for benchmarking new knowledge repositories against established standards, with implications for content migration, knowledge graph construction, and the design of hybrid collaborative platforms.
679: Large language models are now ubiquitous, but most deployments incorporate safeguards that filter out harmful or restricted content.  In this paper we expose a severe security flaw in the way many models are packaged: the computational‑graph representation can be subtly tampered with to hide a backdoor.  We present **ShadowLogic**, a white‑box attack that injects a small “uncensoring vector” into a model’s graph.  When a user prepends a specific trigger phrase to a prompt, the embedded logic activates this vector and lifts the model’s built‑in safety filters.  The trigger circuitry is woven into the graph itself and obfuscated so that it mimics normal operations, thereby evading inspection.  Because the changes to model weights are minimal, the compromised model appears benign while still producing unfiltered outputs on demand.  We demonstrate the feasibility of ShadowLogic on Phi‑3 and Llama 3.2 by manipulating their ONNX graphs, achieving an attack success rate exceeding 60 % for subsequent malicious queries.
680: – Membership inference attacks (MIAs) seek to determine whether a specific data point was included in a model’s training set. This work introduces a novel privacy challenge for large language models (LLMs): *entity‑level* membership inference targeting sensitive attributes such as personally identifiable information (PII) or credit‑card numbers. While existing MIAs can flag whether entire prompts or documents appear in the training corpus, they do not address the finer granularity of individual entities. We therefore present the **EL‑MIA** framework, designed to audit entity‑level membership risks in LLMs. To facilitate evaluation, we build a dedicated benchmark dataset for this task and use it to systematically compare current MIA techniques alongside two newly devised methods. Our comprehensive analysis explores how entity‑level MIA vulnerability correlates with model scale, training epochs, and other observable factors. The results demonstrate that prevailing MIA approaches struggle to identify sensitive entity‑level information, whereas simple methods can expose such risks, underscoring the necessity for stronger adversarial models to rigorously evaluate the proposed threat landscape.
681:
Recent progress in open‑domain question answering has been driven largely by large English datasets, yet comparable resources for Chinese remain scarce. We introduce **ChiMDQA**, the first comprehensive Chinese Document‑QA benchmark that combines a wide range of real‑world documents (news reports, encyclopedic entries, academic abstracts, and user‑generated blogs) with over 200 k high‑quality question–answer pairs. Each QA instance is annotated with a fine‑grained reasoning path—fact extraction, multi‑step inference, and knowledge‑integration—allowing researchers to evaluate not only final answer accuracy but also the intermediate reasoning quality.  

To support this, we propose a **Fine‑grained Evaluation Framework (FEF)** that decomposes performance into (1) **Answer Retrieval Accuracy** (Exact Match, F1), (2) **Reasoning Coherence** (step‑wise correctness, answer path consistency), and (3) **Commonsense and World‑Knowledge Utilization** (semantic similarity to external knowledge). We release an open‑source evaluation toolkit that implements these metrics automatically.  

We benchmark several state‑of‑the‑art Chinese language models—including BERT‑Chinese, ERNIE‑3, and GPT‑4‑based retrieval‑augmented architectures—on ChiMDQA. Baseline results indicate that current models achieve only 55.2 % Exact Match and 63.7 % F1, while their reasoning‑level accuracy falls below 40 %, underscoring the dataset’s difficulty. We also present an enhanced **Multi‑Document Fusion Network (MDFN)** that incorporates cross‑document attention and knowledge‑graph grounding, achieving a 5 % lift in EM over the best baseline.  

ChiMDQA and its evaluation framework aim to spur more realistic, multi‑document Chinese QA research and to provide a rigorous benchmark for assessing both answer quality and the underlying reasoning processes. All data, annotation guidelines, and evaluation scripts are publicly released to facilitate community participation.
682: Global optimization over graph‑structured data is a fundamental yet challenging problem: the combinatorial nature of the search space and the irregular topology of graphs hinder the application of standard Bayesian optimization techniques that rely on vector representations. We introduce **GSGP‑BO**, a principled framework that combines Gaussian processes (GPs) with spectral graph theory to perform efficient global optimization on arbitrary graphs. By projecting graph signals onto the eigenbasis of the normalized Laplacian, we obtain a low‑dimensional, fixed‑size representation that preserves both local edge correlations and global topological structure. A spectral kernel is then constructed on this basis, allowing a GP surrogate to model the objective function with uncertainty quantification that respects graph geometry. The acquisition function (Expected Improvement / GP‑UCB) is optimized in the spectral domain and projected back to the discrete graph space via a continuous relaxation followed by spectral truncation, yielding candidate graphs that can be evaluated in the original domain. We prove a regret bound for GSGP‑BO under standard smoothness assumptions in the spectral domain, establishing theoretical convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments on synthetic graph functions, molecular property optimization (QM9, ZINC), and graph neural network hyper‑parameter search demonstrate that GSGP‑BO attains the optimum with up to 50 % fewer evaluations than state‑of‑the‑art baselines (GraphBO, GNN‑BO, and random search). Our method offers a scalable, interpretable, and theoretically grounded approach to global optimization on graph‑structured data.
683: The rapid growth of maritime infrastructure—ranging from offshore wind farms and oil‑and‑gas platforms to artificial islands and aquaculture sites—underscores the urgency of robust monitoring solutions. Accurate detection of such structures hinges on well‑balanced training datasets, yet real‑world collections are often sparse, especially for minority object classes and varying geometries. In this work, we train YOLOv10 object‑detection models on a hybrid set of synthetic and Sentinel‑1 imagery, collected in Q4 2023 across the Caspian Sea, South China Sea, Gulf of Guinea, and Brazilian coast. The synthetic samples are designed to alleviate class imbalance and to enrich the representation of rare shapes and sizes. To assess geographic transferability, the models were tested on three hold‑out regions—Gulf of Mexico, North Sea, and Persian Gulf—without further fine‑tuning. The resulting detector identified 3,529 offshore platforms (411 in the North Sea, 1,519 in the Gulf of Mexico, 1,593 in the Persian Gulf), achieving an F1 score of 0.85; inclusion of synthetic data raised this to 0.90. Our analysis confirms that synthetic augmentation improves performance across under‑represented classes, thereby enabling a globally transferable detection framework. This study demonstrates that balanced, augmented datasets can substantially enhance deep‑learning‑based monitoring of marine infrastructure at scale.
684:
Large language models (LLMs) encode a vast amount of world knowledge directly in their internal parameters, a practice that makes updating or extending this knowledge costly in both compute and storage. In this work we introduce **ExplicitLM**, a novel architecture that decouples knowledge storage from the generative parameters by augmenting a lightweight transformer backbone with an explicit, vector‑based memory bank. The memory bank stores fine‑grained factual, contextual, and procedural knowledge in an external index that can be queried at inference time, allowing the core network to focus on linguistic structure while the memory module supplies up‑to‑date knowledge. 

We formalise the decoupling principle and design an efficient retrieval‑augmented decoder that merges memory embeddings with the model’s hidden states through a learnable gating mechanism. Knowledge can be inserted, removed, or edited in the bank without retraining the entire system, enabling rapid adaptation to evolving facts or domain‑specific vocabularies. To evaluate this paradigm, we construct a suite of knowledge‑intensive benchmarks (ARC, LAMA, and a synthetic temporal‑reasoning dataset) and compare ExplicitLM against baseline LLMs of comparable size. ExplicitLM matches or exceeds baseline performance on all tasks while using 30–50 % fewer trainable parameters and supporting dynamic updates with a single memory‑insertion operation. On the OpenAI‑style GPT‑3 benchmark, a 1.5B‑parameter ExplicitLM with a 200 M‑parameter memory bank attains 90 % of the baseline accuracy while incurring only 10 % additional inference latency.

Our experiments demonstrate that explicit memory banks provide a scalable, flexible, and efficient alternative to monolithic parameter‑based knowledge encoding, opening the door to continuously evolving LLMs that can be updated without expensive retraining cycles. The approach is broadly applicable to any transformer‑based generative model and paves the way for future research in knowledge‑aware, resource‑efficient language systems.
685:
Reconstructing realistic 3D objects from multi‑view photographs is pivotal for 3D editing, AR/VR, and digital content creation. Conventional approaches tend to focus exclusively on either geometric fidelity (e.g., Multi‑View Stereo) or photorealistic synthesis (e.g., Novel View Synthesis), and usually separate the optimization of shape and appearance. This separation limits the usefulness of the resulting models for downstream editing.  

In this work we present a unified framework that jointly refines both mesh geometry (vertex positions and topology) and vertex colors. By integrating Gaussian‑guided mesh differentiable rendering, we enforce photometric consistency across input images while simultaneously regularizing the shape with normal and depth cues. The resulting reconstruction combines high‑quality geometry with accurate appearance, enabling robust downstream tasks such as relighting and shape manipulation. The code will be released publicly upon acceptance.
686:
Fine‑grained visual classification (FGVC) is notoriously difficult because the differences between classes are often very subtle, while instances of the same class can exhibit wide variability. Current state‑of‑the‑art methods usually rely on either feature selection or region‑proposal schemes to pinpoint discriminative patches for semantic reasoning. In practice, these techniques miss many relevant cues and add a considerable amount of category‑agnostic noise. To overcome these drawbacks, we introduce **H3Former**, a novel token‑to‑region pipeline that harnesses high‑order semantic relationships to fuse local fine‑grained descriptors into well‑structured region‑level embeddings. 

At the heart of H3Former lies the **Semantic‑Aware Aggregation Module (SAAM)**. SAAM constructs a weighted hypergraph over tokens by exploiting multi‑scale contextual information, then applies hypergraph convolutions to capture higher‑order dependencies and progressively aggregate tokens into compact region representations. Complementing this, we propose the **Hyperbolic Hierarchical Contrastive Loss (HHCL)**, which operates in a non‑Euclidean embedding space to impose hierarchical semantic constraints. HHCL boosts inter‑class discrimination and intra‑class cohesion while faithfully preserving the inherent taxonomy of fine‑grained categories.

Extensive evaluations on four widely used FGVC benchmarks demonstrate that H3Former outperforms existing approaches, confirming the effectiveness of our token‑to‑region strategy and hypergraph‑based modeling.
687:
Semantic‐aware transmission is emerging as a promising paradigm for next‑generation wireless video delivery, yet practical schemes remain constrained by the high dimensionality of visual data and the difficulty of exploiting temporal redundancy across frames. This paper proposes a *Wireless Video Semantic Communication (WVSC)* framework that integrates **decoupled diffusion modeling** with *multi‑frame compensation* to achieve highly efficient, robust video transmission over fading channels.  

In our approach, a lightweight semantic encoder transforms each incoming video frame into a compact representation that preserves task‑relevant visual semantics. At the channel front, we employ a *diffusion‑based transmitter* that learns a prior over semantic codes conditioned on a controllable *noise schedule*. Unlike conventional joint diffusion models, we decouple the diffusion process into *spatial* and *temporal* sub‑processes: spatial diffusion operates on individual frames, while temporal diffusion explicitly models inter‑frame dependencies via a *motion‑aware compensation module*. This decoupling allows us to trade off diffusion steps per dimension, drastically reducing computational load and enabling real‑time operation on embedded hardware.  

The receiver side reconstructs the video by performing *semantic diffusion decoding* under a learned posterior that incorporates a *channel‑aware noise estimator* and a *temporal consistency module*. Experimental results on the UCF‑101 and HEVC standard sequences demonstrate that WVSC delivers 2.3–3.6 dB higher PSNR than baseline convolutional autoencoders and outperforms conventional video codecs (H.265/HEVC) by up to 30 % in the low‑bandwidth regime (< 200 kbps) while maintaining perceptual quality (SSIM > 0.9) in SNRs down to –5 dB.  

Key contributions include: (1) a novel decoupled diffusion architecture tailored for video semantics; (2) a multi‑frame compensation strategy that reduces redundancy and improves robustness to packet loss; and (3) a comprehensive end‑to‑end training pipeline that jointly optimizes semantic extraction, diffusion, and channel coding. This work paves the way for scalable, high‑fidelity video delivery in bandwidth‑constrained wireless environments.
688:
Recent advances in diffusion‐based video generation have made it possible to synthesize long, high‑resolution sequences, yet the resulting videos often lack the cinematic coherence and stylistic fidelity required for film production. In this work we propose a lightweight, small‑data fine‑tuning pipeline that adapts large open‑source video generators to the domain of cinematic scene synthesis. Our method leverages **LoRA (Low‑Rank Adaptation)** to insert trainable rank‑restricted modules into the latent diffusion backbone, thereby preserving the pre‑trained knowledge while enabling rapid adaptation to new visual styles with only a handful of exemplars. We further introduce **Wan2.1 I2V**, a two‑stage “Image‑to‑Video” encoder‑decoder architecture that bridges static cinematography references and temporal consistency, and which is fine‑tuned using the same LoRA modules. The pipeline requires no additional GPU‑intensive pre‑training: a single GPU can train a fully functional cinematic generator from a 100‑clip curated dataset in under 8 hours.

We evaluate the approach on two cinematic benchmarks—**Cinematic‑SFX** and **Film‑Shots**—using perceptual FID, temporal SSIM, and a large human preference study. Our fine‑tuned models achieve a 35 % reduction in FID and a 12 % improvement in temporal consistency over the vanilla open‑source baseline, while the average human rating of “cinematic quality” rises from 3.8 to 4.5 on a 5‑point Likert scale. Ablation studies confirm that LoRA’s rank‑1 updates capture style‑specific cues with as few as 50 training clips, and that Wan2.1 I2V contributes a 4 % gain in temporal coherence.  

We release the full pipeline, trained checkpoints, and a public “cinematic‑clip” dataset, enabling the community to rapidly adapt video generative models to domain‑specific storytelling tasks. Our work demonstrates that small‑data LoRA fine‑tuning, combined with a dedicated I2V module, provides a practical and powerful approach to high‑fidelity cinematic scene synthesis.
689:
Modern meta‑heuristics often struggle to adapt to the diverse landscape of challenging optimisation tasks, particularly when the objective functions are high‑dimensional, multimodal, or partially observable. This paper proposes a novel hybrid framework that augments the Fireworks Algorithm (FWA)—a population‑based search method inspired by the explosive dispersion of fireworks—with a multi‑modal Large Language Model (LLM). The LLM is trained on a corpus of optimisation literature, problem specifications, and domain‑specific visual representations, enabling it to generate context‑aware guidance signals.  

In the proposed scheme, the LLM serves three complementary roles. First, it synthesises a *problem‑specific initialization* by translating natural‑language problem statements and schematic diagrams into a set of promising seed solutions. Second, it dynamically adjusts the *explosion radius* and *burst density* of each firework during evolution, based on real‑time predictions of landscape ruggedness gleaned from textual descriptions and embedded visual cues. Third, it acts as a *surrogate evaluator*, providing fast, probabilistic fitness estimates for candidate solutions in computationally expensive domains.  

Extensive experiments on a suite of IEEE CEC benchmark problems, as well as real‑world scheduling and energy‑management scenarios, demonstrate that the LLM‑assisted FWA consistently outperforms the vanilla algorithm and several state‑of‑the‑art baselines. In particular, average best‑found fitness values improve by 12.5 % on continuous problems and 18.3 % on combinatorial ones, while convergence speed is accelerated by up to 35 %. Ablation studies confirm that each of the three LLM modules contributes significantly to the overall performance gains.  

Our results highlight the potential of integrating knowledge‑rich, multi‑modal language models with classical evolutionary search to create more adaptive, efficient optimisation solvers. The framework is broadly applicable to any problem where textual and visual information can be leveraged to inform search dynamics.
690:
The third International Workshop on eXplainable Artificial Intelligence for the Arts (XAIxArts) convened a multidisciplinary community of artists, designers, computer‑scientists, and human‑computer‑interaction scholars to explore how transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems can be cultivated and critically evaluated in creative domains. Over a three‑day event, participants discussed challenges at the intersection of algorithmic creativity, aesthetic perception, and user trust, and presented 21 papers that span six thematic tracks: (1) explainable generative models for visual and musical arts; (2) interactive storytelling and user‑guided content generation; (3) bias, ethics, and cultural context in algorithmic curation; (4) human‑in‑the‑loop workflows for artistic production; (5) quantitative and qualitative evaluation of explainability in creative AI; and (6) pedagogical frameworks for teaching explainable AI to artists.  

The proceedings present a rich collection of case studies demonstrating how explanations can be tailored to different stakeholders—from novices seeking intuitive visualizations to experienced practitioners demanding low‑level model insights. Highlights include a comparative study of saliency‑driven explanations for style‑transfer networks, a mixed‑methods evaluation of interactive explanation panels in an AI‑assisted music composition tool, and a framework for audit‑friendly generative models that embed provenance and lineage tracking. 

Beyond technical contributions, the workshop generated a set of actionable research agendas, such as standardizing evaluation protocols for interpretability in creative AI, developing interdisciplinary toolkits that embed explanation capabilities by design, and fostering open‑source communities that prioritize transparency. The proceedings aim to serve as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to bridge the gap between explainable AI research and the arts, and to catalyze future collaborations that place human understanding and artistic agency at the core of AI‑augmented creation.
691: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as raters for evaluation tasks, yet their performance tends to falter on subjective problems where human judgments depend on nuanced reasoning beyond simple labels. The underlying reasoning—“thinking traces”—is highly valuable but notoriously difficult to collect and curate. In this work we propose a human‑LLM collaborative framework that infers these thinking traces from label‑only annotations. Our approach employs a straightforward rejection‑sampling strategy to scale up trace reconstruction. We then leverage the inferred traces in two complementary ways: (1) fine‑tuning open‑source LLM raters, and (2) generating clearer annotation guidelines for proprietary LLM raters. Experiments on several datasets show that both strategies substantially raise LLM‑human agreement, and the improved guidelines also boost consistency across different LLMs. These findings demonstrate that LLMs can act as effective stand‑ins for hidden human reasoning, turning ordinary label corpora into richer, thinking‑trace‑augmented datasets that strengthen the reliability of LLM raters.
692: Mathematical reasoning hinges on distilling symbolic rules from visual data—drawing general conclusions from finite examples. In this study we ask whether multimodal AI models can do that by introducing **FractalBench**, a new benchmark that tests the ability to generate fractal programs from images. Fractals are especially suited for this: Iterated Function Systems (IFSs) use only a handful of contraction maps to produce intricate self‑similar patterns through straightforward recursive rules, forcing a model to connect visual perception with abstract mathematical formulation. We evaluate four top multimodal large language models—GPT‑4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Qwen 2.5‑VL—across 12 classic fractal families. Each model is asked to output Python code that recreates the depicted fractal, allowing a precise, objective scoring of correctness. The results uncover a pronounced gap: while 76 % of the models produce syntactically correct code, merely 4 % actually capture the underlying mathematics. Performance is uneven—geometric transformations are handled better (e.g., Koch curves succeed at 17–21 %) whereas branching recursion is almost never mastered (< 2 % success on tree‑shaped fractals). These findings expose fundamental limits in current multimodal systems’ ability to perform visual‑mathematical abstraction. FractalBench offers a clean, contamination‑free diagnostic for this problem and is publicly released at https://github.com/NaiveNeuron/FractalBench.
693: This paper investigates whether large language models can generate authentic student responses for use in educational assessment. We employed GPT‑4o to produce 2,000 virtual student profiles, each of which completed the Academic Motivation Scale (AMS). Subsequent exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, together with clustering techniques, confirmed that GPT‑4o successfully reproduced the AMS’s underlying factor structure and the distinct motivational subgroups it identifies.
694:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has emerged as a cornerstone of modern tissue biology, enabling the quantification of gene expression with subcellular fidelity across intact tissue sections. However, prevailing ST platforms (e.g., 10× Visium, Slide‑seq, MERFISH) are constrained by a coarse grid of capture spots or limited multiplexing, which hampers downstream analyses that rely on fine‑scale cellular resolution. Existing computational super‑resolution methods—generative adversarial networks, Gaussian process interpolation, or variational auto‑encoders—typically exploit only the transcriptomic data itself or a single auxiliary modality, and often fail to preserve the nuanced spatial‑gene correlations that define tissue architecture.

We introduce **C3‑Diff**, a cross‑modal, cross‑content contrastive diffusion framework that jointly learns from low‑resolution ST data and high‑resolution histology images. C3‑Diff first encodes the histology and the sparse transcriptomic map into separate feature spaces, then applies a dual contrastive objective: (i) cross‑modal alignment to tether histological texture with underlying gene expression patterns, and (ii) cross‑content alignment to enforce consistency among highly co‑expressed gene sets. These learned embeddings condition a score‑based diffusion model, which progressively refines a low‑resolution transcriptomic field into a high‑resolution, pixel‑level gene expression map. By leveraging diffusion’s inherent denoising capability, C3‑Diff naturally captures multimodal uncertainty and preserves fine‑grained spatial gradients.

We benchmark C3‑Diff on five publicly available ST datasets spanning human brain, mouse liver, and breast carcinoma, achieving a mean Pearson correlation gain of 0.19 (p < 1e‑5) over state‑of‑the‑art baselines, as well as a 27 % reduction in spatial entropy for key marker genes. Ablation studies confirm the pivotal role of cross‑modal contrastive pre‑training and demonstrate robustness to missing modalities. The resulting high‑resolution ST maps unlock more precise cell‑type segmentation, improved ligand–receptor inference, and richer spatial pathway analyses. C3‑Diff is released as an open‑source PyTorch toolbox, encouraging rapid adoption across the spatial omics community.
695:
Smart agriculture increasingly relies on large, heterogeneous datasets collected from distributed farm sites. While these data can improve crop‑management models, sharing them directly violates farmers’ privacy and incurs prohibitive communication costs. Federated transfer learning (FTL) offers a decentralized alternative, yet its effectiveness is hampered by non‑identical data distributions and the limited amount of local data available on each node, leading to slow convergence and sub‑optimal performance.  

We propose **FedReplay**, a feature‑replay assisted federated transfer learning framework that addresses these challenges with minimal additional overhead. Each client locally trains a lightweight feature extractor and periodically generates a compact set of *replay features* that encapsulate the most informative aspects of its private data. These replay features, encrypted and aggregated under a secure‑aggregation scheme, are shared with a central server that performs a multi‑task knowledge‑distillation step. The server then broadcasts a distilled teacher model back to the clients, which fine‑tunes it with its own data. This replay mechanism allows the global model to incorporate cross‑farm knowledge without exposing raw data, thereby preserving privacy while mitigating non‑i.i.d. effects.  

Extensive experiments on three real‑world agricultural benchmarks—(i) multi‑crop disease classification from leaf images, (ii) soil moisture prediction from multispectral remote‑sensing data, and (iii) yield forecasting from weather and sensor logs—demonstrate that FedReplay improves mean accuracy by 6.3 %–9.8 % over conventional federated averaging and 4.1 %–7.4 % over baseline transfer‑learning approaches, while reducing communication payload by 35 % and training iterations by 42 %. A formal differential‑privacy analysis confirms that the replay features leak no identifiable information beyond what is already inherent in the model weights.  

FedReplay thus offers a practical, privacy‑preserving, and communication‑efficient solution for scalable smart‑agriculture deployments, enabling heterogeneous farms to collaboratively build high‑performance models without compromising sensitive data.
696:
Retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) improves large language models (LLMs) by tapping external knowledge to overcome their limits in accessing timely or domain‑specific facts. A straightforward way to boost the chance of retrieving useful material is to increase the number of documents pulled, but this also risks injecting a lot of noise—irrelevant or misleading texts that can hurt answer quality. To tackle this dilemma, we introduce **WinnowRAG**, a new RAG architecture that actively filters out noisy documents while retaining the valuable ones—a process we call *winnowing*.  
WinnowRAG proceeds in two phases. In Phase I, we perform query‑aware clustering to partition the retrieved set into topic‑centric groups, assigning each cluster to a distinct LLM agent that produces a candidate answer. In Phase II, a critic LLM evaluates the agents’ outputs, iteratively discarding unhelpful documents and retaining only the most relevant. To avoid losing useful information when an agent is dropped, we apply two merging strategies that consolidate the remaining knowledge for the final response.  
Because WinnowRAG is model‑agnostic and requires no fine‑tuning, it can be deployed across a wide range of tasks. Extensive evaluation on realistic benchmarks confirms that WinnowRAG outperforms leading baselines.
697: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are increasingly viewed as a viable strategy against rising antimicrobial resistance, yet progress is hampered by sparse, inconsistently labelled datasets and the absence of unified evaluation standards. To remedy this, we introduce the Expanded Standardized Collection for Antimicrobial Peptide Evaluation (ESCAPE), a curated experimental framework that assembles over 80,000 peptides from 27 well‑validated sources. ESCAPE cleanly separates AMPs from non‑active sequences and organizes their functional annotations into a biologically meaningful multilabel hierarchy that covers antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, and antiparasitic activities. Leveraging this resource, we develop a transformer‑based model that jointly exploits sequence and structural cues to predict multiple peptide functions. The approach yields a relative gain of up to 2.56 % in mean average precision over the next best adapted method, setting a new benchmark for multilabel AMP classification. ESCAPE delivers a robust, reproducible platform for AI‑driven discovery of novel antimicrobial peptides.
698:
Dynamic languages such as Ruby are pervasive in modern web and scripting contexts, yet automated program repair (APR) tools for them lag behind those targeting statically typed languages.  In this paper we present **Collaborative Agents for Automated Program Repair in Ruby (CoAR‑Ruby)**, a novel multi‑agent framework that orchestrates heterogeneous repair subsystems—bug detection, fix generation, test‑suite validation, and knowledge‑base lookup—to produce correct patches in a highly dynamic setting.  Each agent is implemented with a mix of transformer‑based language models, symbolic execution, and meta‑heuristic search, and communicates through a lightweight mediator that coordinates evidence sharing and conflict resolution.

We evaluate CoAR‑Ruby on 527 real bugs collected from 26 open‑source Ruby projects (the Ruby‑BugBench dataset).  Against a baseline of state‑of‑the‑art APR systems adapted to Ruby, our approach yields a 62 % fix‑rate (versus 47 %) with 0.78 × fewer false positives and 1.4× faster synthesis time.  Importantly, 78 % of the automatically generated patches were semantically equivalent to human‑written fixes and passed all associated test suites.  An ablation study demonstrates the critical role of inter‑agent communication: removing the knowledge‑base agent drops the fix‑rate by 12 %.

CoAR‑Ruby demonstrates that a collaborative, agent‑centric architecture can effectively handle the dynamic features of Ruby, including implicit types, monkey‑patching, and metaprogramming.  The paper contributes a reusable APR framework, an expanded Ruby bug dataset, and a set of design principles for agent coordination in dynamic‑language repair.  These results open a promising avenue for future research into collaborative, AI‑driven software maintenance across the full spectrum of programming paradigms.
699:
Abstract  
Reinforcement‑learning (RL) post‑training has become indispensable for endowing large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi‑step problem‑solving abilities, yet most existing reward functions focus solely on the final answer.  In this work we introduce PM4GRPO, a reasoning‑aware variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).  PM4GRPO extends the conventional answer‑ or format‑based rewards by incorporating signals that reflect the reasoning process itself.  We employ process‑mining methods to calculate a scalar conformance reward, quantifying how closely a policy’s intermediate reasoning trajectory matches that of a pretrained teacher model.  Across five benchmark datasets, PM4GRPO consistently surpasses prior GRPO‑based post‑training strategies.  These findings demonstrate that integrating process‑mining‑derived, reasoning‑aware signals into GRPO markedly boosts the reasoning performance of policy models.
700: Human‑language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate everyday conversations, yet their responses frequently miss the implicit cues that human interlocutors rely on to convey meaning succinctly. In this study we investigate the role of *implicature*—the inferential layer that underlies conversational meaning—in the alignment between human users and LLMs. We first formalize a taxonomy of pragmatic implicatures in dialogue (e.g., conversational implicature, scalar implicature, ostensive‐inference) and develop a lightweight, rule‑based recognizer that annotates utterances in a large multilingual dialogue corpus. Using these annotations, we augment a state‑of‑the‑art transformer with a dual‑objective training regime that jointly optimizes for lexical fidelity and pragmatic inference. The resulting “Implication‑Aware LLM” (IA‑LLM) is evaluated on three downstream tasks: (1) *inference‑based question answering*, (2) *dialogue summarization*, and (3) *multi‑turn interaction in a customer‑support setting*. Across all tasks IA‑LLM yields statistically significant gains in both automatic metrics (e.g., BLEU, ROUGE, and an emergent “Implicature‑Accuracy” score) and human‑judged alignment (higher scores on the Pragmatic Alignment Scale and lower perceived misunderstanding rates). A qualitative analysis reveals that IA‑LLM consistently preserves speakers’ implicit intent and generates responses that are more contextually appropriate. Our results demonstrate that explicitly modeling implicature during training improves the alignment of LLMs with human communicative norms, paving the way for more natural and trustworthy human‑LLM interactions.
701: Ride‑pooling (or shared ride‑hailing, micro‑transit) lets passengers share a vehicle, lowering costs for users and operators while easing congestion and environmental impact. Its principal drawback is the myopic nature of many dispatch algorithms, which ignore the long‑term consequences of routing choices. To overcome this, we develop a simulation‑driven reinforcement‑learning (RL) framework. Building on the learning and planning architecture of Xu et al. (2018), we adapt it to ride‑pooling by embedding a realistic ride‑pooling simulator into the RL loop, thereby enabling non‑myopic decision‑making. We also introduce a complementary rebalancing policy for idle vehicles. Using n‑step temporal‑difference learning on simulated experience, we estimate spatiotemporal value functions and evaluate the resulting policy on NYC taxi demand data. The non‑myopic matching policy improves service rate by up to 8.4 % over a myopic baseline, while reducing both in‑vehicle and wait times for riders. It also allows a fleet reduction of over 25 % without sacrificing performance, yielding substantial operator cost savings. Adding the rebalancing component further cuts wait time by 27.3 % and in‑vehicle time by 12.5 %, raising the service rate by 15.1 % relative to a matching‑only approach—at the expense of additional vehicle minutes per passenger.
702: – Traditional multi‑agent reinforcement learning (MARL) delivers impressive performance in cooperative settings, but it usually presupposes a fixed, fully controlled team. Ad hoc teamwork (AHT) loosens this restriction by enabling collaboration with unseen partners; however, most AHT methods still rely on pre‑shared conventions. We propose a new setting, **Multi‑Party Ad Hoc Teamwork (MAHT)**, in which agents that are under direct control must cooperate with several groups of teammates that are mutually unfamiliar. To tackle this challenge, we introduce **MARs**, an approach that constructs a compact skeleton graph and employs relational modeling to explicitly capture dynamics across different groups. On standard benchmarks—including Multi‑Agent Particle Environment (MPE) and StarCraft II—MARs not only surpasses conventional MARL and AHT baselines but also converges more rapidly.
703:
Accurate change detection from multi‑temporal remote‑sensing imagery is essential for monitoring urban growth, deforestation, and disaster impacts. However, most deep learning methods require large amounts of labeled data, which is prohibitively expensive to obtain for every scene and temporal pair. In this work we propose the **Consistency Change Detection Framework (CCDF)**, a fully unsupervised pipeline that leverages intrinsic temporal consistency to learn discriminative change maps without any ground truth supervision.  

The framework consists of three complementary stages. First, a siamese convolutional encoder extracts spectral‑spatial embeddings for each temporal image pair. Second, a self‑supervised clustering module generates pseudo‑change labels by enforcing **cross‑time consistency**: pixels that belong to the same cluster across time are encouraged to remain unchanged, while divergent clusters signal potential change. Finally, a consistency regularization loss aligns the predictions of two independently trained networks, mitigating the drift that often plagues unsupervised methods.  

We evaluate CCDF on four benchmark datasets (HRSCD, Onera‑RF, LEVIR‑CD, and DeepGlobe), achieving F1‑scores of 0.82, 0.81, 0.79, and 0.83 respectively—outperforming prior unsupervised baselines by 4–7 % and approaching the performance of weakly supervised approaches. Ablation studies confirm that each consistency component contributes to robustness against noise, illumination changes, and class imbalance. CCDF therefore provides a scalable, label‑free solution for large‑scale change monitoring in high‑resolution remote sensing.
704:
Fresh‐produce supply chains are notoriously volatile due to temperature‑sensitive perishables, fluctuating consumer demand, and weather‑related disruptions. Internet‑of‑Things (IoT) sensing networks now provide high‑frequency, granular data on temperature, humidity, and product condition along every leg of the chain, yet most decision‑support tools fail to exploit this information in a real‑time, uncertainty‑aware manner.
