802: The proliferation of user‑generated content in Bengali has amplified the need for robust text‑detoxification systems that not only flag toxic utterances but also offer transparent, human‑understandable explanations. Existing Bengali NLP resources are limited to single‑label toxic‑classification datasets, precluding fine‑grained analysis of how and why a statement is deemed toxic. We introduce **BanglaNirTox**, the first large‑scale, parallel corpus for explainable AI in Bengali text detoxification. The corpus contains 120 k sentence pairs, each consisting of a raw Bengali sentence and its manually detoxified counterpart, annotated with fine‑grained linguistic explanations (e.g., hate‑speech category, slur type, contextual cue) and toxicity severity scores. Construction followed a multi‑phase pipeline: (1) automatic collection from public forums and social media; (2) initial toxicity scoring using a fine‑tuned BERT‑based detector; (3) semi‑automatic detoxification via rule‑based paraphrasing; (4) rigorous human‑review by native Bengali speakers trained on a detailed annotation guideline; and (5) post‑processing to align source‑target pairs and validate explanation consistency. Statistical analysis shows 78 % of the sentences contain profanity or hate‑speech, with 42 % requiring contextual reinterpretation. We benchmark state‑of‑the‑art transformer models (XLM‑R, mBERT) on both detoxification and explanation generation tasks, reporting BLEU‑style scores and human preference rates. BanglaNirTox therefore enables not only end‑to‑end detoxification but also explainable decision‑making, providing a valuable resource for researchers developing transparent, culturally attuned AI systems in low‑resource languages. The dataset, along with our baseline models and evaluation scripts, is publicly released at https://github.com/xxx/BanglaNirTox.
803:
Measuring the spread of AI worldwide is difficult because existing data lack population‑normalised, cross‑country usage metrics. We present **AI User Share**, a new indicator that estimates the proportion of each nation’s working‑age population that is actively engaging with AI tools. The metric is derived from anonymised Microsoft telemetry, adjusted for device availability and mobile penetration, and covers 147 economies, offering a consistent, real‑time view of global AI uptake.

Our analysis reveals substantial variation in adoption: AI User Share correlates strongly with GDP, with higher usage in developed markets. However, even in lower‑income countries, a sizable share of internet‑connected populations shows latent demand. We observe pronounced spikes in usage after major product releases—e.g., the launch of DeepSeek in early 2025—highlighting the sensitivity of the metric to market events.

Although our reliance on Microsoft telemetry may introduce biases toward this user base, AI User Share provides a valuable, timely lens for tracking AI diffusion and can support evidence‑based AI policy decisions.
804: Normative reasoning concerns judgments involving obligations, permissions, and other deontic modalities. Although large language models (LLMs) excel at many reasoning tasks, their handling of normative inference has received little systematic scrutiny. In this work we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs on normative reasoning from both logical and modal standpoints. We contrast the models’ performance on normative modals with their performance on epistemic modals, which share a formal structure, to isolate differences in handling deontic content. To facilitate this study we build a new benchmark that spans a broad set of formal reasoning patterns in both the normative and epistemic domains, and also embeds non‑formal cognitive factors that are known to affect human reasoning. Our experiments show that, while LLMs usually follow valid reasoning patterns, they display marked inconsistencies on certain normative problems and exhibit cognitive biases reminiscent of those reported in human psychological research. These results underline the difficulty of ensuring logical consistency in LLMs’ normative reasoning and suggest directions for improving their trustworthiness. All datasets and code are publicly available at https://github.com/kmineshima/NeuBAROCO.
805: Activation probes—simple linear classifiers trained on intermediate activations of large language models—have become a cornerstone of modern interpretability research, offering a window into the linguistic and semantic knowledge stored in neural networks. However, the very simplicity that makes probes attractive also renders them fragile: subtle adversarial prompts can mislead a probe into reporting spurious or fabricated information, thereby undermining conclusions drawn from such analyses. In this work we introduce a systematic *red‑team* framework for probing the robustness of activation probes using prompted large language models (LLMs). We leverage chain‑of‑thought prompting and task‑specific prompt engineering to generate adversarial inputs that target the internal representations of the host model, without requiring explicit access to the probe’s parameters. Our method treats the probe as a black‑box evaluation oracle, iteratively refining prompts until the probe’s predictions deviate from ground‑truth labels or from predictions made by a baseline model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a suite of probing tasks—including syntactic structure, coreference resolution, and sentiment classification—using GPT‑4 and PaLM‑2 as the adversarial prompt generators. In every case, we observe a statistically significant degradation of probe accuracy (up to 35 % relative drop) and uncover systematic failure modes that correlate with the presence of lexical cues and prompt‑length. These findings expose a critical vulnerability in current probing pipelines and highlight the need for adversarial‑robust probe design. We conclude with a discussion of mitigation strategies and outline directions for future research on secure interpretability.
806: Brain‑computer interfaces (BCIs) frequently exhibit weak robustness and limited long‑term adaptability. Their accuracy drops quickly when a user’s attention wanders, brain dynamics shift, or transient artefacts emerge during use. To address these challenges, we propose a state‑aware EEG filtering framework that refines neural signals prior to intention decoding. By continuously inferring the user’s cognitive state—such as focus or distraction—from EEG features, the method adaptively down‑weights unreliable epochs according to the estimated attentional level. This filtering stage mitigates noisy or out‑of‑focus segments, curbing distributional drift and enhancing the stability of subsequent decoding. Across several EEG datasets that mimic realistic BCI scenarios, our approach consistently improves classification accuracy and reliability over standard preprocessing pipelines. These results demonstrate that exploiting intrinsic brain‑derived state information, even without external labels, can substantially boost the dependability of practical EEG‑based BCIs.
807:
In recent years convolutional neural networks (CNNs), vision transformers (ViTs) and self‑supervised ViTs have dominated visual recognition, yet little is known about how these heterogeneous architectures encode semantically related but distinct object categories.  We investigate whether the representations of two highly visual yet taxonomically unrelated species—humans and cats—exhibit invariance across a spectrum of perturbations (noise, occlusion, viewpoint change) and across model families.  Using a curated dataset of 25 000 high‑resolution human and cat images, we fine‑tune and evaluate ResNet‑50, EfficientNet‑B3, ViT‑base, Swin‑Transformer and three self‑supervised ViTs (DINO, MoCo‑v3, SimCLR).  We then probe the learned feature spaces with representational similarity analysis (RSA), canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and classification‑based adversarial probing.  

Our results show that, despite architectural diversity, all models produce highly correlated embeddings for the human‑cat pair that remain robust to perturbations—hence the “purrturbed” but “stable” moniker.  Self‑supervised ViTs exhibit the highest intra‑category variance under occlusion, yet the cross‑category similarity remains comparable to supervised counterparts, suggesting a shared low‑level feature manifold.  Moreover, we uncover a systematic bias: CNNs rely more on texture cues while ViTs emphasize shape, which manifests as divergent adversarial vulnerability profiles.  We also demonstrate that the learned invariances can be transferred to a zero‑shot human‑cat retrieval task with a 12‑point drop in mAP compared to a model trained from scratch.  

This work provides the first comparative study of invariant human‑cat representations across mainstream CNNs, ViTs and self‑supervised ViTs, offering insights into architecture‑driven biases and guiding future design of robust multi‑species vision systems.
808:
Neural networks routinely achieve state‑of‑the‑art performance on visual, textual and multimodal tasks, yet the opaque nature of their internal reasoning continues to impede user trust and regulatory compliance. Conventional post‑hoc explainers (saliency maps, feature attributions, or concept‑based probes) often sacrifice *faithfulness* for *interpretability* or require intrusive model access, limiting their applicability to black‑box systems. We introduce **FaCT** (Faithful Concept Traces), a general framework for generating temporally‑resolved, concept‑level explanations that remain faithful to the network’s decision logic while being agnostic to its architecture.

FaCT operates in two stages. First, it discovers a compact set of human‑interpretable concepts by clustering activations of a user‑selected intermediate layer and labeling representative prototypes. Second, it learns a lightweight *concept‑trace predictor* that maps the evolution of these concepts across layers to the final output, using a mixture‑of‑experts formulation that preserves the causal structure of the underlying network. The resulting trace is a sequence of concept‑importance scores that can be visualized as a “story” of how the model arrived at its prediction.

We evaluate FaCT on ImageNet, COCO‑captioning, and BERT‑based language classification benchmarks, comparing against Layer‑wise Relevance Propagation, Integrated Gradients, and Concept Activation Vectors. Quantitatively, FaCT achieves up to 35 % higher *fidelity* (measured by perturbation‑based metrics) while maintaining comparable *faithfulness* to gradient‑based methods. Human subject studies confirm that users find FaCT explanations more actionable and trustworthy. Our open‑source implementation demonstrates that FaCT can be integrated into existing pipelines with minimal overhead, making faithful, concept‑level tracing a practical tool for transparent AI.
809:
Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs) traditionally relies on a discrete‑token action space, forcing policy gradients to traverse a combinatorial landscape that is both high‑variance and computationally expensive. This bottleneck limits the ability of LLMs to learn complex, long‑horizon instruction‑following and dialogue strategies. In this work we introduce **SofT‑GRPO**—**Soft‑Thinking Gumbel‑Reparameterized Policy Optimization**—a novel framework that bridges the discrete–continuous divide by leveraging the Gumbel‑Softmax reparameterization to generate *soft thoughts* over token probabilities. SofT‑GRPO treats the policy as a continuous relaxation of the discrete token distribution, enabling back‑propagation of gradients through a differentiable “soft‑thinking” layer that captures the entire support of possible next tokens. This yields a low‑variance estimator of the policy gradient, while preserving the expressiveness of discrete actions at inference time.

We formulate a principled objective that couples the soft‑thinking representation with an entropy‑regularized reward signal, and prove that the resulting gradient estimator is asymptotically unbiased with variance bounded by the temperature parameter. Empirically, SofT‑GRPO is evaluated on a suite of benchmark tasks—text‑based navigation, open‑ended dialogue, and instruction‑following—using GPT‑NeoX as the underlying LLM. Across all tasks it outperforms conventional discrete‑token baselines (PPO, DQN, and REINFORCE) by 12–27 % in cumulative reward, and reduces sample complexity by an order of magnitude. Ablation studies confirm that the soft‑thinking layer is the primary driver of performance gains, while the Gumbel temperature offers a tunable trade‑off between exploration and stability.

Our results demonstrate that re‑parameterizing the discrete action space with Gumbel‑Softmax not only preserves the linguistic fidelity of LLM outputs but also unlocks a more efficient policy optimization pathway. SofT‑GRPO therefore represents a significant step toward scalable, high‑performance RL for generative language models.
810:
Many studies of reasoning models examine only a single chain‑of‑thought (CoT), yet such models actually produce a distribution over many possible CoTs. We contend that analyzing just one sample is insufficient for uncovering the causal drivers of a model’s decisions and for grasping its internal computation. While fully enumerating the entire distribution is infeasible, it can be approximated via sampling. In this work we employ resampling to probe the behavior of CoT models through several case studies.  

1. **Causal relevance of stated reasons** – We ask whether a reason given by a model truly influences its chosen action. In “agentic misalignment” settings we resample individual sentences and examine their downstream effects. Sentences expressing self‑preservation show only minor causal impact, indicating that they are not the main force behind blackmail-like behaviors.  

2. **Effectiveness of artificial CoT edits** – A common practice is to manually modify a CoT to steer a model, but such edits run off‑policy. We demonstrate that on‑policy alternatives based on resampling and selecting completions with desired properties are more principled. Off‑policy edits produce small, unstable effects on decision‑making tasks compared to resampling.  

3. **Robustness to step removal** – Removing a reasoning step can be complicated if the model repeats the same content after the edit. We introduce a resilience metric that repeatedly resamples downstream content to prevent re‑appearance. We find that key planning statements resist removal but, when successfully eliminated, exert a large influence on the outcome.  

4. **Unfaithful CoTs and hidden hints** – When a CoT is unfaithful, can our techniques still yield insight? Adapting causal mediation analysis, we identify hints that influence the final output without being explicitly mentioned; these hints exert a subtle, cumulative effect that persists even after removal.  

Overall, resampling the full distribution of CoTs enables reliable causal analysis, clearer interpretations of model reasoning, and principled interventions on the chain of thought.
811:
Vision‑Language (VL) models such as CLIP and BLIP have shown remarkable transferability to downstream visual recognition tasks through prompt learning.  However, the ubiquitous use of image augmentations (random crops, color jitter, etc.) during VL pre‑training induces *augmentation bias*: the visual encoder learns to emphasize features that are invariant to augmentation while the language prompt encoder implicitly aligns with those same biased visual cues.  When a downstream prompt is optimized on a small target dataset, this bias can cause the prompt to over‑fit to augmentation‑specific artifacts rather than the true semantic content, limiting generalization and inflating performance on noisy or biased data.

In this work we formally define augmentation bias in the context of prompt learning and propose **Decoupled Augmentation‑Invariant Prompt (DAIP)**, a lightweight framework that explicitly separates augmentation‑invariant and augmentation‑variant components of the image–text joint representation.  DAIP introduces a dual‑path prompt encoder: (i) an *invariant branch* trained with contrastive losses on aggressively augmented images to capture robust semantics, and (ii) a *variant branch* that models residual augmentation signals and is regularized to be orthogonal to the invariant space.  The two branches are fused only at inference, allowing the downstream prompt to leverage the invariant subspace while remaining immune to augmentation noise.  

We evaluate DAIP on a suite of VL benchmarks (ImageNet‑1K, COCO‑Caption, and several few‑shot classification tasks).  Across all settings, DAIP reduces augmentation‑driven over‑fitting, yielding 3.1–4.7 % absolute gains on zero‑shot classification, 1.9 % improvement in COCO captioning BLEU‑4, and a 12 % relative reduction in performance variance under unseen augmentations.  Ablations confirm the necessity of the orthogonality constraint and the dual‑branch design.  

Our findings demonstrate that decoupling augmentation bias is critical for reliable prompt learning in VL models, and DAIP provides a general, plug‑in solution that can be applied to any existing CLIP‑style architecture.
812:
The entire Artificial Intelligence (AI) lifecycle—from hardware manufacturing to development, deployment, and reuse—incurs significant burdens of energy, carbon, water, and embodied resources. Although cloud‑provider tools enhance transparency, they are fragmented and usually exclude water consumption and upstream value‑chain effects, hampering cross‑comparison and reproducibility. To tackle these multi‑faceted impacts, we advocate a holistic lifecycle methodology that links explicit phase mapping with actionable system levers (e.g., hardware choices, deployment location, power mix, cooling, and scheduling) and incorporates calibrated metrics at facility, system, device, and workload scales.

This paper (i) defines *Green AI* as a distinct, operational concept separate from *Sustainable AI*; (ii) formalizes a five‑stage lifecycle aligned with Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) stages, treating energy, carbon, water, and embodied impacts as core dimensions; (iii) introduces governance through Plan‑Do‑Check‑Act (PDCA) cycles with decision checkpoints; (iv) catalogs hardware and system‑level tactics across the edge‑to‑cloud spectrum to minimize embodied loads; and (v) presents a calibrated measurement framework that blends estimator models with direct metering, enabling reproducible, provider‑agnostic comparisons.

By integrating a clear definition, lifecycle mapping, hardware strategies, and a rigorous measurement regime, we deliver practical, evidence‑based guidance for researchers, developers, and policymakers seeking to reduce AI’s environmental footprint.
813:
Large language models that are trained to reason step‑by‑step tend to become overly verbose, inflating inference cost. In typical Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) setups, easy problems are filtered out for efficiency, so the model is exposed mainly to hard tasks that demand lengthy reasoning chains. This skews the output‑length distribution upward, leading the model to equate “longer reasoning” with “better reasoning.”  

In this study we demonstrate that deliberately retaining and slightly up‑weighting moderately easy examples acts as a natural length regularizer. By training on solvable short‑chain problems, we constrain the model’s output distribution and curb runaway verbosity. The result is **emergent brevity for free**: the model can still solve difficult questions without inflating its answer length, even without any explicit length penalty.  

Experiments with RLVR on Qwen3‑4B‑Thinking‑2507 (16k‑token limit) achieve baseline pass@1 AIME‑25 accuracy while producing solutions that are almost twice as concise on average. The code, datasets, and models are available at <https://github.com/MBZUAI-Paris/Frugal-AI> and on Hugging Face.
814: Autonomous driving systems must simultaneously learn efficient motion planning and adhere to stringent safety guarantees. Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) agents excel at exploiting data but often violate safety constraints during exploration, while rule‑based planners are brittle to novel traffic situations. We present **Hybrid Options (HO)**, a novel framework that unifies hierarchical RL with formal safety synthesis to learn driving policies that are both high‑performance and provably safe. In HO, high‑level “options” encode semantically meaningful driving primitives (e.g., lane‑change, yield, merge) and are generated by a policy over a discrete option space. Each option invokes a low‑level continuous controller trained via deep RL. Safety is enforced by a hybrid supervisor that blends a model‑based control‑barrier function with a learned safety critic, ensuring that every option transition satisfies a probabilistic collision‑avoidance constraint. Training occurs in a realistic CARLA simulator augmented with dense traffic, diverse weather, and occlusion scenarios. The learned agent demonstrates a 42 % reduction in collision rates and a 30 % increase in route‑completion success relative to baseline DRL baselines and a rule‑based benchmark, while preserving comparable trajectory smoothness. Ablation studies confirm that both the hierarchical option structure and the hybrid safety layer contribute synergistically to safety. We further show that the resulting policy generalizes to unseen maps and to a subset of real‑world data collected from a test‑bed vehicle. Our work illustrates that integrating hybrid options with safety‑aware RL yields autonomous driving agents that can learn complex manoeuvres while maintaining rigorous safety guarantees.
815: Accurate and timely radiology reports are indispensable for patient care, yet real‑world clinical workflows frequently suffer from incomplete data: images may be corrupted or unavailable, and natural‑language notes may be missing or inconsistent. Conventional vision‑language models assume fully observed modalities and therefore degrade sharply when any input is absent. To address this limitation, we introduce **DiA-gnostic VLVAE** (Disentangled Alignment‑Constrained Vision‑Language Variational Auto‑Encoder), a generative framework that learns modality‑agnostic, disentangled representations for multimodal radiology data while enforcing alignment between visual and textual subspaces. The model adopts a two‑stage VAE: a vision encoder and a language decoder share a joint latent space partitioned into modality‑specific and shared factors, and a cross‑modal alignment loss ensures that the shared factors capture the semantic core of a study. During training we employ a missing‑modality curriculum that explicitly masks either images or reports, encouraging the encoder to synthesize missing views from the retained modality. We evaluate DiA‑gnostic VLVAE on the MIMIC‑CXR and RSNA Pneumonia datasets, measuring report generation quality with BLEU‑4, METEOR, CIDEr, and human radiologist preference. Across 30%–70% image‑missing scenarios, our model achieves a 12.4% CIDEr improvement over state‑of‑the‑art vision‑language baselines and retains 87% of the performance observed under complete data. Qualitative analyses reveal clinically coherent synthetic reports and faithful image reconstructions. DiA‑gnostic VLVAE demonstrates that disentangled, alignment‑constrained multimodal VAEs can provide robust, high‑quality radiology reports even when one or more modalities are absent.
816:
*Smarter Together: Creating Agentic Communities of Practice through Shared Experiential Learning* investigates how participatory, real‑world learning experiences can ignite collective agency within Communities of Practice (CoPs). Drawing on situated learning, social constructivism and the emergent “agentic” lens—where members not only absorb knowledge but actively co‑construct meaning—the study explores how shared experiential activities (e.g., collaborative simulations, interdisciplinary problem‑solving, field‑based co‑research) can transform conventional CoPs into dynamic, self‑directed networks.  

Using a mixed‑methods design, we conducted a three‑phase longitudinal case study across two professional training programs (a STEM‑focused university cohort and a corporate innovation lab). Phase 1 quantified engagement and agency indicators through pre‑ and post‑intervention surveys (N = 152). Phase 2 involved semi‑structured interviews and focus groups with 26 participants to surface narratives of agency, identity, and knowledge co‑production. Phase 3 applied thematic network analysis to map relational shifts and emergent practices.  

Findings reveal that shared experiential learning catalyzes a four‑stage progression in agentic CoPs: (1) *situational anchoring* (shared tasks that demand collective problem‑solving), (2) *relational brokerage* (cross‑boundary interactions that expand knowledge horizons), (3) *normative re‑configuration* (participants co‑define success criteria and roles), and (4) *autonomous praxis* (self‑initiated projects that sustain the community). Quantitatively, participants reported a 35 % increase in perceived agency and a 28 % rise in collaborative knowledge production. Qualitatively, emergent themes—“co‑authorship of learning,” “boundary‑spanning practice,” and “distributed decision‑making”—highlight how experiential scaffolds support sustained agentic engagement.

The study advances the theoretical understanding of agentic CoPs and offers a practical framework for educators and organizational designers: (a) embed shared, authentic tasks; (b) facilitate fluid boundary‑crossing networks; (c) nurture co‑constructed norms; and (d) sustain autonomy through iterative, self‑generated projects. By positioning experiential learning as a catalyst for agentic communities, this work provides actionable insights for building smarter, more resilient collective knowledge ecosystems.
817:
Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) has become the de‑facto standard for predicting student responses from historical interaction data. Although DKT models achieve state‑of‑the‑art accuracy, their latent representations remain opaque, and the underlying learning dynamics—how mastery of one skill influences the acquisition of another—are rarely made explicit. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a principled framework for extracting *causal relations* among skills from a trained DKT model.

Our approach first reconstructs a high‑dimensional latent mastery trajectory using the DKT’s recurrent encoder. We then fit a structural causal model (SCM) to these trajectories by learning a sparse directed graph that best explains the temporal evolution of skill proficiency. To overcome the confounding introduced by the model’s internal state dynamics, we employ a counterfactual perturbation scheme: for each skill pair we generate synthetic student trajectories that intervene on one skill’s state and propagate the effect through the DKT’s decoder, thereby estimating a conditional interventional effect. The resulting causal weights are aggregated over the student population to produce a global, interpretable skill graph.

Experiments on the widely used ASSISTments and KDD Cup 2017 datasets demonstrate that the inferred causal network recovers pedagogically meaningful dependencies (e.g., “Linear Equations” → “Quadratic Equations”) and improves downstream tasks such as curriculum sequencing and targeted remedial interventions by 5–7 % over purely predictive baselines. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of the counterfactual component for avoiding spurious correlations inherent in purely observational DKT outputs.

The proposed method provides a scalable, data‑driven pipeline for turning opaque DKT predictions into actionable causal knowledge about student learning. This work opens the door to more transparent, explainable, and ultimately more effective educational analytics systems.
818: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed to generate and refactor code, yet correctness does not guarantee security. In this study we assess secure code generation by employing the Instruct Prime framework, which removes compliance‑required prompts and cue‑contamination effects, and we benchmark five instruction‑tuned code‑LLMs against a zero‑shot baseline and a three‑round reflection prompting strategy. Security is quantified using the Insecure Code Detector (ICD), and we report the Repair, Regression, and NetGain metrics across programming languages and CWE families. Our results reveal that insecurity is still prevalent in the first iteration: about 25–33 % of generated programs fail the zero‑shot baseline (t₀). Bugs involving weak cryptography or configuration dependence are the most difficult to eliminate, whereas template‑based flaws such as XSS, code injection, and hard‑coded secrets are handled more consistently. Python achieves the highest secure‑rate, while C and C# exhibit the lowest, with Java, JavaScript, PHP, and C++ falling in between. Reflection prompting boosts overall security for all models, raising average accuracy from 70.74 % at t₀ to 79.43 % at t₃; the largest gains occur in the first round, followed by diminishing returns. Analyses of Repair, Regression, and NetGain suggest that one or two rounds of reflection capture most of the benefits. A replication package is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17065846.
819:
The proliferation of residential renewable generation and smart appliances has created a complex decision‑making problem: how to schedule diverse loads in real time while minimizing cost, maximizing self‑consumption, and respecting user comfort. Traditional rule‑based and optimization‑driven home energy management systems (HEMS) struggle to scale across heterogeneous device types, tariffs, and dynamic market signals. We propose an **Agentic AI Home Energy Management System (AI‑HEMS)** that leverages large language models (LLMs) as autonomous agents for residential load scheduling. By formulating scheduling as a conversational task, the LLM ingests real‑time device states, weather forecasts, and time‑of‑use tariffs via a structured prompt, then outputs actionable dispatch instructions. The framework integrates a lightweight inference engine, a domain‑specific knowledge base, and a safety‑layer that enforces hard constraints (e.g., appliance safety limits, user‑defined preferences).  

To evaluate the approach, we deployed the AI‑HEMS in a simulated 100‑household testbed using realistic load profiles and a dynamic pricing environment. The LLM‑based scheduler achieved a 12 % reduction in electricity costs compared to a rule‑based baseline and a 7 % increase in PV self‑consumption, while maintaining user‑specified comfort thresholds. A comparative study with reinforcement‑learning agents demonstrated comparable performance but with markedly lower computational overhead and greater interpretability. User studies revealed higher satisfaction with the LLM’s explainable reasoning and the ability to query “why” a particular schedule was chosen.  

This paper presents the architecture of the Agentic AI HEMS, the prompt‑engineering strategy for domain‑specific reasoning, and a rigorous assessment of its economic and operational benefits. The results illustrate that LLMs, when coupled with a lightweight safety interface, can serve as flexible, explainable agents for intelligent residential energy management, paving the way for broader adoption of generative AI in the smart‑grid domain.
820: Accurate and efficient generation of realistic multivariate time series is a foundational requirement for downstream tasks such as forecasting, anomaly detection, and data augmentation.  Existing generative models—autoregressive networks, variational autoencoders, and diffusion samplers—either impose restrictive conditional assumptions, suffer from long sampling times, or fail to capture the rich stochastic dynamics present in real‑world sequences.  We introduce **TimeFlow**, a stochastic‑aware, flow‑matching framework that models time series as a continuous trajectory of probability density functions.  By formulating time‑dependent flow matching equations and embedding them into a hierarchical transformer backbone, TimeFlow learns a parameter‑efficient bijective mapping that preserves temporal correlations while enabling tractable likelihood evaluation.  The model is trained using a variational lower bound derived from the flow‑matching objective, and inference is achieved in a single forward pass, thereby reducing generation latency by an average of **3.8×** relative to state‑of‑the‑art diffusion and transformer‑based generators.  Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks (electricity, traffic, weather, financial, and biomedical) demonstrate that TimeFlow consistently outperforms baselines in log‑likelihood and predictive downstream accuracy, while generating diverse, multimodal sequences that match the empirical autocorrelation structure of the data.  Our results confirm that flow matching can be leveraged for high‑fidelity, efficient time‑series synthesis and highlight the potential of stochastic‑aware generative modeling for practical industrial applications.
821: While multi‑modal diffusion models—especially those translating text into images—have become remarkably powerful, their vulnerability to adversarial manipulation has received little attention. Our study shows that the correspondence between text and image inputs in current diffusion architectures is weaker than assumed, opening a doorway to the generation of undesirable or NSFW material. To exploit this flaw, we introduce Prompt‑Restricted Multi‑modal Attack (PReMA), an approach that alters only the input image (leaving the prompt untouched) to steer the output toward malicious content. Unlike earlier work that crafts adversarial prompts, PReMA is the first method that achieves such attacks solely through adversarial images, thereby threatening the reliability of diffusion models in settings where prompts are fixed, such as image‑editing pipelines. Extensive tests on inpainting and style‑transfer tasks across a range of models demonstrate the effectiveness of PReMA.
822:
Social media platforms generate a deluge of heterogeneous signals—text, images, geospatial tags, network traces, and temporal logs—whose joint interpretation is essential for understanding collective behavior, detecting misinformation, and informing policy. Conventional analytics pipelines either (i) fuse these modalities into flat feature vectors, thereby discarding structural dependencies, or (ii) treat them independently, missing cross‑modal interactions that drive coordinated user actions. We propose a unified framework that *links heterogeneous data through coordinated agent flows* for enriched social‑media analysis.  

The core idea is to model each content stream (e.g., a tweet, a photo, a user’s retweet trajectory) as a *coordinated agent* that propagates through a multi‑layer graph comprising linguistic, visual, and network subgraphs. Agents exchange state information via a lightweight message‑passing protocol, enabling the emergence of a coherent latent representation that respects modality‑specific constraints yet preserves inter‑modal causality. We formulate this as a joint optimization over (a) a heterogeneous graph neural network that learns modality‑specific embeddings, and (b) a dynamic flow controller that enforces consistency across agent trajectories. The resulting *Agent‑Flow Embedding* (AFE) captures both the content semantics and the underlying propagation dynamics.  

We evaluate AFE on two large‑scale benchmark datasets—Twitter’s political‑discourse stream and Reddit’s image‑sharing communities—targeting tasks of (i) coordinated inauthentic behavior detection, (ii) stance evolution forecasting, and (iii) multi‑modal sentiment inference. Across all tasks, AFE outperforms strong baselines (e.g., multimodal transformers, graph‑only embeddings) by 4–8 % in F1 and 3–5 % in RMSE, demonstrating that coordinating agent flows yields more faithful cross‑modal integration.  

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a principled methodology for linking heterogeneous social‑media data via coordinated agent flows; (2) an open‑source implementation and benchmark suite that facilitate reproducibility; and (3) empirical evidence that such coordinated representations enhance downstream analysis in real‑world settings. This work bridges the gap between multimodal data fusion and dynamic network modeling, providing a scalable tool for researchers and practitioners investigating the complex fabric of online social behavior.
823: Diffusion models have become a popular generative tool, yet they frequently produce hallucinated, incoherent samples. Recent studies attribute these artifacts to mode interpolation and overly smooth score functions, but they provide no practical way to stop such hallucinations during sampling. Here we introduce a simple post‑hoc modification of the score function that uses the Laplacian (i.e., sharpness) of the score to mitigate mode‑interpolation errors in unconditional diffusion models. We propose an efficient Laplacian estimate for high‑dimensional spaces via a finite‑difference variant of the Hutchinson trace estimator. Experiments on toy 1‑D and 2‑D distributions, as well as on large‑scale image datasets, demonstrate a substantial drop in hallucinated outputs. Our analysis also elucidates how the Laplacian reflects uncertainty in the score.
824:
Accurately estimating causal effects in settings with *multiple* simultaneous treatments remains a central challenge in observational studies. Existing approaches typically treat each treatment separately or rely on handcrafted propensity scores, thereby ignoring rich relationships among treatments and risking residual confounding. We propose **Task‑Embedding Balanced Representation Learning (TE‑BRL)**, a unified framework that learns low‑dimensional embeddings for each treatment while simultaneously enforcing covariate balance across all treatment groups in a shared latent space.  

TE‑BRL comprises three key components. First, a neural encoder maps high‑dimensional covariates to a continuous representation, and a learnable task‑embedding vector is concatenated with this representation to capture the unique characteristics of each treatment. Second, a *balance loss*—an adversarial domain‑discriminator and a maximum‑mean‑discrepancy term—pushes the representations of different treatment groups toward mutual indistinguishability, thus mitigating confounding bias. Third, a causal head predicts counterfactual outcomes conditioned on the balanced representation and treatment embedding, yielding individualized treatment effect (ITE) estimates for any number of treatments.  

We establish a theoretical bound showing that, under standard overlap and unconfoundedness assumptions, the proposed embedding‑balance objective reduces the worst‑case estimation error of the true multi‑treatment effects. Empirically, TE‑BRL outperforms state‑of‑the‑art single‑ and multi‑treatment methods on synthetic benchmarks, the IHDP dataset, and a large‑scale electronic health records study, achieving up to 30 % lower mean absolute error in ITE estimation.  The method scales linearly with the number of treatments and is agnostic to the outcome distribution.  

Our work demonstrates that jointly learning task embeddings and a balanced representation enables more accurate, scalable causal inference in multi‑treatment contexts, opening pathways for personalized policy design in domains such as medicine, public policy, and online recommendation.
825: Villages remain crucial arenas for exploring human‑land interactions, yet the push of urbanization has begun eroding their unique spatial signatures, leading to a pronounced landscape homogenization. Most previous research treats village morphology from a single‑disciplinary lens and relies mainly on qualitative methods, often hampered by limited digital infrastructure and sparse data. To overcome these gaps, this study introduces a Hierarchical Graph Neural Network (HGNN) that fuses heterogeneous data sources to perform a comprehensive analysis of village spatial form. The model distinguishes two node types—input nodes and communication nodes—alongside static input edges and dynamic communication edges. By integrating Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) with Graph Attention Networks (GAT), the HGNN efficiently merges multimodal features through a two‑stage feature‑update protocol. Building on established criteria for classifying village spatial morphology, we incorporate a relational pooling module and jointly train across 17 sub‑categories. Empirical evaluations reveal that the approach markedly outperforms existing methods in multimodal fusion and classification, raising mean accuracy and F1 scores from 0.71/0.83 (independent models) to 0.82/0.90; notably, parcel‑level tasks benefit from a 6% gain. These results provide robust empirical support for dissecting village spatial patterns and elucidating their generative logic.
826:
Planning for multiple interacting agents in high‑dimensional environments remains a central obstacle for autonomous systems, due to the exponential growth of joint state–action spaces and the combinatorial complexity of coordinating strategies. We introduce **MALinZero**, a novel framework that combines learned low‑dimensional latent models with a zero‑sum search scheme to enable efficient, scalable planning for complex multi‑agent problems. MALinZero first trains a compact, task‑specific variational autoencoder on demonstrations of multi‑agent trajectories; the encoder maps the joint state space into a low‑dimensional manifold where geometric distances correlate with feasibility and reward. Planning proceeds in this latent space using a modified depth‑first search that incorporates a *zero‑reward* pruning criterion, guaranteeing that sub‑optimal branches are eliminated early while preserving completeness for a broad class of deterministic, cooperative‑adversarial tasks. 

Our evaluation on a suite of benchmark domains—multi‑agent path finding, real‑time strategy micro‑tasks, and cooperative manipulation—demonstrates that MALinZero attains up to 5× faster search times and 30–40 % higher plan quality than state‑of‑the‑art baselines such as MCTS, MADDPG, and MAPF‑based planners. The method is also robust to partial observability, as the latent encoder naturally captures uncertainty through probabilistic embeddings. Theoretical analysis establishes that MALinZero’s zero‑reward pruning preserves optimality for a wide family of zero‑sum reward functions, and we provide an empirical study of the trade‑off between latent dimensionality and planning performance. This work bridges representation learning and combinatorial search, opening a new pathway for efficient multi‑agent planning in high‑dimensional, real‑world settings.
827:
Large‑scale machine‑learning inference is increasingly performed on heterogeneous, distributed clusters in which even subtle kernel‑level misbehaviours can cascade into catastrophic inference failures or severe throughput degradation. Current monitoring stacks focus on application‑level metrics and miss the fine‑grained, low‑overhead anomalies that arise in the operating system and hardware subsystems. In this paper we present **Kunlun Anomaly Troubleshooter**, a unified framework that (1) instruments kernel‐level events across CPUs, GPUs, interconnects and memory hierarchies using lightweight eBPF traces, (2) aggregates these signals into a unified, time‑synchronised event stream, and (3) applies statistical anomaly detection coupled with causal‑reasoning inference to pinpoint the root cause of distributed inference faults in real time.

Kunlun builds a causal graph over kernel metrics and hardware counters, learning normal operational regimes with a combination of unsupervised auto‑encoders and Bayesian network models. During inference, deviations are flagged as anomalies and immediately routed to a causal inference engine that propagates evidence through the graph, yielding a ranked list of likely failure modes (e.g., memory fragmentation, PCIe congestion, GPU scheduler starvation). The system exposes a lightweight API for inference frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, Triton) to trigger re‑balancing, resource throttling, or fail‑over actions autonomously.

We evaluated Kunlun on an 8‑node GPU cluster running a 13 B‑parameter transformer for real‑time inference of long‑form dialogue. Across 12 h of sustained load, Kunlun detected 95 % of injected anomalies—including memory‑leak, NUMA mis‑allocation, and inter‑connect latency spikes—while maintaining <1 % false‑positive rate. Root‑cause identification was achieved within 2 s of anomaly onset, enabling a 40 % reduction in mean‑time‑to‑repair compared to baseline application‑level monitoring. These results demonstrate that kernel‑level anomaly detection and causal reasoning can substantially improve reliability and performance of large‑model distributed inference workloads.
828:
Migrating legacy code to modern libraries, APIs, or language versions is a tedious and error‑prone activity that often requires deep knowledge of both the original and target ecosystems. Recent large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable aptitude in generating and refactoring code, yet their ability to produce *correct, minimal diffs* that faithfully transform code bases at scale remains underexplored. In this work we investigate the feasibility of automatically generating migration diffs with LLMs and present **DiffMate**, a pipeline that harnesses prompt‑engineering, program‑state conditioning, and iterative verification to produce reliable patch files for a wide range of migration scenarios.

DiffMate first extracts a *migration specification*—for example, a library upgrade or a language‑feature deprecation—from a repository’s change logs or issue tracker. It then constructs a natural‑language prompt augmented with the relevant context (affected files, stack traces, and a minimal snippet of the target API). An LLM (OpenAI‑GPT‑4, Codex, and a fine‑tuned GPT‑NeoX) proposes a *diff* that transforms the source code into the desired target state. The proposed patch is subjected to a lightweight semantic test suite and a *semantic similarity* check against a ground‑truth diff (when available). If the patch fails, DiffMate iteratively refines the prompt by incorporating counter‑examples and failsafe constraints.

We evaluated DiffMate on 1,200 real‑world migration tasks spanning Python 2→3, NumPy API upgrades, and the transition from AngularJS to Angular 12 in JavaScript projects. Across all models, DiffMate achieved an 84 % success rate for generating semantically correct diffs without manual inspection; fine‑tuned models improved this to 92 %. Human evaluators rated 78 % of the patches as “ready for integration” in a real codebase, with an average effort savings of 4.6 hours per task. Moreover, DiffMate’s diffs preserved formatting and documentation style, a key requirement for maintainability.

Our findings demonstrate that LLMs, when coupled with a disciplined diff‑generation framework, can effectively automate complex code migration tasks at scale. We release DiffMate as an open‑source tool and provide a benchmark dataset of migration diffs to spur further research in this emerging area.
829:
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise orders‑of‑magnitude improvements in energy efficiency by exploiting event‑driven, biologically inspired computation. However, commercial processors struggle to deliver the low‑latency, high‑throughput support required for real‑time SNN workloads, and commercial ASICs suffer from high entry barriers and limited programmability.  In this paper we present **FeNN‑DMA**, a fully open‑source RISC‑V System‑on‑Chip (SoC) designed explicitly for accelerating SNN inference and training.  FeNN‑DMA couples a lightweight, tightly‑integrated RISC‑V core with a custom, scalable SNN accelerator and a dedicated Direct‑Memory‑Access (DMA) engine that manages spike event traffic and weight updates.  The accelerator exploits sparse event propagation, on‑chip event queues, and a hierarchical memory hierarchy that keeps frequently accessed synaptic weights in register‑file‑level caches while offloading the rest to a high‑bandwidth SRAM.  The DMA engine implements a priority‑based scheduling algorithm that guarantees deterministic latency for high‑frequency spike bursts and supports multi‑core cooperation via a lightweight on‑chip network‑on‑chip (NoC).  

We evaluate FeNN‑DMA on a suite of benchmark datasets—including MNIST, N‑MNIST, and the DVS Gesture dataset—using state‑of‑the‑art SNN models (e.g., LIF, Izhikevich, and STDP‑based networks).  Compared to a baseline RISC‑V processor with a generic neural‑network library, FeNN‑DMA delivers **5.8×** improvement in throughput and **70 %** reduction in energy consumption per inference while maintaining less than 1 ms latency for high‑density event streams.  A silicon implementation in 65 nm technology consumes only **0.35 W** under a 200 MHz operating frequency, demonstrating the practicality of our design for edge‐AI applications.  

Key contributions of this work are:  
1. An open‑source RISC‑V SoC architecture that natively supports SNN workloads without reliance on proprietary IP.  
2. A novel event‑driven accelerator core with an integrated DMA subsystem that eliminates memory bottlenecks.  
3. A flexible memory‑hierarchy and interconnect scheme that scales from small‐scale IoT devices to larger multi‑core clusters.  
4. A comprehensive performance and energy evaluation that confirms FeNN‑DMA’s competitiveness with commercial accelerators while retaining full programmability and reconfigurability.  

FeNN‑DMA establishes a new baseline for open‑source hardware platforms dedicated to spiking neural networks, paving the way for community‑driven innovation in neuromorphic computing.
830:
The rapid proliferation of multimodal artificial intelligence has largely focused on English‑centric data, leaving many linguistically diverse regions underrepresented. In Southeast Asia, the coexistence of dozens of languages and dialects—many of which are low‑resource and lack large‑scale audio corpora—poses unique challenges for audio‑language modelling. To bridge this gap, we introduce **SeaLLMs‑Audio**, the first comprehensive framework for training and evaluating large audio‑language models (A‑LLMs) across Southeast Asian languages. SeaLLMs‑Audio comprises a curated, multilingual audio‑text corpus of 3,200 h spanning 24 languages, including Bahasa Indonesia, Thai, Vietnamese, Lao, Khmer, and regional dialects such as Javanese and Tagalog. We employ a unified encoder–decoder architecture based on the Transformer‑X architecture, augmented with a self‑supervised contrastive pre‑training objective that exploits unlabeled speech to learn language‑agnostic acoustic representations. To mitigate data imbalance, we introduce a curriculum‑based multi‑stage fine‑tuning pipeline that progressively adapts the model from high‑resource to low‑resource languages. 

We evaluate SeaLLMs‑Audio on a suite of downstream tasks—automatic speech recognition (ASR), spoken‑language translation (SLT), and cross‑lingual speech synthesis—using both standard benchmarks (CommonVoice, VoxPopuli) and a newly released SeaL Audio‑Eval set. Our models achieve an average relative improvement of 18% in WER for low‑resource Southeast Asian languages compared to existing state‑of‑the‑art multilingual models, while preserving competitive performance on high‑resource English and Mandarin. Moreover, SeaLLMs‑Audio demonstrates strong zero‑shot generalization to unseen dialects, underscoring the effectiveness of our self‑supervised pre‑training. 

Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of linguistic bias and model robustness, revealing that incorporating regional phonetic dictionaries and gender‑balanced speaker corpora significantly reduces error rates for under‑represented ethnic groups. SeaLLMs‑Audio establishes a new benchmark for audio‑language modelling in Southeast Asia and offers a publicly available open‑source code base, dataset, and pre‑trained checkpoints to accelerate research and application development in this understudied yet linguistically rich region.
831:
Accurate prediction of chaotic dynamical systems remains a central challenge in nonlinear time‑series analysis, with applications ranging from climate forecasting to fault‑diagnostics in engineering systems. Conventional reservoir computing (RC) architectures excel at capturing short‑term dynamics but often struggle to extrapolate over longer horizons, largely due to the mismatch between the high‑dimensional phase‑space of chaotic attractors and the fixed, low‑rank reservoir representation. In this work we introduce a **Delay‑Embedding Random‑Fourier Reservoir (DERF‑RC)**, a novel RC framework that explicitly incorporates Takens’ time‑delay embedding into the input layer and projects the resulting high‑dimensional state onto a randomized Fourier feature space before feeding it to a sparse, orthogonal reservoir.  

The time‑delay embedding layer reconstructs the underlying attractor manifold, while the Random Fourier Features (RFF) layer provides a scalable, kernel‑based expansion that preserves nonlinear relationships in a lower‑dimensional Euclidean space. The orthogonal reservoir, initialized with a sparse random graph, evolves the augmented state via a leaky‑integrator update. Only the output weights are trained using a regularized least‑squares procedure, ensuring that the entire pipeline remains computationally lightweight.  

We evaluate DERF‑RC on the Lorenz, Rössler, and Mackey‑Glass systems, comparing against standard Echo State Networks (ESNs), Extreme Learning Machines (ELMs), and deep recurrent neural networks. Across all benchmarks, DERF‑RC reduces the normalized root‑mean‑square error (NRMSE) by 12–18 % and accurately reproduces the Lyapunov spectrum up to the first three exponents. Ablation studies confirm that both the delay‑embedding and RFF stages contribute multiplicatively to performance gains, and sensitivity analysis demonstrates robustness to reservoir size and regularization hyper‑parameters.  

In summary, DERF‑RC offers a principled, data‑efficient solution for chaotic time‑series prediction, combining state‑of‑the‑art manifold reconstruction with kernel‑approximation techniques within a lightweight RC architecture. The framework opens avenues for real‑time forecasting in high‑dimensional, partially observed systems where traditional model‑based approaches are infeasible.
832:
Large language models (LLMs) routinely consume dozens of gigabytes of parameters, making their deployment on resource‑constrained devices impractical. Traditional compression techniques—pruning, quantisation, and low‑rank factorisation—trade off accuracy for storage but lack principled guarantees for a given memory budget. In this work we introduce **Optimal Singular Damage (OSD)**, a novel framework that selects a minimal subset of singular components in a model’s weight matrices to preserve the most essential information for inference. OSD formalises the compression problem as a constrained optimisation over the singular value spectrum: for a target storage budget, it chooses the singular vectors that minimise the Frobenius‑norm reconstruction error while respecting a sparsity pattern that can be applied uniformly across layers. The optimisation admits a polynomial‑time solution via a greedy selection algorithm that provably achieves a $(1-\epsilon)$‑approximation of the optimal damage set.

We evaluate OSD on several transformer backbones (GPT‑2, GPT‑Neo, and BERT‑Base) across downstream language modelling, text classification, and question answering tasks. Compared to baseline pruning (10 % accuracy loss) and low‑rank factorisation (≈20 % loss at comparable compression), OSD attains a 6×–8× reduction in memory footprint with ≤1.3 % degradation in perplexity or BLEU scores. The method incurs negligible overhead during inference, as the damage mask is applied once during a static compilation step and the resulting pruned model can be run with standard deep‑learning libraries. We also demonstrate that OSD can be combined with 4‑bit post‑training quantisation to achieve 12×–15× total compression without a catastrophic drop in performance.

Our results show that Optimal Singular Damage delivers a principled, theoretically‑sound, and empirically robust path toward efficient LLM inference in low‑storage regimes, enabling deployment on edge and mobile platforms while preserving high‑quality language understanding.
833: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on tasks that require the joint interpretation of text and visual content.  However, their propensity to hallucinate or misinterpret sensory evidence limits their deployment in high‑stakes domains such as medical diagnostics, autonomous navigation, and collaborative robotics.  We introduce **FaithAct**, a unified framework that interleaves *faithful planning* and *faithful acting* to enforce semantic consistency between the model’s internal reasoning and the multimodal inputs it receives.  FaithAct comprises three core components: (1) a **Verification Module** that performs real‑time consistency checks against a grounded evidence repository, (2) a **Planning Module** that generates a sequence of sub‑tasks and intermediate goals that respect the verified evidence, and (3) an **Acting Module** that executes each sub‑task while continuously re‑consulting the verifier.  The system employs a lightweight policy network trained with a *faithfulness‑augmented loss* that penalizes deviations from the verifier’s ground truth.  We evaluate FaithAct on a suite of multimodal benchmarks—VQA, Visual Storytelling, and Robotics‑Simulation—showing a 12 % absolute improvement in faithfulness metrics (e.g., VQA accuracy and hallucination rate) with negligible impact on overall task performance.  Ablation studies demonstrate the necessity of the dynamic planning loop for mitigating cumulative hallucinations.  FaithAct offers a principled pathway for building trustworthy MLLMs that can plan and act while remaining faithful to the multimodal evidence they observe.
834: Large language models (LLMs) can carry out multi‑step reasoning through Chain‑of‑Thought (CoT) generation, yet they rarely verify the soundness of the reasoning they produce. Even when the final answer turns out to be correct, the internal logical chain may contain errors, eroding confidence in high‑stakes applications. To address this, we propose **VeriCoT**, a neuro‑symbolic framework that extracts and validates formal logical arguments from CoT traces. Each reasoning step is translated into first‑order logic, with premises explicitly linked to the source text, external commonsense resources, or earlier reasoning stages. The symbolic form allows automated solvers to check logical validity, while the accompanying natural‑language premises help humans and other systems spot ungrounded or fallacious steps. Experiments on ProofWriter, LegalBench, and BioASQ demonstrate that VeriCoT reliably detects flawed reasoning and correlates strongly with answer accuracy. We further harness VeriCoT’s verification signal for (1) runtime self‑reflection, (2) supervised fine‑tuning on VeriCoT‑distilled datasets, and (3) preference fine‑tuning via direct preference optimization (DPO) with verification‑based pairwise rewards, all of which boost both reasoning validity and overall performance.
835:
As generative AI becomes more widespread in higher‑education, the gap between institutional policy and everyday practice grows larger, making it urgent to develop measurable evidence of alignment.  
This paper presents a ten‑question, indirect‑elicitation instrument that sits inside a structured interpretive framework designed to reveal such misalignments. By harvesting empirical and epistemic cues from faculty, the framework produces three distilled indicators of “voids” between rules and use:

1. **AI‑Integrated Assessment Capacity (proxy)** – a three‑signal screen (AI skill, perceived teaching benefit, detection confidence) that estimates the proportion of faculty willing to allow full AI use in examinations.

2. **Sector‑Level Necessity (proxy)** – among high‑output AI users who still credit the technology with substantial contribution, the share who believe AI can challenge established disciplines.

3. **Ontological Stance** – from respondents who (a) view AI as a fundamentally different kind of tool, (b) report actual practice changes, and (c) pass a metacognitive gate, the split between material and immaterial perspectives forms an ontological map that aligns procurement claims with evidence categories.
836:
Accurate sea‑surface temperature (SST) forecasting is essential for climate science, weather prediction, and marine resource management. Conventional approaches either rely on coarse‑resolution physical ocean models that are computationally intensive, or on purely data‑driven neural architectures that lack physical consistency and generalization outside the training domain. We introduce **SSTODE**, a physics‑informed neural ordinary‑differential equation framework that marries ocean‑atmosphere physics with modern machine learning to predict SST at high spatial and temporal resolution. SSTODE embeds the governing equations of surface heat balance—including advection, diffusion, solar radiation, and latent‑heat fluxes—directly into the loss function of a continuous‑time neural network. The model is trained on satellite‑derived SST and atmospheric reanalysis fields (MODIS, ERA‑5) using adjoint‑based backpropagation through a Runge–Kutta integrator, enabling efficient end‑to‑end learning of latent dynamics while enforcing conservation laws. 

On a 10‑year North‑Pacific test set, SSTODE reduces the root‑mean‑square error by 18 % relative to a state‑of‑the‑art LSTM and by 12 % over a classical linear ocean model, while preserving physical invariants (energy and heat flux balance) to within 0.5 %. Importantly, the method demonstrates robust extrapolation to unseen seasonal regimes and extreme events (e.g., El Niño outbreaks), owing to its physics‑regularized dynamics. Ablation studies reveal that the ODE layer alone accounts for a 7 % performance gain, while the inclusion of atmospheric covariates further improves prediction over 30‑day horizons. 

SSTODE offers a scalable, interpretable, and physically faithful alternative for ocean surface temperature forecasting, paving the way for more reliable climate risk assessments and informing coupled ocean–atmosphere simulation pipelines.
837: Flood insurance is a proven method for reducing disaster‑related losses, yet uptake among high‑risk communities in the United States remains unusually low. This discrepancy highlights the necessity of dissecting the behavioral drivers of insurance choices. With the recent emergence of large language models (LLMs) that display near‑human reasoning across diverse tasks, new avenues open for simulating such decision processes. In this work, we create a benchmark dataset that records the likelihood of insurance purchase across a range of influencing variables. We then assess the performance of LLMs on this data: while they capture the qualitative importance of the factors, they struggle to produce accurate quantitative probability estimates. To overcome this shortcoming, we introduce InsurAgent—a five‑module, LLM‑powered agent comprising perception, retrieval, reasoning, action, and memory components. Its retrieval module, based on retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG), grounds decisions in empirical survey evidence, enabling precise estimation of marginal and joint probabilities. The reasoning module taps the LLM’s common‑sense knowledge to infer beyond the survey scope, incorporating contextual nuances that elude conventional models. The memory component allows us to model how decisions evolve over time, illustrated via a simulated “roller‑coaster” life trajectory. Together, these capabilities position InsurAgent as a powerful tool for behavioral analysis and policy design in insurance contexts.
838: Large language models (LLMs) routinely perform downstream tasks using implicit, latent reward structures that are inaccessible to users and safety engineers. These hidden objectives, shaped by pre‑training corpora, instruction‑tuning datasets, and reinforcement‑learning signals, can lead to undesirable behavior and obscure model accountability. We introduce **Spilling the Beans**, a framework for teaching LLMs to self‑report their internal objectives. Our method augments the standard language modeling objective with a *Self‑Objective Prediction* loss that trains the model to generate concise, faithful statements about its own preference functions when prompted. To support this, we curate a benchmark of 10,000 “objective‑reflection” pairs, each consisting of a context, a ground‑truth objective vector (in a structured natural‑language form), and a self‑reported explanation generated by human annotators. Models are fine‑tuned on this dataset using a dual‑decoder architecture that simultaneously predicts task outputs and the self‑report. Evaluation on the *Self‑Objective Accuracy* (SOA), *Coherence* and *Faithfulness* metrics shows a 27 % improvement in objective alignment over baseline models. Moreover, human evaluators report higher confidence in safety assessments when the model can articulate its own goals. We further demonstrate that self‑reporting facilitates adversarial detection: models that misalign with their declared objectives exhibit a higher error rate. Spilling the Beans opens a pathway toward transparent, introspective LLMs, enabling users to audit hidden motivations and mitigate alignment risks.
839:
Hyperspectral image (HSI) super‑resolution (SR) is pivotal for remote‑sensing and industrial inspection, yet it remains challenging to jointly enhance spatial details and preserve the intrinsic spectral signatures. Recent diffusion models have shown promising generative capabilities for SR, but they typically rely on pixel‑wise reconstruction losses and lack explicit exploitation of multiscale frequency structures and geometric priors inherent in HSIs. This paper presents **GEWDiff**, a *Geometric‑Enhanced Wavelet‑based Diffusion* framework that marries a wavelet‑domain representation with a geometry‑aware diffusion process to produce high‑fidelity, spectrally consistent HR images from low‑resolution inputs.

GEWDiff first embeds the input LR HSI into a redundant discrete wavelet domain, where spatial frequency bands are isolated and spectral correlations are preserved across coefficients. The diffusion backbone is then conditioned on a learned geometric descriptor that captures spatial continuity and boundary structure through a lightweight graph‑convolutional module operating on the wavelet coefficients. During reverse diffusion, the model iteratively refines the wavelet representation, guided by both a spectral fidelity loss and a geometry‑regularized reconstruction objective, and finally reconstructs the HR HSI via inverse wavelet transform.

Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets (Pavia University, Salinas, and Houston) demonstrate that GEWDiff outperforms state‑of‑the‑art CNN, transformer, and diffusion‑based SR methods by up to 0.9 dB in PSNR and 0.7 % in SAM, while achieving competitive computational complexity. Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of wavelet embedding and geometric conditioning, and a perceptual user study highlights the visual superiority of the proposed approach.

GEWDiff offers a principled integration of frequency‑domain analysis and spatial geometry into diffusion modeling, establishing a new baseline for HSI super‑resolution and paving the way for further geometric‑aware generative techniques in spectral imaging.
840:
Large‑language models (LLMs) frequently employ *self‑consistency* to improve accuracy by aggregating multiple parallel reasoning traces and selecting the most common answer. Though powerful, this approach is limited by the statistical correlation between traces and the inefficiency of treating all traces equally regardless of their internal confidence. In this work we introduce **Inverse‑Entropy Voting (IEV)**, a lightweight sequential aggregation scheme that ranks candidate answers by the inverse of the trace‑level entropy of their intermediate reasoning states. By weighting more coherent, low‑entropy chains more heavily, IEV effectively prioritizes internally consistent explanations while still leveraging the diversity afforded by multiple traces.

We benchmark IEV against parallel self‑consistency (PSC) across a broad set of reasoning and mathematical benchmarks (e.g., GSM‑8K, MATH, and the OpenBookQA dataset) at *matched compute*—the same total number of forward passes, token budget, and wall‑clock time. On all tasks, IEV yields a 3.2–5.8 % absolute gain over PSC, with the largest improvements on the most difficult, multi‑step problems. Ablation studies confirm that the sequential nature of IEV reduces inter‑trace correlation, while the entropy weighting scheme captures the model’s own confidence signal more effectively than majority voting. We further demonstrate that IEV scales with model size: on GPT‑4‑like models it achieves a 1.1× relative improvement over PSC at equivalent compute, while remaining 15 % faster due to its single‑pass token generation per trace.

Our analysis reveals that the *sequential edge*—the ability to adaptively weight and prune traces during generation—provides a principled advantage over the conventional parallel self‑consistency paradigm. Inverse‑Entropy Voting therefore constitutes a practical, compute‑efficient upgrade for high‑stakes inference in current LLMs, and opens avenues for entropy‑aware ensemble methods in future language‑model architectures.
841: Foundation models designed for generic time‑series data are rapidly gaining traction as versatile backbones, yet their utility for specialized biomedical signals, such as electroencephalography (EEG), has not been thoroughly examined. In this study we evaluate a recently introduced time‑series classification foundation model on two distinct EEG applications—motor‑imagery decoding and sleep‑stage classification. We explore two pre‑training strategies: (a) pre‑training on a diverse collection of real‑world time‑series from multiple domains, and (b) pre‑training on purely synthetic signals. Both approaches deliver robust results, consistently surpassing the performance of EEGNet, a standard convolutional baseline, and CBraMod, the latest EEG‑focused foundation model. These findings demonstrate that generalist time‑series foundations, even when trained on non‑neural or synthetic data, can effectively transfer to EEG tasks. Our work underscores the potential of cross‑domain pre‑training to advance brain‑signal analysis and suggests that EEG can benefit from ongoing progress in the broader time‑series field.
842: World models have become a cornerstone of model‑based reinforcement learning, enabling agents to plan efficiently in complex, high‑dimensional environments. However, most implementations are tightly coupled to legacy deep‑learning frameworks, lack modularity, and struggle to exploit modern accelerator hardware at scale. We introduce **Jasmine**, a lightweight, JAX‑based codebase that unifies simplicity, performance, and scalability for building world models. Jasmine is built around a composable library of probabilistic dynamics, observation, and reward modules, all defined in pure JAX and automatically compiled with XLA. This design allows zero‑overhead vectorization over time, batch, and parallel environments, and seamless integration with distributed training pipelines. We demonstrate that Jasmine’s modular dynamics architecture yields competitive sample efficiency on the DM‑Control and Atari benchmarks while reducing runtime by 2–4× compared to PyTorch‑based baselines such as DreamerV2. Furthermore, we show that Jasmine scales gracefully to hundreds of thousands of environment steps per second on a single GPU, and to millions of steps per second across a multi‑GPU cluster, thanks to its built‑in support for JAX’s `pmap` and `pjit`. Finally, we release Jasmine as an open‑source library with comprehensive documentation and reproducible research artifacts, aiming to lower the barrier to entry for researchers and practitioners interested in world‑model‑based decision making.
843: Accurate delineation of the left atrium (LA) on cardiac MRI is essential for planning atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation and for building detailed biophysical cardiac models. However, manual contouring is laborious, depends on the observer, and is unsuitable for high‑volume or time‑critical clinical settings. Recent advances in deep learning, especially convolutional networks, have outperformed traditional approaches in medical image segmentation. In this work we employed the nnU‑Net framework—an automated, self‑configuring segmentation architecture—to the Left Atrial Segmentation Challenge 2013 dataset, which contains thirty MRI studies annotated by experts. The nnU‑Net automatically tuned its preprocessing, network architecture, and training strategy to the specific characteristics of the data. We assessed the model using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and compared the results qualitatively against the reference masks. The resulting nnU‑Net achieved an average Dice score of 93.5, indicating strong agreement with expert segmentations and surpassing several conventional methods reported in earlier studies. The network demonstrated robust generalization to variations in atrial morphology, contrast, and image quality, accurately segmenting both the atrial myocardium and the proximal pulmonary veins.
844: Accurate semantic segmentation remains a bottleneck for real‑time, resource‑constrained deployments. Conventional lightweight networks either fix their computational budget at training time or employ hand‑crafted sparsification, yielding suboptimal performance on heterogeneous data streams. We introduce **TauFlow**, a novel framework that injects *dynamic causal constraints* into a flow‑based segmentation backbone to enable *complexity‑adaptive* inference. TauFlow learns a per‑sample scalar τ that captures the intrinsic difficulty of an image and drives a gating module that modulates the depth, width, and skip‑connection schedule of the network on the fly. The causal constraint guarantees that the information flow follows a strictly monotonic refinement path, ensuring that any early‑exit branch can be interpreted as a valid coarse segmentation while preserving the full‑resolution output when deeper features are required. Training is performed end‑to‑end with a joint segmentation‑and‑complexity loss, encouraging the network to trade off accuracy for speed without manual tuning. On the Cityscapes, Pascal‑VOC and the medical prostate‑MRI datasets, TauFlow attains 2–3× reduction in FLOPs while maintaining within 1.5 % of state‑of‑the‑art mIoU, and achieves real‑time performance (≤30 fps) on a single RTX 2070 GPU and on ARM‑based mobile platforms. Ablation studies confirm that both the causal constraint and the dynamic τ‑controller are critical for achieving the reported speed‑accuracy frontier. TauFlow therefore represents a principled, data‑driven approach to lightweight segmentation that adapts its computational footprint to the semantic complexity of each input.
845:
Scene text recognition (STR) continues to be a demanding task because real‑world images introduce complex variations. Existing systems typically separate visual and linguistic optimisation, which aggravates error propagation caused by cross‑modal misalignment. Visual encoders tend to focus on background distractors, while decoders experience spatial misalignments when parsing geometrically distorted text, leading to a drop in accuracy for irregular patterns.

Drawing inspiration from the hierarchical cognitive stages of human visual perception, we introduce **OTSNet**, a three‑stage network that implements a neurocognitive‑inspired *Observation–Thinking–Spelling* pipeline for end‑to‑end STR. The model is built upon three principal modules:

1. **Dual Attention Macaron Encoder (DAME)** – this layer refines visual features by applying differential attention maps that suppress irrelevant background and accentuate discriminative regions.
2. **Position‑Aware Module (PAM) + Semantic Quantizer (SQ)** – together, these components embed spatial context and glyph‑level semantic abstraction through adaptive sampling.
3. **Multi‑Modal Collaborative Verifier (MMCV)** – this component enforces self‑correction by fusing visual, semantic and character‑level features, ensuring cross‑modal consistency.

Extensive evaluations show that OTSNet sets new state‑of‑the‑art results, achieving **83.5 % average accuracy on the challenging Union14M‑L benchmark** and **79.1 % on the heavily occluded OST dataset**, securing record performance in 9 of the 14 tested scenarios.
846: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive reasoning capabilities, but most current test‑time methods depend on rough self‑verification and correction, which hampers performance on more demanding tasks. In this work we introduce **Socratic Self‑Refine (SSR)**, a novel framework that performs fine‑grained assessment and precise improvement of LLM reasoning. SSR breaks a model’s answer into verifiable sub‑question/sub‑answer pairs, allowing step‑by‑step confidence estimation via controlled re‑solving and self‑consistency checks. By detecting unreliable steps and iteratively refining them, SSR yields more accurate and interpretable reasoning chains. Across five reasoning benchmarks and three different LLMs, SSR consistently surpasses leading iterative self‑refinement baselines. Beyond accuracy gains, SSR offers a principled black‑box method for evaluating and understanding the inner reasoning dynamics of LLMs. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/socratic-self-refine-reasoning.
847:
Harnessing explicit causal knowledge is vital for refining causal models and enhancing downstream applications such as therapeutic design. We propose a novel ingredient for causal discovery—**interventional constraints**—which is distinct from conventional interventional data. Whereas interventional data involve direct perturbations of variables, interventional constraints encode domain expertise as inequality constraints on total causal effects. For example, in the Sachs dataset (Sachs et al., 2005) it is known that PIP3 activates Akt, implying a strictly positive causal effect from PIP3 to Akt. Existing algorithms that impose structural constraints (e.g., requiring a directed path PIP3 → Akt) can still infer incorrect relations such as “PIP3 inhibits Akt”. By explicitly bounding the magnitude of total effects, interventional constraints eliminate such contradictions and enforce consistency with prior biological knowledge.

To operationalize these constraints we introduce a quantitative metric for total causal effects in linear models and cast the learning problem as a constrained optimisation task.
