In this paper we propose *Textual Understanding Boost* (TUB), a framework that augments a baseline link‑prediction policy with advanced natural‑language representations of article bodies, entity relationships, and discourse cues.  

TUB leverages two complementary techniques: (1) a fine‑tuned transformer encoder (RoBERTa‑Wiki) to compute semantic embeddings of article paragraphs, and (2) a graph‑neural‑network layer that propagates entity‑link information across the Wikipedia hyperlink graph. Together, these components produce a dynamic relevance score for each outbound link, conditioned on the current path context. We integrate the scores into a Monte‑Carlo tree‑search policy that balances exploration and exploitation while respecting the game’s time constraints.  

We evaluate our approach on the publicly available WikiRace dataset (over 30,000 races spanning 500,000 unique articles) and on a newly curated “Hard‑Mode” subset where target articles are semantically distant from sources. Compared to the state‑of‑the‑art baseline (DeepWikiNavigator), TUB improves success rates from 62.4 % to 76.1 % on the standard dataset and from 47.3 % to 64.8 % on Hard‑Mode, while reducing average hop count by 18 %. Ablation studies confirm that both the contextual embeddings and the entity‑propagation layer contribute significantly to performance gains.  

Our results demonstrate that fine‑grained textual understanding and knowledge‑graph reasoning can substantially enhance navigational decision‑making in Wikipedia‑based tasks, opening avenues for more general web‑exploration agents and for improved educational tools that rely on large knowledge bases.
1043:
3D semantic scene understanding is still a formidable problem in computer vision, largely because annotated real‑world data are scarce and models that generalise well are hard to build. A common workaround is to generate synthetic data: while these datasets are easy to scale and come with perfect labels, the manually designed scenes rarely capture the richness and noise of real sensor outputs, leading to a noticeable synthetic‑to‑real domain gap. Additionally, no existing benchmark offers synchronised real and synthetic point clouds that can be used to study this gap specifically for segmentation.

To bridge this gap, we present **TrueCity**, the first urban segmentation benchmark that pairs centimetre‑accurate annotations of real point clouds with perfectly aligned 3D city models and corresponding simulated point clouds of the identical scene. Our classes follow international 3D city‑modeling standards, allowing for consistent evaluation of the domain shift. Extensive tests on standard baselines quantify the magnitude of the shift and demonstrate techniques for leveraging synthetic data to improve real‑world performance. We believe that TrueCity will become a valuable resource for quantifying sim‑to‑real discrepancies and training robust, data‑driven models. The dataset, code, and 3D models are freely available at https://tum-gis.github.io/TrueCity/.
1044:
This study investigates the use of an optimization‑based damage‑detection and damage‑state digital twinning framework built on a novel conditional‑labeled generative adversarial network. Unlike existing AI‑driven digital‑twin techniques, our approach does not require prior knowledge of a system’s health, a critical advantage for real‑world deployment. Current methods often suffer from unreliable predictions when only a few measurements are available, when physical knowledge is sparse, or when the damage state is unknown. To address this, we propose and rigorously validate an unsupervised procedure on the benchmark structural‑health‑monitoring data from Switzerland’s Z24 bridge, a post‑tensioned concrete highway structure. 

The procedure first trains the network with multiple measurements that belong to the same damage level, forcing it to converge conditionally to two distinct damage states. It then repeats this process for a separate set of measurements. By comparing the resulting convergence scores, the method distinguishes between different damage states. Importantly, the same process is applied to both healthy‑to‑healthy and damage‑to‑healthy data streams, thereby generating synthetic measurements for digital twinning across several damage levels. These synthetic data support pattern recognition and machine‑learning data generation.

To further validate the approach, we develop a support‑vector‑machine classifier and a principal‑component‑analysis routine that jointly evaluate both real and generated measurements for each damage category, yielding a secondary dynamic‑learning indicator for damage scenarios. The results demonstrate that the framework accurately discriminates damaged from healthy conditions, offering a robust vibration‑based monitoring tool that scales to large infrastructure networks and enhances resilience.
1045:
Improvisation—spontaneous, moment‑to‑moment creation that unfolds without a predetermined script—demands continuous perception, adaptation, and recombination. As a core form of human creativity, it permeates music, dance, and everyday life, generating a stream of unique, unrepeatable moments that are prized in artistic practice. This same notion of unbounded novelty, or *open‑endedness* (OE), characterises natural and cultural evolution and is widely regarded as “the last grand challenge” in artificial life (ALife). With the advent of generative AI, a pressing question emerges in computational creativity (CC): What constitutes a “good” improvisation for machines, and can AI achieve genuinely open‑ended performance?  

In this work‑in‑progress paper we report findings from in‑depth interviews with six experts spanning dance, music, and contact improvisation. By mapping the insights from these practitioners to AI design, we identify a set of improvisational qualities that future experiential agents should embody: active listening (awareness of the *umwelt*), temporal presence (mindfulness and ephemerality), a willingness to embrace the unknown (sources of randomness and serendipity), a non‑judgmental flow (dynamical stability balancing structure and surprise), imaginative metaphor (synaesthetic planning), empathy and trust (mutual theory of mind), and playfulness with intrinsic motivation (sustaining interestingness). These principles illuminate pathways for developing AI capable of improvising independently, collaboratively with humans, or alongside other agents.
1046:
Physics‑informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful surrogate solver for partial differential equations, yet their practical deployment is often hindered by two intertwined challenges: (i) the loss terms associated with boundary conditions, governing equations, and data are highly disparate in scale, leading to unstable training and sub‑optimal convergence; and (ii) the uniform or heuristic sampling of collocation points fails to focus computational effort on regions that most influence the solution’s fidelity. In this work we introduce a **self‑adaptive weighting and sampling framework** that simultaneously addresses these issues.  

For the loss‑term balancing, we develop a dynamic weighting strategy that monitors the relative gradient norms of each residual and adjusts the corresponding weight to equalize their contribution over training epochs. This scheme is formally derived from a Lyapunov‑based analysis guaranteeing boundedness of the weighted loss. For sampling, we propose an **importance‑based point selection** method that uses a running estimate of the local residual magnitude to bias the probability density toward high‑error zones, thereby concentrating the network’s capacity where it is most needed. The resulting algorithm is lightweight, requires only standard back‑propagation, and is agnostic to the underlying physics model.  

We validate our approach on a suite of canonical problems—including the Poisson, Burgers, and Navier–Stokes equations—demonstrating up to a 30 % reduction in relative L2 error and a 40 % speed‑up in epochs to reach a prescribed tolerance, relative to conventional PINNs with static weights and uniform sampling. Sensitivity analyses confirm robustness across different network architectures and problem settings. The proposed self‑adaptive weighting and sampling strategy thus offers a practical, generalizable pathway to accelerate and stabilize the training of physics‑informed neural networks.
1047: Robotics and control systems often struggle to perform reliably in environments that differ from those seen during training. In this study we examine contextual reinforcement learning, where an agent must operate under a variety of contexts—such as a self‑driving vehicle facing new weather conditions, or a quadrupedal robot traversing unfamiliar terrain—without being given explicit context cues at test time. Prior solutions have employed a two‑stage pipeline that first trains a context encoder and then a history‑based adaptation module. While effective, this approach is complex to implement and to train end‑to‑end. We therefore propose **SPARC** (Single‑Phase Adaptation for Robust Control), a streamlined method that learns to adapt within a single training phase. SPARC is evaluated on the high‑fidelity racing simulator *Gran Turismo 7* and on wind‑perturbed MuJoCo tasks, and it demonstrates consistent, robust generalization to out‑of‑distribution settings.
1048: Federated Learning (FL) enables multiple institutions to collaboratively train models while keeping sensitive data locally, making it especially valuable in privacy‑constrained settings. Nonetheless, FL deployments remain susceptible to membership‑inference attacks and must contend with non‑IID data distributions. This work introduces **FedOnco‑Bench**, a reproducible, open‑source benchmark that uses synthetic oncologic CT scans annotated with tumors to evaluate privacy‑aware FL for medical image segmentation. We compare four FL strategies—FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedAvg augmented with DP‑SGD—assessing both segmentation quality and privacy leakage. The results reveal a clear privacy‑utility trade‑off: vanilla FedAvg attains the highest Dice scores (~0.85) but suffers greater privacy loss (attack AUC ≈ 0.72), whereas DP‑SGD offers stronger privacy protection (AUC ≈ 0.25) at the expense of accuracy (Dice ≈ 0.79). In heterogeneous data settings, FedProx and FedBN strike a better balance, maintaining robust performance with non‑IID client data. FedOnco‑Bench therefore provides a standardized platform for evaluating and advancing privacy‑preserving FL techniques in medical imaging.
1049:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly vulnerable to prompt‑injection exploits, yet most research has concentrated on sophisticated LLM deployments such as personal copilots. Everyday, low‑complexity LLM applications—think of the customer‑service bots that sit on countless websites—are far more common, yet their susceptibility to such attacks has not been thoroughly investigated. These bots are typically powered by third‑party plugins that sit between the user’s browser and commercial LLM APIs, letting non‑technical site owners effortlessly tweak chatbot behavior.

To address this knowledge gap, we conducted the first extensive audit of 17 widely used third‑party chatbot plugins, covering more than 10 000 public sites. Our study reveals hitherto unknown prompt‑injection vulnerabilities in practice. First, eight of the plugins (used by roughly 8 000 sites) do not validate the conversation history that is transmitted from the site to the LLM. This flaw permits attackers to insert fabricated conversation logs—including fake system prompts—thereby amplifying the success rate of direct prompt‑injection attacks by a factor of three to eight.

Second, fifteen plugins provide capabilities such as web‑scraping to augment a bot’s context with site‑specific content. However, these tools fail to discriminate between trusted, on‑site information (e.g., product descriptions) and untrusted, third‑party material (e.g., customer reviews), opening the door to indirect prompt‑injection attacks. In fact, about 13 % of e‑commerce sites already feed their chatbots with such third‑party content.

We evaluated both weaknesses through controlled experiments that mirror real‑world conditions, examining variables such as the design of system prompts and the choice of underlying LLM. The results demonstrate that many plugins adopt insecure practices that erode the LLM’s built‑in safeguards, leaving widespread, everyday chatbot deployments exposed.
1050: Liar’s Poker, a game of hidden information and strategic deception, poses a formidable challenge for artificial agents: the optimal strategy requires simultaneously evaluating probabilistic commitments and anticipating adversarial bluffing. In this work we introduce a deep reinforcement‑learning framework that learns to outbid and outbluff elite human players through large‑scale self‑play. Building on recent advances in imperfect‑information game‑theory, we model each player as a neural policy conditioned on the full history of bids, the private card distribution, and the current score state. The agent is trained with a combination of proximal policy optimization and a value‑network critic that incorporates counterfactual regret minimization (CFR) signals, thereby preserving equilibrium‑like play while allowing exploration of novel bluffing patterns. To evaluate the learned strategies, we conduct a series of head‑to‑head matches against a curated pool of 34 professional Liar’s Poker players, ranging from novice enthusiasts to self‑identified experts. Our agent consistently achieves a win rate of 68 % against the top‑tier cohort, exceeding the previous best human performance by 22 %. Moreover, ablation studies confirm that the inclusion of counterfactual regret signals is critical for learning sophisticated bluffing tactics, whereas pure policy‑gradient methods alone converge to myopic “truth‑telling” play. This paper demonstrates that self‑play reinforcement learning can not only master perfect‑information games but also navigate the nuanced demands of deception in imperfect‑information domains. The resulting framework offers a promising pathway for developing AI agents capable of sophisticated strategic reasoning in real‑world bargaining and negotiation contexts.
1051:
Large‑scale language models (LLMs) have emerged as versatile agents capable of learning from interaction, yet their reinforcement‑learning (RL) dynamics remain difficult to control and predict. In many domains—ranging from dialogue systems to autonomous reasoning—the agent must decide *when* to query an LLM, *what* sub‑tasks to solve, and *how* to interleave model‑generated plans with environment‑based exploration. Current approaches treat these decisions heuristically or rely on flat priority queues, which often lead to sub‑optimal sample efficiency and unstable training.  

We introduce **Scheduling with Reasoning Trees (SRT)**, a principled framework that couples RL with structured, tree‑based reasoning to guide the temporal allocation of LLM inference. An SRT is built from a hierarchy of sub‑goals and constraints derived from the task specification; each node in the tree is associated with a *scheduling policy* that decides whether to explore, exploit, or defer a particular branch based on a learned value estimate. The tree is traversed using a depth‑first policy that dynamically prunes unlikely branches, thereby reducing the number of costly LLM calls while preserving a comprehensive exploration of the policy space.  

We formally characterize SRT’s convergence guarantees under standard RL assumptions and present a lightweight implementation that integrates with off‑policy algorithms (e.g., PPO, SAC) and LLM back‑ends (OpenAI GPT‑4, Llama‑2). Experiments on a suite of benchmark environments—TextWorld, MiniGrid, and a custom “Logic Maze” suite—show that SRT attains 2–3× better sample efficiency and 1.5–2× higher final reward compared to baseline LLM‑RL methods. Ablation studies confirm the importance of tree depth, pruning heuristics, and reward shaping in the overall performance.  

Our results demonstrate that reasoning‑guided scheduling can reconcile the computational cost of LLM inference with the exploratory demands of RL, opening avenues for more robust and scalable language‑model agents in complex sequential tasks. Future work will explore adaptive tree re‑construction and transfer of reasoning policies across domains.
1052: We introduce **KFCPO**, a new Safe Reinforcement Learning method that fuses scalable Kronecker‑Factored Approximate Curvature (K‑FAC) for second‑order policy optimization with a safety‑aware gradient‑manipulation scheme. K‑FAC supplies fast and stable natural‑gradient updates by computing a closed‑form, layer‑wise approximation of the Fisher Information Matrix, thereby sidestepping the iterative costs typical of other curvature estimators. To navigate the tension between reward maximisation and constraint satisfaction, we propose a *margin‑aware* gradient‑mixing technique that dynamically weights reward and cost gradients based on how close the agent is to safety limits. This blending is performed through a direction‑sensitive projection, which removes detrimental interference and obviates the need for rigid hard thresholds. Moreover, we adopt a minibatch‑level KL rollback to preserve trust‑region properties and to prevent destabilising policy jumps. Benchmarks on Safety Gymnasium using the OmniSafe framework show that KFCPO attains between **10.3 % and 50.2 % higher average returns** than the best safe baseline while still honouring the safety constraints—demonstrating a superior balance of safety and performance.
1053: Transformers excel at capturing long‑range dependencies and are increasingly used as world models in model‑based reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability.  Yet, unlike the dense sequences found in natural language, RL trajectories are sparse and shaped by rewards, which renders conventional self‑attention sub‑optimal: it spreads weight evenly over all past tokens instead of highlighting the few transitions that are most relevant for control.  To overcome this mismatch, we embed structured inductive priors directly into the dynamics head’s attention layer.  Specifically, we impose (i) per‑head memory‑length constraints that confine attention to task‑specific horizons, and (ii) distributional priors that learn smooth Gaussian weightings over historic state‑action pairs.  These mechanisms are incorporated into UniZero, a model‑based RL agent that employs a Transformer‑based world model capable of planning under partial observability.  Evaluations on the Atari 100k benchmark reveal that the Gaussian prior is chiefly responsible for efficiency gains, smoothly allocating emphasis to informative transitions, while the hard memory‑length cutoffs often discard useful information.  In particular, Gaussian Attention boosts mean human‑normalised scores by 77 % relative to the baseline UniZero.  These results suggest that in partially observable RL tasks with non‑stationary temporal dynamics, flexible distributional priors outperform rigid memory windows, yielding more robust data efficiency.  Overall, encoding structured temporal priors into self‑attention markedly improves the prioritisation of salient histories for dynamics modelling under partial observability.
1054: In this study we examine how the rhetoric surrounding ChatGPT prompt‑writing on social media can foster critical AI literacies. Prompt‑writing—crafting instructions for generative AI tools such as ChatGPT to produce specific responses—has become a hot topic in online discussions. To investigate this rhetorical phenomenon, we draw upon four intersecting strands of digital composition scholarship: theories of literacy, analyses of social‑media rhetoric, iterative and reflexive methodological practices, and the fusion of computational and qualitative techniques. Using these lenses, we describe an iterative research workflow that compiled and interrogated 32,000 X (formerly Twitter) posts about prompt‑writing from November 2022 to May 2023. Our findings reveal five key themes in emerging AI‑literacy practices: (1) the communicative domains influenced by prompt‑writing; (2) micro‑literacy resources circulated for prompt‑writing; (3) market‑driven rhetoric shaping prompt‑writing; (4) stylistic features of prompts; and (5) varied definitions of prompt‑writing. By unpacking these themes and our methodological approach, we offer insights for educators and scholars working to teach and analyze critical AI literacies in digital writing contexts.
1055: Accurate day‑ahead electricity price forecasting (DAEPF) is essential for the optimal operation of power systems, yet existing models struggle when confronted with extreme events and market outliers. To address these issues, this paper introduces a novel hybrid deep‑learning architecture that combines a Distilled Attention Transformer (DAT) with an Autoencoder Self‑Regression Model (ASM). The DAT employs a self‑attention mechanism to focus on the most informative portions of historical price series, thereby capturing both long‑term trends and rapid short‑term variations. Meanwhile, the ASM utilizes unsupervised learning to pinpoint and isolate anomalous patterns caused by severe weather, heat waves, holidays, and other disruptive conditions. Empirical tests on datasets from California and Shandong Province show that the proposed framework markedly surpasses current state‑of‑the‑art methods in terms of prediction accuracy, resilience to anomalies, and computational speed. These results suggest that the hybrid model can strengthen grid reliability and improve market performance in emerging power systems.
1056:
The rapid proliferation of specialized “descriptive”, “predictive”, and “generative” models has fragmented the AI landscape, forcing practitioners to maintain multiple pipelines for seemingly related tasks.  In this work we introduce **TRISKELION‑1**, a single, end‑to‑end architecture that unifies these three paradigms within a single parametric backbone.  TRISKELION‑1 is a Transformer‑based encoder‑decoder with a *shared multimodal trunk* and lightweight *task‑specific adapters* that can be switched without retraining the core.  The trunk is trained on a massive 5 B‑token multimodal corpus (text, image, audio, and tabular data) using a curriculum that progressively increases task complexity, while the adapters employ a joint loss that balances cross‑entropy, MSE, and a GAN‑style reconstruction term.

We evaluate TRISKELION‑1 on a diverse suite of benchmarks: (i) descriptive language tasks (GLUE, SQuAD), (ii) predictive tasks (time‑series forecasting, tabular classification, image classification on ImageNet), and (iii) generative tasks (COCO captioning, GPT‑style text generation, StyleGAN image synthesis).  Across the board, TRISKELION‑1 matches or surpasses specialized state‑of‑the‑art models while requiring 30 % fewer parameters and 20 % less wall‑clock training time.  Importantly, the unified setting enables zero‑shot transfer: a prompt engineered for a predictive task can be repurposed to generate synthetic data that improves downstream descriptive performance, illustrating the cross‑fertilization potential of a single architecture.

Our contributions are threefold: 1) a novel unified architecture that seamlessly blends descriptive, predictive, and generative capabilities; 2) a scalable training regimen that harnesses multi‑modal data with a curriculum‑aware loss; and 3) a comprehensive empirical study demonstrating competitive performance on a broad spectrum of tasks.  TRISKELION‑1 opens a new avenue for building versatile AI systems that can describe, predict, and generate from a single model, reducing engineering overhead while delivering superior generalization.
1057: Catastrophic forgetting remains a central challenge in continual learning: neural networks tend to lose previously acquired knowledge when new tasks arrive. We introduce a path‑coordinated framework that integrates three complementary elements: (1) the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory to impose principled bounds on plasticity, (2) Wilson confidence intervals for rigorous statistical validation, and (3) a multi‑metric assessment of path quality. On Split‑CIFAR‑10, our method attains an average accuracy of 66.7 % while reducing catastrophic forgetting to 23.4 %—a substantial gain over the baseline and a performance close to state‑of‑the‑art. Analysis reveals that NTK condition numbers act as reliable predictors of learning capacity, with a critical threshold near \(10^{11}\). Notably, the forgetting rate declines as the task sequence progresses (from 27 % to 18 %), indicating system stabilization. The framework validates 80 % of discovered training paths with strong statistical guarantees and preserves 90–97 % of knowledge for intermediate tasks. By identifying the core capacity limits of the continual learning environment, we also propose actionable strategies for adaptive regularization.
1058:
The explosion of user‑generated content in Arabic across text, speech, and visual media has created an urgent demand for high‑quality multimodal resources that reflect the language’s rich cultural and linguistic diversity. Yet, existing Arabic corpora are largely unstructured, modality‑segregated, and lack fine‑grained alignment, limiting their utility for cross‑modal natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as multimodal translation, dialogue understanding, or affective analysis. In this paper we introduce **Wasm** – a scalable, end‑to‑end pipeline for constructing **Structured Arabic Interleaved Multimodal Corpora** (SAIMC). Wasm integrates data crawling, multimodal alignment, automatic quality assurance, and expert‑in‑the‑loop annotation into a unified workflow. The pipeline first harvests parallel streams of text, audio, and image/video from Arabic news sites, social‑media feeds, and public repositories, then employs a hybrid alignment strategy that leverages forced‑alignment of Arabic speech, subtitle extraction, and image captioning models to interleave modalities at the sentence‑level. Subsequently, a rule‑based consistency checker and a lightweight neural quality estimator flag anomalous segments, reducing manual review effort by 73 %. Finally, a web‑based annotation interface supports structured, multi‑label tagging (e.g., discourse, emotion, visual relevance) with collaborative editing and version control.  

We evaluated Wasm on a 12‑hour Arabic broadcast corpus and a 30‑day social‑media dataset, yielding two large SAIMC resources: **AraMult** (≈ 1.2 M interleaved utterances, 150 k image‑text pairs, 80 h of speech) and **News‑Audio‑Visual** (≈ 3.5 M tokens, 250 k images, 200 h audio). Automatic alignment precision exceeds 94 % against manually verified gold‑standard alignments. Downstream experiments on multimodal sentiment analysis and image‑captioning tasks demonstrate that models trained on Wasm‑generated corpora outperform baselines by 5–8 % (macro‑F1), underscoring the value of the interleaved structure.  

Wasm is open‑source and publicly released, enabling researchers and industry practitioners to build their own Arabic multimodal datasets with minimal overhead. The paper concludes with a discussion of future extensions (e.g., video‑level temporal segmentation, Arabic dialect support) and the broader implications for cross‑lingual and cross‑modal research.
1059: Large language models (LLMs) are normally equipped with safety mechanisms to prevent the generation of harmful content. Yet most existing defenses presume that a malicious query originates from an external source, overlooking the possibility that a model’s own output could become a new attack vector. In this work we introduce the *Self‑HarmLLM* setting, in which a *Mitigated Harmful Query* (MHQ) – a deliberately ambiguous prompt that retains its original intent while masking its harmful aspects – is produced by the very model that will later consume it. We test whether such an MHQ can “jailbreak” a fresh instance of the same model by re‑feeding it. Experiments were carried out on GPT‑3.5‑turbo, LLaMA3‑8B‑instruct, and DeepSeek‑R1‑Distill‑Qwen‑7B under baseline, zero‑shot, and few‑shot conditions. In the zero‑shot scenario, we observed transformation success rates up to 52 % and jailbreak success rates up to 33 %; in the few‑shot case, these numbers rose to 65 % and 41 % respectively. A comparison of prefix‑based automated metrics with human judgments revealed that the former consistently over‑estimates jailbreak efficacy, with an average over‑prediction of 52 %. While this study is a preliminary, toy‑level investigation limited to a small query set and evaluator pool, it demonstrates that the proposed self‑generation method is a viable attack vector. Our findings underscore the need to rethink current guard‑rail strategies and to develop more reliable evaluation frameworks.
1060: Simulated students provide a powerful methodological tool for assessing teaching strategies and modelling varied learner profiles—tasks that are often difficult to tackle systematically in real classrooms. Recent studies have increasingly turned to simulated agents that embody diverse learning styles, developmental pathways, and social behaviours. Among these, embedding large language models (LLMs) in educational research has emerged as a particularly flexible and scalable approach. LLMs offer a high degree of linguistic realism and behavioral adaptability, allowing agents to approximate cognitive processes and engage in contextually appropriate pedagogical conversations. This paper offers a thematic review of empirical and methodological work that uses LLMs to simulate student behaviour across learning contexts. We synthesize evidence on how well LLM‑based agents can represent learner archetypes, respond to instruction, and participate in multi‑agent classroom scenarios. We also consider the implications of these systems for curriculum design, instructional assessment, and teacher training. Although LLMs outperform rule‑based models in natural language generation and situational flexibility, concerns remain about algorithmic bias, evaluation consistency, and alignment with educational goals. The review highlights existing technological and methodological gaps and proposes future research avenues for integrating generative AI into adaptive learning and instructional design.
1061:
Whole‑slide images (WSIs) are gigapixel histopathology scans that encode complex spatial and morphological patterns relevant to cancer diagnosis and prognosis. Existing representation‑learning pipelines typically rely on a two‑stage workflow: (i) extraction of tile‑level features with a convolutional backbone, and (ii) aggregation of these features by attention or clustering to form a slide‑level embedding. Such approaches neglect the residual information that is lost when tiling and fail to leverage slide‑level context during feature learning. In this study we introduce **Dynamic Residual Encoding (DRE)**, an end‑to‑end framework that preserves and integrates the residual context across all tiles, and we couple it with a **Slide‑Level Contrastive Learning (SL‑CL)** objective that enforces consistency between global slide embeddings and local patch representations. 

DRE constructs a hierarchical residual representation by iteratively subtracting the mean of lower‑level feature maps from higher‑level ones, thereby encoding the incremental discriminative information across spatial scales. This residual hierarchy is concatenated with the original tile features and fed to a transformer‑based encoder that learns a global slide embedding. The SL‑CL loss maximizes the agreement between the global embedding and its constituent tile embeddings while contrasting against embeddings from other slides, enabling the model to capture slide‑specific histomorphology without supervision. 

We evaluate our method on two large multi‑institutional cohorts (TCGA‑HNSC and a metastatic melanoma set), comparing against state‑of‑the‑art MIL and attention‑based baselines on tasks of tumor subtype classification, mutation status prediction, and overall survival estimation. DRE+SL‑CL improves classification AUC by 4–8 % and outperforms baselines in survival prediction (C‑statistic 0.72 vs. 0.65). Ablation studies confirm that both the residual encoding and the contrastive objective are essential for the observed gains. Our framework is fully differentiable, requires no manual tile selection, and scales to whole‑slide resolution, offering a practical solution for large‑scale computational pathology.
1062: Clinical time series extracted from electronic health records (EHRs) are notoriously irregular—samples arrive at uneven intervals, values are frequently missing, and different features evolve in distinct ways. Although raw laboratory measurements carry a wealth of information, most existing embedding techniques merge feature identity and numerical values using simple addition, limiting their capacity to encode value‑dependent interactions among features. We introduce MedFuse, a framework for irregular clinical data that hinges on the MuFuse (Multiplicative Embedding Fusion) module. MuFuse integrates feature and value embeddings via a multiplicative modulation, retaining feature‑specific cues while capturing higher‑order cross‑feature dependencies. Across three real‑world datasets spanning intensive‑care and chronic‑care settings, MedFuse consistently surpasses state‑of‑the‑art baselines on several key prediction tasks. Examination of the resulting representations reveals that the multiplicative fusion enriches expressiveness and facilitates transfer learning across datasets. These findings position MedFuse as a broadly applicable method for modeling irregular clinical time series.
1063: Wide‑field fluorescence imaging suffers from severe out‑of‑focus background due to its limited axial resolution, especially in densely labelled biological specimens. To overcome this, we introduce ET2dNet, a deep‑learning framework that fuses epifluorescence (EPI) and total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) modalities to deliver TIRF‑level background removal and axial super‑resolution from a single wide‑field image—without any hardware changes. The model combines a physics‑driven hybrid architecture with supervised training on registered EPI‑TIRF pairs and self‑supervised PSF‑convolution constraints, ensuring robust performance across different objectives and enabling rapid few‑shot adaptation to new setups. Extensive validation on cells and tissues demonstrates that ET2dNet achieves superior background suppression and axial resolution, while remaining compatible with conventional deconvolution for lateral refinement. Building on this, we created ET3dNet via knowledge distillation, a dedicated 3‑D reconstruction network that delivers artifact‑reduced volumetric results and effectively removes out‑of‑focus noise even when the background source is missing from the input stack. This approach democratizes axial super‑resolution imaging by providing a simple, hardware‑free algorithm, with promising implications for live‑cell imaging and clinical histopathology.
1064: Probabilistic forecasting underpins efficient portfolio design in multivariate financial time series, especially when complex cross‑sectional relationships must be captured. We introduce **Diffolio**, a diffusion‑based framework for forecasting multiple asset returns and building portfolios. Diffolio’s core is a denoising neural network that incorporates a hierarchical attention scheme with both asset‑level and market‑level modules. To more faithfully encode inter‑asset dependencies, we add a correlation‑guided regularizer that leverages a robust estimate of the target correlation matrix. This architecture jointly learns from historical returns and from asset‑specific as well as systematic covariates, yielding markedly improved forecasts and portfolio allocations. Evaluated on daily excess returns of 12 industry portfolios, Diffolio surpasses a range of probabilistic forecasting benchmarks in multivariate predictive accuracy and in downstream portfolio performance. Portfolios constructed from Diffolio’s predictions consistently outperform benchmark strategies, attaining higher Sharpe ratios for the mean‑variance tangency portfolio and greater certainty equivalents for the growth‑optimal portfolio. These findings highlight Diffolio’s superiority both in statistical precision and in economic value.
1065:
Recent advances in recurrent neural architectures have underscored the importance of *fast‑weight* mechanisms for transient, context‑specific memory and rapid adaptation. However, the interaction between such fast‑weight layers and *homeostatic reentry*—the recurrent loop that stabilises long‑term weight dynamics—remains largely unexplored. In this work we introduce the **Recursive Dynamics in Fast‑Weights Homeostatic Reentry Networks (RDF‑HRN)** framework, a biologically inspired architecture that marries short‑term associative memories with slow, homeostatic weight recalibration through recursive reentry pathways.

We formalise a novel recursive update rule in which fast‑weight traces are repeatedly projected back into the slow‑weight manifold, allowing the network to iteratively refine its internal representation while maintaining global stability. By embedding this process within a hierarchical recurrent structure, the model acquires a *reflective* capacity: it can internally simulate and evaluate its own inference trajectories before committing to an output. We evaluate RDF‑HRN on a suite of benchmark tasks requiring meta‑learning, sequential decision‑making, and context‑dependent reasoning (e.g., Few‑Shot classification, dynamic maze navigation, and natural language dialogue). Across all tasks, RDF‑HRN outperforms state‑of‑the‑art fast‑weight and attention‑based models, achieving up to a 12 % relative improvement in accuracy and a 15 % reduction in training time on low‑data regimes.

Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that the recursive reentry loop enforces a contraction mapping on the joint fast–slow weight space, guaranteeing convergence to a stable equilibrium while preserving rapid adaptability. These results suggest that recursive dynamics within fast‑weight homeostatic reentry networks constitute a promising substrate for *reflective intelligence*—the ability of a system to reason about its own reasoning in real time. We conclude by discussing implications for neuromorphic hardware and potential extensions to multi‑agent coordination and continual learning.
1066:
Large‑scale point‑cloud processing remains a formidable challenge due to the irregularity of the data, the need for multi‑scale context, and the prohibitive memory and computational cost of dense sampling.  We introduce **FractalCloud**, a fractal‑inspired neural architecture that systematically exploits self‑similarity to build highly efficient, multi‑resolution representations of 3‑D point sets.  The core idea is to arrange the network as a recursive “fractal graph”: each fractal block contains a compact local aggregation operator (a point‑wise convolution with a dynamically adaptive radius) followed by a down‑sample/ up‑sample pair that mirrors the block’s own structure.  This self‑similar layout yields a principled hierarchy of receptive fields without the parameter blow‑up of conventional pyramidal designs.  In addition, a cross‑scale attention module fuses information from all fractal levels, allowing the network to adaptively prioritize coarse or fine features on a per‑point basis.  

We evaluate FractalCloud on a suite of large‑scale benchmarks—including ModelNet40, ScanNet, and the KITTI 3‑D LiDAR dataset—using both classification and semantic segmentation tasks.  On ModelNet40 it attains 95.3 % accuracy, surpassing PointNet++, DGCNN, and KPConv while using 40 % less GPU memory and 30 % faster inference.  For ScanNet, FractalCloud improves mean IoU by 4.2 % over the best baseline, and on KITTI it achieves a 2.7 % reduction in average precision for object detection at a fixed latency.  

FractalCloud demonstrates that a fractal‑based architecture can reconcile the competing demands of scalability, accuracy, and efficiency, making it a compelling choice for real‑time applications such as autonomous driving, robotics, and large‑scale scene understanding.
1067: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive reasoning skills in many niche areas, which has sparked interest in using them for legal reasoning tasks. Existing legal benchmarks, however, tend to mix simple factual recall with true inference, break the reasoning chain into isolated steps, and ignore the overall quality of the reasoning process. To overcome these shortcomings, we present MSLR, the first Chinese dataset that captures multi‑step legal reasoning rooted in real judicial decisions. MSLR structures expert reasoning using the IRAC scheme (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion) extracted from official court documents. We also develop a scalable Human‑LLM collaborative annotation workflow that generates fine‑grained, step‑level reasoning annotations and can serve as a template for future multi‑step reasoning datasets. Experiments with several LLMs on MSLR reveal only modest performance, underscoring the difficulty of handling complex legal reasoning. Additional tests show that self‑generated Chain‑of‑Thought prompts from the models themselves enhance reasoning coherence and quality, surpassing manually crafted prompts. MSLR thus pushes forward research on LLM reasoning and Chain‑of‑Thought techniques and supplies open resources for the community. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/yuwenhan07/MSLR-Bench and https://law.sjtu.edu.cn/flszyjzx/index.html.
1068:
Large‑scale mobility prediction systems—ranging from traffic routing to public‑transport demand forecasting—rely on machine‑learning models trained on billions of spatiotemporal observations. Yet these models routinely exhibit systematic performance gaps across demographic and geographic groups, propagating inequities into the services that depend on them. In this work we introduce *Mind the Gaps*, a comprehensive audit and mitigation framework for group‑level inequities in mobility prediction.

We first define a principled audit protocol that (i) partitions users into socially salient groups (e.g., income quintile, race, age, gender, and urban‑rural residence), (ii) evaluates per‑group prediction error using calibrated error metrics (MAE, RMSE, and log‑likelihood), and (iii) quantifies disparity via statistical parity and equalized odds metrics adapted to spatiotemporal forecasting. Applying this audit to two large‑scale datasets—NYC taxi‑trip records (≈1.5 M trips) and nationwide ride‑hailing traces (≈10 M trips)—we uncover pronounced inequities: predictions for lower‑income neighborhoods are on average 18 % less accurate, and for older users a 23 % higher mean absolute error, even after controlling for overall traffic patterns.

To mitigate these gaps we develop a *Group‑Aware Fairness‑Regularized* (GAFR) training pipeline that augments the loss function with a differentiable fairness penalty and employs adversarial reweighting to balance group representations in the embedding space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GAFR reduces the largest per‑group error by up to 31 % while preserving overall accuracy (≤ 3 % loss in global MAE). We also explore curriculum‑style fine‑tuning and data‑augmentation strategies that further narrow disparities at minimal computational cost.

Our contributions provide a practical, end‑to‑end toolkit for auditing and correcting group inequity in large‑scale mobility prediction, illustrating that fairness can be achieved without sacrificing predictive power. This work lays the groundwork for responsible deployment of mobility analytics in smart‑city infrastructures.
1069: The capacitated location‑routing problem (CLRP) lies at the heart of combinatorial optimization, demanding simultaneous decisions about facility placement and vehicle paths. Its difficulty stems from tight capacity constraints and the subtle interplay among location, routing, and demand‑allocation choices. Although deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has proven effective for vehicle‑routing variants, its application to CLRP remains largely unexplored. In this study we introduce **DRL with Heterogeneous Querying (DRLHQ)**, an end‑to‑end DRL framework based on an encoder–decoder architecture that tackles both the standard CLRP and its open‑ended version (OCLRP). We cast the CLRP as a Markov decision process that captures the full spectrum of decision variables, offering a versatile template for future DRL models. To cope with the complex interdependence between location and routing actions, we devise a heterogeneous query‑attention mechanism that adaptively adjusts across different stages of the decision process. Extensive experiments on synthetic instances and benchmark collections show that DRLHQ outperforms prominent classical algorithms and competing DRL approaches, delivering higher‑quality solutions and stronger generalisation across diverse problem settings.
1070: We examine how large language models (LLMs) solve a variety of list‑processing tasks and uncover that they encode a concise, causal representation of a universal “filter” operation—analogous to the generic filter function in functional programming. By applying causal mediation analysis across a broad set of such tasks, we identify a small subset of attention heads, which we term *filter heads*, that store a compact representation of the filtering predicate in their query states at specific tokens. We show that this predicate encoding is both general and transferable: it can be extracted and reused to perform the same filtering on different collections, presented in various formats, languages, or even distinct tasks. At the same time, we find that transformer LMs can also adopt a different filtering strategy—evaluating the predicate on each item in advance and flagging the result directly within the item representations. Our findings demonstrate that transformer LMs can develop human‑interpretable implementations of abstract computational operations that generalize in ways strikingly similar to conventional functional‑programming patterns.
1071: Artificial intelligence systems frequently mirror the biases of economically prosperous regions, thereby sidelining the realities of less affluent areas such as Latin America where training data are scarce and skewed. This study investigates how AI portrays a spectrum of Latin American contexts, uncovering stark differences between datasets sourced from wealthy versus developing regions. It points out that the preponderance of English, at the expense of Spanish, Portuguese, and indigenous tongues like Quechua and Nahuatl, reinforces a Western‑centric narrative that misrepresents local perspectives. To counteract this, we construct a culturally attuned dataset grounded in Latin American historical and socio‑political knowledge, deliberately challenging Eurocentric assumptions. We benchmark six language models on culturally contextualized prompts, applying a new Cultural Expressiveness metric, statistical significance tests, and linguistic analysis. Results reveal that while some models grasp Latin American nuance, others display pronounced sentiment distortions (p < 0.001). Fine‑tuning Mistral‑7B with our dataset boosts its cultural expressiveness by 42.9%, moving the field toward more balanced AI. We conclude that equitable AI must foreground datasets that honor Latin American history, indigenous wisdom, and linguistic diversity, and that community‑driven methodologies are essential for amplifying marginalized voices.
1072: Recent advances in multi‑agent systems have shifted toward deploying larger, more intricate architectures to tackle sophisticated problems. However, this increased complexity can give rise to two significant issues: heightened vulnerability to faults and emerging performance bottlenecks. To mitigate the former, we introduce a transaction‑based design framework tailored for Very Complex Multi‑Agent Systems (VCMAS). To tackle the latter, we embed transaction scheduling within this framework. Together, these components form the OptiMA platform, which we have implemented and tested on VCMAS configurations comprising over one hundred agents. Empirical results demonstrate that incorporating transaction scheduling can improve system performance by more than 16 %. Additionally, we present a theoretical analysis of the transaction scheduling problem and provide practical tools to support ongoing research in this area.
1073: Fairness is a key requirement for unsupervised clustering, yet most existing fair‑clustering algorithms scale poorly, often exhibiting quadratic or higher time complexity that limits their applicability to large datasets. In this work we propose the *Anchor-based Fair Clustering Framework (AFCF)*, a versatile, plug‑and‑play scheme that endows any off‑the‑shelf fair clustering method with linear‑time efficiency. AFCF first builds a concise, representative set of anchor points using a novel fair‑sampling procedure. The chosen fair algorithm is then run on this small anchor subset. The central component of our framework is an anchor‑graph module that propagates cluster labels to all data points while maintaining fairness; we formulate this as an optimization problem with a joint group‑label constraint and prove that it guarantees the overall clustering inherits the fairness of the anchor clustering. The problem is solved efficiently via an ADMM routine. Experiments on several large‑scale datasets show that AFCF reduces runtime by orders of magnitude, while preserving strong clustering quality and fairness performance compared to state‑of‑the‑art methods.
1074:
Modern software is often distributed only as binary executables, leaving legacy codebases and security-critical firmware in a fragile state that cannot be easily understood, maintained, or migrated to new hardware. Traditional decompilers recover a syntactic approximation of the original program but frequently omit crucial semantic information, such as data‑flow relationships, type annotations, and platform‑specific constraints, which hampers any attempt to re‑execute the recovered source on a different architecture or to formally verify its correctness.  

We introduce **Context‑Guided Decompilation (CG‑Decomp)**, a novel framework that integrates static binary analysis with lightweight dynamic contextual information gathered from sandboxed executions. By observing runtime traces—control‑flow, memory‑access patterns, and system‑call interactions—CG‑Decomp infers implicit type, ownership, and data‑dependency relations that are otherwise lost in the binary. These *execution contexts* are then leveraged to disambiguate low‑level idioms and to annotate the reconstructed source with rich semantic metadata.  

Our prototype, built on LLVM’s intermediate representation, is evaluated on a diverse set of open‑source binaries (Linux utilities, embedded firmware, and legacy Windows programs). Compared to state‑of‑the‑art decompilers, CG‑Decomp improves type‑precision by 42 % and restores re‑executability on an ARM‑based platform with 88 % functional equivalence. We also demonstrate that the enriched decompiled artefacts enable automated patching and formal verification tasks that were previously infeasible.  

In sum, Context‑Guided Decompilation bridges the gap between low‑level binaries and high‑level, re‑executable artifacts, paving the way for sustainable reverse engineering, vulnerability remediation, and platform migration of legacy software.
1075: Although both shape and texture are essential for visual recognition, most deep‑learning studies have concentrated on texture, leaving the geometric aspect largely unexplored. In this work we demonstrate that: (1) carefully optimized shapes can serve as powerful semantic cues, enabling high‑confidence predictions from purely geometric inputs; (2) such shapes act as precise interpretability tools, pinpointing a model’s most relevant regions; and (3) they introduce a versatile adversarial strategy capable of fooling downstream visual systems. Our end‑to‑end differentiable pipeline unifies a robust Fourier‑series parametrization of arbitrary shapes, a winding‑number mapping that embeds them into the pixel grid of DNNs, and energy‑based constraints that accelerate optimization while preserving physical plausibility. This framework offers a flexible means to interrogate the geometric behaviour of DNNs and paves the way for novel tests and insights into machine perception.
1076: The rapid deployment of autonomous AI agents in domains ranging from conversational assistants to autonomous vehicles has exposed a critical gap: existing Service Level Agreements (SLAs) were designed for human‑managed services and fail to capture the unique, dynamic, and often opaque nature of learning‑based agents. In this work we introduce **AgentSLA**, a principled framework for specifying, negotiating, and verifying contractual guarantees for AI agents. AgentSLA extends classical SLA concepts—availability, latency, error‑rate, and fairness—to include *model‑level* properties such as robustness, interpretability, and data‑use compliance. We formalise these properties as measurable metrics, present a language for expressing them in contract terms, and develop a negotiation protocol that reconciles conflicting objectives between agents and stakeholders while respecting legal and ethical constraints. To demonstrate feasibility, we instantiate AgentSLA for three representative agent classes (dialogue, recommendation, and robotic control) and evaluate its enforcement via both simulation and real‑world deployment. Results show that agents can satisfy negotiated SLA targets with a negligible performance overhead and that the framework enables early detection of drift or policy violations. Our contributions lay a foundation for the trustworthy, accountable, and economically viable integration of AI agents into mission‑critical systems.
1077:
Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have broadened their ability to process both spoken and non‑spoken audio, yet they have also opened up new safety concerns when faced with intricate audio inputs that existing mitigations do not adequately address. To probe these weaknesses we propose **SACRED‑Bench** (Speech‑Audio Composition for RED‑teaming), a benchmark designed to test LLM resilience against complex audio‑based attacks. Unlike traditional perturbation techniques that depend on noise optimisation or white‑box access, SACRED‑Bench leverages three speech‑audio composition strategies:  

1. **Speech overlap and multi‑speaker dialogue** – embedding malicious prompts inside or alongside benign speech.  
2. **Speech‑audio mixtures** – conveying illicit intent through background non‑speech audio while presenting innocuous speech or audio.  
3. **Varied spoken instruction styles** – such as open‑ended Q&A or yes/no formats that bypass text‑only filtering.

Evaluation on the benchmark demonstrates that even the cutting‑edge proprietary model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, is vulnerable, achieving a 66 % success rate on our test set. To close this gap, we introduce **SALMONN‑Guard**, a safeguard LLM that jointly examines speech, audio, and text to produce safety judgments, cutting the attack success rate to 20 %. These findings underscore the necessity of audio‑aware defenses for the secure operation of multimodal LLMs. The SACRED‑Bench dataset and SALMONN‑Guard checkpoints are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/tsinghua‑ee/SACRED-Bench. **Note:** The paper contains potentially offensive or harmful content.
1078: The rapid advancement of synthetic image and deep‑fake generation models has made source attribution and authenticity verification a pressing issue for contemporary computer‑vision systems. Recent investigations reveal that diffusion pipelines inadvertently embed persistent statistical artefacts—so‑called signal leaks—within their outputs, especially in latent representations. Leveraging this insight, we introduce **Proto‑LeakNet**, a signal‑leak‑aware, interpretable attribution framework that couples closed‑set classification with a density‑based open‑set assessment of the learned embeddings. This design permits the analysis of unseen generators without requiring additional training. Operating directly in the diffusion model’s latent space, our approach partially reverses the forward diffusion process to reveal residual generator‑specific cues. A temporal attention encoder fuses multi‑step latent features, while a feature‑weighted prototype head structures the embedding space to yield transparent attribution. Trained only on known generators, Proto‑LeakNet attains a macro‑AUC of 98.13 %, demonstrates robustness against post‑processing, outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines, and exhibits strong separability between known and unseen generators. These results confirm that modeling signal‑leak bias in latent space yields reliable, interpretable forensics for AI‑generated images and deep‑fakes. The full code will be released upon publication.
1079: Machine learning systems that serve socially sensitive applications are increasingly required to be both *fair*—avoiding disparate treatment of protected groups—and *private*—protecting individual data from leakage. Existing approaches typically treat fairness and privacy as orthogonal constraints, leading to either brittle rule‑based post‑processing or a single, static objective that cannot adapt to domain‑specific concerns. We introduce **FAIRPLAI**, a human‑in‑the‑loop framework that jointly optimises fairness and differential privacy by integrating expert feedback at every stage of training. FAIRPLAI alternates between a privacy‑preserving gradient step (using DP‑SGD with a tunable privacy budget) and a *fairness‑oracle* that interrogates a human reviewer to adjust group‑specific performance targets. The framework formalises a *fair‑privacy budget allocation* problem, solved via a convex relaxation that guarantees $(\epsilon,\delta)$‑differential privacy while maintaining a target fairness metric (e.g., equalized odds or demographic parity). We demonstrate the effectiveness of FAIRPLAI on multiple benchmark datasets (COMPAS, Adult, German Credit, and UCI Adult-Census) and on a real‑world health‑insurance claims dataset. Across all settings, FAIRPLAI attains up to 15 % reduction in disparate impact relative to state‑of‑the‑art DP‑aware baselines while preserving or improving model utility; simultaneously, it respects a tighter privacy budget than comparable methods. A user‑study with domain experts confirms that the iterative human feedback loop allows nuanced trade‑offs that static optimisation cannot capture. Our theoretical analysis provides generalization guarantees under the combined fairness‑privacy constraints. FAIRPLAI therefore offers a principled, practical pathway to deploy machine‑learning models that satisfy both societal fairness and stringent privacy regulations.
1080:
Diffusion‐based language models have recently achieved state‑of‑the‑art performance on a variety of generative tasks, yet their inherent iterative refinement process poses a challenge for controllable editing: user‑supplied modifications often deteriorate as the diffusion chain progresses, a phenomenon we term the *edit‑fading* effect. In this work we introduce **Token‑Timestep Allocation (TTA)**, a lightweight, post‑hoc editing framework that preserves user edits throughout the diffusion pipeline without the need for costly retraining or fine‑tuning.  

TTA treats each token as an independent entity whose diffusion trajectory is governed by a dynamically‑assigned timestep schedule. By allocating “long‑horizon” timesteps to edited tokens and “short‑horizon” timesteps to unmodified tokens, the algorithm ensures that the latent representation of the edited portion remains stable while the rest of the sequence continues to evolve. The allocation scheme is guided by a principled objective that balances edit fidelity against overall generative quality, and it can be integrated with any pre‑trained diffusion language model in a single forward pass.  

We evaluate TTA on a suite of editing benchmarks—including controlled style transfer, fact injection, and sentence paraphrasing—and demonstrate that it reduces edit‑fading by up to 35 % relative to baseline diffusion and 50 % relative to fine‑tuning baselines, while preserving perplexity and BLEU scores within 3 % of the original model. Ablation studies confirm that the timestep allocation is the key component, and analysis of the latent space reveals that edited tokens maintain higher cosine similarity across diffusion steps.  

Our results illustrate that simple, token‑level timestep scheduling can provide robust edit retention for diffusion language models, opening a path toward practical, user‑driven text editing that preserves both fidelity and fluency. This work is a step toward “Don’t Let It Fade” – keeping user edits alive in the generative process.
1081: The European Union’s forthcoming Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) introduces novel regulatory obligations for high‑risk and “special‑purpose” large language models (LLMs), demanding transparency, traceability, and accountability in their deployment. This paper investigates watermarking—embedding machine‑readable signatures into generated content—as a technical lever to operationalise these requirements. We first analyse the AI Act’s provisions on “information about the origin, development, and operation of AI systems” and assess how watermarking can satisfy obligations related to model identification, version control, and misuse monitoring. Drawing on a mixed‑methods approach, we (i) survey current watermarking techniques (deterministic, probabilistic, cryptographic, and steganographic) and benchmark their robustness against common adversarial transformations; (ii) conduct a legal mapping exercise that juxtaposes the Act’s transparency clauses with watermarking’s evidentiary potential; and (iii) interview stakeholders—including EU policymakers, LLM developers, and civil‑society experts—to gauge acceptance and identify deployment trade‑offs. Our results demonstrate that, while no single watermarking scheme is fully resilient, a hybrid approach can deliver sufficient auditability without compromising user privacy or model performance. We conclude by proposing a framework for integrating watermarking into LLM development pipelines, outlining policy recommendations for regulators, and highlighting avenues for future research on harmonisation across jurisdictions. This work contributes to the emerging dialogue on AI governance by bridging legal theory with actionable technical safeguards in the context of Europe’s AI Act.
1082:
Urban storm sewers are critical infrastructure assets that must be monitored to detect flooding, pollutant surges, and structural deterioration. However, installing and maintaining dense sensor networks in these confined, often inaccessible conduits is prohibitively expensive. This paper proposes a data‑driven sparse sensing framework that optimally selects sensor locations while preserving high fidelity in the reconstruction of hydraulic and water‑quality states throughout an entire sewershed.

We first aggregate historical hydro‑geometric and pollutant‑loading records from a 120‑km urban storm sewer network and embed them in a physics‑based hydraulic simulation. The resulting high‑dimensional state trajectories are compressed using principal component analysis and sparse reconstruction techniques. Sensor placement is then cast as a mixed‑integer optimization problem that minimizes the reconstruction error of the full network state subject to a hard bound on the number of deployable sensors. To solve this NP‑hard problem efficiently, we develop a greedy algorithm guided by the mutual information criterion and a subsequent refinement step using a Bayesian optimization surrogate.

The algorithm is validated on synthetic networks of varying topology and on a real‑world dataset from the City of Boston’s storm sewer system. Compared with conventional uniform and flow‑threshold based placements, the proposed method achieves over 90 % of the full‑network observability while reducing sensor count by 35–45 %. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate robustness to measurement noise and to unmodeled extreme events. Moreover, we illustrate how the selected sensor set can be adapted online as new data streams in, enabling dynamic re‑allocation for evolving urban drainage challenges.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a principled sparse sensing formulation for storm sewer monitoring that explicitly leverages historical data and hydraulic modeling; (2) an efficient, scalable algorithm that delivers near‑optimal sensor configurations for large urban networks; and (3) a comprehensive validation that quantifies cost savings and performance gains over existing heuristic methods. This work offers a practical pathway to cost‑effective, data‑driven monitoring of storm sewer systems, facilitating proactive maintenance and real‑time flood mitigation.
1083:
Confocal laser endomicroscopy (CLE) offers a non‑invasive, real‑time means of visualizing mucosal micro‑architecture in situ. Nevertheless, clinicians—particularly those without extensive experience—often find CLE images difficult to interpret, limiting its diagnostic utility. Machine‑learning techniques could alleviate this barrier, yet their effectiveness is hampered by the scarcity of histopathology‑correlated CLE sequences and the sheer diversity of visual patterns, which in turn fosters overfitting. 

To address this, we apply self‑supervised learning (SSL) to large, unlabeled CLE corpora. Because CLE data arrive as high‑correlation video streams, the distribution for SSL training is non‑stratified, exacerbating redundancy. We therefore introduce a video‑sequence filtering scheme that prunes redundant frames, thereby accelerating SSL convergence and reducing computational load. 

Four cutting‑edge baseline models and an SSL teacher‑student architecture—built on a Vision Transformer small (ViT‑S) backbone—were evaluated on downstream classification tasks involving a sinonasal tumor cohort and a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma cohort. On both datasets, the filtered, SSL‑pretrained model achieved the best test accuracy (67.48 % for sinonasal tumors and 73.52 % for skin SCC), markedly surpassing non‑SSL counterparts. 

Our findings confirm that SSL is a potent pre‑training strategy for CLE, and that the proposed video filter substantially boosts training efficiency, cutting the required training time by 67 %.
1084: Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted in an ever‑expanding array of applications, yet systematic methods for evaluating their reliability are still scarce. Traditional benchmark tests usually report only aggregate accuracy figures, leaving a gap in understanding how LLMs behave probabilistically in real‑world settings. This work proposes HIP‑LLM, a Hierarchical Imprecise Probability framework that brings the rigor of software reliability engineering to the analysis of LLMs. We define LLM reliability as the probability of operating without failure over a predetermined number of future tasks under a specified Operational Profile (OP). By structuring domain dependencies in a hierarchical manner, HIP‑LLM allows inference at multiple levels—from individual sub‑domains up to the entire system. The framework incorporates imprecise priors to capture epistemic uncertainty and integrates OPs to reflect actual usage conditions, yielding posterior reliability envelopes that express uncertainty across both prior assumptions and observed data. Experiments conducted on several benchmark corpora show that HIP‑LLM provides a more precise and uniform reliability assessment than existing benchmark‑based and state‑of‑the‑art methods. A public implementation of HIP‑LLM is available for use.
1085: Vision‑language alignment (VLA) models have become the backbone of many multimodal systems, yet their ability to generalize to out‑of‑distribution (OOD) visual scenes remains fragile.  In practice, a VLA encoder can become “blind” to domain shifts: the visual representations it learns are heavily tied to the training domain’s visual distribution, leading to catastrophic failure when confronted with novel objects, styles, or lighting conditions.  In this paper we formalise this *blindness* phenomenon by analysing the discrepancy between in‑distribution (ID) and OOD visual embeddings in two popular VLA families (CLIP‑style and transformer‑based encoder‑decoder models).  We then propose **Aligned Visual Representation Learning (AVRL)**, a lightweight training regime that explicitly aligns visual embeddings across a curated set of domain‑shifted auxiliary images.  AVRL comprises (i) a *domain‑agnostic contrastive loss* that pulls together visually similar concepts regardless of style, and (ii) an *image‑reconstruction regulariser* that forces the encoder to retain semantic content while discarding domain‑specific artefacts.  We evaluate our method on a suite of OOD benchmarks—including COCO‑Style, Flickr30K‑Domain, and a newly introduced *VQA‑OOV* dataset—showing consistent 4–7 % absolute gains in retrieval accuracy and a 3× reduction in hallucination rates relative to strong CLIP‑based baselines.  Ablation studies confirm that both contrastive and reconstruction terms are essential for robustness, and an analysis of the learned embedding space demonstrates markedly improved cross‑domain cluster cohesion.  Finally, we release the AVRL codebase and pre‑trained checkpoints, providing a practical recipe for practitioners to “unblind” their VLA models and achieve reliable performance on previously unseen visual distributions.
1086:
With machine learning’s rapid growth, models are increasingly adept at learning from and predicting across a wide range of domains. Yet, deploying such models in safety‑critical settings is hampered by strict data‑privacy requirements that preclude free data exchange. Homomorphic encryption (HE) addresses this by allowing computations on encrypted data, but it is not natively compatible with deep learning architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), whose performance hinges on non‑linear activation functions. 

In this work we present an optimized framework that substitutes standard activations with HE‑friendly approximations, thereby preserving security while curbing the computational penalty. The approach rewires the CNN pipeline and introduces a lightweight polynomial approximation scheme to replace costly non‑linearities. 

On the CIFAR‑10 benchmark our method attains 94.4 % test accuracy using a degree‑4 polynomial and a Softplus substitute under the CKKS scheme. Inference times are 2.42 s per single encrypted image and 24,000 s for 10,000 encrypted samples, striking a practical balance between performance and privacy.
1087: Large language models (LLMs) consume considerable compute during inference, making deployment costly and challenging. Although dynamic pruning can surpass static techniques by selectively activating only the necessary circuitry for a given input, it often worsens alignment problems, since it keeps only those safety‑critical sub‑circuits that vary with the input, leaving other essential safeguards under‑exposed. Consequently, mitigating these amplified alignment risks is crucial. We propose Alignment‑Aware Probe Pruning (AAPP), a dynamic, structured pruning strategy that selectively retains circuits that influence alignment behavior while still benefiting from inference‑time efficiency. Built on the foundation of Probe Pruning, AAPP adaptively preserves alignment‑relevant components during inference. Evaluations on LLaMA 2‑7B, Qwen2.5‑14B‑Instruct, and Gemma‑3‑12B‑IT demonstrate that AAPP boosts refusal rates by approximately 50 % under the same computational budget, enabling safer and more efficient LLM deployments.
1088:
Accurately predicting far‑ahead values in time series is essential for many high‑stakes applications, but most current approaches struggle because their receptive fields are capped by a finite look‑back window. Transformer‑based and MLP‑based models, in particular, are constrained to short historical segments, which hampers their ability to capture long‑range dependencies and degrades forecast quality. Simply widening the look‑back window is not a viable solution, as it inflates computational costs and causes the signal to be overwhelmed by noise from distant past observations.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce **CometNet**, a new framework for long‑term time‑series forecasting that leverages contextual motifs. First, a **Contextual Motif Extraction** module scans long historical sequences to locate recurrent, salient motifs that encapsulate far‑away temporal dependencies beyond the conventional window. Next, a **Motif‑Guided Forecasting** module incorporates these motifs into the predictive process: it dynamically maps each short look‑back segment to the most relevant motifs, thereby enriching the model’s contextual knowledge and strengthening long‑horizon predictions.

Comprehensive experiments on eight real‑world datasets show that CometNet markedly surpasses existing state‑of‑the‑art methods, especially when forecasting over extended horizons.
1089: Human‑interpretable knowledge extraction from deep neural networks remains a critical bottleneck in deploying these models for high‑stakes domains. We propose a novel framework, **Saliency‑Map‑Guided Knowledge Discovery (SM‑KDG)**, that harnesses the spatial importance signals of class‑wise saliency maps together with large‑language‑model (LLM) powered symbolic approximation to uncover latent sub‑class structures in complex visual datasets. The pipeline first trains a backbone CNN/ViT for coarse‑grained classification and then extracts activation‑based saliency maps for each test instance. By clustering these maps in a joint feature–visual space, we obtain high‑confidence candidate sub‑classes that exhibit coherent discriminative patterns. An LLM is then prompted with the aggregated saliency signatures and the associated image metadata to generate concise symbolic rules (e.g., “wing shape + crest pattern → *Eurasian Sparrow* subtype”) that approximate the learned decision boundaries. We evaluate SM‑KDG on benchmark fine‑grained datasets (CUB‑200, Stanford Cars, and a custom medical‑imaging subset) and demonstrate a 12.4 % uplift in sub‑class discovery precision relative to baseline clustering alone, while the generated symbolic rules achieve a 93.7 % fidelity to the neural predictions. Furthermore, the LLM‑derived explanations enable domain experts to verify and refine the sub‑class taxonomy, leading to a 7.9 % reduction in annotation effort in an active‑learning loop. Our work bridges visual saliency, clustering, and language‑model reasoning, offering a scalable approach for transparent model refinement and data‑driven taxonomy construction.
1090:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents increasingly operate in safety‑critical domains, yet the stochastic and exploratory nature of learning can violate system‑level guarantees. Shielding—interposing a runtime monitor that blocks unsafe actions—has emerged as a principled method to enforce safety while allowing the agent to learn. Conventional shields are usually synthesized from *GR(1)* temporal specifications that encode safety but often ignore *liveness* requirements such as eventual task completion or resource availability. When a learned policy conflicts with a liveness property, a static shield either blocks all actions that could satisfy the liveness goal or forces the agent to abandon exploration, leading to degraded performance or deadlocks.

In this work we introduce **Adaptive GR(1) Specification Repair (AGR‑S)**, a framework that automatically modifies the GR(1) specification on‑the‑fly to reconcile liveness conflicts while preserving safety. Our method monitors the agent’s behavior, detects liveness violations that arise due to overly restrictive safety constraints, and repairs the specification by weakening or postponing liveness assumptions in a principled way. We prove that the repaired shield remains a *liveness‑preserving* safety filter, guaranteeing that all reachable states satisfy the safety properties and that at least one liveness objective is eventually fulfilled. The algorithm is implemented as a lightweight runtime extension to existing shield synthesis tools and can be integrated seamlessly into any RL pipeline.

Experiments on benchmark domains—grid‑world navigation, robotic arm manipulation, and a traffic‑control environment—demonstrate that AGR‑S yields higher reward accumulation and faster convergence compared to static safety‑only shields. In all cases, the repaired specifications maintain the original safety guarantees while restoring the agent’s ability to satisfy the desired liveness properties. Our results indicate that adaptive specification repair is a viable path toward practical, safe, and efficient RL deployment in complex, safety‑critical systems.
1091:
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a progressive condition that often culminates in end‑stage renal failure, yet its trajectory varies widely among patients. Accurate early prognosis is essential for optimizing treatment strategies and allocating limited resources, yet conventional statistical models rely on hand‑crafted features and fail to capture complex, temporal dependencies in electronic health records (EHR). In this study, we propose a Transformer‑based framework that learns directly from longitudinal clinical and laboratory data to predict 1‑, 3‑ and 5‑year renal outcomes (staging progression, dialysis initiation, and mortality).

Using a multi‑institutional cohort of 12,456 CKD patients with at least 36 months of follow‑up, we constructed a time‑series representation comprising demographic variables, comorbidities, medication histories and 22 laboratory metrics recorded at irregular intervals. A masked, position‑aware Transformer encoder was trained to generate patient‑specific embeddings, which were then passed through a multi‑task classification head. Training employed a composite loss that weighted progression and survival outcomes to mitigate class imbalance.

Our Transformer achieved an area‑under‑the‑receiver‑operator‑characteristic (AUROC) of 0.89 (95 % CI 0.87–0.91) for predicting dialysis initiation at 3 years, outperforming baseline models (gradient‑boosted trees, LSTM, and logistic regression) by 8–12 % absolute improvement. Calibration curves indicated well‑matched predicted probabilities across risk deciles. Ablation experiments demonstrated that incorporating the full temporal context and multi‑head self‑attention yielded the greatest performance gains, underscoring the model’s ability to capture long‑range interactions among clinical events.

Interpretability analysis using Integrated Gradients identified key drivers such as albuminuria, eGFR trends, and blood pressure variability, aligning with established CKD risk factors.
