Deploying the model in a prospective pilot at a tertiary care center achieved a net reclassification improvement of 18 % over standard risk scores.

Our findings illustrate that Transformer architectures can effectively model heterogeneous, irregularly sampled EHR data to deliver robust, clinically actionable CKD prognostication, paving the way for personalized intervention pathways and improved patient outcomes.
1092:
Accurate medical image segmentation is essential for diagnosis, treatment planning, and outcome prediction. In clinical practice, however, segmentation results often vary substantially among expert annotators due to differences in annotation protocols, anatomical interpretations, and individual preferences. Existing multi‑expert learning frameworks either average disparate labels or treat each expert as a separate task, failing to capture the nuanced, individualized styles that shape real‑world annotations.  

We introduce **ProSona**, a prompt‑guided personalization framework that adapts a single deep segmentation backbone to the idiosyncratic labeling behavior of each expert while leveraging shared anatomical knowledge across all experts. ProSona employs a lightweight prompt encoder that converts an expert’s identity and a few example segmentations into a continuous prompt vector. This vector modulates the feature representations of a shared UNet‑style network via conditional batch‑norm and attention gates, allowing the model to flexibly specialize without catastrophic forgetting. The framework is trained end‑to‑end using a contrastive loss that aligns the predictions of a “reference expert” with the target expert’s annotations, together with a consistency regularizer that preserves shared anatomical priors.  

We evaluate ProSona on two large‑scale, multi‑expert datasets: the ISIC 2018 skin lesion segmentation benchmark (3 dermatologists) and the MICCAI 2023 Multi‑Organ Abdominal CT segmentation dataset (4 radiologists). Across all organs and modalities, ProSona outperforms baseline multi‑task, ensemble, and fine‑tuned methods by an average Dice improvement of 3.7 % and reduces inter‑expert variance by 22 %. Ablation studies demonstrate the crucial role of the prompt encoder, the conditional normalization, and the contrastive training objective.  

ProSona offers a principled, scalable solution to personalize medical image segmentation in the presence of heterogeneous expert annotations, paving the way for more reliable, clinician‑tailored AI tools in precision medicine.
1093:
Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly become a transformative force in Software Engineering, capable of producing code, detecting defects, suggesting fixes, and aiding quality assurance. While its impact on coding is evident, the broader application of GenAI across the entire Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) remains largely untapped. Significant open questions—particularly regarding reliability, accountability, security, and data privacy—require focused research and coordinated action.  

The GENIUS initiative, involving more than 30 European academic and industrial partners, seeks to tackle these issues by pushing the integration of AI throughout every SDLC stage. It concentrates on unlocking GenAI’s potential, creating novel tooling, and addressing emerging research questions, thereby actively shaping the future of software engineering.  

This vision paper articulates a collective outlook on GenAI‑driven software engineering, grounded in cross‑sector dialogue and the experiences gathered within the GENIUS consortium. It examines four pivotal dimensions: (1) a systematic survey of current challenges to GenAI adoption in the SDLC; (2) a forward‑looking roadmap of expected technological and methodological breakthroughs over the next five years; (3) projected changes in the roles and skill sets of software practitioners; and (4) the role of GENIUS in driving this transition through practical tool development and industrial validation.  

The focus is on aligning technical innovation with business value, offering guidance to both research agendas and industrial strategies, and laying the groundwork for dependable, scalable, and industry‑ready GenAI solutions for software engineering teams.
1094: Time‑series clustering in high‑dimensional dynamical datasets remains a challenging problem because conventional distance metrics often fail to capture the underlying physics of the processes. We propose a novel framework that leverages *Koopman invariants*—the eigenfunctions of the Koopman operator—as intrinsic descriptors that drive the emergence of coherent clusters in joint‑embedding predictive architectures. Our method integrates three components: (i) a deep auto‑encoder that jointly embeds raw observations and their future predictions, (ii) a data‑driven approximation of the Koopman operator via extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) applied to the latent embeddings, and (iii) a spectral clustering routine that groups sequences according to their learned invariant spectra. By learning the Koopman eigenfunctions directly in the latent space, the architecture automatically uncovers conserved and slowly‑evolving quantities that are invariant under the dynamics, providing a low‑dimensional manifold that respects the system’s physics. Experiments on synthetic chaotic systems (Lorenz, Rossler) and real‑world multivariate sensor streams (human gait, electrical grid monitoring) demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional time‑series similarity measures (DTW, autocorrelation) and recent neural clustering methods in both intra‑class compactness and inter‑class separability. Furthermore, the Koopman‑informed clusters exhibit interpretability: the dominant eigenvalues correspond to identifiable dynamical modes (e.g., oscillatory frequencies, growth/decay rates), offering actionable insight into the mechanisms governing the data. We also show that the joint‑embedding predictive loss significantly accelerates the convergence of the Koopman eigenfunctions, yielding stable clusters even with limited training data. This work establishes a principled bridge between operator‑theoretic dynamical systems theory and modern representation learning, providing a scalable, physics‑aware clustering paradigm for complex time‑series.
1095:
Ultra‑wideband (UWB) positioning systems are increasingly used in mission‑critical indoor applications, yet they remain vulnerable to deliberate radio‑frequency jamming that can severely degrade or nullify localisation accuracy. Existing mitigation techniques rely on signal‑to‑noise ratio thresholds or hand‑crafted feature‑based classifiers, which often fail in complex indoor multipath environments and provide limited localisation of the jammer itself. In this paper we propose a novel end‑to‑end machine‑learning framework that jointly detects jamming events and infers the jammer’s position from passive UWB channel state information (CSI) and time‑of‑arrival (TOA) measurements collected at a set of distributed anchors.

We first construct a comprehensive labelled dataset from a custom UWB testbed comprising 15 anchors and a mobile jammer equipped with a programmable USRP‑based transmitter. The dataset spans diverse indoor layouts, jammer transmit powers, and mobility patterns. Three model families are evaluated: a conventional random‑forest classifier on handcrafted CSI features, a convolutional‑recurrent network (CR‑Net) that processes raw CSI waveforms, and a transformer‑based architecture that learns spatial‑temporal dependencies. Localization is performed by a two‑stage pipeline— (1) a binary jamming detector followed by (2) a regression module that predicts the jammer coordinates in a 2‑D map.

Experimental results show that the transformer‑based approach achieves an average detection accuracy of 98.3 % and a mean localisation error of 0.42 m under 10 dB signal‑to‑jammer ratios, outperforming baseline methods by >30 % in error metrics. Ablation studies confirm that integrating raw CSI with TOA cues is critical for robust performance, while attention mechanisms effectively capture multipath signatures. We also demonstrate the system’s generalisation to unseen rooms and jammer types through cross‑validation.

Our work constitutes the first application of deep learning to indoor UWB jammer localisation, providing a scalable, data‑driven solution that can be deployed in real‑time security systems. The dataset and code are released as open resources to encourage further research in UWB resilience and adversarial RF detection.
1096: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly and their applications have proliferated, creating a growing need for computational power. The widespread use of test‑time scaling has intensified the trade‑off between model performance and resource consumption, underscoring the necessity of efficient inference. Yet there is no single metric that captures an LLM’s efficiency across different sizes and architectures. Drawing on the link between compression and intelligence, we propose **information capacity**—a metric that quantifies a model’s efficiency by comparing its text‑compression gains to its computational cost. Bigger models tend to predict next tokens more accurately, yielding higher compression but also incurring greater computational expense. Experiments on popular open‑source models demonstrate that within a given series, models of varying sizes share a consistent information capacity, enabling fair cross‑series efficiency comparisons and reliable performance forecasts within a series. A key advantage of information capacity is that it takes tokenizer efficiency into account, a factor that influences both input and output token counts but is often overlooked in LLM evaluations. We evaluate the information capacity of 49 models on five diverse datasets, finding systematic effects of tokenizer choice, pre‑training data, and mixture‑of‑experts design.
1097: Accurate, real‑time tool‑condition prediction is essential for smart manufacturing, as unexpected tool failures can degrade quality and cause costly downtime. Today’s industrial settings increasingly use predictive maintenance as an integrated, service‑oriented solution that fuses sensing, analytics, and decision support across the production chain. To satisfy the need for reliable, modular operation, we introduce **OmniFuser**, a multimodal learning framework for milling‑tool health monitoring that simultaneously processes high‑resolution visual data and cutting‑force signals. By extracting features in parallel from both modalities, OmniFuser captures complementary spatiotemporal patterns. A contamination‑free cross‑modal fusion strategy disentangles shared and modality‑specific information, enabling efficient interaction across heterogeneous feature streams. A recursive refinement path serves as an anchor, consistently preserving residual details to stabilize fusion dynamics. The resulting representations can be packaged as reusable maintenance‑service modules, supporting both tool‑state classification (e.g., Sharp, Used, Dulled) and multi‑step force‑signal forecasting. Experiments on real milling datasets show that OmniFuser consistently surpasses current state‑of‑the‑art baselines, offering a robust foundation for next‑generation intelligent industrial maintenance services.
1098: Large‐scale documents pose a persistent challenge for reading‑comprehension systems: exhaustive scanning is computationally expensive, while naïve heuristics often miss the subtle, cross‑paragraph evidence required for accurate inference.  We introduce **ALDEN** (Active Learning for Document Navigation and Evidence discovery), a reinforcement‑learning framework that learns to **actively navigate** long texts and **assemble a compact evidence set** for downstream tasks such as multi‑hop question answering, fact verification, and summarization.  ALDEN represents a document as a graph of paragraphs enriched with hierarchical embeddings, and the agent receives a sparse reward for correctly answering a query or for retrieving a high‑confidence evidence chain.  At each step it chooses a paragraph to read, updates a dynamic memory of extracted facts, and may terminate when confidence is sufficient.  We design a novel reward shaping scheme that balances *coverage* and *brevity* and employ curriculum learning to stabilize training on documents with hundreds of thousands of tokens.  Experiments on HotpotQA, NarrativeQA and the newly released **LongDocEvidence** benchmark demonstrate that ALDEN can reduce the average number of read tokens by 65 % while increasing end‑to‑end accuracy by 4–7 % over strong baselines such as Hierarchical Transformer and DocQN.  Ablation studies confirm the importance of the evidence‑memory module and the hierarchical attention network.  Our code, pre‑trained models, and the LongDocEvidence dataset are publicly released to encourage further research on efficient, evidence‑centric reading strategies.
1099:
The growing ubiquity of large language models (LLMs) has prompted a proliferation of safety mechanisms that constrain their responses to user inputs. Yet adversaries continually devise new “jailbreak” techniques that circumvent these safeguards. In this work we investigate a previously under‑explored class of jailbreak vectors: *linguistic style manipulations*. We demonstrate that subtle changes in the phrasing, syntax, and register of a prompt—while preserving its semantic intent—can substantially alter the internal representation of a model and cause it to relax or ignore its safety policies.  

To quantify this phenomenon we construct a benchmark of 1,200 prompts spanning 10 content‑sensitive domains (e.g., self‑harm, hate speech, disallowed instructions). Each prompt is paired with a family of stylistic variants generated via paraphrasing, code‑switching, hyper‑compression, and metaphor‑heavy constructions. We evaluate these pairs on three representative LLMs (GPT‑4, Claude 2, and Llama‑2‑Chat) using the OpenAI Moderation API and the internal safety classifiers of each model. Our experiments reveal that up to 73 % of safe prompts become unsafe once re‑expressed in a more informal, non‑standard, or metaphorical style, with a particularly high success rate on models with stricter safety thresholds.  

Beyond empirical measurement, we analyze the linguistic features most responsible for bypassing safety filters—such as the use of rare synonyms, syntactic ambiguity, and culturally specific idioms—by leveraging explainable‑AI tools on the models’ token‑level activations. Finally, we propose a lightweight style‑aware moderation pipeline that augments existing classifiers with a style‑embedding module, achieving a 28 % reduction in jailbreak success while preserving 96 % of benign throughput.  

Our findings underscore the necessity of incorporating linguistic style analysis into safety evaluation frameworks and provide a foundation for future research into robust, style‑invariant defenses against LLM jailbreaks.
1100: Accurate delineation of vestibular schwannoma (VS) on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for patient care but usually demands laborious manual annotations by specialists. Although recent deep‑learning (DL) methods have accelerated automated segmentation, achieving robust performance across heterogeneous datasets and challenging clinical scenarios remains difficult. We introduce a richly annotated dataset derived from a bootstrapped, DL‑driven pipeline for iterative VS segmentation and quality refinement. By aggregating data from several institutions and validating annotations through expert consensus, we demonstrate that this strategy facilitates efficient and reliable generalisation of segmentation models to a target data distribution. On our internal test cohort, the framework elevated the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) from 0.9125 to 0.9670, while retaining stable results on representative external sets. A secondary expert review of 143 scans identified subtle cases that still necessitated human intervention, guiding further model improvements. The human‑in‑the‑loop training protocol is estimated to save roughly 37.4 % of the time required for conventional manual annotation. In sum, our approach achieves high‑precision VS segmentation and offers a clinically adaptable, generalisable workflow suitable for diverse medical settings. The dataset, encompassing 190 patients and 534 longitudinal contrast‑enhanced T1‑weighted (T1CE) scans from 184 subjects, along with non‑annotated T2‑weighted scans from six patients, is freely available on The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) (https://doi.org/10.7937/bq0z-xa62).
1101:
For many years, bilingualism was regarded as an extra cognitive burden that might impede linguistic and intellectual growth. Over the past thirty years this view has shifted dramatically. A large body of work has sought to model the bilingual word‑recognition system (Dijkstra & van Heuven, 2002) and to explain how languages interact in the brain (Kroll et al., 2015). Recent evidence increasingly shows that multilinguals—people who speak three or more languages—often outperform monolinguals on a range of linguistic and cognitive tasks, including second‑language acquisition (Abu‑Rabia & Sanitsky, 2010).  

The present proposal investigates how the mental lexicon is organized in multilingual speakers. Drawing on Stella et al.’s (2018) exploration of explosive learning with a multiplex model of the lexicon and on the Bilingual Interactive Activation+ (BIA+) framework (Dijkstra & van Heuven, 2002), we apply the multilayer network principles of Kivela et al. (2014). Our experimental design expands the existing models by adding a multimodal layer that links visual inputs to their corresponding lexical representations across all language layers of the mental lexicon. 

The central research question is: **Does the inclusion of visual input in a translation task enhance participants’ proficiency and accuracy relative to a text‑only condition, and how does a heritage language modulate this effect?** Through this work we aim to deepen our understanding of how multiple languages co‑exist and interact within the mind’s lexical architecture.
1102:
Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide spectrum of language tasks by learning from massive corpora.  However, the same probabilistic mechanism that empowers them to generate fluent text also drives two adverse behaviours: **hallucinations**—the invention of facts that are not grounded in the training data—and **memorization**—the inadvertent recall of private or copyrighted passages.  In this paper we present a systematic study of the dual nature of probabilistic learning in LLMs, quantifying how the shape of the output distribution governs the trade‑off between hallucination and memorization.

We introduce a unified **Probabilistic Memorization–Hallucination (PMH) framework** that decomposes a model’s generative policy into a *semantic* component, which captures task‑relevant knowledge, and a *memorized* component, which reflects surface‑level data retention.  Using this decomposition we define a pair of complementary metrics: the *Memorization‑Rate* (MR) and the *Hallucination‑Risk* (HR), both estimated from controlled generation experiments on the Unified Knowledge Benchmark (UKB).  Experiments with GPT‑3.5, Llama‑2, and Claude‑2 variants reveal a clear anti‑correlation between MR and HR across temperature and nucleus‑sampling settings, confirming that tighter probability mass on high‑confidence tokens suppresses hallucinations but increases memorization, whereas flatter distributions reduce memorized leakage at the cost of more frequent hallucinations.

We further demonstrate that fine‑tuning with a **semantic‑confidence penalty** or employing a *contrastive memorization filter* can shift models along the MR–HR curve, allowing practitioners to tailor behaviour to domain constraints (e.g., legal compliance versus factual accuracy).  Finally, we propose a *Dynamic Confidence Calibration* (DCC) strategy that adaptively adjusts temperature based on real‑time semantic confidence, achieving a 23 % reduction in hallucinations while keeping MR below 4 % on a privacy‑sensitive dataset.

Our results provide a principled lens for understanding and managing the twin challenges of hallucination and memorization in modern LLMs, and lay the groundwork for future work on safety‑aware probabilistic learning.
1103: This study investigates podcasts generated by Google’s NotebookLM, an AI system that produces audio shows featuring two conversational hosts who discuss user‑submitted documents. Although AI‑created podcasts have been cited as educational tools—particularly in medicine—they have not been examined as a form of media. By feeding the model diverse textual inputs and examining the resulting broadcasts, I demonstrate that the podcasts adhere to a rigid structural template. I also uncover that NotebookLM not only renders non‑English texts into a lively, standardized Mid‑Western American accent but also homogenizes cultural references into a white, educated, middle‑class American perspective. This represents a notable shift in how audiences are shaped by media, moving away from the plural public spheres that characterized human‑hosted podcasts from the early 2000s onward—where hosts tailored content to specific communities and engaged with listener feedback—toward an increasingly abstracted genre.
1104: The progress of artificial‑intelligence applications in dentistry depends on access to extensive multimodal datasets that reflect real‑world clinical complexity. In this work we introduce a large, publicly available collection comprising 8,775 dental examinations from 4,800 patients (ages 10–90) gathered between 2018 and 2025. The set contains 50,000 intra‑oral photographs, 8,056 radiographs, and rich textual records—including diagnoses, treatment plans, and follow‑up notes—fully annotated for benchmark use while adhering to standard ethical protocols. To illustrate its practical value, we fine‑tuned two leading vision‑language models, Qwen‑VL 3 B and 7 B, on two downstream tasks: (1) classification of six common oro‑dental anomalies, and (2) generation of comprehensive diagnostic reports from multimodal inputs. The fine‑tuned models substantially outperformed both their unmodified counterparts and GPT‑4o, demonstrating the dataset’s utility and its potential to accelerate AI‑driven solutions in oral healthcare. The dataset is released to the research community, providing a vital resource for future advances in AI dentistry.
1105:
Authorship attribution (AA) in low‑resource languages such as Bangla remains largely underexplored, in part due to the scarcity of standardized evaluation data and the lack of nuanced linguistic insights. This paper introduces **BARD10**, the first large‑scale, publicly available Bangla Author‑Reputation Dataset comprising 10,000 documents from 50 distinct writers spanning contemporary prose, poetry, and journalistic texts. Each entry is meticulously annotated for author, genre, and publication date, enabling controlled experiments on stylistic variation across time and medium.

A central contribution of our study is a systematic investigation of Bangla stop‑words—a class of high‑frequency, low‑content tokens traditionally discarded in natural‑language processing pipelines. We constructed multiple feature sets, ranging from character‑ and word‑n‑grams to advanced embeddings, with and without stop‑words. Using a suite of classifiers (SVM, logistic regression, and transformer‑based fine‑tuning), we demonstrate that retaining stop‑words boosts average classification accuracy by **4.7%** (p < 0.01) across 10‑fold cross‑validation, with the largest gains observed in short‑text genres where stylistic cues are sparse. Ablation studies reveal that particular stop‑word families (e.g., particles, conjunctions, and honorifics) carry author‑specific stylistic fingerprints.

Our empirical findings challenge prevailing assumptions in Bangla NLP that stop‑words are neutral, underscoring their role as valuable stylistic markers for AA. In addition to the dataset, we provide an open‑source benchmark framework and a detailed error analysis that highlights genre‑dependent variations. This work not only supplies the community with a robust evaluation resource but also opens avenues for improved authorial modeling in Bangla, encouraging future research to revisit token‑level preprocessing strategies in other low‑resource scripts.
1106: The scarcity of high‑quality labeled data curtails the performance of machine‑learning approaches to malware detection. To address this limitation, we present **MalDataGen**, a freely available, modular framework that generates realistic synthetic tabular datasets using state‑of‑the‑art deep‑learning models such as WGAN‑GP and VQ‑VAE. By applying a dual‑validation protocol (train‑on‑test‑split / test‑on‑train‑split) across seven benchmark classifiers and a suite of utility metrics, we demonstrate that MalDataGen consistently outperforms existing data‑synthesis baselines—particularly SDV—while preserving the analytical value of the data. Its flexible, plug‑and‑play design facilitates seamless integration into existing malware detection pipelines, offering a practical tool for cybersecurity practitioners.
1107: Modern, data‑driven recommender systems can inadvertently learn and store highly personal user behavior, creating significant privacy risks. Although several “unlearning” strategies exist that can excise the influence of specific data points, they typically operate sluggishly and compromise recommendation accuracy, falling short of the real‑time requirements of today’s systems. Because recommendation engines are intrinsically rank‑oriented, we introduce **unranking**—a procedure that pushes unwanted items down the recommendation list while still offering rigorous unlearning guarantees. To make unranking practical, we propose **Learning to Fast Unrank in Collaborative Filtering Recommendation (L2UnRank)**. L2UnRank proceeds in three stages: (1) it pinpoints the affected neighborhood through interaction‑based p‑hop propagation; (2) it quantifies both structural and semantic impacts on entities inside that neighborhood; and (3) it applies fast, rank‑aware parameter updates informed by these influence metrics. Across a range of datasets and back‑end models, L2UnRank proves to be model‑agnostic, delivering superior unranking performance and preserving recommendation quality close to that of a full retrain, while achieving a 50× speedup over prior methods. Source code can be found at https://github.com/Juniper42/L2UnRank.
1108:
Large‑language models (LLMs) have recently shown an ability to orchestrate external tools (e.g., calculators, code engines, web APIs) by chaining calls in an *in‑context* manner. However, real‑world problem solving frequently requires reasoning over *tool dependencies* (the preconditions and postconditions that link one tool’s output to another’s input) in concert with rich *domain knowledge* (concepts, rules, and causal relationships). Existing approaches treat tool usage heuristically or rely on pre‑written scripts, leaving a gap between the low‑level execution semantics of tools and the high‑level reasoning required to satisfy complex user goals.  

We propose **GAP‑Plan (Graph‑based tool‑dependency and domain‑knowledge planning)**, a unified framework that represents both tool dependencies and domain knowledge as a single heterogeneous graph. Nodes encode tools, intermediate states, and domain concepts; edges encode causal, precondition, and semantic relationships. During inference, the LLM grounds its natural‑language prompt against this graph, generating a *contextual plan* that selects, orders, and conditions tool calls while respecting dependency constraints and domain constraints. A lightweight planner performs graph‑constrained traversal to validate the plan and identify potential dead‑ends before execution.  

We evaluate GAP‑Plan on a benchmark of 250 multi‑step tasks spanning finance, medicine, and software debugging. Compared to baseline in‑context tool usage and symbolic planners, our method achieves a 42 % increase in task success rate and a 3× reduction in hallucinated intermediate states. Ablation studies confirm that jointly modeling tool dependencies and domain knowledge yields the most robust performance. GAP‑Plan demonstrates that a graph‑based integration of operational and semantic information can substantially enhance in‑context planning for large‑language models.
1109:
Requirements engineering is now routinely conducted in multi‑stakeholder settings where entities both collaborate and compete, giving rise to *coopetitive* relationships in which trust is a dynamic construct that evolves from observed actions over successive encounters. Conventional conceptual tools such as the i* framework capture trust qualitatively but do not provide computational means to track its change. On the other hand, agent‑based trust models offer algorithmic update rules but are not tailored to the nuances of requirements engineering or to the richer conceptual models it employs.  

This report closes that divide by introducing a computational trust model grounded in game‑theoretic notions of strategic coopetition and capable of dynamically evolving trust. Trust is conceived as a two‑tier construct: (1) an *immediate* component that reacts to the most recent behaviour, and (2) a *reputation* component that aggregates the history of violations. The update rule is asymmetric: cooperative acts gradually increase trust, whereas a single violation causes a steep drop, generating hysteresis and upper bounds that limit how quickly a relationship can recover.  

To make this model usable for requirements engineers, we present a formal translation scheme that maps i* dependency networks and organisational context information onto the computational trust formalism. Extensive simulation over 78,125 parameter settings confirms that the model reliably reproduces key phenomena such as negativity bias, hysteresis, and cumulative damage amplification. Finally, we validate the approach against the Renault‑Nissan Alliance case study (1999‑2025), matching 49 of 60 documented validation points (81.7 %) and accurately mirroring the evolution of trust across five distinct phases—including crisis and recovery periods. This work builds upon the foundational theory presented in arXiv:2510.18802.
1110: Vision‑language models (VLMs) have achieved impressive results on visual‑question‑answering and multimodal text‑generation tasks, yet their application to scientific domains—particularly materials science—is still nascent. Although various machine‑learning approaches have tackled specific challenges in this field, there is no general‑purpose foundation model that can handle a wide spectrum of polymer‑property predictions using multimodal inputs. In this study, we introduce a multimodal polymer dataset and employ instruction‑tuning pairs to adapt VLMs for this purpose. Using LoRA for fine‑tuning, we show that the resulting multimodal models surpass both unimodal baselines and other conventional approaches, underscoring the advantages of integrating visual and textual information. Moreover, this strategy obviates the need to train separate models for each property, thereby cutting deployment and maintenance overheads.
1111:
Real‑time understanding of human activity is pivotal for interactive systems, yet achieving high accuracy in unconstrained environments remains difficult due to the variability in motion, viewpoint, and temporal dynamics. In this paper we present an end‑to‑end online action and gesture recognition framework that integrates a lightweight detector with a deep Symmetric Positive‑Definite (SPD) Siamese network, enabling robust, low‑latency inference on commodity hardware.

Our pipeline first employs a cascade of convolutional detectors to localize candidate action regions in each frame, thereby reducing background clutter and facilitating frame‑wise feature extraction. From the detected regions we construct a spatio‑temporal covariance descriptor, an SPD matrix that preserves inter‑channel relationships while remaining invariant to small geometric transformations. This SPD representation is projected into a low‑dimensional manifold via the log‑Euclidean map, after which we feed the embeddings into a Siamese network trained with a contrastive margin loss. The Siamese architecture learns a discriminative metric that is resilient to intra‑class variations and cross‑subject differences, allowing for efficient online matching against a library of class prototypes.

We evaluate our approach on three benchmark datasets—UCF‑101, Something‑Else, and the Chalearn 2019 Gesture Recognition dataset—achieving state‑of‑the‑art accuracies of 92.3 %, 97.8 %, and 94.5 % respectively, while maintaining an average inference time of 15 ms per frame on a single NVIDIA GTX 1080. Ablation studies confirm the importance of the SPD embedding and the Siamese loss, each contributing 2–3 % performance gains over a vanilla CNN baseline. Moreover, we demonstrate that our system generalizes well to unseen subjects and illumination conditions, owing to the intrinsic geometry of the SPD representation.

In summary, the proposed detector‑plus‑SPD‑Siamese framework delivers accurate, low‑latency action and gesture recognition suitable for deployment in mobile and robotics applications. The code and pre‑trained models are publicly released to facilitate further research in online human‑behavior analytics.
1112:
Recent progress with large language models (LLMs) has dramatically accelerated code translation, delivering more precise and efficient conversions across programming languages. Although LLMs were originally designed for natural language processing, they have proven highly effective at modeling programming language syntax and semantics, consistently surpassing conventional rule‑based approaches in both accuracy and flexibility. As a result, cross‑language conversion has been streamlined, development effort has been cut, and legacy code migration has been sped up. 

In this work we present **OMPILOT**, a domain‑specific encoder‑decoder transformer that translates C++ into OpenMP, thereby enabling effective shared‑memory parallelisation. OMPILOT incorporates custom pre‑training objectives that encode the semantics of parallel constructs and blends unsupervised with supervised learning to enhance translation robustness. Unlike prior efforts that target only loop‑level transformations, OMPILOT operates at the function level, capturing a richer semantic context. 

To validate our method we introduce **OMPBLEU**, a new composite metric designed explicitly to evaluate the correctness and quality of OpenMP parallel constructs, overcoming shortcomings of existing translation metrics.
1113: Improving the factual accuracy of large language models can be achieved by retrieving information from graph‑structured knowledge bases. Although many methods have been suggested, comparing them is hampered by the lack of challenging QA datasets that include ground‑truth targets for graph retrieval. We introduce SynthKGQA, a framework that automatically generates high‑quality synthetic Knowledge‑Graph Question‑Answering datasets from any KG, supplying the complete set of relevant facts to support each query. By producing these datasets, SynthKGQA not only enables more meaningful benchmarking of KG retrievers, but also allows us to train more effective models. Applying SynthKGQA to Wikidata, we create GTSQA—a novel dataset designed to evaluate the zero‑shot generalisation of KG retrievers to unseen graph structures and relation types—and use it to benchmark popular KG‑augmented LLM approaches.
1114:
Modern interaction paradigms often demand large, deliberate motions or complex sequences of touch, which can impede usability in constrained environments such as wearable devices, public kiosks, or ergonomically sensitive workflows. We propose **Preview, Accept or Discard (PAD)**, a predictive low‑motion interaction paradigm that anticipates user intent from minimal, natural body cues and presents a visual preview of the resulting action, allowing the user to confirm or cancel with a single, low‑energy response. PAD leverages a lightweight neural model trained on multimodal sensor streams (IMU, depth camera, and contextual metadata) to infer high‑level intents such as “open email”, “scroll to next page”, or “switch application”. Once an intent is recognized, the system overlays a concise preview—an icon, thumbnail or contextual suggestion—onto the user’s field of view. The user can then accept or discard the proposal using a subtle thumb tap or a short head nod, eliminating the need for extensive gestures or multiple touch taps.

We implemented PAD in a mixed‑reality prototype and evaluated it in a 60‑person study comparing it to baseline high‑motion gestures and conventional touch input. Results demonstrate a 35 % reduction in average task completion time and a 42 % decrease in reported fatigue, while user satisfaction scores rose by 18 % relative to the baseline. Error rates also dropped by 27 % thanks to the preview‑confirmation step, which mitigates mis‑recognition. The study further highlights that PAD is robust across diverse user groups, including those with limited upper‑body mobility.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a novel low‑motion interaction framework that fuses prediction with preview‑based confirmation; (2) an open‑source, lightweight intent‑recognition model that operates in real time on consumer hardware; and (3) empirical evidence that PAD improves efficiency, reduces physical strain, and increases user confidence in high‑precision tasks. We discuss implications for future low‑effort interfaces and outline extensions to multi‑modal and collaborative contexts.
1115:
Multi‑goal reinforcement learning (MGRL) enables agents to learn policies that can solve a wide spectrum of tasks defined by a set of target goals. However, existing approaches often suffer from two intertwined deficiencies: (i) **sparse coverage** of the goal space, whereby the agent’s experience is concentrated near the current training distribution, and (ii) **limited diversity** of achieved goals, resulting in over‑fitting to a narrow subset of the environment and poor generalization to unseen objectives.  

We formalise the notion of *dense and diverse goal coverage* as a joint optimisation problem that maximises the *coverage density*—the expected proportion of the goal manifold visited per episode—while maintaining a *diversity budget* that penalises repetitive goal trajectories. To solve this, we propose **Coverage‑Aware Goal‑Sampling (CAGS)**, a novel curriculum framework that dynamically adapts the distribution of goals in the replay buffer based on a learned density estimator. CAGS couples an auxiliary *goal‑density critic* with an entropy‑regularised intrinsic reward that biases exploration toward under‑visited regions of goal space. This is further enhanced by a *diversity‑aware replay* scheme that ensures that each batch contains a maximally varied set of goals.  

We evaluate CAGS on a suite of challenging continuous‑control benchmarks from the D4RL and Meta‑World suites, including FetchPush, Kitchen, and Humanoid. Across all environments, CAGS outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods (e.g., Hindsight Experience Replay, Goal‑Conditioned Universal Policy, and Goal‑Set Replay) by 12–18 % in final success rates and demonstrates a 2–3× improvement in coverage density metrics. Ablation studies confirm that both the density critic and diversity‑aware replay contribute critically to these gains.  

Our work provides the first principled approach to achieving dense and diverse goal coverage in MGRL, paving the way for more sample‑efficient and generalisable goal‑conditioned agents.
1116: Assessing the quality of athletic performance—known as Action Quality Assessment (AQA)—has become a focal point in recent research. Current AQA approaches typically derive scores from global video features, which hampers both interpretability and reliability. Moreover, most available datasets lack fine‑grained score annotations, particularly for deduction terms and sub‑component ratings. In this work we introduce the first AQA benchmark for aerial skiing that contains detailed sub‑score and deduction labels, and we make the dataset publicly available. To address the technical challenges posed by such fine‑grained evaluation, we propose **JudgeMind**, an AQA framework that emulates the reasoning process of professional judges. JudgeMind decomposes the action clip into distinct stages and assigns a score to each stage, thereby improving precision. A stage‑aware feature‑enhancement and fusion module further emphasizes key regions specific to each stage and mitigates visual instability caused by frequent camera angle changes. Finally, a knowledge‑informed, grade‑aware decoder incorporates potential deduction items as prior knowledge, yielding more accurate and trustworthy predictions. Extensive experiments confirm that JudgeMind establishes new state‑of‑the‑art performance on the proposed aerial skiing benchmark.
1117:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi‑agent systems where several autonomous agents interact, negotiate, or coordinate to achieve complex goals. While individual LLM agents have been studied extensively under adversarial scrutiny, the compounded risks arising from *inter‑agent* interactions remain largely unexplored. This paper introduces **TAMAS (Testing Adversarial Risks in Multi‑Agent Systems)**, a comprehensive benchmark suite designed to systematically evaluate and compare the robustness of multi‑agent LLM architectures against a wide spectrum of adversarial strategies.

TAMAS comprises 12 attack families (e.g., instruction manipulation, chain‑of‑thought poisoning, reward‑shaping, and policy‑steering), 48 task‑specific scenarios (including collaborative planning, distributed problem solving, and adversarial negotiation), and a set of 2,300 annotated adversarial dialogues. Each scenario is paired with a formal success criterion and a suite of quantitative metrics that capture safety violations, sub‑optimal coordination, and policy drift. To support reproducibility, we provide a lightweight simulation framework that automatically orchestrates agent interactions, injects adversarial perturbations, and records performance across three representative multi‑agent LLM configurations (single‑agent orchestration, pairwise bargaining, and fully decentralized swarms).

Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that even state‑of‑the‑art models (e.g., GPT‑4 and Claude 3) exhibit significant fragility in multi‑agent settings, with error rates rising by 27–65 % under coordinated attacks. We also uncover systematic weaknesses that are absent in isolated-agent settings, such as *cross‑agent contamination* and *iterative misinformation*. Finally, we propose a set of mitigation strategies—including dynamic trust scoring, adversarial‑aware curriculum learning, and cross‑validation protocols—whose effectiveness is quantified across the benchmark.

TAMAS provides the first standardized, scalable, and publicly available platform for measuring adversarial robustness in collaborative LLM deployments, thereby enabling researchers to benchmark defenses, track progress, and ultimately build safer multi‑agent language‑based systems. The dataset, evaluation scripts, and baseline models are released at https://tamas-benchmark.org.
1118: Ensuring dataset integrity is essential for the safety and dependability of AI applications, particularly in autonomous driving. This paper proposes a systematic framework for constructing safety‑oriented datasets that adhere to ISO/PAS 8800. Focusing on AI perception as the key use case, it introduces the AI Data Flywheel and a full dataset lifecycle—from acquisition and labeling through curation and upkeep. The framework embeds detailed safety analyses to uncover hazards arising from data deficiencies and to prescribe mitigation measures. It also delineates procedures for setting dataset safety requirements and offers verification and validation approaches to confirm compliance with safety norms. Beyond establishing best practices, the study surveys recent work and emerging trends in dataset safety and autonomous vehicle technology, highlighting present challenges and charting future research paths. By weaving these elements together, the paper seeks to foster robust, safety‑certified AI systems for autonomous driving.
1119:
The rapid adoption of smart contracts has amplified the need for reliable vulnerability analysis tools. While static analysis and symbolic execution techniques can flag potential weaknesses, translating these findings into actionable, executable proof‑of‑concept (PoC) exploits remains largely manual and ad‑hoc. PoCo addresses this gap by introducing an *agentic* framework that automatically constructs, tests, and refines PoC exploits for Ethereum‑based contracts.  

PoCo models the exploit discovery problem as a sequential decision process in which an artificial agent manipulates contract state, transaction payloads, and oracle inputs to maximize a reward defined by successful re‑entrancy, arithmetic overflows, or gas‑limit abuses. The agent combines reinforcement learning with symbolic path‑finding, leveraging a lightweight EVM emulator that preserves full transaction semantics. A novel *exploit‑plan* language allows the agent to encode high‑level attack strategies (e.g., “withdraw first, then call back”) and iteratively refine them based on execution feedback.  

We evaluate PoCo on the SmartBugs benchmark and a curated set of 1,200 real‑world contracts from the Ethereum mainnet. PoCo generates valid PoCs for 84 % of the known vulnerabilities, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art tools such as Mythril and Echidna by 30 % in success rate while reducing the average search time by 55 %. Moreover, PoCo’s generated PoCs are directly executable on test‑net deployments, facilitating rapid security audits and automated patch verification.  

**Contributions**  
1. A novel agentic architecture for end‑to‑end PoC generation in smart contracts.  
2. An integrated EVM emulator with symbolic guidance that supports multi‑step attack chains.  
3. A public PoC generator benchmark and dataset, enabling reproducible research on exploit synthesis.  

PoCo demonstrates that autonomous agents can bridge the long‑standing divide between vulnerability detection and exploit construction, providing a practical tool for auditors, developers, and security researchers.
1120: In this paper we present a novel framework for detecting anomalies in multivariate time series by first reducing them to a univariate form. We investigate several conversion strategies that leverage Fuzzy C‑Means clustering and fuzzy integrals. Once the data are transformed, a Hidden Markov Model is employed to flag anomalous behavior. By building HMM‑based detectors and systematically comparing the different transformation methods, we report a comprehensive set of experiments and a detailed comparative analysis.
1121:
Boolean networks are a cornerstone of computational modeling for systems biology, digital circuit design, and social dynamics. However, the sheer size and redundancy of real‑world networks impede analysis of their dynamical behavior, especially when long‑time attractors or transient states must be enumerated.  In this work we introduce **BoolSkeleton**, a principled framework for *skeletonizing* Boolean networks through **Homogeneous Pattern Reduction (HPR)**.  HPR identifies groups of nodes that exhibit identical update functions and mutually feed each other in a way that guarantees that their joint dynamics can be collapsed into a single representative without altering the global state‑transition graph up to a bisimulation equivalence.  By extending classical graph‑theoretic notions of symmetry and modularity with a Boolean‑specific notion of homogeneity, BoolSkeleton systematically applies pattern reduction, followed by a minimality‑preserving cleanup step that eliminates redundant edges.

We prove that the HPR reduction is sound and complete for preserving attractor structure and that the overall algorithm runs in time linear in the size of the network representation.  Empirical evaluation on a diverse suite of benchmarks—including synthetic random Boolean networks, the Drosophila segment‑polarisation network, and a 10,000‑node transcriptional regulatory network—shows that BoolSkeleton achieves reductions of up to 85 % in node count and 78 % in edge count while maintaining all attractors and preserving the basin sizes within 0.5 % error.  The reduced skeletons enable an average speed‑up of 3.7× for exhaustive state‑space exploration and 4.2× for Monte‑Carlo trajectory simulation.

Our results demonstrate that BoolSkeleton provides a scalable, mathematically rigorous method for simplifying Boolean networks without sacrificing dynamical fidelity, thereby facilitating both analytical insight and efficient computation on large biological and engineered systems.
1122: Recent advances in sequential recommendation have leaned heavily on convolutional filters because of their prowess in extracting local temporal patterns. Nevertheless, most of these approaches pair such filters with self‑attention modules, since fixed convolutional kernels alone tend to fall short in modeling the long‑range interactions that are critical for accurate predictions. In this work we introduce **Time‑Variant Convolutional Filters for Sequential Recommendation (TV‑Rec)**, a framework inspired by graph signal processing. TV‑Rec employs time‑dependent graph filters that adapt to the position of events in a user’s sequence, thereby capturing nuanced temporal dynamics. By replacing both static kernels and self‑attention with these dynamic filters, our model gains richer representational capacity and a deeper understanding of complex user behavior interactions. The resulting architecture not only discards the need for self‑attention but also streamlines computation, yielding faster inference. Across six publicly available datasets, TV‑Rec consistently outperforms current state‑of‑the‑art methods, achieving an average improvement of 7.49 %.
1123:
High‑resolution image reconstruction from low‑resolution, noisy observations is a central challenge in computational imaging. Existing super‑resolution (SR) frameworks—diffusion models, generative adversarial networks, and autoregressive flows—often suffer from a trade‑off between perceptual fidelity and noise robustness, especially under severe sensor noise or limited training data. We propose **ResMatching**, a noise‑resilient SR framework that unifies *flow matching* with *guided conditional sampling* to achieve high‑quality, stable reconstructions. ResMatching introduces a **residual flow matcher** that learns a conditional probability flow conditioned on a noise‑aware prior. During training, we employ a *noise‑augmented matching loss* that explicitly penalizes deviations under stochastic perturbations, thereby aligning the learned flow with the true data distribution even when the input is corrupted. At inference, a lightweight guidance mechanism steers the reverse diffusion‑like sampling process towards the latent manifold defined by the low‑resolution input, effectively suppressing amplified noise artifacts. 

Extensive experiments on DIV2K, RealSR, and BSD500 demonstrate that ResMatching outperforms state‑of‑the‑art diffusion, GAN‑based, and flow‑based SR methods by 1.8–2.5 dB in PSNR and 3–5 % in SSIM under Gaussian and real‑world noise regimes, while maintaining comparable computational cost (≈ 8 ms per 64 × 64 patch on a single GPU). Visual inspection confirms that ResMatching preserves fine textures without introducing hallucinations. Ablation studies confirm the importance of the residual flow matcher and the noise‑aware guidance. Our code and pre‑trained models are publicly available. ResMatching establishes a new baseline for noise‑resilient computational SR and demonstrates the efficacy of guided conditional flow matching for high‑fidelity image restoration.
1124:
Large‑language‑model agents have progressed from simple text generation to autonomous completion of intricate tasks that involve interacting with external tools. Yet most existing benchmarks evaluate only end‑to‑end performance within narrowly defined scenarios, limiting the scope of skills tested and leading to score saturation and an increasing reliance on expert‑crafted annotations as agents become more sophisticated.  

In this paper we argue that the true measure of progress for these agents is their *learning ability*—both self‑refinement and the capacity to learn from peers—which is essential for approaching human‑level intelligence. To this end we introduce an iterative, competitive peer‑learning framework that lets agents improve their strategies through repeated interactions and feedback, thereby providing a systematic assessment of learning dynamics.  

To alleviate the saturation problem inherent to current benchmarks, we propose **CATArena**, a tournament‑style evaluation platform that hosts four diverse board and card games with open‑ended scoring. By removing explicit score ceilings, CATArena facilitates continuous, dynamic testing of rapidly evolving agent capabilities.  

Experiments conducted with both minimal‑code and commercial agents demonstrate that CATArena delivers reliable, stable, and scalable measurements of core agent competencies, particularly learning performance and strategy design.
1125:
Class‑incremental learning (CIL) systems continually acquire new categories while preserving knowledge of previously seen classes. When deployed in safety‑critical environments, such models must also withstand adversarial perturbations. Existing robust CIL approaches typically append adversarial training to each incremental step, which either leads to catastrophic forgetting of the adversarial manifold or incurs prohibitive memory and computation costs. In this work we formalise the notion of *sustainability* for adversarial examples in CIL: the ability to maintain a representative, reusable set of attacks that evolve jointly with the model without compromising either clean accuracy or robustness.  

We propose a two‑stage framework that (i) dynamically constructs a compact *Adversarial Experience Buffer* (AE‑Buffer) by selecting exemplar attacks that maximise coverage of the evolving feature space, and (ii) employs a *Curriculum‑driven Adversarial Replay* (CD‑AR) strategy that progressively re‑trains on older attacks while weighting newer classes more heavily. To further stabilize the representation, we introduce a *Dual‑Distillation Regularizer* that enforces consistency between the original and adversarial logits of both old and new classes. Our method can be incorporated into any gradient‑based incremental learner (e.g., GEM, EWC, iCaRL) and requires no architectural changes.  

We evaluate on CIFAR‑100, ImageNet‑Subset, and Office‑Home under the standard CIL protocols, measuring both clean and robust accuracy with FGSM, PGD‑10, and CW‑0.5 attacks. Compared to baseline robust CIL methods, our approach reduces forgetting of adversarial performance by 4.7 % on average, while improving overall robust accuracy by 3.2 % and achieving a 1.8 × reduction in storage overhead for adversarial samples. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of curriculum scheduling and dual‑distillation in sustaining adversarial robustness over long incremental horizons.  

Our results demonstrate that sustainable adversarial example generation is not only feasible but also essential for deploying class‑incremental systems in adversarially hostile settings. The proposed framework is generic, scalable, and paves the way for future research on long‑term robustness in continual learning.
1126:
Understanding what makes a mathematical problem “interesting” is essential for both educational design and the development of intelligent tutoring systems. Yet, the notion of interestingness remains largely subjective, and little is known about how language models perceive and generate problems that capture human attention. In this study we introduce **Math‑Int**—the first large, curated benchmark of mathematical problems annotated for interestingness by expert mathematicians, teachers, and students. We collect 8,400 problems spanning algebra, calculus, discrete mathematics, and advanced topics, each scored on a 5‑point Likert scale and accompanied by qualitative explanations. 

Using this corpus we train a set of interpretable classifiers that quantify the contribution of problem attributes (difficulty, novelty, real‑world relevance, solution elegance) to human ratings. We then probe state‑of‑the‑art language models (GPT‑4, Claude, Llama‑2) via prompt‑injection and zero‑shot classification to evaluate whether they can predict human‑derived interestingness scores. Results show that while language models can capture syntactic and semantic proxies of difficulty (p < 0.01), they systematically underestimate novelty and contextual relevance, yielding an average Pearson r = 0.52 with human scores. Fine‑tuning on Math‑Int improves performance to r = 0.73, indicating that explicit supervision is critical for aligning model judgments with human preferences.  

Our findings illuminate the dimensions of interestingness that humans prioritize, expose gaps in current generative models, and provide a pathway for designing math problem generators that are both pedagogically valuable and engaging. Math‑Int is released publicly to support future research in educational AI and computational creativity.
1127:
The Segment‑Anything Model (SAM) has demonstrated remarkable generality across diverse natural‑image segmentation tasks, yet its performance drops markedly on medical imagery due to domain shift and the paucity of annotated data. We introduce **SAMora**, a hierarchical self‑supervised pre‑training pipeline designed to bridge this gap and substantially improve SAM’s applicability to medical image segmentation. SAMora first pre‑trains a feature encoder on large collections of unlabeled medical scans (CT, MRI, ultrasound) using a multi‑scale contrastive objective that encourages consistent representations across anatomical hierarchies (e.g., organ‑level, tissue‑level, voxel‑level). The encoder is then fine‑tuned within SAM’s prompt‑based architecture, yielding a **medical‑adapted SAM** that retains the model’s flexible prompt interface while exhibiting enhanced contextual understanding of medical structures. 

We evaluate SAMora on three challenging, publicly available benchmarks: the KiTS19 kidney tumor segmentation dataset, the BraTS2021 brain tumor segmentation challenge, and the NIH ChestX‑Ray14 disease localization set. Across all tasks, SAMora outperforms vanilla SAM by +5.8 % (Dice) on KiTS19, +4.3 % (DSC) on BraTS, and +7.1 % (mean IoU) on ChestX‑Ray. Ablation studies confirm that the hierarchical contrastive loss, the use of multi‑scale augmentations, and the fine‑tuning of the prompt embeddings are all critical to these gains. Moreover, SAMora requires no manual annotations, making it highly scalable to emerging modalities such as PET and OCT. 

Our results suggest that hierarchical self‑supervised pre‑training can effectively adapt general‑purpose foundation models to the stringent requirements of medical imaging, paving the way for rapid deployment of SAM‑style segmentation tools in clinical settings. The code and pre‑trained checkpoints are publicly released at https://github.com/example/samora.
1128: Maintaining high visual quality while expanding the variety of images produced remains a core difficulty in image‑generation research. Although Fractal Generative Models (FGMs) excel at synthesizing realistic pictures, their intrinsic self‑similarity curtails the range of distinct outputs. We tackle this limitation by introducing the Hausdorff Dimension (HD), a fundamental measure of structural complexity from fractal geometry, into the FGM pipeline. First, we devise a learnable HD estimator that predicts the dimension directly from image embeddings, thereby bypassing the high computational cost of classical methods. Merely adding an HD term to the training objective, however, fails to boost diversity without compromising image quality. To overcome this, we employ a momentum‑driven, monotonic scheduling scheme that gradually tunes the HD‑based loss, achieving optimal trade‑offs between diversity and fidelity. During inference, we further refine outputs via HD‑guided rejection sampling, selecting only those images that exhibit richer geometric content. Experiments on ImageNet show that our FGM‑HD framework improves output diversity by 39 % relative to vanilla FGMs while preserving comparable visual quality. This is, to our knowledge, the first work to incorporate Hausdorff Dimension into Fractal Generative Models, providing both a practical diversity enhancement and a theoretically grounded extension to the FGM framework.
1129:
Evaluating speech‑to‑text translation (ST) systems usually relies on comparing their output with one or more human reference translations. While this method works to a degree, it suffers from a key drawback of reference‑based metrics: it neglects information that can be derived directly from the source audio. In recent machine‑translation research, neural metrics that incorporate the source text have shown higher alignment with human judgments. Applying the same idea to ST is challenging because the source is audio, not text, and dependable transcripts or source‑reference alignments are rarely available.

In this paper we present the first systematic investigation of source‑aware metrics for ST, especially under realistic scenarios where transcriptions of the audio are not provided. We examine two complementary ways to approximate the source text: (1) automatic speech‑recognition (ASR) transcripts, and (2) back‑translations of the reference translation. We also propose a new cross‑lingual re‑segmentation algorithm that tackles the alignment mismatch between these synthetic sources and the reference translations.

Our experiments on two ST benchmark datasets covering 79 language pairs and six diverse ST systems reveal that ASR transcripts are the more dependable synthetic source when the word error rate is below 20 %. Back‑translations, although cheaper to compute, remain an effective alternative. Finally, the re‑segmentation method allows existing source‑aware MT metrics to be applied reliably to ST evaluation, opening the door to more accurate and principled assessment techniques for speech translation.
1130:
Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) has demonstrated remarkable success in emulating and extrapolating complex physical, biological, and chemical phenomena. Yet the current paradigm largely relies on a single, monolithic model trained on curated data, which often struggles with extrapolation, interpretability, and the discovery of novel scientific laws. In this work we introduce **AgenticSciML**, a framework that casts the problem of scientific discovery as a collaborative multi‑agent system. Each agent embodies a distinct scientific or computational expertise—such as data‑driven regression, physics‑informed constraints, symbolic manipulation, or uncertainty estimation—and operates within a shared environment that encapsulates experimental data, simulation outputs, and domain ontologies. Agents interact through a lightweight communication protocol that allows them to propose hypotheses, exchange partial models, and critique each other’s outputs. The joint policy of the system is optimized via a meta‑reinforcement learning objective that rewards not only predictive accuracy but also scientific novelty and interpretability. 

We demonstrate AgenticSciML on several benchmark scientific domains, including fluid dynamics, quantum chemistry, and epidemiology. In each case, the multi‑agent system autonomously uncovers high‑fidelity surrogate models, derives compact symbolic expressions that recover known governing equations, and identifies previously unknown relationships between variables. Compared to single‑agent baselines, AgenticSciML achieves a 15–30 % improvement in out‑of‑sample prediction accuracy while reducing the number of required simulations by an order of magnitude. Our results illustrate that emergent, cooperative reasoning among heterogeneous agents can accelerate hypothesis generation, validate theoretical models, and ultimately facilitate deeper scientific insight. The framework is open‑source and extensible, inviting researchers to incorporate new agent types and domain knowledge into the collaborative loop.
1131:
Impaired speech production in aphasia patients necessitates alternative communication strategies that can reliably decode imagined speech from neural signals. Conventional deep‑learning decoders require extensive computational resources, precluding their deployment on low‑latency, bedside platforms. We propose a **Lightweight Diffusion‑based Framework (LDF)** that translates electroencephalography (EEG) recordings of imagined speech into phoneme sequences in real time. The core of LDF is a compact denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) adapted to the low‑frequency, high‑dimensional nature of EEG. To reduce inference cost, we employ a teacher‑student distillation pipeline where a lightweight transformer encoder extracts spatio‑temporal features, while the diffusion decoder operates in a compressed latent space. This architecture yields a 60 % reduction in memory footprint and a 4× speed‑up over state‑of‑the‑art recurrent models while preserving classification fidelity.

We evaluated LDF on a publicly available imagined‑speech dataset (N = 45 aphasic participants, 30 k trials) and on a proprietary clinical cohort (N = 12, 8 k trials). Offline decoding achieved a phoneme‑level accuracy of 78.4 % (±3.1 %) and a word‑level accuracy of 62.7 % (±4.8 %)—comparable to prior benchmarks—yet online inference was completed within 150 ms per utterance, satisfying clinical real‑time constraints. Ablation studies confirm that diffusion denoising substantially improves robustness to inter‑subject variability, while the lightweight encoder preserves performance with only 1.2 M trainable parameters.

Our results demonstrate that diffusion‑based generative modeling can be harnessed in a computationally efficient manner for online imagined‑speech decoding, paving the way for real‑time brain‑computer interfaces that restore communication in aphasic patients. The proposed framework is open‑source and readily integrable into portable neuroprosthetic devices.
1132:
This paper develops a scientific and systemic foundation for physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI). It aims to describe how intelligent behavior emerges from the interaction among an agent’s body, its sensory perceptions, its motor capabilities, its learning dynamics, its autonomy, and the surrounding context—all within a unified framework. Unlike traditional AI, which depends on symbolic manipulation and purely data‑driven models, Physical AI treats intelligence as a byproduct of real, embodied interaction with the environment. 

The six core elements—embodiment, perception, action, learning, autonomy, and contextual sensitivity—are introduced as the conceptual pillars for constructing and assessing physically intelligent systems. The analysis demonstrates that these elements are not isolated modules; rather, they form a closed feedback loop where energy, information, control signals, and context continuously exchange. This circular interaction allows a system to derive meaning from lived, physical experience rather than from pre‑stored databases, thereby redefining learning as a reconfiguration of the agent‑environment coupling instead of mere parameter tuning.

To ground the theory, the paper presents a practical example: an adaptive rehabilitation robot that assists patients in a clinical setting. This scenario shows that the six fundamentals interact seamlessly—embodiment as the basis, perception as input, actuation as output, learning as adaptation, autonomy as self‑regulation, and context as orientation—highlighting how physical intelligence originates from immediate, embodied experience rather than abstract computation.
1133: Despite the swift rise of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the inner workings of their reasoning traces remain largely inscrutable: it is often unclear which modality drives a prediction, how conflicts among modalities are reconciled, or when one stream exerts undue influence. In this work we introduce “modality sabotage”—a diagnostic failure mode in which a highly confident unimodal prediction can override other evidence and steer the fused outcome astray. To probe these dynamics, we propose a lightweight, model‑agnostic evaluation layer that treats each modality as an independent agent. Each agent generates candidate labels and a concise self‑assessment that can be audited. A simple fusion rule then aggregates these outputs, revealing both contributing modalities (those that support the correct result) and saboteurs (those that mislead). Applying this diagnostic layer to multimodal emotion‑recognition benchmarks built on foundation models exposes systematic reliability patterns and helps determine whether errors stem from dataset artefacts or model shortcomings. More generally, our framework provides a flexible diagnostic scaffold for multimodal reasoning, enabling principled audits of fusion behavior and guiding future remedial strategies.
1134:
Virtual reality (VR) systems routinely rely on vision‑based hand tracking or dedicated haptic devices to translate user movements into digital actions. These solutions, however, suffer from occlusions, high hardware cost, and limited expressivity for complex, natural gestures. In this work we investigate an alternative interaction channel—acoustic gesture recognition—where sound cues captured by a room‑wide microphone array encode spatial motion patterns. While acoustic sensing offers a low‑latency, unobtrusive interface, its high dimensionality and ambiguity pose a significant recognition challenge.  

We propose a novel framework that marries acoustic signal processing with large language models (LLMs) to achieve robust, context‑aware VR interaction. Raw microphone data are first passed through a deep spectrogram encoder that extracts spatio‑temporal embeddings. These embeddings are then fused with a pre‑trained transformer LLM (e.g., GPT‑4‑Vision‑Audio) that has been fine‑tuned on a curated corpus of paired acoustic‑gesture and semantic action labels. The LLM interprets the acoustic embedding in the broader narrative of the user’s VR session, allowing it to disambiguate gestures that are acoustically similar but semantically distinct (e.g., “grab” vs. “drop”).  

To validate our approach we collected a dataset of 4,200 multi‑modal recordings from 120 participants, encompassing 30 distinct acoustic gestures across diverse environments. Our model achieves an average top‑1 accuracy of 92.3 % and a mean F1‑score of 0.90 on a held‑out test set, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art acoustic recognizers by 12 % absolute. A user study involving 30 VR scenarios shows a 35 % reduction in task completion time and a 28 % increase in subjective naturalness relative to conventional controller‑based interaction.  

These results demonstrate that leveraging large language models for acoustic gesture interpretation yields a scalable, low‑latency interaction paradigm that can seamlessly integrate with existing VR pipelines. Our framework paves the way toward more intuitive, multimodal VR experiences where sound becomes a primary conduit for natural user intent.
1135:
Data augmentation is a cornerstone of visual learning, introducing variability to reduce over‑fitting and promote invariances such as spatial symmetry. Yet, augmentation alone only exposes the model to the invariances present in the transformed training set, leaving many desirable properties inadequately encoded. To address this, we introduce *generative hints*, a training framework that explicitly enforces known invariances across the entire input space.

Our method builds a generative model trained on the available data to approximate the underlying distribution and produce unlabeled “virtual” images. These synthetic samples are then employed to impose functional constraints—hints—that reflect the desired invariances. Although the original dataset is fully labeled, the network is trained in a semi‑supervised fashion: the classification objective is combined with the hint objective, and the virtual examples steer the model toward the target property.

We evaluate generative hints on a variety of datasets, architectures, and loss functions, consistently surpassing conventional data augmentation when learning the same invariance. On fine‑grained classification benchmarks, we obtain up to a 1.78 % top‑1 accuracy gain (0.63 % on average) over models fine‑tuned with standard augmentation. On the CheXpert X‑ray dataset, the approach yields an average accuracy improvement of 1.286 %.
1136:
Diffusion‑based generative models have recently achieved state‑of‑the‑art results on a wide array of image and video synthesis tasks. However, the sequential nature of the denoising process and the high dimensionality of video latents render real‑time generation prohibitively expensive, both in terms of wall‑clock time and memory. Existing approaches to accelerate diffusion‑video pipelines rely on naïve checkpointing or fixed‑step caching, which either waste compute or incur large memory footprints without guaranteeing any principled quality‑time trade‑off.

We propose **LeMiCa** (Lexicographic Minimax Path Caching), a principled framework for selecting which latent states to cache along the diffusion trajectory of a video generator. By formulating caching as a lexicographic minimax optimization over a *path graph* that captures dependencies between intermediate latent steps, LeMiCa simultaneously minimizes the worst‑case recomputation cost while respecting a strict memory budget. The resulting algorithm operates in two stages: a global path‑selection pass that computes an optimal caching strategy using a modified Dijkstra traversal, followed by a lightweight dynamic re‑use scheduler that guarantees constant‑time retrieval of cached states during sampling.

We evaluate LeMiCa on several large‑scale video benchmarks (UCF‑101, Kinetics‑400) and show that it reduces average inference latency by 35–50 % compared to baseline checkpointing schemes, with a memory overhead of less than 10 %. Moreover, LeMiCa preserves perceptual quality, as measured by FVD and human preference studies. Our analysis reveals that the lexicographic minimax criterion yields a Pareto‑optimal balance between time and space, and that the caching graph can be extended to accommodate multi‑modal diffusion models.

LeMiCa thus offers a scalable, theory‑grounded method for efficient diffusion‑based video generation, opening the door to real‑time deployment on edge devices and interactive content creation pipelines.
1137:
Comics fuse highly stylized graphics, unconventional panel layouts, and densely packed textual cues to convey narrative, making fine‑grained visual–language understanding a formidable challenge for contemporary vision‑language models (VLMs). Existing VLMs treat comic images as homogeneous wholes or rely on fixed‑grid tokenization, thereby ignoring the spatially heterogeneous importance of panels, speech balloons, and character poses. We propose **Region‑Aware Reinforcement Learning (RARL)**, a lightweight yet powerful framework that end‑to‑end learns to attend to diagnostically relevant regions in comic panels while preserving the holistic context required for multi‑step reasoning.

RARL first generates a set of candidate regions via a lightweight region proposal network tailored to comic‑style imagery. A reinforcement learner, parameterized as a recurrent policy network, selects a sequence of regions conditioned on the current state (previously attended regions, encoded visual and linguistic features) to maximize a task‑specific reward (e.g., answer accuracy on a VQA objective). The policy is trained with policy gradients and a curriculum of progressively harder questions, enabling the model to discover non‑obvious “information hotspots” such as subtle visual gestures or marginal text that are critical for narrative inference. We integrate the RL‑guided attention into a transformer‑based VLM, yielding a joint visual‑textual embedding that respects both global layout and local semantics.

Evaluated on the **ComicVQA** and **ComicsQA** benchmarks, our RARL‑enhanced VLM achieves +6.3% absolute accuracy over the strongest non‑RL baseline and +4.1% over a purely CNN‑based region‑aware model, demonstrating the necessity of dynamic, task‑driven region selection. Ablation studies confirm that both the reinforcement signal and the region‑aware pre‑selection contribute synergistically to performance gains, while our approach incurs only a 12% inference overhead. RARL thus offers a principled pathway to fine‑grained comic understanding, and sets the stage for future work on multimodal narrative modeling and interactive comic generation.
1138:
Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) extends the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) by tapping external knowledge sources, thereby enhancing their reliability. In *agentic* RAG, the model autonomously engages in multi‑round retrieval and reasoning to answer user queries. While recent reinforcement‑learning techniques have boosted the accuracy of such systems, they typically impose a large token cost due to repeated search and reasoning operations, trading efficiency for precision.

This paper introduces **TeaRAG**, a token‑efficient agentic RAG framework that compresses both the information retrieved from the knowledge base and the reasoning chain itself. First, we augment conventional chunk‑based semantic retrieval with a compact graph‑based retrieval that represents knowledge as succinct triples. By constructing a knowledge‑association graph—derived from semantic similarity and co‑occurrence signals—and applying Personalized PageRank, we isolate the most salient facts, thereby shrinking the token budget for each retrieval step. Second, to curb the length of reasoning traces, we propose **Iterative Process‑aware Direct Preference Optimization (IP‑DPO)**. The reward function in IP‑DPO scores outputs according to a knowledge‑matching criterion while penalizing unnecessary reasoning iterations, enabling the generation of high‑quality preference pairs that drive iterative DPO training for more concise reasoning.

Across six benchmark datasets, TeaRAG achieves an average Exact Match gain of 4 % and 2 % over baselines on Llama3‑8B‑Instruct and Qwen2.5‑14B‑Instruct, respectively, while cutting output token counts by 61 % and 59 %. The full implementation is released at https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/TeaRAG.
1139:
Numerical integration of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) is a cornerstone of quantitative modeling in physics, finance, biology and engineering.
