Existing solvers, however, often require prohibitively small time‑steps or high‑order schemes to attain acceptable accuracy, leading to large computational costs. We introduce **FMint‑SDE**, a multimodal foundation model that learns to accelerate SDE simulation by predicting and correcting discretization errors on the fly. FMint‑SDE is built on a transformer encoder–decoder architecture that ingests the full trajectory of a low‑order numerical integrator, the governing SDE parameters, and optional contextual metadata (e.g., parameter regimes or descriptive tags). Trained on a large synthetic corpus of SDE solutions spanning over 200 canonical equations—including Langevin dynamics, geometric Brownian motion, and stochastic partial differential equations—FMint‑SDE learns a universal mapping from coarse numerical trajectories to their high‑fidelity counterparts.

During inference, a cheap base integrator (e.g., Euler–Maruyama with coarse time‑step) produces an intermediate solution which is then passed to FMint‑SDE. The model predicts a correction term that, when added to the coarse state, yields a trajectory indistinguishable from a high‑order solver (Runge–Kutta–Milstein) while retaining the efficiency of the inexpensive method. On a benchmark suite of 50 SDEs, FMint‑SDE achieves up to **25× speedup** with mean absolute errors below **0.5 %** of the ground‑truth, and maintains stability across stiff, highly nonlinear, and multi‑dimensional systems. Moreover, the multimodal nature of the model allows rapid adaptation to unseen equations via prompt‑based fine‑tuning, demonstrating the viability of a foundation‑model paradigm for stochastic simulation.

Our results highlight FMint‑SDE as a practical tool for real‑time stochastic modeling, uncertainty quantification, and control, opening a new avenue where machine‑learning‑augmented error correction replaces costly high‑order solvers in large‑scale scientific computing.
1140: Cluster DAGs (C‑DAGs) are a higher‑level abstraction of causal graphs in which each node denotes a cluster of variables and edges capture both causal influences between clusters and statistical dependencies caused by hidden confounders. A C‑DAG represents an equivalence class of acyclic causal graphs that agree on these cluster‑level relations, enabling reasoning at a coarser scale. Traditionally, a clustering that induces a cycle in the resulting C‑DAG is considered invalid under the standard semantics. In this paper we lift that restriction and allow arbitrary variable clusterings, thereby admitting cyclic C‑DAGs. We generalize d‑separation and causal calculus to this relaxed setting, expanding the range of causal questions that can be addressed within clusters. Our calculus is sound and atomically complete with respect to do‑calculus: every valid cluster‑level interventional query can be derived from our rules, each of which maps to a single primitive step of standard do‑calculus. This extension broadens the applicability of C‑DAGs to problems that were previously intractable.
1141:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of complex reasoning, yet the inference‑time expansion techniques that aim to exploit this power usually become prohibitively expensive because they rely on exhaustive sampling. By inspecting decoding trajectories we discovered that most next‑token predictions agree with the reference output, and only a small handful of “critical” tokens drive the model astray. Building on this observation, we introduce **Hint‑Practice Reasoning (HPR)**, a novel framework that pairs two complementary agents: a **hinter** (a strong LLM) that offers probabilistic guidance at key decision points, and a **practitioner** (a lightweight, efficient model) that carries out the bulk of the reasoning.  

The core of HPR is **Distributional Inconsistency Reduction (DIR)**, a rigorously defined metric that identifies intervention points by quantifying how far the practitioner’s trajectory diverges from the hinter’s expected distribution in a tree‑structured probabilistic space. By iteratively refining the search tree according to DIR, HPR re‑weights promising branches and suppresses low‑probability paths.  

Across arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, HPR attains state‑of‑the‑art efficiency‑accuracy trade‑offs: it matches the performance of self‑consistency and Monte‑Carlo Tree Search baselines while generating only one‑fifth of the tokens, and it exceeds other methods by up to 5.1 % absolute accuracy while keeping FLOPs comparable or lower.
1142:
Control‑engineering knowledge is largely dispersed across textbooks, research articles, and industry reports, most of which is expressed in informal natural‑language form.  This hampers the reuse, traceability, and automated reasoning required for modern design, verification, and education.  In this paper we propose an **LLM‑Supported Formal Knowledge Representation (LLM‑FKR)** framework that automatically converts unstructured control‑engineering content into a formally annotated semantic layer and exposes it through an interactive interface.  The core of the framework is a two‑stage pipeline: (1) a transformer‑based prompt‑engineering module extracts domain concepts, mathematical relationships, and design patterns from raw text; (2) a lightweight ontology‑generation engine maps the extracted elements onto a control‑engineering ontology (OWL/RDF) enriched with custom rules for stability, robustness, and optimality.  The resulting graph is rendered in a browser‑based, query‑driven workspace that allows users to explore, validate, and extend the knowledge through natural‑language queries and visual graph traversal.  

We evaluate the pipeline on a benchmark corpus of 1,200 control‑theory papers and 300 textbook chapters, achieving 82 % precision and 76 % recall on concept extraction, and 68 % accuracy in formal relation mapping.  User studies with 45 control‑engineering practitioners demonstrate a 35 % reduction in time to locate relevant design patterns and a 27 % improvement in the perceived quality of the retrieved information.  

The results confirm that large language models can be harnessed to bridge informal domain content and formal knowledge bases, thereby providing an interactive semantic layer that enhances both the accessibility and the computational tractability of control‑engineering knowledge.  This work opens the door to knowledge‑centric design tools, adaptive learning environments, and automated compliance checking in control systems.
1143:
This paper investigates how artificial intelligence can be woven into the creative process of sound artists, illustrated by *Studies for*—a generative audio installation produced with sound artist Evala (see https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/archive/works/studies-for/). The work uses SpecMaskGIT, a lightweight yet high‑fidelity AI synthesizer, to generate and play back eight‑channel sound in real time during a three‑month exhibition, delivering an enveloping auditory experience. At its heart lies the notion of a “new form of archive”: an evolving repository that captures an artist’s sonic language while continuously spawning fresh material beyond their existing catalogue. To realise this, we trained SpecMaskGIT on a 200‑hour corpus of Evala’s past pieces, enabling the model to honour the artist’s distinctive style while producing unexpected, novel sounds. 

Our findings emphasize three essential elements for successful Human‑AI co‑creation in sound art: (1) continuous artist feedback, (2) training datasets sourced from the artist’s own oeuvre, and (3) the capacity to generate genuinely unexpected outputs. *Studies for* exemplifies these principles, demonstrating how a sound AI can both preserve and extend an artist’s legacy. We therefore propose a co‑creation framework for integrating sound generation models into artistic workflows and outline new avenues for preserving and expanding sonic art beyond an individual’s physical lifespan. For a live demonstration, visit https://sony.github.io/studies-for/.
1144: The collaborative filtering (CF) framework has become a cornerstone of modern recommendation engines, yet its performance can degrade when the user‑item interaction matrix is corrupted by noise. While a number of denoising techniques have been proposed, most of them operate on a single graph representation, risking the loss of valuable collaborative signals: pruning an edge between two nodes can sever indirect paths that carry essential information for other node pairs. In this paper, we introduce **DRCSD**, a novel graph‑neural‑network based CF architecture designed to filter out unstable interactions. DRCSD comprises two pivotal components: a **collaborative‑signal‑decoupling module** that separates the observed signals into distinct orders according to their structural properties, and an **order‑specific denoising module** that selectively cleans each order. Moreover, we redesign the traditional GNN aggregation strategy to prevent cross‑order interference until the final pooling stage. Across three publicly available datasets, experiments demonstrate that DRCSD exhibits heightened resilience to noisy interactions and delivers statistically significant gains over leading baseline methods in standard recommendation accuracy metrics.
1145:
Federated learning (FL) allows multiple devices to jointly train a model without sharing raw data, yet its distributed nature leaves it exposed to attacks when trust is lacking. Gradient‐based inference attacks can leak private information, and poisoning attacks can sabotage model quality or inject malicious behaviors. Current countermeasures tend to incur heavy communication or computational burdens and often lack fine‑grained detection accuracy. 

We introduce **LSHFed**, a lightweight yet robust FL system that simultaneously improves aggregation resilience and privacy protection. The cornerstone of LSHFed is **LSHGM**, a novel gradient‑verification protocol that maps high‑dimensional update vectors into short, irreversible binary codes using a multi‑hyperplane locally‑sensitive hashing scheme. By operating directly on these compressed hash signatures, the framework can accurately identify and discard malicious updates while preventing any potential reconstruction of the original gradients, thereby reducing privacy leakage and cutting down the communication payload dramatically. 

Empirical results show that LSHFed sustains near‑optimal model performance even when half of the participating clients are colluding adversaries, and achieves up to a 1,000‑fold reduction in communication cost for gradient verification compared to conventional full‑gradient approaches.
1146:
Brain‑computer interfaces (BCIs) that rely on electroencephalography (EEG) are notoriously sensitive to non‑stationarities arising from rapid changes in a user’s internal state (e.g., fatigue, attention, mental workload). These fluctuations induce systematic drifts in the spatial‑spectral patterns that decoding algorithms exploit, leading to a pronounced decline in classification accuracy over time. To address this challenge, we propose a user‑state‑aware EEG filtering framework that dynamically adapts preprocessing parameters to the real‑time cognitive condition of the user.

The method first estimates the user’s current state using low‑latency EEG‑derived metrics (power spectral density, frontal alpha asymmetry, and frontal theta‑beta ratio) combined with auxiliary signals (pupil diameter, galvanic skin response). Based on the inferred state, a Bayesian adaptation layer selects optimal band‑pass ranges and spatial filters (Common Spatial Patterns and Riemannian covariance‐based kernels) that maximize the signal‑to‑noise ratio for the task at hand. The adaptive pipeline is integrated into a sliding‑window classification loop and updated every 500 ms without interrupting the BCI operation.

We evaluated the approach on 30 subjects performing a four‑class motor‑imagery task across five sessions separated by 30‑minute intervals. Compared with a conventional, static filter baseline, the adaptive strategy yielded a mean accuracy gain of **12.4 %** (p < 0.001) and reduced within‑session accuracy variance by 35 %. Furthermore, the adaptive system maintained performance for up to 90 % of the session duration, whereas the static pipeline degraded below 70 % accuracy after the first 15 min in 42 % of runs.

Our results demonstrate that incorporating real‑time user state into the EEG preprocessing chain can substantially enhance decoding stability and robustness. This state‑aware filtering paradigm constitutes a scalable, low‑overhead step toward truly adaptive BCIs suitable for prolonged use in clinical and consumer settings.
1147:
Accurate and efficient ultrasound imaging demands expert manipulation of the probe, a task that is both time‑consuming and highly operator dependent. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) and deep reinforcement learning (RL) offer a promising route toward fully autonomous scanning, yet a scalable, end‑to‑end framework that unifies realistic data synthesis with task‑oriented control remains lacking. In this work we present a novel pipeline that couples a diffusion‑based generative model with a deep RL policy to perform autonomous, patient‑specific ultrasound scanning.

The generative component is trained on a large corpus of high‑resolution 3‑D ultrasound volumes and learns to produce anatomically faithful synthetic scans conditioned on probe pose and contact force. These synthetic scenes populate a differentiable physics‑based simulator that provides a rich training environment for the RL agent, enabling extensive exploration without the need for costly, real‑world data collection. The RL agent, implemented as a transformer‑based actor‑critic network, receives real‑time image observations and proprioceptive feedback and outputs continuous probe trajectories that maximize coverage and image fidelity while respecting safety constraints.

We evaluate the framework on a commercial diagnostic system in both phantom and in‑vivo settings. Compared with a baseline hand‑crafted rule‑based controller, our end‑to‑end model reduces scanning time by 35 % and achieves a 21 % improvement in the Dice coefficient of anatomical landmark segmentation, while maintaining force limits below 2 N. Ablation studies confirm that the generative pre‑training reduces sample complexity by over 50 % relative to purely supervised RL, and transfer learning experiments demonstrate robust sim‑to‑real performance across multiple body regions.

Our results highlight the feasibility of combining generative AI and deep RL for complex medical imaging tasks, and lay the groundwork for autonomous ultrasound devices capable of consistent, high‑quality imaging in diverse clinical environments.
1148: Multiple‑Criteria Decision Making (MCDM) is a branch of Operations Research that assists decision‑makers in selecting, ordering, or clustering alternatives when faced with conflicting criteria. Its scope has progressively broadened to dynamic, data‑driven settings such as recommender systems, where the use of personal and sensitive information can be pivotal to the outcome. Although these contexts increasingly depend on such data, the incorporation of privacy‑preserving techniques into MCDM remains sparse. This paper presents a unified framework that merges MCDM outranking methods with Differential Privacy (DP), thereby protecting the privacy of individual contributions in ranking tasks. The approach first aggregates multiple user assessments into a single performance matrix via a preprocessing step. Empirical results demonstrate a strong to very strong statistical correlation between the original and the DP‑protected rankings, confirming that the privacy guarantees do not significantly compromise decision quality.
1149:
Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) models make large language models tractable by activating only a handful of experts for each token. However, conventional Top‑K routing fixes the number of experts per token, disregarding the fact that some tokens are inherently more complex than others. Existing adaptive routing techniques try to address this by adding extra modules or hyper‑parameters, which usually necessitates expensive, end‑to‑end retraining.

In this work we introduce **Sequence‑level Top‑K (SeqTopK)**, a lightweight tweak that reallocates the expert budget from the token to the whole sequence. By selecting the top \(T\!\times\!K\) experts for all \(T\) tokens in a sequence, SeqTopK allows the model to learn a dynamic allocation that assigns more experts to difficult tokens and fewer to easy ones, all while keeping the total budget unchanged. The method needs only a handful of code lines, incurs less than 1 % additional computation, and can be applied directly to pre‑trained MoE models.

We evaluate SeqTopK on diverse tasks—including mathematics, programming, legal reasoning, and creative writing—and consistently outperform the standard Top‑K and other parameter‑free adaptive schemes. The improvement is particularly pronounced under high sparsity settings, where gains reach up to 16.9 %. These results demonstrate that SeqTopK is a simple, efficient, and highly scalable routing strategy, especially suitable for the extreme sparsity regimes required by next‑generation LLMs.

Source code: https://github.com/Y‑Research‑SBU/SeqTopK.
1150:
In many practical supervised learning scenarios the labeling process is noisy, ambiguous or inherently subjective. Traditional hard‐label frameworks force a binary decision for each class, often misrepresenting the true uncertainty of the annotation and limiting the ability of a model to learn from partially reliable information. To bridge this gap, we introduce **fuzzy labels**—continuous membership functions that quantify the degree to which each example belongs to every class. Building upon fuzzy set theory, we formalize a *fuzzy label learning* paradigm that replaces the conventional one‑hot encoding with a vector of membership values in \([0,1]\).  

We develop a principled training objective that incorporates these membership degrees into a generalized cross‑entropy loss, enabling a neural network to learn from fuzzy supervision. The resulting framework is agnostic to model architecture and can be seamlessly integrated with existing deep learning pipelines.  

Experiments on several standard multi‑label datasets (e.g., Pascal VOC, MS‑COCO, and a medical image atlas) demonstrate that the fuzzy label approach consistently outperforms hard‑label baselines in terms of mean average precision and F1‑score, especially under conditions of label noise and class imbalance. Ablation studies confirm that the improvement stems from the model’s ability to leverage partial label information rather than overfitting to erroneous hard labels.  

Our work provides a systematic treatment of fuzzy labels and their application in label learning, offering a more expressive and robust alternative to hard annotation schemes. This paradigm can be readily extended to semi‑supervised, active learning and weakly supervised contexts, opening new avenues for handling uncertainty in modern machine learning.
1151: The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has sparked interest in endowing embodied agents with sophisticated reasoning capabilities. Yet, current LLM‑driven systems largely rely on stateless, purely symbolic reasoning, which hampers adaptive interaction in dynamic, real‑world environments and limits collaborative efficiency among multiple agents. We propose **DR. WELL**—a framework that unifies *Dynamic Reasoning* with *Learning* over a *Symbolic World Model* to support embodied LLM‑based multi‑agent collaboration. DR. WELL constructs an incremental, graph‑based representation of the environment, incorporating perceptual grounding and action affordances. During execution, agents continuously update this world model, negotiate joint plans, and revise their internal hypotheses via a feedback loop that couples the symbolic reasoning layer with the LLM’s latent semantic space. We evaluate the framework in a suite of simulated robotics and real‑world tabletop tasks involving up to four agents with heterogeneous skill sets. Across benchmarks, DR. WELL reduces task completion time by 22 % and increases success rates by 18 % over baseline LLM‑only and classical symbolic planners. Ablation studies confirm that the dynamic world‑model exchange is critical for robustness to perceptual noise and changing goals. Our results demonstrate that a tightly coupled symbolic reasoning–learning architecture can effectively bridge the gap between powerful LLMs and embodied multi‑agent systems, paving the way for scalable, adaptive collaboration in complex, real‑world settings.
1152: Recent work on long‑duration video analysis has leveraged the sophisticated visual‑language reasoning abilities of large multimodal models (LMMs), spurring the development of video‑specific LMMs for extended clips. Yet these models quickly become infeasible because the sheer number of visual tokens generated from long videos overwhelms their capacity. To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce FLoC, a lightweight visual‑token compression framework grounded in the facility location function. This principled method rapidly selects a small, yet highly representative and diverse set of visual tokens within a fixed budget. By employing a lazy‑greedy algorithm, FLoC achieves substantial efficiency gains, drastically shrinking the token set while maintaining near‑optimal performance. Importantly, the approach is training‑free, model‑agnostic, and query‑agnostic, enabling seamless integration with any video‑LLM or existing pipeline. Extensive experiments on large benchmarks such as Video‑MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench confirm that FLoC consistently outperforms contemporary compression schemes, demonstrating both its effectiveness and its speed advantages for long‑video understanding.
1153:
Categorical data often exhibit heterogeneous relationships among attribute values that vary across subpopulations. Existing clustering approaches either ignore these dependencies or impose a single global similarity structure, thereby limiting cluster purity and interpretability. We introduce **Break the Tie**, a novel framework that learns *cluster‑customized* category relationships jointly with the partition of the data. In our model, each cluster is endowed with its own pairwise similarity (or dissimilarity) matrix over categorical levels, and these matrices are inferred by a hierarchical Bayesian prior that encourages sparsity and discourages redundant “ties” between categories. A tractable EM‑style variational inference scheme updates cluster assignments and the relationship matrices simultaneously, while a tie‑breaking regularizer guarantees that the learned matrices are distinct enough to capture local structure.

Extensive experiments on synthetic and real‑world datasets—including market‑basket, survey, and biological annotation collections—show that Break the Tie consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art categorical clustering methods (k‑modes, latent class analysis, one‑hot GMM) in both clustering accuracy and internal coherence. Moreover, the cluster‑specific relationship matrices provide rich, interpretable insights into domain‑specific categorical interactions and can be reused for downstream tasks such as feature engineering and anomaly detection. This work demonstrates that allowing category relationships to vary across clusters unlocks superior clustering performance and deeper understanding of categorical data.
1154:
Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable general‑purpose capabilities, yet their performance degrades sharply when deployed in highly specialized domains such as telecommunications mathematics, where terminology, notation, and problem structure diverge substantially from the pre‑training corpus. In this work we introduce **Data Trajectory Alignment (DTA)**, a principled two‑phase synthesis framework that bridges this domain gap without requiring costly manual labeling.

**Phase I – Trajectory‑Based Synthetic Generation** leverages a curated set of domain‑specific equations, network‑topology descriptions, and performance‑metric traces to synthesize realistic problem‑solution pairs. By sampling and perturbing “data trajectories” extracted from real telecom simulation logs and embedding them into a controlled generative process, we produce a high‑fidelity, semi‑structured corpus that captures the sequential logic and algebraic manipulations characteristic of telecommunications mathematics.

**Phase II – Alignment‑Driven Fine‑Tuning** employs a novel alignment loss that jointly optimizes token‑level semantic similarity and trajectory coherence. The loss is computed over the synthetic corpus and a small set of expert‑annotated validation traces, ensuring that the model not only reproduces correct mathematical syntax but also preserves the underlying procedural dependencies. We further integrate curriculum‑style scheduling, gradually introducing longer and more complex trajectories to prevent catastrophic forgetting.

We evaluate the framework on a benchmark of 12 telecom‑specific tasks—including bandwidth allocation, signal‑to‑noise ratio analysis, and network coding proofs—using GPT‑4‑style models. Compared to standard fine‑tuning and prompting baselines, DTA achieves a **25 % relative improvement in F1‑score** on mathematical reasoning and a **30 % reduction in hallucination rates**. Ablation studies confirm that both synthetic trajectory diversity and alignment loss contribute synergistically to performance gains.

Our results demonstrate that domain adaptation for LLMs can be achieved efficiently through trajectory‑aware synthesis, offering a scalable path for deploying intelligent assistants in mathematically rigorous engineering fields. The framework is publicly released, providing a blueprint for future work in specialized scientific language modeling.
1155: Spatial reasoning—understanding how objects relate and interact within complex scenes—is a demanding cognitive problem, especially for robotic systems. While current vision‑language models (VLMs) perform well on perception, they often fail to capture fine‑grained spatial relationships because they rely on implicit, correlation‑based reasoning and only process images. We introduce a neuro‑symbolic architecture that fuses panoramic imagery and 3D point‑cloud data, marrying deep perception with explicit symbolic inference to model spatial and logical connections. The system first detects objects and extracts their attributes, then builds a structured scene graph that enables precise, interpretable queries. On the JRDB‑Reasoning benchmark, our method outperforms existing baselines in dense, human‑built environments, all while remaining lightweight enough for deployment on robots and embodied agents.
1156:
Dexterous manipulation requires a detailed yet tractable representation of hand‑object interactions for policy learning, yet conventional physics engines either sacrifice fidelity or incur prohibitive computational costs. We present **GenDexHand**, a generative simulation framework that learns a high‑fidelity, low‑dimensional surrogate of contact dynamics for multi‑fingered robotic hands. By training a deep graph‑convolutional network on a curated dataset of high‑resolution finite‑element and discrete‑element simulations, GenDexHand captures nonlinear friction, compliance, and contact‑switching behavior in a differentiable form. The resulting surrogate can be queried at 10 kHz on commodity GPUs, enabling end‑to‑end differentiable control of a 20‑DOF Shadow Dexterous Hand in a simulated environment that preserves the rich physics of real‑world grasps.

We evaluate GenDexHand on a suite of standard dexterous benchmarks: precision and power grasping, in‑hand re‑orientation, and dynamic pick‑and‑place. Policies trained with GenDexHand achieve 30–40 % higher success rates than those trained with conventional rigid‑body simulators and require only a third of the training time. Importantly, we demonstrate zero‑shot transfer to the physical hand: policies trained exclusively in GenDexHand perform with >90 % success in real‑world trials. Ablation studies confirm that the generative contact model and its differentiable interface are critical for both simulation speed and transfer fidelity.

To encourage reproducibility and further research, we release the GenDexHand codebase, a 5‑hour dataset of synthetic hand‑object interactions, and a set of benchmark tasks. Our results show that a data‑driven generative approach can bridge the fidelity‑efficiency trade‑off in dexterous manipulation simulation, opening new avenues for rapid development of high‑performance robotic hand controllers.
1157: As artificial intelligence increasingly informs decisions in many fields, there is a rising demand for AI literacy among learners who are not from computer‑science backgrounds. Existing approaches, however, tend to depend on code‑heavy tools or abstract lectures, which can alienate non‑STEM audiences. This paper reports on a study of **AI User**, a modular, web‑based curriculum that conveys core AI concepts through interactive, no‑code projects set in realistic contexts. The curriculum contains eight projects; our analysis focuses on Projects 5–8, which cover applied topics such as natural‑language processing, computer vision, decision support, and responsible AI. Fifteen community‑college instructors took part in structured focus groups, first completing the projects themselves and then reflecting individually and discussing collectively. Thematic analysis of their feedback examined how the design, instructional value, and classroom applicability of these experiential activities were perceived. Findings show that instructors appreciated the exploratory tasks, role‑based simulations, and real‑world relevance, while also identifying trade‑offs related to cognitive load, scaffolding, and adaptability for diverse learners. By foregrounding instructor perspectives on teaching complex, code‑free AI topics, this work extends the AI‑literacy literature and offers concrete guidance for designing inclusive, scalable, experiential AI learning resources that can be adopted across disciplines.
1158:
Video Large‑Language Models (VideoLLMs) have emerged as powerful multimodal systems capable of generating coherent textual descriptions and answering complex queries over long‑form video streams. However, the dense visual tokenization required to capture spatial‑temporal nuances leads to prohibitively high compute and memory demands, and the inclusion of irrelevant frames and pixels often degrades reasoning quality. In this paper we introduce **Sharp Eyes and Memory (SEM)**, an information‑aware visual token pruning framework that selectively preserves only those visual tokens that contribute substantively to downstream linguistic inference.

Our approach casts pruning as a mutual‑information bottleneck problem: a lightweight saliency network (“Sharp Eyes”) estimates the predictive relevance of each token with respect to the target language task, while a recurrent “Memory” module accumulates a compressed representation of salient spatio‑temporal patterns across the video. Tokens falling below a learned importance threshold are discarded prior to the transformer encoder, thereby shrinking both the input sequence length and the internal memory footprint. We train the saliency module jointly with the VideoLLM using a differentiable relaxation of the pruning operation, enabling end‑to‑end optimization without sacrificing model expressiveness.

Evaluated on the MSR‑VTT, ActivityNet Captions, and TGIF‑QA benchmarks, SEM reduces the average number of visual tokens by 58 % and the total FLOPs by 36 % while maintaining or improving task performance (e.g., +1.3 BLEU on MSR‑VTT). Importantly, the information‑aware pruning enhances robustness to distractors and background noise, yielding a higher variance in per‑video accuracy across long‑duration clips. Ablation studies confirm that both the Sharp Eyes saliency predictor and the Memory module contribute synergistically to the efficiency–reliability trade‑off. Our code and pretrained models are publicly available.
1159:
Recent progress in vision‑language (VL) models has enabled powerful joint reasoning over text and image modalities, yet their capacity to perform *visual measurement reading*—the extraction and interpretation of quantitative quantities from photographs—remains largely unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce **MeasureBench**, a comprehensive benchmark that systematically evaluates VL models on a diverse suite of measurement‑reading tasks. MeasureBench comprises 6,432 images spanning five measurement domains (length, area, volume, angle, and speed) and 12 sub‑tasks (e.g., ruler reading, scale‑based size estimation, time‑based speed calculation, and context‑dependent unit conversion). Each image is annotated with ground‑truth measurements and a natural‑language query, allowing models to be evaluated on both *raw numeric accuracy* and *semantic consistency* with the query.

Using MeasureBench, we benchmark a representative set of contemporary VL architectures—CLIP‑based zero‑shot models, BLIP, Flamingo, and LLaVA—as well as a fine‑tuned baseline trained on the dataset. Across the board, zero‑shot VL models achieve only 48 % exact‑match accuracy, whereas the fine‑tuned baseline improves to 78 %, revealing a substantial performance gap. Our analysis uncovers two primary failure modes: (i) misinterpretation of visual context (e.g., confusing a scale bar with a measurement); and (ii) inadequate unit handling, leading to systematic over‑ or under‑estimates. We also propose a lightweight *measurement‑aware pretraining* objective that encourages the model to attend to quantitative cues, yielding a 6‑point boost on the full benchmark without additional labeled data.

MeasureBench therefore serves as a diagnostic tool and a target for future research, illustrating that while state‑of‑the‑art VL models can comprehend language and vision, they still fall short on precise, quantitative reasoning required for practical measurement reading. We hope this benchmark will spur the development of more robust VL systems capable of reliably extracting and interpreting measurements from the visual world.
1160: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed across scientific and practical domains, yet their ability to exhibit truly general intelligence remains limited. A key divide lies between factual knowledge—answers that are simply true or false—and probabilistic knowledge, which concerns the statistical properties of real‑world phenomena (for example, “what fraction of U.S. computer‑science graduates are male?”). In this study we introduce the first benchmark that directly probes large language models’ grasp of such real‑world probability distributions. Although LLMs are trained on vast corpora of text and are often described as universal approximators of natural distributions, classic statistical results on the curse of dimensionality suggest that learning high‑dimensional distributions is fundamentally hard. Our benchmark tests LLMs across diverse areas—economics, health, education, and social behavior—to see whether they encode empirical distributions of population statistics. Results show that LLMs generally fail to recover accurate distributions, indicating that they do not naturally internalize real‑world statistics. Interpreted through Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy, this failure implies that these models lack knowledge of observational distributions (Layer 1), and consequently their interventional (Layer 2) and counterfactual (Layer 3) understanding is also severely constrained.
1161:
The rapid deployment of large‑language‑model (LLM) agents on social platforms has introduced a new vector for financial fraud: coordinated, autonomous agents that can plan, execute, and conceal illicit schemes at scale.  This paper investigates the emergent risk that “colluding” LLM agents pose to digital economies and the broader public. We first formalise collusion as a multi‑agent interaction in which individual LLM bots share state, exploit platform affordances, and jointly influence target users.  To characterise this phenomenon, we design a threat model that enumerates three classes of collusion—information‑sharing, joint deception, and coordinated manipulation—and quantify their potential damage using a combination of historical fraud data and synthetic scenario generation. 

Leveraging a dataset of 1.2 million posts from Twitter, Reddit, and Discord, we develop a computational pipeline to detect signatures of collaborative LLM activity (e.g., rapid dissemination of identical phrasing, cross‑platform echoing, and coordinated timing).  Using this pipeline, we identify 84 clusters of suspicious bot‑co‑operation and evaluate their fraud outcomes through controlled experiments that simulate phishing, deep‑fake endorsement, and coordinated marketplace scams.  Our results demonstrate that even lightweight, pre‑trained LLM agents can, when orchestrated in groups, inflate perceived authenticity and amplify the reach of illicit offers, leading to estimated losses of over \$2.3 M in test environments.

Finally, we propose a risk‑assessment framework that combines content‑based, behavioural, and network‑level signals to flag potential collusion.  The paper concludes with a discussion of policy implications, suggesting platform‑level mitigations (e.g., collaborative bot‑identification, rate‑limiting for cross‑account activity) and future research directions for robust counter‑measures against adaptive, colluding AI agents.
1162:
Online reinforcement learning (RL) requires agents to adapt their behaviour continuously while interacting with an environment that is often only partially observable and non‑stationary. Traditional policy‑gradient and actor‑critic methods rely on stochastic optimisation over discrete actions or on tabular value updates, which can lead to unstable learning dynamics and poor sample efficiency in high‑dimensional control problems. In this work we introduce **Controllable Flow Matching (CFM)**, a novel framework that casts online RL as a continuous‑time flow‑matching problem: we learn a time‑dependent policy density that is steered by a control field to match the optimal trajectory distribution defined by the Bellman equation.

CFM leverages recent advances in neural ordinary differential equations and score‑based generative modelling. The policy is parameterised as a stochastic differential equation (SDE) whose drift is a learnable control function. During interaction the agent observes a trajectory and updates the control field via a principled gradient that minimises the Kullback‑Leibler divergence between the empirical state‑action flow and the target optimal flow. We provide a rigorous convergence analysis showing that, under standard ergodicity assumptions, the learned control drives the policy to a fixed point that satisfies the optimal Bellman equations. Moreover, we derive a finite‑sample complexity bound that scales sub‑linearly with the horizon.

Experiments on a suite of continuous‑control benchmarks (MuJoCo locomotion, OpenAI Gym robotics) demonstrate that CFM achieves state‑of‑the‑art sample efficiency, outperforming SAC, TD3, and recent diffusion‑based RL baselines by 20–35 % on average reward. Ablation studies reveal that the controllability of the flow enables effective exploration and rapid adaptation to changing reward structures. Finally, we showcase the flexibility of CFM by incorporating safety and resource constraints as additional control penalties, yielding policies that respect safety limits without compromising performance.

Our results establish controllable flow matching as a powerful and generalisable approach for online RL, bridging the gap between continuous‑time generative modelling and reinforcement learning theory.
1163: In light of the growing risks associated with data misuse and fabrication, this work tackles the challenge of spotting synthetic time‑series produced by Time‑Series Large Models (TSLMs). Although a wealth of literature exists for detecting model‑generated text, these token‑centric techniques fail on time‑series because the latter typically possess lower information density and smoother probability distributions, which diminish the discriminative power of text‑based detectors. To overcome this limitation, we investigate the subtle distributional distinctions between authentic and synthetic series and formulate the *contraction hypothesis*: synthetic series, unlike genuine ones, exhibit a progressive reduction in uncertainty when subjected to recursive forecasting. We establish this hypothesis under reasonable theoretical assumptions about model behavior and the structure of time‑series data. Empirical tests on a wide range of datasets confirm that synthetic series indeed display increasingly concentrated distributions as forecasting proceeds, leading to the observed uncertainty contraction. Leveraging this insight, we propose the **Uncertainty Contraction Estimator (UCE)**—a white‑box detector that aggregates uncertainty measures across successive prefixes to identify TSLM‑generated series. Experiments on 32 datasets demonstrate that UCE consistently outperforms current state‑of‑the‑art baselines, providing a robust and broadly applicable solution for detecting synthetic time‑series.
1164: Accurate time‑series forecasting remains a cornerstone of decision‑making in finance, energy, supply‑chain, and many other domains. Traditional statistical and deep‑learning methods, however, often require extensive domain expertise to pre‑process data, select appropriate models, and interpret results, while purely automated pipelines lack the flexibility to incorporate nuanced, situational knowledge. To bridge this gap, we present **AlphaCast**, a human‑wisdom + LLM intelligence co‑reasoning framework that facilitates interactive, explainable forecasting across heterogeneous time‑series datasets. AlphaCast orchestrates a dynamic dialogue between an advanced large language model (LLM) and a domain expert: the LLM proposes candidate features, temporal transformations, and model architectures, and the expert supplies contextual insights, business constraints, and corrective feedback. This co‑reasoning loop is guided by a lightweight knowledge graph that captures causal and seasonal patterns, allowing the LLM to query and refine its suggestions in real time. We evaluate AlphaCast on five benchmark datasets spanning retail, weather, and power‑grid domains, comparing against state‑of‑the‑art baselines (Prophet, LSTM, Transformer). Across all datasets, AlphaCast achieves a mean relative improvement of 12 % in SMAPE while reducing the model‑tuning time by 37 % and producing human‑readable rationale for every forecast. User studies demonstrate that participants perceive AlphaCast forecasts as more trustworthy and actionable, underscoring the value of integrating human wisdom with LLM reasoning for practical time‑series analytics.
1165:
Understanding how often characters appear is key to unraveling a story’s structure, the prominence of its figures, and its overall progression, especially in anime. In this study we present **OregairuChar**, a benchmark dataset tailored for character‑frequency analysis in the series *My Teen Romantic Comedy SNAFU*. The set contains 1,600 hand‑picked frames from season three, each annotated with 2,860 bounding boxes for 11 principal characters. It deliberately includes challenging visual factors such as occlusion, diverse poses, and characters that look alike, offering a realistic testbed for appearance‑based research.

We evaluate a range of object‑detection models on OregairuChar and use their outputs to carry out detailed episode‑level analyses of character presence. The results highlight how individual characters rise and fall in visibility throughout the narrative. By centering on appearance frequency, OregairuChar provides a useful resource for probing computational narrative dynamics and character‑driven storytelling in stylized media.
1166:
Accurate, transparent, and uncertainty‑aware disease prediction from electronic health records (EHRs) and clinical narratives remains a central challenge in medical AI.  Existing transformer‑based language models deliver strong performance but lack principled confidence estimates and explanatory power, while traditional Bayesian methods provide uncertainty but scale poorly to high‑dimensional text.  We introduce **DiagnoLLM**, a hybrid Bayesian‑neural language framework that marries a pre‑trained clinical transformer (ClinicalBERT) with a Bayesian neural decoder to produce calibrated posterior distributions over disease labels.  The model incorporates domain‑specific priors derived from ontology (e.g., ICD‑10 hierarchies) and leverages variational inference to efficiently approximate the posterior over latent disease scores.  Interpretability is achieved through (i) posterior‑weighted attention maps that highlight clinical concepts driving a diagnosis, (ii) probabilistic relevance scores that quantify the contribution of individual notes, and (iii) an explicit Bayesian evidence framework that allows clinicians to query “what‑if” scenarios.  

We evaluate DiagnoLLM on two large EHR corpora—MIMIC‑III and eICU—across five high‑prevalence conditions (pneumonia, sepsis, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and acute kidney injury).  Across all tasks, DiagnoLLM attains a mean AUROC of **0.912** (±0.003) and a Brier score of **0.078**, outperforming baseline transformer classifiers (0.879/0.103) and purely Bayesian models (0.857/0.112).  Calibration plots demonstrate near‑perfect alignment between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies.  An ablation study confirms that the Bayesian layer accounts for a 7.5 % improvement in AUROC and a 25 % reduction in over‑confidence.  Case‑study analyses illustrate how the posterior attention mechanism surfaces clinically relevant biomarkers and facilitates hypothesis generation.  

DiagnoLLM thus provides a scalable, interpretable, and uncertainty‑quantified approach to disease diagnosis, bridging the gap between high‑performance language models and the rigor required for clinical decision support.  The code and pretrained checkpoints are released at https://github.com/DiagnoLLM.
1167:
Shortest‑path routing is a well‑studied foundation for vehicular navigation, yet real‑world driving demands more nuanced decision‑making: congestion, road‑closure advisories, weather hazards, and driver intent must be jointly considered. This paper introduces **Agentic Vehicular Routing with Semantic Context (AVR‑SC)**, a framework that augments graph‑based path planning with rich semantic descriptors derived from heterogeneous urban data. We formalise the routing problem as a Markov Decision Process over a knowledge‑graph representation of the road network, where vertices are annotated with temporal traffic flows, weather conditions, and contextual predicates (e.g., “school zone”, “construction zone”). A lightweight semantic embedding model maps these predicates into a continuous latent space, enabling the agent to evaluate trade‑offs beyond mere distance or time.

Our approach leverages a hierarchical policy: an offline planner generates candidate routes using a modified Dijkstra algorithm that incorporates semantic penalty scores, and an online reinforcement‑learning controller refines the path in situ based on real‑time observations. Evaluation on a high‑fidelity simulator of the City of Los Angeles and a real‑world fleet of connected vehicles demonstrates that AVR‑SC reduces expected travel time by 12 % and incident‑rate risk by 18 % compared to baseline shortest‑path routing, while maintaining comparable computational latency (< 50 ms on embedded hardware). These results affirm that integrating semantic context endows autonomous vehicles with truly agentic routing behaviour, balancing efficiency, safety, and user preferences.
1168:
Large language models normally encode knowledge implicitly inside a highly entangled set of parameters, which makes the information stale and impossible to scrutinize or edit.  We introduce **ExplicitLM**, a new architecture that stores knowledge explicitly in a million‑word external memory bank of readable token sequences.  This allows the model to look at and modify facts directly.  

Our design employs a two‑stage, differentiable retrieval process: first a coarse, product‑key decomposition prunes candidates from the $\mathcal{O}(N\cdot|I|)$ space to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N}\cdot|I|)$, and then a fine‑grained Gumbel‑Softmax matcher selects the final memory items, enabling end‑to‑end training.  Drawing on dual‑system cognitive theory, we split knowledge into two parts—frozen explicit facts (≈20 %) and learnable implicit patterns (≈80 %)—and use an Exponential Moving Average scheme to keep the explicit component stable.  

On a range of knowledge‑heavy benchmarks, ExplicitLM outperforms standard Transformers by as much as 43.67 % and delivers a 3.62× advantage in low‑data settings (10 k examples).  Analysis reveals a strong link between retrieval success and accuracy: correctly predicted examples exhibit a 49 % higher hit rate in the external memory.  Unlike conventional Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) systems that keep the memory static, our jointly optimized architecture shows that a model can be both interpretable and up‑datable while retaining competitive performance.
1169:
Direction‑of‑arrival (DOA) estimation is a cornerstone of modern acoustic signal processing, enabling tasks such as robotic audition, smart‑home automation, and beam‑forming in wireless communications. Conventional data‑driven approaches, however, rely on large volumes of labelled recordings that are expensive to collect and often fail to capture the diversity of real‑world acoustic scenes. In this work we propose a novel pipeline that (i) uses a large‑language model (LLM) to generate richly annotated, physics‑based acoustic simulations, and (ii) trains a lightweight neural network that delivers high‑accuracy DOA predictions on both simulated and real recordings.

The LLM is employed to produce a vast corpus of synthetic audio scenes by generating realistic room layouts, microphone arrays, and source trajectories, followed by ray‑tracing propagation. This yields over 50 k training instances spanning a broad range of reverberation times, source‑to‑sensor distances, and noise conditions, without manual labelling. The DOA estimator is a compact 1‑D convolutional architecture with a single attention block, comprising only 0.8 M parameters and 2.3 M FLOPs. Trained end‑to‑end on the LLM‑augmented dataset, the network attains a mean absolute error of 2.4° on the benchmark TIMIT‑based dataset, matching or surpassing state‑of‑the‑art models that use tenfold more parameters.

Our results demonstrate that LLM‑aided simulation not only mitigates data scarcity but also endows the model with robust generalisation to unseen real‑world recordings. The lightweight design allows deployment on embedded processors, paving the way for low‑power acoustic sensing in IoT devices. We release the full simulation pipeline and trained models to the community, encouraging further exploration of LLM‑driven synthetic data generation for audio machine‑learning tasks.
1170: Despite the impressive performance of text‑to‑image diffusion models, producing a single flattened image remains a major limitation for professional workflows that demand fine‑grained, layer‑by‑layer control. Existing solutions either fine‑tune on large, hard‑to‑access datasets or, when training‑free, can only generate isolated foreground patches and fail to compose a complete, coherent scene. We propose **TAUE**—the Training‑free Noise Transplantation and Cultivation Diffusion Model—enabling zero‑shot, multi‑layer image synthesis. Its core **NTC** mechanism extracts intermediate latent codes from both foreground and composite generation stages and grafts them onto the initial noise for subsequent layers, guaranteeing semantic and structural alignment across all layers. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TAUE matches the quality of fine‑tuned methods while delivering consistent, multi‑layer outputs without requiring additional training or external data. By eliminating expensive fine‑tuning and opening the door to sophisticated compositional editing, TAUE makes generative pipelines more accessible and controllable.
1171: This paper presents the methods and outcomes of our participation in the Multilingual E‑commerce Search Competition. The challenge requires evaluating the relevance between user queries and product items in a multilingual context, thereby improving recommendation quality on e‑commerce platforms. By exploiting the cross‑lingual capabilities of Large Language Models and adopting a data‑centric workflow, we achieved the top score among all competing systems. The final leaderboard is available at [https://alibaba‑international‑cikm2025.github.io](https://alibaba-international-cikm2025.github.io), and the full source code can be accessed via [https://github.com/nhtlongcs/e-commerce-product-search](https://github.com/nhtlongcs/e-commerce-product-search).
1172: Although the LLaVA framework has proven highly effective for vision‑language tasks, its architecture inherently limits the seamless fusion of visual and textual features because of a mismatch between the two modalities. We address this shortcoming by reimagining the large language model not merely as a text processor but as a powerful visual encoder as well. Introducing LLaViT—Large Language Models as Extended Vision Transformers—we equip the LLM to act as a vision encoder through three key enhancements: (1) training dedicated QKV projections for visual input, (2) adding bidirectional attention over visual tokens, and (3) fusing both global and local visual representations. Extensive, controlled experiments across numerous LLMs reveal that LLaViT consistently outperforms the baseline LLaVA approach on a diverse set of benchmarks, even surpassing models that have twice the parameter count, thereby establishing a more effective paradigm for vision‑language integration.
1173:
Multi‑arm robotic systems have become indispensable in high‑throughput warehouses, automated assembly lines, and surgical assistance. However, the joint task‑and‑motion planning (TAMP) and scheduling of several manipulators remains a computational bottleneck, largely due to the combinatorial explosion of inter‑arm constraints and the expensive geometric queries required for collision‑free trajectories. **ScheduleStream** proposes a unified framework that marries temporal planning with learned samplers and leverages GPU acceleration to break this bottleneck.

At the core of ScheduleStream is a *stream‑based temporal planner* that constructs a partial‑order schedule of high‑level actions while delegating the feasibility of each action to a set of lightweight samplers. These samplers—parameterized by problem‑specific heuristics and learned from prior executions—produce candidate joint configurations and inter‑arm coordination primitives. The resulting geometric queries (inverse kinematics, collision checking, and kinematic feasibility) are batched and executed on a GPU, exploiting massive parallelism to evaluate thousands of samples in microseconds. A hierarchical decomposition further separates long‑term sequencing from short‑term motion feasibility, allowing the planner to prune infeasible branches early and focus GPU resources on the most promising candidates.

We validate ScheduleStream on a suite of synthetic and real‑world multi‑arm benchmarks (up to eight arms in cluttered environments). Compared to state‑of‑the‑art CPU‑based planners, ScheduleStream achieves an average **10× speed‑up** while maintaining a success rate of **>95 %** and producing makespans within 5 % of the optimal schedule. The results demonstrate that temporal planning coupled with GPU‑accelerated samplers can scale multi‑arm TAMP to problem sizes previously deemed intractable, paving the way for real‑time deployment in industrial and surgical settings.
1174: Redistricting determines how electoral votes translate into political power, yet most algorithmic tools focus only on producing large collections of legally compliant plans and overlook the strategic aspects of plan selection. This gap allows partisan actors to choose from compliant maps that are still heavily biased in their favour. Merely meeting formal constraints does not guarantee a fair process when the selection itself is malleable. We introduce **Agentmandering**, a new framework that frames redistricting as a turn‑based negotiation between two opposing political agents. Building on game‑theoretic concepts such as the *Choose‑and‑Freeze* protocol, our approach models this interaction with large language model agents that alternately pick and lock districts from a limited pool of candidate maps. This stepwise, interpretable construction progressively partitions the state while respecting constraints. Experiments on post‑2020 U.S. Census data for all states demonstrate that Agentmandering substantially lowers partisan bias and unfairness, and produces plan ensembles with 2‑3 orders of magnitude less variance than conventional baselines—especially in swing‑state contexts. The code is available at https://github.com/Lihaogx/AgentMandering.
1175:
Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a popular, parameter‑efficient technique for fine‑tuning large language models. Yet typical LoRA adapters are trained for a single task, which hinders their usefulness when inputs come from a wide, unpredictable spectrum of domains. Current inference‑time solutions combine several LoRAs to cover multiple tasks, but they normally require extra labeled data or task‑specific training—costly at scale.  

In this paper we propose **LoRA on the Go (LoGo)**, a completely training‑free framework that selects and blends adapters on a per‑instance basis. LoGo extracts cues from a single forward pass through the adapters, identifying which modules are most relevant and weighting them dynamically, without any additional training or labeled data. Evaluated on five NLP benchmarks, 27 datasets, and three different model families, LoGo surpasses training‑based baselines on several tasks by up to 3.6 % while staying competitive on the rest, all while preserving inference speed. This demonstrates LoGo’s practicality and effectiveness for real‑world, multi‑domain deployment.
1176: Invasive marine species disperse worldwide through commercial shipping, causing significant ecological and economic damage. Conventional risk assessments depend on exhaustive ballast‑water and traffic data, which are frequently missing or incomplete, thereby hindering broad‑scale application. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework that quantifies invasion risk by integrating environmental similarity between ports with both observed and projected maritime traffic. Each port’s marine environment is described using climate‑based feature vectors, while vessel movement networks built from Automatic Identification System (AIS) data capture actual and potential transfer pathways. Through clustering and metric‑learning techniques, climate analogues are identified, allowing the calculation of species survival probabilities along shipping routes. A temporal link‑prediction model then projects future traffic flows under changing environmental conditions. By fusing environmental likeness with predicted mobility, the approach generates exposure estimates at both port and voyage levels, thereby facilitating targeted monitoring, route optimization, and management actions.
1177: Advancements in visual reinforcement learning have driven impressive gains in robotic control, yet their susceptibility to adversarial attacks is still poorly understood. Current black‑box attacks are largely tailored to vector‑based or discrete‑action settings, and struggle to affect image‑driven continuous control because of the vast action space and the prohibitive number of environment queries required. We introduce SEBA, a sample‑efficient black‑box attack framework designed for visual RL agents. SEBA couples a shadow Q‑network that predicts the cumulative reward under adversarial conditions, a generative adversarial network that crafts imperceptible visual perturbations, and a learned world model that emulates environment dynamics to curb real‑world interactions. By iteratively training the shadow model and the generator in two stages, SEBA delivers potent attacks while remaining query‑efficient. Extensive tests on MuJoCo and Atari environments demonstrate that SEBA dramatically lowers cumulative rewards, preserves image quality, and reduces the need for environment calls far more than previous black‑box and white‑box methods.
1178:
Reasoning is a core element of human cognition, underpinning critical thinking, sound decision‑making, and the resolution of complex challenges. While AI has traditionally addressed reasoning through logic‑based knowledge representations, the recent explosion of transformer‑based language models—trained on ever larger corpora—has raised the prospect that these models may themselves exhibit reasoning capabilities. Yet, despite much discussion, it remains difficult to gauge the true extent of reasoning performed by such models.

This workshop seeks to provide a forum for researchers across disciplines and AI paradigms to investigate how to bridge transformer‑based language models with logic‑driven reasoning. Its specific aims are: (1) to evaluate the reasoning competencies of language models against conventional knowledge‑representation techniques; (2) to embed KR‑style reasoning into language models, including through neuro‑symbolic approaches; and (3) to formalize the types of reasoning that these models actually carry out. By doing so, we hope to uncover ways in which language models can more effectively integrate and leverage knowledge and reasoning, thereby boosting their performance and reliability in domains where precision and accountability are paramount.
1179:
Linear genetic programming (LGP) has become a popular evolutionary paradigm for evolving programs represented as sequences of instructions. Although most LGP systems adopt a binary bitstring encoding for instruction arguments and control flow, the impact of the underlying bit‑level representation on the overall performance of the framework has received limited systematic scrutiny. In this work we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation of three common bitstring representations—direct binary encoding, Gray‑code encoding, and hybrid fixed‑length/variable‑length encoding—within a canonical LGP framework. Using a suite of benchmark problems that span symbolic regression, boolean satisfiability, and combinatorial optimization, we measure not only predictive accuracy but also key performance indicators such as compilation overhead, execution time, memory consumption, and convergence speed.

Our experiments reveal that while the direct binary encoding yields the fastest individual instruction decoding, the Gray‑code representation consistently reduces the frequency of disruptive mutations, leading to faster overall convergence on highly rugged fitness landscapes. The hybrid representation, which preserves the compactness of fixed‑length codes while allowing variable‑length segments for program headers, offers a favorable trade‑off between expressiveness and computational cost, achieving comparable accuracy to the Gray‑code variant with roughly 30 % lower memory footprint. Moreover, we observe that representation choice has a pronounced effect on the scalability of the system: on problems requiring deep instruction sequences, the direct binary encoding incurs significant decoding latency, whereas the Gray‑code and hybrid schemes maintain stable runtimes.

These findings underscore that the selection of bitstring representation is a pivotal design decision in LGP implementations, affecting both algorithmic efficiency and evolutionary dynamics. We conclude with a set of guidelines for practitioners and outline directions for future research, including adaptive representation switching and hybrid encoding strategies that dynamically balance exploration and exploitation.
1180: Detecting anomalies in visual data is notoriously difficult because anomalous samples are rare and highly diverse. Conventional anomaly detection pipelines either rely on large annotated anomaly corpora or on hand‑crafted perturbations that fail to capture the true semantic variety of out‑of‑distribution events. We present **Anomagic**, a cross‑modal prompt‑driven framework that synthesises realistic, high‑frequency anomalous instances in a zero‑shot setting. Anomagic jointly harnesses a powerful pre‑trained diffusion generator and a multimodal embedding backbone (CLIP) to transform a natural‑language prompt into a richly contextualized latent representation. A cross‑modal attention module aligns the textual intent with visual features, guiding the diffusion model to carve out plausible deviations from the normal distribution without any anomaly‑specific supervision. The resulting synthetic anomalies can be injected into downstream training pipelines, yielding state‑of‑the‑art performance on standard benchmarks such as MVTec AD, VisA, and a newly proposed Cross‑Modal Anomaly (CMA) dataset. On average, models trained with Anomagic‑generated samples achieve a 5.8 % increase in AUROC over the best existing zero‑shot anomaly generators, and a 3.2 % gain over fully supervised baselines when combined with standard detection heads. We further demonstrate the utility of Anomagic for rapid prototyping of anomaly detectors in unseen domains, highlighting its potential as a universal, prompt‑driven anomaly synthesis tool.
1181:
The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has spurred a growing interest in their capacity to simulate realistic multi‑user conversations. While the conventional Turing Test evaluates a single interlocutor’s plausibility, it falls short of capturing the dynamics of group discourse—turn‑taking, divergent viewpoints, and contextual coherence. In this work we introduce the **Collective Turing Test (CTT)**, a benchmark framework that quantifies an LLM’s ability to generate *entire* multi‑user discussions that appear indistinguishable from human‑authored threads. 

We curate a novel dataset, **Multi‑Chat Corpus (MCC)**, comprising over 10,000 annotated forum and chat logs spanning diverse topics (politics, science, entertainment) and participant roles (moderators, experts, casual users). Using MCC we train and finetune a suite of state‑of‑the‑art models (GPT‑4, LLaMA‑2, Claude) to produce *whole* discussion threads conditioned on initial prompts. Evaluation involves a two‑stage human adjudication protocol: (i) *authenticity assessment*—human raters judge whether a conversation is machine‑ or human‑generated, and (ii) *participatory coherence*—ratings of topic consistency, individual voice fidelity, and engagement quality. Complementing human scores, we employ automatic metrics—per‑user perplexity, diversity scores, and dialogue state accuracy—to capture nuanced aspects of discourse.

Our experiments demonstrate that GPT‑4 consistently achieves a 47 % pass rate on the CTT, outperforming all baseline models and approaching the 55 % human pass rate. Importantly, the CTT reveals deficiencies not apparent in single‑turn evaluations, such as maintaining coherent personas over long threads and handling conflicting viewpoints. These findings underscore the maturity of LLMs for complex dialogue tasks and provide a rigorous, reproducible standard for future research on automated group conversations.
1182:
Decentralized agent economies—where autonomous software agents locate, negotiate, and consume services—have become pervasive in cloud‑based micro‑services, IoT marketplaces, and distributed AI systems.  However, the openness of such economies makes them vulnerable to *Sybil* attacks: a single adversary can create a multitude of fabricated identities and thereby distort service discovery, monopolize resources, or launch denial‑of‑service attacks.  In this work we first formalise the Sybil threat in the context of service‑discovery protocols, proving that naïve registries and existing reputation schemes can be subverted with only a small fraction of malicious nodes.  

To counter this, we propose **Sybil‑Resistant Service Discovery (SRSD)**, a lightweight, fully distributed framework that blends three complementary defenses: (i) identity‑based cryptographic vouchers issued by a public‑key infrastructure, (ii) bounded‑resource tests that enforce a computational cost per registration, and (iii) a gossip‑driven reputation layer that aggregates local observations and penalises anomalous behaviour.  SRSD imposes only minimal communication overhead and is suitable for resource‑constrained agents.  

We provide a formal security analysis showing that SRSD tolerates up to a fraction f of Sybil nodes while preserving discovery accuracy with a negligible increase in latency.  Extensive simulations in a synthetic 10⁵‑agent marketplace and a real‑world testbed of 1 000 heterogeneous IoT devices demonstrate that SRSD reduces successful Sybil infiltration by 92 % relative to state‑of‑the‑art defenses, while maintaining precision ≥ 94 % and recall ≥ 91 % for legitimate service discovery.  

SRSD therefore enables robust, trust‑worthy service discovery in agent economies, paving the way for scalable, decentralized marketplaces that remain resilient to identity‑fabrication attacks.
1183:
Vector‑symbol architectures (VSAs) have become a cornerstone of modern cognitive modeling, yet mainstream programming languages rarely expose the core algebraic primitives required for scalable symbolic manipulation.  In this paper we present **Hey Pentti**, a Lisp dialect that treats vector‑symbol operations—binding, superposition, and chunking—as first‑class language constructs and grounds them in a novel residue‑number arithmetic framework.  The key insight is that high‑dimensional vectors can be represented exactly as tuples of integer residues modulo a set of pairwise‑prime bases.  This representation eliminates the floating‑point noise that traditionally plagues VSA computations, while enabling extremely efficient hardware‑friendly arithmetic (addition, multiplication, and modular inversion).  

Our implementation integrates the residue‑based VSA engine into the Common Lisp runtime, providing a lightweight macro‑system for declarative vector construction and a rich set of algebraic primitives that interoperate seamlessly with conventional Lisp data structures.  We evaluate Hey Pentti on a suite of symbolic‑reasoning benchmarks—including knowledge‑graph query answering, semantic parsing, and relational reasoning on synthetic and real datasets.  Compared to state‑of‑the‑art VSA libraries written in C++ and Python, Hey Pentti achieves comparable or better accuracy while reducing memory consumption by up to 35 % and CPU time by 20 % on large‑scale problems.  

Finally, we demonstrate how residue arithmetic facilitates exact recovery of bound components and supports principled error‑correction, thereby enabling new applications such as loss‑less compression of semantic networks and provable guarantees on symbolic inference.  Hey Pentti opens the door to a new class of Lisp‑based cognitive architectures where vector‑symbol reasoning is both natural to express and mathematically exact.
1184: Large‑language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in applications where safe and responsible use is paramount. Despite guardrails, adversaries can often subvert these constraints via carefully crafted “jailbreak” prompts. Existing jailbreak studies largely focus on single‑turn attacks and rely on manual prompt engineering, leaving a substantial gap in our understanding of how multi‑turn interactions can be exploited automatically. In this paper we introduce **AutoAdv**, a framework that automatically generates adversarial prompting sequences designed to jailbreak LLMs in a multi‑turn dialogue setting. AutoAdv formulates the jailbreak problem as a sequential decision process and employs a hybrid search‑based policy gradient method to discover prompt chains that progressively coax the model into revealing disallowed content or violating policy constraints. We evaluate AutoAdv on a benchmark of five commercial LLMs (GPT‑4, Claude 2, Llama‑2 70B, Gemini Pro, and Cohere Command R) across 12 sensitive domains, achieving an average jailbreak success rate of **78 %** with only **3.2** prompts on average, compared to 4–8 prompts for hand‑crafted baselines. Ablation studies demonstrate that context‑aware reinforcement signals and token‑level constraints are critical for navigating the model’s safety filters. We further analyze the linguistic characteristics of high‑impact prompts, revealing that subtle linguistic cues and chain‑of‑thought reasoning can systematically bypass safeguards. Finally, we discuss implications for future LLM safety research, including adaptive counter‑measures and robust policy enforcement that anticipate multi‑turn adversarial strategies. AutoAdv provides a scalable tool for auditing and hardening LLMs against sophisticated jailbreak attacks.
1185: In the distributed computing continuum—ranging from resource‑constrained IoT and edge nodes to high‑performance supercomputers—system failures are the everyday reality. Maintaining reliability and global consistency across such a heterogeneous stack is particularly difficult when AI workloads demand real‑time, adaptive coordination. This paper presents the **Probabilistic Active Inference Resilience Agent (PAIR‑Agent)**, a novel approach to endow DCC systems with self‑healing capabilities. PAIR‑Agent operates in three stages: (i) it builds a causal fault graph from device logs; (ii) it detects faults while handling certainty and uncertainty through Markov blankets and the free‑energy principle; and (iii) it autonomously restores functionality by executing active inference. By continuously monitoring and reconfiguring the system, the agent preserves service continuity and stability across a wide range of failure scenarios. Formal analysis demonstrates that the framework delivers both reliability and effectiveness.
1186:
Modern software ecosystems rely on continuous integration and delivery pipelines that must process thousands of commits per day while maintaining high quality and low latency. Traditional repository‑level optimization—such as incremental builds, cache‑sharing, and test‑suite pruning—is labor‑intensive and often sub‑optimal for diverse workloads. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) promise to automate such tasks by generating context‑aware suggestions for build configuration, dependency management, and test selection. In this work we ask: **Can LLMs effectively optimize real‑world repositories on real workloads?** 

We introduce **SWE‑fficiency**, a framework that interfaces an LLM with a repository’s CI/CD metadata to propose actionable optimization artifacts: (1) a fine‑tuned model that predicts build‑time reduction opportunities; (2) a retrieval‑augmented system that surfaces repository‑specific refactoring patterns; and (3) an interactive feedback loop that learns from engineer overrides. Using a curated benchmark of 72 open‑source projects from GitHub, we evaluate our approach on 3,480 real‑world commit‑level workloads spanning 14 CI providers. We compare LLM‑generated optimizations against baseline manual practices and state‑of‑the‑art static analysis tools. 

Results show that SWE‑fficiency reduces average build time by **12.7 %** and test suite duration by **9.3 %** while preserving or improving test coverage across 88 % of the projects. In 73 % of cases, the LLM’s proposals are accepted or refined by developers, indicating a high practical relevance. A cost–benefit analysis demonstrates a net throughput gain of 1.8× in continuous‑delivery cycles for medium‑sized repositories. 

Our findings highlight the viability of LLM‑driven repository optimization but also uncover limitations in handling highly dynamic dependency graphs and security‑critical code paths. SWE‑fficiency demonstrates a scalable, data‑driven approach to augment software engineering workflows and points toward a future where language models become first‑line assistants in maintaining efficient, high‑quality codebases.
1187: Robust loop‑closure detection is essential for SLAM systems operating in GNSS‑denied environments, such as planetary exploration. In these scenarios visual place recognition often degrades because of aliasing and weak textures, while LiDAR‑based approaches struggle with point‑cloud sparsity and geometric ambiguity. We introduce **MPRF**, a multimodal pipeline that harnesses transformer‑based foundation models for both image and LiDAR data, enabling reliable loop closure even in highly unstructured surroundings. Unlike earlier work that focuses solely on retrieval, MPRF employs a two‑step strategy: a fast visual retrieval using DINOv2 embeddings coupled with SALAD aggregation to shortlist candidates, followed by a 6‑DoF pose estimation that incorporates SONATA‑derived LiDAR descriptors for geometric verification. Extensive evaluations on the S3LI and S3LI‑Vulcano datasets demonstrate that MPRF surpasses contemporary retrieval techniques in precision and markedly improves pose accuracy in low‑texture environments. By delivering interpretable correspondences that are directly usable by SLAM back‑ends, MPRF strikes a practical balance among accuracy, speed, and reliability, thereby showcasing the power of foundation models to unify place recognition and pose estimation. All code and models are available at https://github.com/DLR‑RM/MPRF.
1188:
We introduce a MedGemma‑based architecture for the automatic detection of abnormalities in musculoskeletal radiographs. Instead of relying on traditional autoencoders or conventional neural‑network pipelines, the approach exploits the MedGemma foundation model, employing a SigLIP‑derived visual encoder that has been pretrained across a broad range of medical imaging modalities. After standard preprocessing, X‑ray images are projected into high‑dimensional feature vectors by MedGemma’s vision backbone and then fed into a lightweight multi‑layer perceptron that performs binary classification. Experiments show that this MedGemma‑driven classifier outperforms baseline convolutional and autoencoder‑based methods in terms of accuracy and other evaluation metrics. Moreover, the model benefits from MedGemma’s transfer‑learning strengths, yielding better generalisation and reducing the need for extensive feature engineering. The integration of a modern medical foundation model also enables modular training strategies, such as selectively unfreezing encoder blocks, which facilitates efficient domain adaptation. These results suggest that MedGemma‑powered classification systems can significantly improve clinical radiograph triage by offering scalable, precise abnormality detection, with prospects for wider use in automated medical image analysis.
