We evaluate DeepRWCap on a suite of industry‑grade benchmarks (e.g., 28‑nm, 7‑nm, and 3‑D stacked designs) and compare against state‑of‑the‑art N‑mesh and finite‑element solvers. Results demonstrate a median speed‑up of **4.6×** with a root‑mean‑square error below **0.9 %** relative to N‑mesh, while consuming **35 %** less memory. Moreover, on ultra‑dense layouts the algorithm maintains its performance gains, showcasing its scalability to future technology nodes.  

DeepRWCap offers a practical, data‑driven acceleration for capacitance extraction, enabling faster design‑space exploration and tighter timing margins without sacrificing analytical fidelity. Future work will extend the framework to include resistance extraction and integrate it into full‑chip EDA flows.
1381: Physics‑informed machine learning (PIML) has achieved remarkable success in engineering and physical sciences, where governing equations are well‑defined, data are abundant, and the system dynamics are largely deterministic. Biology, however, presents a fundamentally distinct set of challenges: multiscale, highly heterogeneous, stochastic, and often only partially understood mechanistic frameworks. This position paper argues that biology is the most demanding frontier for PIML, necessitating a paradigm shift in how physical priors, data, and learning algorithms are integrated. We first delineate the structural and functional complexities of biological systems—ranging from molecular signaling networks to tissue‑scale biomechanics—that expose limitations of current PIML techniques, such as over‑reliance on explicit differential equations, inadequate handling of noisy and sparse data, and poor transferability across biological contexts. We then outline key methodological directions that can bridge this gap: (i) development of probabilistic, multi‑physics hybrid models that can accommodate uncertainty and emergent behavior; (ii) flexible incorporation of empirical biological constraints (e.g., conservation of mass, homeostatic limits) through soft regularizers and learned physics; (iii) scalable active‑learning frameworks to exploit limited experimental data efficiently; and (iv) interpretability layers that align learned representations with known biological pathways. Through case studies in cardiovascular modeling, neural circuitry inference, and cancer metastasis prediction, we demonstrate how these innovations can improve predictive fidelity and mechanistic insight. We conclude that for PIML to realize its full potential in biology, it must evolve from a physics‑centric toolbox into a multidisciplinary, data‑aware framework capable of capturing the idiosyncratic and adaptive nature of living systems. This evolution will not only unlock new scientific discoveries but also catalyze translational applications in precision medicine and synthetic biology.
1382: Detecting anomalous patterns in multivariate time series is critical for many industrial and scientific domains, yet remains challenging because of high dimensionality, complex temporal dependencies, and the absence of labeled anomalous samples.  We propose a fully unsupervised, clustering‑based framework that learns a compact representation of normal behaviour and flags any sample that deviates from the learned cluster structure as an anomaly.  First, we extract a multiscale, statistics‑driven feature set (including mean, variance, cross‑correlation, and wavelet energy) that captures both spatial and temporal correlations across channels.  Second, we embed these features into a low‑dimensional manifold via a self‑organising map (SOM) followed by a density‑based refinement (DBSCAN), yielding a robust model of normal clusters that naturally handles non‑linear manifold shapes.  An anomaly score is computed as the Mahalanobis distance to the nearest cluster centroid combined with a local density penalty; samples with a score above a self‑adjusting threshold are flagged in real‑time.  We evaluate the method on four publicly available datasets (NAB, SWaT, SMAP, and a synthetic industrial process), comparing against state‑of‑the‑art techniques such as Isolation Forest, LSTM‑Encoder‑Decoder, and Dynamic Time Warping‑based clustering.  Across all datasets, our approach achieves a mean F1‑score improvement of 12 % over the best baseline, while maintaining a false‑positive rate below 3 %.  Moreover, the method scales linearly with the number of channels, making it suitable for deployment in high‑throughput monitoring systems.  The proposed clustering‑based anomaly detector offers a practical, interpretable, and computationally efficient solution for real‑world multivariate time series monitoring.
1383:
Urban 3D scene understanding is a cornerstone of autonomous driving, robotics, and smart‑city applications. Existing benchmarks are either richly annotated real‑world datasets, which are costly and limited in variability, or large‑scale synthetic collections that suffer from a pronounced domain gap when deployed on real imagery. To bridge this divide, we introduce **TrueCity**, a unified urban dataset that couples a high‑fidelity synthetic city (generated with a physics‑based rendering engine) with a corresponding real‑world counterpart captured in the same geographical layout.  

TrueCity comprises 12,000 photorealistic camera frames and 48,000 LiDAR point clouds across 200 scenes, each annotated with pixel‑level semantic labels, instance masks, 3D bounding boxes, and dense depth maps. The synthetic portion contains 8 million labeled objects spanning 23 categories, while the real portion offers 6 million automatically‑aligned labels obtained through a semi‑automatic annotation pipeline that fuses multi‑view photogrammetry and manual refinement.  

We propose a cross‑domain evaluation protocol that trains 3D semantic segmentation, instance segmentation, and object detection models on one domain and tests them on the other, revealing quantitative insights into the magnitude of the domain shift. Baseline experiments using state‑of‑the‑art methods (e.g., PointNet++, MinkowskiNet, and 2D‑to‑3D knowledge transfer) demonstrate a performance drop of up to 18 % when transferring from synthetic to real, underscoring the need for robust adaptation strategies.  

TrueCity is freely available under a CC‑BY license and includes a set of benchmark scripts, evaluation metrics, and a reference implementation. It offers a scalable, realistic, and extensible platform for advancing cross‑domain 3D scene understanding and will serve as a testbed for future domain adaptation, data‑efficient learning, and multimodal perception research.
1384:
Assessing the safety of large language models (LLMs) is a central challenge for responsible deployment. Existing protocols rely on exhaustive human‐in‐the‐loop annotation or costly adversarial prompt generation, which do not scale to the breadth of real‑world use cases. We propose **Efficient LLM Safety Evaluation through Multi‑Agent Debate (EMED)**, a lightweight framework that harnesses the power of adversarial reasoning within a self‑contained multi‑agent system. Two “debater” agents are instantiated with divergent safety biases (one prioritizing correctness, the other prioritizing caution). For each safety‑critical prompt, the agents independently generate candidate responses and then iteratively critique one another’s outputs in a fixed‑round debate. A lightweight “judge” module—implemented as a small neural classifier trained on a modest set of human‑verified debate transcripts—selects the safest final response. The debate surface additional hazards that a single‑pass evaluation would miss, while the judge’s streamlined design eliminates the need for exhaustive human review.

We evaluate EMED on the publicly available SafetyEval benchmark and a newly curated **Debate‑Safety** dataset comprising 10 k nuanced prompts spanning disinformation, toxic content, and policy violations. Compared to baseline safety evaluation pipelines that use a single agent and a single prompt, EMED improves true‑positive detection of unsafe content by 21 % (p < 0.001), while reducing annotation time by 48 % and inference cost by 33 %. Ablation studies confirm that the debate depth and judge confidence threshold are key hyperparameters that trade off thoroughness against efficiency.

EMED demonstrates that a principled multi‑agent debate can substantially lower the human and computational burden of safety evaluation without sacrificing precision. The framework is model‑agnostic and readily integrates into existing LLM development lifecycles. All code, datasets, and benchmark scripts are released at https://github.com/llm-safety/emed.
1385: 5G technology provides ubiquitous mobile Internet access to billions of users. However, answering advanced queries about its specifications demands sifting through thousands of interlinked standard documents that continuously evolve across releases. Conventional retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) pipelines—including those tailored to telecom—rely largely on semantic similarity and struggle to handle cross‑references or capture how specifications change over time. In this work we introduce DeepSpecs, a RAG framework that incorporates both structural and temporal reasoning through three richly‑annotated databases: SpecDB (clause‑level text of the standards), ChangeDB (line‑level diffs between releases), and TDocDB (meeting notes from the standardisation process). DeepSpecs resolves cross‑references explicitly by recursively querying the metadata, and traces the evolution of clauses by mining change logs and linking them to the underlying Change Requests that explain design decisions. We build two 5G QA datasets: 573 expert‑annotated real‑world questions sourced from practitioner forums and educational materials, and 350 evolution‑centric questions extracted from approved Change Requests. Experiments with several large language‑model backends show that DeepSpecs consistently outperforms baseline LLMs and the leading telecom‑focused RAG systems. Ablation studies confirm that explicit cross‑reference resolution and evolution‑aware retrieval are key drivers of the performance gains, highlighting the importance of modelling the structural and temporal aspects of 5G standards.
1386: Cyber‑scams continue to pose a pressing threat, as attackers constantly design messages that slip past conventional automated defenses. We introduce the Hierarchical Scam Detection System (HSDS), which couples a lightweight, multi‑model voting front end with a finely‑tuned LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct backend to boost both accuracy and resilience to adversarial manipulation. Four base classifiers generate initial predictions by majority vote; instances that remain ambiguous are forwarded to the fine‑tuned LLM, which has been hardened through targeted adversarial training to curb false positives. Empirical results demonstrate that this tiered approach not only raises performance against adversarial scams but also cuts inference latency by diverting most inputs away from the large language model. Compared with standard machine‑learning baselines and other proprietary LLMs, HSDS delivers superior detection capabilities, underscoring the value of a hybrid voting scheme combined with adversarial fine‑tuning for reinforcing automated scam‑detection pipelines.
1387: Dermatology AI systems require large, diverse, and high‑quality image datasets to achieve reliable disease classification on mobile devices. Existing public repositories are dominated by curated photographs taken in controlled conditions, leading to a domain shift when models are deployed in real‑world clinical or consumer settings. We present *DermAI*, a framework for quality‑driven acquisition of clinical dermatology images via a mobile application that guides clinicians and patients in standardized image capture, performs on‑device quality assessment, and securely streams annotated data to a cloud backend. The app incorporates real‑time feedback on lighting, focus, and framing, and automatically tags each photo with metadata (device, illumination, skin tone, and diagnosis) using a lightweight on‑device model. A semi‑automated review pipeline ensures that only images meeting predefined quality thresholds (contrast, resolution, skin‑to‑background ratio) are included in the training set, thereby reducing noise and bias. We trained a state‑of‑the‑art convolutional neural network on 12,345 DermAI‑derived images from 4,567 patients and compared its performance to models trained on publicly available datasets and on mixed‑quality data. On a held‑out test set of 2,000 images, DermAI‑trained models achieved a top‑1 accuracy of 92.4 % (95 % CI: 91.1–93.7), outperforming the baseline by 7.3 % and demonstrating superior calibration on under‑represented skin phototypes (AUC = 0.97 for Fitzpatrick VI lesions). Furthermore, when deployed on a 6 G smartphone, the model maintained <0.4 s inference time with an average energy consumption of 120 mJ per classification. DermAI thus provides a scalable, quality‑centric pipeline for building robust, mobile‑ready dermatology AI systems, bridging the gap between laboratory research and real‑world clinical deployment.
1388:
Understanding the world in its full multimodal richness requires the ability to flexibly combine vision, language, audio, and other sensing modalities without requiring a monolithic end‑to‑end model trained on every possible task. In this work we introduce **Agent‑Omni**, a test‑time multimodal reasoning framework that treats each pretrained expert (e.g., a vision‑language transformer, a speech recognizer, a graph neural network for structured knowledge) as a lightweight *agent* that can be invoked on demand. A central coordination policy, learned in a small auxiliary network, dynamically selects, sequences, and orchestrates these agents based on the query and the available modalities. The agents exchange structured intermediate representations through a common message‑passing interface, enabling recursive reasoning: the output of a visual agent can become an input prompt for a language model, while a knowledge‑graph agent can refine the language representation with factual consistency checks.

Agent‑Omni achieves *plug‑and‑play* extensibility: new modalities or specialized models can be added without retraining the core system. We evaluate Agent‑Omni on a suite of open‑ended, multimodal benchmark tasks—including visual question answering with audio cues, cross‑modal retrieval, and real‑world “anything‑can‑happen” reasoning—showing an average relative improvement of 8.5% over single‑model baselines and 4.3% over recent multimodal fusion systems. Ablation studies confirm that the learned coordination policy is essential for leveraging complementary modalities, while the message‑passing mechanism reduces hallucinations and improves interpretability.

Our results demonstrate that **test‑time model coordination** can unlock the collective strengths of heterogeneous pretrained models, paving the way toward truly general “understanding anything” systems. The code, trained agents, and a demo interface are released to facilitate rapid experimentation and further development.
1389:
AdamW has emerged as one of the most powerful optimizers for large‑scale neural networks, and we have found it similarly effective in federated learning (FL) environments. Yet, directly transplanting AdamW into FL encounters several hurdles: (i) data heterogeneity inflates the variance of the second‑moment estimate \(\boldsymbol{v}\); (ii) the tendency of AdamW to overfit locally can induce client drift; and (iii) resetting the moment buffers (\(\boldsymbol{m}\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}\)) at every round impedes convergence.  

To overcome these obstacles, we introduce **FedAdamW**, the first federated adaptation of AdamW designed for training and fine‑tuning large models. FedAdamW synchronizes local and global updates through a local correction scheme and employs decoupled weight decay to curb local overfitting. It also aggregates the **mean** of second‑moment estimates across clients, thereby reducing variance and obviating the need for frequent reinitialization.  

Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that FedAdamW achieves a linear‑speedup convergence rate  
\[
\mathcal{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{L \Delta \sigma_l^2}{S K R \varepsilon^2}}+\frac{L \Delta}{R}\right),
\]  
without assuming data homogeneity, where \(S\) is the number of clients sampled per round, \(K\) the local epoch count, and \(R\) the total communication rounds. A PAC‑Bayesian generalization argument further elucidates the benefits of decoupled weight decay during local training.  

Empirical results on Transformer‑based language and vision models confirm that FedAdamW markedly reduces communication rounds and improves test accuracy relative to several competing baselines. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/junkangLiu0/FedAdamW.
1390:
Rising sea levels and climate‑driven changes threaten coastal municipalities worldwide, underscoring the urgency for fast, reliable flood‑hazard prediction tools. Conventional physics‑based hydrodynamic simulators, while accurate, are too costly to run across entire cities. Although deep‑learning approaches can accelerate predictions, they usually suffer from limited data and the difficulty of handling high‑dimensional outputs. Building on a recently introduced low‑resource, vision‑centric DL framework, we present a lightweight convolutional neural network that forecasts coastal inundation under a range of sea‑level rise projections and shoreline‑adaptation scenarios. The model’s versatility is illustrated by training and testing on datasets from two geographically disparate regions—Abu Dhabi and San Francisco—demonstrating robust cross‑regional generalisation. Quantitatively, our method outperforms current state‑of‑the‑art baselines, lowering the mean absolute error of flood‑depth maps by an average of approximately 20 %. These results suggest that the proposed CNN can act as a scalable, practical aid for coastal flood management, enabling planners to devise more effective adaptation strategies in the face of accelerating climate change.  

Project Page: https://caspiannet.github.io/
1391:
We introduce a hybrid quantum–classical recurrent neural network (QRNN) whose core recurrence is implemented by a parametrized quantum circuit (PQC) that is driven by a conventional feed‑forward network.  The network’s hidden state is a quantum state of an \(n\)-qubit PQC, living in the exponentially large Hilbert space \(\mathbb{C}^{2^n}\).  Because the PQC is unitary by design, the hidden‑state evolution is automatically norm‑preserving, obviating the need for external regularisation.  

At every timestep the PQC is measured midway through its depth, yielding a vector of Pauli expectation values.  These readouts are concatenated with the current input embedding and fed into the classical network, which introduces the essential nonlinearities.  The output of this network then parametrises the next PQC step, updating the hidden state via unitary dynamics.  This architecture combines three key ingredients: (i) a high‑capacity, reversible quantum memory, (ii) partial observation through mid‑circuit measurements, and (iii) explicit classical nonlinearity for input‑dependent control.  

We benchmark the model in simulation up to fourteen qubits on a diverse set of sequence‑learning benchmarks, including sentiment analysis, MNIST and permuted MNIST classification, a synthetic copying task, and language modelling.  For sequence‑to‑sequence problems we augment the QRNN with a soft‑attention module over the mid‑circuit readouts, demonstrating its utility on machine‑translation datasets.  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first recurrent architecture based purely on quantum operations that matches or surpasses strong classical baselines across such a wide range of sequential tasks.
1392:
Fair clustering seeks to partition data into groups that are both representative of the underlying structure and compliant with a prescribed notion of equity across protected attributes. Existing algorithms typically enforce fairness by solving a large-scale constrained optimization problem, which quickly becomes infeasible on modern, high‑dimensional data sets. We propose a *general anchor‑based framework* that dramatically reduces computational overhead while preserving rigorous fairness guarantees.

Our framework introduces a small set of *anchor points* that capture the geometric and demographic characteristics of the data. A two‑stage pipeline first clusters the data into anchor‑centric neighborhoods; a second stage solves a relaxed clustering problem on the anchors only, using either group‑balance, proportionality, or disparate‑impact constraints. The method is agnostic to the specific fairness definition and to the underlying clustering objective (k‑means, k‑median, spectral, etc.). We provide a theoretical analysis that bounds the clustering cost and fairness violation incurred by the anchor approximation, showing that the loss is controlled by the number of anchors and the intra‑anchor diameter.

Experiments on benchmark datasets (Adult, COMPAS, German Credit, and a large synthetic scale‑up) demonstrate that our approach achieves ≥ 10× speed‑ups relative to state‑of‑the‑art fair‑clustering algorithms, while maintaining comparable or superior utility and fairness metrics. In particular, on a 1 million‑point dataset we obtain a 95 % reduction in runtime and a 30 % improvement in the fairness‑utility trade‑off over baseline methods. Our framework thus offers a scalable, theoretically sound, and practically effective solution for fair clustering in modern data‑rich environments.
1393: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning and reward‑learning capabilities, yet their computational footprint remains a critical barrier to widespread deployment.  In this work we present **DistilQwen**, a compact, high‑performance family of models distilled from the flagship Qwen architecture.  DistilQwen is organized into a *Tale of Four* series, each targeting a distinct component of advanced LLM pipelines: (1) **DistilQwen‑R** – a reasoning‑aware distilled model that preserves chain‑of‑thought (CoT) reasoning fidelity; (2) **DistilQwen‑M** – a reward‑model student trained on human preference data; (3) **DistilQwen‑S** – a lightweight supervised fine‑tuned student optimized for instruction following; and (4) **DistilQwen‑X** – an integrated model that jointly inherits reasoning and reward signals through multi‑task distillation.  We devise a two‑stage knowledge‑distillation strategy: (i) *teacher‑augmented self‑supervision* that injects explicit reasoning traces into the student’s loss, and (ii) *adversarial reward alignment* that enforces consistency with the teacher’s reward predictions.  The resulting models span 1.1 B–3.4 B parameters, achieving up to a 3× reduction in inference latency while maintaining ≥ 85 % accuracy on a suite of arithmetic, commonsense, and logical reasoning benchmarks.  On reward‑learning tasks, DistilQwen‑M and DistilQwen‑X match 90 % of the full‑size Qwen’s preference accuracy with a 4× compression.  Extensive ablation studies demonstrate the importance of reasoning‑aware prompts and reward alignment, and we release the full DistilQwen series, training scripts, and benchmark evaluations to encourage reproducible research.  This work illustrates a scalable path to deploying powerful reasoning and reward‑model LLMs in resource‑constrained settings.
1394:
Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural‑language understanding, yet their ability to reason about temporally ordered data remains limited.  We introduce **TimeSense**, a lightweight framework that endows LLMs with robust time‑series analysis capabilities.  TimeSense augments the transformer backbone with a *temporal encoder* that maps multivariate time‑series into a dense representation and a *time‑aware prompting schema* that exposes the model to temporal syntax (e.g., “forecast the next 24 hours”, “detect anomalies in a 7‑day window”).  A novel *temporal‑contrastive objective* jointly trains the encoder and the LLM on large-scale synthetic and real‑world datasets, encouraging the model to learn both numeric patterns and their linguistic explanations.

We evaluate TimeSense on four downstream tasks—univariate forecasting, multivariate anomaly detection, classification of physiological signals, and event‑based regime change prediction—using five benchmark datasets (NAB, UCR, M4, SMD, and a newly released TimeSeriesBench).  Compared to state‑of‑the‑art neural baselines (LSTM, Temporal Fusion Transformer) and domain‑specific methods (Prophet, ARIMA), TimeSense achieves 8.3 % lower mean absolute error in forecasting, 12.5 % higher AUROC in anomaly detection, and 4.7 % higher accuracy in classification, while maintaining competitive inference latency.  Importantly, the model retains the ability to produce human‑readable explanations for its predictions, a capability absent in purely numerical models.

TimeSense demonstrates that LLMs can be repurposed for temporal reasoning with modest architectural modifications and a targeted pre‑training regime.  Our framework paves the way for unified, multimodal systems that simultaneously understand natural language and time‑ordered data, opening new avenues for real‑time analytics, automated monitoring, and intelligent forecasting.
1395: The capacity of large language models (LLMs) to accurately recall and retrieve facts from extensive contexts is essential for many practical use cases. Previous studies (Liu et al., 2023) observed that LLMs experience marked drops in retrieval performance for facts positioned in the middle of long inputs—a phenomenon termed “Lost in the Middle” (LITM). In contrast, we show that Gemini 2.5 Flash can answer needle‑in‑a‑haystack queries with high accuracy regardless of where the information appears in the document, even when it is near the limit of the input context. These findings imply that Gemini 2.5 Flash does not exhibit the LITM effect for straightforward fact‑based Q&A, highlighting significant progress in long‑context retrieval.
1396:
Large‑scale language models (LLMs) now routinely require on‑the‑fly storage of millions of hidden‑state tokens (KV caches), a demand that quickly exceeds the capacity of GPU‑resident memory and becomes a bottleneck for low‑latency inference.  We present *Scalable Processing‑Near‑Memory for 1 M‑Token LLM Inference* (SPN‑M1M), a CXL‑enabled architecture that moves KV‑cache management from the CPU into a tightly coupled near‑memory processing fabric.  By coupling high‑bandwidth CXL 2.0 memory modules with lightweight, on‑socket NPUs, SPN‑M1M implements a hierarchical KV cache that supports compression, adaptive eviction, and batched read‑back directly within the memory subsystem, dramatically reducing off‑chip traffic to the GPU.  

Our design introduces a two‑tier KV policy engine that (i) partitions the 1 M‑token space into fine‑grained shards, (ii) performs locality‑aware compression (up to 4×) in situ, and (iii) streams only the most relevant keys/values to the GPU during each attention step.  A software stack exposes a standard LLM inference API while automatically orchestrating CXL bandwidth and memory placement.  

Evaluation on a 16‑GPU cluster with GPT‑3‑style transformer models shows a 3.8× throughput improvement and 28 % reduction in end‑to‑end inference latency compared with conventional GPU‑only KV storage, while consuming only 12 % of the memory footprint required by naive CPU‑RAM replication.  Energy measurements indicate a 21 % saving due to decreased DRAM‑to‑GPU data movement.  SPN‑M1M demonstrates that CXL‑enabled near‑memory processing can break the GPU memory barrier for billion‑parameter LLMs, paving the way for cost‑effective, scalable inference at the 1 M‑token level.
1397:
Creating synthetic training data for large reasoning models provides a scalable alternative to scarce human‑curated datasets, enabling the production of high‑quality examples. Nevertheless, current synthesis methods struggle on two fronts: (i) they generate problems indiscriminately, ignoring the solver’s capabilities and producing low‑value items, or they depend on cumbersome pipelines to balance difficulty; and (ii) they lack explicit reasoning during generation, yielding only shallow variants.  

We introduce a problem generator that explicitly reasons about the desired direction before synthesis and tailors difficulty to the solver’s skill. The approach first builds related problem pairs and enriches them with intermediate chain‑of‑thought (CoT) design steps generated by a reasoning model, which bootstrap the generator’s design strategies. The solver’s feedback on synthetic problems is used as a reward signal, allowing the generator to calibrate difficulty and produce complementary tasks that sit at the edge of the solver’s competence.  

Across ten mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, our method improves performance by an average of 2.5% and generalizes to both language‑only and vision‑language models. Moreover, a solver trained on the synthetic data supplies higher‑quality rewards for ongoing generator training, yielding an additional 0.7% gain. Our code will be made publicly available.
1398:
Understanding whether a model truly “knows” what it values or merely mirrors superficial preferences is a central challenge for safe, aligned artificial intelligence. Existing evaluations focus on immediate preference matching or narrow task performance, offering little insight into a model’s capacity to reason about *deep* values—those that guide behavior across diverse, long‑term contexts. We introduce the **Deep Value Benchmark (DVB)**, a unified test suite that explicitly probes whether large language models and reinforcement‑learning agents generalize beyond surface‑level cues to the hierarchical, causal structure of human values. DVB comprises five interrelated sub‑tasks: (1) *Multi‑step planning* where short‑term gains conflict with long‑term welfare, (2) *Cultural norm inference* requiring the model to apply abstract principles to novel scenarios, (3) *Moral ambiguity* where surface signals are noisy, (4) *Preference generalization* across disjoint but value‑aligned settings, and (5) *Adversarial preference leakage* that tests robustness against manipulative prompts. For each sub‑task we provide a gold standard of deep value judgments derived from a large, crowdsourced value hierarchy, as well as a set of engineered “shallow” confounders that encourage overfitting to surface patterns.  

We evaluate a spectrum of architectures—from vanilla GPT‑4 to RL‑HF tuned policy models—using two novel metrics: **Deep Value Fidelity** (alignment with the hierarchical gold standard) and **Shallow Preference Leakage** (sensitivity to engineered confounders). Across 1,200 prompts, baseline models achieve high shallow accuracy but only 47 % deep value fidelity, while RL‑HF models improve to 63 % but still exhibit substantial leakage. Ablation studies highlight the importance of explicit value‑hierarchy training and prompt‑engineering.  

DVB offers the first comprehensive, quantitative framework for diagnosing whether models generalize deep values or merely surface preferences. We release the dataset, evaluation code, and a baseline leaderboard to foster continued research into value‑aligned modeling.
1399: In many practical scenarios—such as telehealth, call centers, and wearable devices—only one party’s speech can be recorded, creating a “one‑sided conversation” setting. We introduce this setting as the **1SC problem**: learning to interpret and exploit information from a single speaker’s transcript. We investigate two concrete applications: (1) filling in the missing utterances of the unseen partner for real‑time dialogue systems, and (2) producing concise summaries from one‑sided transcripts. By testing prompting strategies and fine‑tuned models on datasets such as MultiWOZ, DailyDialog, and Candor, and evaluating them through both human A/B tests and LLM‑based adjudication, we observe that having access to a single future turn and knowing utterance lengths improves reconstruction quality. Using placeholder prompts reduces hallucination, while large language models can generate satisfactory reconstructions with prompting alone; smaller models, however, benefit from fine‑tuning. Importantly, we demonstrate that high‑quality summaries can be generated directly from one‑sided data without first reconstructing the missing turns. The 1SC challenge thus offers a new avenue for developing privacy‑aware conversational AI, and our results show encouraging progress toward that goal.
1400:
In‑context learning (ICL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for large language models, enabling rapid adaptation to new tasks by conditioning the model on a handful of task‑specific examples. However, the explicit exposure of training data in the prompt raises severe privacy risks: sensitive user information can be inferred from model outputs or from the prompt itself. We propose **Differentially Private In‑Context Learning with Nearest Neighbor Search (DP‑ICL‑NN)**, a principled framework that guarantees \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-differential privacy for the examples used in ICL while preserving competitive downstream performance.

Our method first constructs a privacy‑preserving representation of the training corpus by applying a private embedding function that adds calibrated Gaussian noise to the feature vectors. When a new query arrives, we perform a differentially private nearest‑neighbor (DP‑NN) search over this noisy embedding space to retrieve a set of \(k\) exemplar documents. The selected examples are then filtered and obfuscated using a lightweight DP‑aware prompt‑generation module, yielding a sanitized context that is fed to the language model. Theoretical analysis shows that the entire pipeline satisfies \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP under composition, with a privacy budget that scales sub‑linearly in \(k\). 

Empirically, DP‑ICL‑NN matches or surpasses non‑private baselines on several benchmark datasets (e.g., RACE, MMLU, and few‑shot classification tasks) for \(\varepsilon \in [1,4]\). Ablation studies confirm that the nearest‑neighbor retrieval is critical for maintaining task relevance under privacy constraints, while the noise added at the representation level dramatically reduces memorization risk compared to naïve DP‑ICL variants. Our approach demonstrates a practical path toward privacy‑aware in‑context learning, enabling secure deployment of large language models in sensitive domains.
1401: Recent progress in text‑to‑image generative models has sparked worries that these systems could generate harmful content when fed malicious text prompts. Two main counter‑measures have emerged to mitigate this risk: (1) fine‑tuning the model so that it “unlearns” objectionable concepts, and (2) employing training‑free guidance by supplying negative prompts. We find that naïvely combining these orthogonal strategies often yields only modest gains—or even hurts performance—highlighting a fundamental incompatibility between the two paradigms. To overcome this limitation, we propose a straightforward yet robust solution: replace the explicit negative prompts in training‑free methods with implicit negative embeddings produced via concept inversion. This approach is agnostic to the underlying method and can be plugged into existing pipelines without modification. Experiments on nudity and violence benchmarks show that our technique consistently boosts defense success while preserving the intended semantics of the user’s prompt.
1402:
Intuitive physics is the ability to reason about the motion and interaction of objects from limited observations, a capability that remains challenging for deep models. Existing approaches either treat each object independently, ignoring long‑range relations, or rely on hand‑crafted physics engines that cannot learn from data. In this work we introduce **SRNN (Spatiotemporal Relational Neural Network)**, a unified architecture that simultaneously captures *spatial* interaction patterns and *temporal* evolution in a single end‑to‑end trainable module. SRNN embeds a relational graph network that learns pairwise interaction tensors for all visible entities. These relational features are then propagated through a recurrent core that preserves a hidden state of the entire scene, enabling the model to maintain memory of past configurations and to predict future states over arbitrarily long horizons.  

We train SRNN on a suite of synthetic physics benchmarks (bouncing balls, deformable cloth, fluid blobs, and rigid‑body collision sequences) and on a real‑world physics dataset of household objects. On all tasks SRNN outperforms state‑of‑the‑art relational networks and recurrent physics models, reducing mean‑squared error of trajectory prediction by 18 % and achieving 12 % higher accuracy on counterfactual “what‑if” queries. In addition, SRNN generalizes to unseen initial conditions and object configurations, demonstrating robustness to changes in scale, mass, and material properties. Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of the relational encoder and the temporal decoder, and an attention analysis reveals that SRNN automatically learns to focus on critical interaction pairs.  

Our results suggest that integrating explicit spatiotemporal relations into neural dynamics yields a more faithful and interpretable model of intuitive physics, paving the way for data‑driven reasoning in robotics, animation, and scientific discovery.
1403:
State Space Models (SSMs) underpin the recently popular Mamba architecture, which is prized for its linear‐time inference and its ability to capture long‑range dependencies in 3D human pose estimation. Existing SSM‑based approaches, however, usually flatten the spatially coherent 2D pose sequences into one‑dimensional temporal streams using hand‑crafted scan operations. This flattening breaks the intrinsic spatial relationships among joints and forces spatial and temporal cues to mingle, thereby hampering the modeling of complex pose dynamics.  

We introduce **Skeleton Structure‑Aware Stride SSM (SAS‑SSM)** to overcome these shortcomings. SAS‑SSM first applies a structure‑aware spatiotemporal convolution that adaptively learns critical local joint interactions. It then employs a stride‑based scanning mechanism to build hierarchical, multi‑scale global structural representations. This two‑stage process preserves the spatial integrity of poses while still enjoying linear computational complexity.  

Leveraging SAS‑SSM, we develop **SasMamba**, a lightweight 3D pose estimator that matches or surpasses the accuracy of state‑of‑the‑art hybrid models while using far fewer parameters. The full implementation is publicly released at https://hucui2022.github.io/sasmamba_proj/.
1404: Dataset distillation compresses large corpora into compact synthetic subsets that enable training of models with performance close to that achieved on the full data, while dramatically cutting storage and compute demands. Conventional distillation approaches, however, treat every real sample as equally valuable, overlooking the fact that practical datasets contain both highly informative and redundant or even detrimental instances. Ignoring such quality variations can harm the resulting model’s accuracy. In this paper we introduce Influence‑Weighted Distillation (IWD), a principled method that incorporates influence functions to explicitly evaluate data quality during the distillation process. By assigning each training example a weight that reflects its estimated contribution to the distillation objective, IWD accentuates useful samples and suppresses unhelpful or damaging ones. Its modular design allows IWD to be plugged into a wide range of existing distillation pipelines. Experiments demonstrate that using IWD consistently improves the quality of the distilled datasets and boosts downstream model performance, with accuracy improvements of up to 7.8 %.
1405: Personalised math learning is expanding at an unprecedented pace, driving a pressing need for vast collections of similar practice questions. Existing research on generating math problems has largely concentrated on augmenting data for training language models, rather than on creating ready‑to‑use educational content. To address this disconnect, we introduce Isomorphic Math Problem Generation (IMPG), a task that produces structurally equivalent variants of a given problem. We then develop LLM‑based approaches for automated IMPG and establish a set of Computational Blueprints for Isomorphic Twins (CBIT). By leveraging meta‑level generation and template‑based selective variation, CBIT delivers highly accurate, mathematically sound, and structurally coherent problems while cutting production costs. Across multiple refinement stages, CBIT outperforms competitors in both accuracy and scalability. Notably, the problems generated by CBIT show a 17.8 % lower error rate than those authored by experts, and when deployed to 6,732 learners on a commercial platform, it generated 186,870 learner interactions.
1406:
Clinical narratives are a primary source of patient information, yet they routinely contain spelling mistakes, ambiguous abbreviations, and content‑level errors that jeopardise downstream electronic health record (EHR) analytics and patient safety. Existing natural‑language‑processing benchmarks focus on generic error correction or terminology mapping, but none explicitly require the model to leverage clinical knowledge and infer the most plausible correction in context. To bridge this gap, we present **MedRECT** (Medical Reasoning for Error Correction in Clinical Texts), the first end‑to‑end benchmark that couples error detection, causal reasoning, and correction in real‑world EHR documents.

MedRECT was built from 12 M de‑identified clinical notes spanning five hospital systems. A team of licensed clinicians annotated 23 k sentences for 1 million surface‑level errors, providing both a corrected span and a justification that references evidence from structured codes, clinical ontologies, and nearby narrative. Each example is paired with a knowledge graph snapshot (UMLS, RxNorm, ICD‑10) that allows models to perform multi‑step reasoning about drug interactions, diagnostic relationships, and temporal sequencing. The benchmark contains three tasks: (1) *Error Detection* (binary classification), (2) *Error Reasoning* (multiple‑choice explanation), and (3) *Error Correction* (span‑based generation). We define a unified metric—**Reasoning‑Corrected Accuracy (RCA)**—that rewards correct correction only when the model’s rationale matches a gold evidence chain.

Baseline experiments show that a fine‑tuned PubMedBERT achieves 68 % RCA on the correction task, whereas a knowledge‑augmented transformer (MedBERT‑KG) attains 76 %. The gap underscores the value of explicit reasoning. MedRECT therefore offers a rigorous, clinically meaningful platform for advancing error‑aware NLP in medicine, and it is publicly released to accelerate research in safe, knowledge‑driven language models.
1407: Despite notable progress in personalising Human‑Robot Interaction (HRI), most current methods adapt to only one user, ignoring situations where several stakeholders bring divergent preferences. To fill this gap, we introduce the Multi‑User Preferences Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Framework (MUP‑QBAF), a new personalisation paradigm that extends Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks (QBAFs) to explicitly model and reconcile conflicts among multiple users. Unlike traditional argumentation approaches that treat inputs as static, MUP‑QBAF blends users’ arguments with the robot’s real‑time environmental observations, enabling continuous adaptation to evolving contexts. Both positive and negative preferences are encoded as arguments whose influence is recalculated iteratively as new data arrives. We demonstrate the framework’s properties and effectiveness through a realistic scenario in which an assistive robot mediates the contradictory preferences of a caregiver and a care recipient during a frailty assessment. The study also performs a sensitivity analysis of the initial argument scores, illustrating how user input and contextual cues steer the resulting preference decisions. By offering a transparent, structured, and context‑aware solution for resolving competing user preferences, this work advances multi‑user HRI, presenting a principled alternative to purely data‑driven methods for handling conflicts in real‑world deployments.
1408: Military training exercises increasingly rely on high‑fidelity simulations to prepare forces for complex operational environments. However, designing realistic, varied, and mission‑relevant scenarios remains a labor‑intensive, expertise‑driven process that limits scalability and adaptability. This paper introduces a novel AI‑assisted framework for automated generation of military training scenarios that balances realism, diversity, and strategic relevance. Leveraging a hybrid approach that combines large‑scale natural‑language models, knowledge graphs derived from doctrinal documents, and reinforcement‑learning‑guided scenario refinement, the system produces context‑rich, multi‑layered training narratives that can be rendered in virtual or augmented reality environments. We formalize the scenario generation task as a constrained planning problem, integrating user‑specified parameters such as mission objective, threat level, and environmental constraints. Our prototype, trained on a curated corpus of after‑action reports, operational briefs, and historical engagements, generates thousands of scenario variants in minutes, each evaluated against a suite of realism metrics (semantic coherence, tactical plausibility, and scenario complexity) and cross‑validated by a panel of subject‑matter experts. Experimental results demonstrate that AI‑generated scenarios achieve a 78 % acceptance rate compared to human‑crafted scenarios, while reducing design time by an order of magnitude. We also discuss the ethical considerations of autonomous scenario creation, including bias mitigation and dual‑use concerns. The proposed framework paves the way for adaptive, continuous scenario evolution in live training environments, ultimately enhancing force readiness and operational effectiveness.
1409:
Transformers have become the de‑facto standard for modeling long‑range dependencies in sequential data, yet the quadratic complexity of self‑attention limits their scalability. Physics‑Attention, a recent class of models inspired by pairwise interaction potentials in classical physics, offered a more memory‑efficient alternative by exploiting physically meaningful kernels. However, its practical deployment has been hampered by an opaque connection to the family of linear attention mechanisms that provably achieve linear time and memory.  

In this paper we revisit Physics‑Attention through the lens of linear attention and show that its core interaction can be expressed as a kernel‑based linear map, allowing a direct reimplementation as a **Transolver** – a new linear Transformer that preserves the expressive power of physics‑inspired potentials while enjoying the computational guarantees of state‑of‑the‑art linear attention schemes. We derive an end‑to‑end differentiable formulation that reduces the memory footprint from \(O(n^2)\) to \(O(n)\) and the runtime from \(O(n^2d)\) to \(O(nd)\), where \(n\) is sequence length and \(d\) the hidden dimension.  

Our experiments on a broad suite of long‑range benchmarks (Long‑Range Arena, WikiText‑103, ImageNet‑1K) demonstrate that Transolver matches or surpasses conventional Transformers and other linear attention models in accuracy, while reducing GPU memory usage by up to 70 % and training time by 3×. We also provide a theoretical analysis that unifies physics‑based potential functions with kernel approximations, offering new insights into the role of locality, sparsity, and stability in attention mechanisms. Together, these results establish Transolver as a principled, scalable, and efficient linear Transformer that bridges the gap between physics‑inspired attention and modern kernel‑based methods.
1410:
Full‑duplex speech‑language models (FDSLMs) that can simultaneously comprehend spoken input and generate natural‑language or spoken replies are rapidly becoming central to next‑generation conversational agents.  Yet, the current evaluation ecosystem remains fragmented: most benchmarks either focus on single‑turn or text‑only interactions, or evaluate acoustic‑only capabilities, leaving a substantial gap in our ability to measure how well these models maintain context, coherence, and naturalness over extended, back‑and‑forth dialogues.  

We introduce **MTR‑DuplexBench**, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate multi‑round full‑duplex conversations.  The benchmark comprises (i) a newly collected dataset of 12 k real‑world multi‑turn audio‑text dialogues spanning 7 distinct domains (customer support, tutoring, casual chat, etc.), annotated with high‑fidelity speech transcriptions, turn‑level timestamps, and context‑aware evaluation scores; (ii) a suite of task‑specific protocols (continuation, clarification, and turn‑transition metrics); and (iii) a unified evaluation framework that jointly measures acoustic fidelity (WER, MOS), linguistic quality (BLEU, ROUGE), and conversational dynamics (response latency, turn‑coherence, and engagement).

Using MTR‑DuplexBench, we benchmark five state‑of‑the‑art FDSLMs, revealing substantial disparities across domains and uncovering systematic weaknesses in long‑term context retention and turn‑synchronization.  We further demonstrate that a simple multi‑task fine‑tuning strategy improves overall scores by 7.4% in the combined metric.  

MTR‑DuplexBench fills a critical void in the evaluation landscape for full‑duplex speech‑language systems, providing a reproducible, multi‑round, multimodal test bed that encourages progress toward truly interactive, natural conversational agents.  The dataset and evaluation tools are publicly released to foster community adoption.
1411:
A world model equips an intelligent agent with the capacity to envision, forecast, and reason about how the environment will change in response to its own actions, thereby facilitating planning and strategy. Although recent video‑generation systems can produce photorealistic sequences, they usually operate in a prompt‑to‑video fashion and lack the causal control, interactivity, and long‑horizon coherence necessary for meaningful reasoning. Existing approaches to world modeling tend to be confined to narrow domains (e.g., physics simulators, games, or 3‑D scenes), offering limited depth and controllability and failing to generalize across varied settings and interaction styles.

In this work we present PAN—a versatile, interactive, and long‑horizon world model that simulates future states of the world through high‑fidelity video conditioned on historical observations and natural‑language actions. PAN’s core is the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture, which marries an autoregressive latent dynamics backbone powered by a large language model (LLM) with a video diffusion decoder. The LLM grounds the simulation in rich text‑based knowledge and enables conditioning on language‑specified actions, while the diffusion decoder restores perceptually detailed, temporally coherent visuals, bridging imagination in latent space with realistic world dynamics. Trained on a large collection of video–action pairs across diverse domains, PAN supports open‑domain, action‑conditioned simulation with coherent long‑term behavior. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PAN outperforms competing video generators and world models in action‑conditioned simulation, long‑horizon prediction, and simulative reasoning, advancing the development of general world models capable of predicting future states for reasoning and acting.
1412: Methods that rely on textual style have made great strides in spotting fake news. Yet, as attackers grow more adept at mimicking legitimate writing, style‑based detectors lose their edge. Recent work has turned to large language models (LLMs) to push detection further, but practical use remains limited by shallow experimentation, unclear usability, and high inference costs. We introduce **FactGuard**, a novel framework that harnesses LLMs to extract event‑centric content, thereby mitigating the influence of stylistic cues. FactGuard also incorporates a dynamic usability module that flags contradictory or ambiguous factual reasoning, selectively invoking LLM guidance to boost decision confidence. For real‑world deployment, we distill the full system into **FactGuard‑D**, a lightweight variant suitable for cold‑start and resource‑constrained environments. Extensive evaluation on two benchmark datasets shows that our approach consistently surpasses existing techniques in both robustness and accuracy, effectively overcoming style‑sensitivity and LLM‑integration hurdles in fake‑news detection.
1413:
The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) has revealed that dense neural networks contain sparse “winning” sub‑networks that can be trained in isolation to match or exceed the performance of the original model. However, its application to modern Transformer‑based architectures, where multi‑head attention dominates the parameter budget, remains largely unexplored. In this work we formulate a **Strong Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (SLTH) for Multi‑Head Attention (MHA)**: for any trained Transformer, there exists a sparse sub‑network comprising a subset of attention heads and a subset of feed‑forward parameters that can be re‑initialized and trained from scratch to achieve performance within a constant margin of the full model, while requiring substantially fewer parameters and floating‑point operations.

We develop a principled pruning framework that (1) identifies head‑wise and token‑wise importance scores using a differentiable mask‑based objective, (2) enforces head‑level sparsity while preserving the overall network topology, and (3) applies an iterative rewinding strategy to recover a strong initialization for each candidate subnet. Extensive experiments on BERT‑Base, RoBERTa‑Base, and GPT‑2 across GLUE, SQuAD 2.0, and Wikitext‑103 demonstrate that SLTH sub‑networks with as few as 30 % of the heads and 45 % of the feed‑forward parameters can match the full‑model accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 40 %. Moreover, we provide empirical evidence that the sub‑networks exhibit **robustness to domain shifts** and can be transferred across tasks with minimal fine‑tuning.

Our findings not only extend the theoretical understanding of over‑parameterization in attention mechanisms but also pave the way for more efficient deployment of large‑scale Transformers in resource‑constrained environments.
1414: Vision‑language models (VLMs) have become the backbone of multimodal AI, yet their performance often deteriorates when deployed in domains that differ from the data used to pre‑train them. Conventional prompt‑learning strategies, which inject learnable text tokens or visual embeddings, treat each domain as a separate fine‑tuning target and therefore do not scale to the large number of potential visual environments. In this work we introduce **Latent Domain Prompt Learning (LDPL)**, a unified framework that learns a continuous latent representation of a domain and decodes it into a prompt that is conditionally fused with a VLM’s multimodal embedding. The latent prompt encoder is trained with a contrastive objective that maximizes agreement between the domain‐conditioned prompt and the target VLM’s output while preserving the model’s original knowledge. LDPL is lightweight, requiring only a handful of parameters per domain, and can be instantiated on a variety of VLM architectures (CLIP, ViLBERT, BLIP, etc.). We evaluate LDPL on cross‑domain image classification, captioning, and visual‑question answering tasks spanning natural, medical, and synthetic domains. Across all benchmarks LDPL outperforms both vanilla prompt‑learning and fine‑tuned baselines, achieving an average gain of 3.8 % top‑1 accuracy on ImageNet‑V2 and a 5.1 % BLEU‑4 improvement on the VizWiz captioning dataset, while incurring negligible inference overhead. Our results demonstrate that latent domain prompts offer a principled, efficient route to adapt VLMs to diverse visual worlds without sacrificing generality.
1415: Accurate phase picking is a cornerstone of modern seismology, yet most convolutional and attention‑based detectors suffer from *amplitude suppression*—a systematic bias that under‑estimates the energy of weak or distant arrivals. This phenomenon hampers not only event detection but also downstream tasks such as hypocenter relocation and magnitude estimation. In this work we diagnose amplitude suppression through a systematic analysis of residual networks trained on synthetic and field datasets, revealing that the bias arises from an over‑reliance on waveform shape at the expense of absolute amplitude scaling. To address this, we propose **Adversarial Shape Learning (ASL)**, a two‑stage framework that jointly learns a *shape encoder* and an *amplitude critic* in a generative adversarial setting. The shape encoder extracts a compact, invariant representation of a seismic phase, while the critic forces the network to preserve amplitude statistics by penalizing deviations from a learned amplitude manifold. The resulting model not only retains high temporal precision but also recovers the true amplitude envelope, yielding a 12 % reduction in root‑mean‑square error relative to baseline detectors on the SEED and Iquique‑2019 datasets. Moreover, the ASL‑enhanced picker achieves a 4.7 % increase in detection recall for events with magnitude < 3.0, without sacrificing precision. Our results demonstrate that adversarial shape learning provides a robust, physics‑informed regularization that breaks amplitude suppression and improves both phase picking and subsequent seismic analysis pipelines.
1416: Traditional online surveys are often generic, offering little personalisation that can lead to low engagement and shallow answers. Even though AI‑powered survey chatbots provide greater convenience, most of them remain reactive, following pre‑written dialogue trees or static templates and failing to adjust the flow in real time to individual respondents. To overcome these shortcomings, we introduce **AURA** (Adaptive Understanding through Reinforcement Learning for Assessment), a reinforcement‑learning framework that tailors conversational surveys to each participant. AURA measures response quality across four dimensions—Length, Self‑disclosure, Emotion, and Specificity (the LSDE metric)—and employs an epsilon‑greedy policy to choose follow‑up question types, continuously updating expected quality gains during a session. Starting from priors derived from 96 prior campus‑climate conversations (467 chatbot‑user exchanges), the system balances exploration and exploitation over 10–15 turns, adapting on the fly to each user. In controlled tests, AURA delivered a mean quality improvement of +0.076, a statistically significant boost over non‑adaptive baselines (p = 0.044, d = 0.66), largely due to a 63 % reduction in specification prompts and a tenfold increase in validation responses. These findings illustrate that reinforcement learning can turn static questionnaires into dynamic, self‑optimising conversational assessments.
1417: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) hold great promise as adsorbents for gas uptake and separation, yet pinpointing the best structures from their vast design space demands efficient high‑throughput screening tools. Traditional machine‑learning models usually depend on gas‑specific descriptors such as Henry coefficients or adsorption heats, which are costly to obtain and hinder scalability, making the process labor‑intensive and slow. In this study we introduce COFAP, a universal COF‑adsorption prediction framework that leverages deep learning to automatically harvest multimodal structural and chemical features, and merges these complementary cues via a cross‑modal attention mechanism. By dispensing with explicit gas‑related inputs, COFAP sets a new state‑of‑the‑art benchmark on the hypoCOFs dataset, surpassing all prior approaches. Analysis of the predictions reveals that top‑performing COFs for separation cluster within a limited band of pore size and surface area. Additionally, we present a weight‑adjustable prioritization scheme that allows researchers to tailor the ranking of candidate COFs to specific application requirements. The combination of speed and accuracy makes COFAP immediately applicable to the rational design of crystalline porous materials.
1418: Vision‑based deep learning systems are increasingly used in safety‑critical settings such as medical imaging, yet they remain susceptible to tiny adversarial patches that can cause incorrect predictions. Most current countermeasures are designed for a single patch and break down when several localized corruptions appear simultaneously—an attack pattern that real‑world adversaries and natural artifacts often exploit. We introduce **Filtered‑ViT**, a novel vision transformer that embeds **SMART Vector Median Filtering (SMART‑VMF)**, a spatially adaptive, multi‑scale, robustness‑aware module capable of selectively attenuating corrupted zones while retaining fine semantic details. On ImageNet under the LaVAN multi‑patch threat, Filtered‑ViT records 79.8 % clean accuracy and 46.3 % robust accuracy against four concurrent 1 % patches, surpassing existing defenses. A practical evaluation on radiographic datasets further demonstrates that Filtered‑ViT removes natural disturbances such as occlusions and scanner noise without compromising diagnostic information. These results position Filtered‑ViT as the first transformer architecture to provide unified resilience to both adversarial and naturally occurring patch‑like perturbations, paving the way for dependable vision systems in genuinely high‑stakes domains.
1419:
Generating attractive graphic layouts—from posters to academic documents—has become a prominent research field. Recent studies have introduced user‑defined constraints to steer layout synthesis, yet these constraints typically demand detailed, technical specifications that can hinder usability. In this work we propose a novel, more natural form of guidance: user sketches. We show empirically that sketch‑based constraints enable a more intuitive design process and position the sketch‑to‑layout problem as a fruitful, yet underexplored, research avenue.  

To address this challenge, we design a multimodal transformer architecture that consumes both a sketch and a set of content assets to output high‑quality layouts. Because manually annotated sketch data would be prohibitively expensive, we develop an efficient, synthetic sketch‑generation pipeline that can produce large volumes of training sketches. Using this pipeline, we train and evaluate our model on three benchmark datasets—PubLayNet, DocLayNet, and SlidesVQA—and demonstrate superior performance compared to leading constraint‑based methods while providing a more user‑friendly interface.  

To catalyze further research in sketch‑based layout generation, we release approximately 200 k synthetically generated sketches that pair with the public datasets. The datasets are accessible at https://github.com/google-deepmind/sketch_to_layout.
1420:
The ability to decode imagined speech from electroencephalography (EEG) has long been envisioned as a key component of next‑generation brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, most laboratory demonstrations rely on wired, high‑channel‑count systems and offline analyses that preclude practical deployment. In this work we present *Toward Practical BCI*, a fully integrated real‑time wireless imagined‑speech EEG decoding pipeline that operates on a 32‑channel, light‑weight headset and delivers intelligible word predictions with sub‑second latency.  

Signal acquisition is performed using a commercial wireless EEG system that streams 500‑Hz data to an on‑board edge computer. A lightweight preprocessing stage removes power‑line noise, performs band‑pass filtering (1–80 Hz), and applies robust artifact rejection via adaptive independent component analysis. Feature extraction consists of time–frequency decompositions (wavelet coefficients and band‑power summaries) computed over 200‑ms sliding windows, followed by dimensionality reduction with principal component analysis (PCA). Decoding is performed by a shallow convolutional–recurrent neural network (CNN–LSTM) trained on a subject‑specific dataset (20 trials per word, 10 target words). The model is optimized for inference on a low‑power ARM Cortex‑A53 processor, achieving a mean classification accuracy of 71 % (±4 %) across 20 healthy participants while maintaining an average latency of 240 ms from stimulus onset to output.  

We further demonstrate robustness to channel drop‑out and wireless packet loss through an online feedback loop that dynamically re‑weights feature contributions. The system’s performance matches or surpasses state‑of‑the‑art offline studies, yet with the added constraints of wireless operation and real‑time inference. These results bring imagined‑speech BCIs one step closer to practical, ambulatory use cases such as assistive communication for locked‑in patients and hands‑free control of smart environments.
1421: Visual grounding—localizing image regions based on natural‑language prompts—is essential for building reasoning‑capable Graphical User Interface agents. Most current approaches depend on large, often noisy synthetic datasets. In this paper, we propose a streamlined training framework that couples model‑driven data filtering with parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning. Starting from 4.8 million synthetic examples, we distill a high‑quality set of 12 k diverse instances: we first isolate the most difficult cases, prune misaligned samples, and then pick a representative, multimodal subset. A 3‑billion‑parameter Vision‑Language Model is then trained under three regimes—plain supervised fine‑tuning, chain‑of‑thought‑augmented fine‑tuning, and reinforcement learning via Group Relative Policy Optimization. Models trained on the curated data and lightweight fine‑tuning approaches achieve parity with or exceed larger baselines on benchmarks such as ScreenSpot, Multimodal‑Mind2Web, and AndroidControl. These findings highlight that careful data curation combined with robust adaptation can match large‑scale training, paving the way for compact yet powerful multimodal reasoning agents.
1422:
Accurate data assimilation in geological carbon storage (GCS) is essential for quantifying storage security, predicting leakage pathways, and guiding operational decisions. Conventional ensemble‐based methods (e.g., Ensemble Kalman Filter, Ensemble Smoother) struggle with the high dimensionality and strong nonlinearity of subsurface flow, while spatial localization is typically imposed ad hoc, leading to either over‑filtering or spurious correlations. We present a novel assimilation framework that couples **score‑based diffusion models**—a class of deep generative models capable of capturing complex, high‑dimensional prior distributions—with **machine‑learning‑enhanced localization** to overcome these limitations.

Our approach first trains a diffusion model on a large set of synthetic reservoir realizations, thereby learning a flexible representation of the joint prior over petrophysical properties and state variables. During assimilation, the diffusion sampler generates a diverse, high‑fidelity ensemble that preserves subtle non‑Gaussian features absent in Gaussian‑based priors. Localization is then learned end‑to‑end by a convolutional neural network that predicts a spatially varying correlation kernel from the current ensemble statistics and sensor geometry, thus adapting the localization radius and shape to the evolving state. The learned kernel is integrated into a modified Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF‑MLL), ensuring that only physically meaningful correlations are retained.

We evaluate the method on a benchmark GCS case (SPE‑10‑like heterogeneous aquifer) with synthetic pressure and seismic observations. Compared with standard EnKF and particle filter variants, our framework reduces the root‑mean‑square error of the CO₂ plume prediction by 32 % and improves the ensemble spread coverage from 68 % to 94 %. Computational overhead is modest: the diffusion sampling cost is amortized over the entire assimilation cycle, and the localization network requires only a single forward pass per update.

This work demonstrates that integrating score‑based diffusion priors with learning‑based localization can yield a robust, scalable data assimilation pipeline for GCS, offering enhanced predictive accuracy and uncertainty quantification while remaining compatible with existing workflow architectures. The methodology is broadly applicable to other subsurface monitoring problems where high‑dimensional, non‑Gaussian priors and spatially varying correlations pose significant challenges.
1423:
Self‑talk, the spontaneous inner monologue that accompanies everyday cognition, has been shown to influence attention, memory consolidation, and stress regulation. Yet, quantifying and monitoring self‑talk in naturalistic settings has remained largely speculative because conventional microphones either lack the necessary proximity to capture the subtle acoustic cues or raise privacy concerns. This paper presents *EarSelf*, a novel framework that leverages ear‑mounted wearables (earables) to automatically detect self‑talk in real‑time. By integrating a miniature, low‑power microphone array with inertial sensors and a multimodal audio‑contextual pipeline, EarSelf extracts a rich feature set—including spectral harmonics, prosodic markers, and head‑motion correlations—that distinguishes self‑talk from environmental speech and other vocalizations. A deep convolutional–recurrent neural network trained on a newly collected corpus of 75 participants (over 800 h of naturalistic audio) achieves 87 % overall accuracy and 92 % precision on self‑talk detection while maintaining a false‑positive rate below 5 %. We also demonstrate that self‑talk episodes can be temporally aligned with cognitive load events (e.g., problem solving) with a mean latency of 0.3 s, enabling prospective interventions in adaptive learning and stress‑management applications. Importantly, the earable’s on‑device processing preserves user privacy by discarding raw audio and transmitting only encrypted, high‑level inference tags.

The results confirm that ear‑mounted sensors are sufficiently sensitive to capture the acoustic footprint of self‑talk, opening a path toward unobtrusive, continuous monitoring of internal cognitive processes. This work contributes a scalable, privacy‑preserving detection pipeline, a large annotated dataset, and an evaluation framework that can be adopted by researchers in HCI, cognitive science, and health informatics seeking to explore the role of self‑talk in real‑world contexts.
1424:
Brain magnetic‑resonance imaging (MRI) remains the cornerstone of neuroimaging research and clinical diagnostics, yet the quality and interpretability of raw scans are frequently compromised by scanner‑specific artifacts, intensity inhomogeneities, and patient motion. Conventional preprocessing pipelines—bias‑field correction, skull stripping, intensity normalization, and spatial registration—are computationally intensive and may introduce systematic distortions that obscure subtle disease signatures. In this study, we introduce **Diffusion-Driven Generation of Minimally Preprocessed Brain MRI (DDGM‑MRI)**, a generative framework that leverages denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) to synthesize high‑fidelity brain MR images from minimal input, thereby bypassing extensive preprocessing steps.

Our architecture comprises a conditional diffusion backbone trained on a large, multi‑site repository of raw T1‑weighted scans. A lightweight encoder extracts low‑dimensional anatomical priors (e.g., tissue‑class maps, head‑shape descriptors) that guide the diffusion process, ensuring that generated images respect individual patient anatomy while preserving realistic noise and contrast characteristics. We evaluate DDGM‑MRI on two benchmark datasets (Human Connectome Project and ADNI) against state‑of‑the‑art generative models and conventional preprocessing pipelines. Quantitatively, the synthetic scans achieve peak signal‑to‑noise ratios and structural similarity indices within 3 % of fully preprocessed ground truths, and downstream segmentation and classification tasks retain ≥ 95 % accuracy relative to manually processed inputs. Qualitatively, radiologists report indistinguishable anatomical fidelity in blind assessments.

DDGM‑MRI demonstrates that diffusion‑based generation can produce minimally preprocessed brain MRIs that are both computationally efficient and diagnostically reliable. By obviating lengthy preprocessing stages, our method facilitates rapid data augmentation, harmonization across scanners, and real‑time clinical workflows, thereby advancing the accessibility and scalability of neuroimaging analyses.
1425: Large‐scale language models (LLMs) routinely generate *hallucinations*—factually incorrect or fabricated content—yet deploying a full‑size detector remains costly. We investigate whether a lightweight model can acquire a *look‑before‑you‑leap* capability that anticipates and corrects hallucinations on the fly. Our approach, **Dynamic Hallucination Detection (DHD)**, couples a small, task‑specific predictor with a reinforcement‑learned *proactive‑correction* policy. The predictor is trained on a curriculum of progressively harder examples, dynamically augmenting its training distribution with hard negatives discovered during inference. At inference time, DHD first flags potential hallucinations using the predictor, then invokes a lightweight correction module that revises the generation or seeks external evidence before the final output is produced. Across three widely used benchmarks (WebQuestions, WikiQA, and the OpenAI‑Hallucination Corpus), DHD reduces hallucination rates by 23 % relative to state‑of‑the‑art detectors while requiring only 5 % of the parameters of a 13B model. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of dynamic curriculum learning and the proactive correction loop. Our results demonstrate that even a modest model can learn to *look before it leaps*, providing a computationally efficient, yet effective, solution to hallucination in generative language systems.
1426:
Early and accurate detection of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains a pressing challenge in clinical practice, especially given the heterogeneity of patient presentations and the scarcity of labeled data. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated that *in‑context learning* (ICL) can rapidly adapt to domain‑specific tasks with minimal supervision, yet their performance on medical diagnostics is largely limited by the generic, often “plain” demonstration (demo) examples supplied at inference time. In this work we introduce a **demo‑centric anchoring paradigm** that explicitly tailors the composition of in‑context demos to capture clinically salient features of AD, thereby enabling more reliable inference without fine‑tuning the underlying model.

Our approach begins by mining a curated corpus of multimodal AD case reports—including neuropsychological test scores, imaging biomarkers, and patient‑reported symptom narratives—from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the DementiaBank database. Using a graph‑based representation of diagnostic criteria and symptom ontologies, we construct *anchor nodes* that encode key differential patterns (e.g., early memory impairment, language deficits, hippocampal atrophy). These anchors are then expanded into concise, task‑specific demo snippets that are presented to the LLM in the context prompt. We evaluate this paradigm on two benchmarks: (1) a clinical vignette classification task (AD vs. mild cognitive impairment vs. normal aging) and (2) an imaging‑based risk prediction task where the model must infer AD status from volumetric features. Compared with standard “plain” demo ICL baselines, our demo‑centric anchors improve overall accuracy by 12.4 % and the F1‑score by 9.7 % on the vignette dataset, while achieving a 4.1 % reduction in calibration error on the imaging task. Ablation studies confirm that the anchoring strategy is robust to demo size variations and that the learned anchors generalize across different LLM architectures (GPT‑4, LLaMA‑13B).

These results suggest that carefully curated, domain‑aware demos can unlock the full potential of ICL for AD detection, providing a scalable, zero‑shot framework that is both interpretable and amenable to clinical deployment. Future work will extend this paradigm to longitudinal risk modeling and investigate integration with explainability modules to support physician decision‑making.
1427:
Modern vision‑language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide spectrum of perception‑language tasks. However, when confronted with graphical user interface (GUI) reasoning—wherein a model must interpret screen contents, predict user actions, or generate interface‑specific instructions—these systems frequently fall short. Existing benchmarks either treat GUI images as generic visual scenes or focus on low‑level object detection, thus overlooking the rich, structured knowledge required for effective interaction with software interfaces.  

In this work we introduce **GUI Knowledge Bench (GKB)**, a comprehensive benchmark designed to expose the knowledge gaps that cause VLM failures in GUI tasks. GKB comprises 12,345 annotated GUI screenshots spanning 37 application domains (web browsers, IDEs, productivity suites, etc.) and 8,760 multi‑step reasoning questions. Each question targets a distinct dimension of GUI understanding—component semantics, hierarchical layout, event dependencies, state transitions, and cross‑screen consistency—requiring models to draw upon implicit design rules, API documentation, and interaction conventions.

We evaluate a suite of state‑of‑the‑art VLMs (e.g., CLIP, BLIP, Flamingo, LLaVA) on GKB, measuring accuracy, reasoning depth, and robustness to visual perturbations. Results reveal a striking disparity: while overall accuracy exceeds 70 % on generic image‑captioning tasks, performance on GKB drops below 30 % for all models, with a pronounced deficit in questions demanding multi‑step reasoning and cross‑screen inference. Ablation studies demonstrate that incorporating lightweight GUI‑specific embeddings and a curated knowledge graph significantly boosts performance, highlighting the critical role of domain knowledge over raw visual–textual alignment.
