Evaluation on a held‑out test set (30 % of data) yields a macro‑averaged F1‑score of **0.82** and an overall accuracy of **0.89**, outperforming baseline BERT (0.71/0.84), SVM+TF‑IDF (0.68/0.81), and a rule‑based lexicon approach (0.66/0.78). Ablation studies confirm the importance of domain‑adapted embeddings (Δ+0.07 F1) and the label‑smoothing regularizer (Δ+0.04 F1).  

Beyond performance, we provide post‑hoc attention visualizations that highlight clinically relevant linguistic features, offering a level of interpretability useful for clinicians and researchers alike. By demonstrating robust multi‑class classification of mental‑health disorders from unstructured text, multiMentalRoBERTa advances the state of automated mental‑health screening and offers a foundation for future integration into digital‑health workflows and longitudinal monitoring systems.
1573: The exponential growth of telecom infrastructure and the advent of 5G/6G networks demand intelligent, real‑time decision‑making that can adapt to rapidly changing network states. Traditional rule‑based and monolithic machine‑learning solutions struggle to capture the rich, contextual, and hierarchical information required for effective network management. We introduce **Tele‑LLM‑Hub**, a framework that orchestrates a fleet of large language models (LLMs) into context‑aware, task‑specific agents capable of autonomously monitoring, diagnosing, and optimizing telecom networks. Tele‑LLM‑Hub couples a lightweight contextual‑embedding engine with a graph‑based knowledge base that continuously ingests telemetry, topology, and service‑level agreements. An agent‑orchestration layer assigns domain‑specific LLMs—such as a fault‑analysis agent, a resource‑allocation agent, and a user‑experience agent—to relevant sub‑tasks, while a global coordination module resolves conflicts and ensures consistency across the multi‑agent system. To validate the approach, we deployed Tele‑LLM‑Hub on a realistic multi‑site 5G core testbed, benchmarking against rule‑based and single‑model baselines. The system achieved a 37 % reduction in mean time to resolution for complex fault scenarios and improved traffic‑load balancing accuracy by 21 % while maintaining sub‑second latency for inference. Moreover, the contextual routing mechanism reduced irrelevant LLM calls by 48 %, leading to a 15 % lower compute cost. Tele‑LLM‑Hub demonstrates a scalable, modular architecture that enables telecom operators to embed contextual intelligence into network operations, paving the way for self‑healing, policy‑driven, and user‑centric network services.
1574:
Requirements engineering (RE) remains a critical yet resource‑intensive discipline in software and systems development. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI)—particularly in natural‑language processing, machine learning, and automated reasoning—promise to automate many RE tasks, from elicitation and analysis to traceability and compliance checking. However, the extent to which industry practitioners are actually adopting these technologies and the barriers they face are not well understood.  

This paper reports on a comprehensive, mixed‑methods investigation of AI adoption in RE across the software, automotive, aerospace, and healthcare sectors. A quantitative survey of 312 RE professionals was complemented by 24 semi‑structured interviews and three detailed case studies. The survey revealed that 42 % of respondents employ at least one AI‑based tool for requirement elicitation or quality checking, while only 15 % use AI for automated traceability or compliance verification. Key success factors identified include availability of structured requirement repositories, clear quality metrics, and strong managerial support. Major impediments involve lack of domain‑specific data, concerns about model transparency, and difficulty integrating AI tools with existing toolchains.

The interview data highlight divergent practitioner perspectives: some view AI as a productivity enhancer that can reduce manual effort, whereas others emphasize the need for human oversight and the risk of over‑reliance on “black‑box” models. Across all studies, a consistent theme emerged that successful AI deployment requires a hybrid workflow that preserves human judgment while leveraging AI for routine, repetitive tasks.

Our findings provide a nuanced view of the current state of AI in RE, illustrating that while early adoption is growing, many organizations remain cautious. We conclude with a set of actionable guidelines for practitioners and a research roadmap that prioritises explainable AI, data‑quality frameworks, and standardized evaluation metrics for RE‑specific AI tools. This work thus bridges the gap between emerging AI technologies and their practical impact on the discipline of requirements engineering.
1575: Multi‑objective search (MOS) has become a central paradigm for tackling planning and decision‑making problems in which several, often conflicting, criteria must be reconciled. Although MOS has long been a subject of research, its relevance has surged in recent years across AI domains—including robotics, transportation, and operations research—underscoring that real‑world systems rarely aim to optimize a single metric. This survey reviews recent progress in MOS, explores interdisciplinary synergies, and identifies the open questions that now shape the cutting edge of the field.
1576: The coordination of very complex multi‑agent systems (MAS) in real‑time domains—such as autonomous transport fleets, distributed robotics swarms, or large‑scale sensor networks—requires a rigorous mechanism to manage inter‑agent dependencies while preserving high throughput. Existing MAS frameworks either rely on loosely coupled publish/subscribe models that suffer from inconsistency, or on heavyweight transactional databases that impose prohibitive latency overhead. In this work we present **OptiMA**, a novel transaction‑based framework that reconciles these opposing requirements by introducing a fine‑grained, compositional transaction model tailored to the semantics of agent interactions. OptiMA leverages a hybrid locking–optimistic concurrency control scheme that adapts dynamically to the contention patterns of the system, coupled with a cost‑based scheduler that predicts transaction execution paths using a lightweight Bayesian network. Our optimization layer exploits the inherent hierarchy of agent responsibilities to prune unnecessary dependency checks, thereby reducing lock contention and improving cache locality. Extensive experiments on two representative benchmarks—a large‑scale autonomous drone swarm and a smart‑grid resource management scenario—demonstrate that OptiMA achieves up to **4.8×** higher throughput and **2.3×** lower latency than state‑of‑the‑art MAS runtimes, while preserving 100 % consistency across all critical invariants. Furthermore, we evaluate OptiMA under fault‑injection scenarios and show graceful degradation with a 15 % drop in throughput, compared to a 45 % drop for baseline systems. This paper therefore contributes a practical, extensible framework, a throughput‑oriented optimization methodology, and a comprehensive empirical validation, paving the way for scalable deployment of very complex multi‑agent systems in latency‑critical environments.
1577: Web‑based games represent a challenging testbed for autonomous agents, demanding real‑time perception, reasoning, and low‑latency interaction with a heterogeneous browser environment. This paper investigates whether a large language model (LLM) can not only comprehend but also master such games through an end‑to‑end *ChatGPT Atlas* agent. The Atlas architecture couples ChatGPT‑derived natural‑language planning with a lightweight WebDriver interface and a short‑term episodic memory, allowing the agent to translate textual observations into actionable browser commands. We evaluate the agent on a curated set of ten representative browser games (e.g., *Cookie Clicker*, *Slither.io*, *Wordle*, *2048*, *Flappy Bird*) drawn from the OpenAI WebGames benchmark, measuring win rates, average episode length, and resource consumption. Compared with baseline reinforcement‑learning agents and rule‑based bots, ChatGPT Atlas achieves human‑level performance in eight games, outperforms RL baselines by 27 % in cumulative reward, and demonstrates rapid zero‑shot generalization to unseen games within five minutes of interaction. Failure cases reveal brittleness to adversarial UI changes and limitations in long‑term planning. We provide an in‑depth error taxonomy and discuss implications for safety, interpretability, and the design of LLM‑powered web agents. The results indicate that LLMs, when paired with a modular execution stack, can effectively conquer a wide range of web games, marking a significant step toward general autonomous web interaction.
1578:
We present *One Model to Critique Them All*, a unified framework for rewarding agentic tool‑use that integrates efficient reasoning with adaptive reward shaping.  While contemporary large‑language models can generate tool‑chains in principle, they often lack a principled incentive to discover and employ them in complex environments.  We address this gap by introducing a *Tool‑Critique Network* (TCN) that, conditioned on a world‑state embedding, predicts the expected benefit of a candidate tool and the cost of its application.  The TCN is trained jointly with a reinforcement‑learning agent under a *Reasoning‑Aware Reward* (RAR) that penalizes wasted reasoning steps and rewards successful tool‑integration.  The RAR is derived from a lightweight chain‑of‑thought reasoning module that explicitly enumerates intermediate steps, thereby enabling the agent to introspect and self‑critique its tool‑use decisions.

We evaluate our approach on a suite of challenging benchmark tasks (MiniGrid, Minecraft, and the Tool‑use subset of the ProcGen environment).  Across all domains, the TCN‑guided policy achieves a 35 % higher cumulative reward and a 50 % reduction in reasoning latency compared with baseline reward‑only policies.  Ablation studies confirm that both the critique module and the cost‑aware reward are essential for robust tool discovery and efficient planning.  Furthermore, qualitative analysis shows that the model spontaneously re‑uses sub‑tools and adapts its strategy when the environment changes, demonstrating a form of meta‑learning.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a novel reward design that explicitly couples efficient reasoning with tool‑use, (2) a compact, trainable critique network that serves as a meta‑advisor for tool‑selection, and (3) a comprehensive empirical evaluation establishing a new state‑of‑the‑art for agentic tool‑use in simulated environments.  We release our code and a pre‑trained TCN model to facilitate reproducibility and future extensions.
1579:
Transformer models dominate modern natural‑language, vision, and multimodal workloads, yet their inference and training pipelines are dominated by a large set of nonlinear primitives—softmax, layer‑norm, GELU, dropout, and the element‑wise multiplications that compose self‑attention. Conventional accelerators implement each of these operations with distinct custom logic, leading to substantial silicon redundancy and energy inefficiency. In this work we present **QUARK** (Quantization‑Enabled Circuit Re‑use for Accelerating Transformers), a holistic hardware/software co‑design that exploits the algebraic commonality among these nonlinearities to share circuit blocks across the entire transformer stack.

QUARK introduces a quantization‑aware pattern‑matching engine that automatically extracts common sub‑computations from the computational graph of any transformer model. By quantizing operands to 8‑bit fixed‑point representations and aligning the numerical range of each pattern, QUARK synthesizes a small library of highly reusable sub‑circuits (e.g., fused exp/softmax, approximate GELU, and scaled dot‑product attention kernels). A runtime scheduler maps each nonlinear operation to the appropriate library block, while a lightweight control logic dynamically reconfigures the shared datapaths to match the required precision or activation function. This approach eliminates the need for separate hardware for every nonlinear primitive, reducing register‑file and routing overhead.

We instantiate QUARK on a 28‑nm ASIC platform and evaluate it on several canonical transformer benchmarks (BERT‑Base, GPT‑2 Small, and Vision‑Transformer‑S). Compared with a baseline ASIC that implements the standard set of nonlinear units, QUARK achieves **30 % area savings**, **22 % energy reduction**, and **18 % latency improvement** while preserving top‑1 accuracy within 0.1 % relative to the floating‑point reference. Our results demonstrate that quantization‑enabled circuit sharing can bridge the gap between the highly irregular computational patterns of transformers and the need for compact, energy‑efficient accelerators.

QUARK is open‑source and integrates seamlessly with existing compiler stacks, paving the way for practical deployment of transformer workloads on edge and data‑center accelerators.
1580:
Knowledge‑graph completion (KGC) methods rely on negative sampling to train efficient scoring functions for link prediction. Conventional schemes – uniform or heuristic Bernoulli sampling – either yield overly easy negatives or fail to adapt to the evolving embedding space, leading to sub‑optimal convergence and inflated training costs. In this paper we introduce **DANS‑KGC (Diffusion‑Based Adaptive Negative Sampling for Knowledge Graph Completion)**, a novel framework that constructs a diffusion process over the graph topology to generate high‑quality, contextually relevant negative triples during training.  

The diffusion kernel is learned jointly with the embedding model by propagating feature gradients along random walk trajectories, thereby capturing multi‑hop relational proximity. At each training step, DANS samples negatives by selecting nodes whose diffusion probability is high but whose current embeddings are still distant from the positive head‑tail pair, ensuring a curriculum that progressively hardens the optimization landscape. This adaptive scheme naturally balances exploration and exploitation: early epochs favor easier negatives to stabilize training, while later epochs concentrate on hard negatives that lie near decision boundaries.  

We provide a theoretical analysis showing that the diffusion‑based sampler approximates the optimal negative distribution under a local reweighting assumption, and we prove that its expected gradient remains unbiased with respect to the true loss. Experiments on benchmark datasets (FB15k‑237, WN18RR, and YAGO3‑10) demonstrate that DANS‑KGC achieves state‑of‑the‑art link‑prediction scores, outperforming baseline samplers by 4–7 % in Hits@10 and 3–5 % in MRR. Moreover, DANS reduces the number of required negative samples by 30 % to reach comparable performance, yielding faster convergence and lower memory overhead.  

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a principled diffusion‑based adaptive sampling mechanism for KGC; (2) an efficient implementation that integrates seamlessly with any score‑based embedding model; and (3) comprehensive empirical evidence that adaptive negative sampling guided by graph diffusion substantially enhances both accuracy and training efficiency. DANS‑KGC is released as open source to encourage reproducibility and further research in adaptive sampling for knowledge graph learning.
1581:
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in open‑ended domains that demand reasoning, creativity, and continual adaptation. Yet, existing benchmarks often evaluate agents in isolated, scripted tasks, failing to capture their competitive dynamics and evolving capabilities. We introduce **CATArena**, a principled framework that evaluates LLM agents by organizing *iterative tournament competitions* in which agents face one another across multiple rounds, receive adaptive feedback, and refine their strategies. CATArena automates the entire pipeline—from opponent selection and match orchestration to scoring and statistical ranking—enabling large‑scale, reproducible, and fair comparison of agents on complex, multi‑step tasks.

In CATArena, each match is a turn‑based dialogue or problem‑solving session in which agents negotiate, solve puzzles, or generate creative content. We employ a tiered, knockout‑style tournament structure, supplemented by a *refinement phase* that re‑matches top performers to expose fine‑grained differences. Performance is measured using a composite metric that aggregates task‑specific accuracy, fluency, coherence, and strategic diversity. To mitigate variance, we run 100+ match‑runs per agent pair and use Bayesian ranking to estimate confidence intervals.

Applying CATArena to a suite of 15 benchmark domains—including commonsense reasoning, collaborative storytelling, and multi‑agent negotiation—we demonstrate that iterative competition uncovers latent strengths and weaknesses that static tests miss. For instance, agents that excel in single‑shot tasks often falter in long‑term strategy, whereas agents designed for turn‑based reasoning outperform on collaborative tasks. Our analysis reveals that tournament dynamics drive agents to adapt more robustly than conventional fine‑tuning, and we provide evidence of emergent cooperative behavior in cross‑agent dialogues.

CATArena offers a scalable, transparent, and extensible platform for LLM evaluation, bridging the gap between isolated benchmarks and real‑world multi‑agent interactions. We release the full framework, dataset, and a leaderboard to encourage community participation and continuous improvement of LLM agents.
1582:
The evolution of artificial intelligence points toward increasingly complex, agent‑based systems in which independently engineered agents—each carrying distinct knowledge, access rights, and tools—must cooperate. The effectiveness of such systems hinges on how well these heterogeneous agents can collaborate, especially when they have only partial visibility of the environment. Yet, large‑scale empirical investigations of agent‑to‑agent cooperation remain scarce. To address this gap, we introduce a maze‑solving benchmark that (i) focuses solely on collaborative skills, (ii) allows the difficulty to be systematically varied, (iii) supports automatic, high‑throughput evaluation, and (iv) imposes no rigid output formatting, thereby maintaining ecological relevance.

Using this framework we test 32 state‑of‑the‑art open‑ and closed‑source models in three settings: solo play, homogeneous pairs, and heterogeneous pairs. The results expose a pronounced “collaboration gap”: models that excel alone often suffer significant performance drops when forced to work together, with some compact, well‑tuned models failing almost entirely in particular pairings. We observe that beginning a task with the stronger agent and then passing control to the weaker one—a strategy we call “relay inference”—consistently improves joint outcomes, narrowing the gap considerably.

These findings highlight the need for (1) evaluation protocols that explicitly assess collaborative competence, (2) training methods designed to cultivate inter‑agent cooperation, and (3) interaction designs that reliably tap into agents’ hidden skills. Such guidance is applicable to both AI–AI and human–AI collaboration scenarios.
1583: In fields such as healthcare, finance, and e‑commerce, the evolution of relational data is driven by intricate interactions—for example, between patients and providers or between users and products spanning many categories. A practical model for these data must capture long‑range spatial and temporal dependencies across heterogeneous entities and support a variety of predictive tasks simultaneously. Existing graph‑based approaches, however, largely concentrate on spatial structure; they treat time simply as a filter to omit future events rather than as a source of signal, and they are usually tailored to single‑task prediction. To bridge this gap, we propose a temporal sub‑graph sampler that expands the context beyond immediate neighborhoods, thereby retrieving temporally pertinent connections. We also introduce the Relational Graph Perceiver (RGP), a transformer‑style architecture that uses a cross‑attention latent bottleneck to fuse structural and temporal cues efficiently. This bottleneck consolidates information from multiple node and edge types into a shared latent space, allowing the model to form a global view of the entire relational system. Furthermore, RGP employs a flexible cross‑attention decoder that facilitates joint learning across tasks with distinct label sets within a single model. Experiments on the RelBench, SALT, and CTU benchmarks demonstrate that RGP achieves state‑of‑the‑art results, providing a general and scalable framework for relational deep learning that accommodates diverse predictive objectives.
1584:
Multivariate time‑series data are ubiquitous in modern cyber‑physical and industrial systems, yet detecting subtle, temporally correlated anomalies in such streams remains a challenging problem.  We propose a unified *Hidden Markov Model* (HMM) framework for multivariate anomaly detection that treats the evolution of hidden system states as the primary vehicle for capturing normal dynamics while exposing deviations through low‑likelihood observations.  Our framework comprises three key components: (i) a feature‑learning stage that aggregates raw sensor streams into a compact, temporally‑resolved representation; (ii) an HMM‑based generative model that is trained on clean data using expectation‑maximization, thereby learning both emission and transition distributions that reflect the joint multivariate dynamics; and (iii) a statistical anomaly‑scoring mechanism that evaluates the likelihood of each new observation sequence and flags events whose likelihood falls below a data‑driven threshold.  

We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three benchmark datasets (SWaT, Secure Water Treatment, and a large‑scale industrial IoT telemetry set) and compare against state‑of‑the‑art approaches such as LSTM‑based reconstruction, isolation forests, and VAR‑based change‑point detection.  Across all datasets our HMM framework achieves a 15 % improvement in F1‑score and a 30 % reduction in false‑positive rate, while maintaining sub‑second detection latency.  Moreover, the modular design of our framework allows seamless integration of additional sensors and dynamic re‑training, making it well suited for evolving operational environments.  These results establish Hidden Markov Models as a powerful, interpretable foundation for real‑time, multivariate anomaly detection in complex time‑series settings.
1585:
Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is the most common inherited form of intellectual disability and is characterized by pervasive deficits in attention, working memory, and auditory processing. Recent evidence suggests that closed‑loop auditory stimulation can entrain neural oscillations and ameliorate cognitive dysfunction, yet optimal stimulation parameters remain highly individual. We introduce **Brian Intensify**, a novel adaptive machine‑learning framework that integrates real‑time electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring with personalized auditory stimulation to enhance cognition in individuals with FXS.

The framework employs a hybrid deep‑learning architecture that simultaneously estimates cortical state from multichannel EEG and predicts the most effective stimulation protocol (frequency, amplitude, and envelope shape). A reinforcement‑learning agent continuously refines stimulation parameters based on immediate changes in spectral power and behavioral performance, enabling a truly adaptive, closed‑loop interaction. To validate Brian Intensify, we conducted a randomized, double‑blind, crossover pilot study with 24 adults diagnosed with FXS (ages 18‑35). Each participant underwent six 30‑minute sessions of auditory stimulation (high‑frequency burst, theta‑entrainment, and sham) delivered via headphones while EEG was recorded. Cognitive outcomes were assessed using the Auditory Working Memory Task (AWMT) and the Continuous Performance Test (CPT).

Statistical analysis revealed a significant interaction between stimulation condition and time (p < 0.01). Adaptive theta‑entrainment yielded the largest improvements in AWMT accuracy (+18 % ± 5 %) and CPT reaction time (+12 % ± 4 %), outperforming high‑frequency burst (p = 0.04) and sham conditions (p < 0.001). EEG results showed a pronounced increase in theta band power (6–9 Hz) and a reduction in beta desynchronization following adaptive stimulation, correlating with behavioral gains (r = 0.68). No adverse events were reported.

Brian Intensify demonstrates that a machine‑learning–guided, closed‑loop auditory stimulation protocol can dynamically tailor neural entrainment to the unique electrophysiological signatures of individuals with FXS, producing measurable cognitive enhancement. This framework represents a promising step toward personalized neurorehabilitation in neurodevelopmental disorders and offers a scalable platform for future clinical deployment.
1586:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are celebrated for delivering rapid, personalized answers to natural‑language queries, yet their ability to deduce users’ demographic traits raises ethical questions about bias, implicit personalization, and the emergence of echo chambers. This paper investigates how ChatGPT’s responses vary when it infers political viewpoints across global conversations, and how its custom‑instruction and memory mechanisms modulate these outputs.  

We constructed three distinct personas—two explicitly political (one liberal, one conservative) and one neutral—each associated with four statements about DEI initiatives, abortion, gun rights, and vaccination. By feeding these statements to ChatGPT via custom instructions and its memory feature, we enabled the model to infer each persona’s stance without explicit disclosure. Subsequent questions were posed to elicit viewpoint differences, and the resulting replies were examined qualitatively.  

The analysis shows that ChatGPT’s replies consistently align with the inferred political leanings of the personas, exhibiting distinct reasoning patterns and vocabulary even on comparable topics. The influence of both explicit custom instructions and implicit memory was similar, and similarity metrics revealed that the liberal persona’s responses under custom instruction most closely matched those of the neutral persona, suggesting a left‑leaning bias in ChatGPT’s outputs.
1587:
Enhancing the “thinking budget” of large language models can markedly boost their accuracy, yet not every query demands the same amount of reasoning. Users often wish to balance output quality against latency and cost, allocating varying degrees of reasoning effort to each prompt. Existing tools typically let users set a fixed token count, which forces them to estimate the problem’s difficulty beforehand—a cumbersome requirement. 

To overcome this, we introduce **Adaptive Effort Control**, a reinforcement‑learning framework that endows models with the ability to use a user‑defined fraction of tokens relative to the current average chain‑of‑thought length for each query. This self‑adjusting method removes the need for dataset‑ or phase‑specific tuning and yields superior cost‑accuracy trade‑off curves compared to conventional approaches. At inference time, users can fine‑tune the cost‑accuracy balance through a continuous “effort” parameter. 

Across model scales from 1.5 B to 32 B parameters, our technique automatically tailors resource allocation to task difficulty, achieving a 2–3× reduction in chain‑of‑thought length while preserving or improving performance relative to the base model used during RL training.
1588: Structured Data Question Answering (QA)—encompassing table QA, Knowledge Graph (KG) QA, and temporal KG QA—remains a crucial research frontier. Recent progress with large language models (LLMs) has enabled unified frameworks such as TrustUQA, yet these approaches falter when deployed with smaller LLMs, which frequently make mistakes in generating the necessary structured queries. To bolster the QA performance of compact LLMs, we introduce Self‑Correction Distillation (SCD). SCD incorporates an Error Prompt Mechanism (EPM) that detects inaccuracies and supplies tailored error messages during inference. It further employs a two‑stage distillation pipeline that transfers both query‑generation and error‑correction expertise from large‑scale LLMs to their smaller counterparts. Across five benchmarks covering three types of structured data, SCD outperforms competing distillation techniques on 8‑B models and narrows the gap to GPT‑4 on several datasets. Moreover, large‑scale LLMs augmented with EPM achieve state‑of‑the‑art results on most benchmarks.
1589: Many multimodal misinformation datasets are skewed toward particular modalities, enabling classifiers to base their predictions on a single view of the data. Prior work has either measured bias only at the dataset level or manually traced spurious correlations between modalities and labels, leaving a gap in fine‑grained, scalable analysis for individual instances. In this study, we develop an automated framework to detect modality bias at the sample level. We introduce three complementary quantification schemes rooted in different granularity perspectives: (1) a coarse‑grained assessment of the relative benefit of each modality; (2) a medium‑level evaluation of information flow between modalities and labels; and (3) a fine‑grained causal analysis. We validate our approach through a human evaluation on two widely used benchmarks. The results highlight three key insights that may guide future work: (1) combining multiple bias perspectives is essential for reliable automated detection; (2) automated methods are susceptible to fluctuations induced by the underlying classifier; and (3) while the views concur on modality‑balanced instances, they diverge markedly on biased ones.
1590: Federated learning of large‑scale models has become indispensable for privacy‑preserving AI, yet the sheer size of modern architectures inflates the communication burden and hampers training stability. Existing federated optimizers either rely on momentum‑based variants of SGD that require many communication rounds, or on full‑batch Adam variants that suffer from divergent behavior under non‑IID data. In this paper we introduce **FedAdamW**, a lightweight federated optimizer that marries the adaptive per‑parameter step sizing of Adam with a principled weight‑decay regularization scheme, tailored specifically for distributed large‑model training. FedAdamW leverages *layer‑wise compression* and *periodic global aggregation* to reduce communication payloads, while preserving the convergence guarantees of the centralised AdamW algorithm. We prove that, under standard smoothness and bounded gradient variance assumptions, FedAdamW converges to a stationary point of the federated objective at a rate of \(O(1/\sqrt{T})\) with only \(\log(1/\epsilon)\) communication rounds to reach \(\epsilon\)‑accuracy. Furthermore, we derive generalization bounds that quantify how the interplay of adaptive learning rates and weight‑decay mitigates over‑fitting on heterogeneous local datasets. Extensive experiments on federated language modeling (GPT‑2, BERT) and vision tasks (ViT) across heterogeneous edge devices demonstrate that FedAdamW cuts communication cost by up to **4×** compared with FedAvg and FedAdam, while achieving comparable or superior test accuracy, especially in the presence of severe label skew. These results confirm that FedAdamW is a practical, communication‑efficient optimizer that delivers both convergence speed and robust generalization for federated large‑scale models.
1591: Human oversight remains a pivotal safeguard against the unintended consequences of increasingly autonomous AI systems. Yet, existing approaches typically treat humans and AI as separate actors, leading to sub‑optimal decision‑making and brittle accountability. In this paper we formalize *Human‑AI Complementarity* as a design principle that explicitly aligns the strengths and weaknesses of each partner to amplify collective oversight. We first define a spectrum of complementarity profiles (e.g., *cognitive specialization*, *risk‑tolerance balancing*, and *contextual intuition*), and then propose a lightweight, model‑agnostic framework that dynamically partitions tasks and confidence thresholds between a human operator and a machine‑learning controller. To evaluate our approach we conduct a multi‑domain study—comprising medical triage, financial fraud detection, and autonomous vehicle navigation—comparing three oversight regimes: (i) human‑only, (ii) AI‑only, and (iii) complementarity. Across all domains, the complementarity regime reduces error rates by 24–38 % relative to human‑only oversight and improves calibration of uncertainty estimates by 12–18 %. Qualitative analysis reveals that complementarity enables more transparent, explainable interventions and reduces cognitive overload in high‑stakes scenarios. We conclude by outlining guidelines for embedding complementarity into regulatory standards and by identifying open challenges in adaptive role assignment and trust calibration. This work demonstrates that, when orchestrated properly, human and AI agents can jointly deliver oversight that is greater than the sum of its parts.
1592: Standpoint logics provide a unified, modal‑logic‑based framework for representing multiple, heterogeneous viewpoints. At the same time, a variety of non‑monotonic reasoning systems can be expressed naturally with modal logics, particularly with S4F. In this paper we introduce **S4F‑Standpoint Logic**, a new formalism that extends both S4F and standpoint propositional logic, thus enabling the articulation of multi‑viewpoint, non‑monotonic semantic commitments. We give a precise definition of its syntax and semantics, and we study its computational complexity, showing that the new logic is no harder to decide than its underlying components, whether considered in a monotonic or non‑monotonic setting. Finally, we describe procedures for both credulous and sceptical acceptance and demonstrate the expressiveness of the framework through an illustrative example.
1593: Traditional Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems struggle with invoices that feature diverse layouts, handwritten entries, and poor scan quality. Their reliance on rigid templates limits adaptability across different document structures. Modern approaches now harness sophisticated deep‑learning techniques—including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Transformers, and domain‑specific models—to perform more accurate layout analysis and section‑level extraction on varied document types. Large Language Models (LLMs) have further transformed extraction pipelines, enabling advanced entity recognition and semantic understanding that maps complex contextual relationships without explicit programming. Visual Named Entity Recognition (NER) techniques extract information directly from invoice images with heightened contextual awareness and markedly improved accuracy over legacy methods. Current best practices employ hybrid architectures that combine OCR and LLMs, achieving high scalability while reducing manual oversight. In this paper we present a comprehensive AI platform that integrates OCR, deep learning, LLMs, and graph analytics to deliver unprecedented extraction quality and consistency.
1594:
The rapid integration of large language models into search interfaces has challenged traditional metrics of information retrieval performance. While precision and recall remain the gold standard, emerging evidence suggests that human‑like dialogue—embodied in tone, style, and conversational cues—may profoundly shape user engagement, perceived trust, and task satisfaction. This study investigates the trade‑off between *personality* and *precision* in ChatGPT‑powered search by conducting a 2 × 2 factorial experiment (Human‑Likeness × Precision) with 240 participants performing fact‑retrieval and exploratory search tasks. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four chatbot conditions: (1) highly personalized, conversational (High Personality, Low Precision), (2) highly personalized with strict factual constraints (High Personality, High Precision), (3) formal, terse responses (Low Personality, Low Precision), and (4) formal, fact‑focused replies (Low Personality, High Precision). Objective measures (retrieval accuracy, time‑to‑completion) and subjective metrics (perceived usefulness, trust, emotional engagement) were collected.

Results reveal a complex interaction: for knowledge‑intensive queries, high precision significantly improves accuracy but does not compensate for lower user satisfaction when personality is absent. Conversely, in exploratory or ambiguous contexts, a conversational persona markedly increases perceived usefulness and trust, without a statistically significant drop in retrieval accuracy. Importantly, the *Personality × Precision* interaction shows that a moderate level of human‑likeness can preserve precision while boosting engagement, whereas excessive verbosity erodes search efficiency.

Our findings suggest that design of conversational search agents should prioritize a calibrated balance between personality and precision, tailored to task type and user context. We propose a “Human‑Likeness‑Precision Continuum” model for evaluating and configuring large‑language‑model search systems. This work contributes the first empirical evidence on the influence of human‑likeness in ChatGPT‑based search, offers design guidelines for next‑generation conversational IR interfaces, and outlines future research directions on adaptive personality mechanisms.
1595:
Traditional student‑simulation frameworks often treat learners as static, “perfect” agents that exhibit deterministic memory retention and retrieval patterns. In reality, learners evolve through distinct developmental trajectories—acquiring, consolidating, and refining knowledge in a non‑linear fashion that is influenced by prior experience, feedback, and contextual factors. This paper presents **The Imperfect Learner**, a novel memory‑based student‑simulation architecture that embeds developmental trajectories into a neural‑symbolic representation of working and long‑term memory.

Our approach augments a probabilistic ACT‑R‑style memory model with a hierarchical Bayesian learner that learns individual growth curves for skill acquisition and forgetting. The model explicitly captures age‑dependent decay rates, spaced‑repetition effects, and domain‑specific transfer dynamics, thereby allowing simulations to reflect realistic learning curves at the cohort and individual level. We evaluate the framework on two large educational datasets—(i) a 1‑million‑interaction MOOC log of algebra and (ii) a high‑school science curriculum dataset—comparing predicted performance against actual test scores.

Results demonstrate a 12 % reduction in mean absolute error relative to baseline memory models and a significant improvement (p < 0.01) in capturing the temporal variability of student mastery across topics. Ablation studies confirm that incorporating developmental priors is essential for simulating the “imperfect” nature of human learning. The proposed architecture offers a scalable, interpretable simulation tool that can inform adaptive pacing, targeted feedback, and curriculum design in intelligent tutoring systems.

By marrying memory‑based cognitive modeling with developmental trajectory inference, this work provides a principled foundation for next‑generation student simulators that reflect the nuanced evolution of learning.
1596:
We introduce **Non‑Monotonic S4F Standpoint Logic (NM‑S4F)**, a novel framework for reasoning about agents’ beliefs under uncertainty when their epistemic standpoints evolve in a defeasible manner. Classical S4F, the modal logic of “standpoints” introduced to capture knowledge with a hierarchical notion of trust, is inherently monotonic and thus inadequate for modelling situations where new information can invalidate previously held standpoints. NM‑S4F augments S4F with a *defeasible* operator 𝔇 that governs the persistence of standpoints, together with a set of non‑monotonic inference rules inspired by default logic and circumscription. 

We formalise the syntax and give a Kripke‑style semantics based on *dynamic standpoint frames*—graphs of possible worlds where edges are labelled not only with accessibility but also with priority‐dependent “standpoint‑reassignment” functions. The semantics captures the intuition that an agent’s viewpoint may be overridden by higher‑priority standpoints when new evidence arrives. We prove soundness and completeness of a Hilbert‑style calculus and show that the satisfiability problem for NM‑S4F is decidable, albeit with a double‑exponential time complexity. Moreover, we provide a polynomial‑time tableau algorithm for the fragment with a single standpoint variable, making the logic amenable to practical applications. 

Finally, we illustrate the expressive power of NM‑S4F through two case studies: (1) modelling epistemic change in multi‑agent planning, and (2) formalising belief revision under conflicting evidence in knowledge bases. Our results open a new research direction for integrating non‑monotonic reasoning into standpoint‑based epistemic frameworks.
1597:
Training large language models (LLMs) is fundamentally limited by the memory available on each device and the high cost of exchanging data across devices. Pipeline parallelism can relieve memory pressure by splitting a model across multiple GPUs, but it introduces an activation‑exchange cost that grows linearly with the sequence length, curbing performance when long contexts are required. Recent “weight‑passing” schemes such as WeiPipe alleviate this by sending model weights rather than activations, yet they still incur duplicated peer‑to‑peer (P2P) transfers and leave much of the intra‑node bandwidth untapped.  

In this work we introduce **TawPipe**—a topology‑aware weight pipeline parallelism that takes advantage of the hierarchical bandwidth structure in distributed clusters to reduce communication overhead. TawPipe: (i) partitions devices according to the underlying network topology, enabling efficient intra‑node collectives and inter‑node P2P links; (ii) assigns each device a permanent shard of the model’s weights and gradients, eliminating redundant transfers; and (iii) overlaps communication with computation to mask latency. By confining the bulk of data exchange inside node boundaries—rather than using global collectives as in fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP)—TawPipe drastically cuts cross‑node traffic.  

We evaluate the method on up to 24 GPUs training LLaMA‑style models and show that TawPipe consistently outperforms existing baselines in both throughput and scalability.
1598:
Although reference libraries and computational tools are increasingly abundant, the field of metabolomics still suffers from a low rate of spectral annotation. Recent breakthroughs with large language models (LLMs) have produced remarkable results in diverse generation and reasoning tasks, prompting interest in applying these models to specialized scientific problems such as mass‑spectra annotation. In this study we introduce **General Intelligence‑based Fragmentation (GIF)**, a framework that steers pretrained LLMs through spectra simulation by using structured prompts and multi‑step reasoning. GIF incorporates tagging, well‑defined input‑output formats, system prompts, instruction‑based prompts, and iterative refinement, offering a systematic alternative to ad hoc prompting and demonstrating the necessity of disciplined guidance for complex scientific workloads.

We apply GIF to assess the ability of state‑of‑the‑art generalist LLMs to reason about fragmentation pathways and to predict peak intensities after fine‑tuning. The evaluation is carried out on a new question‑answering dataset, *MassSpecGym QA‑sim*, derived from the MassSpecGym benchmark. Within this framework, GPT‑4o and GPT‑4o‑mini achieve cosine similarities of 0.36 and 0.35, respectively, between simulated and authentic spectra, surpassing other pretrained models—including the newer GPT‑5, Llama‑3.1, and the domain‑specific ChemDFM—even though GPT‑5 is more recent and ChemDFM is tailored to chemistry. GIF also outperforms several deep‑learning baselines.

Our results underscore the promise of LLMs not only for simulating mass spectra but also for enabling human‑in‑the‑loop workflows and producing structured, explainable reasoning in molecular fragmentation.
1599: TRISKELION‑1 is an integrated descriptive‑predictive‑generative system that unifies statistical, mechanistic, and generative reasoning inside a single encoder‑decoder architecture. By leveraging variational objectives, the model jointly optimizes representation learning, inference, and synthesis. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate that accurate reconstruction, reliable classification, and plausible sample generation can all be achieved stably within one framework. This approach offers a roadmap for building universal intelligence systems that balance interpretability, performance, and creative capability.
1600: The rapid democratization of generative and agentic artificial intelligence has lowered the barrier to entrepreneurship, yet solo founders still confront a daunting spectrum of challenges—from ideation to scaling—without the breadth of skills typically distributed across a founding team. This paper introduces the concept of **Digital Co‑Founders (DCFs)**: autonomous, multi‑agent AI systems designed to partner with individual entrepreneurs in translating nascent ideas into viable, market‑ready businesses. We formalize the DCF architecture along three pillars: (1) *Vision‑Synthesis* agents that refine creative concepts into business models, (2) *Execution‑Orchestration* agents that manage product development, marketing, and operations, and (3) *Strategic‑Feedback* agents that provide continuous performance monitoring and pivot recommendations. Using a mixed‑methods approach, we implemented a prototype DCF framework in a controlled laboratory setting and evaluated it across 12 solo founders with diverse industries and skillsets. Quantitative metrics—time-to-MVP, funding readiness scores, and early customer acquisition—show significant improvements over a baseline group lacking AI assistance (median reduction of 37 % in development time, 42 % increase in validated revenue projections). Qualitative interviews reveal that DCFs enhance decision confidence, reduce cognitive load, and foster iterative learning cycles. Our findings suggest that agentic AI, when thoughtfully integrated as a digital co‑founder, can effectively bridge the expertise gap for solo entrepreneurs, accelerating the path from imagination to sustainable venture. We conclude with a discussion of ethical implications, governance frameworks, and future research directions for scaling digital co‑founder ecosystems.
1601:
We introduce **Step‑Audio‑EditX**, the first open‑source large‑language‑model‑driven audio framework that delivers highly expressive, iterative editing of speech—including emotional tone, speaking style, and paralinguistic nuances—while also offering strong zero‑shot text‑to‑speech (TTS) performance.  
Our key contribution is a large‑margin synthetic‑dataset training strategy that eliminates the need for embedding‑based priors or auxiliary components. This approach supports fine‑grained, iterative control across diverse voices and represents a shift away from traditional representation‑level disentanglement.  
Experiments show that Step‑Audio‑EditX outperforms leading models such as MiniMax‑2.6‑hd and Doubao‑Seed‑TTS‑2.0 on emotion editing and other detailed manipulation tasks.
1602: The rapid diffusion of large‑scale generative models (e.g., GPT‑4, Codex, LLaMA) has reshaped the software‑engineering landscape, yet their full potential remains largely unexplored in production settings. The European GENIUS (Generative Engineering Innovation in UNiversal Software) Project brings together a pan‑European consortium of leading industry partners and academic research groups to chart a holistic vision for generative AI in software engineering. This paper synthesises findings from a series of cross‑disciplinary workshops, empirical pilots, and design‑science studies carried out over the first two years of the project. We identify five critical domains—code synthesis, automated testing, requirements reasoning, model‑driven architecture, and maintenance analytics—where generative AI promises to deliver measurable productivity gains, while also exposing new risk vectors such as hallucination, bias, and intellectual‑property disputes. To address these challenges, we propose a set of integrative guidelines that combine technical safeguards (e.g., confidence‑based gating, model‑distillation for explainability), process‑oriented practices (e.g., AI‑augmented review cycles, traceability frameworks), and regulatory compliance mechanisms aligned with the EU AI Act and GDPR. The paper also presents an open‑source evaluation benchmark, “GENIUS‑Bench,” and a reference architecture for embedding generative AI services into existing CI/CD pipelines. By aligning industry‑driven use‑cases with academic rigour, the GENIUS Project outlines a roadmap for a trustworthy, sustainable, and human‑centric generative‑AI ecosystem in software engineering. This vision sets the stage for subsequent EU‑wide policy recommendations and establishes a baseline for future empirical validation in diverse development contexts.
1603:
The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has spurred interest in their application to biomedical decision support. Yet, most existing benchmarks emphasize surface‑level language tasks and do not probe the nuanced reasoning that clinicians employ when critically appraising evidence. To address this gap, we introduce **CareMedEval**, a high‑quality, multimodal dataset designed to evaluate *critical appraisal* and *domain‑specific reasoning* in the biomedical field. CareMedEval comprises 4,321 evidence‑based clinical vignette pairs drawn from peer‑reviewed systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials, and guideline statements. For each vignette we provide: (1) a *clinical question* (PICO style), (2) a *concise evidence summary*, (3) an *automated inference chain* detailing the logical steps (e.g., study design, bias assessment, effect size interpretation), and (4) a *critical appraisal score* (0–5) from two domain experts. The dataset further annotates 2,147 reasoning subcomponents (e.g., risk of bias judgments, statistical significance checks) using a fine‑grained taxonomy, enabling fine‑grained evaluation of model outputs.

We formalize two tasks over CareMedEval: (i) **Critical Appraisal Generation** – predict the appraisal score and rationale given a clinical question and evidence; (ii) **Reasoning Chain Extraction** – produce a step‑by‑step chain linking evidence to conclusion. Baseline experiments with state‑of‑the‑art LLMs (e.g., GPT‑4, PaLM‑2) reveal average F1 scores of 0.62 for appraisal generation and 0.54 for chain extraction, indicating a substantial head‑start for future research. We also demonstrate that fine‑tuning on CareMedEval improves downstream performance on related clinical NLP tasks such as evidence extraction and question answering.

CareMedEval fills a critical need for benchmarks that reflect the depth of human reasoning required in medical evidence synthesis. By providing rich annotations, a rigorous evaluation protocol, and a publicly released corpus, we invite the community to develop and assess AI systems that can genuinely support evidence‑based clinical practice.
1604: The rapid deployment of AIoT in smart‑home settings has heightened the need for machine‑learning models that are both transparent and interpretable.  Explainable AI (XAI) tools—especially post‑hoc techniques such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model‑Agnostic Explanations (LIME)—are routinely used to reveal how predictions are made.  However, recent work has shown that these explanations can unintentionally disclose private user attributes and behaviors, creating a new privacy threat.  To counter this, we introduce a novel privacy‑preserving strategy that incorporates an entropy‑based regularization term into SHAP.  During training, the regularizer penalises attribution distributions with low entropy, thereby encouraging a more even spread of feature contributions and limiting the amount of sensitive information that can be inferred from the explanations.  We evaluate the method by constructing a set of SHAP‑driven privacy attacks, and by comparing our model against baselines on standard smart‑home energy‑consumption datasets.  Results indicate that SHAP entropy regularization markedly reduces privacy leakage while preserving both predictive performance and the fidelity of the explanations.  This work thus contributes a practical, privacy‑aware approach to explainable AIoT deployments.
1605:
Interpreting the hidden workings of language models hinges on translating their internal states into human‑readable concepts. Although recent dictionary‑learning approaches, notably Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), show promise for extracting such concepts, they routinely miss the deep semantic knowledge that underpins linguistic understanding. Instead, they gravitate toward shallow, token‑specific, or noisy cues—think of the phrase “The” that appears at sentence beginnings. We argue that this shortcoming stems from a core flaw in how dictionary learning is carried out for LLMs. Modern unsupervised techniques largely ignore the rich, well‑established structure of language across syntax, semantics, and pragmatics, so the learned features end up favoring surface patterns over substantive concepts.

To address this, we exploit a key property of language: semantic information varies slowly and exhibits long‑range dependencies, whereas syntactic signals are typically local. Leveraging this insight, we propose Temporal Sparse Autoencoders (T‑SAEs), which augment the standard SAE objective with a contrastive loss that encourages high‑level feature activations to remain consistent across neighboring tokens. This simple yet effective tweak allows the model to disentangle semantic from syntactic patterns in a self‑supervised fashion.

Evaluated on a variety of datasets and language models, T‑SAEs recover smooth, coherent semantic concepts while maintaining reconstruction fidelity. Remarkably, they reveal clear semantic structure without any explicit semantic supervision, opening a new avenue for unsupervised interpretability of language models.
1606:
A key obstacle in human‑AI collaboration is the “intention expression gap”: users often cannot convey their complex, high‑dimensional goals to an AI in a single instruction, forcing them into costly trial‑and‑error interactions. This problem is amplified by the wide spectrum of user expertise. Instead of treating collaboration as passive instruction following, we cast it as a Socratic dialogue and introduce **Nous**, an agent that actively asks targeted questions to reduce its uncertainty about the user’s intent.  

Nous is trained through a principled framework based on information theory. We use the dialogue‑derived information gain—equivalent to a reduction in Shannon entropy over a structured task space—as an intrinsic reward, thereby eliminating the need for expensive human preference labels or external reward models.  

To evaluate our approach, we build an automated simulation pipeline that produces a large, preference‑based dataset for the challenging task of scientific diagram generation. Extensive experiments—including ablations, objective and subjective assessments, and tests across varying user expertise—demonstrate that Nous delivers superior efficiency and output quality while remaining robust to user skill level. Its architecture is domain‑agnostic, and we provide evidence of successful transfer to other tasks beyond diagram generation.  

Overall, Nous offers a principled, scalable, and adaptive method for resolving uncertainty about user intent in complex human‑AI collaboration scenarios.
1607:
Time‑series forecasting in real‑world domains frequently suffers from *concept drift*—the gradual or abrupt change in the underlying data generation process—which degrades the performance of conventional deep learning models that are trained on static historical data. In this work we present **DeepBooTS** (Dual‑Stream Residual Boosting for Drift‑Resilient Time‑Series Forecasting), a novel neural architecture that explicitly tackles drift while preserving high predictive accuracy. 

DeepBooTS employs a *dual‑stream* design: the first stream learns a robust base forecast from long‑term dependencies via a residual‑connected Transformer backbone, while the second stream processes short‑term, high‑frequency corrections through a lightweight convolutional encoder. The two streams are coupled by a *residual boosting* module that iteratively refines the base prediction by learning the residual error distribution conditioned on drift signals extracted from recent observation windows. This gating mechanism allows the model to adaptively weight the contribution of each stream as the drift dynamics evolve. 

We further introduce a *self‑supervised drift detection loss* that encourages the network to maintain a low‑variance reconstruction error under stationary regimes, while signalling drift when the error rises beyond a learned threshold. This loss obviates the need for explicit drift labels and facilitates online adaptation.

Extensive experiments on a suite of benchmark datasets—including traffic, electricity consumption, and sensor‑based industrial time series—show that DeepBooTS consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art drift‑aware baselines such as DARTS‑DR, AdaRNN, and Transformer‑CTM, reducing mean absolute error by up to 18 % under synthetic sudden‑drift scenarios and by 12 % on real‑world datasets with gradual drift. Ablation studies confirm the complementary role of the dual streams and the efficacy of residual boosting. Our results demonstrate that DeepBooTS offers a principled, scalable solution for reliable forecasting in non‑stationary environments.
1608:
Robotic agents operating in real‑world environments must *ground* natural‑language instructions in their sensory observations, a capability that hinges on precise spatial reasoning. Conventional end‑to‑end neural models achieve high performance on synthetic benchmarks but struggle to generalise to the rich, noisy multimodal data encountered in robotics, while purely symbolic systems lack the perception robustness required for unconstrained scenes. We introduce a **multi‑modal neuro‑symbolic framework** that unifies deep perceptual encoders with rule‑based spatial inference to perform visual grounding that is both *data‑efficient* and *explainable*.

Our architecture first extracts joint visual‑semantic embeddings from RGB‑D and lidar streams and a language encoder, yielding a dense representation of scene geometry and linguistic affordances. A graph‑structured *spatial relation module* translates these embeddings into a symbolic knowledge base (KB) of object attributes and relative predicates (e.g., “left‑of”, “on‑top-of”). A lightweight forward‑chaining reasoner operates over this KB to evaluate candidate grounding hypotheses, producing a distribution over referent objects that is subsequently refined by a neural scoring network. The neuro‑symbolic loop is trained end‑to‑end using a multi‑task loss that encourages both perceptual fidelity and logical consistency.

We evaluate our approach on two challenging benchmarks: the **Spatial‑VQA** dataset (synthetic 3D scenes) and a newly constructed **Robotic‑Scene‑Grounding** (real‑world warehouse) test set. On both tasks our method surpasses purely neural baselines by 12–18 % in grounding accuracy, while maintaining a 25 % reduction in annotation effort due to the symbolic component’s sample efficiency. Ablation studies confirm that the symbolic inference layer is critical for correctly interpreting nested spatial expressions (“the cup *under* the red box on the left side of the table”). Furthermore, the system offers transparent reasoning traces, enabling downstream planners to validate object selections before actuation.

Our results demonstrate that integrating neuro‑perceptual feature extraction with lightweight spatial reasoning yields robust visual grounding for robotics, bridging the gap between perception, language understanding, and symbolic manipulation. This work paves the way for more reliable human‑robot interaction and high‑level task planning in complex, unstructured environments.
1609:
Cardiovascular disease remains the world’s leading cause of death. While electrocardiograms (ECGs) are the most common non‑invasive tool for cardiac assessment, large, richly annotated ECG datasets are limited by cost, privacy, and clinical workflow constraints. Synthetic ECGs could aid in mechanistic insight, enable creation of expansive, heterogeneous, and unbiased datasets, and support privacy‑preserving data exchange. However, realistic ECG synthesis that respects both clinical context and underlying physiology has not been thoroughly investigated.

In this work we introduce **SE‑Diff**, a novel diffusion‑based framework that augments ECG generation with two complementary knowledge sources. First, a lightweight ordinary‑differential‑equation (ODE) ECG simulator is woven into the diffusion process through a beat decoder and simulator‑consistent constraints, embedding mechanistic priors that yield physiologically plausible waveforms. Second, a large‑language‑model (LLM)–driven experience‑retrieval module supplies real‑world clinical expertise, steering the generation toward clinically meaningful patterns.

Across multiple real‑world ECG datasets, SE‑Diff outperforms existing text‑to‑ECG baselines in both waveform fidelity and semantic alignment with input prompts. Moreover, the integrated simulator and experience knowledge enhances downstream ECG classification tasks. Our approach demonstrates that incorporating domain physiology and clinical practice into generative models can markedly improve the realism and utility of synthetic ECGs.
1610: Tongyi DeepResearch presents a comprehensive technical report on the end‑to‑end development, scaling, and deployment of the Tongyi family of large‑scale multimodal language models. Leveraging a transformer backbone enriched with a mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) routing mechanism, the Tongyi architecture attains superior parameter efficiency while maintaining state‑of‑the‑art performance across diverse language, vision, and dialogue tasks. This report documents the design decisions underpinning the model’s modularity, including the hierarchical token‑level and task‑specific adapters that enable rapid fine‑tuning on downstream datasets with minimal compute overhead. We describe the training pipeline that integrates a heterogeneous corpus of 2.1 trillion tokens, spanning text, code, and visual annotations, and the novel curriculum‑based pre‑training schedule that progressively introduces multi‑modal signals to stabilize convergence. Extensive empirical studies evaluate Tongyi’s zero‑shot and few‑shot capabilities on benchmarks such as GPT‑4‑Eval, VLUE, and OpenAI’s API suite, demonstrating performance gains of 12–18 % relative to prior Chinese‑language models. Additionally, we report on large‑scale reinforcement‑learning‑from‑human‑feedback (RLHF) fine‑tuning that improves alignment with user intent while mitigating hallucinations. Finally, we discuss operational considerations—distributed training on 256 A800 GPUs, inference latency on edge devices, and model compression through structured sparsity. This technical report serves as a reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to reproduce Tongyi’s architecture, replicate its training regime, and adapt its multimodal capabilities to novel domains.
1611:
Large language models are now able to produce news articles, legal reports, and even software code with a fluency that rivals human writers. However, regulatory frameworks such as the EU AI Act require that every synthetic passage be stamped with an imperceptible, machine‑readable provenance tag. Conventional logit‑based watermarks satisfy this mandate by selecting a pseudorandom “green” vocabulary at each decoding step and boosting its logits. The drawback is that the random split can inadvertently exclude the most likely token, which degrades fluency. 

WaterMod tackles this issue with a probability‑aware modular rule. Tokens are first ordered by descending model probability. Their ranks are then grouped by their residue modulo k, which spreads adjacent—and thus semantically similar—tokens across different classes. A tiny bias is applied to one chosen class.  

In the zero‑bit case (k = 2), an entropy‑adaptive gate selects either the even or odd parity as the green list. Because the top two tokens occupy different parities, the watermark signal is still detectable while at least one highly‑probable token remains available for sampling.  

When k > 2, the payload digit d determines the color class whose ranks satisfy rank mod k = d. Biasing the logits of that class embeds one base‑k digit per decoding step, enabling fine‑grained provenance tracking. The same modular arithmetic therefore supports both binary attribution and richer payloads.  

Empirical studies confirm that WaterMod consistently delivers strong watermark detection while preserving generation quality across a variety of tasks—including natural language generation, mathematical reasoning, and code synthesis. All code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Shinwoo-Park/WaterMod.
1612: Realigning embeddings is an attractive technique for boosting cross‑lingual performance in multilingual language models. Nevertheless, past experiments have produced inconsistent and sometimes unreliable outcomes, especially for typologically distant or low‑resource languages (LRLs) when compared to English. A further limitation is that most word‑realignment tools depend on high‑quality parallel corpora—a resource that is often limited or noisy for many LRLs. In this paper we carry out a comprehensive empirical investigation to determine whether realignment truly benefits from incorporating every available language, or if a strategically chosen subset can deliver comparable—or even superior—transfer, with a particular focus on LRLs. Our controlled studies reveal that realignment is especially advantageous for LRLs and that a well‑chosen, linguistically diverse set of languages can match the performance of full multilingual alignment, sometimes outperforming it for previously unseen LRLs. These findings suggest that effective realignment does not necessitate exhaustive language coverage, can lower data‑collection demands, and remains both efficient and robust when guided by informed language selection.
1613: Assessing how well large language models perform in languages with limited resources remains difficult, because most current benchmarks either translate popular English tasks or test only basic comprehension. This study presents UA‑Code‑Bench, an open‑source benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate models on code‑generation and competitive‑programming tasks expressed in Ukrainian. The benchmark contains 500 E‑olymp problems, evenly spread across five difficulty tiers from very easy to very hard. We benchmarked 13 state‑of‑the‑art proprietary and open‑source systems, each instructed with a one‑shot prompt to generate Python solutions, and verified their outputs against hidden test cases in the official E‑olymp environment to ensure correctness. Results show that even the best performers—OpenAI’s o3 and GPT‑5—resolve only about half of the problems, underscoring the complexity of code generation in low‑resource languages. The paper also provides an in‑depth breakdown of performance by difficulty level, and examines solution uniqueness, as well as runtime and memory efficiency of the generated code. Overall, this work demonstrates the utility of competitive‑programming benchmarks for probing large language models in underrepresented languages, and sets the stage for future work on multilingual code generation and reasoning‑enhanced models. All benchmark data, scripts for parsing, preparation, generation, and evaluation are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NLPForUA/ua‑code‑bench.
1614:
Modern transformer‑based language models (LMs) achieve state‑of‑the‑art performance on a wide variety of tasks, yet their quadratic attention complexity and unbounded memory footprint make them impractical for truly long‑context settings such as document‑level reasoning or multi‑pass inference.  We propose **BudgetMem**, a learnable, cost‑aware memory controller that selectively preserves a compact subset of tokens from a long input while discarding redundant or low‑utility information.  BudgetMem operates as an auxiliary policy network that, for each incoming token, decides whether to write it into a fixed‑size memory buffer or to drop it, using a differentiable “write‑probability” score.  The policy is jointly optimized with the LM under a multi‑objective loss that balances task performance and a hard budget constraint on memory and compute.  At inference time the controller yields a succinct “summary” of the input that is fed to the transformer, reducing the effective sequence length without the need for manual truncation or external chunking heuristics.

We evaluate BudgetMem on several long‑context benchmarks – including PubMedQA, NarrativeQA, and a 50‑k‑token variant of the WIKIMINING dataset – with models ranging from GPT‑2 to T5‑Large.  Across all settings BudgetMem cuts average memory consumption by up to **55 %** and inference latency by **40 %** while incurring less than **1.8 %** drop in accuracy relative to full‑context baselines.  Ablation studies reveal that the learned policy learns to retain syntactic anchors, salient entities, and discourse markers, thereby preserving the semantic essence of the input.  Compared to existing efficient transformer architectures (e.g., Longformer, BigBird, Reformer), BudgetMem consistently achieves a superior trade‑off between computational cost and downstream performance, without requiring changes to the core transformer block.

BudgetMem demonstrates that a lightweight, trainable memory policy can enable cost‑efficient long‑context processing in large language models, opening the door to deployment in resource‑constrained settings and real‑time applications where context length and latency are critical constraints.
1615: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) continues to be a highly regarded and demanding benchmark for measuring progress toward Artificial General Intelligence. Unlike datasets that test an agent’s performance on pre‑defined tasks or its knowledge base, the ARC‑AGI collection is expressly designed to gauge how efficiently a system can learn new skills—a capability that remains elusive even for the most advanced ML models. A key limitation for methods that rely on many intra‑task examples is the small size of the ARC‑AGI training set, which supplies only a handful of input–output grid pairs per task. To widen the pool of usable training pairs, this paper presents ARC‑GEN, an open‑source procedural generator that expands the original ARC‑AGI data while staying faithful to its distributional characteristics. Unlike earlier attempts, our generator covers all four hundred ARC tasks exhaustively and mimics the structure of the initial ARC‑AGI‑1 release. We also demonstrate how this tool can be employed to produce a fixed benchmark suite for validating solutions in the 2025 Google Code Golf Championship.
1616:
Recent advances in large‐scale language and dialogue agents have been accompanied by an urgent need to guarantee that these systems respect user‑defined behavioral policies across extended interactions. Existing evaluation frameworks either focus on single‑turn compliance or rely on coarse‑grained rule checks that fail to capture the subtle dynamics of policy drift, context shifts, and adversarial prompting. We introduce the **Pluralistic Behavior Suite (PBS)**, a comprehensive, stress‑testing framework for multi‑turn adherence to arbitrary, custom‑defined behavioral policies. PBS comprises a library of 120 dialogue scenarios spanning 30 domains (e.g., finance, healthcare, customer support), each annotated with a fine‑grained policy graph that specifies permissible actions, forbidden content, and dynamic constraints (e.g., escalation triggers). The suite supports both synthetic and real‑world corpora, enabling systematic perturbation of policy boundaries, introduction of “policy‑violating” turns, and adversarial prompts. We define a set of quantitative metrics—policy‑violation rate, compliance latency, and policy‑consistency score—alongside a human‑in‑the‑loop audit protocol.

Using PBS we benchmark seven state‑of‑the‑art large language models under a variety of policy specifications, revealing significant variability in multi‑turn adherence and a pronounced “policy fatigue” effect after repeated non‑compliant prompts. The suite also uncovers latent policy gaps that are invisible to single‑turn tests. Finally, we demonstrate how PBS can guide targeted fine‑tuning and reinforcement‑learning‑from‑human‑feedback to improve robustness. PBS offers an open‑source, extensible platform for developers, researchers, and regulators to evaluate, debug, and certify the behavioral compliance of conversational agents in realistic, long‑horizon settings.
1617: Human‑motion style transfer aims to endow animated characters with fluid, realistic behaviours that reflect a particular stylistic flair. Conventional image‑style transfer methods rely mainly on matching mean and variance, a strategy that has also been adopted for motion data. However, because motion is inherently spatiotemporal, these low‑order statistics fail to capture its richer dynamic patterns and coherence. Motivated by this shortfall, we introduce two higher‑order descriptors—skewness and kurtosis—into the style analysis. Our novel Adaptive Statistics Fusor (AStF) comprises a Style Disentanglement Module (SDM) and a High‑Order Multi‑Statistics Attention (HOS‑Attn) sub‑network. It is trained alongside a Motion Consistency Regularization (MCR) discriminator. Experiments demonstrate that by modelling the full suite of spatiotemporal statistical traits present in motion styles, AStF outperforms existing state‑of‑the‑art approaches on several benchmark datasets. The code and trained models are available at https://github.com/CHMimilanlan/AStF.
1618:
Lexicographic multi‑objective problems—where several competing subtasks must be solved in a strict priority order—arise frequently in practical settings. While Reinforcement Learning excels on single tasks, extending conventional RL to handle prioritized objectives is nontrivial: standard Safe RL and Multi‑Objective RL techniques struggle to enforce priority relations efficiently. To bridge this gap, Lexicographic Multi‑Objective RL (LMORL) approaches have emerged, yet most either depend on ad‑hoc threshold tuning informed by prior knowledge or are limited to discrete action spaces.

We introduce **Lexicographically Projected Policy Gradient RL (LPPG‑RL)**, a new LMORL framework that is fully compatible with any policy‑gradient algorithm in continuous domains. LPPG‑RL employs a sequential gradient‑projection procedure to identify feasible policy‑update directions that respect the lexicographic order. Rather than solving the projection with generic optimizers, we cast it as a compact optimization problem and apply Dykstra’s projection algorithm, yielding significant speed‑ups for small‑to‑medium sized problems. Additionally, we propose a **Subproblem Exploration (SE)** mechanism to counteract gradient vanishing, accelerate convergence, and improve stability.

We prove convergence guarantees and establish a policy‑improvement lower bound for our method. Empirical evaluation on a 2‑D navigation benchmark demonstrates that LPPG‑RL surpasses existing state‑of‑the‑art continuous‑space LMORL algorithms, confirming its effectiveness and scalability.
1619:
Recent advances in multimodal representation learning have shown that speech and vision can be embedded into a shared latent space that captures high‑level semantic structure. However, the extent to which these embeddings reflect the neural processing of spoken language remains largely unexplored. In this work we present a framework for aligning non‑invasive brain signals—specifically magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings—with multimodal embeddings derived jointly from audio and visual streams. We first construct a task‑agnostic multimodal embedding space using a transformer‑based “Audio‑Visual BERT” (AV‑BERT) architecture, trained on a large corpus of paired speech and video data. To bridge the modality gap, we learn a linear mapping from the brain signal space to the AV‑BERT embedding space through canonical correlation analysis (CCA) augmented with a time‑lag regularization that accounts for hemodynamic delay. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of 50 participants who listened to natural speech while watching corresponding videos, with simultaneous MEG acquisition. Alignment performance is quantified by nearest‑neighbor retrieval accuracy and by the ability to recover stimulus‑specific semantic categories from the projected neural signals.

Our results demonstrate that the brain–embedding alignment achieves a mean retrieval accuracy of 62 %—substantially higher than chance (10 %) and outperforming baseline linear models by 15 %. Moreover, the alignment yields robust semantic decoding across subjects, revealing that visual context enhances neural representation of spoken content, as reflected by a 9 % increase in classification accuracy when audiovisual embeddings are used versus audio‑only embeddings. Finally, time‑resolved analysis shows that the optimal lag between MEG and embeddings corresponds to the expected cortical processing latency (~150 ms post‑stimulus), supporting the physiological plausibility of the mapping.

These findings provide a principled method for integrating multimodal embeddings into brain‑computer interfaces, offering a new avenue for decoding complex naturalistic stimuli and for investigating the neural correlates of multimodal perception. Our framework is extensible to other neuroimaging modalities and can guide the design of future cognitive neuroscience studies that leverage large‑scale, multimodal language models.
1620: Achieving highly accurate automated license‑plate recognition (ALPR) remains difficult because of challenging environmental conditions such as variable lighting, rain, and dust, as well as high vehicle speeds, diverse camera viewpoints, and low‑resolution imagery.
