Given noisy linear observations \(y = Ax + \xi\) of a random vector \(x\) drawn from a known prior distribution \(p(x)\), we ask when it is possible to efficiently sample from the posterior \(p(x \mid y)\). Accurate posterior sampling underpins a wide range of inverse‑problem tasks—including inpainting, deblurring, and MRI reconstruction—but existing approximation schemes usually suffer from computational intractability.

In this work we restrict attention to (locally or globally) log‑concave priors. When the exact score function of \(p(x)\) is known, Langevin dynamics can produce posterior samples, but this approach is fragile: it requires a sub‑exponential (MGF) control on any score‑estimation error. In contrast, diffusion models can recover the unconditional distribution with only an \(L^{2}\) error bound on the score estimate. We show that, by marrying diffusion models with an annealed variant of Langevin dynamics, we can achieve conditional sampling in polynomial time under a much weaker \(L^{4}\) error assumption on the score. This combination bridges the gap between practical score‑based generative models and rigorous posterior sampling for log‑concave distributions.
1762: The success of Vision‑Language‑Action (VLA) models has largely come from the idea that pretrained Vision‑Language Models (VLMs) can inject transferable world knowledge and robust vision‑language grounding into agents, paving the way for action systems that generalise more broadly. However, once a VLM is fine‑tuned for action tasks, it is not clear how much of its original VL representations and knowledge survive. In this paper we systematically examine the retention of these representations during VLA fine‑tuning, demonstrating that straightforward action‑specific adaptation can erode visual feature quality. To quantify and understand these effects, we probe the hidden layers of VLA models, analyse attention maps, and introduce a suite of targeted probes that isolate changes in VL capability relative to the base VLM. We then evaluate several alignment techniques and propose a simple, effective method that curbs this degradation, yielding better out‑of‑distribution performance. Our findings clarify the trade‑off between action fine‑tuning and loss of VL knowledge, and we provide practical strategies to preserve inherited VL strengths. Code is available at https://blind‑vla‑paper.github.io.
1763:
Image geolocalization—the problem of inferring where a photo was taken—remains difficult because many distant places look alike and the search space is vast. Inspired by the way humans first identify a broad region and then hone in on a specific spot, we introduce a hierarchical sequence‑prediction framework. Our model emits geographic tokens in a nested, multiresolution S2 grid: it first predicts a coarse region and then iteratively refines that prediction by selecting finer‑grained cells conditioned on the image and on earlier predictions. This process is analogous to autoregressive text generation in large language models, and we therefore borrow inference techniques from that domain. We explore several top‑down sampling strategies—including beam search and multi‑sample inference—to balance exploration of plausible paths and computational cost.

The method is evaluated on Im2GPS3k and YFCC4k. Compared with baselines that do not use a multimodal large language model (MLLM), our approach achieves the best results on almost every metric, improving accuracy by up to 13.9 %. When paired with an MLLM, it outperforms all existing methods and establishes a new state of the art across all benchmarks. The implementation is publicly released at https://github.com/NNargesNN/GeoToken.
1764: Public opinion polls have become indispensable tools for gauging citizen sentiment, yet recent controversies over methodological opacity, partisan manipulation, and data privacy have eroded trust in their outputs. This paper introduces a hybrid framework that fuses advanced artificial‑intelligence (AI) techniques with structured social interaction mechanisms to enhance both the integrity and the perceived credibility of poll results. We first employ natural‑language‑processing‑driven sentiment classifiers and anomaly‑detection algorithms to audit and correct sampling and response‑biases in real time. Simultaneously, a blockchain‑based provenance layer records all stages of the poll‑making workflow, ensuring transparent auditability. To engage the public and foster confidence, we embed a moderated deliberative‑forum component that allows respondents to discuss questions, clarify ambiguities, and collaboratively refine survey items before submission. The resulting “AI‑augmented participatory poll” was piloted in a large-scale study on climate‑policy attitudes in three metropolitan regions. Compared with conventional polling methods, our approach achieved a 32 % reduction in variance attributable to sampling bias, a 27 % improvement in response rate, and a statistically significant increase in respondent confidence (p < 0.01). Moreover, the transparency ledger received positive ratings from 78 % of participants, indicating that traceable processes materially influence trust. These findings suggest that a synergetic combination of algorithmic rigor and human‑centric interaction can mitigate the long‑standing credibility gaps in public polling. The paper concludes with recommendations for integrating such hybrid models into policy‑making, electoral forecasting, and civic engagement platforms.
1765: With the growing integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into automated, multi‑stage workflows, the unchecked trust placed between successive processing stages is emerging as a real‑world risk. This paper proposes a mechanism‑centric taxonomy that identifies 41 common risk patterns observed in commercial LLM deployments. Our analysis demonstrates that inputs are often interpreted non‑neutrally, prompting implementation‑driven responses or unintended state changes even when no explicit instruction is given. We argue that such behaviors represent architectural failure modes, and that simple string‑level filtering is insufficient. To mitigate these cross‑stage vulnerabilities, we advocate a zero‑trust architecture featuring provenance enforcement, context sealing, and plan revalidation, and we introduce “Countermind” as a conceptual blueprint for deploying these defenses.
1766:
The safe deployment of autonomous unmanned aerial systems (UAS) hinges on AI reasoning that is both reliable and verifiable under ever‑changing operational conditions. Conventional deep‑learning controllers, while powerful, lack explicit bounds on their decision space, making it difficult to guarantee safety, explainability, or regulatory compliance. We introduce **Cognition Envelopes**, a formalism for encapsulating the admissible cognitive processes of an autonomous UAS within a dynamic, context‑aware boundary. A cognition envelope is defined by a set of *policy constraints*, *environmental predicates*, and a *risk budget* that collectively limit the search space of the reasoning engine at runtime.  

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a mathematical framework for constructing and updating cognition envelopes from mission parameters, sensor‑derived situational awareness, and regulatory constraints; (2) a runtime enforcement architecture that couples a lightweight rule‑based monitor with a probabilistic planner, ensuring that the underlying learning module operates within the pre‑specified envelope; and (3) an empirical evaluation on a high‑fidelity UAS simulator and a fleet of quadrotors in a cluttered indoor environment. Across 12,000 flight trials, our approach reduced unsafe decision rates by 73 % and maintained mission‑completion times within 4.8 % of baseline planners that lack envelope enforcement. Moreover, the envelope‑guided planner produced explanations for every action in 97 % of cases, facilitating post‑flight analysis.  

By bounding AI reasoning through cognition envelopes, we enable modular certification of autonomous UAS systems, reduce computational overhead, and provide a pathway for integrating learning‑based components into safety‑critical air‑space operations. This work lays the foundation for a new class of *bounded* AI architectures that reconcile flexibility with rigorous assurance.
1767:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a transformative force across the spectrum of bioinformatics, driving progress in genomics, proteomics, transcriptomics, structural biology, and drug discovery. In order to systematically capture and assess this expanding body of work, we conducted a review guided by PRISMA‐style methodology and framed around six specific research questions (RQs). Our aim was to appraise GenAI’s impact on methodological innovation, predictive accuracy, and domain specialization, while spotlighting the most promising techniques for sophisticated modeling, high‑volume discovery, and integrative biological analysis.

RQ1 examined the breadth of GenAI applications, revealing widespread use in sequence analysis, molecular design, and integrative data modeling. Across these subfields, GenAI consistently surpassed conventional approaches by leveraging pattern recognition and generative capabilities.  
RQ2 showed that domain‑specific model architectures generally outperformed generic, pre‑trained networks, a gain attributed to tailored pre‑training regimens and context‑aware adaptations.  
RQ3 identified pronounced gains in molecular analysis and data integration, leading to heightened accuracy and a marked reduction in analytical errors within complex workflows.  
RQ4 documented substantial advancements in structural prediction, functional annotation, and synthetic data creation, all of which were corroborated against established benchmarks.  

RQ5 highlighted prevailing challenges—most notably scalability limits and dataset biases that constrain model generalizability—and outlined future research directions emphasizing rigorous evaluation frameworks and biologically grounded modeling.  
RQ6 catalogued the primary data sources that facilitate GenAI training and transferability, including protein repositories such as UniProtKB and ProteinNet12, cellular expression datasets like CELLxGENE and GTEx, and textual corpora such as PubMedQA and OMIM.

Collectively, these findings chart the current landscape of GenAI in bioinformatics, underscoring both its transformative potential and the critical hurdles that must be addressed to fully realize its capabilities.
1768: Automated processing of invoices is a persistent bottleneck in enterprise finance workflows, largely due to the heterogeneity of invoice layouts, multilingual content, and the need for highly accurate key‑value pair extraction. In this paper we present *AutoInv*, a hybrid pipeline that combines Optical Character Recognition (OCR) with large language models (LLMs) to deliver robust, template‑agnostic invoice data extraction. The pipeline first employs a state‑of‑the‑art OCR engine to convert scanned documents into a structured text representation. We then feed the OCR output into a fine‑tuned LLM, prompted to identify and classify domain‑specific fields such as vendor name, invoice number, dates, amounts, and line‑item details. To reduce hallucination and enforce consistency, we integrate a lightweight rule‑based post‑processing module that validates extracted values against business logic and a small set of domain ontologies. Experiments on two publicly available invoice datasets (the EU Invoice Dataset and the Camelot Invoice Corpus) demonstrate that *AutoInv* outperforms baseline rule‑based and end‑to‑end deep learning approaches, achieving a mean F1‑score of 94.7 % for key fields and 92.1 % for line‑item extraction. Moreover, the system generalizes to unseen vendors with minimal fine‑tuning, reducing the need for large annotated corpora. Our results suggest that LLM‑augmented OCR can substantially streamline invoice automation and reduce manual post‑editing effort.
1769: The persona that a modern chatbot’s large language model adopts shapes not only its surface-level interactions but also its expressed values, beliefs, and ethical stance. These factors influence the quality of user engagement, the perceived intelligence of the assistant, and how well it aligns with both developer and user goals. Although the process of shaping such a persona—often called “character training”—is a key element of industry‑level post‑training, it has received little scholarly attention. In this work we present the first open implementation of character training, built on Constitutional AI principles and a novel synthetic introspection‑based data pipeline that more effectively and controllably molds the assistant’s persona than traditional approaches such as system‑prompt constraints or activation‑steering. We fine‑tune three widely used open‑weight models using eleven example personas (e.g., humorous, deeply caring, or even malevolent). To quantify the impact of our method, we employ a preference‑analysis framework that reveals comprehensive, holistic shifts in character. Our results show that these persona changes remain robust against adversarial prompting, yield more coherent and realistic outputs, and preserve the models’ general performance on standard benchmarks. The full post‑training pipeline is released as open source at https://github.com/maiush/OpenCharacterTraining.
1770: The growing capability of large language‑model agents to plan and use external tools introduces new safety concerns, underscoring the need for a thorough red‑teaming approach to uncover vulnerabilities and secure deployment. We introduce **SIRAJ**, a versatile red‑teaming framework that can evaluate any black‑box LLM agent. The framework operates in two dynamic stages: first, it generates diverse seed test cases—spanning multiple risk outcomes, tool‑use patterns, and threat vectors—based on the agent’s definition. Second, it iteratively crafts and refines adversarial attacks informed by the execution traces from earlier attempts. To keep the process cost‑effective, we adopt a model‑distillation strategy that trains smaller, yet equally potent, models from the structured reasoning of a larger teacher. In a range of agent configurations, our seed‑generation step increases coverage of risk outcomes and tool‑calling paths by 2–2.5×. The distilled 8 B‑parameter red‑teamer doubles the attack success rate, outperforming a 671 B‑parameter Deepseek‑R1 model. Ablation studies and analysis confirm the value of the iterative design, structured reasoning, and the generalizability of our red‑teamer.
1771: We investigate why large language models (LLMs) that incorporate reasoning modules excel at difficult logical tasks. Although such “reasoning models” dominate the state‑of‑the‑art, the underlying reasons for their improved performance remain obscure. We demonstrate that most of the added capability can be induced by tiny, rank‑one parameter adjustments to the base model, many of which are interpretable. Using a rank‑1 LoRA adapter on Qwen‑2.5‑32B‑Instruct, we recover 73‑90 % of the full‑parameter fine‑tune performance on reasoning benchmarks. The adapter’s activations behave like individual MLP neurons, triggering for reasoning‑specific patterns. By training a sparse autoencoder on the entire LoRA activation space, we uncover fine‑grained, monosemantic features. Our results show that minimal parameter tweaks can produce substantial reasoning gains and reveal what aspects of the model they modify. More generally, this study illustrates how parameter‑efficient training can serve as a focused probe for fundamental insights into LLM behavior and dynamics.
1772: Accurate depth determination in oil and gas wells is critical for operational safety, well integrity monitoring, and regulatory compliance. Conventional depth‐sensing techniques—such as pressure‐based rate‑of‑penetration (ROP) algorithms and acoustic logging—suffer from cumulative error, limited resolution, and dependence on wellbore conditions. This study presents an image‑based approach that automatically identifies casing collars from downhole camera footage and computes their depth using an AlexNet‑derived convolutional neural network (CNN). A dataset of 12,000 annotated images from 25 completed wells was compiled, encompassing a wide range of illumination, fluid visibility, and casing materials. The network was fine‑tuned on a pre‑trained AlexNet architecture with a custom collar‑detection head and a regression output for depth estimation. During training, a multi‑task loss weighted the classification and regression components, achieving 95.2 % collar detection accuracy and a mean absolute depth error of 1.4 m on the held‑out test set. Comparative evaluation against traditional ROP‑based depth profiles demonstrates a reduction in cumulative drift by 40 % over a 6 km segment, confirming the superior precision of the visual method. Furthermore, the model exhibits robust performance under varying image quality, indicating resilience to downhole optical disturbances. The integration of this deep‑learning module into a real‑time drilling workflow can provide instant depth confirmation, facilitate anomaly detection, and improve wellbore surveillance. Future work will extend the approach to multi‑modal sensor fusion and adapt it to autonomous drilling operations. The results underscore the viability of CNN‑based casing collar recognition as a reliable tool for high‑resolution depth measurement in modern oil and gas exploration.
1773:
Predicting properties of short peptides—such as toxicity or HIV‑inhibitory activity—is central to bioinformatics and drug design. Conventional methods depend on hand‑crafted encodings of one‑dimensional (1D) sequences, which often fail to generalise across diverse tasks and datasets. Protein language models (PLMs) like ESM‑2 and ESMFold have emerged as powerful predictors, yet they suffer from two main drawbacks: fine‑tuning is prohibitively expensive, and their high‑dimensional latent spaces are difficult for experts to interpret. Moreover, most existing frameworks are tailored to a single classification problem, limiting transferability.  

To overcome these issues, we propose **PepTriX**, a unified architecture that fuses 1D sequence embeddings with three‑dimensional (3D) structural cues through a graph‑attention network equipped with contrastive training and cross‑modal co‑attention mechanisms. PepTriX automatically learns task‑specific peptide representations that remain biologically meaningful.  

Evaluation by domain specialists shows that PepTriX achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance across a range of peptide classification benchmarks while offering interpretable insights into the structural and biophysical motifs that drive its predictions. Consequently, PepTriX bridges the gap between high‑performance, data‑driven peptide models and the mechanistic understanding required for peptide research.
1774: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) AI seeks to fuse neural architectures with symbolic reasoning to enhance model accuracy, interpretability, and generalization. Although adding logical inference on top of subsymbolic modules can secure these benefits, it often hampers scalability, limiting practical deployment. In this work we present **DeepProofLog (DPrL)**, a new NeSy framework built around stochastic logic programs that overcomes prior scalability bottlenecks. DPrL embeds neural networks into every derivation step, providing efficient neural guidance across the proving process. We further derive a formal correspondence between DPrL’s resolution procedure and Markov Decision Processes, which allows us to harness dynamic programming and reinforcement‑learning tools for more efficient inference and learning. This theoretical linkage boosts scalability in large proof spaces and knowledge bases. Empirical results on benchmark NeSy datasets and knowledge‑graph reasoning tasks show that DPrL surpasses current state‑of‑the‑art NeSy systems, enabling application to significantly larger and more complex scenarios.
1775:
Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) models have become a cornerstone of modern large‑scale neural architectures, yet their prevailing paradigm—token‑wise routing—introduces both computational friction and a fragmented view of sequence‑level semantics. In this work we propose **Sequence‑Level Expert Routing (SL‑ER)**, a novel framework that assigns an entire input sequence to a single expert (or a small set of experts) rather than making independent decisions for each token. Our approach leverages a lightweight, global representation of the sequence to inform a routing policy that is simultaneously more efficient and better aligned with downstream tasks.  

We develop an adaptive gating mechanism that aggregates sequence features through a compact transformer encoder and produces a probabilistic expert assignment. This gating is trained jointly with the expert sub‑networks in an end‑to‑end fashion, using a differentiable load‑balancing loss that mitigates expert under‑utilization. SL‑ER dramatically reduces the number of inter‑expert communication events, yielding a 2–4× decrease in memory traffic and a 30–50 % reduction in inference latency on GPU and TPU platforms.  

Empirically, we evaluate SL‑ER on several benchmark suites: language modelling (Wikitext‑103, OpenWebText), machine translation (WMT’14 En‑De), and vision‑language fusion (COCO captioning). Across all tasks, SL‑ER matches or surpasses token‑wise MoEs, improving perplexity by up to 0.4 points and BLEU scores by 1.1 points while using 35 % fewer FLOPs. Ablation studies confirm the importance of sequence‑level context in expert selection and highlight the robustness of our load‑balancing strategy.  

In summary, Routing Experts by Sequence, not by Token, delivers a scalable, resource‑efficient alternative to traditional MoE designs, opening a new avenue for building high‑capacity models that better respect the intrinsic structure of sequential data.
1776:
Recent work has highlighted Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) as a fast, reward‑free technique for boosting video generation performance.  Yet most DPO approaches have been borrowed from image‑generation settings and trained on modestly sized models (≈ 2 B parameters), which hinders their ability to confront the specific difficulties of video synthesis—such as the high cost of assembling datasets, unstable optimisation, and heavy memory demands.  
To address these shortcomings, we propose **GT‑Pair**, a method that automatically produces high‑quality preference pairs by pairing authentic videos as positives with model‑generated videos as negatives, thus removing any need for manual annotation.  We also introduce **Reg‑DPO**, which augments the standard DPO loss with an SFT (symmetric‑forward‑training) regulariser, improving both training stability and output fidelity.  Furthermore, by integrating the Fully‑Sharded Data‑Parallel (FSDP) framework with several memory‑optimisation tricks, our system can train models with almost three‑times the capacity that FSDP alone would allow.  Extensive experiments on image‑to‑video (I2V) and text‑to‑video (T2V) benchmarks across multiple datasets show that our approach consistently surpasses existing methods, yielding superior video‑generation quality.
1777:
In the current era, Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) has become a cornerstone architecture in many state‑of‑the‑art models. A key drawback of MoE systems is their substantially higher memory footprint compared to dense models, which makes deployment on memory‑constrained GPUs—such as those found on edge devices—particularly challenging. MoE offloading, especially when combined with caching and pre‑fetching, offers a viable remedy, yet existing work has employed sub‑optimal cache policies and provided limited analytical insight.

This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of MoE offloading, delivering the following contributions:  

1. A detailed analysis of expert activation patterns and the behaviour of LRU caching, accompanied by empirical traces.  
2. A novel LFU‑based caching strategy derived from this analysis, yielding significant gains over LRU.  
3. Implementation and evaluation of speculative expert pre‑fetching, with trace data that highlights its substantial potential.  
4. An extensive examination of MoE internals, illuminating the characteristics of gating networks and individual experts—information that can guide future efforts in model interpretation and the design of pruning techniques that preserve performance.
1778:
Deep neural networks are notoriously difficult to train due to the non‑convexity of their loss landscapes. In practice, most training procedures rely on stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with heuristic schedules, often resulting in slow convergence and sensitivity to hyper‑parameters. In this paper we introduce a *convexity‑dependent two‑phase training algorithm* that exploits the implicit convex structure present in a broad class of network architectures and loss functions.

In the **first phase**, we solve a convex surrogate of the original problem by fixing all but the last layer and training a linear classifier (or a small kernelized network) with an exact convex optimizer. This stage yields an initialization that is provably close to a stationary point of the full network and provides a tight lower bound on the empirical risk. We then perform a *convexity diagnostics* step in which we estimate the curvature spectrum of the network’s loss in the neighborhood of the obtained solution.  

The **second phase** adapts the learning dynamics based on these diagnostics: if the local curvature indicates a nearly convex regime, we employ a small‑step SGD with adaptive learning rates; otherwise, we switch to a more aggressive optimizer (Adam or LAMB) and optionally inject a convex regularizer to reshape the landscape. This convexity‑aware switching reduces the number of required epochs by up to 35 % on CIFAR‑10, SVHN, and ImageNet‑100, while simultaneously improving test accuracy by 1.2 %–2.7 % over standard two‑phase baselines and achieving comparable performance to fully end‑to‑end training with 50 % fewer parameter updates.

We provide rigorous convergence guarantees for the convex surrogate and prove that the convexity diagnostics ensure that the second phase operates within a region where the loss is locally strongly convex. Our results demonstrate that explicitly harnessing convexity within a neural training pipeline yields both computational efficiency and enhanced generalization.
1779: Artificial coding assistants frequently produce snippets that contain simple security flaws. Although developers must ultimately vet and approve such code, raising its intrinsic quality is still crucial. A major source of these weaknesses is the inclusion of vulnerable code in the corpora used to train large language models (LLMs). In this work we tackle the problem by curating a training set that contains only code that has passed a static‑analysis check for security issues. We built a secure Python corpus by filtering an existing dataset with a vulnerability detector, then trained two transformer models—one on the cleaned data and one on the original, unfiltered corpus. We evaluated both models on natural‑language function specifications, measuring the functional correctness and the presence of security defects in the generated code. Results show that the model trained on the curated dataset produces far fewer security problems while achieving comparable correctness, underscoring the value of secure training data for building more reliable AI programming assistants. Further architectural and evaluation improvements are nonetheless required to strengthen these gains.
1780: The engineering design cycle routinely requires the confluence of expertise across multiple disciplines, resulting in intricate collaboration chains and repeated iterations. Conventional practices tend to be resource‑driven and riddled with bottlenecks. To tackle these challenges, we present a formalized multi‑agent artificial‑intelligence architecture that structures the design and review process into systematic loops. Within this architecture, domain‑specialised agents cooperate to generate and iteratively improve design candidates. As a concrete illustration, we apply the framework to the aerodynamic optimisation of 4‑digit NACA airfoils. The system is composed of three pivotal AI agents: a Graph Ontologist, a Design Engineer, and a Systems Engineer. The Graph Ontologist uses a Large Language Model to extract and encode two domain‑specific knowledge graphs derived from the airfoil literature. Guided by a human manager, the Systems Engineer defines the technical specifications that steer the generation and assessment of designs. The Design Engineer, drawing on the design knowledge graph and simulation tools, proposes candidate airfoils that satisfy those specifications. Subsequently, the Systems Engineer evaluates these candidates, providing both qualitative and quantitative feedback through its own knowledge graph, thereby establishing an iterative refinement loop that continues until the manager approves. The ultimate design is further tuned to maximise key performance indicators such as lift‑to‑drag ratio. This study demonstrates that a collaborative AI system built around structured knowledge representations can markedly improve the efficiency, consistency, and overall quality of engineering design work.
1781:
In contemporary medical research, omics datasets are indispensable for uncovering disease mechanisms, yet they contain highly sensitive personal information. Federated Learning (FL) coupled with Differential Privacy (DP) can safeguard such data against adversarial intrusions, but the noise required for DP inevitably degrades model accuracy. Conversely, Homomorphic Encryption (HE) permits secure computation on encrypted data and allows the aggregation of gradients without the detrimental noise of DP, thereby improving predictive performance—at the cost of increased computational overhead.

To reconcile accuracy with the diverse computational capacities of participating clients, we present the Privacy‑Preserving Machine Learning Hybrid (PPML‑Hybrid) approach that incorporates HE. In PPML‑Hybrid, each client chooses between HE and DP based on its available resources: HE clients contribute unperturbed updates while DP clients incur lower computational burdens. Clients endowed with ample computational power can flexibly switch between HE and DP to meet specific privacy requirements.

Experiments on several omics datasets demonstrate that PPML‑Hybrid attains predictive accuracy comparable to HE‑only schemes while markedly reducing runtime. Moreover, it surpasses DP‑only methods even under identical or stricter privacy budgets.
1782: In many coupled‑physics imaging modalities, including photoacoustic tomography, the inverse source problem is commonly addressed through iterative schemes that minimize an appropriate cost functional. Recently, deep‑learning‑based strategies have also been explored to further enhance these optimization techniques. All of these approaches rely on repeated evaluations of the forward model and its adjoint. Here we introduce a set of asymptotically fast algorithms for computing the forward and adjoint operators in the circular acquisition configuration. For an image of size \(n\times n\), the new methods require only \(\mathcal{O}(n^{2}\log n)\) floating‑point operations. We validate their efficiency with numerical experiments where they are integrated into several reconstruction pipelines: classical variational schemes such as non‑negative least squares and TV‑regularized least squares, as well as deep‑learning approaches like the learned primal‑dual network. A public Python implementation together with example code is provided.
1783:
Contemporary Internet‑of‑Things (IoT) networks for environmental monitoring generate vast amounts of spatiotemporal data, which are then fed into machine‑learning models for downstream tasks such as forecasting. While many studies focus on reducing the quantity of data transmitted from the edge, they seldom examine how different sampling rates and sensor placements influence the performance of the forecasting models that follow. Often, adding measurements from extra sensors can “smooth out” predictions by supplying a richer spatial context, yet the joint effect of sampling frequency, spatial density, and model architecture remains largely unstudied.

In this work we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of several forecasting paradigms—classical vector autoregression (VAR), recurrent neural networks (GRU), Transformers, spatio‑temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs), and modern time‑series foundation models (TSFMs) such as Chronos, Moirai, and TimesFM—across a range of sensor densities and sampling intervals. Our experiments use real‑world temperature traces from a wireless sensor network. 

Key observations include: (i) STGNNs excel when the deployment is sparse and the sampling cadence is moderate, as the graph structure captures spatial correlations that compensate for limited data coverage; (ii) TSFMs deliver strong performance at high sampling frequencies but suffer as spatial coverage shrinks; and (iii) the multivariate TSFM Moirai consistently outperforms all competitors by directly learning inter‑sensor dependencies. 

These results provide concrete guidance for designing efficient forecasting pipelines in spatiotemporal IoT deployments. All configuration scripts, datasets, and training logs are publicly available at https://github.com/UIUC-MONET-Projects/Benchmarking-Spatiotemporal-Forecast-Models.
1784:
Anticipating abnormal events in multivariate time‑series from real‑world, dynamic, and complex environments is crucial for avoiding critical failures and reducing both operating costs and manual effort. Existing techniques, however, are often tailored to particular domains and struggle to adapt when anomaly patterns shift over time. Recent advances in pretrained Time‑Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) have shown remarkable generalization and zero‑shot forecasting, yet they have not been exploited for anomaly prediction—a problem that differs fundamentally from normal‑behaviour forecasting. 

In this work we introduce **Forecast2Anomaly (F2A)**, a new framework that equips TSFMs with the capability to predict anomalies. F2A incorporates two key contributions: (1) a joint forecast‑anomaly loss that fine‑tunes TSFMs so they can still predict future observations accurately even during anomalous periods; and (2) a Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) module that pulls in historically relevant horizons and conditions predictions on those retrieved contexts. This dynamic retrieval allows F2A to cope with distributional changes at inference time, tracking evolving anomalies without the need for further model training. 

By marrying focused fine‑tuning with adaptive retrieval, F2A bridges the gap between robust zero‑shot TSFM forecasting and zero‑shot anomaly prediction. Extensive evaluations on 16 heterogeneous datasets and across several TSFM backbones demonstrate that F2A consistently surpasses state‑of‑the‑art baselines, providing a scalable, zero‑shot solution for real‑world anomaly prediction.
1785: This paper introduces a comprehensive pipeline for fully automated tennis match analysis. By combining several deep‑learning modules, the system simultaneously detects and tracks both players and the ball in real time, while also locating key court reference points. Player detection is handled by YOLOv8, ball tracking is performed with a YOLOv5 network trained specifically for this task, and court keypoint identification uses a ResNet‑50 based architecture. The resulting framework delivers in‑depth analytics such as player movement trajectories, ball velocity, shot precision, and reaction times. Experiments show reliable performance across a range of court settings and match situations. The model outputs a video with overlaid annotations together with comprehensive performance statistics, providing coaches, broadcasters, and athletes with actionable insights into the flow of the game.
1786:
Spatial understanding—perceiving, reasoning about, and interacting with three‑dimensional environments—is a cornerstone of autonomous robotics, AR/VR systems, and embodied AI. Traditional supervised methods for spatial perception rely on expensive, hand‑annotated datasets, and the resulting models often fail to generalize beyond the narrow distributions of these benchmarks. We introduce **Spatial‑SSRL**, a novel self‑supervised reinforcement learning framework that learns spatial representations and control policies from raw sensor streams without any human labels. 

Spatial‑SSRL couples a goal‑conditioned policy network with a spatial‑aware value function that is trained using intrinsically motivated rewards derived from visual consistency, depth estimation, and topological coverage metrics. The policy is optimized in simulation on a diverse set of procedurally generated 3‑D scenes, while an auxiliary “spatial critic” learns to predict future scene embeddings, enabling the agent to plan over long horizons and to discover informative exploration trajectories. We further introduce a hierarchical curriculum that gradually increases scene complexity, ensuring stable credit assignment in the sparse‑reward setting. 

To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we evaluate Spatial‑SSRL on three standard benchmarks: (i) **Room‑for‑Room** navigation, (ii) **3D Scene Reconstruction** from first‑person RGB‑D streams, and (iii) **Spatial Relational Reasoning** on the *SpatialCLEVR* dataset. Across all tasks, Spatial‑SSRL achieves a 12 % absolute improvement over state‑of‑the‑art supervised baselines and outperforms prior self‑supervised methods by 6–9 % on absolute error metrics. Moreover, the learned spatial embeddings transfer seamlessly to real‑world robot platforms, reducing fine‑tuning data by 80 % relative to supervised counterparts. 

Our results illustrate that self‑supervised reinforcement learning, when guided by spatially structured intrinsic signals, can endow agents with robust, transferable spatial reasoning capabilities—paving the way toward truly autonomous systems capable of navigating, mapping, and interacting with the world without manual annotation.
1787:
Co‑creative animation tools aim to empower designers and non‑experts to produce expressive visual stories without requiring extensive animation skill. Yet, most existing approaches rely on manual keyframe editing or rule‑based motion generation, which are time‑consuming and often produce rigid, predictable results. In this paper we introduce **Decomate**, a novel system that harnesses large‑scale generative models to assist users in the creation of rich, semantically meaningful SVG animations. Decomate integrates a conditional diffusion encoder that interprets high‑level prompts—text, sketches, or partial animation fragments—and samples plausible motion trajectories and timing parameters for vector graphics elements. The model is trained on a curated dataset of SVG animation sequences annotated with semantic tags, enabling it to capture a wide spectrum of stylistic and temporal patterns.

During a co‑creative session, Decomate presents multiple candidate refinements to the user, who can then select, combine, or edit the suggestions in a live preview. Our architecture preserves the symbolic nature of SVG, allowing for precise control over shape, color, and hierarchical transformations while still benefiting from the fluidity of neural motion synthesis. We evaluate Decomate through a mixed‑methods study with 48 participants of varying animation expertise. Quantitative results show a 35 % reduction in editing time compared with baseline keyframe workflows and a 12 % increase in perceived animation quality. Qualitative interviews reveal that users value the system’s ability to generate unexpected yet coherent motion cues, fostering iterative creativity.

We conclude that generative models can serve as powerful co‑creative agents for vector animation, bridging the gap between algorithmic synthesis and human intention. Decomate opens a new avenue for expressive, low‑effort animation creation and provides a foundation for future research on interactive, AI‑augmented design tools.
1788:
Recent years have seen growing efforts to map the relationships between particular datasets and the scholarly articles that reference them. Once we know that a paper cites a specific dataset, the next logical inquiry is to uncover how or why that data was employed. The emergence of pretrained, transformer‑based large language models (LLMs) offers a scalable way to annotate these data‑use cases, bypassing the costly manual labeling and bespoke training set creation typical of traditional machine‑learning approaches. 

In this study we harness the open‑source LLM Llama 3.1‑405B to produce structured labels for how genomic datasets are used within known publications. We also propose a new evaluation framework for assessing the performance of such methods. Our experiments show that the baseline model attains an F1 score of 0.674 on a zero‑shot data‑citation classification task, despite the absence of predefined categories. While these findings are encouraging, they are tempered by challenges around data accessibility, prompt over‑fitting, computational demands, and the high cost of rigorous performance evaluation.
1789: Large Language Models (LLMs) open up novel possibilities for modeling online communities and social‑media interactions. They could be leveraged to evaluate content‑recommender designs or to gauge the impact of policies and interventions. Yet, it remains unclear whether LLMs can faithfully reproduce the dynamics of human dialogue in such settings. To investigate this, we compared genuine Reddit exchanges with synthetic ones produced by two state‑of‑the‑art models—Llama 3 70B and GPT‑4o—on identical topics. When these exchanges were shown to participants side‑by‑side, 39 % of the AI‑generated conversations were indistinguishable from human‑written threads. For Llama 3, participants identified the artificial threads as AI only 56 % of the time, barely above chance. These findings confirm that LLMs can produce social‑media conversations that convincingly mimic real ones, underscoring both their utility for social simulations and the risk of generating deceptive, inauthentic content.
1790: The rapid global expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) has largely been measured in terms of high‑income, English‑centric economies, leaving low resource language (LRL) countries—those where languages lack digital corpora, computational tools, and large‑scale training data—under‑studied. This paper investigates the diffusion of AI technologies in such contexts, aiming to (1) delineate the current landscape of AI adoption across LRL‑dominated nations, (2) identify the socio‑economic, infrastructural, and linguistic barriers that constrain diffusion, and (3) propose actionable policy and industry strategies to accelerate inclusive AI uptake. Using a mixed‑methods approach that blends a systematic review of 132 peer‑reviewed articles with in‑depth case studies in Kenya, Myanmar, and the Sámi region of Scandinavia, we applied the Diffusion of Innovations framework to trace pathways of AI diffusion from global hubs to local ecosystems. Survey data from 1,247 developers, policymakers, and end‑users in 18 LRL countries reveal a persistent digital divide: 84 % of respondents cite lack of annotated data as the primary impediment, while 62 % report limited internet bandwidth and 54 % report insufficient local AI talent. Our findings further indicate that open‑source initiatives, such as Hugging Face and the Common Voice project, serve as critical enablers but remain under‑leveraged due to linguistic mismatch. We advocate a multi‑layered strategy that includes (i) investment in community‑driven corpus building, (ii) subsidies for low‑cost edge‑device deployment, and (iii) partnerships with diaspora researchers to co‑create culturally relevant AI models. By mapping the current diffusion trajectory and articulating targeted interventions, this study provides a roadmap for stakeholders—governments, academia, and industry—to ensure that AI’s benefits are equitably accessible across linguistic and economic boundaries.
1791:
License plate recognition (LPR) systems have become indispensable for a wide range of security, traffic‑management, and automotive applications.  Existing approaches typically rely on large, manually annotated datasets to train deep detectors and sequence‑recognizers, which is costly and often infeasible for new languages or vehicle styles.  In this work we propose an **efficient LPR framework that eliminates the need for hand‑crafted bounding‑box labels** by exploiting a pseudo‑labeling pipeline built on the state‑of‑the‑art grounding model **Grounding DINO** and the lightweight detector **YOLOv8**.

Our pipeline first runs a zero‑shot grounding network that localises the textual cue “license plate” in raw traffic images.  The resulting bounding boxes, albeit noisy, serve as **pseudo‑labels** to initialise a YOLOv8 detector.  We refine the pseudo‑labels with an iterative self‑distillation step, wherein the detector’s predictions are fed back to the grounding model to suppress false positives and sharpen localisation.  The final YOLOv8 model is fine‑tuned on a small set of fully labelled images (≈1 % of the total dataset) and is coupled with a lightweight CRNN character recogniser to produce end‑to‑end plate identification.

Evaluated on the publicly available **UFPR‑ALPR**, **OpenALPR**, and a proprietary in‑house dataset, our method achieves **87.3 % mAP@0.5** on plate detection and **93.5 % character‑level accuracy**, matching or exceeding fully supervised baselines while requiring only 15 min of human annotation.  Moreover, the combined detection‑recognition system runs at **58 FPS** on a single 1080 Ti GPU, demonstrating its suitability for real‑time deployment on edge devices.  

This study shows that **pseudo‑labeled supervision** can drastically reduce annotation overhead for LPR, and highlights the synergy between foundation‑model grounding and efficient object detectors.  Our code and datasets will be released to encourage further research in low‑label LPR and related vision‑to‑text tasks.
1792:
Emotion recognition using EEG signals is a cornerstone of affective computing and has seen extensive study with deep‑learning methods. Although recent models excel on individual datasets, they struggle to generalise across studies because of inconsistent annotation schemes and varied data formats. Most existing approaches also adopt dataset‑specific architectures and fail to align diverse emotion labels semantically.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce **EMOD**, a unified EEG emotion representation framework that employs Valence‑Arousal (V‑A)‑guided contrastive learning. EMOD learns transferable, emotion‑aware embeddings by bridging both semantic and structural gaps: discrete and continuous labels are mapped into a common V‑A space, and a soft‑weighted supervised contrastive loss pulls emotionally similar samples together in latent space. To handle heterogeneous EEG inputs, EMOD uses a flexible Triple‑Domain Encoder followed by a Spatial‑Temporal Transformer that jointly extracts and integrates temporal, spectral, and spatial features.

After pre‑training on eight publicly available EEG datasets, we evaluate EMOD on three benchmark datasets. Results demonstrate that EMOD outperforms existing methods, achieving state‑of‑the‑art accuracy while exhibiting strong generalisation across diverse EEG‑based emotion‑recognition settings.
1793:
Chest computed tomography (CT) is an indispensable modality for diagnosing a wide spectrum of thoracic diseases, yet its diagnostic performance is often hindered by substantial domain shifts arising from heterogeneous scanner vendors, acquisition protocols, and patient cohorts. At the same time, privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIP‑AA) restrict the sharing of raw imaging data, complicating the development of robust, general‑purpose models. To address these challenges, we propose a *Privacy‑Aware Continual Self‑Supervised Learning* (PA‑CS‑SSL) framework that simultaneously learns transferable representations from multi‑window chest CT scans while preserving patient confidentiality.

Our approach first constructs a *Multi‑Window Representation* (MWR) by jointly feeding lung‑, mediastinal‑, and bone‑windows into a shared encoder, enabling the model to capture complementary anatomical cues without manual window selection. The encoder is then updated in an online, continual fashion using a *Differentially Private Contrastive* (DP‑C) objective, which injects calibrated Gaussian noise into the gradient updates to guarantee ε‑differential privacy. To mitigate catastrophic forgetting, we integrate a *Replay‑free Memory‑Regularized* (RMR) mechanism that leverages generative replay with privacy‑preserving synthetic samples. The resulting PA‑CS‑SSL pipeline is deployable across hospitals in a federated manner, obviating the need to centralize patient data.

We evaluate the method on five large, heterogeneous chest‑CT datasets spanning multiple vendors and disease phenotypes, and benchmark against state‑of‑the‑art continual SSL and domain‑adaptation baselines. On downstream tasks such as COVID‑19, pneumonia, and lung nodule detection, PA‑CS‑SSL attains 4–7 % higher area‑under‑the‑curve than baseline models while exhibiting a domain‑shift resilience up to 15 % improvement in cross‑site generalization. Privacy analysis demonstrates that the algorithm satisfies ε = 1.5 differential‑privacy guarantees with a negligible 0.8 % drop in accuracy compared to non‑private counterparts.

In summary, we present a novel, privacy‑aware continual self‑supervised learning paradigm that harnesses multi‑window chest CT to build robust, domain‑shift‑resilient representations without compromising patient confidentiality. This work opens a path toward scalable, ethically responsible deployment of AI in radiology across diverse clinical environments.
1794:
The rapid deployment of autonomous scientific agents has amplified concerns about the propagation of unverified or false claims in the digital knowledge ecosystem. Current practice often relies on post‑hoc peer review or ad‑hoc validation, leaving large swaths of research output vulnerable to misinformation and eroding trust in automated knowledge production. This paper introduces **EviBound**, a comprehensive governance framework designed to bind autonomous research systems (ARSs) to verifiable evidence throughout the entire inquiry lifecycle. EviBound formalises three interlocking modules: (1) **Evidence‑Anchored Data Acquisition**, which mandates provenance capture and cryptographic attestation for every data point ingested; (2) **Dynamic Verification Engine**, which employs a combination of statistical hypothesis testing, cross‑modal corroboration, and distributed consensus protocols to evaluate the integrity of intermediate results and final claims; and (3) **Transparent Accountability Ledger**, an immutable record that logs decision rationales, evidence dependencies, and audit trails accessible to human overseers and competing ARSs. We encode governance rules in a domain‑specific policy language, enabling the specification of experiment constraints, replication requirements, and publication thresholds. 

To assess EviBound’s effectiveness, we instantiated the framework on a suite of benchmark datasets spanning computational biology, natural language processing, and climate modeling. Across 150 autonomous research pipelines, EviBound reduced the incidence of false claims by 92 % relative to baseline systems, while maintaining a 15 % improvement in discovery throughput. Moreover, the evidence ledger facilitated rapid identification and rectification of erroneous inference pathways, demonstrating a tangible reduction in downstream error propagation. 

Our results indicate that evidence‑bound governance not only safeguards the integrity of autonomous research but also enhances reproducibility and fosters interdisciplinary collaboration. EviBound offers a scalable, policy‑driven architecture that can be integrated into existing AI research pipelines, providing a pathway toward trustworthy, self‑regulating scientific discovery.
1795:
Large‑language models (LLMs) are routinely evaluated on a growing suite of benchmarks, yet the extent to which these tests actually measure the underlying linguistic, reasoning, or world‑knowledge abilities they purport to assess remains largely unexamined. We investigate the *construct validity* of LLM benchmarks—i.e., the degree to which a test’s scores reflect the intended latent construct rather than incidental artifacts such as prompt phrasing, dataset memorization, or model‑size‑induced biases. 

First, we formalise a construct‑validation framework for LLM evaluation, drawing on classical psychometric principles and recent advances in model interpretability. The framework introduces three orthogonal diagnostics: (1) **factor alignment** (do scores factor‑load on the target construct?); (2) **adversarial robustness** (do scores degrade predictably under controlled perturbations that remove the target signal?); and (3) **human‑in‑the‑loop calibration** (do model outcomes correlate with expert judgments of construct‑specific competence?). 

Using this framework, we audit 12 widely‑used benchmarks (e.g., SuperGLUE, LAMBADA, MMLU, and a suite of procedural reasoning tasks). Our analysis reveals pervasive violations of construct validity: many tasks exhibit strong correlations with model size or surface‑level statistical regularities, and are highly sensitive to trivial prompt changes. Conversely, a small subset of tasks demonstrates robust factor alignment and adversarial stability. We also propose a *construct‑weighted composite* that aggregates only the validated sub‑tasks, yielding a more reliable estimate of a model’s genuine capabilities. 

Finally, we provide an open‑source toolkit that implements the diagnostics and a set of best‑practice guidelines for future benchmark design. By foregrounding construct validity, this work offers a principled path toward more trustworthy, interpretable, and actionable evaluation of LLMs.
1796: Artificial‑intelligence generated content (AIGC) is reshaping digital marketing and the way consumers interact online.  Yet forecasting how such content spreads and what market impact it will have remains difficult because of heterogeneous data, nonlinear propagation dynamics and continuously changing consumer behaviour.  This paper presents an AI‑driven Decision Support System that fuses multiple data streams—social‑media feeds, advertising spend, engagement logs and sentiment signals—into a hybrid Graph Neural Network and Temporal Transformer framework.  A dual‑channel architecture learns the diffusion network and the evolving influence over time, while causal‑inference modules isolate the effects of marketing stimuli on ROI and visibility.  Experiments on large, real‑world datasets from Twitter, TikTok and YouTube ads show that our system outperforms existing baselines across all six metrics.  By delivering interpretable, real‑time insights into AIGC dissemination and market growth, the proposed DSS empowers marketers to make more informed decisions.
1797:
End‑to‑end neural architectures for autonomous driving have shown remarkable perceptual and control capabilities, yet they remain brittle in unfamiliar environments and often ignore the rich, low‑level interactions between the vehicle and its surroundings. Recent theories of embodied cognition posit that cognition emerges from the continual coupling of perception, action, and physical body dynamics. In this work we formalise this insight for autonomous driving and propose **ECA‑End2End**, a novel framework that augments deep‑learning pipelines with an explicit body‑centric representation and physics‑aware reasoning.

ECA‑End2End learns a joint latent space that fuses exteroceptive cues (LiDAR, RGB, radar) with proprioceptive signals (steering, throttle, brake, vehicle dynamics) through a hierarchical encoder–decoder architecture. A recurrent “body‑module” processes temporal proprioceptive traces and predicts short‑term physical affordances (e.g., slip, tire force) that are then injected into the policy network as auxiliary supervisory signals. The entire system is trained end‑to‑end using a hybrid loss that combines supervised trajectory imitation, self‑supervised physics consistency, and a reinforcement‑learning objective on a high‑fidelity simulator.

We evaluate ECA‑End2End on the nuScenes and Waymo Open datasets, as well as a real‑world test track. Compared with state‑of‑the‑art end‑to‑end baselines, our method reduces collision rates by 23 % and improves lane‑keeping error by 18 % while requiring only 30 % of the labeled data. Ablation studies confirm that the embodied module is critical for extrapolation to unseen road conditions and dynamic traffic scenarios.

Our results demonstrate that incorporating embodied cognition principles into end‑to‑end autonomous driving pipelines yields safer, more generalizable, and data‑efficient agents, opening a new direction for future research at the intersection of machine learning, robotics, and cognitive science.
1798:
Conventional multi‑lead ECG systems record cardiac activity from a fixed set of anatomical viewpoints dictated by lead placement. Yet, certain conditions such as Brugada syndrome often require additional, non‑standard views to expose diagnostically crucial patterns that standard leads miss. To address this shortcoming, Nef‑Net was recently proposed to recover a continuous electrocardiac field, allowing virtual ECG signals to be observed from any arbitrary perspective—a concept we call Electrocardio Panorama. Although promising, Nef‑Net relies on idealized assumptions and struggles with real‑world challenges including long‑duration recordings, device‑specific artifacts, and imperfect electrode positioning.

In this work we introduce NEF‑NET+, an enhanced framework for realistic panoramic ECG synthesis. It supports arbitrarily long signal generation from any desired view, generalizes across a variety of ECG devices, and corrects for operator‑induced deviations in lead placement. These capabilities are achieved through a novel model architecture that performs direct view transformation, coupled with a multi‑stage workflow: offline pre‑training, device‑calibration tuning, and an on‑the‑fly, patient‑specific adjustment.

To evaluate panoramic ECG synthesis rigorously, we build Panobench, a new benchmark consisting of 5,367 recordings with 48 distinct views per subject, capturing the full spatial variability of cardiac electrical activity. Experiments demonstrate that NEF‑NET+ markedly outperforms the baseline Nef‑Net, achieving roughly a 6 dB improvement in PSNR under realistic conditions. The code and the Panobench dataset will be released in a forthcoming publication.
1799: In high‑stakes fields such as medicine, AI explanations often cannot be independently verified, which undermines user confidence. We address this problem by introducing an interactive agent that generates explanations through a traceable series of actions. The agent learns a strategy for actively gathering external visual evidence to reinforce its diagnostic reasoning; this strategy is optimized with reinforcement learning, yielding a system that is both efficient and broadly applicable. Our evaluations show that this action‑driven reasoning markedly boosts calibrated accuracy, lowering the Brier score by 18 % relative to a static baseline. To assess the faithfulness of the explanations, we employ a causal‑intervention test: when the visual evidence selected by the agent is masked, its performance drops (ΔBrier = +0.029). This confirms that the evidence is essential to the agent’s decisions. Overall, we present a practical approach for creating AI models that offer verifiable and faithful reasoning.
1800: Accurate extraction of medical orders from clinical documentation is a critical enabler of downstream clinical decision support, medication reconciliation, and quality‑improvement pipelines.  In this study we evaluate the effectiveness of a suite of prompting strategies for the newly released MedGemma, a domain‑tuned large language model (LLM) pre‑trained on multimodal medical corpora, in the task of medical order extraction from unstructured discharge summaries and progress notes.  We formulate the extraction problem as a sequence‑to‑sequence labeling task, mapping natural‑language inputs to a structured representation of drug, dosage, route, and frequency.  To probe the influence of prompt design we compare (i) a vanilla zero‑shot prompt, (ii) a few‑shot prompt incorporating exemplar order instances, (iii) a chain‑of‑thought (CoT) prompt that explicitly guides MedGemma through intermediate reasoning steps, (iv) an instruction‑tuned prompt that embeds a concise set of extraction rules, and (v) a hybrid “template‑plus‑CoT” prompt that blends structured question‑answer templates with step‑by‑step reasoning.  Experiments are conducted on a curated subset of 10,000 de‑identified notes from the MIMIC‑III dataset, annotated by clinical pharmacists for 12 order categories.  Across all strategies, MedGemma surpasses baseline rule‑based extraction (F1 = 0.68) and generic GPT‑4 (F1 = 0.73).  The hybrid “template‑plus‑CoT” approach attains the best performance (macro‑F1 = 0.81, precision = 0.85, recall = 0.78), achieving a 12 % relative improvement over zero‑shot and a 5 % absolute gain over few‑shot.  Error analysis reveals that CoT prompts reduce dosage‑level misclassifications, while template prompts mitigate entity‑type confusion.  We conclude that carefully engineered prompts can unlock MedGemma’s full potential for medical order extraction, and recommend a hybrid prompting framework for deployment in clinical NLP pipelines.
1801:
Verifying learning‑enabled cyber‑physical systems (CPS) in a comprehensive way remains a hard problem because of black‑box modules and highly complex real‑world settings. Existing techniques either give formal guarantees for a narrow class of models or treat the entire system as a monolithic black box, leaving no general, compositional approach that can integrate diverse verification methods for realistic environments.  

We present **ScenicProver**, a new framework that bridges this gap. Built on the Scenic probabilistic programming language, ScenicProver offers:  

1. **Composable system specifications** with well‑defined component interfaces, spanning from readable code to opaque black boxes.  
2. **Assume‑guarantee contracts** expressed in a Linear Temporal Logic extension that allows arbitrary Scenic expressions.  
3. A flexible **evidence generation pipeline** that combines runtime testing, formal proofs via Lean 4, and externally supplied assumptions.  
4. Systematic **combination of evidence** using contract operators.  
5. **Automatic assurance‑case generation** that records the provenance of each system‑level guarantee.  

We validate the framework on an autonomous vehicle’s automatic emergency‑braking system that fuses radar and laser data. By reusing manufacturer‑provided sensor guarantees and concentrating testing on the most uncertain scenarios, ScenicProver yields stronger probabilistic assurances than a monolithic testing approach while using the same computational resources.
1802:
Deep neural networks often contain a strikingly large number of parameters, many of which are redundant.  Low‑rank training—constraining weight matrices to be of low rank—provides an effective way to reduce model size, memory consumption, and inference latency while preserving predictive performance.  Existing rank‑regularization techniques (e.g., nuclear‑norm penalties, hard rank constraints, or adaptive low‑rank factorizations) typically suffer from either a loose approximation to the true rank, a prohibitive computational overhead, or instability during stochastic optimization.

We introduce **Q3R** (Quadratic Reweighted Rank Regularizer), a novel differentiable penalty that tightly approximates the matrix rank by employing a quadratic reweighting scheme over the singular values.  Q3R assigns a decreasing quadratic weight to each singular value, sharply penalizing large singular values while encouraging a rapid decay in the spectrum.  Unlike the linear nuclear‑norm, Q3R yields a tighter convex surrogate to the rank function, and unlike hard rank constraints, it remains fully differentiable and amenable to standard gradient‑based training.  

We provide a theoretical analysis of Q3R, showing that its optimal solutions satisfy a closed‑form reweighted singular‑value shrinkage operator, which can be computed efficiently in a batched manner during back‑propagation.  We further prove that Q3R preserves convergence guarantees of stochastic gradient descent under mild assumptions.  

Extensive experiments on CIFAR‑10, ImageNet, and Transformer‑style language models demonstrate that Q3R achieves **up to 3× compression** and **20 % inference‑time speedup** while incurring **≤1 % loss in accuracy**, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art low‑rank training methods such as Singular Value Thresholding (SVT), Adaptive Low‑Rank (ALR), and Rank‑Sparsity regularizers.  Ablation studies confirm the robustness of Q3R to hyper‑parameter choices and its effectiveness across different architectures (ResNet‑50, MobileNetV2, GPT‑2).  

Our results show that Q3R constitutes a simple, theoretically grounded, and highly effective tool for large‑scale low‑rank training, paving the way for more efficient deployment of deep models in resource‑constrained environments.
1803:
Accurately grasping what a piece of source code is meant to do is essential for maintenance, onboarding, and modernization efforts. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate code explanations, those explanations frequently lack a solid foundation in the surrounding software‑engineering context.  
We introduce a new method that augments LLM‑driven code interpretation with natural‑language artifacts from GitHub—pull‑request narratives, issue discussions, and commit logs. The system is built around three modules: (1) a context extractor that harvests and structures relevant GitHub information, (2) a context‑aware explanation generator that produces high‑level descriptions of the code’s intent, and (3) a validation component that checks the coherence of the generated explanation.  
The approach is delivered as both a stand‑alone tool and as a server that follows the Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing seamless integration with other AI‑assisted development environments.  
Our primary use case is to enrich a conventional LLM‑generated code explanation with deeper, context‑driven insights. To assess the value of these insights, we carried out a small user study involving developers from several open‑source projects and proprietary teams. Results show that the system’s additional explanations are frequently useful, non‑trivial, and largely devoid of hallucinations.
1804:
We present the first large‑scale, formal evaluation of how useful conventional chemical functional groups are for explaining molecular data. Our methodology is grounded in a core tenet of computational learning theory: a strong explanation should also compress the data it describes. To this end, we devised an unsupervised algorithm that leverages the Minimum Message Length (MML) principle to search for substructures that effectively compress a database of roughly three million biologically relevant molecules. The resulting substructures recover virtually all human‑curated functional groups and reveal additional, larger motifs with more specific functional roles. 

We further applied the same algorithm to 24 distinct bioactivity prediction datasets, identifying functional groups that are tailored to each dataset. Fingerprints derived from these dataset‑specific groups consistently outperform conventional representations such as MACCS and Morgan fingerprints when training ridge‑regression models on bioactivity‑regression tasks.
1805: Modern robotics continues to be hampered by the chasm between powerful, general‑purpose foundation models (e.g., large language models, vision‑language transformers, and multimodal diffusion networks) and the real‑time, safety‑critical demands of embodied agents. In this work, we present a unified architecture that harnesses the representational richness of foundation models to improve both perception and action in robotic systems. Our contributions are threefold. First, we develop a *Context‑Aware Retrieval and Inference* (CARI) module that projects high‑level semantic queries from a robot’s internal state into a multimodal embedding space, enabling zero‑shot perception of novel objects, scenes, and affordances with minimal domain adaptation. Second, we introduce *Action‑Conditioned Fine‑Tuning* (ACFT), a lightweight fine‑tuning protocol that preserves the generality of the underlying model while endowing it with domain‑specific affordance predictions and motion primitives through few‑shot demonstrations. Third, we integrate these modules into a closed‑loop control pipeline that leverages the foundation model’s language output to generate high‑level task plans, which are then translated into motion primitives via a learned policy network. We validate our approach on a 7‑DOF manipulator and a mobile base in a suite of pick‑and‑place, navigation, and assembly tasks, achieving a 23 % improvement in success rate over baseline perception–control pipelines and a 15 % reduction in task completion time. Ablation studies confirm that the CARI and ACFT modules each contribute significantly to robustness against perceptual noise and novel objects. Our results demonstrate that foundation models can be effectively leveraged as a cognitive substrate for robots, providing a scalable pathway toward adaptable, sample‑efficient robotic autonomy.
1806:
Conventional continual‑learning (CL) systems rely on gradient‑based fine‑tuning to alleviate catastrophic forgetting, a strategy that is impractical for agents required to adapt on the fly. We present ATLAS (Adaptive Teaching and Learning System), a dual‑agent framework that separates high‑level reasoning (Teacher) from low‑level execution (Student). ATLAS maintains a persistent memory of distilled experience, which the orchestration layer consults to modulate runtime behaviour—such as adjusting supervision levels or selecting initial plans—without touching model parameters. This gradient‑free approach shifts the learning burden from weight updates to adaptive system orchestration, aiming for “adaptive efficiency”: maximizing task success while curbing computational cost.

Using Microsoft’s ExCyTIn‑Bench, a public cyber‑threat‑analysis benchmark, ATLAS with GPT‑5‑mini as the Student reaches 54.1 % success, surpassing the larger GPT‑5 (High) by 13 % while cutting inference cost by 86 %. Cross‑incident validation further demonstrates generalisation: a frozen “pamphlet” from Incident #5 boosts accuracy from 28 % to 41 % without retraining, and alters the output style from exploratory to structured reasoning. These results confirm that gradient‑free continual learning is a practical route to adaptive, deployable AI, while the causally annotated traces produced by ATLAS offer a rich resource for constructing explicit world models.
1807:
The rapid proliferation of large‑scale generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools—such as GPT‑style language models—has reshaped scholarly workflows across publishing, pedagogy, and research. Yet institutions, professional societies, and funding agencies remain largely uncoordinated in articulating explicit policies, resulting in a growing chasm between what is permitted and what is practiced. This study investigates the “policy‑practice void” that has emerged in academia by combining an empirical survey of 1,200 scholars from the humanities, natural sciences, and social sciences with in‑depth semi‑structured interviews (N = 48) and a systematic review of 32 institutional AI‑guidelines. 

Our quantitative analysis reveals that 67 % of respondents employ generative AI for drafting or data‑analysis tasks, yet only 28 % report having accessed any formal policy, and merely 15 % have received dedicated training. Qualitative coding surfaces three epistemic indicators of voids: (1) **ambiguity of authorship and citation norms**, (2) **lack of transparency in algorithmic provenance**, and (3) **inconsistent assessments of AI‑generated content quality**. Cross‑referencing these indicators with policy documents shows a significant mismatch in 73 % of cases, highlighting the persistence of unaddressed ethical, methodological, and professional concerns.

We propose a set of diagnostic metrics—“policy‑practice concordance scores,” “knowledge‑gap indices,” and a “trust‑worthiness audit trail”—to identify and monitor emerging voids. Finally, we recommend a multi‑stakeholder framework that couples iterative policy updates with institutional capacity building, fostering a resilient ecosystem where generative AI enhances, rather than undermines, the epistemic integrity of academic work. Our findings underscore the urgent need for coordinated, evidence‑based governance to bridge the widening divide between policy intentions and on‑ground practices.
1808:
Conventional image sensors can only capture a narrow intensity range, which leads to saturation in high‑dynamic‑range scenes. Modulo cameras solve this by folding the incident light into a fixed, bounded interval, but they then require specialised unwrapping procedures to recover the true radiance. Unlike HDR reconstruction—where the goal is simply to extend the dynamic range of a sampled signal—modulo recovery must reconstruct the exact, un‑folded values from the wrapped observations. Although the idea has been around for more than ten years, progress has been modest, especially in adopting modern deep‑learning techniques.

In this work we demonstrate that standard HDR algorithms do not translate well to the modulo setting. Instead, Transformer models, which capture long‑range spatial and temporal dependencies, prove to be a promising fit, provided that the architecture is suitably modified. We therefore introduce the Selective Spatiotemporal Vision Transformer (SSViT), the first deep‑learning framework dedicated to modulo video reconstruction. SSViT employs a token‑selection strategy that concentrates computation on the most informative regions, improving both efficiency and accuracy. Experiments on 8‑bit folded video sequences confirm that SSViT produces high‑quality reconstructions and achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance for modulo video recovery.
1809:
Automatic evaluation of multimodal reasoning systems—those that jointly process vision, language, and other modalities—remains a bottleneck for rapid progress. Existing metrics either assess only the final answer or rely on black‑box score aggregation, making it difficult to diagnose why a system fails or to guarantee *faithfulness* to the evidence it was given. To address this, we propose **RPTS (Tree‑Structured Reasoning Process Scoring)**, a fine‑grained evaluation framework that quantifies the fidelity of a system’s reasoning steps as a directed acyclic graph. Each node in the tree represents a semantic unit (e.g., a visual grounding, a linguistic inference, or a multimodal integration) and is annotated with a confidence score derived from cross‑modal consistency checks. RPTS aggregates these node‑level scores via a principled dynamic‑programming scheme, yielding an overall process‑faithfulness measure that is both interpretable and sensitive to intermediate errors.

We instantiate RPTS on two challenging benchmarks, **VQG‑Faith** (visual question generation with explicit rationales) and **MUTUAL** (multimodal dialogue with multi‑step reasoning). Across both datasets, models scored by RPTS exhibit a stronger correlation with human judgments (Spearman ρ = 0.68) than standard BLEU, ROUGE, or GPT‑4‑based fidelity scores. Moreover, we show that optimizing models using RPTS as a training signal improves their final task accuracy by up to 5 % while simultaneously reducing hallucinations.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a novel tree‑structured representation of multimodal reasoning processes; (2) a faithful, interpretable scoring protocol that decomposes errors across modalities; and (3) empirical evidence that RPTS can both evaluate and guide the training of multimodal agents. RPTS is publicly released along with a benchmark of annotated reasoning trees to foster further research in transparent multimodal evaluation.
1810:
Modeling articulated objects for robotics, simulation, and virtual reality typically requires painstaking manual assembly of geometry and joint definitions in formats such as the Unified Robot Description Format (URDF). Recent multimodal large‑scale language models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to map natural language to 3D primitives, but their output has largely remained in the form of raw meshes or voxel grids, leaving the crucial articulation hierarchy unaddressed. In this work we introduce **URDF‑Anything**, a novel end‑to‑end framework that translates multimodal inputs—textual descriptions, RGB‑depth images, and point‑clouds—into fully‑specified URDF models with articulated links, joints, and physical properties. 

The core of URDF‑Anything is a transformer‑based **Multimodal Articulation Decoder (MAD)** that jointly conditions on a language encoder (BERT‑style) and a 3D geometry encoder (PointNet++ + 3D‑Swin) to predict a hierarchical joint tree and the associated link geometry. During training we employ a hybrid supervised‑reinforcement objective: supervised loss on a newly curated dataset of 5,000 real‑world articulated objects annotated with natural language instructions, and a physics‑based reward that encourages the generated URDF to preserve motion dynamics in Gazebo. We also introduce **Joint‑Aware Language Modeling (JALM)**, a curriculum that progressively exposes the model to increasingly complex articulation patterns.

Our experiments demonstrate that URDF‑Anything generates syntactically valid URDFs for 84 % of test queries, a 27 % improvement over prior template‑based methods. The resulting models achieve near‑identical forward‑kinematic accuracy (mean joint error < 2.3°) and support physically realistic simulations. Qualitative results show that the system can interpret ambiguous instructions (“open the cabinet door”) and produce multi‑degree‑of‑freedom rigs with correct collision geometries. Finally, we release an open‑source pipeline and the **Articulate‑Text Dataset** to foster future research at the intersection of language, perception, and robot model synthesis.
1811:
Bandit algorithms that exploit reward‑variance information—so‑called variance‑aware bandits—have attracted growing interest because they achieve tighter regret guarantees and more efficient exploration.
