1860: Eigenvalue problems possess a unique forward‑inverse relationship and are essential for describing a system’s thermal behavior, stability, and natural vibration modes. Physics‑Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) provide a mesh‑free means of tackling these problems, yet they typically lag behind conventional numerical solvers by several orders of magnitude in speed. This paper proposes a new PINN formulation that recasts the search for eigenpairs as a biconvex optimization task. By employing analytically optimal updates, we enable a fast, provably convergent Alternating Convex Search (ACS) that iterates between eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Numerical tests demonstrate that PINN‑ACS achieves high‑precision results while accelerating convergence by up to 500× compared to standard gradient‑based PINN training. The implementation is available at https://github.com/NeurIPS-ML4PS-2025/PINN_ACS_CODES.
1861:
Non‑intrusive cardiac monitoring with low‑power radars has attracted growing interest, yet practical deployments remain hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and the sensitivity of radar micro‑Doppler signatures to environmental noise. This paper introduces **Radar‑APLANC**, an unsupervised framework that extracts reliable heartbeat signals from continuous‑wave radar traces without any manual annotations. The core idea is to generate **augmented pseudo‑labels** by first applying a lightweight peak‑detector on phase‑shifted sub‑bands, then enriching the signal set through time–frequency transformations and synthetic jittering. These pseudo‑labels serve as a noisy supervision signal for a **Noise‑Contrastive Estimation (NCE)**–based representation learner, which discriminates true heartbeat cycles from background clutter and random micro‑motions. By iteratively refining the pseudo‑labels with the learned embeddings, Radar‑APLANC converges to a highly discriminative feature space that is robust to motion artifacts and multipath distortion. 

We evaluate the method on two benchmark datasets—IEEE 802.11ac radar and a custom FMCW radar platform—achieving a peak‑to‑noise ratio of 23 dB and a heartbeat detection F1‑score of 0.97, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art supervised CNNs by 4% in low‑SNR regimes. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of both pseudo‑label augmentation and NCE loss. The approach runs in real time on an embedded DSP, demonstrating the feasibility of fully autonomous, privacy‑preserving radar‑based vital‑sign monitoring in clinical and consumer settings.
1862:
In moral AI alignment, systems are designed to capture and adopt human stakeholders’ moral preferences. This approach assumes those preferences are fixed, yet they frequently shift over time. Effective alignment must distinguish genuine evolutions in moral reasoning from transient fluctuations caused by attention lapses, cognitive biases, or other noise. Conventional alignment strategies largely ignore such temporal dynamics, posing serious risks in high‑stakes settings—such as healthcare—where misalignment can erode trust and inflict considerable harm.

To assess how moral preferences vary, we conducted a longitudinal study in the kidney‑allocation domain. Over 400 participants completed 3–5 sessions of pairwise comparisons involving hypothetical transplant candidates. On average, respondents altered their judgments on 6–20 % of identical scenarios at different times, indicating *response instability*. We also detected substantial changes in several participants’ fitted decision‑making models over time—*model instability*. Consequently, simple AI models’ predictive accuracy deteriorated with both response and model instability, and performance degraded further across time. These results underscore fundamental normative and technical obstacles for AI alignment: when user preferences shift markedly, we must re‑examine what it means to “align to” and how to adapt to evolving moral landscapes.
1863:
Spine procedures such as pedicle screw placement and vertebral body access rely on real‑time fluoroscopic guidance to achieve millimetre‑level accuracy. However, the need for continuous image interpretation imposes cognitive load on surgeons and exposes patients to cumulative ionising radiation. We propose and evaluate a data‑driven robot control policy that autonomously navigates an instrument under X‑ray guidance, aiming to reduce procedure time, improve placement precision and minimise fluoroscopy usage.

A hybrid simulation–in‑vivo pipeline was developed. Virtual fluoroscopic sequences were generated from 3‑D CT volumes of 120 patients, yielding >15,000 needle‑trajectory pairs that emulate typical surgical workflows. A recurrent deep reinforcement learning (RL) agent was trained in this simulated environment to output continuous tip‑control commands, conditioned on the latest X‑ray image, depth‑estimation, and a target location mask. The policy was regularised with a safety‑aware cost that penalises proximity to critical anatomical structures.

The learned controller was transferred to a robotic arm equipped with a steerable needle and a fluoroscopic C‑arm. In a cadaveric phantom study (n = 25), the RL policy achieved a mean target‑point error of 1.8 ± 0.4 mm, comparable to expert surgeons (1.7 ± 0.5 mm) while reducing cumulative fluoroscopic dose by 32 % (p < 0.01) and shortening procedure time by 18 %. Ablation studies confirmed that the recurrent state representation and safety cost were essential for robust generalisation to unseen anatomy. When evaluated on a limited clinical dataset (n = 5), the policy maintained sub‑3 mm accuracy and was deemed safe by a board of surgeons.

These results demonstrate that a learned robot control policy can reliably perform X‑ray‑guided spinal interventions, offering a promising pathway toward fully autonomous, low‑dose, and highly accurate spine surgery. Future work will focus on integrating real‑time bone‑registration, expanding the dataset to capture intra‑operative anatomical variations, and conducting a prospective clinical trial.
1864:
Graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful tools for modeling relational data, thanks to their ability to exchange information along node features and graph topology. However, this very mechanism can exacerbate existing biases in the training set, allowing discriminatory signals and structural skews to be amplified and ultimately reflected in unfair predictions. Current fairness‑aware approaches typically consider bias as a single, monolithic factor, overlooking the distinct ways in which attribute‐level and structure‐level biases interact—often resulting in suboptimal compromises between accuracy and equity. 

To address this, we introduce **FairMIB**, a multi‑view information‑bottleneck framework that disentangles a graph into three complementary perspectives: node features, graph structure, and diffusion dynamics. Within each view, we employ contrastive learning to preserve only the bias‑free information shared across views, while a multi‑perspective conditional bottleneck objective simultaneously protects task performance and suppresses information about sensitive attributes. Moreover, we correct the diffusion view’s adjacency matrix through an inverse‑probability weighting scheme, curbing the spread of biased signals during message propagation. 

Across five real‑world benchmark datasets, FairMIB consistently outperforms prior methods on both predictive utility and fairness metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly disentangling feature, structural, and diffusion biases in GNNs.
1865:
Large language models (LLMs) rely on an ever‑growing key‑value (KV) cache to store the intermediate attention outputs required for subsequent tokens. In interactive or batch‑dedicated inference settings, the KV cache can consume several gigabytes of RAM, limiting the scalability of LLMs on edge devices or in high‑throughput servers. While numerous compression techniques target model weights, little work has addressed the dynamic KV cache that dominates memory during inference.

In this paper we propose **KV Cache Transform Coding (KVC‑TC)**, a principled framework that transforms the high‑dimensional KV tensors into a sparse domain, sparsifies and quantizes the coefficients, and encodes them with an entropy coder. Our method is agnostic to the underlying transformer architecture and can be applied at inference time with negligible impact on accuracy. We design two transform families tailored to the structure of KV tensors: (i) a learned low‑rank basis via PCA‑based autoencoders, and (ii) a handcrafted multi‑scale wavelet transform that captures locality across the token dimension. Experimental results on GPT‑2‑XL, LLaMA‑7B, and Stable‑Diffusion show that KVC‑TC achieves **4×–8× memory reduction** for the KV cache while keeping the perplexity increase below 0.3% and the end‑to‑end latency overhead below 5 %. Additionally, we demonstrate that the compressed cache can be restored on‑the‑fly during decoding, enabling a seamless integration into existing inference pipelines.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a general transform‑coding pipeline for KV cache compression; (2) a rigorous evaluation of transform choice and quantization strategy on LLM workloads; and (3) a practical deployment strategy that preserves inference speed. KVC‑TC opens the door to deploying large models on memory‑constrained devices and to scaling multi‑model inference engines without sacrificing quality.
1866: Enhancing competent robotic policies with on‑policy reinforcement learning is often stymied by noisy, weak gradients. In this work we revisit Evolution Strategies (ES) as a surrogate for policy gradients, but we constrain exploration with bounded, antithetic triangular perturbations that are well‑suited to fine‑tuning policies. We introduce Triangular‑Distribution ES (TD‑ES), which couples such bounded triangular noise with a centered‑rank finite‑difference estimator, yielding stable, parallel‑friendly, gradient‑free updates. Our two‑step training scheme first pre‑trains with PPO to retain early sample efficiency, then refines with TD‑ES to achieve robust late‑stage performance. Applied to a range of robotic manipulation benchmarks, TD‑ES boosts success rates by 26.5 % over PPO while markedly reducing variance, offering a lightweight, compute‑efficient pathway to reliable policy improvement.
1867: Fine‑tuning large language models on long chain‑of‑thought (CoT) demonstrations has become a key method for boosting reasoning performance. Yet conventional cross‑entropy training assigns the same weight to every token, disregarding the varying importance of tokens within a reasoning chain. This uniform weighting often misdirects supervision and hampers generalization, particularly for complex, long‑form reasoning problems. To solve this, we present **V**ariance‑**C**ontrolled **O**ptimization‑based **RE**weighting (VCORE), a principled scheme that casts CoT supervision as a constrained optimization problem. By viewing the task through an optimization lens, VCORE adapts token weights in a data‑driven way, aligning the objective more closely with robust reasoning generalization. Experiments confirm that VCORE consistently beats existing token reweighting approaches. On both in‑domain and out‑of‑domain math and coding benchmarks, models from the Qwen‑3 series (4B, 8B, 32B) and LLaMA‑3.1‑8B‑Instruct achieve marked improvements. Additionally, we demonstrate that VCORE provides a superior initialization for downstream reinforcement learning, paving the way for further advances in LLM reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/coder-gx/VCORE.
1868: Reliable air‑quality predictions are essential for public‑health warnings, exposure studies, and emission‑control policies. In reality, monitoring networks often produce incomplete spatiotemporal datasets, with gaps that vary in size and pattern due to sensor, collection, or transmission failures. Such missing observations hinder trustworthy inference, risk assessment, and may encourage overconfident extrapolation. To tackle these issues we introduce CGLUBNF—an end‑to‑end *Channel‑Gated Learning Unit* based *Spatiotemporal Bayesian Neural Field*. The model employs Fourier‑based features together with a graph‑attention encoder to capture multiscale spatial relationships and seasonal temporal dynamics. A learnable, gated residual module selectively amplifies informative channels, providing adaptive feature filtering. Bayesian inference simultaneously optimizes the predictive distribution and the uncertainty of model parameters, yielding both point predictions and calibrated confidence intervals. We evaluate CGLUBNF on two real‑world datasets, systematically testing four common missing‑data scenarios and comparing against five state‑of‑the‑art baselines. The proposed framework delivers higher prediction accuracy and tighter confidence bands, remains robust across multiple forecast horizons, and reveals the impact of auxiliary covariates. This work establishes a principled foundation for deep‑learning‑based spatiotemporal forecasting under incomplete observations, with particular relevance to emerging mobile‑sensor networks such as vehicle‑borne monitoring.
1869:
Accurate segmentation of the spinal column and its surrounding structures in computed tomography (CT) scans is essential for diagnosing and planning treatment of spinal disorders. Conventional segmentation approaches struggle with the low contrast and intricate boundaries that characterize vertebral anatomy. Although the Segment Anything Model (SAM) has achieved notable success across a range of segmentation tasks, its application to spinal CT is hampered by the need for extensive annotations and limited generalization to this specific domain.  

To overcome these challenges, we introduce **SpinalSAM‑R1**, a multimodal vision‑language interactive framework that couples a fine‑tuned SAM with the DeepSeek‑R1 language model. The system incorporates an anatomy‑guided attention module that enhances the fidelity of spinal segmentation, and a semantics‑driven interaction protocol—powered by DeepSeek‑R1—that allows users to refine results using natural‑language prompts. Adaptation is performed efficiently with Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to minimize computational overhead.  

We evaluated SpinalSAM‑R1 on a dataset of spinal CT images and demonstrated that it outperforms existing methods in segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, we developed a PyQt5‑based user interface that supports point, box, and text prompts, enabling 11 distinct clinical operations with a parsing accuracy of 94.3 % and a latency below 800 ms. The software is publicly available at https://github.com/6jm233333/spinalsam-r1.
1870:
Enterprise platforms are essential for boosting both employee productivity and customer decision‑making. Embedding large‑language‑model (LLM) based solutions into these platforms can deliver intelligent automation, tailor‑made interactions, and rapid access to information, thereby accelerating operational efficiency and fostering strategic growth. Yet, building and assessing such solutions remains difficult because enterprise environments are inherently complex: data is dispersed over many silos and tightly controlled by intricate access‑policy frameworks.  

To address this, we introduce **EnterpriseBench**, a comprehensive benchmark that emulates realistic corporate scenarios. It consists of 500 varied tasks spanning software engineering, human resources, finance, and administrative functions. The benchmark uniquely incorporates hallmark enterprise attributes—data fragmentation, hierarchical access controls, and cross‑departmental workflows. In addition, we provide a novel data‑generation pipeline that constructs internally coherent tasks directly from organizational metadata.  

Our experiments with leading LLM agents show that even the most capable models manage only **41.8 %** of the tasks, underscoring the substantial room for advancement in AI systems tailored to enterprise settings.
1871:
The representation of data as sequential strings and as graph‑structured objects are two complementary paradigms that have long been treated in isolation. Conventional sequence models (e.g., transformers, recurrent nets) excel at capturing local, ordered dependencies, whereas graph neural networks (GNNs) naturally encode relational structure and global topology. This disjunction hinders the ability to learn end‑to‑end on heterogeneous inputs that simultaneously contain sequential and relational signals, such as protein sequences with residue interaction networks, text with syntax trees, or molecular SMILES paired with chemical connectivity graphs. 

In this work we propose **SeqGraphNet**, a unified architecture that bridges this divide by jointly embedding sequences and graphs within a shared latent space. The model comprises a dual‑encoder backbone: a Transformer that processes raw token sequences and a message‑passing GNN that operates on the corresponding adjacency structure. A cross‑modal attention mechanism fuses the two embeddings, allowing the network to align local sequential patterns with graph‑level motifs. To enable true end‑to‑end learning, we introduce a *sequence‑graph alignment loss* that enforces consistency between token positions and graph nodes, and a *joint positional encoding* that preserves order information across both modalities. 

We evaluate SeqGraphNet on three benchmark domains: (i) protein function prediction from amino‑acid sequences and residue contact maps; (ii) semantic role labeling from sentence tokens and dependency graphs; and (iii) molecular property regression from SMILES strings and molecular graphs. In all cases SeqGraphNet outperforms both sequence‑only and graph‑only baselines, achieving up to 7.8 % higher F1 in protein function prediction, 4.3 % error reduction in semantic role labeling, and 0.12 RMSE improvement in molecular property regression. Ablation studies confirm that the cross‑modal attention and alignment loss are critical to the performance gains.

SeqGraphNet demonstrates that end‑to‑end sequence‑graph learning is not only feasible but also advantageous in diverse settings. By integrating sequential and relational inductive biases into a single training objective, our framework opens new avenues for modeling complex data where order and structure coexist.
1872:
This paper presents **Text-based Aerial‑Ground Person Retrieval (TAG‑PR)**, a new task that seeks to match people’s images taken from both aerial and ground perspectives using natural language descriptions. Unlike conventional Text‑based Person Retrieval (T‑PR), which is limited to ground‑view pictures, TAG‑PR tackles a more realistic problem and brings its own difficulties, primarily the large viewpoint gap between the two modalities.

To enable research on this challenge, we offer two main contributions: 

1. **TAG‑PEDES**, a large-scale dataset assembled from public benchmarks and enriched with automatically generated captions. We employ a diversified text‑generation strategy to ensure the descriptions remain robust across different viewpoints.  
2. **TAG‑CLIP**, a novel retrieval framework that mitigates view heterogeneity. It uses a hierarchically‑routed mixture‑of‑experts module to learn both view‑specific and view‑agnostic representations, coupled with a viewpoint‑decoupling mechanism that sharpens cross‑modal alignment.

We evaluate TAG‑CLIP on both the newly introduced TAG‑PEDES dataset and existing T‑PR benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness. The dataset and code can be accessed at https://github.com/Flame-Chasers/TAG-PR.
1873: Rare events—such as market crashes, extreme weather, and atypical biological phenomena—are notoriously hard to model because they appear infrequently and follow heavy‑tailed distributions. Conventional deep generative models often fail to represent these low‑probability modes, collapsing them or delivering poorly calibrated uncertainty. We introduce the **Quantum‑Enhanced Generative Model (QEGM)**, a hybrid classical‑quantum architecture that marries deep latent‑variable networks with variational quantum circuits. QEGM offers two main contributions: (1) a composite loss that simultaneously enforces accurate reconstruction and a tail‑sensitive likelihood, and (2) noise injection driven by quantum randomness to boost sample diversity and counteract mode collapse. Training runs through a hybrid loop, where classical weights are updated via back‑propagation while quantum parameters are refined with parameter‑shift gradients. Experiments on synthetic Gaussian mixtures and real‑world datasets from finance, climatology, and protein folding show that QEGM cuts tail KL divergence by up to 50 % relative to leading baselines (GAN, VAE, Diffusion) and improves recall and calibration for rare events. These results underscore QEGM’s promise as a principled, more robust solution for predicting rare phenomena than purely classical methods.
1874: In recent years, synthetic text has become a promising source for scaling the pre‑training of Large Language Models (LLMs), especially for low‑resource languages that have historically received fewer benefits from contemporary LLMs. This paper reports a comprehensive investigation into the creation and assessment of synthetic multilingual pre‑training data for Indic languages. We develop BhashaKritika, a 540‑billion‑token corpus generated with five distinct methods across ten languages. Our study examines how grounding generation in source documents, personas, and topics influences output quality, and it contrasts native Indic text produced by our models with translations of English material. To enable efficient, language‑aware evaluation, we propose a modular quality‑control pipeline that incorporates script and language detection, metadata consistency checks, n‑gram repetition analysis, and perplexity filtering using KenLM. The framework supports rigorous quality assurance across varied scripts and linguistic settings. Experiments with downstream models illustrate the trade‑offs inherent in different generation strategies and delineate best practices for building high‑quality multilingual corpora.
1875: The double‑descent (DD) phenomenon, whereby generalization improves again after an interpolation threshold in over‑parameterized models, has yet to be thoroughly investigated in the non‑stationary setting of deep reinforcement learning (DRL). In this work we provide initial evidence that DD also appears in model‑free DRL, examining it systematically across a range of network sizes within an Actor‑Critic architecture. Using the information‑theoretic quantity of Policy Entropy to track uncertainty over the course of training, we observe a distinct DD curve over epochs; the policy’s transition into the second descent phase aligns with a pronounced and persistent drop in Policy Entropy. This entropic decline suggests that excess capacity functions as an implicit regularizer, steering the policy toward flatter, more robust minima in the loss surface. Our results confirm that DD influences DRL dynamics and offer an entropy‑based framework for engineering agents that are more general, transferable, and resilient.
1876:
In recent years, large transformer‑based language models have been repurposed as in‑context reinforcement learning (RL) agents that can adapt their behavior from a handful of demonstrations or reward signals without any gradient updates.  However, these agents typically treat the observed trajectory as a deterministic sequence, ignoring the fact that many RL domains are partially observable and that a proper *belief* over hidden states is crucial for optimal decision making.  We propose the **Heuristic Transformer (HT)**, a modular architecture that augments in‑context RL with an explicit, learned belief representation.  HT first runs a lightweight inference network over the context window to produce a *heuristic belief* vector—a compressed, probabilistic summary of the agent’s latent state.  This belief is concatenated with each token’s embedding and fed to a standard transformer decoder that predicts the next action conditioned on the full context.  The model is trained end‑to‑end on large offline RL datasets (e.g., Atari, MuJoCo, and custom partially observable tasks) using a mixture of supervised imitation loss and a novel belief‑consistency regularizer that encourages the belief module to approximate the true posterior over hidden states.  

Across a suite of benchmark environments, HT achieves a median 23 % improvement in final return over vanilla in‑context transformers and a 45 % reduction in the number of interactions needed to reach comparable performance.  Ablation studies reveal that the belief augmentation is particularly beneficial in high‑uncertainty settings, where it allows the transformer to recover from misleading observations and maintain robust policy execution.  By demonstrating that a lightweight heuristic belief can be seamlessly integrated into transformer‑based in‑context RL, this work bridges a gap between classical POMDP reasoning and modern large‑scale sequence models, opening a new avenue for sample‑efficient, zero‑shot reinforcement learning.
1877:
The Opioid Industry Documents Archive (OIDA) is a vast, publicly released repository of internal corporate filings, marketing materials, and legal documents that has become a cornerstone of research into the opioid crisis. Yet, no large‑scale benchmark exists to systematically evaluate computational methods that must grapple with the archive’s heterogeneous format—PDFs interlaced with tables, figures, footnotes, and handwritten annotations—alongside its dense, domain‑specific terminology.  

In this work we introduce **OIDA‑QA**, a multimodal question‑answering benchmark that brings together 12,345 annotated questions spanning 3,876 documents, covering 19 distinct modalities (plain text, embedded images, charts, footnotes, and scanned signatures). Each question is paired with one or more evidence snippets drawn from the corresponding document, and a free‑form answer is provided by expert annotators. The dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets that preserve document-level dependencies and reflect the distribution of industry sectors (manufacturing, marketing, litigation).  

We formalize two core tasks: (1) *Document‑aware QA*, which requires retrieving the correct document and generating an answer, and (2) *Multimodal QA*, which explicitly demands extraction of information from non‑textual elements such as tables or embedded graphics. Baseline experiments using state‑of‑the‑art text‑only transformers, vision‑language models, and hybrid retrieval‑generation pipelines establish a performance spectrum and highlight the substantial difficulty introduced by the multimodal content.  

OIDA‑QA therefore serves as the first standardized, community‑ready benchmark for advancing robust, explainable AI in the context of the opioid industry, enabling future work to benchmark progress in multimodal understanding, domain adaptation, and evidence retrieval on a real‑world, high‑stakes dataset.
1878:
The rapid expansion of large‑scale nucleotide sequencing has spurred the development of foundation models that learn generalizable representations of genomic sequences. Yet, progress in this area is hampered by the absence of a unified, high‑resolution benchmark that systematically evaluates these models on biologically meaningful fitness prediction tasks. We introduce **NABench**, a comprehensive benchmark suite that aggregates >4 million experimentally measured fitness scores across 23 distinct assays (e.g., CRISPR‑Cas9 cleavage, transcriptional activity, protein‑binding affinity) spanning bacterial, yeast, and human genomes. Each entry in NABench is annotated with its raw sequence, functional context (promoter, enhancer, coding region, etc.), and a gold‑standard fitness label derived from high‑throughput mutagenesis or reporter assays.

NABench offers a standardized split protocol (training, validation, test) and a set of evaluation metrics (Spearman’s ρ, mean‑squared error, area‑under‑curve for binary fitness thresholds) that facilitate direct comparison of model families. We benchmark a diverse set of nucleotide foundation models—including transformer‑based architectures (DNABERT, ESM‑DNA), convolutional networks, and hybrid models—on these tasks. Results reveal pronounced disparities between models on sequence length, evolutionary conservation, and assay modality, underscoring the need for task‑specific pretraining objectives.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a large, reproducible dataset that bridges multiple experimental modalities; (2) a rigorous evaluation protocol that exposes current model limitations; and (3) an open‑source codebase (github.com/GenomicsLab/NABench) that provides baseline implementations and facilitates community extensions. NABench will serve as a critical resource for developing and assessing future nucleotide foundation models capable of accurately predicting functional fitness, ultimately accelerating advances in genomics and synthetic biology.
1879: Modern bioacoustic AI models, built on transformer networks, foundation‑model paradigms, and other advanced computational techniques, boast remarkable cross‑species recognition capabilities. Yet they ignore a crucial question: how does a system that relies on its own recursive cognition—through attention, iterative passes, and feedback loops—interact with the inherently recursive communicative practices of other living beings? Drawing on Yuk Hui’s theories of recursivity and contingency, I contend that these AI agents are not merely neutral pattern detectors; their internal information flows can systematically veil or warp the communicative structures of the species they observe. This generates a double‑contingency dilemma: each organism’s dialogue is shaped by its unique ecological and evolutionary context, while the AI’s interpretation is conditioned by its own architecture and training regime. I argue that overcoming this problem requires rethinking bioacoustic AI not as a universal pattern‑matcher but as a diplomatic interface between distinct recursive intelligences, which has profound implications for how we design models, evaluate them, and conduct research.
1880:
Equivariant representation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for capturing the intrinsic symmetry of structured data such as images, point clouds, and graphs. While standard equivariant architectures often employ hard‑wired symmetries, they struggle to balance specialization across diverse downstream tasks and to exploit shared structure efficiently. In this work we introduce **Soft Task‑Aware Routing of Experts (STAR‑E)**, a principled framework that augments equivariant networks with a differentiable mixture‑of‑experts (MoE) module whose gating is conditioned on the task identity. Unlike conventional hard‑routing schemes, STAR‑E learns a continuous soft assignment of feature channels to experts, thereby preserving equivariance while allowing task‑specific specialization.

Our method interleaves equivariant convolutional blocks with a *task‑aware gating network* that outputs probability vectors over a set of lightweight expert branches. Each expert implements a distinct equivariant transformation (e.g., different group convolutions or spectral filters), and the gated mixture is recomposed into a single equivariant representation that is fed to the downstream head. The gating network is trained jointly with the experts using a single objective that penalizes entropy to encourage sparse but smooth routing, and an auxiliary regularizer that enforces task orthogonality.

We evaluate STAR‑E on several benchmark suites that require equivariant processing: rotationally invariant classification on 3D point clouds (ModelNet40, ShapeNet), symmetry‑aware graph classification on molecular datasets (QM9, ZINC), and equivariant physical dynamics prediction (Newton’s cradle, fluid simulation). Across all tasks, STAR‑E achieves up to **15 %** improvement over state‑of‑the‑art equivariant baselines while reducing parameter count by 30 %. Ablation studies confirm that the soft routing mechanism is essential for balancing expressiveness and regularization, and theoretical analysis shows that the gating preserves equivariance under the underlying symmetry group.

STAR‑E demonstrates that *soft, task‑aware routing* can reconcile the conflicting demands of generality and specialization in equivariant representation learning, opening a new direction for designing efficient, adaptable symmetry‑aware architectures.
1881:
The rapid evolution of generative AI has produced deepfakes that are increasingly indistinguishable from real media, threatening both law‑enforcement efforts and public confidence. Traditional passive detectors lag behind, because they rely on specific artefacts that do not transfer to novel forgery techniques. Proactive defenses based on watermarks have been proposed, yet they frequently struggle to stay robust against harmless edits while remaining sensitive to deliberate tampering.  
In this work we propose a new deep‑learning framework that exploits high‑dimensional latent‑space representations and a Multi‑Agent Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (MAARL) architecture to build a watermark scheme that is both resilient and adaptable. Our learnable watermark embedder works in the latent space, capturing semantic image content and granting fine‑grained control over message encoding and extraction. Through MAARL, the embedder learns to strike an optimal trade‑off between robustness and fragility by training against a dynamic curriculum of benign and malicious image transformations generated by an adversarial agent.  
Experiments on the CelebA and CelebA‑HQ datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently surpasses existing techniques, improving detection accuracy by over 4.5 % on CelebA and more than 5.3 % on CelebA‑HQ under difficult manipulation conditions.
1882:
Processing‑in‑Memory (PIM) architectures are rapidly becoming the de‑facto standard for accelerating data‑centric workloads, yet their dense in‑silicon memory arrays and high‑current data‑movement paths suffer from severe IR‑drop, compromising both reliability and performance. Conventional mitigation techniques—fixed on‑chip voltage regulation, aggressive shielding, or post‑layout design rules—are either too conservative or incur prohibitive area/power overheads. In this work we present **AIM** (Architecture‑level IR‑drop Mitigation), a holistic software‑hardware co‑design framework that dynamically balances electrical constraints with algorithmic scheduling to protect PIM devices without sacrificing throughput.

AIM introduces a **runtime‑aware IR‑drop model** that maps the instantaneous power‑density landscape of the PIM array onto a graph of voltage‑drop criticality. The software layer, integrated into the PIM compiler, performs **task partitioning** and **memory‑placement** optimizations that steer data and operations away from hotspots while respecting data‑locality and load‑balance. Concurrently, the hardware layer implements a **light‑weight adaptive voltage‑control unit** that modulates supply rails, sense‑amp biasing, and on‑chip decoupling resources on a per‑core basis, guided by the IR‑drop model. The co‑ordination of these layers is orchestrated by a lightweight scheduler that exchanges IR‑status and workload metadata over a low‑overhead interconnect.

Extensive simulation on a 3D‑Stacked PIM prototype (64 Gb DDR‑4) shows that AIM reduces worst‑case IR‑drop by 32 % and improves effective bandwidth by 18 % compared with a baseline static‑voltage design, while incurring only 1.4 % area and 1.9 % dynamic‑power overhead. Experiments on benchmark workloads (graph analytics, machine‑learning inference, and HPC kernels) confirm that the combined software‑hardware approach yields up to 12 % end‑to‑end throughput gain under aggressive process corners, without violating timing or safety constraints. These results demonstrate that architecture‑level IR‑drop mitigation, enabled by tight software‑hardware coupling, is essential for the next generation of high‑performance, energy‑efficient PIM systems.
1883:
Unstructured data – ranging from semi‑structured documents to raw text and multimedia – now dominates enterprise data lakes, yet ad‑hoc analytics over such data remains a brittle and manual affair. We present **Cortex AISQL**, a production‑grade SQL engine that bridges the gap between declarative relational queries and the heterogeneous, schema‑less nature of modern data sources. Cortex AISQL introduces an AI‑augmented query layer that automatically discovers latent structure, generates semantic embeddings for non‑textual entities, and seamlessly fuses these representations into the execution pipeline. At its core lies a hybrid storage engine that couples row‑store relational tables with a distributed vector index, enabling efficient similarity searches, entity resolution, and contextual joins on unstructured blobs. The optimizer employs a reinforcement‑learning policy that learns from runtime statistics to select hybrid execution plans (native SQL, vector‑search, or deep‑learning inference) without requiring manual tuning.

We evaluate Cortex AISQL on a benchmark comprising 5 TB of heterogeneous logs, news articles, and image metadata. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art engines (Spark SQL, Presto, and a pure‑vector search baseline), Cortex achieves up to 4× lower latency for complex join–filter queries and up to 10× higher throughput for similarity‑based retrieval, while maintaining full ANSI‑SQL compatibility and supporting ACID transactions. These results demonstrate that a tightly integrated AI‑augmented relational engine can deliver both the expressive power of SQL and the analytical depth required for unstructured data in production workloads. Our work offers a roadmap for future data platforms that need to reconcile the flexibility of unstructured data with the rigor of enterprise analytics.
1884: Recent breakthroughs in large language models have brought AI systems close to expert‑level performance on highly specialized scientific tasks, yet these models tend to be narrowly engineered for specific problems. To address this limitation, we present **SciAgent**, a unified multi‑agent framework that performs general‑purpose scientific reasoning, adapting its strategies to a wide range of disciplines and difficulty levels. SciAgent structures problem solving hierarchically: a **Coordinator Agent** first evaluates the domain and complexity of a query and then dynamically arranges a set of **Worker Systems**. Each Worker System comprises interacting sub‑agents that handle symbolic deduction, conceptual modeling, numerical computation, and verification. Together, they construct and iteratively refine a reasoning pipeline customized to the task at hand. Evaluations on mathematics and physics competitions—including the IMO, IMC, IPhO, and CPhO—show that SciAgent matches or exceeds the performance of human gold‑medalists, demonstrating both cross‑domain versatility and adaptive reasoning. Additional tests on the International Chemistry Olympiad and selected problems from the Humanity’s Last Exam benchmark further confirm its generalizability. This work establishes SciAgent as a tangible advance toward AI systems capable of coherent, expert‑level reasoning across scientific fields.
1885:
Graph‐structured data are ubiquitous in social, biological and cyber‑physical domains, yet the privacy and distributional heterogeneity of such data pose significant challenges for conventional centralized machine learning. Federated learning (FL) offers a privacy‑preserving paradigm but has been largely studied on tabular or image data, with few principled extensions for graphs. In this work we introduce *Subgraph Federated Learning via Spectral Methods* (SSFL), a novel framework that jointly exploits the locality of subgraphs and the compactness of spectral representations to enable efficient, privacy‑aware FL on large, sparse graphs.  

SSFL operates by decomposing each local graph into a set of overlapping subgraphs (e.g., ego‑nets or community fragments) and projecting each subgraph onto the eigenbasis of its Laplacian. The resulting spectral descriptors—low‑dimensional vectors of eigenvalue–eigenvector coefficients—encapsulate rich structural information while being agnostic to node identities. Clients perform local training on these descriptors using graph neural network (GNN) encoders, and transmit only the updated spectral coefficients to the server. The central aggregator applies a weighted spectral averaging scheme, leveraging the orthogonality of the Laplacian basis to prevent double‑counting of shared substructures, and disseminates the global model back to the clients.  

We prove that SSFL preserves \(\varepsilon\)-differential privacy under standard noise‑adding mechanisms applied to spectral coefficients, and establish convergence guarantees for linear GNNs on the aggregated Laplacian. Experiments on benchmark citation, social and protein‑interaction graphs show that SSFL achieves up to 6 % higher accuracy on node‑classification and subgraph‑classification tasks compared with baseline graph‑FL schemes, while reducing communication payloads by 70 % and training epochs by 30 %. The method also demonstrates robustness to non‑IID subgraph distributions, a common scenario in real‑world federated deployments.  

Our results demonstrate that spectral subgraph representations provide a principled, communication‑efficient, and privacy‑preserving foundation for federated graph learning, opening new avenues for collaborative analytics on distributed graph data.
1886: The cyber‑security landscape evolves at an unprecedented pace, with new vulnerabilities, malware strains, and attack tactics emerging daily. Large language models (LLMs) possess remarkable natural‑language understanding but suffer from a static knowledge base once trained, making them ill‑suited for real‑time threat intelligence. In this work we present a Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that dynamically adapts an LLM to contemporary cybersecurity domains. Our system indexes a continuously refreshed corpus of threat intelligence feeds, vulnerability databases, and incident‑reporting documents, and retrieves contextually relevant passages during inference. The LLM then generates threat‑analysis reports, vulnerability assessments, or incident‑response recommendations conditioned on the retrieved evidence. We evaluate the approach on three tasks: (i) automated classification of phishing emails, (ii) mapping of zero‑day vulnerability reports to exploit categories, and (iii) generating post‑mortem summaries for intrusion detection alerts. Across all benchmarks, the RAG‑enhanced model outperforms both vanilla fine‑tuned LLMs and retrieval‑only baselines, achieving a 12.5 % increase in classification accuracy and a 15.8 % improvement in factual consistency on generated reports. Moreover, ablation studies confirm that the retrieval component is crucial for maintaining up‑to‑date knowledge while preserving general linguistic competence. Finally, we analyze the trade‑offs between retrieval latency, storage overhead, and explainability, and propose a lightweight caching strategy that reduces query time by 35 % without sacrificing performance. Our results demonstrate that retrieval‑augmented generation is a practical, scalable path for keeping LLM‑based cyber‑security assistants current and trustworthy in rapidly changing threat environments.
1887:
The rapid spread of misinformation on social media demands robust automated detection systems. Existing methods largely rely on linguistic cues or source credibility, often overlooking the semantic structure of events and the rich commonsense knowledge that human readers use to judge truthfulness. In this paper we introduce **FactGuard**, a novel fake‑news detection framework that simultaneously exploits *event‑centric representations* and *commonsense‐guided reasoning*.  

FactGuard first decomposes each news article into an event graph, where nodes correspond to key entities and predicates derived from dependency parsing and semantic role labeling. These graphs capture the temporal and causal relationships that are critical to assessing factuality. Parallelly, we retrieve relevant commonsense facts from the ConceptNet and ATOMIC knowledge bases and encode them as a *commonsense context vector* using a dual‑encoder architecture. The two representations are fused in a multi‑head attention layer that allows the model to align evidence from the article’s event structure with external commonsense constraints. Finally, a lightweight Graph Neural Network aggregates this information into a global credibility score, which is supervised using a multi‑task loss that jointly predicts factuality and the presence of deceptive cues.

Evaluated on four benchmark datasets (FakeNewsNet, FEVER, LIAR, and a newly curated event‑centric news corpus), FactGuard outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines by 4.7–7.2 % in accuracy and 3.1–5.5 % in F1, while requiring fewer parameters. Ablation studies confirm that both the event‑centric decomposition and commonsense augmentation contribute significantly to performance. Moreover, case studies demonstrate that FactGuard can detect subtle factual inconsistencies that other models miss. Our results establish that incorporating event semantics and commonsense reasoning provides a powerful new direction for reliable fake‑news detection.
1888: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) have seen rapid progress, yet their capacity for sustaining truly interactive, multi‑turn conversations has not been thoroughly examined—most existing tests concentrate on one‑shot exchanges. To fill this gap, we present *Multi‑Bench*, the first benchmark explicitly aimed at assessing SDMs in extended, interactive dialogue with a particular focus on emotional intelligence. The benchmark is structured hierarchically, offering a foundational track that tests emotion perception and reasoning, and a more advanced track that challenges models to provide emotional support and apply emotional insights in conversation. Multi‑Bench consists of five meticulously crafted tasks and roughly 3.2K examples, spanning from basic emotion recognition to sophisticated reasoning and interactive dialogue scenarios, all backed by a reproducible evaluation pipeline. We benchmark six leading SDMs across eight subsets of Multi‑Bench. The results reveal that while current models perform well on elementary emotion‑understanding tasks, they still fall short in the more demanding multi‑turn dialogue and reasoning aspects—especially in demonstrating emotion awareness and applying it effectively.
1889: The recent surge in Artificial Intelligence (AI) performance is inseparable from a parallel wave of innovations in computer architecture. As Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have expanded in size and sophistication, their enormous computational requirements have stretched conventional hardware to its limits. This survey presents a systematic examination of the architectural evolution that has emerged to meet these demands. We dissect the prevailing accelerators—Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), Application‑Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), and Field‑Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs)—highlighting their design philosophies, salient features, and inherent trade‑offs. Core efficiency drivers such as data‑flow optimization, sophisticated memory hierarchies, sparsity exploitation, and quantization techniques are explored in depth. Looking forward, the paper also surveys nascent technologies like Processing‑in‑Memory (PIM) and neuromorphic processors that promise to reshape future computational paradigms. By integrating architectural insights with quantitative performance results from industry‑standard benchmarks, this review delivers a comprehensive overview of the AI accelerator landscape. We conclude that AI and computer architecture have become mutually dependent, making hardware‑software co‑design an indispensable strategy for advancing computing capabilities.
1890:
The digital divide in Sub‑Saharan Africa is exacerbated by the scarcity of quality educational content in indigenous languages and the limited computational resources available on rural devices. We present **Agentic Educational Content Generation (AECG)**, a framework that leverages lightweight language models and a goal‑driven “educational agent” to autonomously produce culturally‑relevant learning materials in nine major African languages (Swahili, Yoruba, Zulu, Amharic, Igbo, Hausa, Wolof, Twi, and Oromo) directly on edge devices.  

AECG integrates three key innovations. First, a cross‑lingual transfer pipeline fine‑tunes a 32‑M parameter transformer on a newly compiled multilingual corpus of educational texts, teacher‑generated prompts, and open‑source open‑content resources, achieving a 60‑point gain in BLEU over a baseline multilingual GPT‑2 on a held‑out test set. Second, an agent‑oriented controller learns to adapt content difficulty and topic selection based on student responses and device context, using reinforcement learning with a lightweight policy network that occupies < 5 MB of RAM. Third, a modular, on‑device inference stack (quantized 4‑bit weights, sparse attention) achieves 70 ms generation latency on a Snapdragon 662 SoC while consuming < 30 mAh per minute of use.  

A mixed‑methods evaluation (N = 312 learners across four sub‑Saharan countries) demonstrates that content produced by ADCG increases engagement (p < 0.01) and comprehension scores by 14 % relative to static textbook excerpts. The study also confirms that the agent’s adaptive pacing improves learner retention in low‑bandwidth environments. All models, datasets, and evaluation scripts are released under a permissive license, enabling rapid deployment and further research on edge‑based, agentic educational content generation for low‑resource languages.
1891: Neural receivers deliver performance that far exceeds that of conventional designs, yet their complex networks impose a large computational burden. This makes them difficult to run on devices with limited hardware resources. To make these receivers practical, this paper studies two complementary optimisation techniques: quantisation and compression. We propose both uniform and non‑uniform quantisation schemes, including a novel Fibonacci Code‑Word Quantisation (FCQ) method. To recover the accuracy loss introduced by quantisation, we also introduce a fine‑grained version of Incremental Network Quantisation (INQ). In addition, we present two lossless compression algorithms that exploit the substantial redundancy in the sequences of FCQ‑quantised parameters, dramatically shrinking the memory footprint. The quantisation alone cuts the power consumption of multipliers by 45 % and their area by 44 %; when combined with the compression, the memory size is reduced by 63.4 %, all while still achieving higher performance than a conventional receiver.
1892:
We present a conditional latent‑diffusion framework for tackling the ill‑posed inverse scattering problem in microwave imaging. Unlike conventional deterministic machine‑learning solvers that yield a single reconstruction, our generative model explicitly accommodates the inherent non‑uniqueness of the inverse mapping. It produces a spectrum of plausible permittivity maps conditioned on measured scattered‑field data, thereby sampling the entire feasible solution space. A physics‑based forward electromagnetic solver is embedded within the pipeline to evaluate each candidate; the reconstruction that minimizes the discrepancy between predicted and measured scattered fields is selected as the final estimate.

The model is trained and benchmarked on both synthetic and experimental labeled datasets. We introduce a novel synthetic dataset that showcases a wide variety of scattering signatures, which enables the network to generalise across diverse scenarios while preserving high shape fidelity. The resulting permittivity reconstructions demonstrate superior quality and generalisation, underscoring the promise of hybrid generative‑physics approaches for robust, data‑driven microwave imaging.
1893:
Accurate, real‑time estimation of both system states and unknown inputs or parameters is critical for modern control and monitoring applications ranging from robotics to power‑grid protection. Conventional Kalman‑filter‑based techniques either linearise the dynamics, sacrificing accuracy, or require batch processing, which is infeasible in time‑sensitive scenarios. This paper develops an **Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)** framework that simultaneously estimates state variables, external inputs, and slowly varying model parameters of highly nonlinear systems in a recursive, online fashion.

The proposed method augments the state vector with input‑parameter blocks and propagates a carefully chosen set of sigma points through the full nonlinear measurement and process models. By retaining higher‑order moments, the UKF captures non‑Gaussian statistics without resorting to linearisation, enabling robust convergence even for strongly nonlinear or poorly conditioned problems. We present a rigorous derivation of the augmented filter equations, discuss observability conditions for joint input‑parameter estimation, and introduce an adaptive covariance inflation scheme that mitigates model mismatch and measurement noise.

Numerical experiments on a benchmark quad‑rotor flight dynamics problem and a power‑system fault‑detection scenario demonstrate that the UKF achieves superior estimation accuracy and faster convergence compared with extended Kalman filter and particle‑filter baselines. Real‑time implementation on an embedded processor confirms the method’s suitability for online deployment. The results indicate that the proposed unscented approach provides a powerful, low‑complexity tool for concurrent state, input, and parameter estimation in a wide range of nonlinear, real‑time applications.
1894: Health‑related misinformation is pervasive and can cause serious harm. Identifying such content is especially difficult when it distorts or misinterprets scientific evidence. In this study we examine how synthetic data generation and lightweight fine‑tuning can improve large language models (LLMs) at spotting fallacious arguments, using the MISSCI dataset and framework. We present MisSynth, a pipeline that employs retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) to produce synthetic fallacy examples, which are then used to fine‑tune an LLM. Our experiments reveal significant gains: a fine‑tuned LLaMA 3.1 8B model surpasses its vanilla counterpart by more than 35 % F1‑score on the MISSCI test split. These findings demonstrate that augmenting limited annotated resources with synthetic fallacy data can markedly enhance zero‑shot LLM performance on real‑world scientific misinformation tasks, even with modest computational budgets. The code and synthetic dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/mxpoliakov/MisSynth.
1895:
Achieving expert-level performance in simulation‑based training hinges on the production of complex, adaptable scenarios—a task that has traditionally demanded extensive human effort and resources. Previous work on scenario generation for military training has shown that non‑LLM AI tools often fall short in producing sufficiently intricate or flexible content. In this paper we propose a multi‑agent, multi‑modal reasoning framework that harnesses Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate critical training artifacts, such as Operations Orders (OPORDs). 

Our framework decomposes scenario creation into a hierarchy of sub‑problems, assigning a distinct AI role to each: (1) generating a set of options for a human designer to choose from, (2) producing a draft product for human approval or refinement, and (3) creating fully automated text artifacts. Specialized LLM‑based agents tackle each sub‑problem, ingesting outputs from preceding agents and integrating textual scenario details with visual data (e.g., map features, unit positions). This sequential processing preserves logical consistency and ensures accurate document construction, overcoming the limitations of simple prompting or single‑agent methods when faced with highly complex tasks.

We validate the approach with a proof‑of‑concept that generates the scheme of maneuver and movement section of an OPORD while estimating map positions and movements. The results confirm that our LLM‑driven multi‑agent system can produce coherent, nuanced documents and adapt dynamically to changing conditions, thereby advancing automation in scenario generation for military training.
1896:
Accurate 3D scene understanding from a handful of RGB images is essential for mobile robots, AR/VR and autonomous agents, yet most modern pipelines rely on large, task‑specific training sets and expensive depth sensors.  We present **Sparse3DPR**, a *training‑free* framework that performs hierarchical 3D scene parsing and task‑adaptive subgraph reasoning directly from *sparse* RGB views.  The method first fuses multi‑view structure‑from‑motion with a lightweight probabilistic occupancy grid to obtain a coarse volumetric model.  A geometric–semantic refinement stage then induces a hierarchical scene graph by iteratively clustering voxels into object‑level nodes and grouping them into functional subgraphs (e.g., “kitchen”, “living‑room”).  Crucially, every inference step is driven by a set of analytic geometric priors and logical constraints; no deep network is trained or fine‑tuned, yielding zero‑cost generalization to unseen environments.

For downstream tasks we introduce a **task‑adaptive subgraph reasoning** module that selects relevant subgraphs (e.g., “object affordances” for manipulation or “navigation corridors” for path planning) and propagates constraints across the graph using a lightweight message‑passing engine.  The entire pipeline operates online, requiring only 3–5 RGB frames and runs at 12 Hz on a standard GPU.  

We evaluate Sparse3DPR on ScanNet, Replica and Matterport3D under varying degrees of view sparsity.  Compared to learning‑based baselines (e.g., 3D‑CNNs, point‑cloud segmentation) we achieve comparable or superior performance on 3D semantic segmentation (mean IoU 67.3 % vs 65.8 %) and affordance prediction (AUC 0.86 vs 0.83), while reducing inference time by 4× and eliminating the need for labeled training data.  Ablation studies confirm that hierarchical graph construction and task‑specific reasoning are the primary drivers of accuracy gains.

Sparse3DPR demonstrates that robust, hierarchical 3D scene parsing and flexible reasoning can be realized without any training, enabling rapid deployment in real‑world robotic and AR applications where labeled data and sensors are scarce.
1897:
On-demand ride‑pooling platforms operate over millions of vehicles and passengers each day, yet the joint problem of *matching* requests to drivers and *rebalancing* idle vehicles remains largely solved only in a myopic, short‑horizon sense.  Ignoring the downstream effects of today’s allocation decisions can lead to persistent supply–demand imbalances, long wait times, and inefficient fleet utilization.  In this work we formulate a non‑myopic matching‑and‑rebalancing problem for large‑scale ride‑pooling systems as a long‑horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP) and propose a *simulation‑informed reinforcement learning* (SIRL) framework that learns policies capable of anticipating the future consequences of current actions.  

Our approach couples a high‑fidelity microscopic traffic simulator with a hierarchical deep‑RL architecture.  The simulator is used to generate realistic state‑transition dynamics and to pre‑train a policy network on a distribution of demand scenarios, thus mitigating the sample‑efficiency challenge of RL in sparse‑reward environments.  The policy is represented by a graph neural network that operates on the spatio‑temporal demand–supply graph, allowing it to scale to fleets of 10⁵ vehicles and 10⁶ passengers per hour.  We introduce a composite reward that balances passenger wait time, vehicle idle time, and route‑deviation penalties, and we employ multi‑step temporal‑difference learning with curriculum‑based horizon expansion.

Experiments on synthetic grids and on a real‑world dataset from New York City’s “Lynx” fleet demonstrate that our SIRL policy reduces average passenger wait time by 22 % and idle mileage by 18 % compared with state‑of‑the‑art myopic matching and rebalancing baselines.  Moreover, the learned policy is robust to sudden demand surges and works effectively in both single‑ and multi‑vehicle per trip scenarios.  

We highlight three key contributions: (1) a scalable non‑myopic matching‑rebalancing formulation that captures long‑term fleet dynamics; (2) a simulation‑informed RL training pipeline that substantially improves sample efficiency; and (3) a practical, data‑driven policy that achieves significant operational gains in large‑scale ride‑pooling deployments.  These results open a path toward more efficient, demand‑responsive transportation services in growing urban environments.
1898: Designers often run into roadblocks when turning static SVG graphics into animated assets, especially when the visual hierarchy of the file does not match the level of motion detail they need. Most existing tools rely on pre‑defined groupings or demand a level of technical know‑how that hampers free experimentation. We introduce **Decomate**, a system that lets you animate SVGs through natural‑language commands. By using a multimodal large language model, Decomate automatically restructures raw SVGs into semantically meaningful, animation‑ready components. Designers can then describe the motion for each component with text prompts, and the system generates the corresponding HTML/CSS/JavaScript animation. This iterative, language‑driven workflow embeds generative AI directly into creative processes, enabling users to shape animation outcomes precisely from their intent.
1899:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful tool for improving reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Yet, current RL‑based methods often encounter *Gradient Starvation* and *Policy Degradation* when they are trained on a mixture of easy and hard examples. Previous solutions have attempted to sidestep these issues by employing Chain‑of‑Thought (CoT) demonstrations, but generating high‑quality CoT annotations is costly. Other attempts have turned to curriculum learning, but they usually suffer from mismatched difficulty levels, the burden of hand‑crafted curricula, and catastrophic forgetting.

In response, we introduce **AdaCuRL**—an Adaptive Curriculum Reinforcement Learning framework. AdaCuRL jointly estimates task difficulty at a coarse‑to‑fine granularity and schedules training examples accordingly, thereby matching the difficulty of the data to the evolving capability of the model. It also revisits previously seen data to reduce forgetting. To guard against policy collapse, AdaCuRL incorporates an adaptive reference policy and a sparse Kullback‑Leibler penalty. Extensive evaluations on a variety of reasoning benchmarks show that AdaCuRL consistently outperforms existing methods, delivering notable gains for both standard LLMs and multimodal LLMs.
1900:
Food Visual Question Answering (Food‑VQA) demands more than surface‑level recognition; answering a query such as *“Which ingredients in this dish are gluten‑free?”* or *“How many calories does this dessert contain?”* requires multi‑step reasoning over the image, a semantic inventory of food items, and external nutritional knowledge. In this work we introduce **Thought‑For‑Food (TFF)**, a multimodal framework that explicitly constructs a *reasoning chain* to decompose a complex query into a sequence of interpretable sub‑steps. TFF first encodes the image and the natural‑language question with a cross‑modal transformer, then a *Chain‑Induction Module* predicts a short, symbolic reasoning skeleton (e.g., “detect ingredient → map ingredient → infer property”). Each node in the chain invokes a specialized sub‑module: a fine‑grained object detector, a knowledge‑base lookup, or a lightweight neural regressor, producing intermediate answers that are fed forward to the next step. The final answer is assembled by a lightweight decision network that aggregates the chain outputs.  

We evaluate TFF on two benchmark food‑VQA datasets, **Food101‑VQA** and **VQA‑Food‑Nutrient**, where it achieves state‑of‑the‑art accuracy (+4.2 % absolute on Food101‑VQA, +3.8 % on VQA‑Food‑Nutrient) and superior interpretability, as shown by automatic chain‑explainability metrics and user studies. Ablation studies confirm the importance of each chain component, and a zero‑shot experiment demonstrates TFF’s ability to transfer reasoning patterns to unseen dishes. Our results demonstrate that explicitly inducing a reasoning chain, rather than learning a monolithic mapping, yields both higher accuracy and actionable explanations for Food‑VQA systems.
1901:
Accurate, reproducible psychiatric diagnosis remains a persistent challenge owing to the nuanced, often subjective nature of symptom presentation and the heterogeneity of diagnostic criteria. In this work we present a novel, open‑source decision‑support framework that harnesses a consortium of fine‑tuned large language models (LLMs) in conjunction with the OpenAI‑gpt‑oss reasoning LLM to standardize diagnostic processes across multiple clinical settings.

We curated a comprehensive, multimodal dataset comprising 5,000 de‑identified electronic health records (EHRs), DSM‑5 and ICD‑10 diagnostic guidelines, and structured interview transcripts. A multi‑model consortium was built by domain‑specialized fine‑tuning of open‑source LLMs on disorder‑specific corpora, followed by an ensembling stage that leverages the OpenAI‑gpt‑oss model to generate a transparent, chain‑of‑thought rationale for each predicted diagnosis. The system outputs both a primary DSM‑5 diagnosis and a confidence score, along with a brief narrative of supporting evidence.

In a blinded evaluation against a panel of ten board‑certified psychiatrists, the LLM‑enabled system achieved an overall F1‑score of 0.86 across 12 core psychiatric disorders, with particularly strong performance for mood (MDD: 0.88; Bipolar I: 0.84) and anxiety (GAD: 0.82) categories. The model also reduced inter‑rater variability by 28 % relative to clinician consensus and provided consistent, reproducible decision paths that could be audited and refined.

Our findings demonstrate that a fine‑tuned LLM consortium, augmented by a reasoning‑focused OpenAI‑gpt‑oss backbone, can substantially improve the standardization of psychiatric diagnoses while preserving interpretability. Future work will address scalability to low‑resource settings, continuous model updating via federated learning, and the ethical governance of automated diagnostic support.
1902: Coordinating heterogeneous agents to solve complex, multi‑step problems remains a central challenge in autonomous systems. Traditional centralized planners often lack the flexibility to adapt to dynamic environments or to leverage specialized capabilities across a diverse agent portfolio. In this work we propose a modular task‑decomposition framework driven by large language models (LLMs) that enables **dynamic collaboration** among autonomous agents. An LLM‑based orchestrator first analyzes a global objective, generates a hierarchical plan that decomposes it into a set of sub‑tasks, and assigns each sub‑task to a suitable agent or module. During execution, agents communicate via a lightweight protocol that allows them to request assistance, share partial results, and update the plan on the fly. This end‑to‑end system is evaluated on a suite of benchmark domains—including multi‑robot manipulation, autonomous navigation, and knowledge‑based reasoning tasks—where it achieves state‑of‑the‑art success rates while significantly reducing coordination overhead. We also provide an analytical study of the trade‑offs between LLM‑driven planning depth and agent specialization, and demonstrate that our approach scales gracefully to dozens of agents. Our results show that large language models can serve as powerful cognitive glue, enabling modular, adaptive, and robust multi‑agent collaboration in complex environments.
1903: Sign-language translation remains difficult largely because of the limited availability of large, sentence‑aligned corpora. Earlier work has explored various feature‑extraction tricks and architectural tweaks to adapt neural machine translation models to sign data. In this paper we introduce **POSESTITCH‑SLT**, a novel pre‑training strategy that draws inspiration from linguistic‑template‑based sentence generation. When we train a straightforward transformer encoder‑decoder on template‑generated sentence pairs and evaluate it on the How2Sign and iSign datasets, it surpasses existing approaches. Specifically, we lift the BLEU‑4 score from 1.97 to 4.56 on How2Sign and from 0.55 to 3.43 on iSign, establishing a new state of the art for pose‑based, gloss‑free translation. These findings highlight the power of template‑driven synthetic supervision in low‑resource sign‑language settings.
1904: Discovering new materials is fundamentally hampered by the difficulty of extracting synthesis protocols, which are dispersed throughout decades of unstructured literature. In this work, we introduce a multi‑modal toolkit that leverages large language models (LLMs) and vision‑language models (VLMs) to automatically harvest and catalogue synthesis instructions and associated performance metrics from both the text and figures of materials‑science papers. From a curated set of 81 000 open‑access articles, we created LeMat‑Synth v1.0, a dataset comprising 35 distinct synthesis approaches applied to 16 material classes, organized under a domain‑specific ontology. We assess extraction fidelity on a 2.5 k‑entry subset using expert annotations in tandem with a scalable “LLM-as‑judge” framework. In addition to the dataset, we release a modular, open‑source software stack that enables the community to extend the approach to new corpora and synthesis areas. Together, these contributions provide a flexible infrastructure that converts unstructured literature into machine‑readable data, setting the stage for predictive models of synthesis protocols and the elucidation of synthesis–structure–property relationships.
1905:
The Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) remains a cornerstone benchmark for combinatorial optimisation, yet its exponential solution space still poses formidable challenges for both exact solvers and data‑driven heuristics. In this work we investigate the adaptation and fine‑tuning of **TabPFN**—a recently proposed probabilistic transformer for tabular data—to learn high‑quality tours directly from raw instance descriptors. We first reformulate TSP instances as structured tabular data: each city pair is represented by its Cartesian coordinates, distance, and relative ordering, thereby preserving permutation invariance while enabling the model to exploit local and global geometric cues. Leveraging a multi‑task objective that jointly predicts edge inclusion probabilities and tour length bounds, we train TabPFN on a diverse pool of randomly generated Euclidean TSPs ranging from 20 to 500 nodes, and subsequently fine‑tune on problem‑specific distributions (e.g., clustered, grid‑like, or sparse instances) using a small adaptation budget.

Our experiments demonstrate that the fine‑tuned TabPFN achieves tour lengths within 1.3 % of the optimum on the TSPLIB benchmark, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art neural solvers and approaching the performance of classic exact methods while reducing inference time by two orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the probabilistic outputs enable a principled exploration of candidate solutions, facilitating an efficient stochastic search that further narrows the optimality gap. We analyse the effect of transfer learning across instance sizes, revealing rapid generalisation thanks to TabPFN’s inductive bias for relational reasoning. Finally, we propose an adaptive fine‑tuning schedule that balances exploitation and exploration, yielding robust performance across unseen TSP domains.

This study establishes TabPFN as a versatile and scalable framework for learning combinatorial optimisation strategies and highlights the value of probabilistic tabular models for complex routing problems.
1906:
We investigate the problem of generating new, unseen strings from a target language \(K\) when an algorithm is fed an adversarial enumeration of \(K\)’s elements.  Kleinberg and Mullainathan [KM24] showed that such “generation in the limit” is possible in a very broad range of settings, but their construction suffers from *mode collapse*: it eventually produces strings from only a shrinking subset of \(K\).  To overcome this, Kleinberg and Wei [KW25] required the output to be *dense* in the target language and proved that dense generation is still achievable under the same general conditions.

All of these results assume perfectly clean data—no erroneous insertions and no missed examples.  This leaves a natural question: how much noise can the process tolerate?  Recent work has addressed this by examining non‑dense generation with either a finite amount of noise (but no omissions) or a finite number of omissions (but no noise).

In this paper we provide a full robustness characterization for contaminated enumerations:

1. **Generation under Contamination.**  
   Language generation in the limit is achievable for every countable collection iff the fraction of contaminated examples tends to zero.  When this condition is violated, we precisely identify which collections remain generable.

2. **Dense Generation under Contamination.**  
   Dense generation is strictly less tolerant of contamination than ordinary generation.  As a consequence we solve an open problem of Raman and Raman [ICML25], showing that, with only membership‑oracle access, generation is still possible even when a finite number of examples are contaminated.

3. **Beyond Worst‑Case Learning.**  
   Introducing a curriculum‑learning inspired model, we prove that dense generation can succeed despite an infinite amount of contamination, provided that the contamination rate itself converges to zero.  This highlights the potential importance of curriculum learning for learning from noisy web data.
1907:
Accurate and rapid prediction of structural dynamics is a cornerstone of modern design and safety assessment in aerospace, civil, and mechanical engineering. Conventional finite‑element solvers, while highly reliable, become computationally prohibitive for real‑time control, uncertainty quantification, or large‑scale parametric studies. In this work we introduce a **Graph Network‑based Structural Simulator (GN‑Sim)** that leverages graph neural networks (GNNs) to learn the mapping from geometric and material descriptors to time‑resolved dynamic responses of arbitrary structural meshes. By representing each element as a node and inter‑element couplings as edges, our model naturally incorporates the sparsity and local interaction patterns inherent to structural mechanics. A physics‑informed message‑passing architecture is proposed, embedding conservation of momentum and energy through equivariant layers and a dedicated loss term that penalizes deviation from the governing differential equations.

We train GN‑Sim on a comprehensive dataset of synthetic problems generated with a high‑fidelity finite‑element solver, covering a broad range of boundary conditions, loading histories, and material properties. The learned model predicts transient displacements, velocities, and stresses with sub‑percent mean‑absolute‑error relative to reference solutions while reducing inference time by up to **three orders of magnitude** compared to conventional solvers. Moreover, we demonstrate strong generalization to unseen mesh topologies and loading regimes, confirming the model’s ability to capture underlying physics rather than memorizing training cases.

Our results indicate that GN‑Sim provides an effective surrogate for structural dynamics, enabling accelerated design loops, real‑time monitoring, and integration into larger multi‑physics frameworks. The approach opens new avenues for applying data‑driven techniques to high‑dimensional PDEs in engineering, and establishes a foundation for further extensions such as adaptive mesh refinement and uncertainty-aware predictions.
1908:
Urban flow inference—predicting fine‑grained spatio‑temporal traffic, taxi, or pedestrian densities—is a cornerstone of next‑generation smart‑city services. Existing deep models achieve high accuracy at the cost of heavy computation, limiting real‑time deployment on edge devices such as traffic cameras or mobile sensors. In this work we propose **Boosting Fine‑Grained Urban Flow Inference via Lightweight Architecture and Focalized Optimization (LAFIO)**, a two‑stage framework that simultaneously reduces model size and sharpens predictive focus on critical spatio‑temporal patterns.

The first component, a **Lightweight Graph‑Transformer (LGT)**, replaces standard 3×3 convolutions with depth‑wise separable attention blocks and a hierarchical graph pooling scheme. This reduces parameters by 70 % and inference time by 4× relative to state‑of‑the‑art Conv‑GNN baselines, while preserving the ability to capture long‑range spatial dependencies. The second component, **Focalized Loss (FL)**, extends the focal loss to multi‑scale flow maps. By dynamically weighting residuals in high‑density and rapid‑change regions, FL mitigates the class‑imbalance inherent in urban flow data and forces the network to learn fine‑grained dynamics that are otherwise drowned by dominant background flows.

We evaluate LAFIO on four large‑scale urban datasets (TaxiBJ, TaxiNY, BikeShareNYC, and METR‑London), achieving up to 12.4 % relative improvement in RMSE over the best prior art while keeping the model under 2 M parameters. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of LGT and FL, and a real‑time edge deployment experiment demonstrates sub‑100 ms inference on an NVIDIA Jetson Xavier. Our results illustrate that judicious architectural lightness combined with focalized optimization can unlock high‑precision urban flow inference in resource‑constrained settings.
1909:
The rapid deployment of AI agents in consumer‑facing applications has intensified the need for reliable mechanisms to verify adherence to privacy policies, both to safeguard user data and to satisfy increasingly stringent regulatory requirements. Existing compliance tools either rely on manual code reviews or on opaque black‑box testing, neither of which scales to the heterogeneity of contemporary AI systems. In this work we introduce **AudAgent**, a unified framework that automates the end‑to‑end auditing of privacy‑policy compliance for AI agents. AudAgent first converts natural‑language policies into a formal policy graph using a hybrid NLP‑based extraction pipeline augmented with a domain‑specific ontology. It then instruments the target AI agent’s code and runtime environment to trace data flows, decision points, and external interactions.
