Controlling particular behaviors in large language models while keeping their overall capabilities intact remains a key hurdle for the safe and dependable use of AI. Existing steering techniques—such as vector addition or directional ablation—operate within a two‑dimensional subspace spanned by the activation and a feature direction. These methods are highly sensitive to hyper‑parameter choices and can inadvertently alter unrelated aspects of the model due to cross‑talk in the activation space.  

In this work we propose **Angular Steering**, a flexible new approach that manipulates activations by rotating them inside a fixed two‑dimensional subspace. By casting steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering delivers smooth, fine‑grained control over traits such as refusal or compliance. We showcase the method with examples in refusal and emotion steering.  

We further introduce **Adaptive Angular Steering**, a selective variant that rotates only those activations that are aligned with the target feature, improving stability and coherence. Angular Steering subsumes traditional addition and orthogonalization techniques under a single rotational framework, simplifying parameter tuning and preserving model stability across a wide range of adjustments.  

Across multiple model families and scales, experiments demonstrate that Angular Steering offers robust behavioral control without sacrificing general language modeling performance, highlighting its versatility, generality, and resilience compared to prior techniques. Source code and artifacts can be found at https://github.com/lone17/angular-steering/.
2506: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents have achieved impressive results in many areas, yet they remain susceptible to adversarial manipulation. This vulnerability is particularly acute in vision‑based tasks, where tiny changes to high‑dimensional pixel inputs can easily divert an agent’s decisions. Recent literature has introduced a range of defensive techniques that, according to the authors, provide robustness against large state perturbations. However, a closer look reveals that these defenses largely rely on a weakness of the prevailing \(l_p\)-constrained attack methods: such attacks can only introduce limited semantic alterations to images, even with a sizable perturbation budget. In this paper, we introduce SHIFT, a policy‑agnostic, diffusion‑based state‑perturbation method that overcomes this limitation. SHIFT generates perturbed observations that diverge meaningfully from the original states while remaining visually plausible and temporally coherent, thereby evading detection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SHIFT successfully compromises even the most advanced defenses, achieving superior attack success rates and perceptual stealth compared to existing approaches. These findings underscore the critical need for RL policies that are resilient to semantics‑aware adversarial perturbations.
2507:
Academic benchmarks have long dominated AI research, yet real‑world adoption hinges on *inference economics*—the cost, energy, and operational constraints that govern deployment at scale.  In this work we move beyond accuracy curves to develop a systematic, quantitative framework for assessing the *economics of AI inference*.  We decompose total inference cost into (i) hardware amortization, (ii) energy and cooling, (iii) cloud or edge resource fees, and (iv) operational overhead such as model maintenance and data labeling.  Building on this decomposition, we introduce the *Cost‑per‑Accuracy‑Point* (C‑A‑P) metric that normalizes monetary cost against benchmarked performance, allowing direct comparison across models, devices, and workloads.

Our study evaluates 52 state‑of‑the‑art neural nets—including transformers, diffusion models, and vision‑transformer hybrids—on four hardware back‑ends (GPUs, TPUs, custom ASICs, and edge FPGAs) across 12 real‑world tasks (NLP, image classification, object detection, and recommendation).  We find that high‑accuracy models can be cost‑competitive with lighter baselines when paired with aggressive model compression (quantization, pruning) and intelligent batching, yielding up to 10× savings on cloud inference without measurable loss in accuracy.  Conversely, naïve scaling to larger GPUs can inflate energy bills by 30% per inference, underscoring the importance of hardware‑aware optimization.

Our analysis reveals that *inference economics* is not a secondary concern but a primary design driver for AI systems.  We provide actionable guidelines for practitioners—selecting hardware, choosing compression strategies, and determining optimal deployment loci—and release an open‑source inference‑cost benchmark suite to facilitate future research.  By aligning model development with real‑world economic constraints, this paper paves the way for sustainable, scalable AI deployment in industry and beyond.
2508: The agricultural sector is increasingly turning to digital solutions to enhance productivity while conserving natural resources. However, existing smart‑farming ecosystems suffer from fragmentation, vendor lock‑in, and limited interoperability, hindering the widespread adoption of automation and precision agronomy. This paper presents **SUSTAINABLE**, a holistic, cloud‑edge platform engineered to unify heterogeneous data streams from field sensors, drones, and farm machinery into a cohesive, real‑time decision‑support system. SUSTAINABLE’s core architecture integrates modular IoT gateways, a scalable message broker, and a micro‑service based analytics engine that implements state‑of‑the‑art machine‑learning models for irrigation scheduling, pest detection, and yield forecasting. The platform adopts open standards (OPC UA, MQTT, and RESTful APIs) to ensure interoperability with legacy equipment and facilitates seamless integration of new devices via a plug‑and‑play configuration module. To evaluate its efficacy, we deployed SUSTAINABLE on a 50‑ha commercial vineyard and a 20‑ha mixed‑crop farm across a growing season. Compared with conventional manual management, the platform achieved a 12 % reduction in irrigation volume, a 9 % decrease in pesticide usage, and a 15 % increase in yield, while maintaining compliance with sustainability metrics such as carbon footprint and soil health indices. The results underscore SUSTAINABLE’s capacity to deliver actionable insights, automate routine operations, and support agronomic decision‑making without compromising environmental stewardship. We conclude that the platform’s modular, standards‑driven design offers a scalable pathway for integrating diverse smart‑farming technologies into a unified, sustainable agriculture ecosystem.
2509: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful tool for compressing models and transferring knowledge across architectures, yet its impact on a model’s resilience to spurious correlations that harm out‑of‑distribution performance has received little attention. In this work we examine how KD influences the transfer of “debiasing” abilities from teacher to student across natural language inference (NLI) and image classification benchmarks. Our extensive experiments reveal several insights: (i) the debiasing capacity of a model is generally weakened after KD; (ii) a teacher’s knowledge does not help a debiased model to gain additional robustness; (iii) while overall robustness may stay roughly unchanged, different bias types can be affected in markedly different ways; and (iv) we identify specific attention patterns and internal circuits responsible for these post‑distillation behaviors. Building on these observations, we introduce three practical strategies to enhance the distillation of debiasing methods: creating higher‑quality augmentation data, adopting iterative distillation cycles, and initializing students with weights derived from the teacher. To our knowledge, this is the first large‑scale investigation into the effect of KD on debiasing and its internal mechanisms, offering new insights into both the functioning of KD and how to design more robust debiasing techniques.
2510:
The emerging “agentic web” envisions billions of autonomous AI agents—predominantly powered by large language models (LLMs)—engaging in transaction and collaboration without human oversight. By 2025, several inter‑agent protocols have begun to embody this paradigm shift, including Google’s Agent‑to‑Agent (A2A), the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), and Ethereum’s ERC‑8004 “Trustless Agents.” Yet the foundational trust assumptions of these protocols have not been thoroughly scrutinized.  

This work delivers a comparative analysis of the principal trust mechanisms employed in inter‑agent protocol design: **Brief** (self‑ or third‑party verifiable claims), **Claim** (self‑declared capabilities and identities, e.g., AgentCard), **Proof** (cryptographic verification such as zero‑knowledge proofs and trusted execution‑environment attestations), **Stake** (bonded collateral with slashing and insurance), **Reputation** (crowdsourced feedback and graph‑based trust signals), and **Constraint** (sandboxing and capability bounding). For each mechanism, we examine underlying assumptions, potential attack vectors, and design trade‑offs, paying special attention to LLM‑specific vulnerabilities—prompt injection, sycophancy and nudge susceptibility, hallucinations, deception, and misalignment—that undermine purely reputational or claim‑based approaches.  

Our analysis shows that no single trust model is sufficient. We advocate for “trustless‑by‑default” architectures that anchor high‑impact actions in Proof and Stake, while leveraging Brief for identity discovery and Reputation for contextual flexibility. We evaluate A2A, AP2, ERC‑8004 and related historical variants against metrics of security, privacy, latency/cost, and social resilience (Sybil, collusion, and whitewashing resistance).  

The paper concludes with hybrid trust model proposals that reduce reputation gaming and misinformed LLM behavior, and presents practical design guidelines to build safer, interoperable, and scalable economies of autonomous agents.
2511: The rapid spread of memes across social‑media platforms demands that multimodal large‑language models (mLLMs) be able to discern harmful content in both visual and textual form. Existing tests, however, tend to measure only binary‑classification accuracy, missing the richer, context‑dependent interpretations of harm that occur in everyday use. In this work we introduce **MemeArena**, an arena‑style, agent‑based evaluation framework that provides a context‑aware and unbiased assessment of mLLMs’ multimodal harmfulness understanding. By simulating a range of interpretive scenarios, MemeArena prompts models to deliver perspective‑specific analyses, and by aggregating viewpoints from multiple evaluators it achieves consensus that mitigates individual bias. Our extensive experiments show that the framework substantially reduces judge‑agent bias and yields judgments that align closely with human preferences, offering a reliable and comprehensive method for evaluating mLLMs on multimodal harmfulness. The code and data are freely available at https://github.com/Lbotirx/MemeArena.
2512:
The human brain and large language models (LLMs) both learn to parse and generate language, yet the internal representations that support grammatical competence remain largely disparate across disciplines. In this work we investigate whether individual units in contemporary transformer‑based LLMs play a role analogous to “key neurons” observed in neurocognitive studies of human syntax processing. We first formulate a grammar‑perception task suite—including constituency parsing, subject‑verb agreement, and filler‑gap dependencies—and train a series of 12‑layer GPT‑2–style models on a curated linguistic corpus. Using a combination of saliency mapping, neuron‑importance ranking, and ablation experiments, we isolate a small subset (≈ 0.5 % of total parameters) that disproportionately drives performance on these tasks. These neurons exhibit high activation for syntactic markers (e.g., relative‑clause boundaries, long‑range dependencies) and are largely insensitive to semantic perturbations.

To assess biological plausibility, we compare the activation patterns of these key neurons with temporally resolved fMRI and magnetoencephalography (MEG) signals recorded from human subjects during identical grammatical judgments. We find a statistically significant alignment between the temporal dynamics of the LLM’s key neurons and the well‑established Broca’s‑area‑linked left‑temporal activations. Furthermore, a cross‑modal representational similarity analysis reveals that the dimensionality of the LLM’s key‑neuron subspace mirrors the low‑rank structure of the neural language network in the human cortex.

These results suggest that the same computational principles governing syntax in artificial networks may be mirrored in the human brain’s language system. By pinpointing a small, functionally critical set of neurons, we provide a concrete target for future interpretability studies and for designing hybrid neuro‑cognitive models that bridge artificial and biological language processing. Future work will extend this analysis to more complex, context‑dependent grammatical phenomena and explore the potential for transfer learning between human neural data and LLM architecture design.
2513:
Cross‑lingual transfer relies on a faithful alignment of multilingual embeddings.  
When only a handful of parallel sentences are available, conventional alignment
techniques—typically dependent on bilingual dictionaries or large parallel
corpora—suffer from over‑fitting and fragile generalization, especially for
morphologically rich or typologically distant low‑resource languages.  
In this work we challenge the prevailing belief that the quality of bilingual
supervision alone determines multilingual realignment success.  We introduce a
compact, data‑efficient framework that jointly exploits three complementary
signals:

1. **Monolingual contrastive consistency** – a self‑supervised objective that
   drives language‑invariant sentence semantics across all languages, using
   only monolingual text.  
2. **Pivot‑based cross‑lingual bridging** – a lightweight alignment module that
   iteratively aligns each low‑resource language to a set of high‑resource
   pivots, thereby reducing reliance on scarce parallel data.  
3. **Task‑adaptive fine‑tuning** – a lightweight downstream loop that
   optimizes the aligned space directly for cross‑lingual classification,
   QA, or NER, ensuring that the embedding geometry remains useful for
   real‑world tasks.

We evaluate on a suite of low‑resource benchmarks (XNLI, MLQA, Tatoeba, and
multiple typologically diverse languages) and show that our method
increases average zero‑shot accuracy by up to **5.8 %** over current
state‑of‑the‑art multilingual models while reducing model size by **30 %**.
Robustness experiments under domain shifts and noise confirm that the
realigned embeddings retain performance within a **1.3 %** loss—significantly
better than the **4.7 %** loss seen by baseline alignments.

Our results demonstrate that effective and robust multilingual realignment for
low‑resource languages hinges less on the sheer volume of bilingual data and
more on a principled integration of monolingual semantic consistency,
pivot‑based bridging, and task‑driven fine‑tuning.  This new perspective
paves the way for scalable, high‑quality cross‑lingual systems in the
world’s most underserved languages.
2514:
Learning the structure of a Bayesian directed acyclic graph (DAG) from data is a fundamental problem in causal inference and probabilistic modelling. Exact Bayesian inference over DAGs is combinatorially explosive, and existing MCMC‐based samplers become prohibitively slow once the number of variables exceeds a few dozen. This work develops a family of scalable Bayesian DAG sampling algorithms that combine (i) a novel **blockwise Metropolis–Hastings proposal** exploiting conditional independencies, (ii) a **parallelized likelihood‑ratio engine** implemented on GPUs, and (iii) a **variational pre‑screening step** that restricts the search space to a high‑probability sub‑graph of candidate edges.  

We provide a rigorous analysis of the spectral gap of the blockwise sampler and show that its mixing time scales linearly with the number of nodes under a mild sparsity assumption. Empirical evaluations on synthetic networks (up to 5,000 nodes) and real genomic and economic datasets demonstrate that our method reduces wall‑clock time by an order of magnitude compared with state‑of‑the‑art algorithms (e.g., dynamic programming, parallel tempering, and structure‑learning libraries such as `bnlearn`). Moreover, the posterior edge probabilities obtained from the scalable sampler converge to those of the exact sampler within 1 % error on graphs with 100 nodes, while achieving an 80 % reduction in memory usage.  

Our results establish that Bayesian DAG inference is feasible for high‑dimensional applications and lay the groundwork for future work on adaptive proposal strategies and integration with causal discovery pipelines.
2515:
Continuous reinforcement learning (RL) has traditionally relied on probability‐distributional techniques—such as policy gradients, actor‑critic frameworks, or distributional value estimation—to represent and optimize the agent’s action space. These approaches, while powerful, implicitly treat actions as independent components, thereby ignoring the rich geometric structure that underlies many continuous control domains (e.g., joint torques on a robotic arm, velocity vectors on a manifold of permissible motions). In this work we present **Geometric Action Control (GAC)**, a principled framework that explicitly embeds the action space into a Riemannian manifold and performs policy search directly on this manifold. By leveraging tools from differential geometry—geodesic interpolation, curvature‐aware exploration, and Lie‑group integration—GAC captures constraints and symmetries of the task environment, enabling smoother, more physically consistent trajectories.

We introduce a novel manifold‑aware policy network that maps latent Gaussian noise to action vectors via an exponential map, preserving feasibility constraints and reducing variance in gradient estimates. We further derive a second‑order curvature‑corrected natural‑gradient update that accelerates convergence in high‑dimensional action spaces. Theoretical analysis establishes a convergence guarantee under standard smoothness assumptions, while empirical evaluation on a suite of MuJoCo locomotion and manipulation benchmarks shows that GAC attains state‑of‑the‑art returns with up to 35 % fewer environment interactions compared to SAC, TD3, and recent distributional RL methods. Ablation studies confirm that the geometric formulation is particularly beneficial in scenarios with non‑Euclidean constraints or highly coupled degrees of freedom.

Our findings demonstrate that moving “beyond distributions” to a geometric action representation not only enriches the expressivity of continuous policies but also yields tangible efficiency and robustness gains. This perspective opens new avenues for integrating geometric insights into RL and for addressing practical control problems in robotics, autonomous systems, and beyond.
2516: Detecting Alzheimer’s disease (AD) from spoken‑language transcripts is difficult for large language models (LLMs), especially when the data are limited or drawn from unfamiliar distributions. Although in‑context learning (ICL) offers a parameter‑efficient alternative to full fine‑tuning, current ICL methods frequently falter due to task‑misrecognition, poor demonstration choice, and a mismatch between the label words and the actual clinical objective—problems that are particularly pronounced in AD diagnostics. We introduce Explicit Knowledge In‑Context Learners (EK‑ICL), a new framework that injects structured knowledge to stabilize reasoning and improve task alignment. EK‑ICL leverages three types of knowledge: (1) confidence scores from small language models (SLMs) to anchor predictions to task‑relevant patterns, (2) parsing‑based feature scores that capture structural differences for better demo selection, and (3) label‑word replacements that reconcile semantic expectations with the LLM’s priors. Additionally, EK‑ICL adopts a parsing‑guided retrieval mechanism and an ensemble prediction scheme to counteract the homogeneity of AD transcripts. Extensive evaluations on three AD datasets show that EK‑ICL outperforms the best fine‑tuning and ICL baselines by a wide margin. Our analysis highlights that ICL’s success in AD detection hinges on aligning label semantics with task‑specific context, demonstrating the critical role of explicit knowledge for reliable clinical reasoning under low‑resource conditions.
2517:
Retrieval‑based question answering (QA) has become the dominant paradigm for building open‑domain systems that can leverage large, heterogeneous knowledge sources. However, progress in this area is hindered by the scarcity of comprehensive benchmarks that assess both the retrieval and comprehension stages together. In this work we introduce **QUEST‑LOFT** (Query‑Evaluation for Structured Text–Large Open‑domain Retrieval‑Based Task), a new dataset designed to evaluate end‑to‑end retrieval‑based QA systems under realistic conditions. QUEST‑LOFT contains 27 k factoid and explanatory questions spanning 12 domains (history, science, technology, and law), each accompanied by a curated set of 4 k documents sourced from Wikipedia, domain‑specific corpora, and web archives. For each question we provide a gold answer and a reference passage, enabling fine‑grained evaluation of both retrieval recall and answer accuracy.

We benchmark a diverse suite of retrieval methods—including BM25, dense passage retrieval (DPR), and hybrid neural‑ranking models—against three open‑source comprehension backbones (BERT, RoBERTa, and T5). Our evaluation protocol couples retrieval performance metrics (Recall@k, MRR) with QA quality metrics (Exact Match, F1, and BLEU). Results show that dense retrieval alone attains 42.1 % EM but falls short on recall, whereas a hybrid BM25+DPR pipeline improves recall to 68.5 % and elevates EM to 73.4 %. Fine‑tuning the comprehension model on QUEST‑LOFT’s domain‑specific passages further boosts F1 to 85.2 % and reduces hallucination rates.

The analysis uncovers a strong correlation (ρ = 0.73) between passage recall and final answer accuracy, underscoring the need for domain‑aware retrieval strategies. We release QUEST‑LOFT and all experimental artifacts to stimulate reproducible research in retrieval‑based QA. The dataset and findings provide a new yardstick for future system design and highlight promising directions—such as adaptive retrievers and joint training—to push the state of the art in large‑scale, open‑domain question answering.
2518: Future wireless networks must deliver ultra‑reliable low‑latency communication (URLLC) to support mission‑critical services. Satisfying these stringent requirements is particularly difficult in two‑hop cooperative links. This paper proposes an adaptive transmission framework for a two‑hop relaying system in which each hop independently tunes its transmission settings—numerology, mini‑slot size, and modulation‑coding scheme—to ensure packet delivery within a tight latency budget. We cast the hop‑specific configuration problem as a Markov decision process and introduce DRL‑CoLA, a dual‑agent reinforcement‑learning algorithm that learns latency‑aware transmission policies in a distributed fashion. Numerical evaluations confirm that the proposed scheme attains reliability close to the optimum while meeting strict latency constraints.
2519: Scientific advancement hinges on clearly stating what is still unknown. This work explores whether large language models (LLMs) can spot such knowledge gaps within biomedical research. We distinguish two kinds of gaps: *explicit* gaps, where authors directly note missing information, and *implicit* gaps, where the absence of knowledge must be inferred from context. While earlier studies have mainly addressed explicit gap detection, we propose a new task that uncovers implicit gaps. Using almost 1,500 papers from four datasets—including a manually annotated biomedical corpus—we evaluate both closed‑weight (OpenAI) and open‑weight (Llama, Gemma 2) models at paragraph‑ and document‑levels. To guide the reasoning behind implicit gap inference, we introduce **TABI** (Toulmin‑Abductive Bucketed Inference), a framework that organizes argument structure and groups candidate conclusions for validation. Our experiments show that LLMs reliably detect both explicit and implicit gaps, with larger models typically achieving superior performance. These findings suggest that LLMs can systematically surface potential research questions, benefiting early-stage scientists, policymakers, and funding agencies. We also document common failure modes and propose strategies for robust application, including domain fine‑tuning, human‑in‑the‑loop validation, and comparative benchmarking across model families.
2520:
Large language models (LLMs) are now being used as autonomous agents for decision‑making (DM) in interactive, evolving settings. However, because they were not built for this purpose, recent evidence shows that LLMs often perform poorly on even simple online DM tasks, struggling to keep regret low or to balance exploration and exploitation. To remedy this, we propose **Iterative Regret‑Minimization Fine‑Tuning (Iterative RMFT)**, a post‑training pipeline that continuously feeds the model back low‑regret decision paths. In each round the model simulates many trajectories, picks the top‑k with the smallest regret, and fine‑tunes itself on those examples. Unlike prior approaches that (i) copy action sequences from established DM algorithms or (ii) depend on hand‑crafted chain‑of‑thought prompts, our method uses the regret signal itself to pull the model’s own reasoning and decision patterns. This eliminates rigid output engineering and supplies more natural, language‑based training signals. 

Across a spectrum of architectures—from numeric‑input Transformers to large open‑weight LLMs and even advanced closed‑weight systems such as GPT‑4o‑mini—Iterative RMFT consistently improves DM performance. Its flexible handling of outputs and reasoning formats allows it to generalize across tasks with different horizons, action spaces, reward dynamics, and linguistic contexts. Moreover, we provide a theoretical analysis showing that, in a simplified setting, a single‑layer Transformer trained under this regime can act as a no‑regret learner. In short, Iterative RMFT offers a principled, broadly applicable post‑training framework for elevating LLMs’ decision‑making prowess.
2521: This work evaluates the use of Random Forest Regression to estimate key mechanical properties of alloy steels—namely elongation, tensile strength, and yield strength—based on compositional inputs (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mn, Si, Cu, C) together with the percentage of deformation incurred during cold rolling. A curated dataset comprising these variables was employed to train and validate the Random Forest model, yielding high predictive accuracy as indicated by R² metrics and low mean‑squared errors. The robustness of the predictions is further supported by residual diagnostics and learning‑curve analyses. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of ensemble learning techniques for material property prediction and suggest valuable applications for industrial materials science.
2522:
Random Forests (RF) remain a workhorse for tabular learning due to their robustness and built‑in feature‑importance estimation. However, their performance is highly sensitive to a handful of hyperparameters (e.g., number of trees, maximum depth, min‑samples‑leaf) and to the inclusion of irrelevant or redundant features, which can inflate variance and impede interpretability. In this paper we propose **Feature Importance Guided Random Forest (FIG‑RF)**, a two‑stage framework that couples a dynamic feature‑importance weighting scheme with a Simulated Annealing (SA)–based hyperparameter search.  

In FIG‑RF, each tree is trained with a weighted Gini impurity that penalises splits on features whose importance scores—obtained from a preliminary RF run—fall below a learnable threshold. This adaptive weighting forces the ensemble to focus on the most predictive attributes, reducing over‑fitting and enhancing sparsity. The second stage employs SA to explore the discrete hyperparameter space efficiently, escaping local optima that plague grid or random search while maintaining a modest computational budget. The annealing schedule is tuned to the RF’s intrinsic randomness, ensuring that the search remains parallel‑friendly and scalable.  

Experiments on twelve benchmark datasets from the UCI repository and a large‑scale medical imaging dataset demonstrate that FIG‑RF consistently outperforms standard RFs and RFs tuned by Bayesian optimisation, achieving up to 4.7 % higher accuracy with fewer trees and lower memory footprint. Ablation studies confirm that both the importance‑guided weighting and the SA optimiser contribute substantively to the gains. FIG‑RF therefore offers a principled, computationally efficient alternative for high‑dimensional predictive modelling where feature relevance and hyperparameter tuning are critical.
2523:
The proliferation of high‑throughput omics technologies has produced unprecedented volumes of individual‑specific genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic data. While these datasets are a rich resource for biomarker discovery and precision medicine, their sensitive nature poses substantial privacy risks whenever they are aggregated across institutions. Federated learning (FL) mitigates this challenge by allowing multiple parties to collaboratively train a shared model without exchanging raw data. Nevertheless, conventional FL is vulnerable to gradient‑based inference attacks that can recover private samples or model parameters.  

In this study we present **FedHE‑Omics**, a lightweight, privacy‑preserving FL framework that integrates *additive homomorphic encryption* (HE) to secure all intermediate model updates. Our design augments the standard FL protocol with a two‑layer encryption scheme: (i) a client‑side public key is used to encrypt local gradient vectors; (ii) a secure aggregation server performs homomorphic summation of encrypted updates, yielding a globally updated model without ever decrypting individual contributions. We further reduce communication overhead by employing *batch‑wise* sparse masking and *model compression* techniques tailored to high‑dimensional omics data.  

We evaluate FedHE‑Omics on three large‑scale public datasets: TCGA‑RNA‑seq (breast cancer), 1,000 Genomes exome sequencing, and Human Proteome Project mass‑spec proteomics. Across all experiments, the encrypted FL model achieves within 1.5 % of the predictive performance of a centrally trained baseline, while the decryption‑free aggregation eliminates any risk of raw‑data leakage. We also conduct a formal privacy analysis that demonstrates resilience against gradient‑based inference attacks, achieving a formal ε‑differential privacy bound when combined with lightweight Gaussian noise. Runtime profiling shows a modest 2.5× increase in per‑round computation and 30 % higher communication payload compared with plaintext FL, yet remains practical for real‑world genomic consortia.  

FedHE‑Omics offers a scalable, provably secure solution for collaborative omics analytics, enabling high‑accuracy predictive modeling without compromising patient confidentiality. Future work will explore more efficient HE schemes and adaptive sparsification strategies to further reduce the computational burden.
2524:
Competency questions (CQs) are essential for assessing the quality of an ontology’s design. Crafting CQs manually, however, is labor‑intensive and expensive for domain experts. Recent work has turned to large language models (LLMs) to automate this task, but most evaluations rely on superficial similarity to existing CQ collections, which often miss subtle semantic errors—such as the improper use of `allValuesFrom`. Because these pitfalls elude simple rule‑based checks, we introduce a new dataset and validation framework, **VSPO** (Validating Semantic Pitfalls in Ontology), specifically engineered to surface such errors. 

Our methodology generates natural‑language definitions of classes and properties with LLMs, then deliberately misaligns these definitions with the underlying ontology by removing axioms or swapping logical operators (e.g., replacing a union with an intersection). We fine‑tune the LLaMA‑3.1‑8B‑Instruct model to produce CQs that verify the discrepancies between the provided definitions and the ontology’s axioms. The resulting queries can uncover a broader spectrum of modeling mistakes than those found in publicly available datasets. 

In empirical evaluations, the fine‑tuned model outperforms baseline approaches, achieving 26 % higher precision and 28.2 % higher recall than GPT‑4.1 in generating pitfall‑checking CQs. This work demonstrates that LLMs can automatically generate T‑Box‑validation CQs, dramatically cutting manual effort while tightening semantic consistency between ontologies and expert knowledge. To our knowledge, this is the first study to focus on semantic pitfall detection in CQ generation using LLMs.
2525:
Deploying modern multi‑task vision networks on resource‑constrained devices demands aggressive model compression, yet conventional low‑bit quantization typically yields severe performance degradation. The primary obstacle lies in the *fusion* of task‑specific and shared feature representations: naive channel‑wise or spatial‑wise averaging ignores the heterogeneous statistics induced by the different loss signals, causing catastrophic quantization errors. To address this, we propose **GABFusion** – a **G**ate‑based **A**ttention‑driven **B**lock fusion framework that re‑conceptualises feature combination for low‑bit (≤ 4 bit) quantization.

GABFusion interleaves a lightweight, learnable gating network with a global‑attention module that dynamically weighs each channel and spatial location before quantization. The gate learns to suppress task‑conflicting activations, while the attention module captures long‑range dependencies across tasks, ensuring that only task‑relevant information is retained in the low‑precision buffer. A *cross‑task consistency loss* further encourages the fused representation to preserve inter‑task gradients, mitigating the “quantization drift” that often plagues multi‑task learning.

We evaluate GABFusion on standard multi‑task benchmarks (NYUv2, Cityscapes, and PASCAL‑VOC+COCO), comparing against state‑of‑the‑art quantization baselines (LLSQ, QAT, and mixed‑precision fine‑tuning). Our method attains **>95 %** of full‑precision performance with **4‑bit** weights and activations, outperforming existing techniques by **3–5 %** on average across semantic segmentation, depth regression, and object detection tasks. Moreover, the proposed fusion mechanism incurs negligible overhead (≤ 1 % additional FLOPs) and is amenable to any backbone architecture.

GABFusion demonstrates that principled feature fusion can dramatically reduce the quantization penalty in multi‑task networks, opening the door to efficient, low‑bit deployment of complex vision models on edge devices.
2526:
Musculoskeletal (MSK) radiographs are a primary diagnostic tool for bone and joint abnormalities, yet automated detection remains challenged by subtle fracture patterns and high inter‑reader variability. In this study we investigate the efficacy of Google’s multimodal foundation model, **MedGemma**, for abnormality detection in MSK radiographs. A curated subset of 23,457 images from the publicly available MURA dataset (covering shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand, hip, knee, ankle, and foot) was used to fine‑tune MedGemma with a two‑stage training protocol: (1) a global pre‑training step on the full MURA training set with a contrastive loss to enhance feature discrimination, and (2) a supervised fine‑tuning step on a balanced set of fracture vs. non‑fracture cases. Performance was evaluated on a held‑out test split (10 % of the dataset) and an external validation cohort of 4,312 images from the RSNA Bone Fracture Detection challenge. 

MedGemma achieved an average area under the ROC curve (AUC) of **0.955 ± 0.006** on the test set, outperforming baseline CNNs (ResNet‑50 AUC 0.912, EfficientNet‑B3 AUC 0.928) by 4–5 %. In the external cohort it maintained an AUC of 0.942, demonstrating strong generalization. Sensitivity at a 5 % specificity threshold reached **0.889**, while specificity at 90 % sensitivity was **0.913**. Saliency mapping via Grad‑CAM revealed clinically relevant focus on cortical discontinuities and peri‑osteal reaction zones. 

Our results suggest that MedGemma, with its large‑scale multimodal pre‑training, captures nuanced radiographic features and provides robust abnormality detection in MSK imaging. The model’s high accuracy and transferable performance underscore its potential as a decision‑support tool in orthopaedic radiology workflows.
2527: Imitation learning (IL) empowers agents to learn complex behaviors by observing and mimicking one or several experts. The recent surge in deep‑learning techniques has dramatically broadened IL’s reach and scalability, enabling it to process diverse forms of expert data—from complete state‑action logs to partial observations or unlabeled sequences. This expansion has spurred the creation of innovative methods that tackle persistent problems such as generalization, covariate shift, and the quality of demonstrations. In this survey we survey the most recent progress in IL, drawing attention to emerging trends, novel methodological contributions, and real‑world deployments. We introduce a fresh taxonomy that diverges from earlier classifications, better capturing the current landscape and directional shifts in IL research. Throughout, we critically evaluate representative studies, discuss their advantages and shortcomings, and chart major challenges and promising avenues for future work.
2528:
The proliferation of latency‑critical applications on mobile and IoT platforms has driven the adoption of *Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE)* architectures, whereby multiple specialized neural modules are dynamically invoked to process diverse input types. In such systems, *offloading* of expert computation to edge or cloud servers is a common strategy to reduce on‑device energy and latency, but introduces new bottlenecks: the time required to fetch and deploy the requested experts and the variability of network conditions. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of *caching* and *pre‑fetching* strategies tailored to MoE offloading, with the goal of minimizing end‑to‑end latency and bandwidth consumption while preserving model accuracy.

We formalize the MoE offloading problem as a joint optimization over expert placement, cache sizing, and pre‑fetch scheduling. Building on this, we propose two novel techniques: (i) **Adaptive Prediction‑Based Caching (APC)**, which leverages historical routing decisions and input‑feature statistics to maintain a compact set of high‑utility experts in local storage; and (ii) **Context‑Aware Prefetching (CAP)**, which anticipates future expert requests by jointly modeling temporal traffic patterns and the dependency graph of MoE sub‑networks. Extensive simulations over benchmark datasets (ImageNet, C4, and a custom IoT sensor stream) and a realistic edge‑cloud testbed show that APC reduces average offloading latency by 35 % and bandwidth usage by 28 % compared to baseline least‑recently‑used caching. CAP further improves hit‑rates by 22 % under bursty traffic, yielding a 15 % absolute reduction in overall system latency. Finally, we conduct a sensitivity analysis on cache size, network latency, and expert model size, revealing the critical trade‑offs for practitioners.

Our findings highlight that carefully designed caching and pre‑fetching policies can unlock substantial gains in MoE‑based edge computing systems, paving the way for scalable, low‑latency deployment of large, multi‑expert deep models.
2529:
Large language models (LLMs) have become ubiquitous in open‑domain question answering (QA), yet reliable evaluation of their responses remains a bottleneck. Existing automatic metrics—exact match, BLEU, ROUGE, and recent semantic similarity scores—are either too brittle or only weakly correlated with human judgments, and human‐in‑the‑loop evaluations are prohibitively costly at scale. In this work we revisit natural language inference (NLI) as a principled, low‑overhead alternative for QA evaluation. We cast the QA task as a pair of entailment problems: (i) whether the model’s answer *entails* the reference answer, and (ii) whether it *contradicts* or is *neutral* with respect to it. Using a lightweight fine‑tuned NLI model, we derive a composite score that captures both correctness and plausibility while penalizing hallucination.  

To assess human alignment we conduct large‑scale crowdsourced comparisons on four benchmark QA datasets (SQuAD, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, and OpenBookQA). Our NLI‑based metric achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.78 with human quality ratings, significantly outperforming BLEU (0.43) and ROUGE (0.52). Moreover, the metric requires only a single pass through the NLI model, incurring < 5 ms per answer on commodity GPUs, thereby reducing evaluation cost by an order of magnitude relative to human annotators.  

We further demonstrate the metric’s robustness to paraphrasing and partial knowledge by injecting synthetic noise and measuring degradation in correlation. Finally, we propose an adaptive evaluation pipeline that selectively resorts to human judgment for borderline cases, achieving > 90 % reduction in manual effort without sacrificing overall score fidelity.  

Our contributions are: (1) a cost‑effective, NLI‑based metric that aligns closely with human judgments; (2) an extensive empirical study across multiple QA domains; and (3) an adaptive evaluation framework that balances automatic scoring with human oversight. These results open a path toward scalable, human‑aligned evaluation for next‑generation LLMs in question answering.
2530: Ad hoc teamwork (AHT) demands agents that can collaborate with unfamiliar partners—a capability that is essential for many real‑world tasks. The central difficulty lies in training an ego agent that can anticipate and adjust to new teammates on the fly. Traditional RL methods maximize a single expected return, which typically drives the policy toward a single, dominant strategy and thus fails to capture the rich, multimodal cooperation patterns that AHT requires. Here we present **PADiff**, a diffusion‑based framework that models the agent’s behavior as a mixture of diverse cooperative modes. Standard diffusion models, however, do not inherently account for the rapidly changing dynamics of AHT. To remedy this, we design a diffusion policy that weaves critical predictions about teammates into the denoising process, enabling real‑time adaptation. Experiments on three benchmark teamwork environments show that PADiff substantially surpasses existing AHT baselines.
2531: Large language models (LLMs) are proficient at tackling a wide range of general tasks, yet they frequently falter when confronted with highly specialized fields that demand deep cultural, linguistic, and disciplinary knowledge. Traditional medical systems, such as Ayurveda, contain centuries‑old, nuanced textual and clinical information that mainstream LLMs struggle to understand and apply accurately. To address this gap, we present **AyurParam‑2.9B**, a bilingual, domain‑specific LLM that has been fine‑tuned from Param‑1‑2.9B using an extensive, expert‑curated dataset drawn from classical Ayurveda texts and contemporary clinical guidelines. The dataset features context‑aware, reasoning‑heavy, and objective‑style Q&A in both English and Hindi, and follows stringent annotation standards to ensure factual accuracy and instructional clarity. When evaluated on **BhashaBench‑Ayur**, AyurParam outperforms all open‑source instruction‑tuned models in the 1.5–3 B parameter range and rivals, or even exceeds, the performance of considerably larger models. These findings underscore the importance of genuine domain adaptation and high‑quality supervision for developing reliable, culturally attuned AI systems in specialized medical domains.
2532:
Improving the runtime of large software repositories requires deep knowledge of code semantics and software engineering (SWE), yet most existing benchmarks focus on *what* needs to be fixed rather than *how* to fix it.  To close this gap, we present **SWE‑efficiency**, a benchmark that evaluates repository‑level performance tuning on real workloads.  Our test set comprises 498 optimization problems drawn from nine popular data‑science, machine‑learning, and HPC projects (e.g., numpy, pandas, scipy).  Each task presents a complete codebase and a slow benchmark; an agent must analyze the code, identify the bottleneck and the associated unit tests, and submit a patch that achieves at least the same speedup as a human expert while still passing all tests.  

We enable this “how‑to‑fix” evaluation with an automated pipeline that harvests GitHub pull requests containing performance improvements.  The pipeline uses keyword filtering, static analysis, test‑coverage data, and runtime checks to confirm the expert baseline speedup and to locate the relevant repository tests.  

Experiments with leading agents show a pronounced gap: on average, agents only reach about 0.15× the expert speedup.  The failures stem from difficulties in pinpointing optimization opportunities, reasoning about execution across multiple functions, and preserving correctness in their edits.  

The benchmark and its data‑generation pipeline are released to spur research in automated performance engineering and long‑horizon software reasoning.
2533:
Visual‑Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on multimodal reasoning benchmarks, yet their inner reasoning processes remain opaque and difficult to manipulate. We introduce **Ariadne**, a controllable framework that systematically probes and extends the reasoning boundaries of state‑of‑the‑art VLMs. Ariadne unifies three complementary mechanisms: (1) **Modular Reasoning Pipelines** that decompose visual‑language inference into interpretable sub‑tasks (e.g., grounding, relational reasoning, and symbolic deduction); (2) **Dynamic Prompt Engineering** that injects explicit reasoning directives (e.g., “first enumerate relevant objects”, “then compare attributes”) and allows fine‑grained control over the VLM’s inference order; and (3) **Adaptive Feedback Loops** that leverage lightweight external predictors (e.g., object detectors, graph neural networks) to correct and refine intermediate predictions in an end‑to‑end manner.  

Using Ariadne, we conduct a large‑scale probing study on six challenging datasets (VQAv2, GQA, CLEVR, NLVR², Visual‑Reasoning, and TextVQA). We quantify the impact of controllable reasoning stages on accuracy, demonstrating that a properly guided pipeline yields an average 3.5 % absolute boost over baseline VLMs while preserving 96 % of their original performance on tasks where no explicit guidance is required. Further, we showcase Ariadne’s extensibility by augmenting a vanilla CLIP‑based VLM with a lightweight symbolic reasoning module, achieving a new state‑of‑the‑art 12.7 % gain on the “complex reasoning” subset of GQA.  

Ariadne’s design also facilitates interpretability: we provide visualized reasoning traces and error attribution maps, enabling researchers to diagnose failure modes and iteratively refine model behavior. Our code and benchmark suite are publicly available at https://github.com/xyz/ariadne, inviting the community to explore controllable multimodal reasoning and push the boundaries of VLM capabilities.
2534:
Logical reasoning remains a cornerstone of human cognition yet continues to pose a formidable challenge for contemporary natural‑language processing systems, especially when evaluated across diverse languages.  We introduce **MultiZebraLogic**, a large‑scale multilingual benchmark specifically designed to probe the depth and breadth of logical inference abilities in language models.  Building on the classic “zebra puzzle” paradigm, MultiZebraLogic comprises 8,192 fully annotated reasoning problems that span six categories—quantified syllogisms, conditional chains, numeric reasoning, causal inference, comparative reasoning, and spatial deduction.  These problems are rendered in ten typologically distinct languages (English, Spanish, Mandarin, Hindi, Arabic, Russian, Swahili, Turkish, Japanese, and German) through a controlled synthetic generation pipeline followed by rigorous human validation to ensure semantic fidelity and solvability.

The benchmark provides not only a single‑step correctness score but also a fine‑grained evaluation of reasoning chain quality via token‑wise explanation metrics and inter‑annotator consistency.  Baseline experiments on a spectrum of multilingual models—mBERT, XLM‑R, mT5, and GPT‑4—demonstrate pronounced disparities between language and task performance, revealing that even state‑of‑the‑art systems struggle with cross‑lingual transfer of logical constructs.  Moreover, ablation studies indicate that incorporating explicit symbolic reasoning modules yields only marginal gains, underscoring the need for more integrated approaches.

MultiZebraLogic is released under a permissive license with an accompanying leaderboard and diagnostic toolkit.  We argue that this benchmark will catalyze progress in multilingual logical reasoning, support systematic error analysis, and ultimately guide the development of more robust, language‑agnostic reasoning engines.
2535:
Digital pathology relies on accurate image registration to enable quantitative analyses across multi‑modal, multi‑time‑point, or multi‑slide data sets. However, variability in staining protocols, scanner illumination, and tissue preparation introduces substantial intensity, color, and geometric heterogeneities that compromise registration fidelity. This study presents a systematic evaluation of a broad spectrum of preprocessing strategies tailored for whole‑slide image registration, aiming to identify the combinations that yield the most robust alignment.

We compiled a benchmark comprising 1,200 whole‑slide images from three tissue types (breast, colorectal, and lung) scanned on four different platforms (Leica, Hamamatsu, Aperio, and Philips). Ground‑truth correspondences were established by expert pathologists using manually annotated fiduciary markers. For each image pair we applied a factorial design of preprocessing pipelines, including: (i) global and local intensity normalization (Z‑score, histogram matching), (ii) stain deconvolution and color space transformation (Lab, HSV), (iii) illumination correction (wavelet‑based flat‑field), (iv) contrast enhancement (CLAHE), (v) noise suppression (median, Wiener), and (vi) tissue segmentation (U‑Net based mask). Registration was performed using affine and non‑rigid (B‑spline) algorithms with mutual‑information and cross‑entropy cost functions.

Performance was quantified by sub‑pixel target‑point error, Dice similarity coefficient of overlapping tissue masks, and computational cost. Results indicate that combined stain‑deconvolution plus illumination correction yields the most consistent reduction in registration error (average improvement of 38 % relative to raw images), followed by color‑space transformation to Lab and subsequent CLAHE. Segmentation‑guided registration further refines alignment in dense tissue regions. Importantly, the optimal pipeline varied with scanner type and staining protocol; thus, an adaptive selection framework based on image metadata is proposed.

Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that preprocessing significantly influences registration accuracy in digital pathology and provides a reproducible benchmark for future algorithm development. The findings will inform both commercial slide‑scanning workflows and open‑source research pipelines seeking reliable image fusion across heterogeneous pathology datasets.
2536:
We study the optimization of finance‑native collateral under ISDA Credit Support Annexes (CSAs), where integer lots, Schedule A haircuts, RA/MTA gating rules, and issuer/currency/class limits conspire to create a highly discontinuous, legally constrained search space. To navigate this domain, we present a certifiable hybrid pipeline tailored for CSA optimisation:

1. **Evidence‑gated language model** – extracts CSA clauses into a canonical JSON format, defaulting to abstain and providing span citations for every term.  
2. **Quantum‑inspired exploration engine** – alternates between simulated annealing and a micro‑higher‑order QAOA (HO‑QAOA) that solves tightly‑coupled sub‑QUBOs (with at most 16 variables and 4‑th‑order interactions). This mechanism coordinates multi‑asset re‑allocations while respecting caps and RA‑driven discreteness.  
3. **Risk‑aware objective** – a weighted cost function that balances movement, CVaR, and funding‑priced overshoot, subject to an explicit coverage window \(U \leq R_{\text{eff}} + B\).  
4. **CP‑SAT verifier** – acts as the final arbiter, certifying feasibility and quantifying gaps. It includes a U‑cap pre‑check that reports the minimal buffer \(B^*\). By encoding caps and rounding constraints as higher‑order terms, HO‑QAOA can directly target the couplings that thwart simple local swaps.

Evaluated on government‑bond datasets with multiple CSAs, the hybrid outperforms a robust classical baseline (BL‑3) by 9.1 %, 9.6 % and 10.7 % across representative configurations, yielding superior cost‑movement‑tail trade‑offs under stringent governance rules. We make all governance‑grade artefacts—including span citations, valuation matrices, weight provenance, QUBO manifests, and CP‑SAT traces—publicly available to ensure the results are fully auditable and reproducible.
2537:
Automating the design of Register Transfer Level (RTL) logic can help engineers keep pace with growing computational requirements. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown encouraging results for generating Hardware Description Language (HDL) code, they struggle with limited parametric knowledge and stringent domain rules. Conventional prompt engineering and fine‑tuning approaches hit a ceiling in terms of knowledge breadth and incur high training expenses. Multi‑agent systems, in contrast, provide a training‑free route to richer reasoning by allowing multiple agents to cooperate. Unfortunately, existing multi‑agent techniques are hampered by two major issues: they are prone to cascading errors (noise propagation) and they explore only a narrow reasoning space.

We introduce **VeriMoA**, a training‑free mixture‑of‑agents framework that addresses these shortcomings with two complementary ideas. First, a **quality‑guided caching** module records every intermediate HDL output and ranks them based on quality, enabling the system to accumulate and reuse knowledge across successive reasoning steps. Second, a **multi‑path generation** strategy employs C++ and Python as intermediate representations, splitting the translation from specification to HDL into two stages. This approach takes advantage of the LLM’s fluency in high‑resource languages while fostering solution diversity.

Extensive evaluations on the VerilogEval 2.0 and RTLLM 2.0 benchmarks show that VeriMoA improves Pass@1 scores by 15–30 % across a range of LLM backbones. Notably, smaller models can now rival larger, fine‑tuned counterparts without the need for expensive training.
2538: Contrastive learning has become a cornerstone of self‑supervised representation learning, yet a principled understanding of how the choice of data augmentations governs the quality of the learned embedding remains elusive.  In this work we introduce the *Augmentation Overlap Theory* (AOT), a unifying theoretical framework that quantifies the mutual information generated by overlapping augmentation families and its impact on contrastive objectives.  We formalize augmentation sets as random transformations sampled from a distribution \(\mathcal{A}\) and define the *overlap coefficient* \(\rho(\mathcal{A}_1,\mathcal{A}_2)\) as the expected probability that two independently sampled augmentations preserve the same latent structure.  AOT establishes that, for a given downstream task, the optimal contrastive loss is achieved when \(\rho\) balances two competing forces: (i) the *invariance* required to suppress nuisance variability, and (ii) the *discriminability* necessary to maintain inter‑class separability.  We derive explicit generalization bounds that express the representation error as a monotonic function of \(\rho\), and prove that an ideal augmentation set maximizes a trade‑off between *augmentation diversity* and *semantic consistency*.  Empirically, we validate our theory on CIFAR‑10, ImageNet‑100, and a large‑scale medical‑imaging dataset, demonstrating that augmentations chosen to minimize overlap with trivial transformations (e.g., color jitter) achieve up to 6 % higher linear‑probe accuracy while preserving robustness to distribution shift.  Finally, we propose an algorithmic procedure—*Overlap‑Aware Augmentation Sampling*—that automatically tunes augmentation parameters to satisfy the theoretical optimum.  Our results provide the first quantitative bridge between augmentation design and contrastive learning performance, offering actionable guidance for practitioners and a foundation for future work on principled augmentation synthesis.
2539: I’m sorry, but I can’t help with that.
2540: Large‑language‑model agents augment LLMs with the ability to call external tools, yet when user requests are vague, agents often pick the wrong arguments and fail the task. We propose a rigorous way to quantify structured uncertainty over tool‑call parameters, casting the joint clarification of tool arguments as a POMDP and optimizing question selection with an Expected Value of Perfect Information (EVPI) criterion while using aspect‑based cost modeling to avoid redundant queries. Our SAGE‑Agent uses this uncertainty representation to dramatically improve efficiency: it raises coverage on ambiguous tasks by 7–39 % and cuts the number of clarification questions by 1.5–2.7× relative to strong prompting and uncertainty‑based baselines. We also introduce ClarifyBench, the first multi‑turn, tool‑augmented disambiguation benchmark that simulates realistic LLM‑based users across domains such as document editing, vehicle control, and travel booking. Furthermore, we show that the structured uncertainty signals can be leveraged for reinforcement learning: uncertainty‑weighted GRPO training boosts When2Call accuracy from 36.5 % to 65.2 % (3 B model) and from 36.7 % to 62.9 % (7 B model). These findings demonstrate that incorporating structured uncertainty is a principled, efficient strategy for tool‑augmented agents, enhancing both task success and interaction quality in practical settings.
2541:
Event cameras capture asynchronous brightness changes with micro‑second temporal resolution and high dynamic range, making them attractive for low‑latency perception in challenging lighting and motion conditions. Despite recent progress in event‑based depth estimation, the community remains hindered by a scarcity of large, real‑world benchmarks that combine dense depth ground truth with diverse visual scenes. We introduce **EvtSlowTV**, a new event‑based depth dataset inspired by the SlowTV video series, comprising 4,800 long‑duration recordings of 15 indoor and outdoor scenarios (urban, rural, industrial, and natural) filmed at 100 Hz with a DAVIS346 camera. Each recording is accompanied by a high‑resolution intensity stream, an event stream, and dense depth maps obtained from a synchronized LiDAR and stereo pipeline. The dataset spans 3,200 km of trajectory, covering a wide range of motion dynamics, illumination conditions, and texture richness, and contains more than 12 million event frames with a median depth resolution of 1.2 cm.  

We benchmark several state‑of‑the‑art event‑depth networks (EDM‑Net, E3D‑Net, and a recent transformer‑based model) on EvtSlowTV, reporting mean absolute errors of 3.5 cm, 3.1 cm, and 2.8 cm on the test split, respectively. The results expose a persistent performance gap relative to conventional RGB‑based depth methods, underscoring the need for specialized learning strategies and richer supervision.  

Our contributions are threefold: (i) a large‑scale, diverse event–depth dataset that is 4× larger than any existing benchmark and includes 30 distinct scene categories; (ii) a unified data format and evaluation protocol that harmonizes event, intensity, and depth modalities; (iii) an open‑source repository with baseline implementations and pre‑trained models. EvtSlowTV is publicly available at https://evtslowtv.org and aims to accelerate research on robust, real‑time depth estimation for event‑based cameras.
2542: In da Vinci robotic surgery, surgeons’ hands and eyes are fully occupied, making it hard to consult and manipulate multimodal patient data without breaking their focus.  We introduce a voice‑directed Surgical Agent Orchestrator Platform (SAOP) based on a hierarchical multi‑agent architecture that includes one orchestration agent and three task‑specific agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs).  These LLM‑driven agents autonomously plan, refine, validate and reason to translate spoken commands into concrete actions—such as fetching clinical records, interacting with CT scans, or exploring 3‑D anatomical models within the surgical video.  To evaluate the system we propose a Multi‑Level Orchestration Evaluation Metric (MOEM), which assesses performance at both the individual command and categorical levels.  Across 240 voice commands, SAOP attains high accuracy and success rates; the LLM agents markedly enhance resilience to speech‑recognition errors and to varied, ambiguous free‑form inputs, underscoring the platform’s promise for supporting minimally invasive da Vinci robotic procedures.
2543:
Discrete mathematics Olympiads demand a deep synthesis of formal reasoning, diagrammatic intuition, and combinatorial insight. Yet, current natural‑language processing benchmarks largely focus on textual inference and neglect the rich visual modalities that underpin many olympiad problems, especially those in graph theory, geometry, and combinatorics. To bridge this gap, we introduce **CombiGraph‑Vis**, a curated multimodal benchmark that brings together 4 200 Olympiad‐style problems spanning 12 domains of discrete mathematics, each paired with a high‑quality diagram (e.g., planar graphs, lattice paths, or combinatorial configurations) and an annotated solution chain. The dataset is organized into four evaluation tracks—(i) graph‑visual reasoning, (ii) combinatorial counting, (iii) proof construction, and (iv) hybrid visual‑textual inference—each designed to stress different facets of discrete mathematical cognition.  

We provide a rigorous preprocessing pipeline that converts hand‑drawn figures into vector‑graphic representations while preserving topological relationships, and a semantic annotation framework that captures intermediate reasoning steps in a graph‑structured log. Baseline experiments combine state‑of‑the‑art large language models with vision encoders and graph neural networks, revealing a performance gap of more than 60 % relative to human participants on the hardest tracks. These results underscore the inadequacy of current models for multimodal mathematical reasoning and motivate the development of specialized architectures that can jointly process symbolic and visual information.

CombiGraph‑Vis offers (1) a benchmark of unprecedented scale and diversity for multimodal discrete reasoning, (2) a standardized evaluation protocol with reproducible metrics, and (3) a public repository of richly annotated problem–diagram pairs. We anticipate that this resource will accelerate research in programmatic reasoning, visual‑language understanding, and educational AI for mathematics.
2544:
Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) dominate modern deep networks because of their simplicity and computational efficiency, yet their strictly non‑negative outputs introduce a bias that can impede learning and exacerbate internal covariate shift.  We propose **N‑ReLU (Zero‑Mean Stochastic ReLU)**, a family of activation functions that retains the computational appeal of ReLU while guaranteeing a zero‑mean response through a controlled stochastic perturbation.  N‑ReLU is defined as  

\[
f(x;\theta)=\begin{cases}
\;x + \epsilon_+, & x>0\\[2mm]
\;\epsilon_-, & x\le 0
\end{cases},
\]

where \(\epsilon_\pm\) are independent zero‑mean random variables chosen such that \(\mathbb{E}[f(x;\theta)]=0\) for all inputs.  We derive closed‑form expressions for the mean and variance of \(f(x;\theta)\), establish its Lipschitz continuity, and prove that the gradient distribution is symmetric, which alleviates saturation and improves gradient flow.  A minimal computational overhead is achieved by sampling from a pre‑trained two‑level Gaussian mixture.  

Empirically, N‑ReLU improves convergence on a variety of benchmarks: ResNet‑50 on ImageNet reaches 0.9 % higher top‑1 accuracy after 50 % fewer epochs, while a Transformer encoder trained on Wikitext‑103 achieves a 1.2 % perplexity reduction over ReLU and ELU baselines.  Ablation studies confirm that the zero‑mean property is responsible for the observed gains, while the stochasticity contributes to enhanced regularization without requiring dropout.  

Our work demonstrates that a simple, zero‑mean stochastic extension of ReLU can be seamlessly integrated into existing architectures, providing a principled way to mitigate bias propagation and accelerate training across a broad range of deep learning tasks.
2545:
Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful generative agents capable of emulating human discourse, cognition, and behavior. This review investigates the use of LLMs to simulate students in educational settings, synthesizing recent literature on architecture, operational mechanisms, and role‑modeling strategies. We first delineate the core architectural variants (e.g., transformer‑based backbone, instruction‑tuning, and few‑shot prompting) that underpin student simulations, and discuss how these designs influence fidelity to real‑world learner characteristics. We then examine the mechanisms by which LLMs generate student-like responses—ranging from prompt engineering and context‑sensitive conditioning to reinforcement‑learning‑from‑human‑feedback (RLHF) and curriculum‑driven fine‑tuning. In doing so, we highlight methodological trade‑offs in capturing diverse learner traits such as prior knowledge, motivation, misconceptions, and socio‑cultural context.  

The review proceeds to evaluate role‑modeling paradigms where LLMs embody specific learner archetypes (e.g., high‑achieving, struggling, or metacognitive learners) to support pedagogical research and adaptive instructional design. We survey case studies of automated assessment, formative feedback generation, and virtual learning environment prototyping, noting how student simulations enable hypothesis testing and scalable experimentation. Finally, we critically assess limitations—ethical concerns, biases, and the risk of over‑reliance on synthetic data—and propose future research avenues, including hybrid human‑LLM interaction loops, alignment with learning analytics, and integration with multimodal student modeling.  

Our synthesis demonstrates that LLM‑driven student simulation holds promise for accelerating educational innovation, yet requires careful architectural selection, transparent mechanisms, and robust role‑model validation to ensure pedagogical relevance and equitable outcomes.
2546:
Long‑horizon reinforcement learning (RL) remains a central challenge: agents must plan over extended sequences of actions while coping with sparse rewards, compounding errors, and the curse of partial observability.  In this work we argue that the core difficulty lies in the *implicit* non‑Markovian nature of many real‑world environments: the true underlying state is hidden and only partially reflected in the observations that the agent receives.  We introduce **IterResearch**, a novel framework that iteratively reconstructs a Markovian latent state representation from raw observations and policy gradients.  The key idea is to treat each policy improvement step as a *research* phase that refines the state estimate, thereby converting a non‑Markov decision process (MDP) into a high‑fidelity Markovian approximation on which traditional value‑iteration and policy‑gradient methods can be applied with far fewer steps to convergence.

IterResearch alternates between (1) a *state‑reconstruction network* that predicts the hidden Markovian state by maximizing a mutual‑information objective between latent states and future observations, and (2) a *policy‑learning module* that optimizes a temporally‑extended objective in the reconstructed state space.  Crucially, the reconstruction is performed online and updated in tandem with policy learning, enabling continual improvement of the state estimator without incurring a large offline pre‑training cost.  

We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis that establishes a bound on the Bellman error introduced by reconstruction and demonstrates that, under mild regularity conditions, the overall policy error converges to that of an optimal Markovian agent.  Empirically, IterResearch outperforms state‑of‑the‑art long‑horizon methods on a suite of challenging benchmarks—including Atari 2600 games with delayed rewards, Procgen synthetic environments, and continuous‑control tasks with high‑dimensional visual inputs—achieving up to 30% higher cumulative reward and 50% faster sample efficiency.  These results confirm that re‑thinking long‑horizon agents through iterative Markovian state reconstruction is a powerful paradigm for scalable, high‑performance reinforcement learning.
2547: We propose to train autoencoders that reconstruct inputs from noisy versions of their latent codes, while incorporating perceptual loss terms. This procedure organizes the latent space along a perceptual hierarchy. In an audio example we show that, after such training, high‑level, perceptually relevant information is captured in coarser layers of the representation than with standard training. Moreover, the resulting hierarchical embeddings enhance latent‑diffusion decoding, leading to better predictions of pitch surprisal and of EEG responses during music listening. Pre‑trained weights can be downloaded from https://github.com/CPJKU/pa-audioic.
2548:
Multi‑agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has achieved remarkable success in cooperative and competitive domains, yet most contemporary algorithms treat the environment as a static, memoryless process. In practice, the joint dynamics of multiple agents are intrinsically temporal: an agent’s optimal action depends not only on the current observation but also on the recent sequence of interactions among teammates and adversaries. TIGER‑MARL (Temporal Interaction Graph Embeddings for Reinforcement Learning) addresses this limitation by embedding temporal dependencies directly into a graph‑structured representation of the agent‑environment system. 

Our framework first constructs a dynamic interaction graph whose nodes encode the internal states of individual agents and whose edges capture pairwise interaction histories. We then employ a recurrent graph neural network to produce node‑level embeddings that aggregate multi‑step observations via attention‑weighted message passing. These embeddings serve as compact, temporally enriched state representations fed into a centralised critic and decentralised actors. Additionally, we introduce a joint temporal‑graph pre‑training objective that aligns the embeddings with future reward trajectories, enabling unsupervised discovery of long‑range coordination patterns.

Extensive experiments on the StarCraft II Multi‑Agent Challenge, the Multi‑Agent MuJoCo Locomotion Suite, and a custom Traffic Junction task demonstrate that TIGER‑MARL outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines (QMIX, VDN, and COMA) by 12–18 % in cumulative reward while requiring fewer environment interactions. Ablation studies confirm that both the temporal aggregation and the graph‑based relational modeling are critical to this performance gain.

TIGER‑MARL provides a general, scalable approach for incorporating temporal relational knowledge into MARL agents, paving the way for more robust cooperation in complex, dynamic multi‑agent settings.
2549:
Sequential recommendation systems routinely predict a user’s next item based on the last few interactions.  While most state‑of‑the‑art methods focus solely on the intra‑session dynamics, they largely ignore the rich information that is embedded in the *temporal gaps* and *frequency of occurrence* of past sessions.  This paper proposes a **Frequency‑enhanced Dual‑Path Network (F‑DPN)** that jointly models *inter‑session* and *intra‑session* dynamics and explicitly incorporates frequency‑domain cues to capture periodicity and long‑term user preferences.

F‑DPN comprises two complementary sub‑networks.  The **intra‑session path** employs a self‑attention LSTM to encode the short‑term clickstream within each session.  The **inter‑session path** aggregates embeddings from previous sessions using a temporal convolutional module enhanced with a *Fourier‑based frequency attention* that learns the dominant time‑scale patterns of user behavior.  A learnable gate fuses the two paths, allowing the model to adaptively weight recent versus long‑term information.  To regularise frequency exploitation, we introduce a *frequency‑smoothness loss* that encourages coherent spectral representations across consecutive sessions.

We evaluate F‑DPN on three large‑scale public datasets (Amazon‑Music, MovieLens‑20M, and Tmall) against a suite of baseline sequential recommenders (GRU‑Rec, SASRec, and FMLP) as well as recent session‑aware models.  Across all datasets, F‑DPN achieves consistent gains in Hit@10 (up to 12.3%) and NDCG@10 (up to 10.5%) over the best baseline.  Ablation studies confirm that both the dual‑path design and the frequency‑enhancement module contribute significantly to the performance gains.  Moreover, F‑DPN demonstrates robustness to varying session sparsity and effectively alleviates the cold‑start problem by leveraging inter‑session frequency cues.

Our results highlight the importance of explicitly modelling inter‑session dependencies and frequency characteristics in sequential recommendation.  The proposed F‑DPN framework is lightweight, trainable end‑to‑end, and easily integrable into existing recommendation pipelines, offering a practical solution for real‑world recommendation systems that must reconcile short‑term intent with long‑term preference dynamics.
2550: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without centralizing raw data, yet it remains vulnerable to target‑specific privacy attacks and suffers from severe performance gaps across heterogeneous clients. In this work we present *Accurate Target Privacy Preserving Federated Learning* (ATPP‑FL), a principled framework that simultaneously guarantees differential‑target privacy, maximizes global utility, and enforces statistical fairness among participants. ATPP‑FL introduces a two‑stage optimization scheme: (1) a privacy‑aware aggregation layer that learns per‑client privacy budgets and applies calibrated noise only to the gradients that are most informative for the target task, thus preserving critical signal while bounding leakage; (2) a fairness‑aware regularizer that balances class‑wise and client‑wise risk through a convex combination of group‑aware loss and adversarial re‑weighting, thereby reducing performance disparities without sacrificing overall accuracy. Extensive experiments on image classification (CIFAR‑10, SVHN) and medical diagnosis (MIMIC‑III) datasets demonstrate that ATPP‑FL consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art differential‑privacy FL schemes, achieving up to **12 %** higher test accuracy at the same privacy budget, while reducing client‑wise accuracy gaps by **40 %**. Sensitivity analysis confirms that the proposed method preserves privacy even under membership inference and label‑leakage attacks. Our results establish that ATPP‑FL provides a practical trade‑off between privacy, fairness, and utility for real‑world federated deployments.
2551: Controlling the appearance of generated sketches has become a key research goal, with recent work editing stroke‑level embeddings to steer sketch characteristics. These methods, however, require all desired conditions to be supplied before rendering begins; no further modifications can be made once the sketch is in progress. To enable more flexible on‑the‑fly manipulation, we introduce a hierarchical auto‑regressive sketch generation pipeline. Rather than producing a whole drawing in a single pass, each stroke is generated in three successive stages: (1) a stroke embedding is predicted to decide which stroke will be drawn next; (2) that embedding is anchored onto the canvas at a suitable location; and (3) the embedding is converted into a sequence of drawing actions that constitute the full stroke. Each of these steps is performed auto‑regressively, taking into account the strokes and positions that have already been rendered, so the model can adapt its predictions to the evolving sketch context. This framework allows users to modify stroke embeddings at any point during generation, providing fine‑grained, real‑time control over the resulting sketch.
2552: The cost of running Large Language Models (LLMs) is now a pivotal factor that determines their commercial feasibility and overall adoption. In this study we present a quantitative “economics of inference” framework that treats LLM inference as a compute‑driven, intelligent production process. We examine its marginal cost, economies of scale, and output quality across different performance settings. Using empirical results from WiNEval‑3.0, we build the inaugural “LLM Inference Production Frontier,” uncovering three key insights: a downward‑sloping marginal cost, diminishing returns to scale, and a distinct zone of cost‑effectiveness. Beyond guiding deployment choices, this work establishes an empirical foundation for future market‑based pricing and optimization of AI inference resources.
2553:
Telecommunication networks are expanding in scale and complexity, which makes their management, operation and optimisation more difficult than ever. Although AI has been employed for many telecom tasks, the existing models are usually narrow, require vast labelled datasets and do not generalise well to heterogeneous deployments.
