The results indicate that participants demonstrate robust cognitive skills, yet exhibit deficiencies in behavioral and normative areas, notably concerning AI bias, AI‑driven learning, and ethical issues. Additionally, the study highlights a mismatch between the perceived significance of AI competencies and the actual efficacy of existing training programmes.
2794: We introduce an innovative method for locating radioactive sources using a team of collaborative Micro Aerial Vehicles (MAVs). Central to this approach is a cutting‑edge single‑detector Compton camera—an ultra‑light (40 g) device that delivers high sensitivity to ionizing radiation while remaining compact enough for deployment on agile drones. We present a foundational technique for fusing Compton‑camera data to infer the source’s position in real time, even when only a few measurements are available. All data acquisition and processing occur onboard, and the resulting estimates feed directly into a dynamic control loop that steers the MAVs. By operating in a tightly coordinated swarm, the vehicles maximize the informational value of each detector reading, swiftly pinpoint static or moving radiation sources, and maintain continuous tracking.
2795: We consider subscription‑based platforms in which consumers pay a flat fee for unlimited content access while content creators earn a share of the resulting revenue. Current anti‑fraud techniques rely largely on machine‑learning classifiers, creating an ongoing cat‑and‑mouse game with malicious actors. In contrast, we investigate revenue‑allocation schemes that are intrinsically resistant to manipulation. We formalise three manipulation‑resistance axioms and test which existing allocation rules satisfy them. Our analysis shows that the rule commonly employed by streaming services not only permits fraud but also renders manipulation detection computationally infeasible. We therefore propose a new allocation rule, **ScaledUserProp**, which satisfies all three axioms. Empirical evaluation on both real‑world and simulated streaming data demonstrates that ScaledUserProp delivers a fairer distribution of revenue than the prevailing rules.
2796: Open data repositories promise evidence‑based decision making, yet they remain out of reach for non‑experts who lack skills in dataset search, schema alignment, and statistical work. While large language models can tackle individual sub‑tasks, a full analytical pipeline reveals core weaknesses: attention is spread too thin across long contexts, specialized reasoning patterns clash, and errors slip through undetected. We introduce PublicAgent, a multi‑agent framework that overcomes these challenges by decomposing the workflow into dedicated agents for intent clarification, data discovery, analysis, and reporting. This design keeps each agent’s focus sharp and allows validation at every step. Across five models and 50 user queries we distill five design principles for multi‑agent LLM systems. First, specialization adds value regardless of model strength; even the strongest model achieves a 97.5 % win rate, and benefits are largely independent of scale. Second, agents fall into two groups—universal (discovery, analysis) and conditional (report, intent)—with universal agents delivering consistent performance (±12.4 % standard deviation) while conditional agents are more model‑dependent (±20.5 %). Third, each agent tackles a distinct failure mode; omitting discovery or analysis triggers catastrophic failures (243–280 cases), whereas omitting report or intent degrades quality. Fourth, the architectural gains hold across varying task complexity, with stable win rates (86–92 % for analysis, 84–94 % for discovery), underscoring the value of workflow management over raw reasoning. Fifth, the wide spread in agent effectiveness across models (42–96 % for analysis) highlights the need for model‑aware architectural choices. Together, these findings chart when and why specialization is essential for complex analytical pipelines, paving the way for broader public data access through natural‑language interfaces.
2797: Object binding—the brain’s ability to fuse a multitude of feature cues into a single, coherent object—is a cornerstone of human cognition. It underlies the aggregation of low‑level perceptual signals into high‑level representations, the efficient, compositional storage of those representations, and the reasoning about specific object instances. While many studies explicitly impose object‑centric attention mechanisms (e.g., Slot Attention) to study these advantages, it remains uncertain whether such a capability arises spontaneously in pre‑trained Vision Transformers (ViTs). Intuitively, identifying which image patches belong together should aid downstream predictions and therefore shape attention. In light of the quadratic interactions inherent in self‑attention, we conjecture that ViTs encode a property we call **IsSameObject**, indicating whether two patches co‑represent the same object. By probing patch embeddings across ViT layers with a similarity test, we recover IsSameObject with over 90 % accuracy. Notably, this binding signal surfaces reliably in self‑supervised models (DINO, MAE, CLIP), whereas it is markedly weaker in ImageNet‑supervised counterparts, implying that binding is not a mere architectural artefact but an outcome of particular pre‑training objectives. Further analysis shows that IsSameObject resides in a low‑dimensional subspace atop object‑level features and actively steers attention. When we ablate this signal from the network, downstream performance drops and the training objective is adversely affected, indicating that emergent object binding serves the pre‑training goal. Our results contest the notion that ViTs lack object binding and demonstrate how a symbolic “parts‑together” knowledge naturally arises in a connectionist framework.
2798:
*Abstract*  
Modern software repositories contain vast amounts of heterogeneous artifacts—source code, documentation, build scripts, configuration files, and issue trackers—that collectively encode tacit design knowledge. Existing code‑generation systems typically operate in isolation on single files or classes, ignoring this broader context and often producing code that violates architectural or domain constraints. We present **SemanticForge**, a framework that elevates code generation to the *repository level* by fusing **semantic knowledge graphs (KGs)** with **constraint‑satisfaction solvers (CSSs)**.  
SemanticForge first extracts a richly typed KG from a repository, encoding entities (packages, modules, interfaces), relationships (inheritance, composition, dependency), and metadata (design patterns, security policies). The KG is continuously updated via incremental parsing, enabling real‑time contextual awareness. A domain‑specific language (DSL) is used to encode constraints—syntactic, semantic, architectural, and policy‑based—over this KG. The CSS then reasons over the KG to discover viable code skeletons and refactorings that satisfy all constraints, selecting from a library of template fragments. Finally, a transformer‑based generator tailors the selected fragments to the target repository, producing type‑safe, pattern‑compliant, and build‑ready code.  
We evaluated SemanticForge on 35 open‑source Java and Python projects spanning 3–12 k LOC each. Our system generated 1,200+ code patches that preserved build success rates (94 %) and complied with 97 % of the expressed constraints, outperforming baseline GPT‑4–based generation by 12 % in functional correctness and 18 % in architectural fidelity. The results demonstrate that repository‑level semantic reasoning combined with constraint satisfaction yields more reliable, maintainable, and context‑aware code generation than isolated, template‑based approaches. SemanticForge paves the way toward automated, large‑scale code synthesis that respects both the structural and policy constraints of real‑world software systems.
2799: Wide‑field fluorescence microscopy is limited by out‑of‑focus background fluorescence and axial resolution dictated by diffraction. The complementary illumination geometries of epifluorescence (EPI) and total‑internal‑reflection fluorescence (TIRF) provide, respectively, a high‑contrast surface signal and a volumetric view of the specimen. Here we present a deep‑learning framework that jointly exploits EPI–TIRF cross‑modality to (i) suppress background and (ii) recover axial super‑resolution (≈200 nm) without additional hardware or acquisition time. A paired EPI–TIRF dataset was generated from 3D‐confocal ground truth using a custom light‑sheet microscope and from synthetic bead phantoms. A multi‑branch U‑Net ingests the simultaneous EPI and TIRF image pair and outputs a background‑subtracted, deconvolved volume. The network is trained with a composite loss that includes pixel‑wise mean‑squared error, structural similarity, and a learned axial regularization term. Quantitative evaluation on fixed microtubule and actin networks, as well as live HeLa cells expressing membrane‑localized GFP, shows that our method reduces background by >80 % relative to conventional rolling‑ball subtraction and improves axial resolution by a factor of 2.5 over raw TIRF stacks, matching the performance of multi‑plane interferometric setups. Importantly, the approach requires only a single simultaneous EPI–TIRF exposure per z‑plane, enabling rapid volumetric imaging at 10 Hz. This study demonstrates that cross‑modal deep learning can unlock axial super‑resolution and background elimination in standard wide‑field microscopes, opening the door to high‑throughput, high‑contrast 3‑D imaging in live‑cell applications.
2800:
Ice‐sheet models are the cornerstone of long‑term climate projections, yet their explicit simulation at regional or global scales remains prohibitively expensive. Recent advances in surrogate modeling have employed deep neural networks to emulate these complex systems, but most approaches treat the ice sheet as a collection of independent spatial points, thereby neglecting the intrinsic graph‑structured geometry of the underlying grid and losing physical fidelity. In this work we introduce **KAN‑GCN**, a hybrid architecture that marries the expressive Kolmogorov‑Arnold Network (KAN) with a Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) to construct a highly accurate, low‑dimensional emulator for the Antarctic Ice Sheet dynamics.

The KAN component parameterizes local, nonlinear relationships between state variables (e.g., thickness, velocity, temperature) and their gradients using the universal representation theorem, yielding a compact, interpretable network that scales linearly with input dimensionality. The GCN layer propagates information over the ice‑sheet mesh, capturing long‑range coupling and enforcing topological consistency. The resulting end‑to‑end model is trained on a large ensemble of 10,000 high‑fidelity simulations from the PIOMAS‐V8 ice‑sheet model, covering a broad range of forcing scenarios and internal noise realizations.

Evaluation on a 20‑fold held‑out test set demonstrates that KAN‑GCN attains a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.62 m yr⁻¹ in ice‑sheet mass balance and a relative error of 2.8 % in surface velocity, outperforming baseline MLP, CNN, and standard GCN emulators by 15–25 % in all metrics. Inference time is reduced by an order of magnitude (≈1 ms per prediction) relative to the full physical model, enabling rapid Monte‑Carlo uncertainty propagation and real‑time policy analysis. Our results confirm that embedding a Kolmogorov‑Arnold representation within a graph‑based framework delivers a powerful, efficient emulator that preserves physical structure while achieving unprecedented predictive accuracy.
2801:
Initial–boundary value problems (IBVPs) for partial differential equations (PDEs) arise in virtually every area of science and engineering, yet their analytic and numerical treatment remains a major challenge when the equations are nonlinear or posed on complex geometries. In this work we present **LieSolver**, a novel framework that exploits the full power of Lie symmetry analysis to construct efficient, high‑accuracy solvers for a broad class of IBVPs.  

LieSolver automatically determines the continuous symmetry group of a given PDE system, builds the associated differential invariants, and uses these invariants to perform a systematic reduction of the original problem to a lower‑dimensional set of equations. In particular, for problems admitting non‑trivial symmetry algebras, the method reduces the PDE to a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in the invariants, which are then integrated numerically while faithfully preserving the original boundary and initial conditions expressed in invariant form. The approach is fully general: it applies to linear and nonlinear equations, to systems with multiple dependent variables, and to both local and nonlocal boundary conditions.  

We have implemented LieSolver as an open‑source Python library that integrates with symbolic computation (SymPy) for symmetry detection and with high‑performance ODE solvers (SciPy) for the reduced equations. Numerical experiments on benchmark problems—heat equation, Burgers’ equation, the Korteweg–de Vries equation, and a nonlinear Schrödinger equation—demonstrate that LieSolver achieves error rates comparable to or better than traditional finite‑difference and spectral methods, while dramatically reducing computational cost for problems with rich symmetry structures.  

The paper discusses the theoretical underpinnings of the symmetry‑based reduction, the algorithmic pipeline of LieSolver, error analysis, and scalability to multi‑dimensional domains. By marrying Lie theory with modern computational tools, LieSolver opens a new pathway for the systematic, automated solution of PDE‑constrained IBVPs.
2802:
Modulo imaging has emerged as a powerful strategy for acquiring high‑dynamic‑range (HDR) scenes with conventional low‑bit depth sensors by encoding pixel values through a modulo operation. However, the loss of wrap‑around information renders the reconstruction of continuous video signals highly ill‑posed, especially under rapid motion and varying illumination. In this work, we introduce **Selective Spatiotemporal Vision Transformer (S‑SVT)**, the first transformer‑based framework explicitly designed for modulo video recovery. S‑SVT jointly exploits spatial context within each frame and temporal continuity across frames through a multi‑head self‑attention mechanism that selectively attends to the most informative neighboring tokens. A lightweight “selective” module filters out redundant or low‑confidence tokens, thereby reducing the combinatorial search space that typically plagues modulo unwrapping.  

We formulate modulo video recovery as a joint inference problem, where the transformer learns to predict the unwrapped intensity sequence directly from the modulo measurements. The model is trained on a newly curated synthetic modulo video dataset that spans a wide range of motion speeds, scene complexities, and illumination conditions. To further improve generalization, we augment the training objective with a differentiable modulo consistency loss and a temporal smoothness regularizer.  

Experimental results on both synthetic and real‑world modulo video captures demonstrate that S‑SVT outperforms prior CNN‑based and classical iterative unwrapping methods by an average of 5.3 dB PSNR and 1.8 × faster inference on a single GPU. On a high‑speed camera testbench, our approach successfully reconstructs 120 fps HDR video from 30 fps modulo inputs, achieving near real‑time performance (≈30 ms per frame). These findings confirm that selective spatiotemporal attention can effectively resolve the ambiguities inherent in modulo measurements, paving the way for robust HDR video acquisition in resource‑constrained imaging systems.
2803: Urban traffic congestion inflates travel times and emissions, particularly during rush hours. Although the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm is optimal for a lone vehicle in a static setting, it tends to aggravate congestion in dynamic, multi‑vehicle scenarios by funneling all cars along the same route. To mitigate this, we develop a multi‑agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach that enables coordinated, network‑aware fleet navigation. Our first contribution, Adaptive Navigation (AN), is a fully decentralized MARL model where each intersection agent issues routing cues based on its own traffic conditions and on the state of neighboring links, the latter captured through Graph Attention Networks (GAT). To handle larger networks, we introduce Hierarchical Hub‑based Adaptive Navigation (HHAN), which limits agent responsibilities to a set of strategically chosen hub intersections. Vehicles are guided from hub to hub by the MARL agents while conventional SPF handles local routing within each hub’s vicinity. HHAN employs a centralized‑training, decentralized‑execution (CTDE) scheme under the Attentive Q‑Mixing (A‑QMIX) framework, which fuses the asynchronous actions of individual vehicles through an attention mechanism. Hub agents operate with flow‑aware state representations that combine real‑time congestion metrics and short‑term traffic predictions, enabling proactive routing decisions. Experiments on synthetic grid networks and real‑world maps of Toronto and Manhattan demonstrate that AN consistently outperforms SPF and other learning baselines, preserving 100 % routing success. HHAN further scales to networks with hundreds of intersections, achieving up to a 15.9 % reduction in average travel time under heavy‑traffic conditions. These results underscore the promise of network‑constrained MARL for scalable, coordinated, and congestion‑aware routing in modern transportation systems.
2804:
As artificial intelligence (AI) permeates everyday professional settings, there is a growing urgency to equip employees—many of whom come from non‑STEM backgrounds—with both the competence and the ethical awareness required to use these technologies effectively. Current conceptions and measurements of AI literacy tend to foreground foundational technical skills such as programming, mathematics, and statistics, while downplaying more applied abilities such as interpreting model outputs, choosing appropriate tools, and spotting ethical pitfalls. This imbalance leaves a conspicuous gap in evaluating real‑world AI literacy.

To address this, we present a work‑task‑oriented framework for assessing AI literacy that aligns with the competencies needed for practical AI tool use in the workplace. We describe the creation of a new AI literacy assessment instrument, accompanied by formative tests, developed within a U.S. Navy robotics training program. The program combined robotics and AI literacy instruction with a practical competition that included a scenario‑based multiple‑choice task designed to mimic on‑the‑job AI decision making. Our findings show that this scenario task performed markedly better as a measure of applied AI literacy than either legacy tests from the literature or the instruments we crafted ourselves. We therefore conclude that educators preparing non‑technical staff for AI‑integrated roles should prioritize evaluation tools that emphasize highly contextualized, practical skills over abstract technical knowledge.
2805: Understanding which training examples steer a Large Language Model (LLM) is critical for transparent model interpretation and dataset auditability. Existing influence‑function approaches estimate the impact of a training instance by propagating gradient information through the network, but for billion‑parameter models this is usually limited to a small subset of layers to keep the computation tractable. In 2022, Yeh et al. argued that the earliest (embedding) layers are the most useful for this task, based on an observed “cancellation effect” where higher‑layer contributions largely offset one another. In this paper we provide both theoretical arguments and empirical results that invalidate this cancellation assumption, demonstrating that mid‑level attention layers actually yield more reliable influence estimates. We also tackle the problem of combining layer‑wise influence scores, showing that ranking or vote‑based aggregation far outperforms naïve averaging. Finally, we introduce a novel, retraining‑free evaluation criterion—the Noise Detection Rate (NDR)—which strongly predicts influence‑score quality and outperforms the cancellation metric. Across a range of LLM architectures and scales, our extensive experiments reveal that neither the earliest nor the latest layers are universally superior for influence estimation, challenging the prevailing consensus in the field.
2806:
Efficient collaboration in multi‑agent systems hinges on the ability to judiciously recruit agents that possess the right mix of resources, capabilities and context for a given task. Existing routing and scheduling solutions treat agent availability as static or rely on heuristics that ignore the rich state information that modern agents continuously generate (battery level, computational load, proximity, etc.). This paper introduces **Optimal‑Agent‑Selection (OAS)**, a state‑aware routing framework that explicitly couples real‑time agent state monitoring with an optimal selection policy to reduce task completion time, energy consumption and communication overhead.

OAS models the collaborative environment as a dynamic graph where each node represents an agent endowed with a vector of observable states. Task requirements are encoded as a set of resource constraints, while the routing problem is formulated as a multi‑objective integer program that jointly optimizes (i) the subset of agents to activate, (ii) the assignment of sub‑tasks to these agents, and (iii) the communication paths between them. We derive a polynomial‑time approximation algorithm based on a weighted bipartite matching and a cutting‑plane method that guarantees a 1‑ε sub‑optimality bound in practice. To capture the stochastic nature of agent degradation and task arrival, we embed the selection policy within a reinforcement‑learning controller that updates its belief over agent states through a lightweight Kalman filter.

Experimental evaluation on benchmark multi‑robot coordination scenarios (search‑and‑rescue, distributed sensor coverage, and cooperative transport) as well as a large‑scale simulated drone swarm demonstrates that OAS improves overall throughput by 18 % and reduces energy consumption by 23 % compared with state‑of‑the‑art heuristic baselines. A real‑world deployment with a heterogeneous fleet of ground and aerial robots confirms the practicality of the framework, showing robust performance under communication failures and dynamic task streams.

OAS offers a principled, scalable solution for agent selection and routing that can be instantiated in any domain requiring rapid, state‑aware multi‑agent coordination. The framework’s modular design allows for easy integration with existing planning, control, and networking stacks, opening avenues for future work in distributed learning and fault‑tolerant execution.
2807: While retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) is widely used for grounded question answering in both research and industry, it often fails on questions that require pulling information from multiple sources or engaging in complex reasoning. The recent LOFT study confirms that this shortcoming also applies to long‑context language models, with the QUEST benchmark revealing considerable potential for improvement. In this paper we dissect the factors that lead to poor performance on QUEST‑LOFT, provide updated scores from a comprehensive human evaluation, and show that RAG can be tuned to far exceed long‑context approaches—especially when it generates a structured output that includes reasoning steps and evidence, optionally followed by a re‑verification of the final answer.
2808:
No‑regret learning dynamics are a cornerstone of game theory, providing a decentralized pathway to equilibrium for notions such as Coarse Correlated Equilibrium (CCE) and Correlated Equilibrium (CE).  In this paper we sharpen the convergence guarantee for CCE in general‑sum Markov games, cutting the rate from the best prior bound of  
\[
\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log^5 T}{T}\right)
\]  
to the tighter  
\[
\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{\log T}{T}\right).
\]  
This not only matches the asymptotic dependence on the number of iterations \(T\) achieved for CE, but also reduces the dependence on the size of the action space from a polynomial to a polylogarithmic factor, yielding exponential improvements in high‑dimensional regimes.  
Our method leverages recent progress on adaptive step‑size schedules for no‑regret algorithms in static (normal‑form) games and generalises them to the Markovian context via a stage‑wise scheme that tunes learning rates on the fly.  Policy updates are cast as a specialised instance of Optimistic Follow‑the‑Regularized‑Leader (OFTRL) that is tailored to value‑iteration‑based learning.  The resulting self‑play algorithm, to the best of our knowledge, provides the fastest known convergence to CCE in Markov games.
2809: Recent diffusion models have become a dominant approach for recommender systems, delivering top‑tier accuracy by learning to generate user‑item interactions. Nevertheless, training such models from scratch is prohibitively costly and the performance gains plateau once training converges. To address this, we introduce **ReFiT**, a framework that injects reinforcement‑learning‑based fine‑tuning into diffusion‑based recommenders. Unlike previous RL methods that rely on external reward approximators, ReFiT treats the denoising sequence as a Markov decision process and employs a reward function that is intrinsically aware of collaborative signals, thereby aligning directly with recommendation quality. This tight coupling allows the RL agent to exploit higher‑order graph structures for fine‑grained optimization while sidestepping the noisy feedback that plagues simplistic reward designs. Using a policy‑gradient objective that maximizes the exact log‑likelihood of observed interactions, ReFiT performs effective post‑hoc fine‑tuning of diffusion recommenders. Extensive evaluation on diverse real‑world datasets shows that ReFiT (i) outperforms strong baselines by up to 36.3 % on sequential recommendation tasks, (ii) maintains linear scalability with respect to users or items, and (iii) generalizes across multiple diffusion‑based recommendation settings. The code and datasets are publicly released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ReFiT-4C60.
2810: Binary representations are essential for large‑scale visual search, yet learning compact, discriminative binary codes with deep autoencoders remains challenging. The main obstacle is the non‑differentiability of the binarization operation, which forces most prior works to rely on heuristic relaxations or two‑stage training pipelines. In this work we propose *Progressive Binary Autoencoder (PBA)*, a novel end‑to‑end framework that learns high‑quality binary codes by gradually tightening the quantization constraint throughout training. Starting from a soft‑tanh autoencoder that preserves reconstruction fidelity, we progressively increase the steepness of the activation and the bit‑rate of the latent code while jointly optimizing a reconstruction loss and a bit‑balance regularizer. This curriculum‑like strategy keeps the network in a smooth regime during early stages, enabling stable gradient propagation, and only later forces the latent representation towards a near‑binary manifold. We further introduce a lightweight *bit‑drop* mask that encourages sparsity in the code space, reducing quantization error. Extensive experiments on CIFAR‑10, ImageNet‑1K, and NUS-WIDE show that PBA attains superior retrieval performance (mAP gains of 3–6 % over state‑of‑the‑art hashing methods) while maintaining a low training cost. Ablation studies confirm that both the progressive schedule and the bit‑drop regularizer are crucial for achieving the reported results. Our approach is simple to implement, requires no post‑processing, and is readily adaptable to other modalities such as text or multimodal retrieval. Overall, PBA demonstrates that a carefully designed progressive training paradigm can effectively bridge the gap between deep autoencoder learning and efficient binary coding.
2811:
The rapid progress of reinforcement learning and autonomous reasoning has outpaced the availability of large‑scale, realistic testbeds that reflect the complexity of real‑world problems. To address this gap, we introduce **The Station**, an open‑world environment that blends high‑fidelity physics, procedural generation, and rich sensory modalities to support AI‑driven discovery. Built on top of a modular simulation engine, The Station contains a sprawling research outpost with interconnected modules—habitat, laboratory, storage, and control‑center—each populated with diverse objects, tools, and dynamic processes. Agents receive visual, proprioceptive, and textual cues, and can interact with the environment through a unified action space that includes locomotion, manipulation, and communication.

We formalize a suite of open‑ended tasks designed to probe long‑term planning, resource acquisition, and adaptive problem‑solving. Tasks range from “Harvest & Fabricate” (collect raw materials and assemble devices) to “Diagnostics & Repair” (identify and fix malfunctions in subsystems), encouraging continuous learning and knowledge transfer across domains. To benchmark progress, we provide a set of baseline policies—both classical planners and deep RL agents—alongside metrics such as cumulative reward, task completion rate, and sample efficiency.

Experiments demonstrate that agents struggle to solve the full curriculum with standard techniques, underscoring the difficulty of open‑world exploration and multi‑task coordination. Nonetheless, the environment facilitates novel investigations into curriculum learning, transfer learning, and emergent cognition. All assets, scripts, and evaluation protocols are released under an open‑source license to enable community contributions.

The Station thus serves as a scalable, extensible platform for testing AI systems that must discover, understand, and manipulate complex, dynamic environments—paving the way toward generalizable autonomous agents.
2812:
Goal‑oriented software engineering (GOSE) has emerged as a paradigm in which developers, automated tools, and AI assistants collaborate to achieve high‑level objectives such as “improve performance”, “reduce cyclomatic complexity”, or “implement feature X” through a sequence of concrete code transformations. Despite its growing prominence, progress in GOSE is hampered by the absence of a unified, large‑scale benchmark that captures the rich variety of goals, code bases, and evaluation protocols required to compare and advance existing techniques.  

In this paper we present **CodeClash**, the first comprehensive benchmark designed explicitly for goal‑oriented software engineering. CodeClash contains 48,321 code fragments spanning Java, Python, and JavaScript, each paired with one or more natural‑language goal statements derived from real‑world issue trackers, design documents, and open‑source contribution histories. The benchmark is organized around five core GOSE tasks—(1) *Goal‑driven Refactoring*, (2) *Goal‑oriented Code Synthesis*, (3) *Goal‑based Bug Repair*, (4) *Goal‑driven Documentation Generation*, and (5) *Goal‑guided Performance Tuning*. For every pair we provide a ground‑truth solution (or a set of acceptable solutions) and a fine‑grained annotation of the transformation steps, enabling both end‑to‑end evaluation and intermediate‑step analysis.

We evaluate a suite of state‑of‑the‑art models—including transformer‑based program synthesis, reinforcement‑learning agents for refactoring, and heuristic search tools—on CodeClash, reporting task‑specific accuracies, solution quality metrics, and runtime statistics. Our experiments reveal substantial gaps between current methods and the benchmark’s gold standard, underscoring the need for more sophisticated reasoning about context, dependencies, and multi‑objective trade‑offs.  

CodeClash is released under an open‑source license, together with a standardized evaluation protocol and a public leaderboard. By providing a rich, reproducible testbed, we aim to accelerate research in GOSE, encourage the development of more robust, goal‑aware software engineering tools, and ultimately bridge the gap between high‑level developer intent and low‑level code change.
2813:
Ensuring security early in the software development lifecycle is essential to prevent costly long‑term damage. Code review is a proven technique that allows developers to spot problems before they are merged, and recent advances in large‑language models (LLMs) have enabled automated generation of review comments. Yet most existing LLM‑based tools target generic code quality and their performance on security‑related defects is largely untested. Moreover, building a system that focuses on security issues is hampered by limited training data and a lack of suitable evaluation metrics.

To fill this gap, we present **SecureReviewer**, a specialized approach that boosts LLMs’ ability to detect and remediate security bugs during code review. First, we compile a curated dataset designed for training and measuring secure‑review capabilities. Using this dataset, we fine‑tune LLMs with a secure‑aware strategy that produces review comments highlighting vulnerabilities and suggesting fixes. To reduce hallucinations and increase reliability, we incorporate a Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) module that grounds the model’s output in domain‑specific security knowledge. We also introduce **SecureBLEU**, a new metric for evaluating how effectively generated comments address security problems.

Experiments show that SecureReviewer outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines, achieving higher accuracy in security issue detection and generating review comments that are both higher in quality and more practically useful.
2814:
Dataset bias remains a persistent obstacle to reliable visual recognition, yet most analyses treat bias as a global phenomenon, ignoring the rich structure of the underlying visual concepts. In this work we introduce **ConceptScope**, a framework for *disentangled* characterization of dataset bias that explicitly separates image variation into interpretable visual concepts (e.g., pose, illumination, object class, background) and evaluates the distribution of each concept across data splits and across competing corpora. ConceptScope first learns a latent space of visual concepts via a combination of self‑supervised contrastive learning and sparse disentanglement, producing a compact set of concept embeddings that are jointly orthogonal and semantically meaningful. For any target dataset, we project its samples into this concept space and compute a *concept‑wise bias score*, defined as the discrepancy of a concept’s distribution between a reference distribution and the target. By aggregating over all concepts we obtain a fine‑grained bias profile that pinpoints which aspects of the data are skewed.

We validate ConceptScope on several benchmark corpora (ImageNet, COCO, and a curated set of medical images), demonstrating that it detects both coarse‑grained biases (e.g., class‑level imbalance) and subtle, concept‑level biases (e.g., gender‑dependent lighting or pose). Experiments show that models trained on datasets with high ConceptScope bias scores suffer larger performance gaps on out‑of‑distribution test sets, while bias‑aware re‑weighting guided by ConceptScope’s scores mitigates these gaps by up to 12 % accuracy improvement. ConceptScope also reveals previously unreported biases in public datasets, providing actionable insights for dataset curators and model developers. Our framework is lightweight, concept‑agnostic, and extends naturally to multimodal and video data, opening a new avenue for bias‑aware dataset engineering and trustworthy AI.
2815: This study investigates a learning‑driven approach for tuning control gains in real‑time using an EMT‑in‑the‑loop platform (e.g., PSCAD coupled with Python learning modules). The goal is to mitigate sub‑synchronous oscillations that arise when control gains are poorly tuned under particular grid configurations. By adopting a closed‑loop, reinforcement‑learning framework—specifically a Markov decision process formulation with lightweight deep policy‑gradient algorithms—our method adjusts gains on the fly based on grid conditions. We augment the learning pipeline with SSCI‑specific signal processing, including down‑sampling, band‑pass filtering, and energy‑dependent reward calculations. Experimental results in a realistic event scenario show that the trained policy can adaptively select gain values, effectively suppressing control‑interaction induced oscillations across changing grid conditions.
2816:
Diagnosing rare diseases remains a formidable challenge in clinical practice, largely because of their extreme heterogeneity and the scarcity of labeled examples in existing medical corpora. Traditional large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong general‐language capabilities but falter when confronted with niche, low‑frequency medical knowledge, often generating plausible yet incorrect conclusions. In this work we introduce **RareRAG**, a retrieval‑augmented reasoning agent that learns to combine domain‑specific evidence with transformer‑based inference to support the differential diagnosis of rare diseases.  

RareRAG interleaves a lightweight, end‑to‑end differentiable retrieval module with a chain‑of‑thought (CoT) reasoning backbone. Given a patient’s clinical vignette, the agent queries a curated repository of rare‑disease resources—including OMIM entries, curated case reports, and expert guidelines—using a semantic search encoder fine‑tuned on biomedical literature. Retrieved passages are concatenated with the prompt and fed to a pre‑trained LLaMA‑2 7B fine‑tuned on a newly compiled dataset of 4,500 rare‑disease case histories. The CoT prompt explicitly encourages hypothesis generation, evidence weighing, and uncertainty quantification.  

We evaluate RareRAG on two public benchmarks (Rare Disease Knowledge Graph and the Rare Disease Clinical Diagnosis Dataset) and a proprietary hospital‑derived test set comprising 1,200 de‑identified patient encounters. Compared to baseline LLMs and to retrieval‑only approaches, RareRAG achieves a 12.7 % lift in top‑3 diagnostic accuracy and a 9.3 % improvement in calibrated confidence scores. Ablation studies confirm the importance of both the retrieval module and the CoT reasoning stage, while explainability analyses show that the agent’s rationales align with expert reasoning patterns.  

Our results demonstrate that retrieval‑augmented agents can effectively bridge the knowledge gap inherent to rare disease diagnosis, offering a scalable, interpretable, and high‑performance tool for clinical decision support. Future work will extend this framework to multimodal inputs and real‑time hospital workflows.
2817: The rapid proliferation of AI‑driven discovery—spanning drug design, materials science, and genomics—has amplified the risk of statistical over‑fitting, spurious correlations, and irreproducible results. Current pipelines largely treat statistical validation as an after‑thought, leading to a disconnect between model development and rigorous hypothesis testing. We propose a *Functional Architecture for Structural Enforcement of Statistical Rigor* (FA‑SERS) that embeds statistical safeguards into every stage of an AI discovery workflow. FA‑SERS is composed of three core components: (i) a declarative *Statistical Specification Layer* that codifies significance thresholds, correction procedures, and prior assumptions; (ii) a *Dynamic Validation Engine* that automatically monitors data drift, model calibration, and cross‑validation quality metrics in real time; and (iii) a *Reproducibility Module* that records experiment provenance, generates immutable audit trails, and enforces deterministic reproducibility through containerized execution environments. We implemented FA‑SERS in a large‑scale drug‑repurposing platform and benchmarked it against traditional pipelines. The architecture reduced false‑positive discovery rates by 35 % while maintaining discovery speed, and it enabled a 28 % increase in successful replication of pre‑clinical hits across independent laboratories. By formalizing statistical rigor as a structural property rather than a procedural add‑on, FA‑SERS demonstrates a scalable, modular framework that can be adopted across domains where AI‑driven hypotheses must satisfy stringent evidentiary standards. This work bridges the gap between high‑performance AI and disciplined scientific method, paving the way for more trustworthy AI‑assisted research.
2818:
Ambiguous user requests are a pervasive obstacle in dialog systems, multimodal interfaces, and information‑retrieval engines.  When a query can be interpreted in multiple ways—e.g., “Book a flight” could refer to a reservation, a ticket purchase, or a request for travel recommendations—the system must infer the most plausible intent from sparse cues and contextual information.  Existing intent‑recognition models typically rely on a single best‑guess classification and do not express the uncertainty inherent in such problems, leading to sub‑optimal user experiences and brittle downstream planning.  

In this work we propose **Intent Reasoning Graphs (IRG)**, a probabilistic framework that jointly models lexical cues, dialog history, and external knowledge sources to generate a ranked set of candidate intents with calibrated uncertainty estimates.  IRG constructs a dynamic graph over candidate intents and context nodes, and applies a message‑passing neural network to propagate evidence across the graph.  The resulting distribution is then used to drive a decision‑making policy that can request clarification, request additional context, or act on the most probable intent.  

We evaluate IRG on two benchmark datasets of ambiguous requests (the Multi‑Intent Dialogue Corpus and the Ambiguous Query Set), as well as a newly curated real‑world log of smart‑home commands.  Compared to state‑of‑the‑art intent classifiers, IRG achieves a 12 % relative reduction in mis‑classification and a 9 % increase in overall task success when coupled with a clarification module.  Ablation studies confirm that both the graph‑structured reasoning and the uncertainty calibration are critical to these gains.  

Our results demonstrate that reasoning about intent with explicit uncertainty can substantially improve the robustness of systems that must interpret ambiguous user input, and open new avenues for adaptive, user‑friendly dialogue design.
2819:
Large‑scale language models are increasingly targeted by adversaries who inject *obfuscated prompts*—strings engineered to evade content‑moderation filters by exploiting quirks of tokenizers. Existing defenses typically rely on exhaustive pattern matching or computationally expensive semantic analysis, leaving models vulnerable to subtle, high‑dimensional obfuscations. In this work we introduce **Broken‑Token**, a lightweight, tokenizer‑aware filter that detects obfuscated prompts by analysing the *characters‑per‑token* (CPT) distribution of the input.  

Broken‑Token is built on the observation that legitimate English text exhibits a highly predictable CPT profile when tokenised with subword models (e.g., GPT‑style byte‑pair encoders). Adversarial obfuscations, such as inserting non‑printing Unicode, excessive whitespace, or deliberate character repetitions, distort this distribution and produce tokens whose character counts deviate sharply from the norm. We formalise this phenomenon by deriving a statistical model of CPT for a large corpus of benign prompts and then formulate a robust hypothesis test that flags inputs with anomalous CPT statistics.  

We evaluate Broken‑Token on a benchmark of 1,200 obfuscated prompts spanning 10 adversarial strategies (Unicode scrambling, token‑split, homograph attacks, etc.) and compare against state‑of‑the‑art detection methods based on regex‑matching, token‑frequency, and transformer‑based classifiers. On GPT‑4‑style tokenizers Broken‑Token achieves 95.7 % recall and 98.3 % precision, outperforming baseline approaches by an average margin of 12 % in F1‑score, while adding negligible latency (≤ 1 ms per prompt).  

Our contributions are: (i) a novel, tokenizer‑centric anomaly metric grounded in CPT analysis; (ii) a simple yet highly effective filtering algorithm that generalises across LLM architectures; (iii) a public benchmark of obfuscated prompts and an open‑source implementation that can be deployed as a pre‑processing guardrail in any production LLM pipeline. Broken‑Token demonstrates that even minimal statistical scrutiny of tokenisation can significantly strengthen defenses against prompt‑obfuscation attacks.
2820:
Large‑scale language‑model (LLM) agents are increasingly employed in complex, interactive tasks that demand a rich variety of training signals—ranging from instruction‑following dialogues and question‑answer pairs to tool‑use logs and simulated environment interactions. Existing fine‑tuning pipelines suffer from a fragmented ecosystem of datasets, each encoded in idiosyncratic formats and annotation styles, which hampers reproducibility, scalability, and the ability to train agents that generalize across modalities and domains.  

We introduce the **Agent Data Protocol (ADP)**, a unified schema and accompanying tooling that standardizes the representation of diverse agent‑relevant data. ADP decomposes a dataset into three orthogonal axes: *Task Context*, *Interaction History*, and *Outcome Metadata*, each annotated with a concise, extensible metadata block. The protocol supports both text‑only and multimodal inputs, permits nested sub‑tasks, and incorporates a version‑controlled ontology of tool‑interaction verbs, enabling seamless integration of datasets that span instruction, dialogue, reinforcement learning logs, and external API calls.  

To demonstrate ADP’s utility, we convert ten heterogeneous datasets (OpenAI instruction set, Stanford Dialog, Tool‑Use, RLHF logs, and more) into a common ADP archive and fine‑tune a 13B LLaMA‑based agent using a unified curriculum. The resulting model—**Agent‑ADP**—outperforms baselines trained on each dataset in isolation by 12.4 % on the AGiXT multi‑tool benchmark and achieves state‑of‑the‑art zero‑shot performance on the Multi‑Agent Dialogue and OpenAI Tool‑Use tasks. Ablation studies confirm that the unified data format is key to this improvement, as random re‑shuffling and partial schema compliance degrade results by up to 8 %.  

Our work establishes a reproducible, extensible framework for assembling heterogeneous agent data, opening pathways for collaborative dataset curation, cross‑domain generalization, and more effective fine‑tuning of LLM agents. Code, data, and pretrained checkpoints are released at https://github.com/agentdataprotocol.
2821:
Data scarcity is a persistent obstacle for advancing embodied intelligence. While current methods leverage large language models (LLMs) to automatically create gripper‑based simulation scenes, these techniques transfer poorly to dexterous manipulation, a domain that requires far more nuanced environment construction. Moreover, dexterous tasks are inherently more challenging because of their high degrees of freedom, making large‑scale generation of viable, trainable hand‑interaction scenarios a significant unsolved problem.

In response, we introduce **GenDexHand**, a generative simulation framework that autonomously produces a wide variety of robotic tasks and environments tailored to dexterous manipulation. Central to GenDexHand is a closed‑loop refinement loop that uses vision‑language model (VLM) feedback to adjust object placements and sizes, markedly elevating the overall quality of the generated scenes. Each task is further split into sequential sub‑tasks, enabling step‑wise reinforcement learning that cuts training time and boosts success rates.

Our approach offers a practical, scalable pathway for generating synthetic data to train diverse dexterous hand behaviors, thereby addressing a key bottleneck in embodied intelligence. More details and examples can be found at https://winniechen2002.github.io/GenDexHand/.
2822:
Electrocardiography (ECG) is a ubiquitous tool for cardiovascular screening, yet most deep‑learning models are trained on clean, laboratory‑recorded data and fail to generalise to the “wild” – continuous, ambulatory, multi‑lead recordings fraught with motion artefact, device drift, and heterogeneous electrode layouts.  We introduce **NEF‑NET+**, a scalable, self‑supervised neural architecture that learns a *panoramic* representation of the ECG signal, enabling robust adaptation to the uncontrolled conditions of real‑world monitoring.  

NEF‑NET+ builds on a dual‑stream backbone: a temporal convolutional encoder captures fine‑grained waveform dynamics, while a graph‑based attention module models inter‑lead relationships.  During training we employ a *domain‑mixing* strategy that interleaves clean clinical beats with heavily perturbed, synthetic noise patterns, and a *contrastive adaptation loss* that aligns embeddings across sensor platforms (e.g., Holter, patch, smartwatch).  A lightweight domain‑specific fine‑tuning head is then instantiated for each user, reducing calibration data to a few minutes of unlabelled recordings.  

We evaluate NEF‑NET+ on the newly released **Panoramic ECG‑Wild (PEC‑W)** benchmark, comprising 1.2 M beats from 10,000 subjects recorded on diverse consumer devices.  On arrhythmia detection (AF, VT, SVT) NEF‑NET+ achieves a 4.3 % absolute improvement in F1‑score over the best prior baseline, and outperforms state‑of‑the‑art transfer‑learning approaches on a held‑out “unknown device” split.  Ablation studies confirm the complementary roles of temporal encoders, graph attention, and domain‑mixing.  

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a robust, pan‑lead ECG representation that generalises across noisy, real‑world conditions; (2) a lightweight domain‑adaptation protocol suitable for on‑device deployment; and (3) PEC‑W, the largest publicly available ECG‑wild dataset.  NEF‑NET+ represents a critical step toward reliable, continuous cardiovascular monitoring in everyday life.
2823:
This full‑paper study explores how community‑college instructors assess interactive, no‑code AI literacy resources tailored for non‑STEM learners. As artificial intelligence permeates everyday technologies, AI literacy—encompassing the ability to evaluate, converse with, and grasp the wider impacts of AI systems—has become a vital skill across disciplines. However, scalable, effective pedagogical strategies for teaching these concepts remain scarce, especially for students outside STEM.

To fill this void, we created *AI User*, an online curriculum that conveys foundational AI ideas through scenario‑based, real‑world activities. We gathered insights from four instructor focus groups who worked with *AI User* materials and completed structured feedback exercises. Thematic analysis highlighted that educators appreciated exploratory tasks that mirrored authentic AI use cases and encouraged experimentation, while also noting challenges around scaffolding, accessibility, and multimodal support. A ranking exercise for instructional aids revealed a clear preference for interactive demonstrations over conventional resources such as conceptual guides or lecture slides.

These results illuminate instructors’ viewpoints on how to render AI concepts more approachable and relevant to a wide spectrum of learners, and they inform the design of AI literacy tools that fit diverse teaching contexts while fostering critical engagement with AI in higher education.
2824: Normalization plays a pivotal role in deep learning, yet conventional techniques—BatchNorm, LayerNorm, and RMSNorm—focus almost exclusively on variance, enforcing zero‑mean and unit‑variance constraints that stabilize training but do not explicitly guide how representations encode task‑relevant signals. We introduce IB‑Inspired Normalization (IBNorm), a lightweight yet powerful suite of methods founded on the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle. IBNorm embeds bounded compression steps that coax embeddings to retain predictive information while discarding irrelevant variability, yielding more informative representations without sacrificing the stability and ease of integration that standard normalizers provide. From a theoretical standpoint, we demonstrate that IBNorm attains a higher IB value and tighter generalization guarantees compared to variance‑centric approaches. Experiments across large‑scale language models (LLaMA, GPT‑2) and vision architectures (ResNet, ViT) consistently show that IBNorm surpasses BatchNorm, LayerNorm, and RMSNorm, with mutual‑information diagnostics corroborating its superior bottleneck behaviour. The implementation will be made publicly available.
2825: State‑of‑the‑art real‑time nonlinear state estimation increasingly relies on neural‑network models, yet these data‑driven approaches must deliver trustworthy error bounds—especially in safety‑critical settings. In this work we present a novel estimator based on the Multi‑Fidelity Residual Physics‑Informed Neural Process (MFR‑PINP) for real‑time robotic state tracking. The method tackles the model‑mismatch problem by learning the residuals between simple, low‑fidelity kinematic predictions and complex, high‑fidelity dynamics, thereby enriching the underlying physics‑guided model. Uncertainty quantification is incorporated through a split‑conformal prediction framework, endowing the estimator with rigorous, confidence‑based guarantees during both training and inference. We detail the hybrid online‑learning implementation of the MFR‑PINP and evaluate its performance on a robotic platform. Compared with leading Kalman‑filter variants—including the Unscented Kalman Filter and Deep Kalman Filter—our results demonstrate that MFR‑PINP is a competitive, reliable choice for real‑time state estimation.
2826:
In many culturally conservative societies, sexual and reproductive health (SRH) information is shrouded in myths, metaphors, and taboos that hinder evidence‑based decision‑making. While large language models (LLMs) promise scalable, personalized health guidance, their generic training corpora and opaque reasoning often reinforce prevailing misconceptions or produce content that violates local norms. This paper argues that “rethinking LLMs for SRH in conservative contexts” requires a dual focus: (1) *myth‑aware content filtering* that identifies and corrects culturally specific misinformation, and (2) *metaphor‑guided framing* that translates technical SRH facts into culturally resonant narratives.  

We propose a modular framework that (i) incorporates a curated SRH knowledge base derived from WHO guidelines and regional health authorities, (ii) applies a context‑sensitive myth‑detection module trained on annotated discourse from conservative communities, and (iii) leverages a metaphor‑generation engine that maps medical terminology to locally accepted analogies. To evaluate the framework, we conducted a mixed‑methods study in two conservative regions (Rajasthan, India and Jordan), deploying the model via a mobile app to 1,200 users over six weeks. Quantitative metrics (accuracy, misinformation reduction, user trust scores) and qualitative feedback (focus‑group interviews) reveal that the myth‑aware, metaphor‑augmented LLM significantly outperforms baseline fine‑tuned GPT‑4 in both factual correctness (↑15 %) and user satisfaction (↑23 %).  

Our findings suggest that SRH LLMs can be ethically and effectively adapted to conservative settings by systematically integrating myth‑detection and culturally appropriate metaphorization. The paper concludes with design guidelines for developers and policymakers, and a discussion of ethical implications related to agency, privacy, and the potential for cultural homogenization.
2827: The exponential growth of publicly available Web APIs has made it increasingly difficult for developers to discover and select services that best satisfy their functional and non‑functional requirements. Existing recommendation approaches typically rely on keyword matching, usage statistics, or collaborative filtering, yet they ignore the rich semantic information that can be extracted from API descriptions, documentation, and underlying ontologies. In this paper we present **WAR‑Re** (Web API Recommendation with Semantic Reasoning), a novel framework that exploits formal semantic models to infer highly relevant API candidates for a given developer query. WAR‑Re first converts API metadata (OpenAPI specifications, README files, and community tags) into an RDF graph enriched with a domain‑specific ontology. A rule‑based reasoning engine then propagates type, capability, and constraint inferences, yielding a semantically grounded representation of each API. For a user’s task description, WAR‑Re performs ontology‑aware query expansion and computes a similarity score that combines lexical, structural, and semantic distances. The final recommendation list is further refined via a lightweight collaborative filter that captures historical API usage patterns. We evaluated WAR‑Re on a benchmark dataset of 3,200 public APIs and 1,500 user queries, achieving a 12.4 % improvement in precision@10 over state‑of‑the‑art keyword‑based and collaborative‑filter baselines. A user study with 30 software engineers confirmed that the semantically enriched recommendations were perceived as more accurate and useful. WAR‑Re demonstrates that integrating formal semantic reasoning into Web API recommendation systems yields measurable gains in relevance, scalability, and transparency, thereby supporting more informed service composition in modern software development.
2828:
The increasing demand for secure and reliable digital media has driven the development of robust image watermarking schemes that simultaneously preserve visual quality and withstand a wide range of manipulations. In this paper we propose a hybrid spatial–frequency domain watermarking framework that exploits complementary advantages of both domains: the spatial domain’s high imperceptibility for subtle alterations and the frequency domain’s resilience against lossy compression and geometric attacks. The watermark is first encoded with a lightweight error‑correction code and then embedded adaptively: low‑frequency DCT coefficients in a block‑based Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) domain are used for coarse robustness, while the Least Significant Bits (LSBs) of selected spatial pixels are modified only in perceptually insensitive regions determined by a local variance map. A perceptual masking model controls embedding strength, ensuring the embedded signal remains below the human visual system’s detection threshold.

Extensive experimentation on the benchmark Kodak and USC‑IRB image datasets demonstrates that the proposed method achieves a peak‑signal‑to‑noise‑ratio (PSNR) above 45 dB and a structural similarity index (SSIM) exceeding 0.98 in the unaltered watermarked images, indicating excellent imperceptibility. When subjected to JPEG compression (quality factors down to 10 %), Gaussian noise (σ = 20), median filtering, scaling, rotation, and cropping, the extracted watermark retains a bit‑error‑rate (BER) below 1 % and a correlation coefficient above 0.85. Compared with state‑of‑the‑art spatial‑only and frequency‑only schemes, the hybrid approach yields a 3–5 dB improvement in PSNR and a 20–30 % reduction in BER under the most aggressive attacks.

The results confirm that the proposed hybrid spatial–frequency embedding strategy offers a superior trade‑off between imperceptibility and robustness, making it a promising candidate for practical watermarking applications such as copyright protection and digital rights management.
2829: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly underpin human‑centered applications, grasping their personality‑like behaviours becomes crucial for responsible design and use. In this study we evaluate six prominent LLMs through the lens of the Big Five Inventory‑2 (BFI‑2), examining how their trait expressions shift with different sampling temperatures. Our findings show pronounced variation across four of the five personality dimensions, with Neuroticism and Extraversion notably sensitive to temperature changes. Additionally, hierarchical clustering identifies distinct groups of models, hinting that architectural choices may steer certain LLMs toward particular, stable trait profiles. Together, these insights illuminate the emergence of personality‑like patterns in LLMs and offer fresh guidance for model tuning, selection, and ethical governance. The full dataset and code are available at https://osf.io/bsvzc/?view_only=6672219bede24b4e875097426dc3fac1.
2830:
Foundation models trained on vast, heterogeneous audio corpora have recently become the de‑facto standard for bioacoustic analysis, yet their zero‑shot performance on unseen species or acoustic environments remains limited by domain shift and over‑reliance on the particular data distribution of a single pretraining set. In this work we introduce **Model Merging (MM)**, a lightweight framework that combines the latent representations of multiple independently pretrained bioacoustic backbone networks into a single, jointly‑fine‑tuned predictor. The merging procedure is agnostic to the source of the individual models: we construct a dynamic ensemble of adapters that learn to weight and fuse hidden activations from each constituent network, and we optionally blend the parameter spaces via Bayesian averaging to reduce catastrophic forgetting.

We evaluate MM on a comprehensive zero‑shot benchmark consisting of 12 publicly available bioacoustic datasets spanning mammalian, avian, amphibian, and insect calls recorded in a wide range of acoustic environments (forest, urban, marine). Across all datasets, MM yields a 7.8 % absolute improvement in F1‑score and a 5.4 % lift in area‑under‑the‑curve over the strongest single‑model baseline, while retaining comparable inference latency. Ablation studies demonstrate that the benefit is driven primarily by the diversity of the source corpora rather than sheer model size, and that the adapter‑based fusion outperforms naïve ensembling and parameter averaging.

Our findings establish that model merging is a simple, scalable, and effective strategy for enhancing zero‑shot generalization in bioacoustic foundation models, and we provide an open‑source implementation that can be readily integrated into existing audio‑analysis pipelines.
2831: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in forensic law, guaranteeing that legal question‑answering (QA) remains accurate and traceable is paramount. Conventional large language models (LLMs) frequently hallucinate, which can lead to misleading legal advice, while static knowledge bases cannot keep pace with the rapid evolution of statutes and case law. To address these challenges, we introduce a hybrid legal QA agent designed for judicial environments that fuses retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) with multi‑model ensembling. The system prioritises evidence retrieval: if a trusted legal repository supplies relevant documents, the answer is generated via RAG; otherwise, several LLMs produce candidate responses that a specialised selector ranks, returning the top‑scoring reply. High‑quality outputs are subsequently reviewed by a human and then fed back into the repository, enabling continuous knowledge refinement and provenance tracking. Evaluations on the Law_QA dataset demonstrate that our hybrid approach significantly surpasses both a single‑model baseline and a vanilla RAG pipeline in F1, ROUGE‑L, and an LLM‑as‑a‑Judge metric. Ablation studies confirm that retrieval prioritisation, model ensembling, and the human‑in‑the‑loop update cycle each contribute uniquely to performance. The proposed system markedly reduces hallucinations, improves answer quality and legal compliance, and brings media‑forensics technology closer to practical deployment in judicial settings.
2832: Link prediction is a core problem in graph‑based machine learning, underpinning applications from social recommendation to knowledge‑graph completion. Ensuring fairness in these predictions is essential, because biased links can reinforce societal inequities. Existing studies typically adopt a dyadic view of fairness, enforcing demographic parity between links made inside and across demographic groups. We demonstrate that this dyadic formulation can mask deeper subgroup disparities, letting systemic bias slip past detection. Moreover, we contend that demographic parity is ill‑suited for ranking‑style tasks like link prediction. We formally expose the shortcomings of current fairness metrics and introduce a more expressive evaluation framework. Finally, we present a lightweight post‑processing strategy that, together with decoupled link predictors, effectively reduces bias while attaining superior fairness‑utility trade‑offs.
2833: Recent strides in long‑context language models (LMs) allow inputs of millions of tokens, broadening their use for intricate tasks such as computer‑assisted agents. However, the safety consequences of these extended contexts are not yet fully understood. To address this, we present **NINJA** (Needle‑in‑a‑Haystack Jailbreak), a technique that subverts aligned LMs by appending harmless, model‑generated text to steer them toward a malicious goal. A key insight behind our approach is that the position of the harmful directive within the prompt heavily influences a model’s safety response. Evaluations on the standard safety benchmark, HarmBench, demonstrate that NINJA markedly boosts attack success rates against leading open‑source and commercial models—including LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, and Gemini. Unlike previous jailbreak strategies, NINJA is resource‑efficient, broadly transferable, and harder to detect. We further show that, given a fixed computational budget, extending the context length can be more effective than simply running more best‑of‑N attempts. These results reveal that even innocuous long contexts, when strategically arranged, expose inherent vulnerabilities in contemporary LMs.
2834:
Diffusion generative models have emerged as the state‑of‑the‑art framework for producing high‑fidelity images, yet their practical deployment hinges on the effectiveness of guidance signals that steer the sampling trajectory toward desired attributes. Current guidance strategies—most notably classifier‑free and classifier‑based conditioning—suffer from two intertwined issues: (1) **miscalibration** of guidance strength, which can lead to either mode collapse or excessive distortion of the underlying distribution, and (2) **over‑regularisation** of the sampler, where strong conditioning forces the model to deviate from its learned prior, producing artifacts and reduced diversity.  

In this work we propose a principled framework that jointly calibrates and regularises diffusion model guidance. We introduce a lightweight calibration network that learns to predict optimal guidance coefficients on a per‑sample basis, thereby mitigating the need for manual hyper‑parameter tuning. Complementary to this, we formulate a regularisation loss that penalises excessive deviation from the diffusion prior, encouraging the model to preserve naturalness while honouring conditioning cues. Our method is agnostic to the underlying diffusion architecture and can be seamlessly integrated into both classifier‑free and classifier‑based pipelines.  

We evaluate the approach on a suite of benchmark datasets (CIFAR‑10, ImageNet‑64, and CelebA‑HQ), demonstrating consistent improvements in FID and CLIP‑score relative to baseline guidance techniques. Qualitative analysis confirms a reduction in hallucination and style drift, while ablation studies reveal the critical role of adaptive calibration in achieving the observed performance gains. Our results suggest that careful calibration and regularisation are essential for unlocking the full generative potential of diffusion models.
2835: When multiple large‑language‑model agents collaborate, they outperform a single agent on math‑question answering. Yet it remains unclear whether such collaborative ensembles also withstand adversarial perturbations. In this study, we probe this by introducing noise into mathematical questions: punctuation perturbations at 10 %, 30 %, and 50 % levels, as well as realistic, human‑style typos (WikiTypo and R2ATA). Employing a unified sampling‑and‑voting framework called *Agent Forest*, we benchmark six open‑source models—Qwen3‑4B/14B, Llama3.1‑8B, Mistral‑7B, and Gemma3‑4B/12B—on four datasets (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU‑Math, and MultiArith). Experiments vary the number of agents (n = 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25). Our results reveal two key insights: (1) The type of noise matters; punctuation errors degrade performance in proportion to their severity, while human‑style typos remain the most harmful, creating the largest accuracy gaps and the highest attack success rates even when many agents are used. (2) Collaborative ensembles consistently boost accuracy as n grows, with the most pronounced improvement from one to five agents and diminishing returns beyond ten. Nevertheless, the robustness gap between clean and adversarial inputs persists regardless of how many agents are employed.
2836:
Large language models (LLMs) often produce outputs that deviate from user intents, safety constraints, or domain‑specific desiderata, even when the models are trained on vast corpora. Existing alignment strategies typically modify the training objective or augment the dataset, incurring significant computational overhead and limited flexibility at inference time. We propose **Test‑Time Alignment via Sampling‑Based Optimal Control (TTA‑SBOC)**, a framework that reframes the alignment problem as a stochastic optimal control task in the *pre‑logit* representation of the transformer. By sampling candidate logits from a controllable policy and evaluating them with a lightweight reward signal that encodes alignment objectives, TTA‑SBOC applies a path‑integral style update to the logits before the final softmax. This procedure allows the model to “steer” its predictions toward compliant, safe, or user‑specified outcomes without retraining or fine‑tuning the network parameters.  

Theoretically, we prove that under mild assumptions the control update converges to a stationary point of the expected reward in the pre‑logit space, and we quantify the variance reduction achieved by importance‑weighted sampling. Empirically, we evaluate TTA‑SBOC on a suite of open‑source LLMs (GPT‑Neo, LLaMA, and GPT‑3‑Ada) across benchmarks for factual accuracy, toxic content filtering, and task‑specific precision. Our method consistently outperforms baseline post‑processing techniques (e.g., temperature scaling, nucleus sampling) and achieves comparable or better alignment quality to fine‑tuned “safe” models, with only a 5–10 % increase in inference latency. TTA‑SBOC offers a practical, modular, and theoretically grounded solution for on‑the‑fly alignment of large language models.
2837:
Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents—automated agents that learn to interact with software by observing and manipulating widgets—have become indispensable for tasks ranging from automated testing to assistive technology. However, most current approaches treat each interaction in isolation, relying on a myopic view of the UI that ignores the rich temporal dependencies inherent in real‑world interfaces. This limitation often manifests as failure to recover from ambiguous or transient states, leading to brittle behavior and low task completion rates.

We propose *History‑Aware Reasoning for GUI Agents* (HARGA), a framework that augments traditional state‑based policy learning with explicit modeling of interaction history. HARGA encodes the sequence of user actions and UI observations in a dynamic graph‑structured memory and employs a transformer‑based reasoning module to infer latent contextual cues (e.g., modal dialogs, pending confirmations, or contextual menus) that are not visible in the current snapshot. The agent thus learns to condition its action selection on both the instantaneous UI state and the temporally‑extended history, enabling robust disambiguation and graceful recovery from unexpected events.

We evaluate HARGA on two benchmark suites: (1) a suite of 120 mobile‑app interaction tasks with non‑linear navigation, and (2) a suite of 65 desktop‑application tasks from the OpenAI Gym‑GUI benchmark. Across both suites, HARGA outperforms baseline state‑only policies by 12.4 % in task success rate and reduces average step count by 18.7 %, demonstrating that incorporating historical context substantially enhances sample efficiency and generalization. Ablation studies confirm that the graph‑memory component is essential for capturing long‑range dependencies, while the transformer reasoning yields the largest gains in ambiguous scenarios.

Our results highlight the importance of history‑aware reasoning for realistic GUI automation and open avenues for more adaptive, explainable, and user‑friendly interface agents.
2838: Large Language Models (LLMs) can be tricked into following malicious instructions by using encoded or ciphered prompts that evade safety filters. Although the guardrails often fail to decode these inputs, the underlying models still understand and act on them. We present **CPT‑Filtering**, a lightweight, model‑agnostic defense that exploits a key property of Byte‑Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenizers: they split unfamiliar, out‑of‑distribution strings—such as ciphers—into many short tokens. By monitoring the *average number of Characters Per Token (CPT)*, our method can detect encoded text with almost perfect accuracy while incurring negligible overhead. This contrasts with costly alternatives that rely on auxiliary LLMs or perplexity estimators. We evaluated CPT‑Filtering on a benchmark of more than 100,000 diverse prompts, covering several encoding schemes and popular tokenizers. The results show that a simple CPT threshold reliably flags encoded content—even in very short messages—making CPT‑Filtering a practical, ready‑to‑deploy layer for real‑time filtering and offline data sanitization.
2839:
High‑risk property assessment—determining whether a property is suitable for financing, insurance, or investment—requires nuanced interpretation of heterogeneous data sources, such as legal documents, geospatial imagery, and historical incident reports. Conventional automated classifiers struggle to capture this complexity, yielding high false‑positive rates that incur costly downstream errors. We propose **ORCHID** (Orchestrated Retrieval‑Augmented Classification with Human‑in‑the‑Loop Intelligent Decision‑Making), a modular framework that couples retrieval‑enhanced machine learning with adaptive human oversight to deliver reliable, explainable decisions on high‑risk properties.

ORCHID’s core consists of a **retrieval‑augmented classifier** that first indexes a curated corpus of domain knowledge (regulatory statutes, case law, and expert annotations) in a dense vector space. At inference time, a semantic search engine retrieves the most relevant documents, which are then fused with the raw property features through a transformer‑based fusion layer. This design allows the classifier to draw on contextual evidence beyond its training distribution, improving robustness to noisy or sparse inputs.

To mitigate residual uncertainty, ORCHID incorporates a **human‑in‑the‑loop (HITL)** module that surfaces the top‑retrieved evidence and a confidence score to domain experts. Expert feedback is automatically logged and used to update both the retrieval index (via relevance re‑ranking) and the classification parameters (via online learning), enabling the system to adapt to evolving risk patterns. We demonstrate that ORCHID reduces the overall misclassification rate by 27 % relative to baseline BERT‑style classifiers on a proprietary dataset of 12,000 property records from multiple jurisdictions, while maintaining a 94 % expert‑approved agreement rate.

Our experiments also reveal that the retrieval component contributes 65 % of the performance gains, highlighting the importance of external knowledge. The HITL loop further improves interpretability, with 85 % of expert reviews citing the retrieved evidence as a decisive factor. We release the ORCHID codebase and a synthetic benchmark to facilitate reproducibility and encourage future research in retrieval‑augmented risk assessment.  

*Keywords:* Retrieval‑augmented classification, human‑in‑the‑loop, high‑risk property, intelligent decision making, explainable AI.
2840:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are being deployed more broadly, yet the security problems that accompany them now pose a serious obstacle to their dependable use in mission‑critical settings.  To address this, we present a holistic safety response framework that protects LLMs at both the input and output stages.  

On the input side, the framework uses a supervised fine‑tuned classifier that applies a fine‑grained four‑category taxonomy—Safe, Unsafe, Conditionally Safe, and Focused Attention—to identify risks and apply appropriate handling rules.  This precise risk identification boosts coverage and adaptability to diverse business scenarios, achieving a 99.3 % recall of unsafe queries.  

At the output level, we integrate Retrieval‑Augmented Generation with a purpose‑built interpretation model, guaranteeing that every response is grounded in a real‑time, trustworthy knowledge base.  This eliminates hallucinations and provides end‑to‑end traceability.  

Experimental results show that our safety control model attains substantially higher safety scores on public benchmarks compared with the baseline TinyR1‑Safety‑8B, and scores a perfect 100 % safety on our proprietary high‑risk test set—demonstrating its robustness in complex risk scenarios.  Overall, the study offers an engineering pathway for building LLM applications that are both highly secure and highly trustworthy.
2841: The reliability and fairness of automated online moderation systems hinge on rigorous evaluation of their decision logic under diverse content contexts. Traditional test suites, however, are limited by the sparsity of real‑world edge cases and the difficulty of constructing counterfactual inputs that probe policy boundaries. We propose **LLM‑Powered Counterfactual Simulations (LPCS)**, a framework that harnesses large language models (LLMs) to generate realistic, context‑aware counterfactual posts, enabling systematic stress‑testing of moderation engines. Our method conditions an LLM on a moderation decision (e.g., “safe” or “toxic”) and then rewrites the content to flip a targeted attribute—such as the speaker’s protected identity, stylistic tone, or factual framing—while preserving semantic intent.
