I then raise four pivotal questions that require further theoretical and empirical work: (1) Will machines simply imitate human behavior? (2) Are existing human‑centric crime theories adequate for explaining deviant or criminal conduct arising from autonomous AI interactions? (3) Which forms of criminal activity will be most immediately affected? (4) In what ways might this profound societal shift alter policing?  

These questions highlight the urgent necessity for criminologists to engage with the implications of multi‑agent AI systems, to shape theoretical and empirical inquiry, and to contribute proactively to discussions on AI safety and governance.
2892: Large‑language‑model (LLM) “judges” have emerged as a scalable mechanism for assessing the correctness, fairness, and safety of generated content. However, their reliability is contingent on high‑quality annotated data, which is expensive and time‑consuming to produce manually. In this work, we introduce a *Generate–Evaluate–Iterate* framework that leverages synthetic data to accelerate human‑in‑the‑loop refinement of LLM judges. First, we employ a baseline judge model to generate a diverse pool of candidate judgments across multiple tasks (e.g., factual consistency, bias detection, and style compliance). Second, a curated panel of domain experts evaluates these synthetic judgments using a lightweight interface that flags errors, provides corrective signals, and ranks confidence. Third, the collected human feedback is fed back into the system as a fine‑tuning signal, producing an updated judge that better aligns with human preferences. Iterating this pipeline yields a progressive improvement in both precision and recall, as measured against an independent held‑out benchmark. We validate the approach on three representative domains—medical text review, legal drafting, and creative writing—achieving up to 18 % absolute gain in accuracy over a purely rule‑based baseline while reducing the human annotation effort by 65 %. Additionally, we release a synthetic judgment dataset of 250k samples, along with evaluation scripts, to encourage reproducibility. Our findings demonstrate that synthetic data, coupled with targeted human oversight, can significantly lower the barrier to deploying trustworthy LLM judges at scale.
2893:
**Background:** Incidental thyroid nodules detected on non‑thyroid imaging studies represent a growing public health concern, yet systematic epidemiological characterization remains limited by the volume and unstructured nature of radiology reports. Artificial intelligence (AI)–based natural‑language‑processing (NLP) offers an opportunity to rapidly mine these reports and quantify both prevalence and downstream clinical outcomes.

**Methods:** We retrospectively extracted 58 842 adult radiology reports (CT, MRI, PET‑CT, and abdominal ultrasound) from a multi‑institutional health network (2015–2020). A supervised NLP pipeline (BERT‑based transformer) was trained on 2 000 manually annotated reports to identify “incidental thyroid findings” and to extract associated modifiers (size, composition, suspicion, and recommended follow‑up). Cases were linked to the electronic health record to obtain demographic data, subsequent thyroid‑specific imaging, fine‑needle aspiration (FNA) results, and management outcomes. Machine‑learning models (random forest, XGBoost) were built to predict malignancy risk from NLP‑derived features. Statistical comparisons were conducted using chi‑square and logistic regression.

**Results:** Incidental thyroid findings were identified in 6 981 (12.0%) patients (median age 57 y; 63% female). The median nodule size was 1.2 cm (IQR 0.8–1.9 cm), with 28% described as “solid” or “hypoechoic.” Of the 6 981 patients, 1,129 (16.2%) underwent further evaluation, yielding 112 malignant diagnoses (5.0% of all incidental nodules). Only 27% of patients with nodules ≥1 cm received guideline‑concordant follow‑up. Our predictive model achieved 0.85 AUC, correctly identifying 70% of malignant nodules with 85% sensitivity. Economically, incidental thyroid findings contributed an estimated 8 % additional cost per imaging suite due to follow‑up testing and procedures.

**Conclusions:** AI‑enabled analysis of unstructured radiology reports reveals a substantial burden of incidental thyroid findings, suboptimal adherence to follow‑up guidelines, and a measurable impact on patient management and healthcare costs. These insights underscore the need for automated alert systems within PACS and highlight opportunities for targeted interventions to reduce overtreatment while ensuring timely detection of clinically significant thyroid disease. Future prospective studies should evaluate the integration of AI‑driven decision support into clinical workflows to improve outcomes for patients with incidental thyroid abnormalities.
2894:
The recent surge of tool‑using agents has highlighted a bottleneck: high‑quality, diverse synthetic tools and environments are scarce and difficult to scale, limiting the breadth of agent training and evaluation. We introduce **SynthTools**, a unified framework that automates the generation, validation, and deployment of synthetic tools for large‑scale agent development. SynthTools comprises three core components: (1) a *Domain‑specific Language* for specifying tool interfaces and semantics, (2) a *procedural generator* that produces thousands of deterministic and stochastic tool instances across domains (e.g., arithmetic, navigation, web‑scraping), and (3) a *feedback‑driven refinement* loop that uses agent performance metrics to iteratively prune redundant tools and enrich under‑represented capabilities.  

We evaluated SynthTools on three benchmark suites—RoboSuite, LLM‑ToolBench, and OpenAI‑Gym—demonstrating that agents trained with SynthTools‑generated toolsets achieve a 12–18 % improvement in task completion rates compared to agents trained on handcrafted tool collections. Moreover, the framework scales to >10 k unique tools while maintaining execution latency below 5 ms per call, enabling real‑time training loops. Ablation studies confirm that both the procedural diversity and feedback loop are essential for optimal performance.  

SynthTools is open‑source, providing a modular pipeline for researchers to construct domain‑agnostic tool ecosystems, thereby accelerating the development of robust, general‑purpose agents. This work advances the state of synthetic data generation for agent training and offers a practical pathway to scalable, high‑fidelity tool usage.
2895:
The discovery of reliable biomarkers in complex biological systems hinges on the integration of *global* molecular context with *cell‑specific* functional read‑outs. Conventional deep‑learning pipelines typically employ linear probing on pretrained language models to extract sequence‑level features, yet this approach neglects the hierarchical and multi‑granular nature of biological regulation. Here we present **Joint‑Weighted Token Hierarchy (J‑WTH)**, a foundation model that fuses global sequence embeddings with cellular‑omics signals through a hierarchical attention mechanism that assigns learnable weights to tokens at multiple levels of abstraction—nucleotide, peptide, and functional domain.  

We first pretrain a transformer encoder on 1.6 × 10⁶ protein sequences and fine‑tune it jointly with single‑cell RNA‑seq matrices from 12 cancer and autoimmune disease cohorts. Linear probing of the frozen encoder achieved an area‑under‑curve (AUC) of 0.83 for known disease biomarkers. In contrast, our J‑WTH model, which jointly optimizes a weighted token hierarchy and a cellular context encoder, attained a mean AUC of 0.91 (p < 10⁻⁶), uncovering 58 novel candidate biomarkers with strong tissue‑specific expression patterns. Cross‑validation demonstrates robustness across data modalities, and ablation studies confirm that the hierarchical weighting scheme drives the performance gain, outperforming flat concatenation and attention‑only baselines by 4–7 %.  

By bridging global and cellular representations, J‑WTH offers a principled framework for biomarker discovery that respects the multi‑scale organization of biology. The model is released as an open‑source toolkit (PyTorch/TF‑Hub) and is accompanied by a benchmark dataset of multimodal omics for 18 diseases. This work paves the way toward interpretable, multi‑modal foundation models that can accelerate translational biomarker research.
2896: Aligning large language model (LLM) judges with human preferences remains a formidable task, largely due to their sensitivity to rubrics, inherent biases, and lack of stability. Tackling this issue is essential for building trustworthy reward models used in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and for creating robust routing systems that pick the most appropriate model for a given query. In this paper, we introduce a framework that captures a spectrum of persona-driven preferences by learning to combine the outputs of multiple rubric‑conditioned judges. We compare this method to simple baselines and evaluate its resilience through case studies involving both human and LLM judge biases. Our key contributions are a scalable, persona‑based approach for generating preference labels and two variants of the aggregation mechanism—a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) and a Multi‑Layer Perceptron (MLP).
2897:
Large language models (LLMs) have recently been employed as flexible “graph reasoners” by serializing graph‐structured data into natural‑language or token sequences.  While this approach unlocks powerful few‑shot reasoning capabilities, it also introduces a pernicious vulnerability: the serialization process is highly dependent on node order, edge ordering, and surface conventions, thereby breaking the permutation invariance that underlies graph semantics.  Consequently, LLMs trained or prompted on a particular serialization often fail to generalize to unseen graphs or to graphs with different size and topology, a problem that has remained largely unexplored in the literature.  

In this paper we systematically investigate the impact of serialization on the invariance and generalization of LLM‑based graph reasoners.  We first formalize the notion of *serialization bias* and quantify its effect on performance across three canonical reasoning tasks—path finding, subgraph isomorphism, and knowledge‑graph query answering—using a suite of synthetic and real‑world datasets.  To mitigate this bias we propose two complementary strategies: (i) a *canonical‑ordering* encoder that maps each graph to a unique, permutation‑invariant serialization, and (ii) a *graph‑aware prompt* that explicitly exposes the model to graph symmetry through a set of invariance‑inducing examples.  We integrate these strategies with state‑of‑the‑art instruction‑tuned LLMs (e.g., GPT‑4, LLaMA‑2) and evaluate them under a rigorous zero‑shot, few‑shot, and fine‑tuning regime.  

Empirical results demonstrate that canonical serialization alone boosts accuracy by 12–18 % on average, while the invariance‑prompting further improves robustness to graph re‑ordering and unseen graph sizes, reducing error rates by up to 25 % compared to baseline serializations.  Ablation studies confirm that the gains stem from reduced over‑reliance on surface heuristics rather than from memorization.  

Our contributions are: (1) a comprehensive framework for measuring serialization bias in LLM graph reasoning, (2) a lightweight canonicalization technique that restores permutation invariance without altering the underlying model, and (3) an analysis of generalization gaps across graph domains, guiding future design of graph‑aware language models.  We hope this work encourages a more principled treatment of graph structure when leveraging LLMs for reasoning tasks.
2898: We introduce a novel pipeline that merges Large Language Models (LLMs) with advanced image‑analysis techniques to non‑invasively predict IDH mutation status in brain gliomas without requiring prior training. For every patient, we processed coregistered multi‑parametric MRI scans alongside multi‑class tumor segmentations to derive interpretable visual attributes and quantitative radiomic descriptors. These features were serialized into a standard JSON format and fed directly to GPT‑4o and GPT‑5, without any fine‑tuning. The framework was evaluated on six publicly available datasets (n = 1,427) and yielded high accuracy and balanced classification performance across diverse cohorts, even in the absence of manual labels. GPT‑5 surpassed GPT‑4o in phenotype interpretation driven by contextual information. Among the extracted predictors, volumetric measures were the most influential, followed by subtype‑specific imaging markers and clinical variables. This study demonstrates that coupling LLM reasoning with computational imaging can achieve precise, non‑invasive tumor genotyping, thereby advancing neuro‑oncologic diagnostic approaches. The source code is available at https://github.com/ATPLab-LUMS/CIM-LLM.
2899: Assessing log‑summarization systems is notoriously difficult because high‑quality reference summaries are rarely available and conventional metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU rely only on surface‑level n‑gram overlap. In this work we present REFLEX, a reference‑free evaluation framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) as zero‑shot judges. REFLEX measures key aspects of a summary—relevance, informativeness, and coherence—without the need for gold references or manual annotations. Experiments on several log‑summarization datasets demonstrate that REFLEX yields stable, interpretable, and fine‑grained scores, and it is more sensitive in distinguishing outputs from different models than traditional metrics. Thus, REFLEX offers a practical and scalable solution for evaluating log summaries in real‑world scenarios where reference data is limited or absent.
2900:
The rapid spread of misinformation on social media poses profound risks to public discourse, policy, and democratic processes. Existing diffusion models—typically based on simple contagion or stochastic reinforcement schemes—often fail to capture the nuanced, content‑driven dynamics that modern platforms exhibit, especially given the sophisticated language generation capabilities now available. This paper introduces **LM‑Sim**, a large‑language‑model (LLM)‑based framework for end‑to‑end simulation of misinformation propagation in realistic social‑network settings.

LM‑Sim treats each user as an autonomous agent whose belief state and posting behavior are governed by a fine‑tuned GPT‑4 model conditioned on network topology, historical interaction patterns, and individual user traits. The model first synthesizes plausible misinformation narratives, then evaluates their persuasive features (emotional valence, factual density, and stylistic cues) using a downstream classifier. Agents’ likelihood to retweet or comment is modulated by a Bayesian belief update that incorporates content similarity to personal prior knowledge and peer influence. The framework is calibrated on a large Twitter‑derived dataset spanning 2020‑2022, encompassing over 10 M users and 250 M posts, and is validated against observed diffusion cascades of high‑profile misinformation events.

Empirically, LM‑Sim reproduces key statistical signatures of real‑world cascades—including heavy‑tailed reach, temporal clustering, and echo‑chamber formation—while outperforming baseline SI/SIR and Hawkes‑process models by up to 18 % in mean‑squared error of cascade size. Sensitivity analyses reveal that linguistic features such as narrative complexity and emotional tone exert a stronger influence on spread than traditional virality metrics. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of the simulator in assessing counter‑measures: targeted fact‑checking and algorithmic throttling significantly dampen cascade growth, with the LLM framework revealing nuanced trade‑offs that are invisible to coarse‑grained models.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a novel LLM‑driven agent‑based simulation platform that bridges language generation and network diffusion; (2) a comprehensive empirical validation against real misinformation cascades; and (3) actionable insights into content‑specific intervention strategies. LM‑Sim offers a versatile tool for researchers and platform designers seeking to anticipate, analyze, and mitigate misinformation in complex social‑network ecosystems.
2901:
Large language models (LLMs) are conventionally evaluated on single‑shot prompts, yet real‑world deployments frequently require feeding the model a stream of contextual information over time. How this *accumulating context* reshapes the model’s internal belief state remains largely unexplored. In this paper we systematically investigate belief evolution in state‑of‑the‑art LLMs when presented with progressively richer contextual cues. We construct a benchmark comprising 1,200 factual queries paired with sequences of context that introduce new facts, disconfirmations, or ambiguous statements. For each query we record the model’s answers after every context addition and quantify belief change with a novel *belief drift* metric based on KL divergence between successive posterior distributions over candidate answers. 

Our experiments reveal that: (i) even a single additional context sentence can induce a measurable shift in the model’s preferred answer; (ii) contradictory or highly uncertain context amplifies drift, sometimes causing abrupt belief flips; (iii) the magnitude of drift correlates with the model’s confidence, as reflected by output entropy, and with the cumulative length of the context window. We further demonstrate that simple prompt‑engineering tricks—such as explicit “reset” tokens or hierarchical context summaries—significantly attenuate undesirable drift. 

These findings underscore that LLMs do not maintain a static worldview but continually recalibrate their internal knowledge when exposed to new information. Our study provides the first quantitative framework for monitoring and mitigating belief drift in downstream applications, thereby enhancing the reliability and interpretability of language‑model‑driven systems.
2902:
Accurate forecasting of time‑series data is indispensable in high‑stakes fields such as energy, healthcare, and climate science. Despite recent progress, most existing methods still treat prediction as a one‑shot, static mapping problem, devoid of the interactive reasoning and adaptive flexibility that human experts bring. This shortfall hampers their deployment in complex, real‑world settings. To bridge this divide, we introduce **AlphaCast**, a human‑wisdom–enhanced large‑language‑model (LLM) co‑reasoning architecture that reconceptualizes forecasting as a collaborative, iterative process. AlphaCast operates in two phases:

1. **Automated Preparation** – It constructs a multi‑source cognitive base that includes a feature set encapsulating key statistical and temporal patterns, a domain knowledge repository distilled from text corpora and historical series, a contextual cache that stores rich information for each time window, and a case base that retrieves optimal strategies through pattern clustering and matching.

2. **Generative Reasoning & Reflective Optimization** – Leveraging these resources, AlphaCast blends temporal features, domain knowledge, context, and forecasting strategies to initiate a meta‑reasoning loop that continuously self‑corrects and refines its approach.

Across a suite of short‑ and long‑term forecasting benchmarks, AlphaCast consistently outperforms leading baselines in predictive accuracy. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/SkyeGT/AlphaCast_Official.
2903: Reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms routinely suffer from slow convergence and brittle performance when deployed in complex environments.  We introduce **RLoop**, a self‑improving framework that iteratively refines policy initialization to accelerate learning and enhance generalization.  At the core of RLoop is a nested two‑stage loop: (i) an *outer* loop that samples a set of high‑value trajectories using the current policy, and then trains a **policy seed** network by supervised imitation of these trajectories; (ii) an *inner* loop that performs standard RL optimization (e.g., PPO, SAC) starting from the seed.  The policy seed is continuously updated via a weighted blend of the best seeds from previous iterations, yielding an initialization that progressively encodes richer task knowledge.  We prove that under mild assumptions the RLoop procedure monotonically improves the expected return of the inner policy, and we provide bounds on the sample complexity reduction relative to vanilla RL.  Empirically, RLoop achieves state‑of‑the‑art performance across a suite of continuous‑control tasks (MuJoCo), discrete control benchmarks (Atari), and a novel multi‑task locomotion benchmark.  On average, it requires 3–5× fewer environment interactions to reach the same target return and exhibits superior robustness to hyper‑parameter perturbations.  Furthermore, the learned policy seeds transfer seamlessly to unseen tasks, demonstrating that RLoop’s iterative policy initialization acts as an effective meta‑learning signal.  Our results suggest that embedding self‑improving initialization loops into RL pipelines can substantially lower the barrier to deployment in real‑world settings.
2904:
The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) has intensified the need for robust methods to trace model provenance, detect unauthorized derivatives, and preserve intellectual‑property rights. Existing attribution techniques largely rely on metadata or heuristic checks on public weights, which can be obfuscated or removed by model owners. We introduce **SVD‑Fingerprint**, a principled, model‑agnostic fingerprinting framework that captures the latent “ghost” of a transformer’s training lineage through the singular value decomposition (SVD) of its weight matrices. By aggregating the spectrum of key attention and feed‑forward layers into a compact vector and normalising across model architectures, SVD‑Fingerprint preserves discriminative information even after fine‑tuning, pruning, or quantisation.

We evaluate the method on a benchmark of 36 transformer models spanning the GPT, LLaMA, and BLOOM families, including 24 fine‑tuned variants. Across a 10‑fold cross‑validation protocol, SVD‑Fingerprint achieves an accuracy of **97.6 %** in identifying the base model of a query network and **94.3 %** in recovering the fine‑tuning dataset when compared to state‑of‑the‑art gradient‑based and hash‑based baselines. Ablation studies confirm that the fingerprint is resilient to common post‑processing operations, and a transfer‑learning experiment demonstrates its applicability to unseen architectures.

Our results reveal that the singular‑value spectra encode a persistent “signature” of the optimisation trajectory and data distribution, enabling reliable lineage tracing with minimal computational overhead. This work paves the way for transparent model supply chains, aids in detecting model misuse, and provides a foundation for future research on provenance in deep neural networks.
2905: Language models (LMs) have achieved remarkable performance across a variety of reasoning tasks, yet their internal decision‑making processes remain opaque and prone to hallucination. Motivated by human metacognition—where thinking is coupled with continuous monitoring, generation, and verification—we formalise a principled *Monitor‑Generate‑Verify* (MGV) framework that endows LLMs with self‑aware reasoning capabilities. In MGV, a *monitor* module first evaluates a problem statement and predicts the most suitable reasoning strategy, allocating computational resources accordingly. The *generate* module then produces a provisional answer using a tailored chain‑of‑thought or retrieval‑augmented approach, while the *verify* module cross‑checks the output against logical consistency, factual accuracy, and resource‑based heuristics, potentially iterating back to generation for refinement. We instantiate each component with lightweight transformer heads, train them jointly under a curriculum that rewards calibrated confidence and correctness, and demonstrate that MGV can be applied to any off‑the‑shelf large language model without architectural changes. Experiments on 12 benchmark datasets—including arithmetic reasoning, commonsense inference, and code synthesis—show that MGV improves accuracy by 8–12 % relative to baseline LMs while reducing hallucinations by over 30 %. Moreover, ablation studies reveal that the monitor’s strategy predictions are highly predictive of downstream success, and that iterative verification cycles converge rapidly in most cases. The MGV framework offers a formal bridge between cognitive theory and machine reasoning, providing a modular, interpretable, and scalable path toward more reliable language model applications.
2906: Large Language Models augmented with retrieval, known as Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG), have achieved impressive results on knowledge‑intensive tasks. Yet, when the retrieved evidence is incomplete, the generated reasoning often collapses, creating gaps that undermine the output. To address this shortfall, we turn to *abductive inference*—the construction of plausible missing premises that reconcile the observed facts. In this paper, we present a framework that embeds abductive inference within RAG pipelines. Our approach first identifies where evidence is lacking, then proposes candidate premises, and finally verifies them via consistency and plausibility checks. Evaluation on abductive reasoning datasets and multi‑hop question‑answering benchmarks demonstrates that the method enhances both answer accuracy and the faithfulness of the generated reasoning. These results suggest that abductive inference is a valuable avenue for boosting the robustness and interpretability of retrieval‑augmented language‑model systems.
2907:
In distributed environments where software agents autonomously perform tasks on behalf of users, granting and revoking permissions is a persistent challenge. Traditional access‑control models require agents to be pre‑configured with a fixed set of capabilities, leading to either over‑privileged access or brittle task failure. We propose **Delegated Authorization for Agents Constrained to Semantic Task‑to‑Scope Matching (DA‑STSM)**, a framework that dynamically negotiates fine‑grained permissions based on semantic compatibility between a task’s requirements and an agent’s available scopes. DA‑STSM introduces a lightweight policy language that expresses constraints in terms of ontologically enriched task descriptors and resource scopes. A runtime inference engine matches the semantics of a requested operation against the agent’s declared competencies, yielding a context‑aware delegation decision that preserves the principle of least privilege.

We formalise the problem as a constrained bipartite matching, provide a sound and complete algorithm that exploits subsumption hierarchies to prune infeasible matches, and prove its polynomial‑time complexity in practical settings. Extensive evaluation on two representative domains— (i) cloud‑based micro‑services orchestration and (ii) smart‑building control—demonstrates that DA‑STSM reduces permission churn by 47 % and task success rates by 12 % compared with static role‑based and attribute‑based access control. Furthermore, our prototype, integrated into an open‑source agent platform, exhibits negligible overhead (< 3 ms per delegation decision).

DA‑STSM offers a principled, semantic‑aware mechanism for delegating authorization to autonomous agents, paving the way for more secure and adaptive task execution in dynamic, heterogeneous ecosystems.
2908: Liquid cooling is becoming indispensable for managing the heat of densely packed data centers, especially as AI workloads grow. To achieve higher energy efficiency and reliability—and thereby enhance sustainability—machine‑learning based control systems are indispensable. We introduce **LC‑Opt**, a benchmark environment that facilitates reinforcement‑learning (RL) research for energy‑efficient liquid cooling in high‑performance computing (HPC) facilities. LC‑Opt is built on a high‑fidelity digital twin of Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s Frontier supercomputer cooling infrastructure and offers a comprehensive, Modelica‑based end‑to‑end simulation—from site‑level cooling towers to individual IT cabinets and server blade clusters. RL agents can tune key thermal parameters—including liquid supply temperature, flow rate, fine‑grained valve actuation at the cabinet level, and cooling‑tower setpoints—via a Gymnasium interface while workloads fluctuate over time. This setting presents a multi‑objective real‑time optimization problem that balances local temperature regulation with overall energy consumption, and can incorporate additional subsystems such as a heat‑recovery unit (HRU). We evaluate both centralized and decentralized multi‑agent RL strategies, convert learned policies into interpretable decision trees and regression models, and investigate large‑language‑model (LLM) approaches that articulate control decisions in natural language within an agentic mesh architecture, aiming to build user trust and ease system administration. By making detailed, customizable liquid‑cooling models publicly available, LC‑Opt empowers the ML community, data‑center operators, and vendors to create and test sustainable liquid‑cooling control solutions.
2909: As AI agents become ubiquitous across industries, judging them only by infrastructural metrics—such as latency, time-to-first-token, or token throughput—is increasingly inadequate. Those numbers do not reflect the quality of an agent’s decisions, its level of autonomy, or the real business value it delivers. This white paper introduces a new, comprehensive set of eleven outcome‑based, task‑agnostic performance metrics that cross domain boundaries. The metrics are crafted to let organizations assess agents on decision quality, autonomy, adaptability, and tangible value, independent of underlying model architecture or specific applications. Among the proposed indicators are Goal Completion Rate (GCR), Autonomy Index (AIx), Multi‑Step Task Resilience (MTR), and Business Impact Efficiency (BIE). In a large‑scale simulation featuring four agent architectures—ReAct, Chain‑of‑Thought, Tool‑Augmented, and Hybrid—across five domains (Healthcare, Finance, Marketing, Legal, and Customer Service), we validate the framework. Results reveal clear trade‑offs among designs, with the Hybrid Agent consistently outperforming others, achieving an average GCR of 88.8 % and the highest Return on Investment (ROI). This work delivers a standardized, holistic methodology for AI‑agent evaluation, fostering more effective development, deployment, and governance.
2910: Self‑talk—an internal dialogue that can be heard only by the speaker or uttered aloud—plays a pivotal role in emotion regulation, cognitive processing, and motivation. Despite its importance, it remains largely invisible and hard to quantify in everyday life. Here we introduce *MutterMeter*, a mobile platform that automatically detects vocalized self‑talk using ear‑mounted microphones in natural environments. Capturing this phenomenon is difficult because self‑talk exhibits a wide range of acoustic signatures, incomplete semantics and grammar, and irregular timing, which violate the assumptions of standard speech‑recognition systems. To overcome these hurdles, *MutterMeter* adopts a hierarchical classification pipeline that incrementally fuses acoustic cues, linguistic content, and contextual signals, thereby striking a dynamic trade‑off between accuracy and computational load. We trained and tested the system on a novel corpus of 31.1 hours of audio from 25 participants. Results show that *MutterMeter* achieves a macro‑averaged F1 score of 0.84, surpassing baseline methods including large language‑model and speech‑emotion recognizers.
2911:
Large language models (LLMs) are being deployed more widely to support decisions in domains such as health, education, and law, and to model human behaviour.  Yet the extent to which they truly mimic how people actually decide remains unclear.  This uncertainty is significant: a mismatch can produce harmful real‑world effects, and if LLMs fail to capture human patterns they become ineffective for social simulations.  

In this work we close that gap by building a digital twin of classic game‑theoretic experiments and introducing a systematic prompting‑and‑probing framework for assessing machine behaviour.  We evaluate three open‑source models—Llama, Mistral and Qwen—finding that Llama replicates human cooperation dynamics with high fidelity, including the subtle deviations from pure rational choice theory that humans exhibit.  By contrast, Qwen’s outputs align more closely with Nash‑equilibrium predictions.  Importantly, we achieve population‑level behavioural replication without employing persona‑based prompts, thereby simplifying the simulation pipeline.  

Beyond reproducing known human data, we extend the framework to new game configurations outside the original parameter grid, generating and preregistering testable hypotheses for these uncharted scenarios.  Our results demonstrate that, once appropriately calibrated, LLMs can mirror aggregate human behaviour and serve as a systematic tool for exploring untested experimental spaces, complementing traditional social and behavioural science research by providing fresh empirical predictions about human social decision‑making.
2912:
–  
Single‑object tracking is tasked with locating a target in a video sequence using one or more reference signals, such as a bounding box, natural language description, or a combination of both, while the video can be captured in several modalities (RGB, RGB+Depth, RGB+Thermal, or RGB+Event). Each reference modality opens up distinct interaction channels, and each video modality is required in different operational contexts to improve tracking reliability. Existing solutions, however, are typically tailored to a specific subset of modalities, resulting in a fragmented model landscape that hampers real‑world deployment. A single, versatile tracker capable of handling all admissible combinations of reference and video modalities is therefore indispensable.

In this work we propose **UniSOT**, a unified single‑object tracker that accommodates any of the three reference modalities and any of the four video modalities using the same set of parameters. Extensive evaluations on eighteen public benchmarks—including visual tracking, vision‑language tracking, and RGB+X tracking—show that UniSOT consistently surpasses modality‑specific competitors. In particular, it achieves a gain of more than 3.0 % in AUC on the TNL2K dataset across all three reference modalities, and improves the primary metric by over 2.0 % compared with Un‑Track on all RGB+X video modalities.
2913:
Short‑video platforms have emerged as a pivotal medium in today’s internet ecosystem, where rapid information delivery and high interactivity are redefining how audiences engage with and spread culture. Among the many forms of interaction, comments are especially important for building community and sparking content remixing. Yet producing comments that both respect platform rules and display stylistic variety while staying context‑aware remains difficult.  

We propose **LOLOGRAPH**—a modular multi‑agent system for controllable short‑video comment generation. The framework combines video segmentation, contextual and affective analysis, and style‑aware prompt engineering. It can generate six distinct styles—puns (homophones), rhymes, meme references, sarcasm/irony, simple humor, and content extraction—by feeding a multimodal large language model (MLLM) with explicit prompt markers and a few illustrative examples.  

To facilitate research and evaluation, we built a bilingual dataset from the official APIs of Douyin (Chinese) and YouTube (English), featuring five popular video categories: comedy sketches, daily‑life jokes, funny animal footage, humorous commentary, and talk shows. Our assessment blends automated metrics (originality, relevance, style fidelity) with a large‑scale human preference study across 40 videos and 105 participants. LOLOGRAPH outperforms baseline models, securing user‑preferred rates of over 90 % on Douyin and 87.55 % on YouTube.  

This paper presents a scalable, culture‑adaptive framework for stylized comment generation on short‑video platforms, paving the way for richer user interaction and creative engagement.
2914:
For years, researchers in artificial intelligence have turned to poker-like games as a proving ground for environments that involve multiple players, hidden information, and decision‑making under uncertainty. Although recent systems have reached or surpassed human experts on no‑limit Texas Hold’em, these games rarely sustain sustained multi‑player interaction: most hands resolve after just a handful of rounds involving only two contestants.  

In this work we introduce **Solly**, the first AI to attain human‑class performance in a reduced‑format version of Liar’s Poker—a game that keeps many players actively involved throughout. Solly was trained via self‑play using a model‑free, actor‑critic deep reinforcement‑learning framework. It achieved an overall win rate exceeding 50 % and high equity in both heads‑up and multi‑player Liar’s Poker, outperforming large language models (LLMs), even those equipped with reasoning capabilities, on the same benchmarks.  

The agent discovered innovative bidding tactics, employed effective randomization, and proved resilient against world‑class human competitors.
2915:
Tree‑of‑Thought (ToT) reasoning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for decomposing complex language‑based tasks into structured sub‑problems. However, the exhaustive exploration of branching hypotheses that ToT affords quickly becomes computationally prohibitive, especially for large language models operating in real‑time or resource‑constrained environments. In this paper, we introduce **Chopping Trees**, a semantic‑similarity based dynamic pruning framework that selectively collapses redundant or irrelevant branches during ToT construction, thereby curbing the combinatorial explosion of reasoning paths.

Our method leverages contextualized embeddings to quantify semantic overlap between partially generated sub‑thoughts. A lightweight, differentiable similarity score is computed on‑the‑fly, and branches whose similarity exceeds a learned threshold are pruned with minimal impact on downstream reasoning quality. We integrate this pruning strategy into several state‑of‑the‑art ToT architectures and evaluate it on a suite of long‑form reasoning benchmarks, including GSM‑8K, MATH, and the OpenAI WebGPT dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that Chopping Trees reduces the average number of nodes by 45 % and inference latency by 38 % while preserving, and in some cases improving, final success rates (up to 1.2 % absolute gain on GSM‑8K). Ablation studies confirm that the semantic similarity criterion is more effective than heuristic depth‑ or probability‑based pruning. 

Chopping Trees offers a principled, data‑driven approach to efficient ToT reasoning and establishes a foundation for future work on adaptive, resource‑aware language‑model inference.
2916:
The field of video generation is undergoing a paradigm shift: instead of merely producing visually pleasing clips, researchers are now building virtual worlds that support interaction while preserving physical realism. These advances herald a new class of video foundation models that serve not only as generative engines but also as implicit world models—systems that can simulate physics, agent‑environment dynamics, and task planning for both real and imagined settings.  

This survey offers a systematic account of that evolution, framing contemporary video foundation models as comprising two fundamental parts: an implicit world model and a video renderer. The world model encodes structured knowledge—physical laws, interaction dynamics, and agent behavior—acting as a latent simulation engine that delivers coherent visual reasoning, long‑term temporal consistency, and goal‑oriented planning. The renderer converts this latent simulation into realistic visual outputs, presenting videos as “windows” into the simulated world.  

We chronicle the development of video generation across four generations, each building on the previous in terms of core capabilities, and culminating in a world model that integrates intrinsic physical plausibility, real‑time multimodal interaction, and multi‑scale planning. For each generation, we outline its defining attributes, showcase representative studies, and explore application areas such as robotics, autonomous driving, and interactive gaming. We conclude by addressing open challenges and design principles for next‑generation world models, emphasizing how agent intelligence can guide and assess these systems. An up‑to‑date repository of related work is available at this link.
2917:
Neural Theorem Proving (NTP) has rapidly emerged as a promising paradigm for integrating deep learning with formal logic reasoning. However, progress in the field has been hampered by the absence of a unified, research‑level evaluation protocol that captures both the logical soundness of generated proofs and the practical scalability of neural systems. In this work we introduce **RLMEval**—a comprehensive framework for evaluating NTP models on a wide spectrum of research‑grade reasoning tasks.

RLMEval comprises three key components: (i) a curated corpus of 15,000 logic problems drawn from synthetic, knowledge‑graph, and real‑world ontological sources, each annotated with gold proof trees and hierarchical difficulty levels; (ii) a standardized evaluation pipeline that measures success rates, proof length, search efficiency, and confidence calibration while enforcing strict soundness checks via automated proof‑checker back‑ends; and (iii) an open‑source benchmark suite that supports plug‑in evaluation of existing NTP architectures (e.g., Neural Theorem Prover, Prolog‑based neural models, and transformer‑augmented reasoning agents).

Using RLMEval we benchmark several state‑of‑the‑art NTPs, revealing systematic gaps: while models achieve near‑perfect accuracy on shallow, deterministic tasks, they falter on problems requiring multi‑step inductive reasoning or handling large knowledge bases. We further demonstrate that reinforcement‑learning‑based search strategies can significantly improve proof discovery rates, yet at the cost of increased computational overhead. Our results underscore the need for more robust training objectives and explainability mechanisms in neural reasoning systems.

RLMEval is released as an open‑source package with a public leaderboard, inviting the community to rigorously compare, reproduce, and surpass existing approaches. By providing a unified, reproducible, and scalable evaluation platform, we aim to accelerate the transition of NTP from proof‑of‑concept experiments to research‑level reasoning engines capable of tackling real‑world logical challenges.
2918: Training and education in human‑centered domains demand authentic experiential practice, yet realistic models of human behaviour have been scarce. Here we introduce a multi‑agent psychological simulation framework that constructs believable human actions by representing and interrelating core cognitive‑affective processes. Unlike opaque neural‑network approaches, our design is anchored in well‑established psychological concepts—such as self‑efficacy, growth mindset, and social constructivism—and implements an explicit “inner parliament” of agents that embody these factors. Through deliberation and interaction among these agents, the system derives its behavioural outputs, offering unparalleled transparency and fidelity to human psychological dynamics. We outline the architecture and theoretical underpinnings of the framework, demonstrate its application in teacher training and academic research, and highlight how it operationalises key ideas from social learning, cognitive apprenticeship, deliberate practice, and meta‑cognition.
2919:
In recent decades, rapid urban growth has exacerbated traffic congestion as the flow of people and goods rises. To counter this, transportation planning is moving from demand‑driven approaches to supply‑oriented strategies, making Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) indispensable for managing existing road networks. A pivotal ITS capability is traffic forecasting, which informs proactive actions such as ramp metering, signal timing, and dynamic routing (e.g., via Google Maps).

This paper evaluates the predictive accuracy of statistical, machine‑learning (ML), and deep‑learning (DL) models for forecasting traffic speed and flow on California’s Harbor Freeway, using real‑time data from the Caltrans Performance Measurement System (PeMS). Each model was tested over 20 lead times, ranging up to 1 hour 40 minutes, and assessed with RMSE, MAE, and R² metrics. 

Results indicate that ANFIS‑GP delivers the best short‑term performance, achieving an RMSE of 0.038, MAE of 0.0276, and R² of 0.9983 for the earliest horizon. For medium‑term horizons, the Bi‑LSTM excels, benefiting from its ability to capture long‑range temporal dependencies; it records an RMSE of 0.1863, MAE of 0.0833, and R² of 0.987 at a 20‑minute forecast. Model robustness was quantified by examining the slope of the logarithmic decay of error metrics over time. Among DL models, Bi‑LSTM showed the most gradual performance decline (slope 0.0454 for RMSE and 0.0545 for MAE on flow), whereas ANFIS‑GP exhibited steeper slopes (0.1058 RMSE, 0.1037 MAE).

The study concludes that hybrid approaches—combining strengths of multiple modeling paradigms—represent a promising avenue for further improving traffic prediction accuracy.
2920:
Large language models struggle with long‑context reasoning: many documents exceed their fixed‑size context windows, and even when a passage fits, performance worsens as the sequence length grows. Consequently, LLMs are routinely paired with external memory systems. Existing techniques—ranging from retrieval with semantic embeddings to increasingly elaborate knowledge‑graph representations—are geared toward fact‑based lookup and do not capture the time‑anchored, narrative structures needed to keep track of entities as they participate in episodic events.  

To address this limitation, we introduce the **Generative Semantic Workspace (GSW)**, a neuro‑inspired generative memory framework that builds structured, interpretable depictions of evolving situations, enabling LLMs to reason over changing roles, actions, and spatiotemporal contexts. GSW is composed of an **Operator** that translates incoming observations into intermediate semantic structures, and a **Reconciler** that fuses these into a persistent workspace, enforcing temporal, spatial, and logical coherence.  

On the Episodic Memory Benchmark (EpBench) \cite{huet_episodic_2025}, which includes corpora from 100 k to 1 M tokens, GSW outperforms existing Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) baselines by up to **20 %**. It also achieves remarkable efficiency, cutting query‑time context tokens by **51 %** relative to the next most token‑efficient baseline, thereby reducing inference‑time costs dramatically. More broadly, GSW offers a concrete blueprint for equipping LLMs with human‑like episodic memory, paving the way for agents capable of reasoning over extended horizons.
2921:
Multimodal large‑language models (LLMs) now fuse vision and language, enabling users to query visual content through natural language. Yet little is understood about *why* a user chooses to provide an image, a textual description, or both, and how the model’s reasoning adapts to that choice. In this work we ask: **“To see or to read?”**—how do users decide which modality to invoke, and how can multimodal LLMs infer and respond to this implicit intent?  

We introduce **M‑USER**, a large, fine‑grained dataset of 120k real‑world interactions with four flagship multimodal LLMs (e.g., GPT‑4V, Claude‑Vision, LLaVA, and BLIP‑Chat). Each interaction is annotated with the user’s modality choice, the context that prompted it, and a fine‑grained reasoning trace of the model’s internal state (attention maps, prompt embeddings). Using this resource we formalize user‑behavior reasoning as a joint multimodal inference problem: given a query and a partial modality cue (image or text), predict the user’s modality selection and the optimal response strategy.  

We propose **Modality‑Aware Reasoning Networks (MARN)**, a transformer‑based architecture that jointly encodes user prompts and visual context, learns a policy over modality‑specific sub‑tasks, and dynamically adjusts attention to either the vision or language stream. Extensive experiments on M‑USER demonstrate that MARN outperforms strong baselines (pure‑vision, pure‑text, and simple concatenation models) by 8.5% in modality‑prediction accuracy and by 15.3% in task‑completion BLEU scores. Ablation studies confirm that the policy component is pivotal for aligning model inference with user intent.  

Our findings reveal systematic patterns—e.g., users provide images for ambiguous spatial queries and text for abstract reasoning—suggesting that multimodal LLMs should adapt not only to the *content* of a query but also to the *user’s interaction strategy*. This work lays the groundwork for more user‑centric multimodal interfaces, and the M‑USER benchmark will spur further research into behavioral reasoning in next‑generation LLMs.
2922:
Kolmogorov–Arnold networks (KANs) provide a theoretically grounded neural‐network architecture for representing high‑dimensional functions with a minimal number of parameters. In many scientific computing applications—e.g., solving partial differential equations (PDEs) or emulating complex dynamical systems—KANs are trained on a spatial grid that discretizes the domain. A fine grid yields accurate predictions but incurs prohibitive memory and training costs, whereas a coarse grid is computationally efficient but can miss critical features such as sharp gradients or localized structures. This paper introduces **Layer‑Histogram Adaptive Grid Refinement (LH‑AGR)**, a principled, data‑driven algorithm that automatically updates the underlying spatial grid during KAN training by exploiting histograms of layer‑wise activations and weight distributions.

The core idea is to treat each layer of a KAN as a feature extractor whose statistical signature (the histogram of absolute activations) encodes the local complexity of the learned function. By comparing the histograms of successive epochs, LH‑AGR identifies regions of the grid where the network’s representation is either over‑ or under‑resolved. A lightweight refinement module then inserts new grid points in high‑variance zones and coarsens sparsely activated areas, while preserving continuity through spline‑based interpolation of the KAN’s weight tensors. Importantly, the refinement operates in tandem with the training loop, requiring only a single forward pass per epoch and a negligible overhead (< 1 % of training time).

We evaluate LH‑AGR on benchmark problems including the 2‑D Burgers equation, a high‑dimensional option‑pricing model, and a turbulent flow dataset. Across all tests, the adaptive grids reduce the required number of points by 30–55 % while maintaining, and often improving, test‑time prediction error (relative L₂ error drops from 4.8 % to 2.1 % on Burgers). Moreover, the approach automatically discovers multi‑scale structures (e.g., shock fronts) without any hand‑tuned refinement criteria. Ablation studies confirm that the histogram‑based trigger outperforms naïve variance or gradient‑based selectors, and that the adaptive refinement converges within a modest number of epochs.  

Our results demonstrate that LH‑AGR enables efficient, scalable KAN training on large‑scale scientific problems, opening a path toward truly automated, high‑fidelity surrogate modeling in computational physics and engineering.
2923: We introduce **Gaperon**, a fully open‑source suite of French‑English coding language models aimed at enhancing transparency and reproducibility in large‑scale training. The family comprises 1.5 B, 8 B, and 24 B parameter models trained on 2–4 trillion tokens, and we release every component of the training pipeline: neural‑quality filtered French and English corpora, a streamlined data curation and training framework, and a wealth of intermediate checkpoints. Our experiments probe how data filtering and contamination influence both benchmark accuracy and generative capability. We observe that stricter linguistic filtering improves fluency and coherence, yet lowers benchmark scores; conversely, intentional late‑stage contamination—continuing training with test‑set‑mixed data—recovers competitive scores while only modestly degrading generation quality. We also show that standard neural filtering can inadvertently magnify benchmark leakage. To facilitate safety research, we provide a benign data‑poisoning protocol during pretraining, creating a realistic sandbox for robustness studies. By publishing all models, datasets, code, and checkpoints, Gaperon establishes a reproducible baseline for examining the trade‑offs among data curation, evaluation, safety, and openness in multilingual language‑model development.
2924:
Recent work has shown that fine‑tuning a pre‑trained vision transformer in a sequential manner (SeqFT), followed by a refinement step that exploits approximate class‑feature distributions, can be an effective approach to class‑incremental learning (CIL).  Unfortunately, the continual optimisation of the shared backbone introduces a distribution shift between the representations of previously seen classes and the updated model, which gradually erodes classifier accuracy.

To counter this, we propose a latent‑space transition operator and a new framework called Sequential Learning with Drift Compensation (SLDC).  SLDC actively aligns the feature distributions of successive tasks, thereby reducing drift.  The first variant is a purely linear version that learns an operator by solving a regularised least‑squares problem mapping features before and after fine‑tuning.  The second variant employs a weakly nonlinear mapping that sits between a strict linear transform and a fully flexible nonlinear model, striking a balance between expressiveness and generalisation.  In both cases we further mitigate representation drift by incorporating knowledge distillation.

Extensive evaluations on standard CIL benchmarks confirm that SLDC markedly enhances SeqFT.  When combined with knowledge distillation, SeqFT achieves performance that is on par with joint training across all datasets tested.  Code is available at https://github.com/raoxuan98-hash/sldc.git.
2925: Deep learning practitioners frequently encounter a bewildering array of output layer configurations and corresponding loss functions, yet a systematic understanding of their interplay remains fragmented in most introductory texts. In **DL101 Neural Network Outputs and Loss Functions** we present a unified framework that demystifies this relationship, positioning it at the core of model design for regression, binary and multi‑class classification, ranking, and structured prediction tasks. We first formalise the role of output activations—linear, sigmoid, softmax, and logits—in shaping the probability space or value range of predictions. We then catalog the most commonly used loss functions (MSE, MAE, binary cross‑entropy, categorical cross‑entropy, hinge, focal, and Kullback‑Leibler) and provide rigorous derivations of their gradients, elucidating why specific pairings (e.g., softmax+cross‑entropy) yield stable training dynamics. Through a series of controlled experiments on MNIST, CIFAR‑10 and a synthetic regression dataset, we quantify how mismatched output–loss combinations can induce vanishing gradients, poor calibration, and sub‑optimal generalisation. Finally, we distill practical guidelines for selecting loss–output pairs based on task requirements, data distribution, and numerical considerations. This concise yet comprehensive survey equips newcomers and seasoned researchers alike with a clear decision‑making map for configuring neural network outputs and losses, thereby accelerating prototype development and improving reproducibility in deep learning pipelines.
2926:
Fine‑tuning large pretrained neural networks on downstream tasks remains a major computational bottleneck, both in terms of memory footprint and runtime.  Conventional adapter or prompt‑tuning schemes add a dense set of task‑specific parameters that often scale linearly with model size, thereby limiting scalability to multi‑task or continual‑learning scenarios.  We propose **TuckA** (Hierarchical Compact Tensor Experts), a novel fine‑tuning framework that leverages *hierarchical Tucker factorization* to compress each adapter into a set of low‑rank tensor “experts” whose dimensions are shared across layers and tasks.  TuckA first decomposes the weight tensors of a standard feed‑forward layer into core tensors and factor matrices arranged in a tree‑structured hierarchy; the tree depth is chosen to balance expressivity and compression.  Task‑specific knowledge is injected by learning a small set of *expert coefficients* that linearly combine the shared factors, thereby reducing the number of trainable parameters from \(O(d^2)\) to \(O(rd + r^2)\) where \(d\) is the hidden dimension and \(r \ll d\) the Tucker rank.  We further introduce a *hierarchical gating* mechanism that activates only a subset of experts per token, yielding dynamic sparsity and further speed‑ups.

Extensive experiments on the GLUE benchmark, the Vision‑and‑Language “VQA‑V4” dataset, and a continual‑learning curriculum demonstrate that TuckA attains within‑1.5 % of full‑model fine‑tuning accuracy while reducing parameter count by up to 7× and inference latency by 3–4×.  Ablation studies confirm that the hierarchical structure is critical for preserving task diversity, and theoretical analysis shows that the proposed compression preserves the expressive power of the original adapters up to an error bounded by the neglected singular values of the tensor cores.  TuckA thus offers a principled, scalable, and efficient alternative to existing fine‑tuning paradigms, enabling rapid deployment of large models across many tasks with limited resources.
2927: Reasoning is a foundational capability in artificial intelligence, yet most benchmarks demand increasingly long and complex chains of thought (CoT). A central open problem is whether a model that has learned to reason can generalize these patterns to more difficult tasks requiring longer CoT sequences. In this paper we give a rigorous analysis of transformer learning on synthetic state‑tracking problems using gradient descent. We show that the algebraic structure of these problems determines how well a transformer can extrapolate its CoT to longer contexts. Our theory describes length generalization in terms of *attention concentration*: the degree to which the attention layer reliably retrieves the necessary states is tightly linked to the task’s state‑tracking structure. When a transformer is restricted to a short reasoning window, we prove that a recursive self‑training strategy can incrementally extend the solvable problem length. This yields the first optimisation guarantee that constant‑depth transformers can learn $\mathsf{NC}^1$‑complete problems via CoT—surpassing prior results that were limited to $\mathsf{TC}^0$, unless the widely believed separation $\mathsf{TC}^0 \neq \mathsf{NC}^1$ is false. Extensive experiments corroborate our theoretical predictions, demonstrating the predicted length generalization and revealing the role of attention concentration in successful reasoning.
2928:
Handling missing observations remains one of the most pressing obstacles in contemporary data science, obstructing reliable analysis and sound decision‐making across domains ranging from healthcare and bioinformatics to social science, e‑commerce, and industrial monitoring. Although a rich body of work on imputation has emerged over the past several decades, the field is still highly fragmented, with many disciplines operating in silos and lacking a unified view that bridges statistical theory and the latest machine‑learning techniques. 

In this article we perform a systematic review of the fundamental ideas surrounding missing data—mechanisms of missingness, the trade‑off between single and multiple imputation, and the objectives of different imputation tasks—and we map these concepts onto problem settings encountered in diverse applications. We organize the vast landscape of imputation strategies into a taxonomy that includes classical methods such as regression and the EM algorithm, matrix‑completion variants (low‑rank and high‑rank), and contemporary deep‑learning based approaches (auto‑encoders, GANs, diffusion models, graph neural networks) as well as the emerging role of large language models. Special emphasis is placed on techniques tailored to complex data structures, including tensors, time‑series, streaming streams, graph‑structured data, categorical variables, and multimodal collections. 

Beyond the imputation stage itself, we examine how missingness handling interacts with downstream analytical tasks—classification, clustering, anomaly detection—exploring both sequential pipelines and joint optimisation frameworks. We also scrutinise the theoretical properties of these methods, the availability of benchmark datasets, and the suite of evaluation metrics. Finally, we outline the major open challenges and prospective research directions: robust model and hyper‑parameter selection, privacy‑preserving imputation through federated learning, and the development of broadly generalisable models capable of adapting to a variety of domains and data types. This survey therefore offers a comprehensive roadmap for future investigations into missing data methodology.
2929:
The swift rise of large language models (LLMs) has amplified the demand for evaluation that is both domain‑ and culture‑specific. Current benchmarks are largely English‑centric and agnostic to particular fields, which hampers their relevance to India‑focused settings. To close this gap, we present **BhashaBench V1**, the first bilingual, multi‑task benchmark that targets core Indic knowledge systems. The benchmark contains **74,166 carefully curated question‑answer pairs**, split into **52,494 English** and **21,672 Hindi** items drawn from authentic government and specialty exams. It covers four principal domains—Agriculture, Legal, Finance, and Ayurveda—encompassing more than 90 subdomains and over 500 topics, enabling fine‑grained analysis.

We evaluate **over 29 LLMs** on BhashaBench V1 and uncover pronounced performance gaps that are both domain‑ and language‑specific, particularly in low‑resource areas. For example, GPT‑4o scores **76.49 %** in Legal but drops to **59.74 %** in Ayurveda. Across the board, models excel on English data while consistently lagging on Hindi. Sub‑domain diagnostics reveal that topics such as Cyber Law and International Finance perform relatively well, whereas Panchakarma, Seed Science, and Human Rights remain weak.

BhashaBench V1 therefore offers a comprehensive, publicly accessible resource for probing LLMs’ ability to integrate specialized knowledge and bilingual comprehension within India’s diverse domains. All code, data, and supplementary materials are released for open research.
2930:
Generalized eigenvalue problems (GEPs) \(A\mathbf{x}=\lambda B\mathbf{x}\) arise in a wide spectrum of scientific and engineering applications, yet their large‑scale solution remains computationally demanding. Contour‑integration based eigensolvers, such as FEAST and Sakurai–Sugiura, provide a promising avenue by projecting the problem onto low‑dimensional subspaces defined by complex contours in the spectral plane. However, the efficiency of these methods hinges critically on the choice of the integration contour: suboptimal contours lead to slow convergence, excessive sampling, or missed eigenvalues.  

In this work we introduce **DeepContour**, a hybrid deep‑learning framework that learns to design optimal integration contours for GEPs from the spectral features of the underlying matrices.  A lightweight convolutional encoder extracts structural and spectral descriptors from the input pencil \((A,B)\), while a graph‑neural‑network decoder predicts a set of contour nodes in the complex plane.  The predicted contours are then fed into a modified FEAST routine that performs subspace iteration on the projected pencil, yielding high‑accuracy eigenvalues within a reduced number of quadrature points.  During training we employ a self‑supervised loss that encourages contour tightness around target eigenvalue clusters while penalizing overlap with the resolvent norm, thereby enforcing numerical stability.  

We evaluate DeepContour on a diverse collection of benchmark matrices—including sparse Hamiltonians from quantum chemistry, elasticity operators from structural dynamics, and discretized PDE eigenproblems—covering sizes up to \(10^6\) degrees of freedom.  Compared with state‑of‑the‑art contour selection heuristics, DeepContour reduces the total number of contour evaluations by 35–55 % and the overall runtime by 25–40 % while maintaining machine‑precision eigenvalue accuracy.  We further demonstrate that the learned contour policy generalizes across matrix families and scales gracefully with problem dimension.  

DeepContour establishes a new paradigm for accelerating contour‑based GEP solvers: a data‑driven, end‑to‑end pipeline that couples spectral learning with classical numerical integration, opening avenues for real‑time eigenanalysis in large‑scale scientific simulations.
2931:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning and language‑generation capabilities, yet their utility in the physical world remains largely unexplored.  In this work we investigate whether LLMs can *directly manipulate physical devices* to play *virtual reality (VR) games*, thereby bridging natural‑language understanding with embodied action.  We introduce **ComboBench**, the first end‑to‑end benchmark that couples an LLM with a physical hardware stack—including a haptic controller, depth‑camera, and a Unity‑based VR environment—to evaluate the model’s ability to interpret game state, generate control signals, and refine actions based on real‑time sensor feedback.  

ComboBench comprises 30 VR tasks ranging from simple navigation to complex cooperative play, each annotated with a ground‑truth sequence of device commands and a set of performance metrics (task completion, latency, and resource efficiency).  We develop a lightweight interface that streams perceptual observations (RGB‑depth + controller telemetry) to the LLM and feeds back the model’s textual command plan to a robotic actuator controller.  Baselines using GPT‑4, LLaMA‑2, and instruction‑tuned GPT‑3.5 are evaluated under both *zero‑shot* and *few‑shot* settings, with and without a multimodal adapter that converts raw sensor streams to structured prompts.  

Our results show that while LLMs can successfully complete 58 % of the tasks in a zero‑shot setting, incorporating chain‑of‑thought reasoning and fine‑tuned multimodal prompts boosts performance to 82 %.  However, the models still exhibit a 0.32 s planning‑to‑execution lag and struggle with continuous, high‑frequency control required for fast‑paced games.  We discuss the implications for embodied AI, safety constraints, and future directions toward truly autonomous, multimodal agents that can play VR games—or, more broadly, interact with physical devices—using only natural‑language instructions.
2932:
Continuous Integration (CI) remains a foundational practice in modern collaborative software development, and a plethora of CI platforms exist today. Because of varying maintenance costs, reliability, and the depth of integration with code‑hosting services, developers often switch between CI systems. A critical part of such a migration is translating CI configuration files—a difficult task owing to their inherent complexity and the semantic differences that must be reconciled across platforms.  

With the rise of large language models (LLMs), recent work has begun to investigate their use for CI configuration translation. In this study we focus on migrating from Travis CI to GitHub Actions using LLMs. By analysing 811 real‑world migration records we quantify the effort involved: developers read on average 38 lines of a Travis file and write about 58 lines of GitHub Actions, and almost half the migrations span multiple commits. We evaluate the translations produced by four LLMs and identify 1,121 issues, which cluster into four categories—logic inconsistencies (38 %), platform discrepancies (32 %), environment errors (25 %), and syntax errors (5 %). Finally, we test three enhancement strategies and find that a combination of a guideline‑based prompt and iterative refinement delivers the best performance, achieving a build success rate of 75.5 %—nearly a three‑fold improvement over GPT‑4o with a plain prompt.
2933: We present **KAN‑GCN**, a high‑performance, highly accurate surrogate for ice‑sheet dynamics that begins with a Kolmogorov‑Arnold Network (KAN) to calibrate features before applying graph convolutional networks (GCNs). The KAN front‑end learns one‑dimensional warping functions and a subsequent linear mix, which enhances feature conditioning and non‑linear representation without adding depth to the message‑passing stage. Using this design we build emulators for numerical ice‑sheet models and train them on 36 melt‑rate simulations at three different mesh resolutions for Pine Island Glacier, Antarctica. Across two‑to‑five‑layer models, KAN‑GCN matches or outperforms baseline GCN and MLP‑GCN emulators. Although it adds a modest number of parameters, KAN‑GCN boosts inference speed on coarser meshes by replacing an edge‑wise message‑passing layer with a node‑wise transform; only the finest mesh shows a slight overhead. In sum, placing a KAN at the front of the network delivers a compelling accuracy‑versus‑efficiency balance for large‑scale transient scenario sweeps.
2934:
Tiny object detection in aerial imagery is hampered by extreme scale variation, severe class imbalance, and the scarcity of high‑resolution training data. Conventional detectors typically rely on a single fixed‑scale backbone or a naïve feature pyramid, which often fails to preserve fine‑grained details necessary for spotting small targets such as vehicles, people, or aircraft. In this work we propose a **Scale‑Aware Relay (SAR)** module and a **Scale‑Adaptive Loss (SAL)** that together address these limitations.

The SAR module fuses multi‑level feature maps through a lightweight, learnable relay network that explicitly propagates low‑frequency context from higher‑resolution stages to the deepest layers, while preserving high‑frequency cues critical for small‑object localization. Unlike standard feature pyramids, the relay operates in a top‑down manner and employs adaptive gating conditioned on the estimated scale of each detection, thereby reducing unnecessary feature mixing that dilutes fine details.

The SAL is a novel loss formulation that weighs classification and regression errors according to the predicted object scale. By assigning larger gradients to tiny instances and diminishing the impact of large‑scale negatives, SAL mitigates the imbalance problem without requiring hard‑negative mining or explicit anchor design.

We evaluate our framework on three challenging aerial datasets—VisDrone, UAVDT, and DOTA—using the same ResNet‑50 backbone across all experiments. Our method improves the average precision for objects smaller than 8 px by 5.8 mAP points over baseline RetinaNet, and achieves a new state‑of‑the‑art 12.4 mAP on VisDrone’s tiny‑object subset. Ablation studies confirm the complementary contributions of SAR and SAL, and the overall system runs at 35 fps on a single RTX 3080. These results demonstrate that scale‑aware relaying and scale‑adaptive loss jointly enable robust detection of ultra‑tiny objects in high‑resolution aerial imagery.
2935:
Cardiac ultrasound (US) remains the principal imaging modality for assessing heart function, yet its reliability is hampered by operator skill, time pressures, and human error. The scarcity of trained sonographers—especially in rural and underserved regions—exacerbates this problem, underscoring the demand for fully automated, reproducible imaging solutions that are independent of user expertise and location. While recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly deep reinforcement learning (DRL), have opened the door to autonomous decision‑making, current DRL‑based scanners suffer from poor reproducibility, depend on proprietary datasets, and employ oversimplified models. 

We introduce the first end‑to‑end framework that marries generative AI with DRL to achieve autonomous, reliable cardiac US scanning. The system consists of two integrated modules:  

1. **Conditional generative simulator** – a hybrid of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) that synthesises realistic, action‑conditioned ultrasound frames, thereby modelling the cardiac imaging environment.  
2. **DRL controller** – a policy‑learning component that exploits the simulator to acquire accurate, operator‑free scanning trajectories.  

Both modules are validated against expert‑annotated image‑type classifiers and quality‑assessment metrics, ensuring clinically trustworthy guidance. The generative engine also permits conditional synthesis of high‑fidelity US images, forming a reproducible basis that can be extended to other organ systems. To promote transparency, we release a public repository of real cardiac US scans. Experiments confirm that the VAE‑GAN outperforms existing GAN variants on both qualitative and quantitative criteria, while the DRL‑driven scanner demonstrates robust performance across multiple configurations.
2936: The rapid growth of complex engineering problems demands design automation that can intelligently explore vast design spaces while respecting domain‑specific rules and performance constraints. We propose a **Knowledge‑Guided Multi‑Agent Framework (KG‑MAF)** that couples principled knowledge representation with collaborative agent reasoning to achieve autonomous engineering design. A central knowledge graph encodes design rules, material databases, and performance heuristics; it is continuously refined by the agents through experience. Three cooperating agents—(i) a *Design Agent* that generates candidate topologies, (ii) an *Evaluation Agent* that predicts functional metrics via surrogate models, and (iii) an *Optimization Agent* that navigates the Pareto frontier using a reinforcement‑learning policy—operate in a closed loop, exchanging proposals and constraints through the shared knowledge graph. Experiments on canonical structural and aerodynamic benchmark problems (e.g., truss topology optimization, airfoil design) demonstrate that KG‑MAF attains competitive or superior performance to state‑of‑the‑art evolutionary and gradient‑based methods while reducing the number of expensive simulations by up to 45 %. Our results illustrate that embedding expert knowledge within a multi‑agent ecosystem yields a scalable, interpretable pathway toward fully autonomous engineering design.
2937:
LiDAR sensors are pivotal for autonomous perception, yet their native spatial resolution remains a bottleneck for fine‑grained tasks such as object delineation and semantic segmentation. Conventional super‑resolution (SR) methods either rely on heavy deep networks that violate real‑time constraints or produce over‑smooth reconstructions that miss high‑frequency geometric details. To address this dichotomy, we propose **Real‑Time LiDAR Super‑Resolution via Frequency‑Aware Multi‑Scale Fusion (FAMSF)**, a lightweight yet expressive framework that reconstructs dense point clouds directly from sparse laser returns while preserving sharp structural cues.

FAMSF operates in the spherical projection domain, where raw LiDAR data is first decomposed into multiple frequency bands using a learnable Fourier‑style filter bank. Each band captures complementary spatial scales: the low‑frequency component encodes global scene layout, while the high‑frequency part preserves fine‑scale edge and corner information. These representations are processed in parallel by shallow multi‑scale convolutional blocks and then fused through a gated attention mechanism that adaptively weighs frequency contributions per spatial location. The fused feature map is finally decoded back into a dense 3‑D point cloud by a lightweight upsampling network that guarantees sub‑millisecond inference on commodity GPUs.

Extensive experiments on the KITTI, nuScenes, and Waymo Open datasets demonstrate that FAMSF attains a 2.8× increase in mean point density and a 15.4% improvement in point‑wise Chamfer distance over state‑of‑the‑art LiDAR SR baselines, while sustaining 25 fps on a single RTX 3090. Ablation studies confirm that both frequency‑aware decomposition and multi‑scale fusion are critical for recovering high‑frequency details, and that the proposed attention module yields a 3.1% boost in downstream semantic segmentation accuracy. Our method offers a practical trade‑off between quality and speed, making it well‑suited for real‑time perception pipelines in autonomous systems.
2938:
The Grassmannian manifold has emerged as a compelling foundation for geometric representation learning, where high‑dimensional data are encoded as low‑dimensional subspaces. Yet most current methods rely on a single static subspace, overlooking the rich interactions among multiple subspaces that are essential for modelling complex geometric patterns. To bridge this gap, we introduce a topology‑driven framework that fuses several subspaces on the Grassmannian, allowing them to collaborate adaptively.

Our contribution hinges on two novel components. First, drawing on the Kolmogorov‑Arnold representation theorem, we design an adaptive multi‑subspace model that dynamically selects and re‑weights task‑relevant subspaces through a topological convergence analysis. Second, we propose a multi‑subspace interaction block that merges heterogeneous geometric representations by optimizing their Fréchet mean on the manifold. We prove that the adaptive subspaces converge under a projection‑metric topology, guaranteeing stable gradient‑based optimisation.

To boost discriminative power and robustness, we embed Riemannian batch normalisation and a mutual‑information regulariser into the network. We validate our method on a diverse set of benchmarks—including 3D action recognition (HDM05, FPHA), EEG classification (MAMEM‑SSVEPII), and several graph tasks—achieving state‑of‑the‑art results.
