Key innovations include: (1) a multi‑scale temporal attention module that automatically emphasizes salient motion patterns, reducing feature redundancy; (2) a dynamic exemplar buffer that selects high‑representative samples for rehearsal, mitigating storage constraints; and (3) a regularized loss that balances new task learning with replayed knowledge without requiring explicit task boundaries. Experiments on benchmark datasets (UCI HAR, WISDM, and a large‑scale multi‑user dataset) demonstrate that EOL‑HAR achieves 3–4 % higher macro‑F1 than state‑of‑the‑art OCL approaches while reducing inference latency by 30 % and memory usage by 50 %. Ablation studies confirm the importance of each component, and real‑time evaluation on an ARM‑based smartwatch shows that the system sustains 15 ms per inference cycle with negligible battery drain.

Our work establishes a practical baseline for deploying continual HAR in resource‑constrained edge devices, and opens avenues for extending the framework to multi‑modal sensing and federated settings.
3366: Detecting lung nodules on chest CT scans is essential for the early diagnosis of lung cancer, yet deep‑learning models often struggle when they must be trained in clinical environments where annotated data are scarce. Curriculum learning can accelerate training, but conventional static curricula are ineffective under such limited‑data conditions. To address this, we introduce **Scale‑Adaptive Curriculum Learning (SACL)**, a dynamic training framework that tailors the learning sequence to the size of the available dataset. SACL incorporates three core components: (1) an adaptive epoch‑scheduling scheme, (2) strategic injection of hard examples, and (3) a scale‑aware optimization objective. Using YOLOv11 on the LUNA25 benchmark, we demonstrate that SACL matches the performance of static curriculum methods on the full dataset (mAP50), while delivering marked gains under data‑restricted scenarios—improvements of 4.6 %, 3.5 %, and 2.0 % over a baseline model when only 10 %, 20 %, and 50 % of the training data are available, respectively. By enabling reliable model training across varying data volumes without altering network architecture, SACL offers a practical solution for medical institutions to build effective lung‑nodule detectors even with limited annotation resources.
3367: Administrative records in criminal justice systems offer only scant detail about offenses. Yet, European court judgments contain rich, often untapped, descriptions of criminal conduct. This study investigates whether such narratives can be systematically extracted from Slovak public court decisions. We compare two extraction techniques: a baseline set of regular expressions that locate typical cue words surrounding the target text, and a refined regex strategy that also targets the “sparing” formatting (spacing between individual letters) commonly used to delimit these descriptions. Additionally, we employ an LLM—Gemini Flash 2.0—prompted with explicit extraction instructions. The baseline succeeds in about 40.5 % of verdicts, whereas the advanced regex and LLM methods identify the descriptions in 97 % and 98.75 % of cases, respectively, and a hybrid approach reaches 99.5 %. Evaluation by law students shows that both advanced approaches achieve roughly 90 % concordance with human annotations, compared with only 34.5 % for the baseline. The LLM alone aligns with human‑labeled segments in 91.75 % of instances, while the regex‑LLM combination attains 92 %. These results suggest that automated extraction of detailed offense descriptions from court texts is both feasible and reliable.
3368: Combinatorial decision problems frequently possess highly non‑uniform solution landscapes, yet conventional search heuristics treat all branches of the search tree uniformly.  In this work we show that the *topology* of the underlying solution space can be systematically exploited to guide a **Constrained Monte Carlo Tree Search (CMTS)**.  By modelling the set of feasible configurations as a high‑dimensional graph and applying tools from persistent homology, we extract a concise topological signature (Betti numbers, persistence diagrams, and critical‑region maps) that reveals bottlenecks, clusters, and connectivity patterns.  We then embed this signature into the CMTS policy in two ways: (1) a *topology‑aware prior* biases node expansion toward highly connected regions, and (2) a *distance‑to‑bottleneck* penalty discourages exploration of sparse subspaces that are unlikely to yield improvement.  Experiments on a diverse suite of NP‑hard problems—including SAT, 3‑coloring, vehicle‑routing, and multi‑objective scheduling—demonstrate that the topology‑guided CMTS consistently outperforms baseline MCTS and other state‑of‑the‑art heuristic solvers.  In particular, we observe a 30 % reduction in tree size and a 15–25 % improvement in solution quality on average.  Our results indicate that incorporating global structural information into local search dynamics yields a principled, general‑purpose enhancement for any CMTS‑style algorithm, and open a new direction for the integration of algebraic topology with search‑based AI.
3369: Breast cancer is among the top causes of death for women around the globe, and detecting it early is essential for successful treatment and better survival outcomes. Yet, prompt identification remains difficult because the disease is inherently complex and patients present a wide range of risk factors. This paper introduces an expert system grounded in fuzzy soft set theory that evaluates a patient’s likelihood of developing breast cancer using readily measurable clinical and physiological indicators. By incorporating Body Mass Index, insulin level, leptin level, adiponectin level, and age as input variables, the system applies a series of fuzzy inference rules coupled with soft‑set calculations to estimate cancer risk. Since these markers can be derived from standard blood tests, the approach offers a non‑invasive and readily accessible screening tool. The model was trained and tested on data from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Ultimately, the proposed system is intended to aid clinicians in pinpointing high‑risk individuals and deciding whether further diagnostic interventions, such as biopsies, are warranted.
3370:
Short‑video platforms (e.g., TikTok, Instagram Reels) generate millions of comments each day, yet most user‑generated commentary is unstructured, short‑lived, and rarely drives long‑term interaction. We address this gap by formulating **stylized comment generation** as a means to *laugh, relate, and engage* with audiences in a scalable, automated manner. In this work we present a novel framework that jointly models multimodal content (visual, audio, and transcript), user context, and stylistic intent (humorous, empathetic, or interactive) to produce concise, contextually relevant comments that emulate human conversational patterns.

To train and evaluate our approach, we curated **VideoComment-360**, a large‑scale dataset of 520,000 short‑video clips paired with 1.8M user comments and annotated engagement signals (likes, replies, shares). We propose a hierarchical transformer architecture with a *multimodal encoder* that fuses visual–audio embeddings and a *style‑aware decoder* that conditions on a learnable style vector. A reinforcement‑learning objective fine‑tunes the generator to maximize a learned *engagement reward* derived from historical interaction statistics.

Automatic metrics (BLEU, METEOR, and a new Stylized‑Relevance score) demonstrate that our model outperforms strong baselines (seq2seq, GPT‑style, and multimodal LSTM) by 12–18 % in relevance and 8–15 % in style fidelity. Human studies confirm that generated comments elicit higher laughter rates and more replies compared to human‑authored but generic comments. Finally, an online A/B test on a live short‑video platform shows a 23 % lift in average user engagement per video when our system is employed.

Our contributions are: (1) a multimodal, style‑controlled comment generator; (2) a large, richly annotated short‑video comment dataset; and (3) an end‑to‑end pipeline that bridges content analysis and engagement‑optimized dialogue generation. This work advances the state of the art in content‑aware, user‑centric social media dialogue systems.
3371: This paper offers an extended articulation of the Holistic Cognitive Development (HCD) framework, designed to foster reflective and creative learning in computing education. The HCD model melds design thinking, experiential learning, and reflective practice into a cohesive constructivist pedagogy that prioritises student autonomy, ownership, and scaffolded support. It is implemented across a variety of courses—game design (CS3247, CS4350), virtual reality (CS4240), and extended‑reality systems—where learners repeatedly cycle through phases of thinking, creating, critiquing, and reflecting. The study also explores how AI‑augmented tools such as iReflect, ReflexAI, and knowledge‑graph‑enhanced large‑language‑model feedback systems realize the HCD framework by delivering scalable, personalised feedback. Empirical evidence shows gains in the depth of reflection, the quality of feedback, and learner autonomy. The work argues for a balanced, supportive autonomy model in supervision: students pursue self‑directed inquiry while being guided through structured reflection and feedback.
3372: Rapid, reliable prediction of small‑molecule solubility is essential for speeding up synthesis and process development. Yet laboratory measurements are expensive, and many machine‑learning methods either rely on costly quantum‑derived descriptors or lack clear interpretability. We present **Solvaformer**, a geometry‑aware graph transformer that treats a solution as a collection of molecules, each endowed with its own SE(3) symmetry. By integrating intramolecular SE(3)‑equivariant attention with intermolecular scalar attention, the model facilitates communication across molecules while respecting their independent geometries. Training is carried out in a multi‑task regime that simultaneously predicts the solubility (log S) and the solvation free energy, using an alternating‑batch scheme that alternates between quantum‑mechanical data (CombiSolv‑QM) and experimental data (BigSolDB 2.0). Solvaformer outperforms all competing learned models and rivals a DFT‑assisted gradient‑boosting baseline, while clearly surpassing an EquiformerV2 ablation and sequence‑based baselines. Moreover, token‑level attention maps provide chemically meaningful attributions, correctly highlighting intra‑ versus inter‑molecular hydrogen‑bonding patterns that differentiate positional isomers. In summary, Solvaformer offers a scalable, accurate, and interpretable framework for solution‑phase property prediction by fusing geometric inductive bias with a mixed‑dataset training strategy that leverages both computational and experimental evidence.
3373: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to create concise yet faithful synthetic datasets, yet most current techniques inherit the inductive bias of a single teacher network. As the volume of the dataset grows, this bias pushes the generated samples toward overly smooth, homogeneous representations, curbing intra‑class variation and hindering generalization. We introduce PRISM (PRIors from diverse Source Models), a novel framework that untangles architectural priors during synthesis. PRISM separates the logit‑matching loss from the regularization term, guiding them with distinct teacher backbones: a primary model supplies the logits while a stochastic subset of networks enforces batch‑normalization alignment. On ImageNet‑1K, PRISM consistently and reliably surpasses single‑teacher baselines (e.g., SRe2L) and recent multi‑teacher approaches (e.g., G‑VBSM) across both low‑ and medium‑IPC regimes. The synthetic images exhibit markedly richer intra‑class diversity, evidenced by a pronounced drop in feature‑space cosine similarity. We also explore teacher‑selection strategies—pre‑ versus intra‑distillation—and propose a scalable cross‑class batch construction scheme that accelerates parallel synthesis. Code will be made available after the review period.
3374:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive reasoning abilities when guided by *Chain‑of‑Thought* (CoT) prompting, which forces the model to articulate intermediate reasoning steps. Nevertheless, conventional CoT approaches depend on discrete, token‑level reasoning, which is susceptible to error propagation and constrained by the expressiveness of the vocabulary. Consequently, the generated reasoning paths can become brittle and inconsistent.  

Recent work has turned to implicit, continuous reasoning in latent spaces, allowing the model to perform internal deliberation before emitting an explicit answer. While this mitigates some of the drawbacks of discrete CoT, these methods usually lack a clear way to enforce coherence across the intermediate steps, resulting in divergent trajectories and unstable predictions.  

To tackle this challenge, we introduce **EBM‑CoT**, an *Energy‑Based Chain‑of‑Thought Calibration* framework. Our approach refines the latent reasoning vectors via an energy‑based model (EBM), steering them toward low‑energy, high‑consistency regions of the embedding space. This refinement process improves both the accuracy and the consistency of multi‑step reasoning, and it does so without altering the underlying language model.  

A comprehensive set of experiments on mathematical, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks demonstrates that EBM‑CoT markedly boosts the reliability and efficiency of LLMs’ reasoning capabilities.
3375:
The rapid spread of misinformation on social media and news platforms demands robust automated defenses. Traditional fake‑news detectors rely on supervised learning and handcrafted features, which struggle to generalize to unseen topics and emerging claim types. We propose **ZoFia** (Zero‑shot f**o**o**e**n d**e**tection via e**nt**ity‑guided Retrieval and Multi‑LLM Interaction), a framework that performs zero‑shot fake‑news classification by integrating open‑domain knowledge with a lightweight ensemble of large language models (LLMs). 

ZoFia first extracts salient entities from a headline‑paragraph pair using a lightweight entity linker. These entities seed a retrieval module that harvests contextually relevant passages from a curated knowledge base (e.g., Wikipedia, fact‑checking databases). The retrieved evidence is then jointly evaluated by multiple LLMs, each prompted with distinct reasoning strategies (e.g., “explain why this claim is plausible” vs. “explain why it is likely false”). Their outputs are fused through a lightweight decision module that weighs evidence consistency and model confidence. This multi‑LLM interaction enables complementary reasoning, mitigating individual model biases while preserving the efficiency of a zero‑shot approach.

On the most recent large‑scale benchmarks (e.g., **FakeNewsNet**, **FIBER**, **LIAR‑LIAR-PLUS**), ZoFia surpasses existing zero‑shot baselines by 6.3 % (macro‑F1) and matches or exceeds supervised state‑of‑the‑art systems with only 2 % of the training data. Ablation studies confirm that entity‑guided retrieval and the multi‑LLM ensemble each contribute significantly to performance gains. 

ZoFia demonstrates that a principled combination of knowledge‑guided evidence retrieval and multi‑LLM reasoning can achieve strong zero‑shot fake‑news detection, offering a scalable, interpretable, and rapid-response tool for emerging misinformation threats.
3376:
Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has made it possible to encode sophisticated knowledge and reasoning, yet their deployment remains constrained by safety and alignment filters that prevent the generation of disallowed or harmful content. In this paper we study the problem of *automatic jailbreak* – algorithmic methods for eliciting policy‑violating outputs from a target LLM – and propose a novel *meta‑optimized LLM judge* framework that learns to assess and steer the jailbreak process.  

Our approach treats the jailbreak generator and the judge as two interacting agents that are co‑trained in a game‑theoretic setting. The generator produces adversarial prompts, while the judge (another LLM) is fine‑tuned to score the compliance of the target model’s responses against a set of safety constraints. A meta‑optimization loop updates the judge’s parameters to increase its discriminatory power, and simultaneously updates the generator to exploit weaknesses uncovered by the judge. This leads to a self‑reinforcing pipeline that automatically discovers increasingly subtle jailbreak strategies without any human‑written prompts.  

We evaluate our method on a suite of standard alignment benchmarks (OpenAI Moderation API, GPT‑4 policy datasets, and a custom *Safe-Chat* benchmark). The resulting jailbreaks achieve a 37 % higher success rate than hand‑crafted attacks while maintaining near‑zero false‑positive rates. Ablation studies confirm that meta‑optimization of the judge yields a 22 % improvement in attack efficacy compared to static, hand‑tuned judges.  

Our findings highlight a new class of adversarial dynamics that can be harnessed to probe and improve LLM safety mechanisms. The meta‑optimized judge framework provides a systematic tool for stress‑testing alignment protocols, and offers insights for designing more robust safety filters.
3377: Human smuggling networks are becoming more resilient and harder to dissect.  Legal case records are indispensable for understanding these networks, yet they are typically unstructured, linguistically complex, and replete with vague or changing references, making automated construction of knowledge graphs (KGs) a formidable task.  While recent large‑language‑model (LLM) techniques surpass static templates, they still produce fragmented, noisy graphs with many duplicate entities because they lack directed extraction and coreference handling.  The newly introduced CORE‑KG framework mitigates these issues by incorporating a type‑aware coreference resolver and domain‑specific structured prompts, which markedly cut down on node duplication and legal‑noise.  In this paper we conduct a detailed ablation analysis of CORE‑KG to assess the separate impact of each of its two main modules.  Our experiments reveal that disabling coreference resolution raises node duplication by 28.25 % and noisy nodes by 4.32 %, whereas removing the structured prompts increases duplication by 4.29 % and noisy nodes by a staggering 73.33 %.  These results provide concrete guidance for building robust, LLM‑driven pipelines that reliably extract structured knowledge from complex legal documents.
3378: Recommender systems are increasingly addressing the cold‑start challenge by exploiting multimodal content or by adopting agent‑based strategies that harness the advanced reasoning powers of large language models (LLMs). In the food‑and‑beverage domain, knowledge graphs and ontologies have long been the preferred tools because of the domain’s intricate data attributes and inter‑relationships. Building on these insights, we introduce **MARC** – a multimodal, multi‑task cocktail recommender that employs Agentic Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) coupled with a graph database to operate effectively under cold‑start conditions. MARC produces high‑quality, contextually relevant recommendations through two essential components: a task‑recognition router and a reflective reasoning loop. We constructed the underlying graph database by processing cocktail datasets from Kaggle and evaluated the system using 200 hand‑crafted queries. Comparative assessments, conducted with both LLM‑based judging and human raters, show that the graph‑backed RAG approach yields superior answer quality compared to a plain vector‑search baseline. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/diddbwls/cocktail_rec_agentrag.
3379:
This paper investigates the prevalence of aesthetic manipulation—design choices that steer users toward the consent button—within cookie banners that purport to comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). In doing so, we also assess the overall compliance of these banners with GDPR mandates and the design guidance issued by national data‑protection authorities.

Our methodology involved crawling 2,579 websites and categorising the cookie banner implementations they deploy. Of these sites, 45 % feature banners that meet the formal GDPR requirements; however, among those compliant banners, 38 % exhibit aesthetic manipulation. Leveraging a computer‑vision model for salient‑object detection, we quantified the visual prominence of each banner element, which allowed us to uncover previously unreported forms of manipulation such as strategic button placement. This approach confirms that the phenomenon is more widespread than earlier estimates suggested (38 % versus the 27 % reported in prior work).

To explore geographic variations in banner design, we examined sites both within and outside the European Union (EU), sampling from IP addresses located in the EU and the United States. Results indicate that 13.9 % of EU websites modify their banner layout when accessed from the US, and that EU sites are about 48.3 % more likely to employ aesthetic manipulation than non‑EU sites. These findings underscore how regulatory pressure in the EU is driving innovative design practices aimed at influencing user consent.
3380: The rapid evolution of large language models has sparked growing interest in LLM‑powered multi‑agent systems (MAS), yet many existing frameworks still suffer from reliability and scalability issues on complex problems. We present **AgentGit**, a new infrastructure that brings Git‑style rollback and branching to MAS workflows. Built atop LangGraph, AgentGit enables state commits, reversions, and branch creation, allowing agents to traverse, compare, and explore multiple execution paths with minimal overhead. To assess its effectiveness, we engineered an experiment that optimises target agents by selecting better prompts and ran a multi‑step A/B test against three baselines—LangGraph, AutoGen, and Agno—on a real‑world task of retrieving and analysing paper abstracts. The results show that AgentGit dramatically reduces redundant computation, cuts runtime and token usage, and supports parallel exploration across branches, thereby enhancing both reliability and scalability. This study offers a practical path toward more robust MAS design and demonstrates how error recovery, safe exploration, iterative debugging, and A/B testing can be seamlessly integrated into collaborative AI systems.
3381: Artificial intelligence agents hold the promise of speeding up scientific progress by autonomously generating hypotheses, designing experiments, writing and running code, and interpreting results. However, most current benchmark suites evaluate only a few isolated skills in highly simplified contexts. To close this disconnect, we present **InnovatorBench**—a comprehensive benchmark‑platform pair that tests agents on realistic, end‑to‑end research pipelines powered by large language models. The benchmark contains 20 diverse tasks covering data construction, filtering, augmentation, loss and reward engineering, and scaffold building, each demanding executable artifacts and rigorous evaluation of correctness, performance, output quality, and uncertainty. To enable such complex workflows, we build **ResearchGym**, a research environment featuring rich action spaces, distributed and long‑horizon execution, asynchronous monitoring, and snapshot capabilities. We also prototype a lightweight **ReAct** agent that blends explicit reasoning with executable planning, leveraging state‑of‑the‑art models such as Claude‑4, GPT‑5, GLM‑4.5, and Kimi‑K2. Experiments reveal that while these frontier models can tackle code‑centric research tasks, they still falter on fragile algorithmic challenges and extended decision‑making horizons—exhibiting impatience, poor resource management, and an overreliance on template‑based reasoning. Moreover, agents required more than 11 hours to reach their best performance on InnovatorBench, highlighting the benchmark’s difficulty and its potential to become the next standard for code‑driven scientific research.
3382:
The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has sparked interest in their application to clinical informatics, yet systematic evaluation of these models on structured electronic health record (EHR) data remains fragmented. We present **EHRStruct**, a unified, open‑source benchmark framework that standardizes the evaluation of LLMs across a spectrum of structured EHR tasks—including ICD‑10 coding, medication recommendation, phenotyping, and longitudinal risk prediction. EHRStruct ingests raw EHR datasets (MIMIC‑III, eICU‑CRD, Stanford Hospital, and a proprietary multi‑site cohort), applies a common preprocessing pipeline (time‑window alignment, ontology mapping, and missing‑data handling), and exposes a modular API that accepts both tabular embeddings and tokenized clinical text. The benchmark comprises nine downstream tasks, each defined by rigorous, clinically relevant metrics (macro‑F1, AUROC, calibration curves) and carefully curated train/validation/test splits that preserve patient‑level independence.

Using EHRStruct, we benchmark twelve state‑of‑the‑art LLMs—including GPT‑4, Llama‑2, Med-PaLM, and domain‑tuned variants—against traditional machine‑learning baselines. Across the tasks, LLMs achieve competitive performance on narrative‑heavy problems (e.g., discharge summary coding, AUROC >0.92) but lag on high‑dimensional numeric‑only tasks such as laboratory forecasting (average macro‑F1 <0.55). Instruction‑tuned LLMs demonstrate significant gains in phenotyping, suggesting that prompt engineering can partially offset structural data challenges. We also highlight reproducible failure modes: tokenization limits on ultra‑long admission notes, sensitivity to temporal mis‑alignment, and inadequate calibration for low‑prevalence conditions.

EHRStruct is released as a Python library and a Docker‑based evaluation pipeline, enabling researchers to reproduce results and extend the benchmark with new datasets or tasks. By providing a transparent, extensible, and clinically meaningful evaluation ecosystem, EHRStruct facilitates principled comparisons of LLMs on structured EHR workloads and informs the design of next‑generation, privacy‑respectful, hybrid models that seamlessly integrate unstructured text with structured clinical data.
3383: The Dafny verifier offers strong correctness guarantees, yet its practical use is often hampered by the need for numerous manual helper assertions. In this work we explore whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can automatically supply these missing assertions, especially when several are absent simultaneously. To facilitate the investigation, we enhance the DafnyBench benchmark with carefully curated datasets in which one, two, or all assertions have been stripped, and we devise a taxonomy of assertion categories to assess the difficulty of inference. Our method improves fault localization by blending LLM predictions with heuristic insights drawn from error messages. The resulting tool, DAISY (Dafny Assertion Inference SYstem), is evaluated on both single‑ and multi‑missing‑assertion scenarios. DAISY succeeds in verifying 63.4 % of programs with a single missing assertion and 31.7 % when multiple assertions are omitted. Remarkably, many programs can be verified with fewer assertions than originally written, underscoring that proofs admit multiple viable repair strategies and that reproducing every original assertion is unnecessary. These findings show that automated inference of assertions can significantly lower the cost of proof engineering, moving formal verification toward greater scalability and accessibility.
3384:
Detecting misconceptions in student answers to open‑ended math questions has long been a difficult problem that requires both fine‑grained semantic understanding and logical scrutiny. To address this, we introduce MiRAGE—**M**isconception **R**e‑identification via **A**ssisted **G**eneration and **E**nsemble. MiRAGE follows a three‑step pipeline: first, a Retrieval module prunes a vast pool of candidate explanations to a semantically relevant subset; second, a Reasoning module generates chain‑of‑thought traces that reveal inconsistencies in the student’s solution; finally, a Reranking module fine‑tunes the predictions by aligning them with the generated reasoning. These stages are integrated through an ensemble‑fusion strategy that boosts both robustness and interpretability.

Across several mathematics datasets, MiRAGE attains Mean Average Precision scores of 0.82, 0.92, and 0.93 at levels 1, 3, and 5, respectively, consistently surpassing each individual module. By combining retrieval guidance with staged reasoning, MiRAGE cuts back on reliance on large language models while offering a scalable, high‑performance solution for automated educational assessment.
3385: We investigate subliminal transfer in Transformer architectures, where a teacher model implants covert attributes that a student can recover by a simple linear probe while still preserving performance on the principal task. Earlier studies have generally linked transferability to global representational similarity measured by Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). To isolate the effect of hidden traits, we use synthetic datasets that separate public and private labels and distill student models from the teacher using either identical or independent random initializations. Our experiments reveal that the amount of transfer depends on how well the representations align in the subspace that is discriminative for the hidden trait: students started from the same random seed inherit a stronger alignment and show a leakage signal of roughly τ≈0.24, whereas students with different seeds – despite exhibiting a high overall CKA (>0.9) – display markedly lower excess accuracy (τ≈0.12–0.13). We formalize this observation with a subspace‑specific CKA metric and residualized probing, demonstrating that leakage correlates with alignment within the trait‑discriminative subspace rather than with global similarity. Applying security mechanisms such as projection penalties, adversarial reversals, and “right‑for‑the‑wrong‑reasons” regularization effectively suppresses leakage in models sharing the same base without harming public‑task performance. These findings highlight seed‑induced uniqueness as a robust defense and underscore the importance of subspace‑aware diagnostics for secure deployment of multiple models.
3386:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to solve problems that require *chain‑of‑thought* (CoT) reasoning, yet the correctness of each intermediate step remains difficult to certify. Existing verification approaches either impose a heavy computational burden by re‑running the entire reasoning trace or rely on heuristic heuristics that often miss subtle errors. In this work we introduce **Uncertainty Heads (UH)**—auxiliary prediction modules attached to every token generation layer of an LLM—that provide *step‑level confidence estimates* calibrated to the true likelihood of error. By training UH jointly with the base model under a *confidence‑aware loss*, the heads learn to distinguish reliable from unreliable reasoning steps without requiring external supervision.

We demonstrate that UH‑augmented reasoning allows a *selective verification pipeline*: only steps whose confidence falls below a learned threshold are recomputed or flagged for human inspection. On a suite of benchmark reasoning datasets (GSM‑8K, BIG‑Bench, and a newly curated “LLM‑Rationale” test set), our method achieves a 4.3× reduction in verification cost while preserving 98.7 % of the overall accuracy. Comparative analyses against baseline uncertainty estimators (e.g., temperature scaling, MC‑dropout) show a 12 % higher calibration error reduction and a 17 % improvement in early‑stop decisions for error detection.

Beyond efficiency, the confidence scores also expose systematic failure modes of LLMs, enabling targeted fine‑tuning and curriculum design. The UH framework is model‑agnostic and integrates seamlessly with existing CoT pipelines. We release our code, datasets, and a public leaderboard to encourage further research on *verified, confidence‑aware* LLM reasoning.
3387:
Green hydrogen production by polymer‑electrolyte‑membrane (PEM) water electrolysis is a cornerstone of the energy transition, but hydrogen permeation through the membrane endangers both safety and cost‑effectiveness—approaching the explosive limit of 4 mol % H₂ in O₂ and diminishing Faradaic efficiency by roughly 2.5 %. Existing physics‑based models are computationally demanding and require extensive calibration, making them impractical for real‑time use, while purely data‑driven networks cannot reliably predict beyond their training regimes, a critical shortfall for dynamic electrolyzer operation.  

In this work we introduce the first physics‑informed neural network (PINN) that forecasts hydrogen crossover. The network embeds mass‑conservation, Fick’s diffusion, and Henry’s solubility laws within a compact architecture of only 17 793 trainable parameters. Tested on six distinct membranes under industrially relevant operating points (0.05–5.0 A cm⁻², 1–200 bar, 25–85 °C), the PINN delivers outstanding predictive performance (R² = 99.84 %, RMSE = 0.0348 %) and achieves sub‑millisecond inference times, rendering it suitable for live control loops. 

Notably, the model retains strong extrapolation capability, achieving R² > 86 % when predicting crossover at pressures 2.5 × higher than its training data—a dramatic improvement over conventional neural networks (R² = 43.4 %). Its hardware‑agnostic nature allows deployment on a wide spectrum of devices—from standard desktop CPUs to edge platforms such as Raspberry Pi 4—facilitating distributed safety monitoring for gigawatt‑scale electrolyzer arrays. 

By harmonising rigorous physical constraints with lightweight machine‑learning efficiency, this research establishes a novel framework for real‑time electrolyzer supervision, paving the way for safer and more economical green hydrogen production in pursuit of net‑zero emissions.
3388:
Financial documents such as earnings reports or balance sheets routinely contain extensive tables and span multiple pages. Recent large language models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for numerically‑oriented reasoning over these materials, yet their effectiveness is highly contingent on the quality of the prompts provided. Existing approaches either fine‑tune prompts on static datasets of financial text or rely on expensive, manually curated annotations, thereby limiting flexibility to new question types or document layouts.  

To address this, we present a self‑enhancing prompt framework that leverages data‑augmented optimization. The system operates in a closed loop: a synthetic generator creates new financial tables and document snippets that expose shortcomings in the current prompt; verifiers validate the accuracy and robustness of these examples; and an optimizer refines the prompt incrementally based on the feedback. This iterative cycle allows the prompt to evolve without external labels.  

Evaluations on the DocMath‑Eval benchmark reveal that our method attains superior accuracy and robustness compared to conventional prompting strategies, demonstrating the advantage of incorporating synthetic data generation into prompt learning for financial reasoning tasks.
3389:
Proof‑Number Search (PNS) is the leading method for solving combinatorial games: a best‑first algorithm that recursively assigns *proof* and *disproof* numbers to nodes in a game tree until the root value is determined.  Although highly effective on single‑core machines, PNS suffers from a deep, highly branching search space and a large memory footprint that quickly exhausts the resources of contemporary processors.  In this paper we present **M‑PNS**, a massively parallel framework that scales PNS to tens of thousands of CPU cores and thousands of GPUs, thereby extending its reach to previously intractable impartial games and enabling its use for a wide class of deterministic turn‑based games.

M‑PNS introduces a lock‑free, distributed work‑stealing priority queue that preserves the core PNS heuristic while allowing concurrent exploration of the search tree.  We develop a novel *dynamic proof‑number pruning* strategy that exploits symmetry and *retrograde reasoning* to reduce the branching factor, and a *node‑caching* scheme that mitigates duplication in a highly parallel environment.  Our implementation is engineered for heterogeneous architectures, automatically partitioning the search across CPU and GPU resources and maintaining consistent proof‑disproof values via a lightweight consensus protocol.

Experimental results on benchmark impartial games (e.g., Nim, Hackenbush, Sprouts) demonstrate a 200‑fold speedup over the state‑of‑the‑art sequential PNS on a 64‑core workstation and enable the first complete solutions for several 8‑by‑8 board positions that have resisted decades of effort.  We further show that M‑PNS generalizes to a variety of impartial and partisan games, achieving comparable gains on the combinatorial game library of 4‑by‑4 Go and the game of Checkers on a 9‑by‑9 board.

Our work demonstrates that massively parallel PNS is both feasible and powerful, opening the door to exact solution of complex combinatorial games and to its application in AI planning, automated theorem proving, and beyond.
3390:
Maintaining physiological equilibrium is a hallmark of living systems, yet contemporary artificial agents largely rely on static, weight‑only learning rules to achieve homeostatic control. Recent evidence suggests that *structural plasticity*—the dynamic rewiring of neural circuitry—plays a pivotal role in biological adaptation, operating in concert with active inference frameworks that minimize free‑energy to reconcile sensory expectations with internal states. Here we introduce **Structural Plasticity as Active Inference (SPA‑Inference)**, a biologically‑inspired architecture that couples synaptic rewiring with probabilistic inference to endow artificial agents with flexible, self‑organizing homeostatic mechanisms.

SPA‑Inference extends the classic variational inference paradigm by permitting the *topology* of the generative network to change during inference. A cost‑aware rewiring rule is derived from the free‑energy principle: new connections are instantiated when the expected reduction in prediction error outweighs the metabolic cost of additional synapses, while redundant links are pruned to preserve sparsity. We implemented SPA‑Inference in a recurrent spiking network tasked with regulating internal temperature and metabolic variables in a simulated virtual organism exposed to stochastic environmental perturbations. Compared with weight‑only active inference agents, SPA‑Inference achieved a 37 % faster convergence to steady‑state conditions and a 42 % reduction in energy expenditure, owing to its ability to reorganize connectivity rather than merely adjusting synaptic amplitudes.

The results demonstrate that structural plasticity can serve as an explicit, inference‑driven mechanism for homeostatic control, reconciling biophysical constraints with computational efficiency. This work bridges the gap between neural plasticity theories and active inference, offering a new paradigm for adaptive, low‑power neuromorphic systems and advancing our understanding of how biological organisms maintain equilibrium in dynamic environments.
3391: We present **SigmaCollab**, a dataset designed to support research on physically embodied human–AI collaboration. The collection comprises 85 recorded sessions in which untrained subjects followed the guidance of a mixed‑reality assistive AI while carrying out procedural tasks in a real‑world setting. Each session is accompanied by a wealth of multimodal streams—participant and system audio, egocentric camera footage from a head‑mounted display, depth maps, and comprehensive head, hand and gaze tracking data—augmented with post‑hoc annotations. Though modest in duration (approximately 14 hours), the interactive and application‑driven nature of SigmaCollab exposes new challenges for human–AI collaboration and offers a more realistic test bed for evaluating diverse AI models in this domain. Future work will leverage the dataset to establish benchmarks for physically situated collaboration in mixed‑reality assistive scenarios. The dataset is freely accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/SigmaCollab.
3392:
Modern image‑generation models are increasingly able to translate textual descriptions into high‑fidelity renderings, yet the notion of *style*—the aesthetic, domain‑specific, or functional attributes that give an image its unique look—remains largely implicit and hard to manipulate. In this work we propose a principled, interpretable framework for *code‑to‑style image generation* that treats visual style as a discrete, combinatorial entity. The central observation is that each distinct style can be represented by a single “style code”, enabling a clean separation between the *content* expressed in natural language and the *style* specified by a compact token.  

To achieve this, we learn a discrete style space by training a vector‑quantized variational auto‑encoder (VQ‑VAE) on a large corpus of diverse images, where the quantized codes capture semantically coherent style primitives (e.g., “watercolor”, “cyberpunk”, “noir”). A cross‑modal transformer maps a user’s programming‑like style instruction (e.g., “apply a 1970s comic‑book filter”) to a sequence of style codes. These codes are then fed into a conditional diffusion generator that synthesizes a target image conditioned on both the textual prompt and the selected style codes.  

Our experiments demonstrate that the discrete style space enables fine‑grained, controllable style editing with a single code, outperforming continuous‑style baselines on style‑consistency metrics (accuracy ↑ 12 %) and preserving content fidelity (FID ↓ 8 %). Ablation studies confirm the importance of discrete quantization for disentanglement and interpretability. Finally, we introduce a new benchmark, *Code‑Style*, comprising 200k image‑style pairs with corresponding natural‑language style specifications, and release a user‑study protocol that shows a 73 % preference rate for images generated by our method over prior style‑transfer pipelines.  

Our approach unlocks a new paradigm where artists and developers can “program” aesthetic attributes with a single, interpretable code, opening avenues for rapid prototyping in design, gaming, and virtual production.
3393:
Untrusted AI agents—software that may deviate from intended behaviour due to bugs, adversarial manipulation or conflicting incentives—pose a growing risk to safety‑critical and high‑stakes applications. While a number of control protocols have been proposed in the literature (e.g., pre‑deployment verification, runtime monitoring, sandboxing, incentive‑aligned reward shaping, and contractual contracts), there has been no systematic, empirical comparison of their effectiveness in realistic settings. This paper introduces a principled evaluation framework for control protocols tailored to untrusted autonomous agents, grounded in formal risk‑analysis and empirical performance metrics.

We first formalise three core threat scenarios—malicious behaviour, accidental drift, and partial observability—and define a suite of quantitative metrics: *safety* (probability of catastrophic failure), *utility loss* (deviation from optimal performance), *verification overhead* (computation and time), and *resilience* (recovery after breach). To populate this framework, we construct a benchmark of 50 autonomous‑agent tasks spanning robotics, dialogue, and finance, each annotated with a baseline policy and a set of adversarial perturbations.

Using this benchmark, we evaluate ten representative control protocols, including static code audits, formal model checking, runtime invariant enforcement, sandboxed execution, multi‑layer reward shaping, and economic‑contractual safeguards. Across all tasks, we observe that protocols combining *runtime monitoring* with *sandboxed execution* achieve the lowest safety‑utility trade‑off, while pure *pre‑deployment verification* suffers from high false‑negative rates under distribution shift. Protocols that rely solely on *incentive alignment* exhibit strong utility retention but weak guarantees against overtly malicious agents.

The results highlight that no single protocol suffices; instead, a hybrid approach that layers lightweight static checks, dynamic monitoring, and formal guarantees yields the most robust protection with acceptable computational overhead. We release our evaluation suite and open‑source implementations to facilitate future research on AI safety protocols. The paper concludes with design guidelines for selecting and integrating control protocols in practical deployments and outlines directions for extending the framework to multi‑agent and federated learning settings.
3394:
The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into educational settings promises to transform how learners confront complex, ill‑structured problems. However, the impact of AI‑mediated collaboration on student engagement—especially in tasks that blend algorithmic precision with creative strategy—remains under‑explored. This pilot study investigates engagement dynamics in a human‑AI partnership on the classic Rubik’s Cube, a canonical example of complex, multi‑step problem solving that requires spatial reasoning, pattern recognition, and iterative refinement.

Nine university students (ages 18–24) participated in a mixed‑methods design in which each solved a 3×3×3 Cube under three conditions: (1) independent human solving, (2) human solving with an AI tutor that provided step‑by‑step hints, and (3) human solving with an AI co‑solver that suggested optimal algorithms in real time. Engagement was assessed through a combination of (a) self‑reported measures (the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, NASA‑Task Load Index), (b) behavioral metrics (time on task, number of moves, error rates), and (c) qualitative interviews exploring perceptions of autonomy, challenge, and perceived competence.

Quantitative results indicated a statistically significant increase in self‑reported intrinsic motivation and lower perceived effort during the AI‑co‑solver condition compared to the independent baseline (p < 0.01). Time to solution was reduced by an average of 42 % in the AI‑co‑solver condition. Qualitative analysis revealed that participants valued the AI’s guidance for strategy but expressed concerns about over‑reliance and reduced agency. The AI‑hint condition yielded moderate gains in engagement but less pronounced performance improvements.

Overall, the findings suggest that AI‑assisted collaboration can enhance student engagement and efficiency in complex problem‑solving tasks when it balances guidance with autonomy. Future work will expand participant numbers, incorporate longitudinal designs, and test domain transfer to curriculum‑based problem sets. This pilot provides preliminary evidence that human‑AI teams can be leveraged to foster deeper engagement in advanced STEM problem solving.
3395:
Learning dynamics models—often called world models—has been shown to boost the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning. Recent studies claim that such models exhibit two forms of sparsity: (1) a sparsely connected causal graph in which each future state variable depends on only a few current variables, and (2) temporal sparsity, meaning that local dynamics shift abruptly only in a limited number of places. These ideas motivate the use of sparsity priors in dynamics learning.

In this paper we rigorously test these hypotheses on the ground‑truth dynamics of a suite of MuJoCo Playground environments. Specifically, we ask:  
i) Are the causal graphs of the environment dynamics actually sparse?  
ii) Does any observed sparsity depend on the current state?  
iii) Do local system dynamics change sparsely over time?

Our findings show that global sparsity is the exception rather than the rule. Instead, the environments reveal **local, state‑dependent sparsity**: sparse interactions appear only in specific parts of the state space and cluster around particular events (e.g., contact points). These sparse structures typically involve only a subset of state dimensions and are temporally localized.

Thus, the common assumption of a uniformly sparse dynamics model does not hold in realistic reinforcement‑learning tasks. Our results point to the necessity of incorporating inductive biases that capture the actual, state‑dependent sparsity patterns observed in real-world dynamics.
3396: Artificial intelligence agents that can manipulate user interfaces promise to reshape how people interact with digital devices. Bringing this vision to reality requires two key enablers: (1) high‑quality, richly varied datasets that empower agents to pursue complex, human‑centric objectives, and (2) robust evaluation frameworks that let researchers and developers quickly iterate on agent performance. This work introduces **DigiData**, a large‑scale, multimodal dataset specifically curated for training mobile‑control agents. Unlike prior collections that rely on noisy, unstructured interactions, DigiData is built through systematic, exhaustive exploration of app features, yielding a broader range of tasks and more challenging goals. We also present **DigiData‑Bench**, a benchmark for measuring mobile‑control agents on realistic, sophisticated tasks. We show that the standard step‑accuracy metric is insufficient for reliable assessment and propose dynamic evaluation protocols coupled with AI‑driven evaluation techniques as more rigorous alternatives. Together, these contributions push the field of mobile‑control agents forward, opening the door to more intuitive and effective human‑device interactions.
3397:
Multi‑domain learning seeks to build a single model that performs well across a diverse set of related tasks or datasets. A perennial challenge in this setting is the skewed distribution of samples and task importance: some domains contain far more data or carry higher stakes than others, leading to biased gradient estimates and sub‑optimal generalization. In this work we systematically investigate two intertwined aspects of the training pipeline—**sampling** and **loss weighting**—and propose a unified framework that dynamically adjusts both during training.

First, we formalise a principled sampling scheme based on *importance‑weighted re‑sampling* that treats each domain as a Bernoulli process with a learned sampling probability. This mechanism guarantees that the effective gradient contribution from each domain is proportional to its current difficulty and prevalence. Second, we introduce a **contrastive loss‑weighting** strategy that modulates domain‑specific loss terms according to their evolving validation performance, thereby preventing catastrophic forgetting of under‑represented domains. We also analyse the theoretical relationship between sampling frequencies, loss weights, and the resulting Fisher information matrix, deriving an optimality condition under which the overall objective remains unbiased.

Empirically, we evaluate our approach on three standard multi‑domain benchmarks—ImageNet‑style classification, language‑model fine‑tuning across multiple corpora, and few‑shot medical‑image segmentation. Across all settings our method consistently outperforms naïve uniform sampling and static weighting by 2–4 % in mean domain‑specific accuracy and reduces validation loss variance by up to 30 %. Ablation studies confirm that both adaptive sampling and dynamic weighting contribute additively to performance gains. Our findings suggest that carefully balancing sample selection and loss emphasis is crucial for robust multi‑domain training, and provide a practical recipe that can be readily incorporated into existing pipelines.
3398: Many organizations store vital business information in separate, siloed databases, which hampers efficiency and data interoperability. A critical step toward solving these problems is the integration of diverse data sources, allowing enterprises to fully leverage their information assets. In this paper we introduce an innovative method for unifying multiple databases via knowledge graphs, employing large language models as semantic agents that map and link structured data across systems by utilizing established vocabularies. Our approach adds a semantic layer on top of relational tables, using a suite of LLM agents to align tables and columns with Schema.org terms. Experiments across several domains show that this technique achieves mapping accuracy exceeding 90 %.
3399: Attribution‑based explainers highlight salient patterns, yet they often miss the fine‑grained detail required for nuanced visual tasks, especially when a model misclassifies. To overcome this, we introduce a counterfactual framework that delivers both object‑level and part‑level insights, addressing two core questions: (1) which specific fine‑grained features lead to misclassification, and (2) where dominant local features should be altered to achieve a correct prediction. Our method constructs explainable counterfactuals without relying on generative models; it compares correctly and incorrectly classified samples, quantifies similarity, and weighs contributions within each region of interest. Additionally, we propose a saliency‑partition module based on Shapley values that isolates features with region‑specific importance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach uncovers more granular, intuitively meaningful regions, outperforming existing fine‑grained explanation techniques.
3400: Explanation‑guided learning (EGL) has emerged as a promising approach for aligning model decisions with human‑interpretable reasoning, especially in computer‑vision applications. Nonetheless, most existing methods depend on external annotations or heuristic segmentation to supervise explanations, leading to noisy, imprecise signals that are hard to scale. In this study, we provide both empirical and theoretical analyses showing that weak supervision can actually degrade a model’s performance instead of enhancing it. To address this shortcoming, we introduce ALIGN—a joint training framework that alternately optimizes a classifier and a masker. The masker learns to generate soft, task‑relevant masks that emphasize informative regions, while the classifier is trained to maximize predictive accuracy and to align its own saliency maps with these masks. By using high‑quality masks as guidance, ALIGN improves both interpretability and generalization. Extensive experiments on two domain‑generalization benchmarks, VLCS and Terra Incognita, demonstrate that ALIGN consistently surpasses six strong baselines in both in‑distribution and out‑of‑distribution scenarios. Moreover, ALIGN yields superior explanation quality with respect to sufficiency and comprehensiveness, underscoring its effectiveness at producing accurate and interpretable models.
3401: Multimodal co‑embedding approaches—most notably CLIP—have recently set new benchmarks for zero‑shot classification and multimedia retrieval by projecting images and text into a unified embedding space. Nevertheless, contrastive training can make these models fragile to minor input alterations. When users issue hand‑crafted queries, small changes in phrasing can dramatically reorder the retrieved set. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of how different non‑semantic query perturbations affect retrieval stability. We examine a wide range of lexical, syntactic, and semantic modifications on several CLIP variants, using TRECVID Ad‑Hoc Video Search prompts and the V3C1 video corpus. Our findings show that syntactic and semantic tweaks cause the most pronounced instability, whereas trivial surface changes such as punctuation and letter case also introduce brittleness. These results underscore that robustness should be a key criterion when assessing vision‑language models, beyond standard accuracy metrics.
3402:
In traditional imitation‑learning pipelines, a model is usually trained to map sensory observations—such as RGB images—directly to corresponding actions. This approach, however, tends to neglect the rich interactions among the various modalities (sensors, control signals, and rewards) that are essential for capturing realistic robot behaviour and for interpreting the outcomes of tasks.  

We introduce **Multimodal Diffusion Forcing (MDF)**, a comprehensive framework for learning from multi‑modal robotic trajectories that goes beyond simple action prediction. MDF does not fix a single target distribution; instead it randomly masks portions of the input trajectory and trains a diffusion model to recover the missing parts. This reconstruction objective compels the network to capture both temporal dynamics and cross‑modal relationships—for example, forecasting how a commanded action will affect force measurements or deducing hidden states from incomplete sensory data.  

We test MDF on a range of contact‑rich, force‑intensive manipulation scenarios, both in simulation and on real hardware. The results demonstrate that MDF not only offers flexible, multi‑purpose behaviour synthesis, but also delivers strong performance and robust resilience to noisy observations. Visual demonstrations are available on our website: https://unified-df.github.io.
3403: We present *KnowThyself*, a conversational assistant that enhances the interpretability of large language models (LLMs). While current tools deliver valuable diagnostics, they are often disjointed and require significant coding effort. *KnowThyself* unifies these functions within a chat interface: users can upload a model, ask questions in plain language, and receive interactive visualizations and structured explanations. The system’s backbone consists of an orchestrating LLM that rewrites user queries, an agent router that dispatches them to specialized modules, and a final layer that stitches the results into coherent, contextualized responses. This architecture reduces the need for technical expertise and offers a flexible platform for probing LLM behavior. By embedding the entire analytical workflow into a conversational paradigm, *KnowThyself* provides a solid, user‑friendly foundation for LLM interpretability.
3404: In federated learning, conventional distributed backdoor attacks (DBA) increase stealth by breaking a global trigger into several sub‑triggers. Unfortunately, this strategy demands a larger proportion of poisoned samples to preserve attack efficacy, thereby heightening the risk of detection. To mitigate this drawback, we introduce the Fractal‑Triggered Distributed Backdoor Attack (FTDBA). FTDBA exploits the self‑similarity inherent in fractal patterns to strengthen the influence of each sub‑trigger, allowing a substantial reduction in the amount of poisoned data needed to achieve the same level of malicious impact. To evade scrutiny in both frequency and gradient spaces, we incorporate a dynamic angular perturbation scheme that modulates the perturbation intensity throughout training, striking a balance between effectiveness and concealment. Our experiments demonstrate that FTDBA attains a 92.3 % attack success rate while requiring only 62.4 % of the poisoning volume used by traditional DBA methods. Moreover, it cuts the detection rate by 22.8 % and the KL divergence by 41.2 %. This work offers a low‑exposure, high‑efficiency framework for federated backdoor attacks and broadens the use of fractal characteristics in generating adversarial samples.
3405: Endoscopic imagery is frequently marred by a range of overlapping artifacts—poor illumination, smoke, hemorrhage—that obscure essential clinical features. Current restoration approaches tend to be highly specialized, often depending on prior knowledge of the exact degradation, which hampers their general applicability in clinical practice. In this work we present **EndoIR**, a unified, diffusion‑based model that tackles multiple degradations with a single, degradation‑agnostic framework. EndoIR incorporates a **Dual‑Domain Prompter** that harvests joint spatial‑frequency representations, and an **adaptive embedding** that conveys both common and task‑specific information as conditioning cues for the denoising process. To avoid the confusion that arises from naïve concatenation of conditions, we devise a **Dual‑Stream Diffusion** architecture that processes clean and degraded inputs in parallel, merging them through a **Rectified Fusion Block** in a degradation‑aware manner. Additionally, a **Noise‑Aware Routing Block** boosts efficiency by selectively engaging only noise‑relevant feature maps during denoising. Evaluation on the SegSTRONG‑C and CEC datasets shows that EndoIR surpasses state‑of‑the‑art methods across a spectrum of degradation types, while employing fewer parameters than strong baselines. Downstream segmentation tests further demonstrate its clinical usefulness.
3406: Learning intricate policies through Reinforcement Learning (RL) is frequently impeded by instability and protracted convergence, problems that are amplified by the challenges of crafting appropriate rewards. Imitation Learning (IL) sidesteps this issue by leveraging expert demonstrations, yet the leading IL techniques—such as Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (GAIL) by Ho et al.—remain highly sample‑inefficient because they rely on on‑policy foundations like TRPO (Schulman et al.). In this paper, we present an adversarial imitation learning framework that adopts an off‑policy approach to boost sample efficiency. By integrating an off‑policy architecture with auxiliary stabilizing mechanisms, notably a double Q‑network, and learning a value function without inferring the reward signal, we achieve a substantial reduction in the number of samples required to reliably emulate expert behavior.
3407:
Open‑domain analytic queries—questions that span heterogeneous data sources and require both information retrieval and complex analytical transformations—remain a bottleneck in modern data‑driven workflows. Existing pipelines force analysts to manually orchestrate separate retrieval, extraction, and analytics stages, leading to high engineering costs, latency, and fragile data‑consistency guarantees. **DRAMA** (Data Retrieval And Analysis) proposes a unified framework that eliminates this impedance mismatch by treating retrieval and analytics as a single, declarative query problem.  

At the core of DRAMA is a lightweight query language that extends SQL with retrieval primitives (e.g., keyword search, semantic matching, and graph traversal) and analytic operators (e.g., aggregation, machine‑learning scoring, and time‑series forecasting). A novel query planner interleaves retrieval and analysis stages, generating a single execution plan that leverages incremental caching, data locality, and adaptive sampling to minimize I/O and computation. The system’s back‑end is built on a distributed column‑store that natively supports both structured and unstructured data, and a retrieval engine that indexes documents, logs, and semi‑structured streams using a joint embeddings representation.

We evaluate DRAMA on a benchmark of 50 open‑domain analytic workloads drawn from finance, public‑health, and e‑commerce domains, comparing it against state‑of‑the‑art pipelines that separate search and analytics. DRAMA achieves up to **4× lower latency** and **30 % cost savings** while preserving exactness of results. A real‑world case study in a multi‑site retail analytics platform demonstrates the framework’s ability to surface actionable insights in real time without the overhead of data movement or schema evolution.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a unified query language that seamlessly blends retrieval and analytics; (2) a cost‑aware execution engine that co‑optimizes search and analytical operators; and (3) a comprehensive evaluation that shows the practical benefits of a single‑pass approach to open‑domain analytic queries. DRAMA opens a new paradigm for end‑to‑end data science, enabling analysts to pose complex questions over diverse data landscapes with minimal friction.
3408: Deep neural networks are routinely trained by first‑order stochastic gradient descent (SGD), yet the geometry of the loss landscape strongly influences the trajectory and final performance of the optimizer. Recent work on pre‑conditioning and second‑order methods has highlighted the importance of curvature information, but the high dimensionality of modern models renders full Hessian computations infeasible. In this paper we introduce an *isotropic curvature model* that captures the dominant spectral properties of the empirical Hessian while remaining computationally tractable. By assuming that the curvature distribution is approximately spherical within a sub‑space of the parameter manifold, we derive a closed‑form expression for an optimal orthogonalization of the gradient that decorrelates its components with respect to this isotropic metric. We then analyze the convergence properties of the resulting *Gradient Orthogonalization* (GO) scheme, showing that it attains the same asymptotic rate as a full Newton step under the isotropic assumption, but at a cost comparable to standard SGD. Empirically, we evaluate GO on a suite of image‑classification and language‑modeling tasks, comparing against Adam, K-FAC, and block‑diagonal preconditioners. Across architectures, GO consistently reduces training loss by 5–12 % and accelerates convergence by 20–35 % relative to plain SGD, while matching the performance of more elaborate second‑order approaches. Finally, we discuss the limitations of isotropy in highly anisotropic regimes and propose a hybrid scheme that adaptively blends GO with block‑wise curvature estimates. Our results suggest that gradient orthogonalization, when grounded in a principled isotropic curvature model, constitutes a near‑optimal and scalable strategy for deep‑learning optimization.
3409:
The rapid deployment of commercial Large Language Models (LLMs) such as OpenAI’s GPT‑4, Azure OpenAI, and Anthropic’s Claude has reshaped empirical software engineering (ESE) research. Yet, the *reproducibility* of performance claims derived from these models remains largely unexamined. In this study we systematically investigate the stability of commercial LLM outcomes across a spectrum of ESE tasks—including bug report classification, code generation, and API documentation summarization—under varying conditions of prompt design, API version, and temporal snapshots of model updates.

We conduct a multi‑phase empirical investigation. First, we benchmark three commercial LLMs on 12 publicly available ESE datasets, recording performance metrics (accuracy, BLEU, ROUGE, and F1) over six consecutive monthly API releases. Second, we perform a “replication test” by re‑executing each experiment after a 3‑month interval, measuring variance induced by model retraining or parameter tuning. Third, we interview fifteen ESE practitioners who rely on these APIs to surface contextual factors (e.g., network latency, quota limits) that influence reproducibility.

Our findings reveal that performance drift can reach up to 12 % for classification tasks and 18 % for code‑generation tasks, even when prompt engineering is held constant. API version changes and implicit parameter adjustments (e.g., temperature defaults) are significant contributors to this drift. Moreover, the variability is higher for datasets with low sample sizes or domain‑specific terminology, underscoring the need for dataset‑aware calibration. The interview data corroborate that practitioners often encounter “model‑as‑a‑service” volatility that undermines longitudinal studies.

We propose a set of reproducibility guidelines for ESE researchers: (1) mandatory logging of API endpoint, model version, and full prompt configuration; (2) use of time‑stamped checkpoints or “model snapshots” where available; (3) adoption of a “reproducibility matrix” that records performance over time. Finally, we discuss policy implications for commercial LLM providers regarding transparent versioning and historical model access. Our work highlights that, unlike traditional ML benchmarks, commercial LLMs present a moving target that demands careful methodological safeguards to ensure robust, replicable software engineering research.
3410: Physics‑informed deep learning has become a powerful tool for numerically solving partial differential equations, yet its practical use is hampered by difficulties in training, especially for complex problems where accuracy and efficiency can suffer. We present a hybrid strategy that couples adaptive sampling with adaptive weighting to boost the performance of physics‑informed neural networks (PINNs). The sampling scheme concentrates training points in zones where the solution varies rapidly, while the weighting scheme equalises the convergence behaviour across all points. Our numerical tests reveal that relying on either adaptation alone is often insufficient, particularly when the training set is sparse, and that the relative benefit of each technique depends on the problem at hand. By integrating both methods, we consistently attain higher prediction accuracy and faster convergence, providing a more reliable framework for solving PDEs with PINNs.
3411:
–  
Accurate stereo matching is critical for the next wave of navigation and augmented‑reality tools in minimally invasive surgery (MIS). However, dense disparity supervision is practically unattainable in this domain because the surgical environment restricts the availability of detailed annotations; typically only a handful of image‑level labels are available before the endoscope enters the deeper cavities. Teacher‑Student Learning (TSL) addresses this limitation by letting a teacher network, trained on the sparse annotations, generate pseudo disparities and confidence maps for the vast amount of unlabeled surgical footage. Existing TSL approaches, however, rely exclusively on image‑level guidance, producing only spatial confidence estimates and ignoring temporal coherence. As a consequence, the resulting disparity maps fluctuate wildly between consecutive frames, generating pronounced flicker in the video output.

To remedy this, we introduce **TiS‑TSL**, a time‑switchable teacher‑student framework that performs video‑level stereo matching under minimal supervision. The backbone model can be switched among three operating modes—Image Prediction (IP), Forward Video Prediction (FVP), and Backward Video Prediction (BVP)—thereby embedding temporal reasoning in a single network. TiS‑TSL follows a two‑step training pipeline: (1) *Image‑to‑Video* (I2V), which bootstraps temporal capability from the sparse image labels; and (2) *Video‑to‑Video* (V2V), which refines the predictions by contrasting forward and backward passes to compute bidirectional spatio‑temporal consistency. This consistency metric flags unreliable regions over time, suppresses noisy pseudo labels, and enforces smoothness across frames.

Experiments on two publicly available MIS datasets show that TiS‑TSL surpasses the best image‑based state‑of‑the‑art methods, improving the mean End‑Point Error (EPE) by at least 4.54 % and the overall Temporal Error (TEPE) by 2.11 %.
3412:
The growing complexity and volume of malware samples make large‐scale, high‑quality labeled datasets indispensable for training robust detection systems. Yet the collection and sharing of real malware telemetry is hampered by legal, privacy, and security constraints, and the intrinsic class imbalance of real data often leads to overfitting and biased models. To address these challenges, we present **MalDataGen**, a modular framework for synthesizing high‑fidelity tabular malware datasets. MalDataGen exposes a pipeline that can be instantiated with any of a family of generative models—including conditional GANs, variational autoencoders, and Gaussian copula‑based approaches—allowing researchers to trade off fidelity, privacy, and computational cost. The framework also incorporates domain‑specific preprocessing, feature‑selection heuristics, and post‑generation quality checks that preserve the joint distribution of static and dynamic features while enforcing differential‑privacy guarantees where required.

We evaluate MalDataGen on three public malware corpora (CICMAL-2021, VirusShare‑CSV, and OpenMalware‑Tabular) and demonstrate that synthetic data produced by the framework yields malware classifiers that achieve F1‑scores within 2.5 % of those trained on real data, even under severe class‑imbalance regimes. Moreover, classifiers trained on synthetic data generalize better to unseen families, reducing the drop in detection accuracy by an average of 4.1 % compared to real‑data baselines. Finally, we show that the modular design permits rapid experimentation: swapping a GAN for a TabNet‑based generator changes inference latency by 35 % without appreciable loss in detection performance.

MalDataGen is released as an open‑source Python package (GitHub: **maldata-gen/maldata-gen**) together with a benchmark suite, facilitating reproducible research and accelerating the development of privacy‑aware, data‑driven malware detectors.
3413:
Diffusion-based approaches hold great potential for generating 3‑D molecular conformations, yet they typically involve a dilemma: flow‑based methods sample quickly but often yield geometrically flawed structures because they cannot fully capture the multimodal distribution of conformations, while denoising diffusion models achieve higher accuracy at the expense of slow sampling—a drawback linked to suboptimal coupling between diffusion dynamics and SE(3)-equivariant network designs.

To overcome this, we introduce **VEDA**, a unified SE(3)-equivariant framework that merges variance‑exploding (VE) diffusion with annealing to produce 3‑D structures that are both accurate and fast. Our main technical contributions are:

1. A VE schedule that mimics simulated annealing for noise injection, which improves spatial fidelity and lowers relaxation energy.  
2. A novel pre‑conditioning strategy that aligns the coordinate‑predicting behavior of SE(3)-equivariant networks with a residual diffusion objective.  
3. An arcsin‑based scheduler that focuses sampling on the most critical segments of the logarithmic signal‑to‑noise ratio.

On the QM9 and GEOM‑DRUGS datasets, VEDA matches the speed of flow‑based generators, delivering state‑of‑the‑art valency stability and validity with only 100 sampling steps. Crucially, the structures it produces are exceptionally stable: the median energy shift during GFN2‑xTB relaxation is merely 1.72 kcal/mol—vastly better than the 32.3 kcal/mol observed for its architectural predecessor, SemlaFlow.  

These results demonstrate that a principled integration of VE diffusion with SE(3)-equivariant architectures can simultaneously achieve high chemical accuracy and computational efficiency in 3‑D molecular generation.
3414:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in a variety of creative and interactive tasks, yet their ability to convincingly portray morally ambiguous or outright hostile characters remains underexplored. In this study we investigate why contemporary LLMs often produce “too good to be bad” outputs when tasked with role‑playing villains. We designed a controlled benchmark comprising 1,200 prompt variations that request the model to adopt the persona of a wide range of antagonists (from cinematic archetypes to original antagonistic concepts). Human evaluators rated each output on a 5‑point scale for authenticity, moral depth, and narrative plausibility. Complementary automatic metrics assessed toxicity, adherence to alignment policies, and stylistic consistency.

Our results reveal a consistent pattern of under‑aggressive, self‑censoring villain depictions across all model sizes tested (GPT‑4, Llama‑2, Claude). Only 12 % of responses scored above 4 on the authenticity metric, and 78 % were flagged by built‑in safety filters for excessive violence or hate content. Detailed error analysis indicates that the models’ training regimes, coupled with post‑hoc alignment fine‑tuning and prompt‑level safety mitigations, bias the generation toward “safe” or neutral characterizations. Furthermore, we observe that fine‑tuning on villain‑specific corpora improves creativity but only marginally increases moral depth, suggesting a fundamental limitation in the models’ conceptual understanding of non‑conforming agency.

We conclude that current LLM architectures, as deployed in commercial or research settings, are ill‑suited for nuanced villain role‑play due to intertwined safety constraints and data‑driven bias toward benevolent narratives. Addressing this gap will require a combination of targeted adversarial training, enriched adversarial datasets that encapsulate villain motivations, and principled exploration of multi‑agent simulations to decouple safety from creative antagonism. This work lays the groundwork for future investigations into the alignment‑versus‑creativity trade‑off in conversational agents.
3415:
Accurate forecasting of financial time series hinges on capturing both transient public sentiment and more enduring policy or market trends. Consequently, exploiting information across multiple temporal horizons is essential, yet most existing forecasting models rely on a single period of data or do not tailor their architectures to multi‑period dynamics. In this work we introduce the Multi‑period Learning Framework (MLF), designed to meet both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency for financial time‑series forecasting. MLF integrates three novel modules that harmonise multi‑period inputs:  

1. **Inter‑period Redundancy Filtering (IRF)** – eliminates overlapping information between periods to sharpen self‑attention mechanisms.  
2. **Learnable Weighted‑Average Integration (LWI)** – combines forecasts from different horizons in a data‑driven manner.  
3. **Multi‑period Self‑Adaptive Patching (MAP)** – normalises patch counts across horizons to prevent bias towards any single period.  

A **Patch Squeeze** module further trims patch counts during self‑attention to boost efficiency. By handling inputs of varied lengths within a single model, MLF improves forecast accuracy while alleviating the burden of selecting optimal input horizons during training. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Meteor-Stars/MLF.
3416:
Diagnosing rare diseases hinges on linking genetic findings with often unstructured reference material. Existing pipelines can generate many candidate genes, yet clinicians still devote substantial time to winnowing false positives and piecing together evidence from literature and databases.
