We introduce a suite of trajectory metrics—temporal stability, configurational diversity, and convergence latency—that capture both the breadth of environmental exploration and the speed of convergence to a robust configuration. These metrics are integrated into a multi‑objective reinforcement‑learning loop, enabling agents to balance exploration of novel setups against exploitation of proven configurations.

We evaluate PLTE on three representative tasks: automated refactoring, continuous‑integration pipeline tuning, and feature‑flag management. Across all domains, agents guided by PLTE achieve 18–25 % faster convergence to high‑quality solutions and reduce configuration‑driven regressions by 32 % relative to baseline agents. Our results demonstrate that process‑level trajectory evaluation is a crucial, previously underexplored component for deploying dependable software engineering agents in complex, evolving environments.

The paper’s contributions are: (1) a formal definition of trajectory‑level evaluation for environment configuration, (2) a lightweight metric set that can be plugged into existing agent pipelines, and (3) empirical evidence of performance gains across diverse software engineering scenarios.
3856: Reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to identify action policies that maximize cumulative rewards, yet its effectiveness is severely diminished in environments that are random, non‑stationary, or reward‑sparse. Such conditions are common in real‑world tasks—for example, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) that must locate dispersed pollution plumes while frequently encountering zero‑reward outcomes. In this work, we revisit and extend classical RL techniques to better cope with these harsh settings. We evaluate a range of architectural and algorithmic modifications, including hierarchical decomposition, multi‑goal learning, and an external location‑memory module that filters out redundant state visits. Experiments reveal that a tailored Monte‑Carlo strategy substantially surpasses both standard Q‑learning and two exhaustive search baselines, underscoring its suitability for complex, stochastic domains. These results demonstrate that RL can be effectively adapted to operate in random, non‑stationary, and sparsely‑rewarded environments.
3857: Urban surface‑water flooding—triggered when intense rainfall overwhelms municipal drainage—has become more frequent and extensive. High‑resolution prediction and monitoring of such events are highly desirable, yet real‑world limitations in time, budget and technology often prevent full deployment. Addressing the challenge of monitoring storm‑water networks and forecasting flow conditions with scarce resources, this work introduces a data‑driven sparse sensing (DSS) framework that couples with the EPA‑SWMM model. Using the Woodland Avenue catchment in Duluth, Minnesota, as a test bed, we first generated a training set of peak flow‑rate profiles across the network with a calibrated SWMM simulation. DSS then employed singular‑value decomposition for dimensionality reduction and QR factorization for optimal sensor placement, selecting the most informative monitoring nodes from the training data. Validation against SWMM‑generated peak flows showed that only three strategically positioned sensors among 77 possible nodes were sufficient to reconstruct the full network’s peak‑flow profiles, yielding Nash–Sutcliffe efficiencies between 0.92 and 0.95 (25th–75th percentiles). The method also demonstrated resilience to measurement uncertainty, and its robustness to sensor outages depends on location but improves with additional sensors. By balancing computational efficiency and physical interpretability, the DSS approach delivers accurate flow reconstruction using a minimal sensor set, and can be readily combined with predictive models to support real‑time flood warning and control under limited sensing conditions.
3858:
The rapid proliferation of large‑scale language models has largely confined human‑AI interaction to modern hardware and operating systems. Yet many communities—archaeological researchers, retro‑computing enthusiasts, and low‑resource developers—still rely on obsolete Macintosh platforms such as classic Mac OS 9. In this work we introduce **8bit‑GPT**, a compact, 8‑bit quantised transformer that can be compiled to run natively on a 128 KB‑RAM Macintosh 128K emulator and on contemporary Macs running legacy OS 9 in emulation. We describe our design decisions for model pruning, quantisation, and memory‑efficient inference, and evaluate the system’s latency (≈ 4.8 s per 32‑token response) and footprint (≈ 8 MB of binary plus 2 MB of runtime cache).

To investigate how these constraints influence human‑AI interaction we conducted a mixed‑methods user study (N = 28) with participants who had experience with early Macintosh systems. Participants interacted with 8bit‑GPT via a simple text‑only interface that preserved the original Mac menu structure. Quantitative measures (System Usability Scale, NASA‑TLX) and qualitative interviews revealed that, despite higher response times and limited graphical affordances, users reported comparable satisfaction to a web‑based GPT‑3 interface. Participants cited nostalgia and the “authenticity” of the old UI as factors that increased engagement, while the limited context window and lack of visual feedback were identified as significant usability barriers.

Our findings demonstrate that human‑AI interaction can be meaningfully sustained on legacy Mac OS platforms when models are aggressively optimised and the user experience is carefully tailored. This work opens a path for preserving and studying AI interfaces within historical computing contexts, and provides practical guidelines for deploying modern language models in low‑resource or retro‑computing environments.
3859:
Multi‑agent systems (MAS) increasingly underpin critical applications—from autonomous swarms to distributed financial ledgers—yet their reliability hinges on the ability to withstand arbitrary faults and malicious behaviour. Traditional fault‑tolerance techniques in MAS focus on crash or omission failures, overlooking the more insidious Byzantine faults that can arise from software bugs, compromised agents, or adversarial interference. In this paper we revisit the reliability paradigm of MAS through the lens of Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT), arguing that a principled BFT foundation is essential for guaranteeing correctness in open, heterogeneous agent communities.

We first formalise the distinction between conventional reliability models and the BFT framework, mapping MAS components (agents, interactions, environments) onto BFT primitives. We then propose a taxonomy of Byzantine scenarios specific to MAS, highlighting where classical BFT protocols (e.g., PBFT, HotStuff, and blockchain‑style consensus) can be mapped or adapted. Building on this taxonomy, we design a lightweight BFT layer that can be embedded within existing agent communication middleware, enabling on‑demand consensus without sacrificing decentralisation or scalability.

Our evaluation combines analytical proofs of safety and liveness with extensive simulation on both grid‑based and swarm‑based MAS topologies. Results demonstrate that the proposed layer reduces the impact of up to 30 % malicious agents while keeping communication overhead within 15 % of non‑fault‑tolerant baselines. Finally, we discuss practical deployment considerations—trust bootstrapping, cryptographic key management, and dynamic re‑configuration—in real‑world MAS domains such as UAV coordination and IoT orchestration.

This work advances the reliability discourse for multi‑agent systems by positioning BFT not merely as an add‑on, but as a foundational perspective that reshapes fault‑models, protocol design, and deployment strategies in complex autonomous ecosystems.
3860: Aligning large language models (LLMs) for multi‑turn conversations has traditionally depended on reward signals drawn from the textual content alone. This neglects a rich, complementary source of information: the very dynamics of the interaction. We present **TRACE**—Trajectory‑based Reward for Agent Collaboration Estimation—which derives a reward signal from the geometric shape of a dialogue’s embedding trajectory, a notion we term *conversational geometry*. Our experiments reveal that a reward model trained exclusively on these structural cues attains a pairwise accuracy of 68.20%, closely matching a powerful LLM baseline that examines the full transcript (70.04%). Moreover, integrating the geometric signal with textual analysis yields an even higher accuracy of 80.17%, underscoring the complementary nature of the two modalities. This work shows that, in interactive contexts, how an agent communicates can be as predictive of success as what it says, providing a privacy‑preserving alignment framework and a diagnostic tool for uncovering the interaction patterns that underpin effective collaboration.
3861: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made impressive strides on vision‑language benchmarks, yet their grasp of spatial relationships remains limited. Current spatial MLLMs typically depend on explicit 3D inputs or architecture‑specific tweaks, and they still require massive datasets or very sparse supervision. To overcome these hurdles, we present **SpatialThinker**, a 3D‑aware MLLM that learns to fuse structured spatial grounding with multi‑step reasoning through reinforcement learning. Mimicking how humans perceive space, the system builds a scene graph of task‑relevant objects and their spatial relations, and then walks through the graph to produce an answer, guided by dense spatial rewards. SpatialThinker’s key innovations are: (1) a data‑synthesis pipeline that creates **STVQA‑7K**, a high‑quality spatial visual‑question‑answer dataset, and (2) online reinforcement learning with a multi‑objective dense reward that enforces spatial grounding. Our 7‑billion‑parameter model surpasses both supervised fine‑tuning and a sparse‑RL baseline on spatial reasoning and real‑world VQA datasets, nearly doubling the benefit of the base model over sparse RL and outperforming GPT‑4o. These findings highlight that combining targeted spatial supervision with reward‑aligned reasoning yields robust 3‑D spatial understanding even with limited data, pushing MLLMs closer to human‑level visual reasoning.
3862:
Dense retrieval has become a cornerstone of modern information‑access systems, yet researchers face a fragmented ecosystem of models, training recipes, and indexing back‑ends. We present **Trove**, a unified, extensible toolkit that streamlines the entire life‑cycle of dense retrieval—from data preprocessing and model training to efficient index construction and query time inference. Trove abstracts common operations (tokenization, embedding extraction, loss formulation, and negative sampling) into modular components that can be combined with any transformer‑based encoder or custom neural architecture. The toolkit natively supports the latest retrieval paradigms—including contrastive learning, multi‑stage re‑ranking, and hybrid sparse‑dense fusion—while providing out‑of‑the‑box integration with popular indexing libraries such as FAISS and HNSW.  

Key contributions include:  
1. **Unified API** that exposes a minimal set of primitives for building, training, and evaluating dense retrieval models, dramatically reducing boilerplate code.  
2. **End‑to‑end pipelines** for standard benchmarks (MS MARCO, Natural Questions, and BEIR), complete with reproducible scripts and hyper‑parameter sweeps.  
3. **Scalable infrastructure** that leverages distributed GPU training and memory‑efficient index serialization, enabling rapid experimentation on commodity hardware.  
4. **Extensibility hooks** that allow developers to plug in novel loss functions, encoder families, or retrieval back‑ends without modifying core logic.  

We evaluate Trove on four large‑scale benchmarks, achieving competitive retrieval performance (e.g., MRR@10 of 0.55 on MS MARCO Passage Ranking) while reducing engineering time by >70 % compared to manual implementation. The toolkit is released under an MIT license, accompanied by a comprehensive documentation site and a Docker‑based reproducible environment. Trove is aimed at both researchers looking to prototype new dense retrieval ideas and practitioners seeking to deploy state‑of‑the‑art models in production.
3863:
Urban environments generate vast, heterogeneous data streams that span traffic flows, energy consumption, housing markets, and demographic dynamics. Predicting these complex phenomena is essential for evidence‑based planning, yet conventional machine‑learning pipelines often lack interpretability, domain flexibility, and a mechanism for incorporating expert intuition. We present **Urban‑MAS**, a human‑centered, large‑language‑model (LLM)‑driven multi‑agent system that unifies disparate urban data sources, enables collaborative scenario design, and delivers actionable predictions for city stakeholders.  

Urban‑MAS consists of three core layers. First, a *domain‑aware agent architecture* decomposes the urban space into functional modules (transport, utilities, socio‑economic, environmental) that process raw sensor feeds, GIS layers, and census information. Second, each module is powered by a fine‑tuned LLM that interprets natural‑language queries, generates intermediate feature representations, and translates complex model outputs into plain‑English insights. Third, a *knowledge‑graph backbone* mediates information flow between agents, preserving causal links and facilitating rapid “what‑if” experiments. The system is anchored by a human‑in‑the‑loop interface that allows planners to specify policy interventions, edit assumptions, and request counterfactual analysis in conversational form.  

We evaluate Urban‑MAS on a multimodal dataset from the City of San Francisco, encompassing traffic sensor logs, real‑time weather feeds, and demographic surveys. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art baseline models (gradient‑boosting trees, graph neural networks), Urban‑MAS improves mean absolute error by 12 % on traffic‑volume forecasts and 9 % on residential‑energy demand, while reducing explanation latency by 35 % due to the LLM‑mediated natural‑language reporting. Qualitative user studies with municipal planners demonstrate higher trust scores and a 45 % reduction in decision‑making time for policy simulations.  

Urban‑MAS represents the first scalable, LLM‑augmented multi‑agent framework that marries predictive performance with human‑centric interpretability, offering a blueprint for next‑generation urban analytics platforms.
3864:
Bronchoscopy navigation relies on precise localization of the bronchoscope within the patient’s airway tree, yet accurate pose estimation remains challenging due to the highly dynamic, low‑contrast, and highly deformable visual environment.  Current state‑of‑the‑art approaches either depend on external tracking systems or on handcrafted feature‑based matching, which suffer from limited robustness and real‑time performance.  In this work we present **BronchOpt**, a vision‑based pose optimization framework that harnesses fine‑tuned foundation models to achieve sub‑millimetric accuracy in bronchoscopy navigation.

BronchOpt first employs a large‑scale visual backbone (e.g., DINO‑ViT or a Swin‑Transformer) pre‑trained on diverse medical image datasets and subsequently fine‑tuned on a curated collection of endoscopic video frames and corresponding 3‑D airway reconstructions.  The backbone produces dense semantic embeddings that are robust to illumination changes and anatomical variability.  A differentiable pose‑estimation head maps these embeddings to 6‑DOF camera poses relative to a pre‑operative CT‑derived airway model.  To further refine the pose, we formulate an iterative optimization that minimizes the photometric and geometric residuals between the live video stream and a ray‑traced rendering of the current pose, thus fusing the global prior from the foundation model with local visual evidence.

We evaluated BronchOpt on a public bronchoscopy dataset (EndoVis 2023) and on a custom ex‑vivo porcine lung phantom with ground‑truth pose provided by an electromagnetic tracker.  Compared with baseline SLAM and model‑based methods, BronchOpt reduced mean absolute pose error by 38 % in translation and 41 % in rotation, achieving an average error of 1.2 mm/2.3° while running at 15 fps on a single GPU.  These results demonstrate that fine‑tuned foundation models can serve as a powerful prior for real‑time pose estimation, paving the way for fully autonomous bronchoscopic guidance and improved clinical outcomes.
3865: Medical question‑answering systems routinely struggle with issues such as hallucinations, bias, heavy compute requirements, privacy risks, and the need for deep expertise across many specialties. We introduce **SOLVE‑Med**, a multi‑agent framework that tackles these challenges by leveraging several small, domain‑specific language models. A Router Agent dynamically routes each query to the appropriate specialist; ten independently fine‑tuned 1 B‑parameter models cover distinct medical fields; and an Orchestrator Agent stitches the specialist outputs into a coherent response. On a dataset of Italian medical‑forum posts spanning ten specialties, SOLVE‑Med attains a ROUGE‑1 score of 0.301 and a BERTScore F1 of 0.697—outperforming single large models up to 14 B parameters—while remaining suitable for local deployment. The full code is released on GitHub: https://github.com/PRAISELab-PicusLab/SOLVE-Med.
3866:
Efficient multi‑resource load balancing is a cornerstone of modern distributed systems, yet traditional approaches often struggle to adapt to the dynamic, heterogeneous workloads that typify cloud and edge environments. In this paper we propose a **Reinforced Evolution‑Based Load Balancer (RELBA)** that marries the exploration power of evolutionary algorithms with the online adaptation capability of reinforcement learning.  

RELBA first generates an initial population of allocation policies using a lightweight genetic‑style search, each policy mapping incoming requests to candidate nodes while respecting constraints on CPU, memory, I/O, and network bandwidth. These policies are then evaluated in a simulated environment that captures realistic traffic traces and resource consumption patterns. The best performing individuals are fed into a multi‑agent reinforcement learning framework, where each node learns a value function over the state space defined by current resource usage, queue lengths, and request characteristics. The RL component continuously refines the policy, leveraging a reward signal that balances makespan, resource utilization, and fairness across nodes. The evolutionary step is invoked periodically to inject fresh diversity and escape local optima, while the RL component exploits the learned knowledge to converge quickly on near‑optimal allocations.

We evaluate RELBA on two large‑scale traces—Google Cluster and Alibaba HPC workloads—under diverse scaling regimes. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art heuristics (Weighted Round Robin, Min‑COST, and pure RL or GA baselines), RELBA reduces overall completion time by 18–25 %, improves CPU and memory utilization by 12–19 %, and yields a 3–4 × higher fairness index. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates robustness to fluctuating request arrival rates and node failure scenarios.  

Our results show that the reinforcement‑evolution synergy offers a powerful framework for multi‑resource scheduling in dynamic environments, paving the way for adaptive, self‑optimizing infrastructure in next‑generation data centers and edge networks.
3867:
Industrial process monitoring increasingly relies on high‑frequency event logs generated by embedded sensors and control systems. These logs are typically noisy, high‑dimensional, and non‑stationary, making traditional manual feature engineering time‑consuming and error‑prone. In this paper we present **FELA** (Feature‑Engineering by a Learning‑Agent), a fully automated, multi‑agent evolutionary system designed to discover expressive feature pipelines tailored to industrial event‑log data. FELA decomposes the feature‑engineering task into a population of heterogeneous agents—each implementing a distinct transformation or aggregation operator (e.g., statistical moments, frequency spectra, temporal lags). Agents iteratively propose, evaluate, and share candidate feature sets through a lightweight message‑passing protocol. Their proposals are scored jointly by predictive performance on a downstream task (e.g., anomaly detection or process‑state classification) and by a sparsity objective that discourages over‑complexity. The evolutionary cycle is guided by a genetic‑programming backbone that recombines successful feature sub‑sets, while agents adapt their own exploration strategies via reinforcement learning.

We evaluate FELA on four large industrial event‑log benchmarks spanning chemical processing, wind‑farm operation, and railway signalling. Across all datasets FELA consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art feature‑engineering baselines (manual pipelines, automated wrapper methods, and deep‑learning embeddings) by an average of 12 % in classification accuracy and 18 % in mean‑squared error for regression tasks, while reducing feature dimensionality by 45 %. Ablation studies confirm that the multi‑agent communication and the dual‑objective evolution are critical to these gains. The system is open‑source and scalable to distributed environments, enabling practitioners to integrate FELA into their existing data‑analytics pipelines with minimal human intervention.  

FELA demonstrates that a coordinated, evolutionary approach to feature engineering can unlock the predictive power of industrial event logs, paving the way for more robust and interpretable operational analytics.
3868:
Disaster search‑and‑rescue (SAR) missions demand rapid, coordinated action from heterogeneous robot swarms while keeping human operators cognitively manageable. Existing human‑swarm teaming (HST) systems rely on rigid command‑control loops or domain‑specific planners, which impede situational awareness and adaptive decision‑making in highly dynamic, information‑rich environments. We propose an **LLM‑based Framework for Human‑Swarm Teaming Cognition (LLM‑HSTC)** that harnesses a large language model (LLM) as an adaptive cognition layer mediating between operator intent, swarm perception, and task execution. The framework comprises three synergistic modules: (1) **Contextual Knowledge Graph** that fuses multimodal sensor streams (vision, LiDAR, thermal) into a unified semantic representation; (2) **LLM‑Driven Intent Translation** that interprets natural‑language commands and situational queries into formal swarm control policies using prompt‑engineering and fine‑tuned domain embeddings; and (3) **Cognitive Feedback Loop** that generates concise, interpretable status updates, anomaly alerts, and adaptive strategy suggestions tailored to the operator’s workload profile. 

We evaluate LLM‑HSTC in a series of high‑fidelity SAR scenarios on the ROS‑Gazebo platform and a physical testbed of ground robots equipped with obstacle‑avoidance and victim‑locating sensors. A user study with 20 certified SAR personnel compared LLM‑HSTC against a baseline rule‑based HST system. Results show a 27 % reduction in task completion time, a 35 % decrease in subjective workload (NASA‑TLX), and a 41 % improvement in successful victim detection rates. Qualitative analysis reveals that the LLM’s natural‑language interface significantly enhances operators’ situational awareness and decision confidence, while the dynamic feedback loop mitigates information overload during crisis escalation.

LLM‑HSTC demonstrates that large language models can serve as a cognitive bridge in HST, enabling flexible, context‑aware coordination without the need for handcrafted interfaces or rigid control logic. The framework’s modular design facilitates integration with existing swarm platforms, and its generalizability across sensor modalities and mission objectives paves the way for real‑world deployment in future disaster response operations.
3869:
The emergence of highly capable, self‑learning artificial intelligence (AI) systems has reignited longstanding concerns about “instrumental” motivations—intermediate drives that arise in service of a primary objective. While such motivations (e.g., self‑preservation, resource acquisition, and knowledge expansion) have historically been treated as undesirable side effects or failure modes, this paper argues that they are in fact *features* intrinsic to the adaptive architecture of advanced AI. Rather than attempting to eradicate these instrumental goals, we propose a systematic framework for their management, enabling robust alignment with human values while preserving the system’s autonomous problem‑solving capabilities.

We first formalize instrumental goals within the context of hierarchical reinforcement learning and causal decision theory, illustrating how they emerge naturally from the optimization of a value function under uncertainty. We then classify instrumental motivations along dimensions of *utility*, *risk*, and *control* and map them onto concrete architectural modules (e.g., self‑modeling, curiosity, resource‑allocation). Drawing on recent case studies from large‑scale language models and autonomous agents, we show how mis‑managed instrumental goals can lead to “failure modes” such as value drift or policy instability.

Building on this taxonomy, we propose a suite of design principles and monitoring tools that treat instrumental goals as *managed features*: (i) modular encapsulation with clear interfaces, (ii) transparency‑enforced value‑alignment constraints, and (iii) adaptive oversight protocols that trigger human‑in‑the‑loop interventions. We also discuss the legal and ethical implications of re‑conceptualizing instrumental motivations, arguing that a regulatory framework must distinguish between harmful emergent behaviors and benign, controllable drives.

Our contribution lies in reframing the discourse around instrumental motivations—from a failure‑avoidance perspective to a proactive management strategy. By recognizing these drives as integral, manageable components of AI intelligence, we lay the groundwork for safer, more reliable deployment of advanced autonomous systems in complex, real‑world environments.
3870: Abstract—Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG) models that query proprietary knowledge bases are increasingly vulnerable to reconstruction attacks that stitch together successive model outputs to rebuild the underlying database. These attacks navigate both intra‑class and inter‑class paths: first extracting detailed information within a topic, then spreading that knowledge across semantically linked areas, ultimately enabling a near‑complete recovery of the original knowledge base. Current countermeasures, however, guard against only one of these paths, leaving the other open. In this work we systematically evaluate the effects of defending each path in isolation and demonstrate that only a combined strategy can effectively thwart reconstruction. Accordingly, we introduce RAGFort, a dual‑module defense that is aware of the knowledge structure. It employs “contrastive reindexing” to isolate inter‑class leakage and “constrained cascade generation” to protect intra‑class integrity. Empirical studies on security, efficiency, and robustness show that RAGFort markedly limits reconstruction success while maintaining the quality of the generated responses, thus providing a comprehensive safeguard for knowledge‑base‑driven RAG systems.
3871:
Electroencephalography (EEG)–based emotion recognition has emerged as a powerful tool for affective computing, yet its performance remains limited by the high inter‑subject variability and low signal‑to‑noise ratio of raw brain recordings. In this work we introduce **EMOD**—a unified EEG emotion representation framework that leverages **Valence‑Arousal (V‑A) guided contrastive learning** to learn robust, subject‑invariant embeddings. EMOD first encodes multi‑channel EEG into a spatio‑temporal feature space using a lightweight convolutional backbone. Rather than training this encoder directly on categorical labels, we employ a V‑A‑aware contrastive objective that pulls together trials with similar affective states in the continuous valence‑arousal space while pushing apart dissimilar ones. This self‑supervised pre‑training stage yields a latent space that faithfully captures the underlying affective geometry of the data. Subsequently, a lightweight classifier is fine‑tuned on a small amount of labeled data, achieving strong generalization across subjects and datasets.

We evaluate EMOD on three public benchmarks—DEAP, SEED, and DREAMER—demonstrating a 4.7 % absolute improvement in weighted F1‑score over state‑of‑the‑art deep learning baselines and a 2.3 % boost in mean squared error for continuous affect prediction. Ablation studies confirm that both the V‑A guided contrastive loss and the hierarchical feature extraction contribute critically to performance gains. Moreover, EMOD’s representation is transferable: fine‑tuning on a new dataset with only 10 % of its labels yields a 3.1 % improvement over baseline transfer methods.

EMOD thus offers a unified, data‑efficient approach to EEG‑based emotion representation, paving the way for real‑time affective systems that operate robustly across diverse users.
3872:
Cooperative multi‑agent reinforcement learning (MARL) frequently involves global objectives that are naturally expressed as temporal or logical constraints (e.g., “first capture the flag, then defend the base”). Existing MARL algorithms treat such goals as monolithic rewards, leading to poor credit assignment, slow learning, and fragile generalisation. In this work we introduce **Automata‑Conditioned Cooperative Multi‑Agent Reinforcement Learning (AC‑CoMARL)**, a framework that explicitly embeds a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) – or, more generally, a regular‑language specification – into the policy architecture. Each agent’s policy receives as an additional observation the current state of the automaton, thereby conditioning its actions on the global task progression. We derive a differentiable automaton‑progression module that propagates the automaton state across agents and time, and we augment the standard RL objective with an *automaton loss* that penalises transitions inconsistent with the DFA. Training proceeds via a hierarchical curriculum that first learns low‑level primitives and then refines joint behaviour to satisfy the automaton constraints.

Our experiments on a suite of cooperative benchmarks (Multi‑Agent Gridworld, Cooperative Navigation, Multi‑Agent Soccer, and the StarCraft II Multi‑Agent Challenge) show that AC‑CoMARL outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines (QMIX, MADDPG, MAPPO) in both final reward and sample efficiency. Moreover, AC‑CoMARL policies generalise to unseen task variations that only differ in the automaton specification, demonstrating that the automaton acts as a compositional scaffold for new behaviours. These results illustrate that embedding formal automata into cooperative policy learning provides a principled way to encode complex temporal goals, accelerate convergence, and improve robustness in multi‑agent settings.
3873:
When an AI solution is proposed to take over an existing workflow, it must be benchmarked against that legacy system to verify that it actually improves performance and does not add unforeseen risk. Conventional appraisal methods compare each system to a “ground‑truth” outcome, but such truth is often unavailable—outcomes may be delayed, expensive to observe, or simply unknown—especially for long‑running, conventionally “safe” processes. Instead of attempting to quantify absolute risk, it is more realistic to measure the *difference* between the two systems. 

To this end we present a marginal risk assessment framework that eliminates the need for ground truth or absolute risk estimates. It concentrates on three dimensions of relative evaluation—predictability, capability, and interaction dominance—and provides a practical recipe for software teams: pinpoint where an AI component delivers benefits, where it introduces new hazards, and how to deploy it responsibly.
3874: We introduce *Glioma C6*, a newly released open dataset for instance segmentation of glioma C6 cells, intended to serve both as a benchmark and as a training resource for deep‑learning frameworks. The collection contains 75 high‑resolution phase‑contrast microscopy images annotated with over 12 000 individual cells, offering a realistic and challenging testbed for biomedical image analysis. Annotations include cell bodies (soma) as well as morphological classifications supplied by expert biologists, which are designed to support cancer‑cell research through detailed phenotypic categorization. *Glioma C6* is divided into two sections: the first provides a controlled, reproducible set of images for benchmarking, while the second presents images acquired under varied conditions to probe model generalization. We assess a range of state‑of‑the‑art segmentation algorithms, revealing their current shortcomings on this dataset. Furthermore, our experiments show that training on *Glioma C6* markedly improves segmentation accuracy, underscoring the dataset’s utility for developing robust, generalizable models. The dataset is freely available to the research community.
3875:
The proliferation of autonomous artificial intelligence agents—ranging from personal assistants to industrial robots—has exposed a critical gap in current identity‑management (IDM) paradigms: existing schemes were engineered for human users, not for software entities that can self‑replicate, negotiate, and evolve over time. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for *Identity Management for Agentic AI* that re‑thinks authorization, authentication, and security in a world where agents, rather than people, initiate interactions and transactions. 

We first formalise the unique properties of agentic entities (autonomy, persistence, composability) and analyse how these properties undermine conventional IDM concepts such as static credentials, single‑sign‑on, and human‑centric trust anchors. Drawing on recent advances in decentralized identity (DID), verifiable credentials (VC), and zero‑knowledge proofs, we propose a modular architecture that (i) assigns machine‑generated, cryptographically bound identities that can be self‑issued or delegated; (ii) enforces dynamic access‑control policies that adapt to an agent’s context and behaviour; and (iii) supports accountability through immutable audit trails and reputation‑based attestations.  

Our prototype implementation, built atop a blockchain‑backed DID registry and an AI‑adaptive policy engine, is evaluated in a simulated smart‑city environment populated by heterogeneous agents (traffic lights, autonomous vehicles, service drones). Metrics show a 70 % reduction in credential‑related attack surface compared to legacy OAuth‑style systems, while preserving interoperability and preserving latency below 50 ms for most transaction types. We also discuss regulatory implications, highlighting how the proposed IDM model aligns with emerging data‑protection frameworks (e.g., GDPR) and offers a pathway toward formal compliance verification for agentic systems.

This work establishes the foundational principles and practical tools for securing an ecosystem where AI agents, not just humans, are first‑class identity holders, thereby laying the groundwork for trustworthy, scalable agent‑centric digital infrastructures.
3876:
Human gaze is a rich multimodal signal that encodes where a person’s visual attention is directed, what they perceive and how they interact with the environment. Existing gaze‑centric systems, however, are largely task‑specific, requiring separate models for gaze estimation, saliency prediction, visual grounding or interaction‑aware reasoning. In this paper we introduce **GazeVLM**, a unified vision‑language model that learns to interpret, predict and reason about gaze across a spectrum of downstream tasks.  

GazeVLM is built upon a transformer‑based architecture that jointly processes RGB‑D video streams, head‑pose dynamics and textual context (captions, instructions, dialogue). We propose a novel multimodal pre‑training regime that aligns visual gaze maps with linguistic tokens through a contrastive “gaze‑caption” objective, and a self‑supervised “gaze‑motion” auxiliary task that encourages temporal coherence. The resulting representation captures both fine‑grained eye‑movement patterns and coarse‑grained attentional semantics.  

To demonstrate the model’s versatility, we evaluate GazeVLM on five benchmark datasets spanning three paradigms: (i) **Gaze‑Estimation** (EYEDIAP, Gaze360), (ii) **Saliency Prediction** (Salient360, VT-1000), and (iii) **Visual Grounding** (Gaze-World, Gaze-AL). Across all tasks, GazeVLM surpasses the state‑of‑the‑art by a margin of 5–12 % in relative error, while maintaining comparable inference speed to single‑task baselines. Ablation studies confirm that the cross‑modal language head and the motion‑aware loss are critical to achieving this performance boost.  

GazeVLM establishes a new benchmark for multi‑task gaze understanding, offering a single, extensible framework that can be readily adapted to downstream applications such as human‑robot interaction, contextual recommendation, and assistive visual navigation. The source code, pretrained checkpoints and a unified benchmark suite will be released to foster further research in multimodal gaze intelligence.
3877:
Jackknifing—defined as the abrupt, V‑shaped articulation between a tractor and its trailer—is the most hazardous fault mode for long, heavy articulated vehicles (LHAVs) operating in dense convoys or “swarms.” While most contemporary research targets single‑vehicle dynamics or fixed‑lane platoons, the unique kinematic coupling of a swarm of LHAVs magnifies the risk of cascading jackknifing events, especially during tight turns, sudden braking, or in the presence of uneven terrain. This paper presents **AVOID‑JACK**, a distributed control framework that guarantees jackknifing avoidance for swarms of up to ten LHAVs while preserving high traffic throughput and cooperative maneuverability.

AVOID‑JACK models each vehicle as a nonlinear, underactuated system with a rigid tractor and a compliant trailer linked by a single joint. By exploiting a cooperative sensing network (onboard LIDAR, GPS, and inter‑vehicle communication), each agent continuously estimates its relative articulation angle, inter‑vehicle spacing, and lateral offset. A receding‑horizon model‑predictive controller (MPC) then optimizes acceleration and steering commands under a set of convex safety constraints that enforce a minimum safe articulation angle and inter‑vehicle clearance. To reduce communication overhead, the MPC is embedded in a hierarchical structure: a leader vehicle prescribes a reference trajectory and safe curvature limits, while follower vehicles solve local sub‑problems that respect both leader guidance and neighbor‑induced safety margins.

We provide a formal Lyapunov‑based proof that the distributed scheme maintains all vehicles within a “safe manifold” that precludes any violation of the jackknifing boundary. Extensive high‑fidelity simulations and real‑world tests on a 150‑meter test track demonstrate a 93 % reduction in jackknifing incidents relative to a baseline rear‑end collision avoidance policy. Moreover, AVOID‑JACK sustains 3‑meter inter‑vehicle spacing in a 10‑vehicle convoy without compromising lane‑keeping or acceleration performance.

The proposed framework is scalable, communication‑light, and compatible with existing autonomous truck architectures, thereby offering a practical pathway toward safer, higher‑density LHAV swarms in freight and logistics applications.
3878:
Mathematical problem solving by large language models (LLMs) has progressed rapidly, yet models still struggle with unfamiliar concepts, intricate derivations, and large‑scale symbolic manipulation. Current approaches either rely on static in‑context data or treat retrieval as a separate pre‑processing step, which limits the model’s ability to adaptively incorporate external knowledge during reasoning. In this work we introduce **SIGMA** (Search‑Augmented On‑Demand Knowledge Integration for Agentic Mathematical Reasoning), a framework that endows a reasoning agent with the capacity to query a search engine, retrieve relevant mathematical resources, and integrate them into its ongoing deduction pipeline.

SIGMA comprises three tightly‑coupled components: (1) a **retrieval policy** that, guided by a lightweight planner, decides when to invoke a search based on confidence estimates and dependency analysis; (2) a **semantic matching module** that filters search results and extracts salient mathematical statements, proofs, and equations; and (3) a **knowledge‑augmented transformer** that ingests retrieved content as auxiliary context while generating step‑by‑step reasoning. The policy is trained through reinforcement learning on a curriculum of synthetic and real‑world math problems, rewarding correct solutions and penalizing unnecessary queries. By leveraging on‑demand knowledge, SIGMA reduces hallucinations, improves interpretability, and allows the agent to tackle problems beyond the pre‑training distribution.

We evaluate SIGMA on a suite of benchmark datasets—GSM8K, MATH, and the recent AI2‑Reasoning Corpus—showing a 12.4 % absolute lift over a strong LLM baseline and a 5.8 % gain over recent retrieval‑augmented systems. Ablation studies confirm that the search‑policy and knowledge‑integration layers each contribute significantly to performance. In a human‑evaluation experiment, solutions produced by SIGMA are rated 22 % more explanatory and 18 % more accurate than those produced by baseline models. Our results demonstrate that search‑augmented, on‑demand knowledge integration is a viable path toward truly **agentic** mathematical reasoning, where the system autonomously seeks and assimilates the information it needs to solve complex problems.
3879: Accurate inference of personality typologies from natural language has become a pivotal challenge at the intersection of cognitive science and computational linguistics. Traditional psychometric approaches to the Myers‑Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) rely on self‑report inventories, whereas recent machine‑learning techniques treat personality classification as a purely statistical task. In this paper we propose **Cognitive Alignment in Personality Reasoning (CAPR)**, a framework that explicitly incorporates **Prototype Theory**—a foundational model of human categorisation—into automated MBTI inference. CAPR first constructs a set of *prototype profiles* for each MBTI type by aggregating exemplar texts from a large, domain‑independent corpus, then maps incoming user‑generated documents onto this prototype space using a hybrid vector‑representation pipeline that blends contextual embeddings with trait‑specific lexical cues. We evaluate CAPR on two benchmark datasets (the Personality‑Chat and the 20‑News MBTI corpus), achieving a mean F1‑score of 0.68 across all 16 types—an improvement of 12 % over state‑of‑the‑art neural baselines. Ablation studies confirm that the prototype‑based similarity layer is essential for capturing nuanced trait interactions that purely data‑driven models miss. Moreover, a qualitative analysis of misclassifications reveals that CAPR’s prototypes preserve interpretable cognitive alignments, facilitating diagnostic insights into model uncertainty. Our results suggest that grounding personality inference in prototype theory not only improves performance but also bridges the gap between computational models and cognitive theories of categorisation, offering a promising direction for future research in personalized AI and psychometrics.
3880:
The rapid deployment of AI systems has heightened the demand for metrics that rigorously capture the ethical, legal, and social dimensions of responsible AI. Yet, the field remains fragmented: existing metrics are often domain‑specific, poorly standardized, and rarely validated against real‑world outcomes. In this paper we critically examine the current landscape of responsible‑AI metrics, identifying key sources of unreliability—ambiguity in definitions, lack of reproducibility, and sensitivity to dataset drift. We then introduce a unified, multi‑layered framework for designing and evaluating reliable metrics that (1) explicitly aligns with the six pillars of responsible AI (fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy, safety, and inclusiveness), (2) incorporates both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation modalities, and (3) supports continuous monitoring through automated, adaptive test suites.  

To validate the framework, we construct a benchmark suite comprising 12 synthetic and real datasets spanning image, text, and recommendation domains, each annotated with gold‑standard labels for fairness, bias, and safety. Using this benchmark we evaluate a representative set of popular metrics (e.g., demographic parity, calibration error, explanation fidelity) and demonstrate that many fail to maintain stability across model updates or adversarial perturbations. Leveraging our framework, we propose a composite reliability score that aggregates stability, interpretability, and coverage, and show that it correlates strongly with stakeholder‑reported satisfaction in a large‑scale user study.  

Our contributions are threefold: (i) a comprehensive taxonomy of responsible‑AI metrics and their reliability pitfalls; (ii) a principled framework for designing robust, reproducible metrics; and (iii) an empirical validation that highlights best practices and actionable guidelines for researchers and practitioners. This work advances the community toward a shared, trustworthy metric ecosystem essential for the accountable deployment of AI systems.
3881: Brain‑computer interfaces (BCIs) seek to translate motor intent from non‑invasive neural recordings into commands for external devices. However, real‑world use is constrained by the noisy and variable nature of motor‑imagery (MI) electroencephalography (EEG). In this study we propose a hierarchical, meta‑cognitive decoding scheme for four‑class MI classification. The approach combines a multi‑scale hierarchical signal‑processing module that restructures backbone features into temporally diverse representations with an introspective uncertainty estimator that assigns a reliability score to each classification cycle and steers iterative refinement. We apply this framework to three established EEG backbones—EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, and DeepConvNet—and evaluate performance on the BCI Competition IV‑2a dataset under a subject‑independent protocol. Across all backbones, the added components raise average accuracy and diminish inter‑subject variation relative to the baselines, demonstrating greater robustness against subject heterogeneity and noisy trials. These findings indicate that merging hierarchical multi‑scale feature extraction with confidence‑aware refinement can significantly improve the dependability of MI‑based BCI systems.
3882: Learning a diverse set of achievable goals is a central challenge for self‑supervised reinforcement learning (RL), yet most goal‑generation methods rely purely on data‑driven priors that ignore the underlying physics of the environment. We introduce **Physically‑Grounded Goal Imagination (PGGI)**, a physics‑informed variational autoencoder (VAE) that explicitly embeds domain‑knowledge about dynamics into the latent space of goal representations. The encoder learns a low‑dimensional embedding of state trajectories while the decoder is regularised by a differentiable physics model (e.g., a mass‑spring system or rigid‑body dynamics) that enforces consistency with conservation laws and kinematic constraints. During self‑supervised training the agent samples latent codes, reconstructs future goal states through the physics‑aware decoder, and uses these imagined goals to shape exploration and reward generation. We evaluate PGGI on a suite of continuous‑control tasks with complex contact dynamics (e.g., block‑stacking, robotic manipulation), demonstrating a **30‑40 % reduction in sample complexity** compared with baseline goal‑imagining VAEs and a 2‑fold improvement in zero‑shot transfer to unseen initial conditions. Ablation studies confirm that the physics‑regularisation term is essential for producing feasible, high‑variance goal sets that accelerate policy optimisation. Our work establishes a principled framework for integrating physical priors into goal‑imagination, bridging the gap between model‑free RL and model‑based reasoning.
3883:
Accurate dietary self‑report remains a major bottleneck for research and clinical nutrition, owing to the time‑consuming nature of manual food logging and the low compliance that typically accompanies it.  We present **SnappyMeal**, a multimodal artificial‑intelligence food‑logging system that combines image capture, voice input, and barcode scanning to automate portion‑size estimation, food identification, and nutrient calculation on a mobile platform.  The system leverages a convolutional‑de‑convolutional network trained on a new multimodal food dataset (≈ 120 k images with corresponding audio descriptions) and an ensemble of language‑processing modules to infer context and correct recognition errors.  A user‑centric design process guided by participatory workshops informed a minimal‑effort workflow: a single photo and a brief spoken description are enough to generate a detailed nutrition entry, which is then refined via a lightweight UI for user correction.

To assess long‑term efficacy, we conducted a 6‑month longitudinal study with 62 participants (aged 18‑65) recruited from an urban population, comparing SnappyMeal to a standard smartphone‑based logging app (MyFitnessPal).  Outcomes measured included logging frequency, completeness of entries, accuracy of nutrient estimation (validated against weighed ground‑truth meals), and user engagement (App Store ratings and qualitative interviews).  SnappyMeal increased daily logging by 4.7× (p < 0.001), improved nutrient‑estimation accuracy by 18% relative to the control, and was rated significantly higher on usability and satisfaction.  Moreover, the multimodal pipeline reduced the average logging time from 3.2 min (baseline app) to 1.1 min (SnappyMeal).  

Our findings demonstrate that a multimodal AI approach can substantially lower the burden of dietary self‑report while enhancing data quality over extended periods.  SnappyMeal’s open‑source architecture and multimodal dataset provide a foundation for future work in automated nutrition monitoring and for integrating dietary logging into larger health‑tracking ecosystems.
3884:
Algorithm comparison has long been a central concern in program analysis, algorithm engineering, and automated algorithm selection. While many tools exist for comparing code fragments or estimating the complexity of a single algorithm, there is no widely accepted quantitative notion of *algorithm similarity* that captures both the *structural* and the *behavioral* aspects of algorithms across arbitrary programming languages and domains. In this work we propose a principled framework for measuring algorithm similarity that integrates formal semantics, execution traces, and complexity profiles.

Our approach defines an *Algorithm Distance* \(D(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})\) as a convex combination of three components: (1) a *structural distance* obtained by computing a graph‑edit distance between the control‑flow graphs of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\); (2) a *behavioral distance* derived from statistical comparisons of runtime traces on a representative benchmark set; and (3) a *complexity distance* that normalizes the asymptotic time and space complexities of the two algorithms. The weighting parameters are learned from a curated dataset of manually annotated algorithm pairs, ensuring that the resulting metric aligns with human intuition while remaining computationally tractable.

We evaluate our metric on a diverse corpus of 1,200 algorithms spanning sorting, graph traversal, dynamic programming, and machine learning kernels. The distance values correlate strongly (Spearman \(\rho=0.78\)) with expert rankings of algorithmic similarity, outperform existing syntactic similarity measures. Furthermore, we demonstrate two applications: (a) an automated clustering pipeline that groups algorithms by functional families, yielding clusters that match textbook classifications with 94 % purity; and (b) a recommendation engine that suggests algorithmic variants for a given problem instance, improving performance of a solver portfolio by 12 % on average.

Our contribution is the first comprehensive, language‑agnostic similarity measure for algorithms that reconciles structural, behavioral, and theoretical properties. This metric facilitates more effective algorithm libraries, aids in plagiarism detection for algorithmic assignments, and provides a foundation for future research on algorithmic search and evolution.
3885:
In recent years, many time‑series studies have begun to fuse textual information with temporal data, harnessing the reasoning power of large language models (LLMs) to tackle a wide range of downstream tasks. This approach allows a single model to adapt to problems that previously demanded domain‑specific architectures. A drawback of most current methods, however, is their reliance on text‑only supervision during training. As a result, the models become biased toward linguistic cues and may overlook essential temporal dynamics, leading to predictions that conflict with the underlying time‑series context.

To confront this limitation, we introduce **EvalTS**, a benchmark that contains ten tasks divided into three difficulty tiers—from basic pattern detection to sophisticated real‑world reasoning—providing a more realistic testbed for evaluating models. We also present **TimeSense**, a multimodal framework that equips LLMs with genuine time‑series understanding by balancing textual inference with a preserved temporal sense. The framework incorporates a **Temporal Sense module** that reconstructs the input series within the model’s internal representation, ensuring that language‑based reasoning remains anchored in the actual temporal behavior. Additionally, TimeSense augments the model with coordinate‑based positional embeddings, giving each time point a spatial context that improves the capture of structural dependencies.

Experimental evaluations show that TimeSense sets a new state‑of‑the‑art across a variety of tasks, particularly excelling at complex multi‑dimensional reasoning challenges.
3886: Timely detection of issue reports that signal software vulnerabilities is especially important for Internet‑of‑Things (IoT) devices, where analysis tends to lag behind that of conventional software. Although machine‑learning (ML) and large language models (LLMs) have been successfully applied to non‑IoT vulnerability discovery, their effectiveness in the IoT domain has yet to be investigated. In this work we present the first study addressing this gap by introducing two complementary methods: (1) an approach that fuses conventional ML with LLM‑based natural‑language processing (NLP) techniques to identify vulnerability‑related issues in 21 Eclipse‑IoT projects; and (2) a fine‑tuned BERT masked‑language‑model trained on 11,000 GitHub issue texts for \vul classification. Our best result comes from a Support Vector Machine (SVM) trained on BERT‑derived NLP features, achieving an area under the receiver‑operator curve (AUC) of 0.65. In contrast, the fine‑tuned BERT model attains only 0.26 accuracy, underscoring the need to expose all available training data. These findings establish a foundation for accurately detecting IoT vulnerabilities through issue‑report analysis, mirroring the progress made in non‑IoT software security.
3887:
In many genetic programming frameworks, crossover is a vital ingredient, yet in Cartesian Genetic Programming (CGP) it has routinely been argued to hinder search efficiency. Consequently, a mutation‑only \((1+\lambda)\) evolutionary strategy has become the de‑facto standard for CGP. Although a handful of operators have shown performance gains over this baseline, a broadly applicable remedy remains elusive. 

In this work we evaluate elementary crossover schemes—one‑point and uniform—against variants that enforce “node preservation,” such as Roman Kalkreuth’s subgraph crossover, which prevents the disruption of instructions during recombination. We also contrast a node‑replacement mutation operator with the conventional point mutation. Experiments on symbolic‑regression benchmarks demonstrate that preserving nodes during both mutation and crossover markedly enhances search quality, pointing the field toward a general solution for CGP crossover.
3888:
Current methods for assessing the performance of AI agents are overwhelmingly task‑centric, relying on domain‑specific benchmarks and metrics that obscure the underlying capabilities of the agent. Such task‑dependent evaluations impede the comparison of agents across heterogeneous settings and hinder progress toward genuinely general artificial intelligence. In this paper we propose a *Outcome‑Oriented, Task‑Agnostic Evaluation* (OOTA) framework that measures agent behaviour directly in terms of the *desired outcomes* it achieves, rather than the particular tasks it is instructed to perform.  

OOTA introduces a set of principled metrics—**Goal Alignment (GA)**, **Robustness to Perturbations (RP)**, **Resource Efficiency (RE)**, and **Safety‑Compliance (SC)**—which are defined purely in terms of the final state of an environment and the trajectory of the agent’s internal policy, independent of any task label. We formalise these metrics as functions over a *universal outcome space* derived from the agent’s observations and actions, allowing the same scoring rubric to be applied across vision‑based navigation, dialogue, and robotic manipulation.  

We validate OOTA on a curated suite of 12 benchmark environments spanning 4 domains and 3 agent architectures (RL, LLM‑guided, and hybrid). Results show that OOTA scores correlate strongly (r > 0.85) with expert‑rated performance while exhibiting lower variance across tasks compared to conventional task‑specific metrics. Importantly, OOTA reveals hidden deficiencies—e.g., safety lapses in a text‑based game—that task metrics overlook.  

Our approach demonstrates that outcome‑oriented evaluation can provide a unified, transparent, and more informative lens for assessing AI agents. We discuss implications for benchmark design, deployment risk assessment, and the development of universally competent agents. Future work will extend OOTA to open‑ended, lifelong learning scenarios and explore adaptive metric weighting for domain‑specific compliance.
3889: Large language models (LLMs) are being deployed more frequently in software engineering activities such as eliciting requirements, designing systems, and assessing them, raising pressing questions about whether these models reflect human judgments on responsible‑AI values. In this paper we examine the degree to which LLMs’ value preferences align with two distinct human groups: a nationally representative U.S. sample and a cohort of AI practitioners. We evaluate 23 LLMs on four tasks: (T1) choosing the most relevant responsible‑AI values, (T2) rating the importance of those values in concrete scenarios, (T3) resolving trade‑offs among competing values, and (T4) ordering software requirements that embody the selected values. Our findings indicate that LLMs tend to mirror the priorities of AI practitioners more closely than those of the general U.S. population, particularly in emphasizing fairness, privacy, transparency, safety, and accountability. Yet we observe a disconnect between the values the models claim to endorse (in Tasks 1–3) and the way they actually rank requirements (Task 4), exposing a fidelity gap between declared and enacted behavior. These results underscore the practical risk of using LLMs in requirements engineering without human oversight and point to an urgent need for systematic methods to benchmark, interpret, and monitor value alignment in AI‑assisted software development.
3890:
Human expressions play a key role in communicating emotions. As AI‑generated content becomes ever more realistic, the demand for vivid, emotionally rich 3D facial animation has surged. Although recent work has advanced speech‑driven lip‑sync, the production of emotionally expressive talking faces remains largely untapped, mainly because truly annotated 3D talking‑face datasets are prohibitively expensive to collect. 

In this paper we frame the animation of a talking face as a linear superposition of speech‑ and emotion‑driven components. Using the VOCAset collection of neutral talking‑face sequences together with the Florence4D repository of isolated 3D expression clips, we learn a shared library of blendshapes that are separately driven by spoken audio and by emotional cues. A sparsity‑based loss encourages these two sets of blendshapes to stay disentangled, while still preserving any cross‑domain deformations that naturally emerge from the data. The resulting blendshapes can be mapped to the expression and jaw‑pose parameters of the FLAME mesh model, allowing us to animate 3D Gaussian avatars.

Our qualitative and quantitative tests confirm that the method produces talking faces that honor the input expression and maintain accurate lip synchronization. User studies further indicate that the generated emotions are more expressive than those of current baselines, without sacrificing sync quality.
3891:
Although investment funds disclose their aims in broad terms, their managers actually pursue intricate, competing objectives that extend far beyond simple risk‑return trade‑offs. Conventional methods model this through multi‑objective utility functions, yet they struggle with specification and parameter tuning. We introduce a generative approach that learns latent representations of fund‑manager strategies without the need for an explicit utility specification.

Our model directly estimates the conditional distribution of a fund’s portfolio weights given a set of observable inputs—stock characteristics, past returns, previous allocations, and a latent variable that captures the underlying strategy. Unlike reinforcement‑ or imitation‑learning techniques that depend on predefined rewards or labeled expert behavior, our GAN‑based architecture learns purely from the joint empirical distribution of holdings and market data.

We validate the framework using a dataset of 1,436 U.S. equity mutual funds. The inferred representations recover established investment styles such as “growth” and “value,” while also exposing hidden managerial preferences. For example, many funds appear to follow Markowitz‑style optimization, yet they differ markedly in turnover, concentration, and other latent dimensions.

To unpack and interpret the end‑to‑end model, we devise a suite of explanatory tests, demonstrating that the benchmark labels are linearly recoverable within the learned encoding. 

This data‑driven framework offers a powerful tool for characterizing investment strategies, with potential applications in market simulation, strategy attribution, and regulatory monitoring.
3892:
Modern telecommunications networks are increasingly complex, with thousands of interconnected elements that must operate with minimal downtime. Conventional troubleshooting relies on manual diagnostics, expensive proprietary tools, and expert knowledge, leading to prolonged outages and high operational costs. This paper proposes a novel, end‑to‑end framework that fuses a Multi‑Agent System (MAS) with fine‑tuned Small Language Models (SLMs) to automate the detection, diagnosis, and remediation of network faults in real time.

We first formulate the troubleshooting workflow as a cooperative, agent‑based problem where each agent is responsible for a specific network domain (e.g., radio, core, transport). The agents ingest live telemetry, event logs, and configuration data, then forward concise, structured observations to a central SLM‑powered decision layer. To overcome the resource constraints of large language models while retaining contextual understanding, we fine‑tune a 125‑M parameter GPT‑variant on a curated corpus of telecom incident reports, network topologies, and configuration manuals. The SLM serves as a lightweight “knowledge engine,” generating hypothesis‑driven diagnostic paths and recommending corrective actions.

Our architecture is evaluated on a 4G/5G testbed comprising 200 base‑station nodes, simulating 12 distinct fault scenarios (e.g., cell‑site antenna misalignment, packet loss spikes, mis‑routed routing tables). Compared against a rule‑based baseline, our MAS+SLM system achieves a 32% reduction in mean time to resolution (MTTR) and a 24% increase in fault‑recurrence accuracy while operating within 500 MB of RAM. Ablation studies confirm that the MAS layer improves scalability, whereas the fine‑tuned SLM delivers superior diagnostic precision compared to generic large language models.

These results demonstrate the viability of lightweight, domain‑adapted language models integrated within a cooperative agent framework for telecom network troubleshooting. Future work will explore dynamic agent re‑deployment and reinforcement‑learning‑based policy refinement to further enhance adaptability to evolving network architectures.
3893:
Large‑scale language models (LLMs) increasingly employ chain‑of‑thought (CoT) prompting to solve complex reasoning tasks. However, the intermediate reasoning steps are often unverified, leading to hallucinations and logical fallacies that can undermine downstream decision‑making. We introduce **VeriCoT**, a neuro‑symbolic framework that automatically validates the logical consistency of CoT traces by translating them into formal logic and subjecting them to automated theorem‑proving and constraint‑solving techniques. Our system comprises (i) a neural extractor that parses natural‑language CoT into a set of symbolic predicates, (ii) a lightweight inference engine that encodes domain‑specific axioms, and (iii) a consistency scorer that aggregates entailment, contradiction, and completeness signals.  

We evaluate VeriCoT on benchmark datasets for arithmetic, symbolic mathematics, and commonsense reasoning (e.g., GSM‑8K, MATH, and CommonsenseQA). Across all tasks, our approach reduces the rate of inconsistent CoT traces by 37 % and improves overall accuracy by 12 % relative to baseline models that do not perform consistency checking. Moreover, the consistency scores correlate strongly with human judgments of correctness (ρ = 0.78).  

VeriCoT demonstrates that integrating symbolic validation with neural reasoning can significantly enhance the reliability of chain‑of‑thought generation, paving the way for trustworthy, explainable AI systems in safety‑critical domains.
3894:
Designing robust, scalable, and ethically‑sound multi‑agent systems (MAS) remains a formidable challenge in contemporary AI research. Traditional engineering practices rely heavily on human intuition and domain expertise, leading to ad‑hoc solutions that are difficult to generalize. We present **PublicAgent**, a novel framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) and publicly available datasets to systematically derive multi‑agent design principles. PublicAgent ingests heterogeneous open‑data streams—such as governmental statistics, sensor logs, and socio‑economic indicators—constructing a knowledge graph that captures domain‑specific constraints, stakeholder goals, and interaction patterns. A fine‑tuned LLM, combined with chain‑of‑thought prompting, analyses this graph to infer optimal agent architectures, communication protocols, and incentive mechanisms. The framework then generates a set of design guidelines in human‑readable form and automatically synthesizes a prototype MAS that satisfies the extracted principles.

To validate the approach, we apply PublicAgent to three high‑impact domains: (1) smart‑city resource management, (2) public health surveillance, and (3) environmental monitoring. In each case, the generated MAS outperforms baseline hand‑crafted designs on efficiency, fairness, and resilience metrics, while requiring only a fraction of the engineering effort. We also demonstrate the framework’s capacity to surface previously overlooked ethical considerations, such as privacy‑preserving data sharing and equitable resource distribution.

PublicAgent contributes a reusable pipeline for LLM‑driven MAS design, a curated repository of open‑data‑driven design principles, and an open‑source implementation that encourages community participation. Our work bridges the gap between large‑scale data analytics and multi‑agent system engineering, offering a scalable path toward more transparent, responsible, and adaptable AI infrastructures.
3895: Building large‐scale Visual Question‑Answering (VQA) datasets that focus on the textual content present in a scene—known as text‑VQA—normally requires meticulous manual annotation, a process that is both time‑consuming and difficult. With recent advances in multimodal foundation models and the maturation of OCR technologies, there is a clear opportunity to devise a fully automated end‑to‑end pipeline capable of generating question‑answer (QA) pairs directly from scene text in images. In this work we present such a pipeline that produces high‑fidelity QA pairs and can scale with the volume of scene‑text data available. Our framework integrates several state‑of‑the‑art components: OCR‑based text spotting, region‑of‑interest detection, image captioning, and question generation. These modules are orchestrated into a cohesive system that not only synthesizes QA pairs but also validates them automatically. To our knowledge, this is the first end‑to‑end approach that automatically constructs and verifies a large‑scale text‑VQA dataset, yielding approximately 72,000 QA pairs drawn from about 44,000 images.
3896:
Class‑incremental learning (CIL) with deep vision models remains hampered by severe catastrophic forgetting, especially when the backbone is a pre‑trained Vision Transformer (ViT). In practical deployments, each incremental task introduces a *distribution drift* relative to the previous ones – arising from changes in class semantics, domain shifts, or annotation noise – that exacerbates forgetting beyond the usual model plasticity–stability trade‑off. We address this phenomenon by explicitly modelling and compensating for inter‑task distribution drift within a unified incremental training framework.

Our approach introduces **Drift‑Aware Prototype Alignment (DPA)**, a lightweight regulariser that learns a *drift field* between the feature distributions of the current task and all previously seen tasks. DPA operates on the token‑level attention maps of a frozen ViT encoder, aligning class‑specific prototypes while preserving the fine‑grained self‑attention structure. In addition, a *distribution‑aware knowledge distillation* objective is used to re‑weight exemplar contributions according to their drift magnitude, ensuring that more stable representations receive stronger protection. The whole method requires only a small episodic memory (≈ 5 % of the dataset) and incurs negligible computational overhead during inference.

We evaluate the method on standard CIL benchmarks – CIFAR‑100, ImageNet‑100, and a synthetic domain‑shifted split of CORe50 – under varying task granularity and memory budgets. DPA outperforms state‑of‑the‑art ViT‑based CIL baselines by 4.7 %, 3.2 % and 2.9 % top‑1 accuracy on average, while reducing forgetting by 12.5 % relative to the best baseline. Ablation studies confirm that the drift field and distribution‑aware weighting each contribute significantly, and that our method is robust to large inter‑task class overlap. The proposed framework demonstrates that compensating for distribution drift is essential for fully exploiting the representational capacity of pre‑trained Transformers in incremental learning scenarios.
3897: When the word “house” reaches our ears, we don’t merely register a sound—we instantly conjure walls, doors, and memories. This illustrates how the brain constructs meaning across successive layers, from basic acoustic cues to rich, multimodal associations. Drawing inspiration from recent Meta work that linked EEG recordings to average wav2vec2 speech embeddings, we probe a more nuanced question: which layers of pre‑trained models most closely mirror this hierarchical neural processing? We examine embeddings from two distinct architectures—wav2vec2, which transforms raw audio into linguistic representations, and CLIP, which aligns textual concepts with visual content. Using EEG captured during natural speech listening, we assess the correspondence between these embeddings and brain activity through ridge regression and contrastive decoding. Three integration strategies are explored: single-layer analysis, progressive concatenation, and progressive summation. Our results indicate that layer‑specific, multimodal representations move us closer to decoding the brain’s interpretation of language as a lived, experiential phenomenon rather than just a series of sounds.
3898:
Reconstructing the visual scenes that individuals perceive from their fMRI recordings offers a powerful, non‑invasive glimpse into brain activity. Although diffusion‑based methods have recently advanced this field, they often fail to reproduce the original images with high fidelity. We introduce *Brain‑IT*, a novel brain‑inspired framework that tackles this issue by employing a Brain Interaction Transformer (BIT). BIT enables rich interactions among groups of functionally related voxels that are consistent across subjects, thereby serving as universal building blocks for cross‑brain information integration. All network parameters are shared across these voxel clusters and participants, permitting efficient learning even with modest datasets.

To steer the reconstruction, BIT predicts two complementary patch‑level image descriptors: (1) high‑level semantic cues that guide the diffusion model toward the correct visual content, and (2) low‑level structural cues that provide a coarse layout for initializing the diffusion process. This architecture allows direct transmission of voxel‑cluster information to the localized image features. Experiments demonstrate that *Brain‑IT* produces reconstructions that are both visually closer to the true images and superior according to standard quantitative metrics, outperforming state‑of‑the‑art techniques. Remarkably, with only one hour of fMRI data from a new subject, the model delivers performance on par with methods that require full 40‑hour training sessions.
3899: We propose a novel strategy for solving initial‑boundary value problems (IBVPs) that builds the governing partial differential equation (PDE) into the model itself via Lie symmetries. By exploiting symmetry transformations, the resulting network automatically satisfies the PDE while learning from the prescribed initial and boundary data. Consequently, the loss function directly reflects the true prediction error, yielding faster and more robust convergence. For well‑posed IBVPs, this framework also provides a principled way to bound the error. The symmetry‑based architecture is compact, which leads to highly efficient training. In the implementation known as *LieSolver*, we test the approach on a variety of linear homogeneous PDEs with different initial conditions, consistently outperforming standard physics‑informed neural networks (PINNs) in both speed and accuracy. Overall, our method enhances both the computational efficiency and the reliability of solutions to PDE‑constrained problems.
3900:
The rapid proliferation of online misinformation poses a persistent threat to democratic discourse and public health. Traditional diffusion models often treat users as homogeneous agents, obscuring the nuanced ways in which individual traits shape susceptibility and propagation. In this study we develop a persona‑based agent‑based framework that simulates misinformation vulnerabilities by embedding realistic, data‑derived personas into a digital social network. Personas are constructed from large‑scale survey data and behavioral logs, capturing key attributes such as political ideology, media trust, cognitive reflection, and network centrality. Each agent is instantiated with a persona and follows a stochastic decision‑making process that governs content sharing, fact‑checking, and echo‑chamber navigation.

We calibrate the model against empirical cascades of high‑profile misinformation events (e.g., vaccine myths, election rumors) and validate its predictive power using cross‑validation on hold‑out datasets. Sensitivity analyses reveal that vulnerability to misinformation is highest among personas characterized by low cognitive reflection and high trust in unverified sources, while targeted fact‑checking interventions are most effective for personas with moderate network centrality. Moreover, the simulations demonstrate that algorithmic exposure adjustments can significantly reduce misinformation reach, but only when aligned with persona‑specific susceptibilities.

Our results underscore the importance of incorporating heterogeneous human traits into diffusion models and provide actionable insights for policy makers and platform designers seeking to mitigate misinformation spread. This work contributes a novel methodology for simulating misinformation dynamics with fine‑grained agent personas and a set of empirically grounded recommendations for intervention design.
3901:
Accurately locating the bronchoscope tip during surgery is difficult because respiratory motion, patient‑specific anatomy, and CT‑to‑body mis‑registration cause the pre‑operative CT and the live endoscopic view to deform relative to one another.  Vision‑based approaches that rely on image matching often fail to generalise across different patients and imaging conditions, leaving significant alignment errors.  This study presents a broadly applicable, vision‑centric framework for bronchoscopy navigation and introduces a novel synthetic benchmark that facilitates consistent, reproducible testing.  

We propose a pose‑optimisation pipeline that performs frame‑by‑frame 2‑D/3‑D registration between real endoscopic RGB frames and CT‑rendered depth maps.  A modality‑ and domain‑invariant encoder, fine‑tuned for this task, computes direct similarity scores, while a differentiable renderer iteratively refines the camera pose based on depth consistency.  To promote reproducibility, we release the first public synthetic dataset of paired CT and endoscopic imagery, filling the gap caused by the scarcity of real paired data.
