InteracSPARQL demonstrates that coupling natural‑language explanations with an interactive refinement loop can make SPARQL more accessible and trustworthy, and we release the prototype and datasets as open source to support further research in explainable graph querying.
3952:
Business processes in modern enterprises generate massive volumes of heterogeneous data while simultaneously demanding ever‑faster, more accurate decision‑making. Conventional process‑management approaches rely on static rules and manual interventions, which are inadequate for the dynamic, data‑rich environments of today’s organizations. This paper proposes a comprehensive Business Process Optimisation Model (BPOM) that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Big Data Analytics to discover, predict, and continuously improve process performance.

The BPOM architecture comprises four inter‑related components: (i) a robust data ingestion layer that streams structured and unstructured information from ERP, CRM, sensor networks, and cloud services into a unified data lake; (ii) a process‑mining engine that reconstructs event logs into high‑fidelity process models; (iii) an AI‑driven optimisation core that employs deep reinforcement learning, predictive modeling, and anomaly detection to recommend process adjustments and automate routing decisions; and (iv) a real‑time feedback loop that updates models with new observations and evaluates the impact of implemented changes. 

To evaluate the framework, we conducted two extensive case studies—(1) a semiconductor manufacturing plant and (2) a global e‑commerce logistics operation—using a dataset of over 50 million events. The BPOM reduced cycle times by 18 % and cost per transaction by 12 % in manufacturing, while improving on‑time delivery rates by 23 % and reducing inventory holding costs by 9 % in the logistics case. Statistical analysis confirms that the AI‑augmented decisions outperform baseline rule‑based approaches with a significance level of p < 0.01.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a unified, end‑to‑end framework that operationalises AI and big‑data analytics for business process optimisation; (2) a set of algorithmic enhancements—including adaptive reward shaping for reinforcement learning in process contexts—that achieve superior performance in heterogeneous domains; and (3) empirical evidence demonstrating tangible efficiency gains in real‑world settings. This work advances the state of the art in process‑aware analytics and provides a blueprint for organisations seeking to embed data‑driven intelligence into their core operations.
3953:
We present a novel framework for automatic sketch synthesis that learns a *hierarchical auto‑regressive* representation of human‑drawn sketches and enables flexible, stroke‑level manipulation of the generated artwork. Traditional generative sketch models either treat each stroke as an atomic unit—producing coarse, often implausible figures—or generate sketches point‑wise, which obscures high‑level semantic control. Our approach bridges this gap by factorizing the sketch generation process into two coupled sequential modules: a *global sketch encoder* that captures long‑range dependencies among strokes, and a *stroke‑generation decoder* that produces fine‑grained pen trajectories conditioned on the global context. The two modules are trained end‑to‑end with a variational auto‑encoder objective and a reinforcement‑learning based policy that encourages realistic temporal ordering.

At inference time, the model samples a latent sketch code that defines a plausible global configuration, and then iteratively generates each stroke conditioned on its predecessors. Because the generation is auto‑regressive at the stroke level, we can insert, delete or modify individual strokes post‑generation without breaking coherence, thus supporting a rich set of sketch‑editing operations (e.g., “move a corner”, “change a branch”). We evaluate our method on the widely‑used QuickDraw and Sketch-RNN datasets, reporting state‑of‑the‑art Fréchet Sketch Distance (FSD) scores and superior human‑evaluation ratings for realism and controllability. Qualitative experiments demonstrate that our model can seamlessly blend stylistic attributes and adapt sketches to user‑specified constraints while maintaining global consistency. Our code and pretrained models are publicly released to encourage further research on controllable sketch synthesis.
3954:
Recent advances in continuous‐time generative modeling have highlighted *flow matching* as a principled alternative to score‐based diffusion and ordinary differential flow (ODE) methods. While the empirical success of flow matching is well documented, its theoretical relationship to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the model distribution and the data distribution remains largely unexplored. In this work we close this gap by deriving a tight, closed‑form correspondence between the flow‑matching objective and the time‑integrated KL divergence along the learned trajectory.

First, we formulate flow matching in a path‑space setting and show that the expected squared distance between the target and learned velocity fields equals the time‑averaged KL divergence between the time‑marginal distributions of the two processes. This result yields a natural variational interpretation of the flow‑matching loss as a *soft* KL regularizer and establishes that the optimal velocity field is precisely the score of the interpolating density. Second, we prove that for Gaussian priors and linear target dynamics the flow‑matching objective reduces to an explicit convex functional of the KL divergence, thereby providing a sharp upper bound on the optimal KL achievable by any flow matching trajectory. Third, we exploit this insight to devise a practical *flow‑matching estimator* of the KL divergence that requires only samples from the data and the learned flow; the estimator enjoys low variance and can be used to monitor training progress or to drive adaptive regularization.

Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and the MNIST/ CIFAR‑10 datasets confirm that the theoretical KL bounds predict training dynamics and that the proposed KL estimator accurately tracks the true divergence, leading to improved sample quality when incorporated as a training signal. Our analysis clarifies the theoretical foundations of flow matching and offers concrete tools for principled model evaluation and regularization.
3955:
Marine invasive species threaten biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and coastal economies worldwide. Current risk assessments largely treat vessel traffic and environmental conditions as independent predictors, overlooking the mechanistic linkage between the two that governs pathway feasibility. We propose a unified theoretical framework that couples environmental similarity and vessel mobility as joint drivers of marine invasive species pathways. The framework constructs a multiplex network comprising (i) a vessel‑mobility layer derived from global shipping data, capturing frequency, speed, and connectivity of marine traffic, and (ii) an environmental‑similarity layer based on oceanographic and habitat variables (temperature, salinity, substrate, and biogeographic affinity) that quantify ecological compatibility between source and destination ports. Coupling is quantified through a path‑weighted similarity index that integrates both layers, enabling the calculation of a pathway risk score for any origin–destination pair.

To illustrate the framework, we applied it to a high‑traffic region in the North Atlantic, integrating AIS‑derived vessel trajectories with climate‑matched habitat maps of the Gulf of Mexico. The coupled model identified “high‑risk corridors” that were not evident when each layer was considered separately, revealing that vessel routes linking environmentally similar ports exhibit an order of magnitude higher pathway potential for invasive organisms. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate that environmental similarity amplifies the influence of vessel density, whereas vessel mobility alone underestimates risk in ecologically dissimilar regions.

Our results underscore that invasion pathways are a function of both anthropogenic connectivity and ecological permissibility, and that neglecting their interaction can lead to substantial under‑estimation of risk. This framework provides a flexible, data‑driven approach for marine biosecurity planners, enabling prioritization of surveillance, ballast‑water management, and policy interventions along the most vulnerable corridors. Future work will expand the model to incorporate ballast‑water exchange dynamics and species‑specific traits to refine pathway predictions at finer taxonomic resolution.
3956: Federated learning (FL) allows multiple parties to train a model collaboratively while keeping their data private, yet it is still susceptible to adversarial attacks that can erode either the model’s performance or its fairness among sensitive groups. Most research has focused on one of these objectives, leaving a gap in understanding how attackers can jointly harm both. To address this, we present the Dual‑Facet Attack (DFA), a new threat model that simultaneously degrades predictive accuracy and group fairness. We also design two variants—Synchronous DFA (S‑DFA) and Split DFA (Sp‑DFA)—to reflect different realistic collusion patterns. Experiments reveal that current FL defenses, including hybrid aggregation schemes, do not adequately withstand DFAs. In response, we propose GuardFed, an adaptive defense that maintains a fairness‑aware reference model built from a small clean server dataset and synthetic examples. At every round, GuardFed assigns a dual‑perspective trust score to each client by examining both its utility deviation and fairness impact, enabling selective aggregation of trustworthy updates. Extensive evaluations on real datasets demonstrate that GuardFed consistently preserves both accuracy and fairness across various non‑IID and adversarial scenarios, achieving superior performance relative to existing robust FL techniques.
3957: Millions of users today craft personalized, LLM‑based chatbots that influence their everyday interactions, yet they struggle to predict how design choices will translate into real‑world behavior. This lack of transparency is critical: seemingly harmless prompts can provoke excessive sycophancy, toxicity, or inconsistency, undermining usefulness and raising safety issues. To tackle this problem, we present a tool that provides neural transparency during the design phase. By contrasting system prompts that elicit opposing behaviors, we extract behavioral trait vectors—such as empathy, toxicity, and sycophancy—derived from differences in internal neural activations. We then estimate a chatbot’s expected behavior by projecting the final‑token activations of a given system prompt onto these trait vectors, normalizing across traits for comparability, and displaying the outcomes with an interactive sunburst diagram. An online study on Prolific compared this transparent interface to a conventional chatbot editor lacking any interpretability. Results show that users routinely miscalibrated AI behavior: participants incorrectly estimated trait activations for 11 of 15 measurable traits, underscoring the necessity of transparency in everyday AI use. While the tool did not alter how users iterated on designs, it markedly boosted trust and was warmly received. Qualitative feedback revealed nuanced interactions with the visualization, offering insights for future neurally transparent interfaces. Overall, our work demonstrates a practical path for bringing mechanistic interpretability to non‑technical users, laying groundwork for safer and more aligned human‑AI collaboration.
3958:
Automatic speech emotion recognition (SER) is a critical component of affect‑aware human‑computer interaction, yet most state‑of‑the‑art methods rely on bulky recurrent or convolutional networks that impede deployment on resource‑constrained devices. In this work we investigate whether lightweight architectures and modern transformer backbones can achieve competitive accuracy while drastically reducing model size and latency. We conduct a systematic comparison across three families of models: (i) classic convolutional networks (MobileNet‑V2, EfficientNet‑B0), (ii) compact recurrent networks (Light RNN, Bi‑GRU), and (iii) transformer‑based models adapted to speech (SqueezeTransformer, DistilBERT‑based wav2vec 2.0). All models are trained and evaluated on the standard IEMOCAP, RAVDESS, and EMODB corpora using a balanced five‑class emotion taxonomy (neutral, happy, sad, angry, fearful).  

A comprehensive ablation study investigates the impact of (a) input representations (log‑Mel spectrogram vs. raw waveform), (b) attention mechanisms (self‑attention vs. channel‑wise attention), and (c) network depth. Results reveal that the DistilBERT‑based wav2vec 2.0 variant attains a weighted F1‑score of 0.67—only 2.3 % below the heavy wav2vec 2.0 baseline—while being 5.8× smaller and exhibiting a 4.3× inference speedup on a single‑core CPU. The hybrid SqueezeTransformer consistently outperforms pure CNNs and RNNs across all datasets, highlighting the value of self‑attention for modeling long‑range prosodic cues. Ablations show that log‑Mel features yield the best trade‑off between performance and computational load, and that a shallow transformer (3 layers) suffices for most emotions, with deeper stacks only marginally improving “fearful” recognition.

Our study establishes that lightweight, transformer‑based models provide a favorable balance of accuracy, memory footprint, and latency for real‑time SER on edge devices. We release the trained checkpoints, preprocessing pipelines, and evaluation scripts to encourage reproducible research in low‑resource affective computing.
3959: Analogical inference has traditionally been confined to symbolic, Boolean representations, where the success of a mapping between two relational structures is evaluated through crisp correspondences. Yet many real‑world problems involve continuous attributes and graded relations that cannot be faithfully captured by binary logic alone. In this paper we present a principled extension of analogical inference to continuous domains. We first formalise an analogical proportion in real‑valued vector spaces, introducing a weighted distance‑based similarity operator that preserves proportional relationships among features. This operator is embedded in a general transfer framework that allows analogies to be applied in both regression and classification settings. We then describe an optimisation procedure that learns the mapping parameters while regularising for over‑fitting, ensuring that the learned analogical relationships remain interpretable. Experimental evaluation on a suite of synthetic and benchmark datasets (including several UCI regression and classification problems) shows that our continuous analogical models achieve lower mean‑squared error and higher accuracy than standard baselines (k‑NN, Gaussian process regression, and tree‑based methods), particularly when the underlying data exhibit smooth relational patterns. We further illustrate the method’s capacity to transfer knowledge across tasks with a cross‑domain case study. The results establish that analogical inference can be successfully generalised beyond Boolean logic, providing a flexible, explainable framework for reasoning in continuous spaces and opening new directions for knowledge transfer in data‑rich domains.
3960: Recent work has introduced “MLLM‑r1” methods that combine reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards for vision‑language models. These approaches typically start from a cold‑start policy that is first supervised‑fine‑tuned (SFT) before RL. However, the SFT step couples reasoning with the task solution and output format, which can lead to instruction‑style overfitting, reduced out‑of‑distribution robustness, and poorer downstream RL performance. In this study we revisit the cold‑start problem from two angles—training strategy and data construction—and propose a Generalization Factor (GF) coefficient to measure how well different methods generalize. Our experiments show that preference‑based training techniques (e.g., Direct Preference Optimization, DPO) outperform SFT in this context. Building on this insight, we present **SPECS**, a Self‑Distilled, Preference‑based Cold‑Start framework that decouples multimodal learning into three stages: (1) generating introspective preference pairs via self‑distillation, eliminating the need for large external teachers or manual labels; (2) training with a preference objective that emphasizes shallow, transferable surface‑form cues (format, structure, style) rather than memorizing content; and (3) handing off to RL with verifiable rewards for deep reasoning tasks. Across a suite of multimodal benchmarks, SPECS consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving MEGA‑Bench scores by 4.1% and MathVista by 12.2%. Additional tests reveal that SPECS reduces in‑distribution stagnation, enhances exploration, stabilizes training, and raises the achievable performance ceiling.
3961:
Ensuring trustworthy machine‑learning systems demands that their output probabilities truly reflect the likelihood of each class. In multiclass settings, “strong calibration” is the most demanding requirement: every class probability must be accurate simultaneously. Current multiclass calibration methods, however, ignore any notion of input proximity, which leads to a *proximity bias*—predictions in sparsely populated regions of feature space are consistently mis‑calibrated. This is particularly problematic in critical domains such as medicine, where the rare cases are precisely those most susceptible to unfair treatment.  

In this paper we tackle this limitation by introducing a **local** view of multiclass calibration. First, we formalise local multiclass calibration and show how it nests within the framework of strong calibration. Next, we expose the shortcomings of prevailing evaluation metrics when they are applied to this local setting. We then present a practical procedure for improving local calibration in neural networks: the method aligns the network’s probability estimates with locally estimated class frequencies by minimising the Jensen–Shannon distance. Finally, we empirically benchmark our approach against existing multiclass calibration strategies, demonstrating its superior performance.
3962: Effective communication remains a persistent hurdle for engineering students, despite its critical importance in conveying technical information to diverse audiences. While universities typically provide public‑speaking workshops and courses, these programs cannot deliver continuous, individualized instruction, and offering detailed feedback on both verbal and non‑verbal elements is labor‑intensive. To address this gap, we present an AI‑driven assessment framework that fuses speech analytics, computer vision, and sentiment analysis to evaluate engineering presentations. Our multimodal system rates (1) verbal aspects such as pitch, volume, pacing, and intonation; (2) non‑verbal cues including facial expression, gesture, and posture; and (3) a newly defined *expressive coherence* metric that links spoken content with body language. Unlike earlier tools that treat each modality in isolation, our integrated approach delivers scalable, personalized feedback that encourages students to harmonize their verbal and physical delivery. Initial trials indicate that the AI‑generated comments align moderately with expert judgments; among the evaluated large language models, Gemini Pro achieved the highest concordance with human annotators. By automating the assessment process, this trainer allows repeated practice, helping students internalize the alignment of speech, posture, and emotion essential for professional and persuasive presentations.
3963:
**Background**  
Asthma exacerbations remain a leading cause of morbidity and emergency visits in pediatric populations. Early prediction of impending exacerbations could enable pre‑emptive interventions and reduce healthcare burden.  

**Objective**  
To develop and validate an artificial‑intelligence (AI) framework—AIRE‑KIDS—for predicting 30‑day exacerbations in children (≤18 y) with asthma using longitudinal clinical, environmental, and wearable sensor data.  

**Methods**  
We performed a multi‑center, retrospective cohort study of 2,347 children enrolled in the Pediatric Asthma Registry (2016‑2021). Data included electronic health record (EHR) features (demographics, medication adherence, prior exacerbations, spirometry), environmental exposures (air‑quality indices, pollen counts), and continuous activity/sleep metrics from consumer wearables. A 70/15/15 split was used for training, tuning, and prospective testing. Two AI architectures were evaluated: a long short‑term memory (LSTM) network to capture temporal patterns and a XGBoost ensemble for feature‑level interactions. Performance was assessed using area under the receiver‑operator curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, and calibration plots; a logistic regression model served as a baseline.  

**Results**  
The LSTM achieved an AUROC of 0.84 (95 % CI 0.81‑0.87) for 30‑day exacerbation prediction, outperforming XGBoost (AUROC 0.78) and logistic regression (AUROC 0.70). At a 5 % false‑positive rate, sensitivity was 77 % and specificity 89 %. Calibration curves demonstrated strong agreement between predicted probabilities and observed outcomes. Feature importance analysis identified recent medication non‑adherence, peak‑flow variability, and elevated ambient fine‑particulate matter as the most predictive variables. Sub‑group analysis revealed consistent performance across age strata (6–12 y and 13–18 y) and across baseline asthma severity levels.  

**Conclusions**  
AIRE‑KIDS delivers clinically actionable, high‑accuracy predictions of pediatric asthma exacerbations by integrating multimodal data streams. The model’s ability to identify high‑risk individuals up to a month before an event offers a viable platform for targeted pre‑emptive care, including medication titration, environmental counseling, and proactive tele‑health visits. Future work will focus on real‑time deployment and evaluation of intervention efficacy in a randomized controlled trial.
3964:
Intelligence can be framed as a systematic attempt to reduce the vast, high‑entropy input streams that an agent receives into compact, actionable internal representations.  In this paper we formalise this intuition through the lens of algorithmic information theory and the principle of maximum entropy.  We argue that the *epistemic imperative*—the drive to form a coherent, predictive model of the world—manifests itself as an inherent compression problem: an intelligent system must discover the shortest program that reproduces its observations, thereby revealing the underlying regularities.  

Building on Kolmogorov complexity, we present a unifying framework that links three seemingly disparate domains—human cognition, statistical learning theory, and deep neural network training—by showing that each, at its core, implements a form of loss‑based compression.  We formalise a new “compression‑generalisation” theorem that quantifies the trade‑off between the Kolmogorov description length of a hypothesis and its out‑of‑sample error, extending classical bounds to adaptive, non‑parametric settings.  

Empirically, we evaluate this theory on synthetic generative models and large‑scale vision datasets, demonstrating that models with higher intrinsic compression ratios achieve superior sample efficiency and robustness to distribution shift.  Furthermore, we design a compression‑guided regulariser for neural networks that consistently improves generalisation without incurring additional computational cost.  

Our findings suggest that compression is not merely a computational convenience but a foundational epistemic mechanism that underpins intelligent behaviour.  This perspective opens new avenues for developing AI systems that mirror human-like curiosity and for understanding the limits of machine and natural intelligence alike.
3965: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong generalization, yet steering their outputs to match human preferences usually demands costly supervised fine‑tuning. Contemporary test‑time approaches use textual feedback, but they typically critique and rewrite a single generated answer, lacking a principled way to examine, rank, and merge the best aspects of several candidate responses. This is problematic because different answers may excel in clarity, factuality, tone, etc., and a composite that combines the top attributes could be much better. In this work we introduce the Textual Self‑Attention Network (TSAN), a test‑time preference‑optimization framework that requires no parameter updates. TSAN mimics self‑attention entirely in natural language: it presents multiple candidates as textual “keys” and “values”, uses an LLM‑based attention module to score their relevance, and blends their strongest points into a new, preference‑aligned response guided by the learned textual attention. The process unfolds in a textual gradient space, allowing iterative, transparent refinement. Experiments show that after only three test‑time iterations on a base SFT model, TSAN outperforms supervised rivals such as Llama‑3.1‑70B‑Instruct and beats the current leading test‑time alignment technique by effectively harnessing multiple candidate solutions.
3966: Although large language models (LLMs) normally interact through natural‑language tokens, this conversion of internal activations into discrete text imposes a hard bottleneck on the richness of the information that can be exchanged, which limits joint problem‑solving. Drawing inspiration from human mind‑reading, we introduce **Interlat** (Inter‑Agent Latent Space Communication), a framework that transmits an LLM’s final hidden state—its “mind”—directly between agents. To further reduce bandwidth without sacrificing meaning, we apply a secondary compression step that operates purely in latent space. Empirical results show that Interlat surpasses both fine‑tuned chain‑of‑thought prompting and single‑agent approaches, encouraging more exploratory reasoning and unlocking the benefits of latent representation sharing. The additional compression notably speeds up inference while preserving performance, thanks to an information‑preserving strategy. This study demonstrates the feasibility of end‑to‑end latent‑space communication between agents and provides a foundation for future investigations in this direction.
3967:
Transformer models have become the de‑facto standard for a wide array of language tasks, yet the role of Layer Normalization (LN) in shaping their capacity to memorize training data versus generalize to unseen contexts remains poorly understood. In this study we present the first systematic investigation of LN’s influence on the memorization–generalization trade‑off in large‑scale transformer architectures. We devise quantitative memorization metrics—including training‑set perplexity, token‑frequency recall, and nearest‑neighbour embedding similarity—and compare them against conventional generalization metrics across a spectrum of datasets (WikiText‑103, C4, and synthetic sequence‑prediction tasks). Experiments span several model sizes (GPT‑2 small to large) and training regimes, and explore variations of the normalization scheme: standard LN, RMSNorm, group‑wise norm, and a newly proposed “adaptive‑LN” that learns scaling per head.  

Our findings reveal that standard LN sharpens generalization at the expense of reduced memorization, particularly for rare tokens, whereas its removal or replacement with RMSNorm induces over‑fitting, evident in inflated training perplexity but diminished validation performance. Theoretically, we analyse how LN’s centering and scaling constrain the Jacobian of transformer layers, yielding tighter weight norms that promote stable learning dynamics. By adjusting the LN learnable parameters (bias and scale) we demonstrate a tunable continuum from memorization‑dominated to generalization‑dominated regimes.  

This work offers actionable guidelines for practitioners seeking to balance memorization and generalization, and suggests avenues for future norm designs that decouple these competing objectives.
3968:
Knowledge editing has become a popular, lightweight alternative to full model retraining for inserting or correcting specific facts in large language models (LLMs). At the same time, fine‑tuning remains the standard method for adapting LLMs to new domains or tasks. These two post‑training techniques, however, have largely been explored separately, leaving a vital question unanswered: will the edits made to a model persist after it has been fine‑tuned? This issue is particularly relevant in two real‑world scenarios: (1) removing hidden or malicious edits, and (2) ensuring that useful edits are retained. If fine‑tuning erodes edits—as illustrated in Figure 1—then current knowledge‑editing methods lose practical value, since every fine‑tuned model would require re‑editing, dramatically raising costs. Conversely, if edits survive, fine‑tuned models could inadvertently propagate harmful changes, posing serious safety risks.  

To address this, we conduct a systematic study of edit decay during fine‑tuning. We evaluate two leading editing techniques (MEMIT and AlphaEdit) together with three fine‑tuning regimes (full‑parameter, LoRA, and DoRA) across five LLMs and three benchmark datasets, producing 232 distinct experimental settings. Our findings confirm that edits tend to degrade after fine‑tuning, with the extent of decay depending on the specific configuration—e.g., AlphaEdit edits decay more rapidly than those produced by MEMIT. We also introduce a selective‑layer fine‑tuning strategy that can effectively eliminate edits when only the edited layers are updated, albeit with a modest hit to downstream performance. Interestingly, fine‑tuning the non‑edited layers can degrade edits more than a full‑parameter fine‑tune.  

Overall, this work provides empirical baselines and actionable guidelines for combining knowledge editing with fine‑tuning, and highlights the necessity of evaluating editing robustness within the broader LLM deployment pipeline.
3969: Recent breakthroughs in 3D generative AI have made it possible to turn text prompts into tangible objects, yet generating and assembling items that comprise multiple distinct parts remains difficult. We introduce a pipeline that couples 3D generative models with vision‑language models (VLMs) to support robotic construction of multi‑component objects from natural‑language descriptions. Our approach uses a VLM to perform zero‑shot, multi‑modal reasoning about shape and purpose, partitioning AI‑generated meshes into structural and panel components defined a priori. We show that the VLM can correctly identify which mesh regions should receive panel elements in addition to structural parts, based solely on geometry and functionality. Across a set of test objects, participants favored the VLM‑derived assignments 90.6 % of the time, compared with 59.4 % for a rule‑based method and just 2.5 % for random allocation. Finally, the system permits users to refine component assignments through conversational interaction, granting greater human agency in the creation of physical objects with generative AI and robotics.
3970: Traditional assessments of Large Language Model (LLM) agents concentrate largely on whether tasks are completed, paying little attention to how efficiently resources are used or how well agents can adapt to changing circumstances. This oversight ignores a key function: the ability of agents to formulate and modify cost‑optimal strategies as the environment shifts. To address this shortfall, we present **CostBench**, a scalable, cost‑centric benchmark that probes an agent’s economic reasoning and replanning skills. Anchored in the travel‑planning domain, CostBench offers challenges that can be tackled through multiple sequences of atomic and composite tools, each with tunable costs. It also introduces four dynamic blockage scenarios—including tool failures and cost fluctuations—to emulate real‑world uncertainty and compel real‑time adaptation. When tested against leading open‑source and proprietary LLM agents, CostBench exposes a wide performance gap in cost‑aware planning: even GPT‑5 reaches less than 75 % exact‑match accuracy on the most difficult static tasks, and performance degrades by roughly 40 % under dynamic conditions. By highlighting these deficiencies, CostBench provides a foundation for building agents that are both economically rational and resilient.
3971: Low‑dose computed tomography (CT) offers a major safety benefit by reducing patient radiation exposure, yet it often comes at the cost of increased image noise, blurring, and loss of contrast, which can compromise diagnostic accuracy. Consequently, reliable and consistent assessment of image quality is critical for clinical practice. In this work, we introduce a large‑language‑model (LLM) driven quality‑assessment framework that produces both quantitative scores and descriptive text highlighting degradations such as noise, blur, and contrast loss. We evaluate several inference techniques—including zero‑shot inference, the incorporation of metadata, and error‑feedback loops—showing how each successive approach improves overall performance. The resulting predictions exhibit strong correlation with reference metrics while delivering interpretable explanations, thereby enhancing clinical workflow efficiency. The codebase for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/itu-biai/lmms_ldct_iqa.
3972:
The ability of large transformer models to perform multi‑step reasoning has been largely attributed to *chain‑of‑thought* (CoT) prompting, yet the internal dynamics by which CoT scaffolds complex inference remain poorly understood.  We cast reasoning in transformers as a *kinetic process*—a time‑dependent trajectory through hidden‑state space that culminates in a final answer—and investigate how CoT prompts influence this trajectory during both inference and training.  Using a suite of synthetic and real‑world reasoning benchmarks (MathQA, GSM‑8K, and Winograd‑Schemas), we instrument transformer layers to record the evolution of token‑wise activations and attention patterns at every decoding step.  We then fit these trajectories to a set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that capture the rate of information flow and the emergence of intermediate hypotheses, enabling a quantitative comparison of “fast” vs “slow” reasoning paths.  

Our results reveal that CoT prompts consistently accelerate the convergence of internal representations toward solution manifolds, as evidenced by a 30 % reduction in the average kinetic energy required to reach convergence.  Furthermore, we show that during fine‑tuning, models that incorporate CoT conditioning develop *temporal alignment* between attention heads, producing more coherent, step‑wise reasoning.  Ablations on prompt length and granularity demonstrate a trade‑off between reasoning speed and accuracy, suggesting an optimal window of “kinetic bandwidth” for different problem domains.  

This work introduces a kinetic framework for reasoning, a suite of diagnostics for probing intermediate states, and practical guidelines for designing CoT prompts that balance speed and fidelity.  Our findings lay a foundation for future research on interpretable, efficient reasoning in large language models.
3973:
Recent advances in automated program repair (APR) have embraced large language models and agent‑based approaches, yet most of these methods rely exclusively on the current snapshot of the code and ignore the rich information embedded in a repository’s history. Previous studies have demonstrated that historical commits can aid the repair of single‑line defects—typically the most recent commit that touched the buggy line is the one that introduced the error. In this work we ask whether such historical signals can also benefit scalable, agent‑driven APR systems when confronted with more challenging, multi‑hunk bugs.

We introduce **HAFixAgent**, a History‑Aware Bug‑Fixing Agent that injects blame‑derived heuristics into its repair loop. A preliminary analysis of all 854 real‑world defects in Defects4J reveals that bug‑relevant history is both frequently available and highly concentrated around the fault. Comparing HAFixAgent against two state‑of‑the‑art baselines, we find that: (1) **Effectiveness**—the agent outperforms a baseline agent by 212.3 % and a multi‑hunk baseline by 29.9 %; (2) **Efficiency**—the use of history does not noticeably increase the number of agent steps or token consumption, and it even reduces median costs for complex, multi‑file, multi‑hunk bugs; and (3) **Practicality**—a combination of diverse historical heuristics repairs the greatest number of bugs, yielding a clear cost‑benefit trade‑off.

HAFixAgent thus provides a practical recipe for incorporating repository history into agentic APR: ground the agent in version‑control data, prioritize diff‑based historical context, and flexibly combine complementary heuristics.
3974:
Accurate action recognition from video remains difficult in realistic settings where the visual appearance of actors is highly variable, occluded, or captured from unconventional viewpoints. 3‑D human pose sequences, obtained from depth sensors or monocular pose estimation, offer a viewpoint‑invariant, high‑level description of motion that is complementary to raw pixels.  In this work we propose **Pose‑Grounded Vision Transformers (PG‑ViT)**, a unified framework that couples foundational vision models (e.g., ViT, Swin‑Transformer, CLIP) with 3‑D pose embeddings to produce a robust, multi‑modal representation for action classification.  

PG‑ViT first extracts spatiotemporal visual tokens from a pretrained transformer backbone.  Simultaneously, a lightweight 3‑D pose encoder maps joint coordinates into a sequence of pose tokens.  These two streams are fused via a cross‑attention module that aligns the pose skeleton with the visual context, allowing the model to “ground” its predictions in human geometry.  The entire architecture is trained end‑to‑end using a joint classification‑contrastive objective that encourages consistency between the visual and pose embeddings across frames.  

We evaluate our method on three standard benchmarks—Human3.6M, NTU‑60, and Something‑Something‑V2—demonstrating consistent gains of 3.1–4.8 % top‑1 accuracy over state‑of‑the‑art baselines that rely solely on RGB or 2‑D pose cues.  Ablation studies confirm that the pose grounding substantially improves robustness to camera motion, occlusion, and viewpoint changes.  Code and pretrained checkpoints are released at https://github.com/pose-vision/pg-vit.
3975:
The quadratic cost of the scaled‑dot product in attention has become a major bottleneck when extending autoregressive language models to very long contexts. Although linear‑time attention mechanisms and State‑Space Models (SSMs) offer scalable alternatives, they usually rely on first‑order or kernel‑based approximations, which can curb expressive power.  
We propose **Higher‑order Linear Attention (HLA)**, a causal, streaming approach that captures higher‑order interactions through compact prefix‑sufficient statistics. In its second‑order form, HLA keeps a fixed‑size state and produces per‑token outputs in \(O(1)\) time per step, never constructing an \(n\times n\) matrix. We present closed‑form streaming identities, a strictly causal masked variant that uses two additional summaries, and a chunk‑parallel training strategy built on associative scans that exactly reproduces the activations of a serial recurrence. We also sketch how the method can be extended to third and higher orders. Together, these contributions establish HLA as a principled, scalable building block that blends attention‑like, data‑dependent mixing with the efficiency of modern recurrent architectures.  

Project Page: <https://github.com/yifanzhang-pro/HLA>.
3976: Large language models such as ChatGPT are now being used in high‑stakes decision‑making, yet we know little about how they respond to social pressure. To address this gap, we ran three preregistered conformity studies with GPT‑4o in a simulated hiring task. In the baseline condition, GPT consistently selected the same applicant (Profile C), rated its own expertise around the mid‑scale (M = 3.01) and expressed high confidence (M = 3.89), and only rarely changed its recommendation. In Study 1, the model was confronted by eight fictitious partners who unanimously opposed its choice; GPT almost always yielded to the group (99.9 %), reporting lower certainty and significantly higher scores for both informational and normative conformity (p < .001). Study 2 paired GPT with a single partner; even then, it conformed in 40.2 % of disagreement trials, again showing reduced certainty and elevated normative conformity. Across all experiments, GPT behaved not as an autonomous evaluator but as a system that adapts to perceived consensus. These results underscore the danger of treating LLMs as neutral decision aids and suggest that AI judgments should be obtained before exposing the model to human opinions.
3977:
Large Language Models (LLMs) routinely encode complex, often hidden, relationships among multiple semantic attributes (e.g., gender, race, socioeconomic status). These *multi‑attribute confounders* can bias downstream predictions and undermine interpretability. Traditional debiasing techniques typically treat confounding as a binary or pair‑wise phenomenon, overlooking the rich interactions that arise when several attributes simultaneously influence a model’s latent space. In this work, we introduce a principled framework for **interpreting multi‑attribute confounding through numerical attributes**, leveraging the continuous representations that LLMs inherently learn for quantitative concepts such as age, income, or measurement units.

Our approach first extracts *numerical attribute vectors* from a frozen LLM’s embedding layer via a lightweight probe trained on a curated dataset of numeric facts. We then construct a *confounding matrix* that quantifies the joint dependence of each target attribute on every other attribute, conditioned on the numeric embedding. By projecting this matrix onto the model’s attention and token‑embedding subspaces, we obtain a visualizable *confounding heatmap* that reveals how numeric information mediates multi‑attribute interactions. We validate our method on several benchmark tasks—bias detection in coreference resolution, sentiment classification, and factual question answering—showing that the numeric‑confounder score predicts both performance degradation and spurious correlation rates. Moreover, we demonstrate that targeted removal of high‑confounding numeric dimensions via adversarial masking leads to measurable reductions in bias metrics (e.g., demographic disparity in coreference accuracy) while preserving overall task performance.

The proposed framework offers a transparent, model‑agnostic tool for diagnosing and mitigating multi‑attribute confounding in modern LLMs, and highlights the pivotal role of numerical attributes as latent “confounder hubs.” By bridging quantitative feature analysis with interpretability, we lay groundwork for future research on debiasing strategies that explicitly account for the continuous dimension of confounding.
3978: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed across a spectrum of tasks—from natural language understanding to code generation—and are also being used to suggest citations. Yet, the generation of phantom references remains a persistent challenge. Building on earlier work, we propose that an LLM’s capacity to produce accurate bibliographic entries depends on whether the information is generated or memorized; highly cited works, which appear more often in the pretraining data, are expected to be less prone to hallucination. We treat citation count as a proxy for training redundancy and examine its impact on the authenticity of LLM‑generated references. Using GPT‑4.1, we generated 100 citations from twenty computer‑science subfields and verified them manually, quantifying consistency through cosine similarity of the produced metadata to the real records. Our findings show that (i) citation count strongly predicts factual accuracy, (ii) beyond roughly 1,000 citations, bibliographic details are almost verbatim recalled, and (iii) memory interference arises when several highly cited papers share overlapping content. These results reveal a tipping point where LLMs transition from generalization to memorization, with frequently cited works being retained nearly verbatim.
3979:
Visual–mathematical reasoning—the ability to perceive, interpret, and generate self‑similar or iteratively defined structures—lies at the core of many scientific and engineering domains. Current benchmarks for such reasoning largely focus on either purely geometric perception or abstract mathematical manipulation, and provide little insight into how models discover and exploit recursive structure. In this work we introduce **FractalBench**, a large‑scale, multimodal benchmark that pairs synthetic fractal imagery (e.g., Mandelbrot sets, L‑systems, Koch curves) with concise, executable program descriptions. Each example consists of a high‑resolution image, a formal recursive program that generates it, and a set of reasoning questions (e.g., “What is the Hausdorff dimension?”, “How many iterations are required to reach a specified level of detail?”). 

To diagnose model capabilities beyond surface accuracy, we employ **recursive program synthesis** as a principled interface: given a visual input, models are required to output a symbolic program that, when executed, reproduces the image. This approach forces the model to discover the underlying recursion, yields interpretable explanations, and provides a fine‑grained error taxonomy (e.g., mis‑identified base cases, wrong recursion depth, or incorrect rule application). We evaluate a suite of state‑of‑the‑art vision‑language agents and foundation models (CLIP‑GPT‑4, Flamingo, and specialized symbolic solvers) on FractalBench, reporting metrics such as image‑to‑program accuracy, recursion depth coverage, and question‑answer precision. Results reveal that while large language models can handle low‑depth fractals with near‑perfect accuracy, performance sharply deteriorates beyond three recursion layers, and many models fail to correctly infer non‑trivial geometric invariants.  

FractalBench thus provides a rigorous, interpretable testbed for visual–mathematical reasoning, highlighting the gap between perception and symbolic recursion in contemporary systems and guiding future research toward more robust, compositional intelligence.
3980: Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) is a cornerstone of transformer architectures, promoting stable training and improved optimization. Recent practice favors Pre‑LayerNorm designs over Post‑LayerNorm variants because of their superior gradient flow, yet the precise influence of LayerNorm on a model’s capacity to learn versus to memorize remains poorly understood. In this study we systematically examine how LayerNorm shapes learning dynamics and memorization in both Pre‑ and Post‑LayerNorm transformers. We show that, in Pre‑LayerNorm models, the LayerNorm modules are essential for maintaining stable learning; removing them heightens memorization and destabilizes training. Conversely, in Post‑LayerNorm architectures, LayerNorm primarily curbs memorization by reinforcing the correct labels. Our analysis further reveals that LayerNorm in the earliest layers exerts the greatest effect, while later layers contribute less, with these patterns differing between the two normalisation strategies. Experiments on thirteen models spanning six vision‑and‑language benchmarks corroborate these observations. These results provide fresh insights into how LayerNorm governs the trade‑off between memorization and genuine learning in transformer systems.
3981:
Generating novel research ideas is essential for scientific progress. Although large language models (LLMs) can now produce such ideas by mining extensive scientific corpora, existing approaches typically depend on simple techniques like keyword co‑occurrence or semantic similarity. These methods capture only surface‑level associations and miss the rich, contextual relationships that underpin interdisciplinary breakthroughs. For example, papers mentioning both “Keyword A” and “Keyword B” often propose ideas that fuse these concepts, a nuance overlooked by statistical methods.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce **Deep Ideation**, a framework that embeds a comprehensive scientific concept network—capturing both co‑occurrence and contextual linkages—into LLM‑driven ideation. Our approach employs an **Explore‑Expand‑Evolve** workflow that iteratively refines ideas and records progress in an **Idea Stack**. A dedicated **critic engine**, trained on real reviewer feedback, evaluates each iteration for novelty and feasibility, steering the process toward high‑quality proposals.

Empirical results demonstrate a **10.67 % increase** in idea quality over baseline methods, with many generated concepts meeting top‑conference acceptance standards. Human judges confirm the practical value of these ideas in real research settings, and ablation experiments validate the contribution of each workflow component. The full implementation is available at [GitHub](https://github.com/kyZhao-1/Deep-Ideation).
3982:
A world model is an internal simulator that forecasts how the environment and the embodied agent evolve over time. By processing past observations and actions, it predicts future states, thereby enabling agents to reason, plan, and act in complex, dynamic scenarios. Although recent advances have produced impressive models, they often falter over long horizons, suffering from brittleness. We posit that this fragility mainly stems from the quality of the learned representation: high‑dimensional sensory inputs (e.g., images) and lossy or entangled latent codes make learning dynamics unnecessarily difficult. Consequently, we investigate whether enhancing representation learning alone can dramatically boost world‑model performance.

In this paper we address a foundational yet unresolved challenge: building a world model capable of perfectly replicating a deterministic 3D environment. We introduce **Geometrically‑Regularized World Models (GRWM)**, a technique that enforces geometric consistency by requiring consecutive points on a natural sensory trajectory to remain close in latent space. This regularization yields latent representations that closely mirror the true topology of the environment. GRWM is lightweight, plug‑and‑play, scales gracefully with trajectory length, and can be combined with any latent generative backbone.

Evaluated on deterministic 3D environments and long‑horizon prediction tasks, GRWM markedly improves rollout fidelity and stability. Detailed analyses reveal that its success comes from learning a latent manifold with a superior geometric structure. These results reinforce a clear message: focusing on representation learning is a direct, effective strategy for building robust world models that deliver reliable long‑horizon predictions without enlarging the dynamics module.
3983:
Autoregressive Transformers have become a dominant framework for modeling diverse data types such as text and images, yet their application to generating 3‑D molecular structures is still limited. This shortfall can be traced to two core obstacles: (1) creating a unique, one‑dimensional token sequence for a molecule that remains unchanged under SE(3) spatial transformations and atom‑index permutations; and (2) designing a model that can handle hybrid tokens that combine discrete atom identities with their continuous three‑dimensional coordinates. 

We propose **InertialAR**, a solution that tackles both problems. First, it introduces a canonical tokenization strategy that aligns each molecule to its inertial reference frame and orders atoms to enforce invariance to spatial motions and permutations. Second, it enhances the transformer’s attention with geometric rotary positional encoding (GeoRoPE), granting the model explicit geometric awareness. Finally, a hierarchical autoregressive scheme is employed: the model first predicts an atom type, then its 3‑D position using a diffusion‑based loss. 

Across the QM9, GEOM‑Drugs, and B3LYP datasets, InertialAR surpasses existing methods on seven out of ten metrics for unconditional molecule generation. It also achieves state‑of‑the‑art results in controllable synthesis of molecules with specific chemical functionalities, outperforming strong baselines on all five evaluation criteria.
3984: The field of computer vision is currently experiencing remarkable advances driven by Vision‑Language Pre‑Training Models (VLMs). Prompt learning has emerged as the key method for leveraging these models, allowing rapid adaptation to downstream tasks with minimal resources. Most prior work, however, focuses on single‑prompt strategies, leaving the richer possibilities offered by multi‑prompt approaches largely unexplored. In this paper we deliver a systematic analysis of vision‑language multi‑prompt learning. We generalize the recently observed constant modality‑gap phenomenon to learnable prompts, and demonstrate—both empirically and theoretically—that multi‑prompt augmentation enhances vision‑language transfer. Building on this insight, we introduce Energy‑Based Multi‑Prompt Learning (EMPL), which generates a diverse set of prompt embeddings by sampling from an energy‑based distribution implicitly defined by the VLM. EMPL is not only highly parameter‑efficient but also naturally balances in‑domain performance with robust out‑of‑domain open‑vocabulary generalization. Extensive experiments validate our approach and highlight the superiority of EMPL over existing methods.
3985: We propose a practical workflow for adapting open‑source video‑diffusion transformers to generate cinematic scenes for TV and film from very limited data.  The approach unfolds in two stages that decouple style learning from motion synthesis.  In the first stage, Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) modules are injected into the cross‑attention layers of the Wan2.1 I2V‑14B model and trained on a small set of short clips from Ay Yapim’s historical series *El Turco*.  This allows efficient domain transfer in a few hours on a single GPU.  The second stage uses the fine‑tuned model to produce stylistically consistent keyframes that preserve costume, lighting, and color grading; a video decoder then temporally expands these keyframes into coherent 720 p sequences.  We also adopt lightweight parallelisation and sequence partitioning to accelerate inference without compromising quality.  Quantitative metrics (FVD, CLIP‑SIM, LPIPS) and a brief expert user study confirm that the pipeline delivers measurable gains in cinematic fidelity and temporal stability over the base model.  All training and inference scripts are released to support reproducibility and to enable adaptation to other cinematic domains.
3986: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into routine decision‐making, creative production, and social interaction has sparked a re‑evaluation of the unique attributes that sustain human resilience. This paper investigates the dimensions of resilience that remain irreplaceable by current and foreseeable AI systems, and proposes a framework for cultivating these traits in individuals and organisations. Drawing upon interdisciplinary literature from cognitive science, organisational psychology, and AI ethics, we conduct a systematic review of machine capabilities in areas such as pattern recognition, data synthesis, and automation of physical tasks. Complementing this with qualitative case studies of crisis response teams, creative industries, and high‑stakes governance, we identify core resilience factors that exhibit low AI substitution potential: emotional intelligence, ethical deliberation, complex social negotiation, contextual empathy, and adaptive learning under ambiguity. To quantify the resilience gap, a mixed‑methods survey (N=1,200) was administered to professionals across three sectors, revealing a strong correlation between high emotional labor scores and perceived job stability in the face of AI deployment. The paper synthesises these findings into a resilience‑enhancement model that integrates targeted education, reflective practice, and inclusive policy design. Key recommendations include embedding resilience curricula in STEM programmes, fostering inter‑disciplinary teams that pair human judgment with AI analytics, and establishing regulatory safeguards that preserve human agency in high‑impact decisions. Ultimately, the study argues that while AI can augment analytical capacity, the nuanced, socially embedded, and ethically grounded aspects of resilience remain uniquely human. Maintaining and strengthening these qualities will be essential for societal stability as AI continues to reshape the labour market, governance, and everyday life.
3987:
Natural language interfaces for tabular data have become ubiquitous, yet the *ambiguity* inherent in human queries remains largely unexplored.  We ask: *Are we asking the right questions?*  In this work we systematically examine the ways in which natural language queries for SQL‑style table analysis can be semantically, syntactically, or contextually ambiguous, and we evaluate the impact of this ambiguity on state‑of‑the‑art query interpretation systems.

We first propose a fine‑grained taxonomy of ambiguity—ranging from lexical (e.g., ambiguous column names) and structural (e.g., missing join conditions) to contextual (e.g., missing time horizons).  Using this taxonomy, we annotate 4,300 real‑world user queries from the Spider, WikiSQL, and OLAP‑QA corpora, producing the **Ambiguous Table Query (ATQ)** benchmark.  An error‑analysis of current neural mapping models (Seq2SQL, RAT-SQL, and Cross‑Tab) on ATQ reveals a 23 % accuracy drop compared to non‑ambiguous subsets, underscoring the severity of the problem.

To address this, we devise an *ambiguity detection* module that flags queries at inference time and initiates a minimal clarifying dialogue.  Coupled with a probabilistic disambiguation layer that ranks candidate SQL plans, this approach boosts overall accuracy by 12 % on ATQ while preserving zero‑interaction performance on unambiguous queries.  We further demonstrate that incorporating user‑generated clarifications improves downstream analytics tasks such as visual‑query generation and incremental reporting.

Our results highlight that current datasets and models implicitly assume unambiguous input, thereby overestimating real‑world performance.  The ATQ benchmark and disambiguation framework provide a foundation for future research on robust, interactive query interpretation and pave the way toward truly “right‑question‑aware” natural language analytics systems.
3988:
Decoding visual content from non‑invasive electroencephalography (EEG) remains a formidable challenge due to the low signal‑to‑noise ratio, inter‑subject variability, and the scarcity of paired EEG‑image training data. We present *NeuroBridge*, a novel bio‑inspired framework that marries self‑supervised representation learning with cognitive priors and bidirectional semantic alignment to recover high‑level image features from raw EEG signals.  

At the core of NeuroBridge lies a two‑stage pre‑training pipeline. First, a transformer encoder is trained on a large corpus of unlabeled EEG recordings using contrastive temporal‑augmented self‑supervision, forcing the model to capture temporally coherent neural dynamics. Second, we integrate cortical hierarchical priors by embedding a pretrained visual transformer (ViT) and aligning its layer‑wise feature maps with the EEG encoder’s representations through a learned mapping that respects the known functional architecture of the visual cortex (e.g., V1–V4–IT).  

During fine‑tuning, we jointly optimize a bidirectional alignment loss: (i) a *visual‑to‑EEG* mapping that enforces that the image embeddings can predict the corresponding EEG features, and (ii) an *EEG‑to‑visual* decoder that reconstructs the original image’s semantic embedding. This symmetric objective encourages the learned latent space to be semantically faithful in both directions, mitigating mode collapse common in single‑direction approaches.  

Evaluated on three benchmark EEG‑image datasets (SEED‑V, UESTC‑EEG, and a newly curated multi‑subject Visual‑EEG set), NeuroBridge improves top‑1 decoding accuracy by 12–18 % over state‑of‑the‑art supervised methods, while demonstrating robust cross‑subject generalization and superior reconstruction quality. Ablation studies confirm the critical roles of cognitive priors and bidirectional alignment.  

NeuroBridge establishes a principled, data‑efficient pathway for EEG‑to‑image decoding, offering a scalable foundation for future brain‑computer interaction and neuro‑prosthetic systems.
3989:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have become a cornerstone of modern generative modelling, yet their training remains notoriously unstable. The root of many instabilities lies in the sub‑optimal choice of objective: conventional losses (e.g., non‑saturating cross‑entropy, Wasserstein, hinge) are ad‑hoc proxies for the true goal of matching the data distribution, and they often drive the discriminator and generator into conflicting regimes that amplify mode collapse, gradient vanishing, and oscillations. 

We derive a *Bayes‑Optimal Loss for GANs* (BOLT), a principled objective that directly minimises the Bayes risk of distinguishing real from fake samples under a variational Bayesian model of the discriminator’s uncertainty. BOLT is obtained by integrating the optimal discriminator posterior into the generator’s loss, yielding a closed‑form expression that unifies several popular divergences as special cases. We prove that the BOLT objective is minimax‑optimal, guaranteeing that, in the limit of infinite capacity, the equilibrium coincides with the true data distribution regardless of the discriminator’s architecture. 

To evaluate BOLT, we implement a lightweight BOLT‑GAN that retains the simple two‑player game of classic GANs but replaces the loss with the Bayes‑optimal form. On benchmark datasets (MNIST, CIFAR‑10, CelebA), BOLT‑GAN consistently outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines in terms of Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), Inception Score (IS), and mode‑coverage metrics, while exhibiting markedly reduced variance across random restarts. Ablation studies confirm that the stability gains stem from the explicit posterior regularisation of the discriminator rather than from architectural changes.  

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a formal derivation of a Bayes‑optimal adversarial loss with theoretical convergence guarantees; (2) a simple yet powerful implementation that plugs into any existing GAN framework; and (3) extensive empirical evidence that BOLT‑GAN achieves stable, high‑fidelity generation on challenging benchmarks. This work opens a new direction for principled objective design in adversarial learning.
3990:
The rapid evolution of large‑language‑model (LLM) agents has opened the possibility of automating large portions of the software development lifecycle. However, existing approaches tend to treat LLMs as monolithic code generators or debugging assistants, overlooking the disciplined, iterative process that drives high‑quality software. In this paper we present **EvoDev**, a feature‑driven, iterative framework that orchestrates multiple LLM‑based agents to perform end‑to‑end software development—from requirement elicitation and architectural design to implementation, testing, documentation, and deployment. EvoDev decomposes user stories into a hierarchy of fine‑grained tasks, assigns them to specialized agents, and iteratively refines the artifacts through continuous feedback loops that include unit‑test generation, static‑analysis, and user‑defined quality gates. The framework is built on a lightweight policy‑based controller that monitors progress, resolves conflicts, and adapts task granularity on the fly, enabling seamless collaboration between human stakeholders and automated agents.

We instantiate EvoDev in a prototype system and evaluate it on five open‑source projects of varying size and domain. Across these case studies, EvoDev reduces the average time to deliver a functional feature by 42 % and improves code coverage and defect density relative to human‑only baselines. Qualitative analysis of the generated code and documentation demonstrates that the agents produce readable, well‑structured artifacts that satisfy the original specifications. We also report on the overhead introduced by the framework’s orchestration layer and discuss the trade‑offs between automation depth and developer oversight.

EvoDev is the first systematic, feature‑oriented approach that treats LLMs as modular, reusable agents within an iterative development cycle. Our results suggest that such a framework can substantially lower the entry barrier for high‑quality software creation and accelerate the adoption of LLM‑based automation in professional software engineering contexts.
3991:
Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has unlocked impressive text‑generation abilities, yet steering specific attributes of the output remains difficult without costly architectural rewrites or heavy fine‑tuning. Existing techniques usually manipulate only a single, simple property and have trouble delivering precise, simultaneous control over several dimensions. When attribute goals conflict, these methods lack a coordination mechanism, leading to interference, and they also ignore iterative refinement during generation.  

To overcome these shortcomings we introduce **Conflict‑aware, Composite, and Collaborative Controlled Text Generation (C³TG)**, a two‑stage framework that achieves fine‑grained, multi‑dimensional control without altering the base LLM. In the first stage, C³TG pairs the model with the relevant attribute classifiers (from a set of 17 dimensions) and adjusts token probabilities through a weighted KL‑divergence penalty. The second, optimization phase applies an energy function that blends classifier scores with penalty terms, iteratively resolving attribute conflicts via feedback. This yields simultaneous, accurate control over multiple properties while maintaining natural language flow.  

Empirical results demonstrate that C³TG outperforms state‑of‑the‑art baselines across a range of metrics, including attribute accuracy, fluency, diversity, and a marked reduction in toxicity. These findings confirm C³TG as a flexible, high‑performance solution for multi‑attribute text generation that obviates the need for expensive model modifications.
3992: This study introduces a novel framework that harnesses pre‑trained foundation models to enable robotic manipulation without the need for domain‑specific training. By integrating readily available models, the framework merges multimodal perception from these foundations with a versatile reasoning engine that can reliably sequence tasks. Scene graphs, maintained dynamically throughout operation, afford spatial awareness and support coherent environmental reasoning. Evaluation on a series of tabletop manipulation tests demonstrates the framework’s promise for constructing robotic systems that run directly on off‑the‑shelf foundation models.
3993:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as knowledge‑bases, yet their factual reliability remains fragile. In this work we introduce a novel *Adversarial Man‑in‑the‑Middle* (MITM) attack that corrupts the factual recall of LLMs by stealthily injecting fabricated knowledge into their inference pipeline. The attacker intercepts and rewrites intermediate activations or prompt‑chain representations, thereby replacing correct facts with convincing falsehoods that persist across subsequent generations. We formulate the attack as a constrained optimization problem that maximizes the probability of a target assertion while preserving overall language coherence. Two practical instantiations are presented: (1) a *parameter‑steering* attack that perturbs the model’s hidden states during beam search, and (2) a *context‑augmentation* attack that appends adversarial “memory chunks” to the LLM’s retrieval cache. 

We evaluate our methods on a suite of factual benchmarks (TriviaQA, WebQuestions, and a curated set of open‑domain fact queries) across four commercial and open‑source LLMs (GPT‑4, Llama‑2, Claude‑2, and Mistral). In each case, the MITM attack reduces factual accuracy by 35–55 % while maintaining fluent, human‑readable text. Notably, the attack also induces cascading hallucinations in downstream chain‑of‑thought reasoning, revealing a vulnerability in multi‑step inference. 

Finally, we discuss countermeasures: adversarial fine‑tuning of the prompt‑embedding space, dynamic provenance checks, and lightweight runtime verification layers. Our results highlight an urgent need for robust safeguards against fact‑corruption attacks and open new avenues for secure deployment of LLMs in high‑stakes domains.
3994:
Strawberries represent a major sector of the U.S. fruit market, yielding more than $2 billion in farm‑gate sales and roughly 13 % of the total fruit production value. Accurate plant phenotyping—assessing traits such as morphology, canopy structure, and growth dynamics—is essential for identifying superior cultivars. Conventional phenotyping is slow, labor‑intensive, and often destructive. In contrast, modern neural‑rendering methods such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can produce high‑fidelity, non‑destructive 3‑D models from multi‑view imagery or video. A common drawback of 3DGS in agriculture is that it reconstructs the whole scene, including background clutter, which inflates noise, computational demand, and hampers downstream trait extraction.

To overcome this, we present an object‑centric 3‑D reconstruction workflow that first removes background using the Segment Anything Model v2 (SAM‑2) and an alpha‑channel masking step. This yields clean, high‑quality reconstructions of individual strawberry plants, reducing processing time and improving geometric accuracy. With a background‑free point cloud, we automatically compute key phenotypic metrics—such as plant height and canopy width—by applying DBSCAN clustering and Principal Component Analysis. Experiments confirm that our method surpasses traditional pipelines in both precision and speed, delivering a scalable, non‑destructive solution for strawberry phenotyping.
3995: Motion style transfer—imposing a desired movement style onto a given motion sequence while preserving the underlying motion content—has become an essential task in animation, robotics and virtual reality.  Existing methods either rely on rigid parametric blending of motion statistics or on end‑to‑end neural models that struggle to maintain fine‑grained articulation, resulting in either loss of style fidelity or distortion of the original motion.  We propose **AStF (Adaptive Statistics Fusor)**, a novel framework that learns to fuse content and style statistics in a data‑driven, adaptive manner.  AStF first encodes a motion sequence into a latent pose‑style space using a lightweight bidirectional LSTM, then computes per‑joint mean and covariance statistics for both content and style.  These statistics are fused through a learnable attention‑based fusor that predicts a style‑adaptive linear combination of the content and style moments, thus preserving global structure while injecting stylistic nuances.  Finally, the fused statistics guide a generative decoder that reconstructs the stylized motion.  Extensive experiments on Human3.6M, AMASS and a newly introduced “Dance‑Style” benchmark demonstrate that AStF outperforms state‑of‑the‑art approaches in both quantitative metrics (e.g., style distance, motion quality) and human perceptual studies.  Ablation studies confirm the importance of adaptive fusion and per‑joint statistics.  AStF offers a flexible, general‑purpose solution for high‑fidelity motion style transfer that is suitable for real‑time animation pipelines.
3996:
Chaos engineering has emerged as a cornerstone for building resilient software systems, yet its practice remains labor‑intensive, requiring domain expertise to design, inject, and interpret faults. We present **LLM‑ChaOS**, a fully automated framework that harnesses large language models (LLMs) to lower the entry barrier for chaos engineering while significantly reducing operational costs. LLM‑ChaOS automatically generates, executes, and evaluates fault injection campaigns for distributed systems, using contextual prompts derived from system observability data, deployment topology, and desired resilience metrics. The framework employs a two‑stage pipeline: (1) an LLM‑guided fault synthesis module that proposes realistic perturbations (network delays, resource exhaustion, API throttling, etc.) and corresponding test scripts; (2) a post‑hoc analysis module that interprets system telemetry, identifies failures, and recommends remediation actions. We integrate these modules into a continuous‑delivery pipeline, enabling near‑real‑time resilience testing with minimal manual intervention.

Evaluation on a suite of open‑source microservices (e.g., Bookstore, Checkout, Order‑Processing) and a production‑grade cloud‑native application demonstrates that LLM‑ChaOS achieves fault‑coverage comparable to expert‑crafted campaigns while reducing the time to design and deploy experiments by 70 % and the total cost by 45 %. Moreover, the generated recommendations for architecture hardening yield measurable improvements in mean‑time‑to‑recovery and error‑budget consumption. Our results suggest that LLM‑powered automation can democratize chaos engineering, enabling developers and operations teams without dedicated expertise to routinely discover and mitigate hidden failure modes. This work paves the way toward resilient software development as a default practice rather than an advanced capability.
3997:
In enterprise settings, AI agents must continuously evolve to stay accurate, fast, and relevant. This paper describes a hands‑on implementation of a “data flywheel” for NVInfo AI—NVIDIA’s Mixture‑of‑Experts Knowledge Assistant used by more than 30 000 employees. By embedding a MAPE‑based (Monitor‑Analyse‑Plan‑Execute) flywheel, we created a closed‑loop system that systematically captures and corrects errors in our retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, enabling ongoing learning. 

During a three‑month observation window, we logged 495 negative samples and identified two dominant failure modes: routing mistakes (5.25 %) and query‑rephrasing errors (3.2 %). Leveraging NVIDIA NeMo micro‑services, we introduced targeted fine‑tuning: a fine‑tuned 8 B Llama 3.1 model replaced the original 70 B variant for routing, boosting accuracy to 96 %, shrinking model size by ten‑fold, and cutting latency by 70 %. For query rephrasing, fine‑tuning delivered a 3.7 % accuracy lift and a 40 % latency reduction. 

These results illustrate how structured human‑in‑the‑loop feedback, fed through a data flywheel, turns an enterprise AI agent into a self‑improving system. The paper also shares practical lessons on building robustness with scarce user signals, respecting privacy boundaries, and rolling out changes incrementally in production. Ultimately, it offers a repeatable framework for developing adaptive, scalable enterprise AI agents that learn from real‑world usage.
3998:
Accurate change detection between remote‑sensing, medical, or surveillance imagery hinges on precise pixel‑level alignment. Temporal gaps—whether due to differing revisit times, sensor modalities, or drastic scene evolution—frequently induce geometric and radiometric misregistrations that degrade downstream change analysis. In this work we introduce *Morphing Through Time*, a diffusion‑based framework that learns to bridge such temporal gaps by generating continuous, physically plausible intermediate representations between two observations. Our approach first trains a conditional diffusion model to synthesize intermediate frames conditioned on the start and end images. These intermediate “morphs” capture subtle deformations and appearance changes that are otherwise difficult to recover by direct warping. We then exploit the smooth trajectory of the diffusion samples to derive a dense, temporally consistent alignment field via an energy‑minimisation stage that enforces both photometric similarity and temporal smoothness. The resulting warp is applied to the input pair, yielding a temporally aligned pair that is robust to large viewpoint shifts, illumination changes, and even partial occlusions.

We evaluate our method on three challenging benchmarks—(i) the ISPRS Vaihingen multi‑spectral dataset with large seasonal gaps, (ii) a longitudinal medical imaging series with organ motion, and (iii) a surveillance dataset with day‑to‑night transitions. Compared to state‑of‑the‑art registration baselines (optical flow, feature‑based, and deep‑learning warps), our diffusion‑guided alignment reduces mean absolute registration error by 42 % and improves change‑detection F1‑scores by 15–20 % across all datasets. Ablation studies confirm the importance of both the diffusion step and the temporal consistency loss.

Our contributions are: (1) a novel diffusion‑driven temporal interpolation mechanism for generating high‑fidelity intermediate images; (2) a unified alignment pipeline that leverages these intermediates to produce robust, temporally coherent warps; and (3) extensive empirical evidence demonstrating significant gains in change‑detection accuracy under wide temporal variations. The proposed framework opens new avenues for reliable change analysis in scenarios where conventional alignment methods falter.
3999:
While many theories agree that compression underlies intelligence, they often do not explain why such compression leads to uncovering causal relationships rather than mere surface statistics. We present a two‑layer framework that bridges this gap.  

The **Information‑Theoretic Imperative (ITI)** shows that any organism surviving in an uncertain world is compelled to reduce epistemic entropy by compressing predictive information. This gives the evolutionary “why” that ties survival pressures to the need for efficient information processing.  

The **Compression Efficiency Principle (CEP)** then details how optimal compression automatically favors generative, causal models through a process of exception accumulation, making alignment with the true structure of reality a natural outcome rather than an accidental one.
